Syrian intelligence authorities have arrested Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, the chief suspect in the 2013 Baniyas massacre who has also been implicated in the deadly twin bombings in Türkiye’s Reyhanli district, state media reported on Thursday.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) said the General Intelligence Directorate detained Kayali as he was allegedly trying to flee across a border. The report did not specify where the arrest took place or which border he was attempting to cross.
Kayali, a former militia leader loyal to Syria’s ousted regime leader Bashar al Assad, has long been accused of involvement in mass killings in Baniyas and the nearby village of al Bayda during the early years of the Syrian uprising.
He has also been implicated in the twin bombings in Reyhanli, in Türkiye’s southern Hatay province, on May 11 2013. The attacks killed dozens of people and were among the deadliest bombings in Türkiye’s recent history.
His arrest comes less than two weeks after Syrian counterterrorism authorities detained Jamal Trabulsi, his former deputy in the pro-Assad Syrian Resistance militia, on October 4.
Syrian authorities have accused Trabulsi of taking part in military operations alongside forces loyal to Assad, including the 2013 massacres in Baniyas and al Bayda.
Mass killings during Syria’s uprising
On May 2 2013, Syrian regime forces and allied militias stormed al Bayda in Tartus province, killing hundreds of civilians, according to accounts of the massacre.
Survivors said forces carried out mass executions, burned homes and killed women and children during the assault.
Since Assad’s ouster in December 2024, Syrian authorities have intensified efforts to arrest former regime officials and militia commanders accused of crimes against civilians during the country’s civil war.

Belgium reports first two deaths from West Nile virus
BRUSSELS – Belgium’s Flanders region on Oct 15 confirmed the deaths of two people from the West Nile virus, a mosquito-borne infection currently sweeping across Europe.
The virus can cause symptoms similar to the flu but in extreme cases it can result in tremors, fever, comas and a lethal swelling of the brain tissue known as encephalitis. It can also cause meningitis.
Officials did not provide details about the two deaths but said they were individuals at risk of severe illness.
The northern Belgian region has confirmed 14 cases including the two deaths, according to local media.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said last week that 18 European countries had recorded more than 1,850 cases in 2026. AFP

Stolen diamonds and locked archives: The desperate balancing act of the British Crown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

20:51:35 KST

Stolen diamonds and locked archives: The desperate balancing act of the British Crown
On September 7, a Jamaican delegation delivered an unprecedented legal petition to London – directly to the Privy Council, a royal advisory body functioning as a court for issues related to the British Empire and Commonwealth realms.
In a historical irony, the petition was addressed to Charles III in his capacity as King of Jamaica, a role he still holds. The filing demands that the British Crown answer the call of its subjects in Jamaica, asking him, as their head of state and the inheritor of one of history’s darkest chapters, to formally define the legality of slave trade and his royal family’s role in it.
Long before this, in March 2022, the King’s elder son and heir, William the Prince of Wales, had also found himself cornered while touring the Caribbean, including Jamaica. While in the capital Kingston, he was greeted by protesters demanding accountability. He expressed his “profound sorrow” for Britain’s role in the slave trade, admitting that the atrocity will “forever stain our history.”
It is becoming a habit for activists and politicians to up the pressure on the British throne, tracking it wherever royal family members appear in international settings. In October 2024, during a joint tour of Australia and Samoa culminating at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Apia, Samoa, King Charles – attending his first Commonwealth summit as reigning monarch – faced intense pressure from African and Caribbean leaders demanding a reckoning over slavery and colonialism. In fact, that summit was heavily anchored by the debate over historical accountability. Addressing the gathering, while seeking to soften his audience’s stance on the dispute, Charles noted that “none of us can change the past,” adding that he understood “from listening to people across the Commonwealth how the most painful aspects of our past continue to resonate,” while carefully stopping short of a formal apology or any commitment to financial reparations.
While he was still Crown Prince, King Charles III had already experienced his share of being chased by the same questions. In June 2022, while attending another Commonwealth summit in Kigali, Rwanda, he spoke openly about the “most painful period of our history,” stating that he could not describe the depths of his “personal sorrow” at the suffering caused by the slave trade and its enduring impact.
Before King Charles inherited the crown, his mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, faced her own share of reckoning with the ghosts of empire. During her state visit to India in October 1997, the Queen faced intense controversy and calls for accountability when she visited the site of the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar, ultimately stopping short of a formal apology while navigating a volatile political reception. Throughout her seven-decade reign, particularly during later milestones like her Diamond and Platinum Jubilees, her visits to former colonies or Commonwealth summits were increasingly overshadowed by organized protests demanding structural apologies and financial amends for Britain’s imperial history. Most notably, as republican movements gained ground in realms like the Caribbean, activists and academics continually deflected from her personal image as a “constitutional monarch” to challenge the enduring institutional wealth accumulated on the backs of enslaved ancestors.
Most royals, when finding themselves in such awkward situations, offer a few carefully chosen words of regret while steadfastly refusing to issue a formal apology, let alone entertain discussions of financial reparations. Even more telling is their fierce refusal to open the Royal Archives to shed light on that dark period – decades spanning not only the slave trade orchestrated by the royal family and their affiliated business partners, but also systemic human trafficking and the systematic extraction of wealth from British colonies across the globe, stretching from the Caribbean and Latin America all the way to India and beyond.
It is worth noting that the Royal Archives are housed in Windsor Castle and managed separately from the UK National Archives with special arrangements for access. Clearly, the royal family retains extraordinary control over what the world can find out about its history of human trafficking, enslavement, and wealth theft across continents.
Take the Imperial State Crown itself, that glittering emblem of power. It is set with stones stolen from at least two continents, among them a diamond looted during the colonial era. So, the evidence is not only in the archives but on the monarch’s head. Worn by Charles as he left Westminster Abbey after his coronation in 2023, the crown carries the Cullinan II diamond, cut from the largest gem-quality diamond ever found, discovered in South Africa in 1905 and later given to King Edward VII by the colonial government while the territory was under British rule.
The Sovereign’s Sceptre holds the even larger Cullinan I, and some South Africans called for its return in the days before Charles III was coronated. Elsewhere in the Crown Jewels, the Koh-i-Noor was forcibly surrendered to Queen Victoria, Charles III’s great-great-grandmother, by Duleep Singh, a boy of ten, proclaimed as Maharaja of the Sikh Empire as a child. Regardless of the legal issues surrounding this “gift” or “treaty,” these were objects acquired under the shadow of imperial power, and the Crown has so far shown no appetite to discuss returning them.
The scale of the problem becomes even clearer when one considers what lies beyond the Crown Jewels in Britain’s museums. During a visit to India in 2010, then-Prime Minister David Cameron was asked about returning the Koh-i-Noor diamond. His response was revealing: “If you say yes to one you suddenly find the British Museum would be empty.” He rejected the idea of returning it, saying it would “have to stay put.”
Cameron’s extraordinary warning made clear that the Koh-i-Noor is part of a much wider restitution problem: accepting one claim could open the door to countless others. And Britain’s museums do not just preserve this imperial inheritance for posterity. They display it to millions of visitors, use it to enhance their international prestige and, through exhibitions, tourism, shops, licensing, and other activities, derive continuing economic value from collections that include objects acquired through conquest, colonial expeditions, and unequal imperial power.
What makes this ongoing reckoning different is that former colonies are no longer treating these grievances as isolated historical footnotes or polite talking points during diplomatic summits. Instead, African and Caribbean states, most of which were British colonies, have synchronized their political diplomatic and legal strategies into a coordinated structural challenge, moving from moral appeals to hard international law. This momentum crystallized at the United Nations General Assembly, where African and Caribbean nations spearheaded a landmark resolution classifying the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans as the gravest crime against humanity, establishing that historical atrocities generate continuing legal obligations.
Reinforced by continental milestones such as the African Union’s declaration centering reparations, amplified by frameworks like the Algiers Declaration, and spearheaded diplomatically by nations like Ghana, this coalition has upended traditional diplomatic containment. By weaponizing multilateral platforms, regional summits, and formal legal routes like the Privy Council petition, these nations are dismantling the monarchy’s decades-old strategy of deflection, exposing an imperial institution whose modern wealth remains directly tethered to an unreckoned past.
The British Crown’s desperate balancing act can no longer convince anybody let alone entire nations who were victimized. The monarchy can no longer hide behind the polite fiction that colonialism and the slave trade are closed chapters safely confined to history textbooks. When legal challenges bypass royal protocol to land directly on the doorstep of the Privy Council, and when international bodies codify chattel slavery as a continuing crime against humanity, the illusion of untouchability begins to crack.
The question now is how long the Crown can afford to wait. Each royal tour, Commonwealth summit and court filing adds to a record that cannot be unwritten, and the pressure keeps mounting. The Royal Archives remain the obvious test. Opening them would let historians and the descendants establish what the monarchy and its commercial partners actually did, and would show whether Buckingham Palace is prepared to move from sorrow to substance. Continued silence will be read, in Kingston, Accra, and beyond, as an answer in itself.

Sally Rooney's books withdrawn in U.K. over author's support for designated terror group Palestine Action
London — World-renowned Irish author Sally Rooney's books will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the U.K. due to her public support for Palestine Action, a group banned as a terrorist organization in Britain.
Rooney, the bestselling novelist behind "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends," both of which have been adapted into television shows, and her publisher Faber have agreed to halt the supply of her books to British retailers, according to a statement from Faber.
"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher," Faber said.
Rooney previously said she intended to use proceeds from her work to financially support Palestine Action, potentially exposing her and her publisher to prosecution under British anti-terrorism laws.
In an article published in The Irish Times in August 2025, Rooney wrote: "I want to be clear that I intend to use these proceeds of my work, as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."
What is Palestine Action?
Founded in 2020, Palestine Action is a British direct-action group that has targeted arms manufacturers and other companies it accuses of supplying weapons to Israel with protests and sabotage.
The group describes itself as a "movement committed to ending global complicity with Israel's genocidal apartheid regime."
The British government designated Palestine Action as a terrorist organization in July 2025, citing the group's history of criminal damage and escalating attacks on defense infrastructure, including a factory belonging to U.S. defense company Teledyne Technologies in 2022.
The 2025 decision came after the group claimed responsibility for breaking into a major air base, RAF Brize Norton, northwest of London, and damaging aircraft. The AP and other outlets cited British police as putting the cost of the damage at around $9.4 million, though authorities have not publicly confirmed that figure.
Under U.K. law it is a crime to be a member of a designated terrorist group, or to publicly support one.
The ban on Palestine Action has prompted widespread protests and thousands of arrests across the U.K. According to the latest figures from Britain's Home Office, which oversees all domestic law enforcement, the average age of those arrested on suspicion of supporting Palestine Action is 59, compared to 28 for other terrorism-related arrests.
The legality of the ban remains the subject of a Supreme Court challenge.
"Sally Rooney is finding out that she can't have her cake and eat it," a spokesperson for the U.K. activist group Campaign Against Antisemitism told CBS News, adding that it had reported the author to counterterrorism police over her vow to financially support Palestine Action.

Breadcrumb
Israeli attacks keep southern Lebanon in limbo as reconstruction stalls
Israeli attacks continue to devastate parts of southern Lebanon, with reports that Israel is planning to deepen its invasion adding to uncertainty and leaving development and reconstruction efforts on hold.
Airstrikes, shelling and demolitions have continued across Lebanon despite a US-sponsored framework agreement signed by Lebanon and Israel in June, which has done little to halt Israel's attacks.
Talks are due to resume in Florida on 20 October, although expectations of a breakthrough remain low.
Earlier this week, Lebanon's Health Ministry said Israeli attacks over the past three years had killed 8,596 people and wounded 30,660, many of them civilians.
A New York Times investigation earlier this week found that Israeli forces had razed 48 of the roughly 60 towns and villages under their occupation in southern Lebanon since the April ceasefire agreement, destroying homes, schools, mosques and roads.
The destruction has been concentrated in predominantly Shia Muslim communities, from which Hezbollah draws much of its support, fuelling fears that Israel is pursuing a scorched-earth campaign aimed at permanently depopulating large parts of southern Lebanon.
On Wednesday night, Israeli forces set fire to and destroyed a school in Kfar Tebnit, near Nabatieh. An Israeli airstrike on the village of Haddatha in the Bint Jbeil district also wounded two people, including a four-year-old child.
Invasion could reach Zahrani
For months, Israeli operations have focused on the Nabatieh district, which lies north of the Litani River. The seizure of strategic sites such as Beaufort Castle, Ali al-Taher Ridge and other highlands by Israeli troops this year gives them a vantage point overlooking Nabatieh, raising concerns that they could attempt to storm the city in the event of another full-scale Israeli offensive.
Lebanese news site Almodon recently reported that Israel intends to expand its occupation of southern Lebanon as far as the Zahrani River, taking control of the Zahrani oil refinery. The move would form part of what the report described as Tel Aviv's efforts to exert further pressure on Lebanon, militarily, politically and economically.
According to Asharq al-Awsat newspaper, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun received US assurances this week that Israel would not be given the green light to expand its operations into areas of the south it does not already occupy. The assurances were reportedly conditional on Lebanon ensuring that no pretexts were provided for further Israeli action, referring to Hezbollah attacks.
On Wednesday, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz threatened to seize more territory in southern Lebanon and forcibly displace residents of Beirut's southern suburbs if Tehran-backed Hezbollah joined Iran in a future attack on Israel.
Hezbollah is reportedly replenishing its depleted weapons stockpile and reorganising its ranks in the south in preparation for another full-scale Israeli offensive. The group has been significantly weakened by years of Israeli attacks and fighting but has insisted it will not disarm before Israel ends its occupation of Lebanese territory.
Gulf state planning 'major project'
Last month, Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said the estimated total cost of Israel's wars on Lebanon could exceed $27 billion, adding that the state could not bear the cost of reconstructing areas devastated by Israeli attacks.
He has nevertheless pledged to launch projects in the south to facilitate the return of residents, including by restoring electricity, water and internet services.
During a meeting earlier this week with MPs representing southern constituencies from Hezbollah and the Shia Amal Movement, Salam said around $70 million had been earmarked for projects in the south by the end of the year. Their implementation would depend on the security situation amid continuing Israeli attacks.
Lebanese newspaper Annahar reported on Wednesday that an unnamed Gulf state was planning a major development project in southern Lebanon, with its launch conditional on Israel withdrawing from occupied areas, stability returning to the region and displaced residents going back to their homes.
The newspaper said the state's ambassador had held discreet talks with several Lebanese ministers about the initiative, and that Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri had also been briefed.
The Gulf state is also working with other countries in the region, in coordination with Salam's government, to support residents of southern Lebanon whose homes have been destroyed or damaged by Israeli attacks.

Study identifies immune cells that can attack deadliest lung cancer
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:47:57 CST
20:47:57 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have identified a previously overlooked type of immune cell that can recognize and kill small cell lung cancer (SCLC), revealing a new immune pathway for fighting the deadliest form of the disease.
The study, led by Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research (WEHI), found that patients with higher levels of gamma delta T cells in their tumors tended to live longer, uncovering a hidden immune defense that could be exploited to attack these hard-to-treat tumors, according to a WEHI statement released on Thursday.
Researchers also showed two existing drugs could be repurposed to boost the cancer-killing abilities of these immune cells, potentially paving the way to enhance therapies for a disease with limited treatment options.
SCLC has a five-year survival rate of less than 7 percent. Although immunotherapy has improved outcomes for several cancers, only a small proportion of SCLC patients experience long-term benefits, partly because these cancers are often invisible to the conventional immune cells that treatments rely on, according to the study published in Cancer Cell.
The study found that gamma delta T cells could detect and attack these lung cancers that are able to evade conventional cancer-fighting immune cells, overcoming a major treatment challenge.
The researchers created miniature tumors in the laboratory using patient samples and found that gamma delta T cells taken from the patients' blood could effectively recognize and kill SCLC cells.
"This could open an entirely new avenue for personalized treatment approaches in SCLC and other solid cancers that are often missed by conventional immune cells," said Jin Ng, first author of the study at WEHI. ■

Players walk into the pitch at Xinjiang Special Education Vocational Secondary School in Changji Hui Autonomous Prefecture, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 14, 2026. Xinjiang's first blind football team is known as the "Wei Wei Wei" team. It takes its name from the call players shout to locate teammates and avoid collisions. This call is the communication code of this special sport.
In blind football, players wear light-blocking blindfolds throughout the match. They track the ball by the bell inside it and keep calling "wei, wei, wei" to gauge teammates' positions, enabling them to dribble, pass and shoot without sight. In training, they run, collide, feel the boundary boards, and build muscle memory through countless falls and getting back up. For visually impaired teenagers who rarely dare to sprint at full speed in daily life, this enclosed pitch is a place where they can run freely.
"We cannot see the world, but we strive to make the world see us." In the darkness, guided by their calls and the sound of the ball, these young athletes break through barriers and shine brightly on the green pitch. (Xinhua/Ding Lei)

China releases probe results on formamide-related safety issues in infant diapers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:47:41 CST
20:47:41 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A joint investigation team comprising four Chinese government departments on Thursday released findings of a probe into safety concerns over formamide in infant diapers, concluding that no formamide was detected in tested diaper products.
The joint investigation was conducted by the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR), together with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the National Health Commission, and the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration, following recent public discussions over the issue.
The investigation team carried out spot checks on 168 domestic baby diaper manufacturers, including contract manufacturers, covering 368 batches of finished diaper samples from 180 brands, according to a statement released by the SAMR.
Testing was entrusted to authoritative institutions, including the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention and the Chinese Academy of Quality and Inspection & Testing. No formamide was detected, the statement said.
All inspected enterprises met the hygiene requirements for the production of disinfection products, and no addition or presence of formamide was found in production processes or raw materials.
The investigation confirmed that several testing entities at the center of the public concern, which claimed to have detected formamide in baby diapers, were found to have deficiencies, including unclear principles for qualitative determination, failure to conduct blank and parallel sample tests, flawed testing procedures and criteria for determination, and the deletion of raw data, making it impossible to reach a conclusion that formamide was detected.
The joint investigation team also commissioned academicians and experts to develop a blood sample formamide testing method through repeated verification. Using this method, a re-test of the blood samples tested by an institution of public concern found no formamide.
Based on current investigation and test results, no formamide-related health hazards from baby diapers have been found, the statement said.
Testing for formamide in baby diapers is a rigorous and professional activity, and research into formamide-related health hazards, in particular, should be conducted in a prudent and objective manner, the statement said.
The statement added that relevant authorities will continue to strengthen supervision of infant products and welcome public participation to jointly create a safe and reassuring consumption environment. ■

The vote came after Parliament Speaker Andreas Norlen nominated Andersson on Tuesday to lead a single-party Social Democratic government, despite the failure of negotiations among four parties that together secured a narrow parliamentary majority in the September election.
The Social Democratic Party, Left Party, Green Party and Center Party won a combined 176 seats, but remain divided over the composition of a new government.
According to SVT, coalition talks have been hampered mainly by disagreements between the Center Party and the Left Party, with the latter insisting on joining the government and securing cabinet posts, while the Center Party refuses to serve in the same government.
The Left Party, Green Party and Center Party all announced ahead of Thursday's vote that they would oppose a single-party Social Democratic government.
Andersson acknowledged Tuesday that although progress had been made in coalition negotiations, conditions were still not in place to form a government capable of securing sufficient parliamentary support.
The former PM was first tasked with exploring the formation of a new government on Sept. 18, after outgoing PM Ulf Kristersson requested to be relieved of his duties following the election.
However, she returned the mandate on Sept. 28 after the Left Party backed the Moderate Party's candidate rather than the Social Democratic Party's candidate in the parliamentary speaker election. Norlen subsequently reassigned her the task in early October, but negotiations remained inconclusive.
Under Sweden's system of negative parliamentarism, a PM candidate can take office unless at least 175 of the 349 lawmakers vote against the nomination.
Following Thursday's rejection, Norlen will have to put forward another candidate. Under Sweden's constitution, if parliament rejects four proposed PM candidates, an extraordinary election must be held. ■

KYIV -- Ukrainian forces have struck an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region, Russian officials said, hours after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian energy facilities and voiced anger over a "dangerous" disruption of satellite intelligence from the United States.
Defying an "energy cease-fire" announced unilaterally last week by US President Donald Trump, Zelenskyy told the Financial Times in an interview published on October 15 that "we're done" with holding off on launching attacks on Russia oil structures.
Hours later, Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram that "our region came under a massive drone attack," adding that "a fire broke out at the oil refinery."
Russia's Defense Ministry later said Ukraine had attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery, adding that falling drone debris had sparked a fire at the facility.
The Ukrainian military has not immediately confirmed the attack, which would be the first by Kyiv since Trump announced the cease-fire on October 11. The Rosneft-owned Ryazan refinery has been targeted by drones several times in recent months and accounts for nearly 5 percent of Russia's total oil refining capacity.
Neither of the warring parties officially confirmed agreeing to the truce announced by Trump, and while Ukraine halted attacks on Russian refineries for three days, Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy facilities and other installations.
"The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy told the Financial Times in the interview.
Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was willing to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow agreed to stop striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian leader's sharp tone continued when discussing a recent crisis involving a cut in the supply of US intelligence to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy told the FT that the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, an idea he dismissed while calling the disruption in the Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite communications system, "dangerous."
Pressure On The Pentagon
Pressure is mounting on the Pentagon to explain the reported restrictions on satellite communications used by Ukraine’s military, with Republican Senator Thom Tillis calling for an inspector-general investigation and warning that Ukrainian civilians and US personnel may have been put at unnecessary risk.
Tillis, a Republican, said on October 14 he would ask the Defense Department’s inspector-general to investigate what he described as a potentially dangerous breakdown involving Starshield, which is controlled by the US government.
“The latest reporting suggests this strategic snafu may have occurred more locally within DOD Starshield systems, not with Starlink or SpaceX,” Tillis wrote on social media.
He said Ukrainian civilians and US diplomatic and security personnel had been placed at unnecessary risk without warning.
“At best, this was an unacceptable error or lapse, and at worst a conscious decision to clear the field for a Russian attack,” Tillis added.
RFE/RL has learned from congressional sources that a group of lawmakers was circulating a letter on October 14 calling on the Defense Department’s inspector-general to investigate the episode. The letter was expected to be sent in the coming days.
The call for an investigation comes amid mounting bipartisan concern over reports that satellite connectivity restrictions have disrupted Ukrainian military operations. Some have also speculated that it could possibly be a move by the administration to pressure Kyiv into refraining from oil refinery attacks on Russia.
But it remains unclear who authorized the restrictions, whether they affected commercial Starlink or Starshield, and whether Washington also reduced intelligence support to Kyiv.
Axios, quoting sources, reported that the White House told Ukraine they do not control Elon Musk's SpaceX, the owner of Starlink.
Musk wrote on X, which he owns, that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Dan Rice, president of American University Kyiv and a former special adviser to the commander in chief of Ukraine’s armed forces, warned that restrictions could have grave consequences if they prevented Ukrainian forces from directing interceptors against incoming Russian drones.
“When you have 500 inbound Shaheeds, jet-powered Shaheeds, and I was hit within 400 meters twice this week,” Rice told RFE/RL, “you need to have interceptors going out to protect Ukrainian civilians.”
He warned that if satellite connectivity prevented high-speed interceptors from reaching their targets, Russian drones could strike civilian locations, killing women, children and other noncombatants. He also noted that Russian forces had targeted universities, schools and children’s hospitals.
Retired Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery, senior director of the Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation and a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told RFE/RL that the reported limits impaired Ukraine’s ability to control medium-range drone strikes against Russian logistics routes and command-and-control facilities supporting Moscow’s forces in occupied Ukrainian territory.
He described the affected operations as involving targets roughly 150 to 250 kilometers behind Russian lines. He also distinguished the satellite-service issue from the reported failure to provide warnings of incoming attacks, saying the Pentagon inspector general should investigate both.
Meanwhile, Moscow continued its attacks on Ukraine on October 15, a day after Russian missile and drone strikes pounded civilian and energy infrastructure across the country, killing at least nine people and leaving hundreds of thousands without power.
Ukraine's Air Force reported on the morning of October 15 that Russia had launched 580 drones and two Kh-59 missiles at Ukraine overnight, adding that the attack was ongoing.

Energy prices rose for the third consecutive month, increasing 3.9 percent month on month in September, compared with 3.4 percent in August and 2.3 percent in July. Manufactured goods prices rose 0.5 percent, slowing from 1.6 percent in August, while food prices increased 0.1 percent, down from 0.4 percent. Tobacco prices remained stable for the second consecutive month.
Core inflation stood at 1.5 percent year on year in September, up from 1.1 percent in August, the statistics organization said. ■

Frozen Russian Assets: Europe Rejects US Control Plan – FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:46:58 UTC
20:46:58 KST

The US proposed that European countries unfreeze some Russian sovereign assets and place them under Washington’s oversight to help revive negotiations over Russia’s war against Ukraine, according to a report published on Thursday, Oct. 15.
The Financial Times reported, citing four people briefed on the discussions, that US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner presented the idea during talks in Miami. European representatives rejected it.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“They were told that this was just simply not going to happen,” one person told the newspaper.
The proposal involved transferring some immobilized reserves into a new financial vehicle overseen by Washington. A US official told the FT that possible uses of the assets were being discussed as part of a comprehensive peace agreement, with the mechanisms for releasing and spending the money still under consideration.
The Miami talks brought together representatives of Ukraine, Britain, France, Germany, the European Commission, and NATO alongside American negotiators. The meeting ended without an announced breakthrough.
Europe opposes surrendering control
European officials at the meeting opposed both handing control of the assets to another party and returning any of the funds to Moscow, according to the report.
Western countries immobilized roughly €260 billion ($291 billion) in Russian sovereign assets after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Around €210 billion ($235 billion) remains blocked in the EU, with much of it held through the Brussels-based securities depository Euroclear.
Military Starlink Service Restored in Ukraine, Defense Sources Say
These are Russian central bank reserves, distinct from the private property of sanctioned businesspeople. EU restrictions prohibit transactions involving the management of those reserves, preventing Moscow from freely accessing them.
European leaders have repeatedly said the assets should remain immobilized until Russia ends its war and compensates Ukraine. In December 2025, the EU adopted additional emergency measures prohibiting transfers of the central bank’s assets or reserves back to Russia. Those measures strengthened the freeze without transferring ownership of the underlying reserves to Ukraine.
European governments nevertheless remain divided over how far they should go in using the funds. Belgium has raised legal and financial concerns about proposals to mobilize the principal, while Ukraine has pressed its partners to use Russian reserves more broadly to finance its needs.
The assets already help finance Ukraine
The EU currently channels extraordinary earnings generated by the immobilized reserves toward assistance for Ukraine, while keeping the underlying assets frozen.
According to the Council of the EU, the assets have generated €8 billion ($9 billion) in windfall profits. Of that amount, €3.8 billion ($4.2 billion) has reached Ukraine, while €4.2 billion ($4.7 billion) has contributed to repayment of EU-G7 loans or been set aside for that purpose.
Under the current distribution rules, 95 percent of those revenues goes through a mechanism helping Ukraine repay approximately €45 billion ($50 billion) in EU-G7 loans. The remaining five percent support the European Peace Facility, which finances military assistance.
A separate €90 billion ($101 billion) EU support loan for 2026-27 is financed through European borrowing backed by the EU budget. European leaders agreed that Ukraine would repay that loan once it receives Russian reparations, while reserving the EU’s right to use immobilized Russian assets for repayment in accordance with international and EU law.
The dispute therefore concerns more than the location of the reserves: European governments have already tied them to Ukraine’s financing and eventual compensation for war damage.
Washington has floated economic incentives before
The latest proposal follows earlier discussions about offering Moscow economic incentives for a limited ceasefire.
Those discussions included releasing some frozen Russian reserves, authorizing a transaction involving Lukoil’s foreign assets, and easing restrictions on Belarusian potash exports. The incentives were reportedly presented as measures that could encourage a partial halt to fighting, including attacks on energy infrastructure or maritime routes.
Ukrainian negotiators sought safeguards in those discussions, including matching financial releases for Ukraine and guarantees of faster military assistance if Russia violated a prospective truce.
Frozen reserves also featured in a 28-point US-backed draft peace plan published in 2025. That draft proposed investing $100 billion in Russian assets in US-led reconstruction efforts in Ukraine, with Washington receiving 50 percent of the profits. It also envisaged a separate US-Russian investment vehicle.
The new asset proposal comes amid a broader disagreement over sanctions relief. European governments have opposed following Trump’s Russian diesel agreement, arguing that pressure on Moscow should remain in place while Russian attacks continue.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said earlier this week that following Washington’s diesel decision was “out of the question” for Germany and Europe, while maintaining that European governments remained in contact with the US over a common approach to ending the war.

Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:45:39 UTC
20:45:39 KST

Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify
Reduced missile warnings increase threat to civilians as Trump pushes an ‘energy ceasefire’ and peace negotiations.
Kyiv, Ukraine – The supernova-like blasts of exploding Russian ballistic missiles are followed by thunderous thumps, shockwaves, fires and deaths – and the staccato of Ukrainian air defence systems.
This week’s nightly attacks on Ukraine that killed at least 15 and wounded dozens resembled hundreds of previous raids – with one exception.
The air raid sirens began howling just seconds before or after yet another wave of missiles struck apartment buildings, power plants and warehouses.
But Ukraine’s partners did not provide the country with intelligence data from NATO’s early-warning satellites, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, as tensions between Washington and Kyiv rise.
He did not name the United States and President Donald Trump has denied that Washington has stopped sharing intelligence.
The constellation of military satellites detects Russian ballistic missile attacks by the rockets’ thermal flames seconds after launch.
The warnings give Ukrainians up to 10 minutes – precious, life-saving time to sound air raid sirens and send emergency text messages to prompt evacuations to bomb shelters.
“That’s what helps prevent the killings,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s ground radars can only detect the incoming missiles as their speed ranges from 6,000 to 12,000km/h (3,730 – 7,260 miles per hour).
‘Trump pressures our president’
Despite Trump’s denial, Ukrainian observers have a simple yet harrowing explanation – the US president wants to help Republicans win more congressional seats in upcoming midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv into declaring an “energy ceasefire” with Moscow that would drive global oil prices down.
“Trump pressures our president, pressures Ukraine” as he strives to “get advantage by any means necessary in the election campaign,” Lieutenant-General Ihor Romanenko, former deputy head of Ukraine’s general staff of armed forces, told Al Jazeera.
The lack of intelligence data “significantly affects the effectiveness of air defence, we don’t have time to respond,” he said.
Without the satellite data, Ukrainian drones and missiles also “lose precision when striking targets deep in Russia,” he said.
On Sunday, Trump announced the ceasefire that envisages no mutual strikes on energy infrastructure – from Russian oil refineries and fuel depots to Ukrainian power and heating stations.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on social media.
Kyiv said the announcement was a surprise, while Moscow declined to say whether it backs the idea – and kept on hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The pressure goes beyond the refineries as Trump wants to quickly reopen, arbitrate and complete peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow – even if they benefit the Kremlin.
“He needs peace talks to succeed. Ideally, it is a certain unblocking of the peace settlement process, when Kyiv shows more willingness to agree with Russia’s demands,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.
The pressure will continue until “Kyiv shows readiness for a compromise and concessions towards Russia,” he said.
Moscow “simply abuses” the pressure and the suspension of air raid warnings to escalate attacks on Ukraine, he said.
Kyiv’s ‘priority’: The destruction of oil refineries
The suspension of data-sharing was especially shocking, given that Kyiv did stop hitting Russian refineries for three days.
It was only on Wednesday that its drones attacked refineries in Saratov and Ryazan regions, said Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister, Aleksander Novak.
However, Kyiv’s focus on striking oil refineries is ineffective and counterproductive, another observer said.
“Kyiv’s strategic priority is still the destruction of oil refineries,” Nikolay Mitrokhin of Germany’s Bremen University, who has penned hundreds of authoritative analyses of the hostilities, told Al Jazeera.
However, Russia overcame the initial shock by transporting gas from refineries in Siberia and exporting it from neighbouring Belarus and Kazakhstan.
No economic collapse, massive joblessness or public protests followed the strikes, while Moscow continued its air raids, adding jet-powered drones that resemble cruise missiles and are hard to down with Ukraine’s existing air defence system, he said.
“What is the basis for Kyiv’s and its backers’ conviction that strikes on oil refineries and depots will lead to Russia’s strategic defeat before Ukraine is defeated? I don’t understand,” he said.
However, Ukrainian attacks on data centres, bridges and factories where drones are assembled are far more effective, he said.
Recent strikes on data centres of Russian online giant Yandex and the state-run Sberbank resulted in disruptions of services in Russia and even former Soviet republics where Yandex operates its online payment, food delivery and taxi services.
Trump “didn’t ask him to stop the war, to give away cities or stop striking Russian rears in general,” Mitrokhin said.
Kyiv has repeatedly reiterated that it was ready to start peace talks if they are preceded by a ceasefire, but Moscow wanted to continue ground assaults and air raids until the peace terms were finalised – which could take months or even years.
‘We’re ready for any turn of events’
On Wednesday, Ukraine’s drone czar accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite terminals that are part of the military-grade Starshield system.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said that SpaceX abruptly and without any warning limited services for terminals placed on drones flying over 160km/h (100mph).
The limit affected crucially-important interceptor drones and followed Trump’s request, presidential adviser Serhii Sternenko said.
Musk said that the White House owns and controls the Starshield systems and that any limits on speed are decided by Trump.
Some military analysts warn that the limit may be followed by a total shutdown of Starlink for Ukraine that could damage the quality of all military communications.
“But we were getting ready for everything,” Andriy Pronin told Al Jazeera. “We already know it may happen, that’s why we’re ready for any turn of events.”
In September 2022, Musk secretly ordered engineers to switch off Starlink coverage in the Russia-occupied Kherson region, effectively thwarting Kyiv’s push to retake it, Reuters reported.
In 2023, Musk threatened to cut off Ukrainian military access to Starlink unless the US defence department took over the costs.
Later, the Pentagon, Poland and other European allies took over the costs.

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The Ankara Climate Transition Forum, held in the runup to next month’s COP31 UN Climate Change Conference, to be hosted in the southern Turkish city of Antalya, kicked off on Thursday in Ankara, the nation's capital.
The forum aims to showcase local climate action initiatives for Antalya, in line with the COP31 Presidency’s goal of delivering a conference focused on implementation, with participation from EU representatives, the UN Development Program, municipalities, international financial institutions, and scientists.
Halil Hasar, head of climate change at Türkiye’s Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, said at the forum’s opening that tackling climate change requires collective action.
Stressing the importance of early warning systems and data, Hasar said: “One neighborhood is facing a heat wave, while another is dealing with rain and flooding. We are living in a different era where even normal conditions are changing.”
Hasar said 2024 was Türkiye's hottest year on record, while 2025 was its driest.
He said long-term precipitation levels have fallen 28%, adding that rainfall of 300 kilograms (661 pounds) per square meter in a single day reflects the consequences of the climate crisis rather than ordinary precipitation.
Hasar stressed the importance of local climate action and science-based planning, saying preventive measures could reduce costs.
He said Türkiye would showcase pilot projects at the conference in Antalya, adding: “We will try to demonstrate these efforts to everyone through a pilot project in Antalya at COP31.”
COP31, the UN Climate Change Conference, is due to be held on Nov. 9-20 in Antalya on the Turkish Riviera, with Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum serving as president.
According to the UN, the conference “is where the world comes together to agree on the actions to address the climate crisis, such as limiting the global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7F), helping vulnerable communities adapt to the effects of climate change, and achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.”
The conference will bring together world leaders and negotiators from the member states of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) to further global progress, with business leaders, young people, climate scientists, Indigenous peoples, and civil society “sharing insights and best practices to strengthen global, collective, and inclusive climate action,” the UN added.

Gaza's patients face death as Israel restricts Rafah crossing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:43:07 UTC
20:43:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's patients face death as Israel restricts medical evacuations via Rafah
Khitam Doghmosh, a Palestinian cancer patient in Gaza battling lymphoma and breast cancer, fears she will die before getting any chance to seek treatment outside the war-torn enclave.
Despite receiving an urgent medical referral, the 45-year-old mother of five remains stranded in the besieged territory, where shortages of medicines and medical equipment have left her without the treatment she needs because of Israeli policy.
On 5 February 2024, the Israeli army killed Doghmosh's husband in an airstrike. Two months later, in April, she was diagnosed with lymphoma and breast cancer and spent more than two months in hospital without receiving adequate treatment.
"The doctors did everything they could, but there are no medicines or treatments available for my condition, which is why they issued an urgent medical referral," she described to The New Arab. "Since that day, I have been waiting in vain. Only a small number of patients manage to leave Gaza, and there are others ahead of me in the queue. I am terrified I will die before my turn arrives."
Doghmosh has lost more than 40 kilograms because of her illness. "I am in my forties, yet I look like I am in my sixties as if I was an elderly woman worn down by disease," she said, sharing fears about what would happen to her children if she died.
Her ordeal reflects the plight of thousands of patients awaiting medical evacuation as Israel continues to prevent sick and wounded Palestinians from leaving through the Rafah crossing, which has remained closed to patient evacuations for more than two weeks, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health.
Mohammed Abu Afash, director of Medical Relief in Gaza, told TNA that 2,027 patients had died while awaiting treatment and medical evacuation since October 2023, amid the continued Israeli closure of crossings and restrictions on the entry of medicines and medical supplies.
"More than 21,000 patients require medical evacuation," Abu Afash said, adding that no patients had left through Rafah in the preceding five days.
"Those awaiting travel include cancer patients, people with kidney failure and heart disease, and others with chronic illnesses requiring specialised care unavailable in Gaza. Delays can worsen their conditions and lead to potentially fatal complications," he explained.
The healthcare system is also struggling with severe shortages of medicines, medical supplies and diagnostic services, including laboratory tests, radiology and operating theatres.
Out of more than 574 healthcare centres operating before the war, only 227 remain functional, many with limited resources, undermining services for pregnant women, children and other patients, he explained.
Thousands face years-long wait
Beyond the illegal Israeli closure itself, the scale of the waiting lists and the limited number of patients permitted to leave have deepened the crisis.
Gaza's Medical Referral Committee at the Ministry of Health warned that evacuating the more than 21,000 patients and wounded people currently awaiting travel could take four years under the existing mechanism, even if no new cases were added.
With new medical referrals continuing to be approved each month, clearing both the accumulated backlog and incoming cases could take approximately eight years, the committee said.
For patients whose conditions require urgent intervention, such delays could prove fatal.
In a press statement, the Ministry of Health said the closure of Rafah was depriving patients and wounded people on approved travel lists of access to medical treatment, while adding to the burden on hospitals already struggling to accommodate critical cases.
The closure also prevents patients from departing on the three days each week designated for coordinating medical evacuations, disrupting travel schedules and prolonging waits for those who have already completed medical and security procedures.
The ministry called on international, UN and human rights organisations to pressure Israel to ensure the sustainable reopening of Rafah and other crossings and facilitate the immediate departure of critically ill patients and those with severe injuries.
War survivors stranded without care
The crisis also affects Palestinians wounded during the war who require specialised treatment abroad, including survivors who have lost entire families and are now struggling to secure care for themselves and their children.
Tamer Mahmoud was injured in an Israeli strike on his home in al-Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza in May 2024. The Israeli army attack killed his mother, sisters, nieces and nephews, wife and three children. He survived alongside one of his children and his father.
Mahmoud requires treatment abroad for his injuries, while his surviving child, who is already a disabled child, requires spinal cord-related therapy that was unavailable in Gaza even before the war.
"I survived alongside my child, who has special needs. I used to travel with him constantly to Egypt for spinal cord treatment therapy that wasn't even available in Gaza before the war, let alone now," he told TNA.
Both have received medical referrals, but neither has been able to travel.
About two weeks ago, Mahmoud received a call from the World Health Organisation telling him to prepare for travel, reviving his hopes of obtaining treatment for himself and his child.
The crossing's closure soon dashed those hopes, leaving him uncertain about when they could leave.
"A few days ago, I felt that relief was near and that I would finally be able to travel and receive treatment, but the crossing was shut," he said. "Today, I do not know whether we will travel or not."
The wait continues for Doghmosh, Mahmoud and thousands of others as their health deteriorates and treatment remains out of reach due to Israeli restrictions.
With more than 21,000 people awaiting medical evacuation and thousands of patients facing conditions that cannot withstand prolonged delays, the continued Israeli closure of Rafah threatens to turn the wait for treatment into a death sentence.

Taxing Orlen windfall profits risks straining ties with Warsaw, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:42:00 UTC
20:42:00 KST

Lithuania’s finance minister has questioned the feasibility of imposing a windfall profits tax on Orlen Lietuva, the country’s oil refinery owned by Poland’s Orlen, saying the measure could strain bilateral relations while generating limited revenue for the state.
Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said Thursday that the government had examined the proposal but identified significant risks and little potential financial benefit.
“There are a number of risks related to international relations. We also received an informal opinion from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that it would not be inclined to support the measure due to certain risks to bilateral relations, so we have analysed the issue in detail,” Valys said.
“The risks are high, while the potential impact is small – ranging from zero to 46 million euros – and our situation is fundamentally different from Poland’s,” he added.
Liberal lawmaker Simonas Gentvilas noted that Poland had already introduced a similar tax.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said discussions on a potential windfall tax in Lithuania remained at an early stage, with no political consensus reached. Preliminary estimates of the possible revenue range from zero to tens of millions of euros, he said.
Sinkevičius said the government must consider Orlen Lietuva’s importance as a major employer, as well as the implications for international relations and ties with neighbouring countries. No concrete political decisions have been made, but possible measures are being assessed.
Poland has introduced a 60% tax on fuel companies’ profits exceeding a threshold based on standard profit margins. The government expects the measure to raise about 4 billion zlotys (940 million euros) to help finance reductions in fuel prices.
Ramūnas Dilba, an aide to Lithuania’s president, said last week that taxing Orlen Lietuva’s windfall profits could be one way to mitigate the impact of rising fuel prices.
He compared the proposal with a similar windfall tax – dubbed “solidarity contribution” –imposed by the previous government on large commercial banks’ profits. Although such a tax would not directly lower fuel prices, the additional budget revenue could be used to cushion the impact of higher fuel costs, he said.
Former Finance Minister Kristupas Vaitiekūnas had pledged to initiate a temporary tax on fuel wholesalers, saying that taxing Orlen Lietuva’s windfall profits would be more complicated than imposing a levy on commercial banks.
In April, then-Energy Minister Žygimantas Vaičiūnas said Lithuania could introduce such a tax if Poland did the same. He said the decision would need to be coordinated with Poland to avoid market distortions and potential fuel shortages, given that Poland’s Orlen owns the Mažeikiai refinery.

US-Iran stalemate: What are Trump’s next military options?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:41:05 UTC
20:41:05 KST

US-Iran stalemate: What are Trump’s next military options?
Trump has ruled out attacks before the midterms. Analysts weigh what he could do next, and at what cost.
United States President Donald Trump has stated on his social media platform Truth Social that he will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.
But he also told a Republican convention in September that the conflict “is going to end immediately after the elections”, and the US military has been sending more forces to the region in recent weeks.
Meanwhile, Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have surged to their highest level since the war began, with an Iranian official telling the Reuters news agency that Tehran has begun using different offensive tactics against vessels it considers to violate its restrictions.
As control of the Strait of Hormuz remains central to the US-Iran conflict, what military options does Trump have left, and what would each cost?
Al Jazeera spoke to military analysts to find out more:
Where does the US-Iran war stand?
Deadlocked.
The US and Israel first launched an attack on Iran on February 28, triggering counterattacks by Iran against US military assets and other infrastructure in Gulf countries and Jordan in the following months.
Iran also closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carried at least 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies before the war, sending global energy markets into chaos. The price of Crude Oil – the global benchmark – rose from about $72 a barrel the day before the war began to a high of nearly $120 a barrel earlier this year. On Thursday, it was trading at about $104.
A June ceasefire agreement collapsed over control of the strait, and Washington has kept up a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports while Iran has continued to attack ships attempting to pass through. Indirect talks via Pakistan and Qatar continue – along with the exchange of various proposals from each side – but Trump rejected Iran’s latest offer to reopen the strait last month.
The US has “enormous military capability that Iran can’t match”, but it has not delivered the outcomes Washington wants, Afzal Ashraf, a visiting fellow in international relations and security at Loughborough University in the United Kingdom and a former senior Royal Air Force officer who served in Iraq, told Al Jazeera.
What forces does the US have in the Middle East right now?
It has at least three aircraft carrier strike groups in the Gulf, or heading towards it.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, carrying about 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines, is sailing to the Middle East to join the carriers already there.
The US also maintains a host of military assets and about 50,000 soldiers at different bases in Middle East countries.
What are Trump’s military options?
Keep squeezing Iran
The US naval blockade on Iranian ports and the naval escorts for commercial ships it has been providing through the Strait of Hormuz are the status quo, which it can continue. This is the most likely course of action, Patrick Bury, a senior associate professor at the University of Bath and former NATO research analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Before the war began, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day, carrying an average of 17.1 million barrels of oil. This collapsed with the closure of the strait in March.
In recent weeks, with the help of US Navy escorts, Gulf oil flows through Hormuz – excluding Iran’s – had recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler. However, this has again reversed with Iran’s recent stepping up of attacks on ships in the strait. According to Kpler, only 2.9 million barrels of oil were carried through the waterway on October 11, the lowest level this month.
Washington is trying to maintain patrols and surveillance over the southwestern side of the strait, “enough to give ships some sort of protection to get out”, Bury said. Increasingly, drones do the grunt work of feeding intelligence and carrying out attacks, which is cheaper than keeping aircraft on long sorties. “I mean, it’s been somewhat effective,” he said, adding that high oil prices and crew bonuses mean “people are willing to take some risk.”
But now, Iran has changed tactics.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre recorded 15 attacks on ships between October 6 and 14. Iran appears well prepared, Bury said, pointing to “the asymmetry of costs”. “By dint of its geography”, he explained, Iran still enjoys “a kind of easier starting point.”
Resume air and missile attacks
This is another option.
Trump has said it may be “possible” to ramp up bombing after the elections, but has not given details.
If the situation does escalate, however, Bury said he expects “further strikes in fairly limited packets” against targets on Iran’s coastline and further inland.
A new campaign could “actually achieve a lot less” than the hits earlier this year, Ashraf said, because Iran has adapted. “They have fewer, but they can conceal them better,” he said of its weapons.
The costs would also be high for the US, which has already depleted much of its stockpile of very expensive defensive missile systems.
Each relatively cheap Iranian drone or missile can force the US to fire “an interceptor of a million [dollars] or more”, he said, and “the United States is running out of missiles for its own defence.”
Furthermore, the US has fired more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles at Iran during the course of the war. Fully restoring its pre-war inventory could take until the end of 2030, according to estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
Getting back to pre-war levels across key munitions would take “three to four years”, Bury said. “The problem is to solve that issue takes a long time, even when you press Go with the money.”
Tehran has also promised to hit back harder. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf declared last month that the era of “proportionate responses” was over.
Renewed attacks could also cost Washington access to some Gulf bases, Ashraf said.
Iran’s recent retaliation has targeted Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain, sparing other Gulf states that Ashraf said may have reached an understanding with Tehran to stay out of the fighting.
Could a US ground operation against Iran be an option?
It is very unlikely, experts say.
One target could be Kharg Island, 26km (16 miles) off Iran’s coast, which handles about 90 percent of Iran’s exports.
Joseph Votel, a former US Central Command (CENTCOM) commander, has said 800 to 1,000 soldiers could take it, but they would be highly exposed to fire from the mainland, according to Reuters.
Ashraf said US forces could launch a limited invasion, likely preceded by electronic warfare to blind Iranian defences.
But Iran would then attack the island itself. “They don’t need very much in the way of targeting information, once they know the island is occupied by American forces,” he said. “And the appetite for casualties is low in a war that is already very unpopular.”
Iran could also hit oil infrastructure across the Gulf in return, he warned, concluding that the seizure of Kharg Island would be “the most irrational of the irrational decisions”.
Is a full-scale US invasion of Iran possible?
This is also highly unlikely.
Trump has largely ruled out a ground offensive, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in March that ground troops would not be needed to achieve the administration’s goals.
“I don’t think they’re going to do it anyway,” Bury said, adding, “I don’t think they can do it, to be honest with you.”
Why does the timing matter?
This war is deeply unpopular with the US public, and Trump is facing mid-term elections in a matter of weeks.
About 65 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of it, according to the Pew Research Center.
Bury argued that the bigger question is whether the US can rebuild its military strength in a short amount of time. “Can America over the next few years regenerate that as a military power?” he said.
The task would outlast Trump’s term, he added, as “the next president would need to do the same thing anyway.”
The longer the war goes on, Ashraf warned, the greater the risk of unrest across the region, arguing that “we should not divorce the military options from the enormous capacity for political instability.”
On Sunday, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran had been striking vessels in the US-backed shuttle through the Strait of Hormuz every night for weeks.
“You are smuggling,” he said, “but the strait is under Iran’s control.”

My autumn of comfort TV and comfort food
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:40:11 UTC
20:40:11 KST

After a summer spent travelling here, there and everywhere, I am welcoming more time at home and bingeable telly with open arms. And, like a lot of the nation, I am obsessed with this season’s Celebrity Traitors. It is my achilles heel; so much so that, earlier this year, I politely declined an invite to a hot industry party because it clashed with the final, and there is no amount of free champagne or hobnobbing that would’ve got me off my sofa. The beauty of such shows is that they are on early enough to make an evening of it. Strictly has become our Saturday night family ritual, while my eldest will usually join us for Tuesday nights watching Bake Off. There are bowls of food, eaten by the spoonful, mugs of tea and endless biscuits. It’s a small, cosy ritual that makes the passing of summer feel a little less bleak.
For ease, I try to live by the rule of one meal for everyone. On nights when we eat on the sofa, I like to make something in advance that the girls can eat after school and that we can return to later on. Nigella Lawson’s chicken barley, for instance, is a firm favourite and, importantly, if a little less glamorously, it reheats well. The same goes for Laura Goodman’s mac’n’cheese, a surefire hit and a fixture in our house.
Essentially it’s all about batch cooking, comfort and being prepared. I also love to make big pots of congee and dal, which I freeze in portions for a rainy day. Both are perfect for feeding a range of appetites, too, with toppings and accompaniments added to suit. Ravinder Bhogal’s seasonal pumpkin and miso variation is firmly on my to-make list, as is pe hin, a Burmese dal recipe from Amy and Emily Chung.
Sofa food isn’t all savoury, of course. If you’ve ever watched Bake Off, you’ll know that doing so without a sweet treat to hand is a form of torture. A mug of tea and a plate of biscuits will usually do that trick, particularly if those biscuits are homemade. Current favourites in our house are Ana Ortiz’s alfajores de dulce de leche and Rebecca Bishop’s brown butter nutmeg shortbread. If something more substantial is required – because, let’s be honest, sometimes only a warming bowl of pudding will do – my first port of call is Felicity Cloake’s sticky toffee pudding (pictured top) with her proper custard on the side, naturally. And, being autumn, I’m also a sucker for Nigel Slater’s apple and blackberry crumble, ideally with more of that custard, too. Nothing says, “hello, autumn”, like a hedgerow-inspired crumble after all.
My week in (sweet) food
A slice of Jamaica | I was recently lucky enough to be on the receiving end of one of Doreen’s homemade Jamaican rum cakes, and I cannot stop thinking about it. I’m looking for any opportunity I can to send one as a gift. You can select a variety of shapes and sizes, but I do think the heart one is particularly endearing, as well as a gorgeous sentiment. Set up by Jackie Christian, the recipe was passed down to her from her Jamaican-born mum, Doreen. It’s a beautiful story and a stunning gift, and I’m already planning on buying myself another.
Malt loaf magic | Friend and fellow food writer Nicola Miller recently introduced me to Wooster’s Bakery, a 30-plus-year-old family business that takes bread and baking seriously. Based in Suffolk, it’s not somewhere I can frequent regularly, but luckily for those of us who aren’t local, you can order their incredible malt loaf online. Mail-a-malt is divine: a delicious, sticky, plump and rich loaf that comes in a glorious circular box.
Sweet innovation | Hello, my name is Georgina Hayden and I am a full-blown chocoholic. And, fortunately for me, one of my favourite pastry chefs, Philip Khoury, has created an online shop where his chocolate creations can be enjoyed by everyone. They are all outstanding, but his latest ingenious creation may be my favourite to date: namely, fig chocolate. Made in the style of white chocolate, it’s packed with fresh figs, fig leaves and a little almond. Elegant yet playful, it feels like a more grown-up chocolate orange. Just don’t wait until Christmas.

Hezbollah admits explosives shipment, defies Lebanon weapons ban

Breadcrumb
Hezbollah admits explosives shipment, defies Lebanon weapons ban
Hezbollah has admitted ownership of a massive explosives shipment seized by Lebanese security forces, insisting the materials were intended for use against Israel while openly rejecting a government ban on its military activities.
Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah confirmed on Thursday that the vehicle and its cargo belonged to the group, demanding the immediate release of two detained men and the return of the confiscated explosives.
The admission marks a significant escalation in the confrontation between Hezbollah and the Lebanese government, which has launched an investigation into the shipment amid fears that the materials could be used in political assassinations.
Speaking from parliament, Fadlallah said Hezbollah had contacted security and judicial authorities immediately after the vehicle was intercepted at the Dahr al-Baidar checkpoint, along a major highway connecting Beirut to the Bekaa Valley and Syria.
He said the group had informed authorities that "the vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance" and demanded "the immediate release of the detainees and the return of the vehicle and its contents".
Fadlallah insisted that the explosives were intended exclusively for use against Israeli forces occupying Lebanese territory, rejecting suggestions that they could be used to carry out political assassinations inside Lebanon.
He accused Prime Minister Nawaf Salam of exploiting the seizure to fuel internal divisions, describing suggestions that the explosives were intended for assassinations as a politically motivated campaign.
The Hezbollah lawmaker claimed that elements within the government were using the incident to serve Israeli and American interests, warning that the group would not tolerate attempts to undermine what it considers its right to resist Israeli occupation.
He also accused the Lebanese authorities of abandoning their responsibility to protect the country and its people.
Fadlallah went further by rejecting the Lebanese government's 2 March decision banning Hezbollah's military and security activities, describing it as unconstitutional and imposed under foreign pressure.
He said the group did not recognise the decision or its consequences on the ground, accusing the government of abandoning southern Lebanon to Israeli occupation.
The lawmaker warned authorities against exploiting Hezbollah's commitment to civil peace and stability to undermine the group or its supporters, arguing that such actions could threaten Lebanon's internal security.
Explosives shipment raises assassination fears
The admission follows the seizure of approximately 500 kilograms of explosives from a grey Dodge Caravan intercepted at the Dahr al-Baidar checkpoint.
Interior Minister Ahmad Hajjar said on Tuesday that security personnel became suspicious of the vehicle because it appeared to be carrying an unusually heavy load.
A search uncovered explosive materials, prompting officers to arrest the driver and a passenger. Both suspects, along with the seized cargo, were handed over to military police on the instructions of judicial authorities.
Salam previously revealed that the vehicle was travelling from the Bekaa Valley towards Greater Beirut and was carrying hundreds of kilograms of explosives, including the powerful military-grade explosive C4.
He warned that similar materials had been used in some of Lebanon's most notorious political assassinations.
Sources familiar with the investigation previously told The New Arab that the explosives were of a type used in past political killings, raising concerns about their possible intended use.
"The case is sensitive, and the quantity of materials seized was not small. These materials have been used in political assassinations in Lebanon," the sources said.
However, investigators have not publicly established that the shipment was intended for assassinations, and Hezbollah has insisted that the materials were destined for use against Israeli forces.
The Lebanese army's intelligence directorate and the Internal Security Forces' Information Branch have been instructed by the public prosecutor to expand their investigations and identify everyone involved in transporting the explosives.
Salam has called for the investigation to continue until all those responsible are identified and referred to the judiciary.
He also praised security forces for uncovering an additional quantity of explosives in the Qasr-Hermel area near the Syrian border.
Justice Minister Adel Nassar has called for the case to be referred to the Judicial Council, a special court responsible for cases involving serious threats to national security.
Nassar previously warned that storing explosives in densely populated areas would constitute a serious crime regardless of their intended use.
He also cited concerns over reports that explosive materials had been transported towards Beirut's southern suburbs, warning that the quantities involved could cause devastating destruction.
Pressure mounts over Hezbollah's weapons
The seizure has intensified Lebanon's internal dispute over Hezbollah's arsenal, with opponents of the group urging the government to accelerate efforts to bring all weapons under state control.
On Wednesday, a committee pursuing legal action against Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem held an emergency meeting at the office of MP Ashraf Rifi.
The committee said the explosives seizure could not be treated as a minor security incident and pledged to continue pursuing its criminal complaint against Qassem as new information emerges.
It called on judicial and security authorities to establish the shipment's origin, intended destination and the identities of those involved, while demanding that the investigation remain free from political interference.
The committee also urged authorities to keep investigations into past political assassinations open and ensure that those responsible are held accountable.
The developments come amid mounting international pressure on Hezbollah to disarm, with Washington linking billions of dollars in reconstruction assistance to the group surrendering its weapons.
A US State Department spokesperson said this week that Washington was working with Gulf and European partners on a reconstruction assistance package for Lebanon but insisted that Hezbollah must first give up its arsenal.
The confrontation unfolds against the backdrop of Israel's continuing military campaign in Lebanon, which has caused widespread destruction and displacement.
Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and damaging infrastructure and agricultural land in southern Lebanon, while occupying parts of the border region.
Hezbollah maintains that its weapons remain necessary to confront Israeli occupation and attacks.

Frankfurt Airport facing kerosene shortage: Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:36:55 UTC
20:36:55 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Frankfurt Airport is facing a kerosene shortage, forcing Lufthansa aircraft to carry additional fuel before arriving at the airport, according to German media reports and statements from the companies involved.
According to Lufthansa, one reason for the tight kerosene supply situation at Germany’s largest airport is reduced capacity in the pipeline connection.
Frankfurt Airport operator Fraport said routine maintenance is currently underway on a pipeline that also supplies the airport with jet fuel. However, no disruptions are expected from the maintenance, as alternative supply routes and sufficient fuel storage capacity are available.
“The airport’s operations will therefore not be affected,” Fraport said.
Meanwhile, daily Bild cited the low water level of the Rhine River as another possible factor affecting supply, as tankers can navigate the river only with limited cargo.
Lufthansa has responded to the situation by taking precautionary measures to maintain flight operations. These include having aircraft on select routes take on additional fuel before departing for Frankfurt.
The practice, known as “tankering,” is intended to reduce the need for additional refueling in Frankfurt. The report said short- and medium-haul routes are primarily affected, while long-haul flights are also increasingly being included.
According to Bild, guidelines for aircraft in the Airbus A320 family set an upper limit of eight metric tons of additional fuel. At the same time, flight planning should ensure that the added weight does not result in restrictions on the transport of passengers or cargo.
Lufthansa emphasized that the measures are intended to ensure reliable flight operations. They will remain in effect until further notice and be adjusted as the situation evolves, the report said.
