Ukraine bins 'energy cease-fire' with attacks on Russian refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:36:00 UTC
20:36:00 KST

Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared the end of a brief, unreciprocated truce amid growing rift with Washington.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia’s Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
The strike could further complicate Kyiv’s relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks.
The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the cease-fire, but Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Ukraine never stopped its strikes on Russian refineries. It wasn't possible to independently verify each side's claims.
Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump’s demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals. Both are vital for Ukrainian defenses and attack operations.
The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We’re done," he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4 1/2 years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist’s YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Putin, the energy cease-fire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.
"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."
He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he’s in the middle."
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink, called Starshield, is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Amid fears that the Trump administration may be withdrawing support for Ukraine, Zelenskyy was due in Brussels for talks with European Union leaders attending a summit.
He was traveling to Belgium after visiting London, where he won pledges of more help from U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Asked whether the EU still trusts Trump, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, replied: "We definitely have a different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender."
"Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that is why Europe is standing beside Ukraine," Kallas told reporters at the summit, which Zelenskyy is scheduled to attend on Friday.
Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine’s Emergency Services said Thursday.
Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said.
"It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security," he added.
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

Documents
Military Court Centre Listings 16 October to 30 October 2026
PDF, 130 KB, 5 pages
Details
In line with the government’s transparency and open data initiative, the Military Court Service is to publish the court listings for the military court centres.
Each court listing covers the next one or two week assize period. This will be published on the internet by the last working day in advance of the assize period.
In addition to this, the court listings are published using digital signage technology within the reception areas of both military court centres.
Please be aware that the court listings are subject to change after publication, if you wish to find out more please contact the relevant military court centre. Details can be found at the bottom of each court listing.

Russia’s largest drone attack on Kirovohrad Oblast since the full-scale invasion kills three in Kropyvnytskyi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:33:09 UTC
20:33:09 KST

Russia hit central Ukraine’s Kirovohrad Oblast with its largest attack since the full-scale invasion, killing residents of the oblast capital, Kropyvnytskyi, the oblast’s head said. Russian strikes hit more than a dozen oblasts, and Ukraine’s president said Moscow escalated deliberately after sanctions relief.
Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine continues on the front line and behind it, where its drones, missiles, and glide bombs strike towns daily. Kyiv is drafting winter crisis plans as Russia targets the biggest cities, and logistics is hit too: Russia struck one retailer’s warehouse hub 10 times in a day.
Three dead in Kropyvnytskyi
Oblast head Andrii Raikovych counted almost 360 Russian drones over Kirovohrad Oblast and hits on 26 locations, mostly in Kropyvnytskyi. In his words, “the enemy deliberately struck critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities, and residential buildings.” In a post after midnight, he reported a third death and six injured, five of them in hospital.
Air-raid alerts around the city ran from 15:20 on 14 October to 05:33, and Suspilne correspondents heard more than 20 explosions in Kropyvnytskyi, the public broadcaster reported. The national emergency service counted 25 struck locations, and rescuers were still putting out fires in the morning, the service’s spokesperson in the oblast said.
A wave Kyiv ties to sanctions relief
Nationwide, Russia launched 580 drones and two Kh-59 guided missiles from 18:00 on 14 October, and air defenses downed or suppressed 536 drones by 08:00, the Air Force reported. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia killed three people in Kropyvnytskyi and three in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, where oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported two dead.
Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles
Zelenskyy counted more than 850 Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones between the start of 14 October and 09:00 the next day, “precisely at the time of an artificial speed limitation for our defensive capabilities.” Overnight into 14 October, SpaceX capped speeds on its military Starshield satellite service, disrupting Ukrainian missions. He added that Russia escalated “deliberately, having received a relaxation of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine.” Last week, Washington cleared Russian diesel trade after a call between US President Donald Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Strikes from Kyiv to Odesa Oblast
In Kyiv, a drone fell into a residential yard, Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote, later putting the injured at six. Drones hit two industrial enterprises in Poltava Oblast, its head Vitalii Diakivnych wrote, and a later strike on Poltava injured three people, rescuers said in a preliminary count. Ukraine’s state gas company Naftogaz said a drone set one of its gas production facilities in the oblast on fire, halting its work.
Russian guided aerial bombs injured two women and a man in Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, on 15 October, according to preliminary data from oblast head Oleh Syniehubov, who had counted nine injured in the oblast over the previous day. Over that day, Russian attacks killed three people in Donetsk Oblast, the oblast police said, and one in Kherson Oblast, where oblast head Oleksandr Prokudin reported five more injured. In Kherson city, a drone injured a man, the oblast administration said. In Sumy Oblast, a drone hit a house and left two people in acute stress, its administration said.
In Odesa Oblast, strikes damaged two apartment blocks, a company, and a bank office without casualties, oblast head Oleh Kiper said. Later, a jet-powered Shahed hit a store in the oblast, Zelenskyy wrote, and Kiper counted four injured in a preliminary tally. Drones also hit an enterprise in Ternopil Oblast, and five people sought medical help, rescuers said, while drones damaged two homes in Rivne, oblast head Oleksandr Koval said.

John Healey vows to give ‘breathing space’ to consumers and businesses in first budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:33:08 UTC
20:33:08 KST

John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules.
Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs.
“I want the budget to be a budget that gives Britain a bit of breathing space – but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans and the strength of our resilience and our economy for the future,” he said.
The government has already cut VAT on electricity bills, but Healey is expected to announce a further package of energy support at his 28 October tax and spending statement, before what is expected to be a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January.
He said: “The prime minister’s talked about recognising the cost of business, not just the cost of living.”
Healey also reiterated his insistence that he would be sticking to the spending plans set out by his predecessor Rachel Reeves at last year’s spending review – and that cabinet colleagues would have to find any additional resources within their existing budgets.
“When the second half of a spending review is in place, there are pressures on departments, and colleagues are doing a good job of managing with what they’ve got,” he said, adding: “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things.”
The UK has been praised by the IMF this week for setting out a plan to tackle its deficit, with the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urging the government to “stay the course”.
Healey stressed he would stick to the rules set out by Reeves. “We will meet those fiscal rules, and I think one of the hallmarks of the IMF’s backing of our fiscal plans is recognition that there isn’t just a forecast for the future, but there’s some evidence of performance already.”
He declined to say whether he would increase taxes on banks, or raise capital gains tax, to offset the expected pressure on his budget from higher energy prices and government borrowing costs.
“If you think back to the run-up to previous budgets, the speculation about what was set to be in those budgets was actually deeply damaging,” he said. “It led to people cashing in their pensions early when they didn’t need to. It led to people holding back or not investing in their businesses when they didn’t need to. So I’m just not going to get drawn into any speculation.”
Healey, a former defence secretary, also hinted he was working on an additional package of support for Ukraine, to be announced at the budget.
He said: “I’m working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine: military, diplomatic and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it’s what we see coming out of Ukraine, with [Vladimir] Putin targeting these energy systems with thousands without power, as we’ve got a harsh winter approaching.
“The step back from this is that the future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that’s why it’s so crucial that Putin doesn’t prevail.”
Healey and the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, chaired a meeting of G20 policymakers on Thursday morning, in the absence of the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent.
The chancellor will fly back to London on Thursday evening to put the finishing touches to the budget.

Former OpenAI engineer booked flight to Saudi Arabia before arrest in bugging case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:32:21 UTC
20:32:21 KST

Dilara Hamit
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device at the company’s San Francisco office booked one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia for himself and two family members before his arrest, according to a newly unsealed US court filing.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, his wife and another family member were scheduled to fly from San Francisco via Istanbul on Oct. 12, prosecutors said.
The FBI arrested Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national and US permanent resident, three days before the planned departure.
Prosecutors disclosed the bookings in an Oct. 8 motion requesting that the criminal complaint, arrest warrant and related documents remain sealed until his arrest.
“The defendant has the means – and will have an incentive – to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested,” Justice Department lawyers wrote.
Alfozan is charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine if convicted.
He had worked as an OpenAI engineer since July 2025 and was dismissed on the day of his arrest, the Justice Department said.
According to the complaint, OpenAI personnel discovered an audio recorder on Sept. 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room. Its stored files appeared to be encrypted.
The conference room was frequently used for confidential discussions about research, product plans, business opportunities, government engagements and company strategy.
Security footage allegedly showed Alfozan near the room on several occasions despite not being authorized to attend meetings there. Footage from Oct. 5 also appeared to show him looking behind the television, according to the complaint.
Prosecutors alleged that he used an internal productivity tool to search for building addresses, conference-room capacities, meeting calendars and locations used by executives and external partners.
A chatbot account associated with his wife also allegedly submitted prompts about building, concealing and remotely accessing an audio recorder, including continuous recording, live listening, encrypted storage and Wi-Fi connectivity.
The complaint does not accuse Alfozan’s wife of committing an offense or allege that she personally submitted the prompts.
OpenAI security personnel later found a similar recorder in a bag containing Alfozan’s wallet and identification, prosecutors said.
The Justice Department has not publicly identified a motive or alleged that he acted for the Saudi government or another foreign entity. He has not been charged with espionage or stealing trade secrets.
Alfozan remains in federal custody, with a detention hearing scheduled for Oct. 19, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California.

Russia plans to continue importing gasoline until end of year — Novak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:32:12 UTC
20:32:12 KST

MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Russia plans to continue importing gasoline at least until the end of 2026 for supplying the market and replenishing reserves, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week.
"We will continue imports at least until the end of the year as we need to both supply the domestic market and increase reserves, which went down in the summer period to meet domestic demand," he said.
The volume of imported gasoline on the Russian market remains stable at 10%, Novak added.
The Russian Energy Week (REW) International Forum is taking place in Moscow from October 14 to 16. It is being held with the support of the Government of the Russian Federation, the Ministry of Energy of the Russian Federation, and the Government of Moscow. The Roscongress Foundation organizes the forum. TASS is the information partner of Russian Energy Week.

Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries as Zelenskyy says 'we're done'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:32:00 UTC
20:32:00 KST

Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries, Zelenskyy says
October 15, 2026
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Thursday said that his country's military had resumed strikes on Russian energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.
Zelenskyy made the statement in an interview with London's Financial Times (FT) newspaper, saying: "The block [on energy infrastructure attacks] is out. We're done."
The announcement came after Russia reported Ukrainian attacks on oil processing plants in Ryazan, where fire broke out, and Saratov.
Kyiv had refrained from making attacks to give Trump's "energy ceasefire" a chance for success.
On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised "vigorous [US] efforts to initiate the peace process," and claimed that by resuming attacks, Ukraine "is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators."
Russia, however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, for instance on Wednesday, when Russian strikes cut power to 600,000 Ukrainian citizens.
Kyiv's blasts dangerous lack of US intel
Ukraine had gone along with Trump's public proposal — despite not being notified of any "ceasefire" ahead of time — but it seemed to have helped little in the eyes of US leadership.
To that end, Zelenskyy railed against a "dangerous" lack of US intelligence information this week as well as the throttling of SpaceX Starlink satellite access for Ukraine's troops after Trump last week announced a number of decisions that have had adverse consequences for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president said his country's military leaders had been warned that they would not be receiving US intelligence if they did not abide by Trump's "ceasefire."
Despite Ukraine's restraint, that withholding of intelligence was on full display this week when Kyiv was blindsided by Russian drones and missiles without any prior warning from the US.
"We will find a way out," said Zelenskyy of the situation as Ukraine's Western allies scramble to pick up the intelligence and defensive slack left by the US.
Zelenskyy said he would be willing to halt energy infrastructure attacks again but only if the US supplied Patriot interceptors that would allow Kyiv to down incoming the Russian ballistic missiles and drones that have been raining down on Ukraine since February 24, 2022.
Zelenskyy: Starlink throttling a question of US 'will'
Despite US claims that the Starlink situation was the result of a technical glitch, Zelenskyy told the FT, "It was not a technical problem, it was will."
SpaceX owner Elon Musk said the US owns and operates the Starshield military version of Starlink used by Ukraine, adding that he and his company had nothing to do with the issue.
The FT interview comes in the wake of Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil as well as his promise to buy "millions of barrels" of Russian diesel fuel amid high fuel prices caused by the US war with Iran.
The deal, just weeks from the US midterm elections, is unlikely to bring down oil prices. But it does extend a lifeline to Russian President Putin, allowing him to continue his illegal invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy and went so far as to call for him to be replaced this weekend.
Trump's sanctions actions fly in the face of nearly five years of allied political efforts to pressure Moscow to end its invasion.
Trump's actions have enraged NATO allies and European leaders, with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, for one, calling the US agreement to purchase Russian diesel "a very risky decision."
Meloni pointed out that the spike in oil prices was clearly precipitated by Trump's war in Iran and that his dealings with Putin would result in the Russian leader continuing his invasion of Ukraine rather than ending it.

'It melts all sides': Slovenia takes drastic measures to stop its last glacier from vanishing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:31:14 UTC
20:31:14 KST

Locals say ‘unique ecosystems’ are vanishing and rivers are losing water as Slovenia’s last glacier melts away.
Drop by drop, Slovenia is losing its ice. The Skuta Glacier is now the last glacier left in the country. Its other glacier on Mount Triglav, Slovenia’s highest peak, has almost completely melted away.
Mountain guide Andrej Slak has watched Slovenia’s glaciers shrink for 35 years. Climbing over rocky terrain toward what remains of Skuta, he says the change has been especially noticeable over the past decade and that its impact on the local community has been devastating.
"We are standing next to Slovenia's last remaining glacier and just look at what is left of it – nothing but a small patch of ice covered in grit and debris; the change is striking.
"These glaciers serve as vital water reservoirs for us in the valley throughout the year. Shepherds used to utilise icy hollows like this to store and preserve meat, but they can no longer do that as such ice pockets are nowhere to be found in the mountains anymore."
What remains is a patch of ice on the surface of the mountainside, and the rest buried under stones, with a narrow opening leading into a crevasse.
How quickly is Slovenia’s last glacier shrinking?
In Ljubljana, scientists have been gathering data on the glaciers.
This year marks 80 years since the Anton Melik Geographical Institute at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts began monitoring both glaciers.
"When we started, there were about two and a half to three hectares of ice under Skuta. Now it has shrunk to 1.5 hectares, and ice has mostly thinned out. On Skuta, it has thinned from several tens of metres to just a few metres. Back when we started, the Triglav Glacier covered a little over 14 hectares. Later, five or 10 years ago, we were still talking about half a hectare to one hectare. In recent years, it has been less than 0.2 hectares, but the ice, as I said, has now completely disappeared," explains Miha Pavsek.
Pavsek says the change is due to a combination of two factors.
"The turning point comes when we have a combination of very little snow, meaning a very low maximum seasonal snow depth, followed by a very warm summer,” he says. “And those two factors coincided very well this year.”
On Skuta, a marker painted on a rock shows how high the glacier reached in 1994. The ice has pulled back from this point since then.
“Skuta is following the same path as the Triglav Glacier. The ice is now protected. We were in the mountains a week ago, and about 80 to 90 per cent of the ice surface is covered by gravel, which provides additional protection, but it melts from all sides," says Pavsek.
Glacier melt has knock on effects on rivers and groundwater
Gravel gives the ice’s surface some protection from the sun, but inside the cave beneath the ice, water falls from the ceiling.
The effects reach well beyond the mountains.
"The waters from the glaciers feed our great rivers, including the Drava, in Croatia, as well as the Mura, which originates in Austria. There, according to the latest forecasts, all glaciers below 3,500 metres will disappear by 2050. So, these rivers will have much less water. And normally, these rivers feed the groundwater, where we have wells and pumps for drinking water," explains Pavsek.
For hikers who still come to the mountain, the loss is easy to see.
"I am concerned about this from a broader perspective, specifically regarding climate change in general, because glaciers serve as a vital reserve of Earth's water," says Tanja Plavec, a local hiker. "As they disappear, that reserve disappears with them. Furthermore, glaciers host a unique ecosystem that also vanishes as the perennial ice disappears."
This year, Europe sweltered under an exceptionally hot and arid summer, the intensity of which scientists say would have been "virtually impossible" without climate change from humans' burning of fossil fuels.
The continent is the world’s fastest-warming, with temperatures increasing twice as fast as the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Ahmad Adil
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
India on Thursday said it was “deeply concerned” over an alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting targeting a Hindu temple in the US state of Illinois.
A 19-year-old man from Palatine, Illinois, was arrested following an investigation into threats involving a potential mass shooting targeting a Hindu temple, according to CBS News.
Alexandros Paporakis was arrested outside his home Sunday evening after authorities received a tip about a possible mass shooting targeting a Hindu temple.
“We are deeply concerned by reports of an alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting targeting a Hindu temple in the Aurora area of Illinois,” the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.
“The reported anti-Hindu and racist nature of the alleged plot, including references to violence against people of Indian origin, is particularly disturbing,” it said.
Noting that the incident added to “growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US,” New Delhi said it “had taken note of the action taken by US law enforcement authorities,” including the “arrest and detention of the suspect and the charges brought against him.”
“There is a need for greater vigilance, zero tolerance for hate-motivated violence, and decisive action to ensure the safety and security of the Indian community,” the ministry said.

Donald Trump claims ‘Iran war will end very soon’ as midterm rallies heat up – US politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

Trump returns to Washington amid midterms campaign blitz as new polls reveal voters’s concern about US economy – live
Key voting groups are increasingly disenchanted with the economy, new Harris polls finds; about 8 in 10 people say the economy or the cost of living is top voting issue, new AP poll finds
Trump returns to White House amid weak polls ahead of midterms
Donald Trump is returning from the campaign trail to Washington DC this morning amid weak polls that could point to trouble for the Republican Party in the midterm elections.
According to an exclusive new poll for the Guardian, voting groups that are key to winning votes in the midterms – including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans – are increasingly disenchanted with the economy. Three in four Americans are now concerned about the potential for a recession.
In another poll conducted by the Associated Press, about 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about healthcare and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump – like immigration or crime – are lower priorities.
While Trump is in DC today, vice-president JD Vance will be in Monroe, Michigan, for a rally in support of Mike Rogers, the former Republican congressman vying to flip the open Senate seat against progressive Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed.
After back to back rallies in Arizona and Montana, Donald Trump’s day in Washington will consist of closed-door meetings, a private Rose Garden lunch and two tele- rallies. None of his scheduled events today are open to the press, but we’ll let you know if anything changes.
Tomorrow, the president will be back on the trail to campaign in Dalton, Georgia.
Key US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, new Harris poll finds
Lauren Aratani
The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession.
The poll shows growing weariness across the political spectrum over high prices.
Republicans, fighting to keep control of Congress, are losing support with independent voters, who are expected to be the deciding factor in key swing races. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of independents said the economy is worse, up from 48% who said the same in September 2024 in the heat of the 2024 presidential election.
Even within the Republican ranks, optimism has waned. In February 2025, just a few weeks after Trump was inaugurated, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By February 2026, just before the US launched attacks against Iran, that optimism was up to 49%. In the latest poll, just 28% of Republicans said the economy is getting better.
In the new poll, a vast majority of Americans agreed that there is an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans. But Americans still remain divided over who has a solution.
Democrats (71%) were more likely than Republicans (59%) to say that their own party had a solution.
Republicans were more likely (26%) to say neither party has a solution compared with Democrats (17%)
Half of independents said neither party has a solution, while 14% sided with Democrats and 10% with Republicans.
Trump returns to White House amid weak polls ahead of midterms
Donald Trump is returning from the campaign trail to Washington DC this morning amid weak polls that could point to trouble for the Republican Party in the midterm elections.
According to an exclusive new poll for the Guardian, voting groups that are key to winning votes in the midterms – including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans – are increasingly disenchanted with the economy. Three in four Americans are now concerned about the potential for a recession.

Other issues that are stronger for Trump – like immigration or crime – are lower priorities.
US voters overwhelmingly want change in Washington, new poll finds
A strong majority of voters believe president Donald Trump is falling short at home and abroad, and they want significant change in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a new AP-NORC poll.
The survey, which was conducted less than four weeks before Election Day, finds that registered voters who identify as Democrats are more enthusiastic than Republican voters about casting a ballot.
More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans.
The poll’s findings paint a difficult picture for Republicans, who are clinging to control of Congress under the weight of an unpopular war with Iran and surging prices in the US.
About 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about healthcare and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump — like immigration or crime — are lower priorities.
James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, sat face to face with several undecided voters who grilled him on a slew of contentious issues including Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, abortion and foreign aid, during a CNN town hall on Wednesday evening.
Jodi Hunt, a self-described single-issue voter, probed Talarico’s pro-choice stance, asking: “How would you convince me as a Catholic voter that I can trust you would protect the most innocent among us?”
Talarico described the Bible as being silent on abortion, to which Hunt countered quoting “Thou shalt not kill”.
“We may have different, moral conclusions when it comes to this particular ethical question, but we actually have the same public policy goal,” Talarico said, framing abortion as a public health issue that could be solved with a reduction in unplanned pregnancies.
During the night, Talarico cast himself as a moderate, who would put the needs of Texans over party allegiances. He railed against the ultra-wealthy, framing them as the common enemy.
Turning to James Talarico, the Democratic candidate fighting for a Texas US Senate seat might not have sparred with his Republican rival Ken Paxton last night but that doesn’t mean he was spared from attacks.
At a rally in Texas on Wednesday, JD Vance responded to an audience member who shouted his praise by responding: “I love you too sir.” He then added: “In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the vice president, not James Talarico.”
It’s part of the Republican strategy to cast doubt down on Talarico’s Texan credentials and whether he’s “man enough,” according to the New York Times.
Recent polls have shown that the Democratic candidate is leading against his Republican counterpart.
Meanwhile Paxton, who declined an invitation to meet voters with Talarico last night, has focused his efforts in an ad blitz. Already more than $500m has been spent on television ads for the Texas race, according to CNN.
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after halting those attacks to show that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.

Saxony-Anhalt: AfD and BSW demand an end to aid for Ukraine
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:27:43 CEST
20:27:43 KST

Saxony-Anhalt: AfD and BSW demand an end to aid for Ukraine
At a special session on 14 October, the parliament of Saxony-Anhalt adopted a joint resolution submitted by the Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), entitled ‘Peace talks instead of expanding the war in Ukraine’. The AfD (39 MPs) and BSW (5) hold a majority in the 83-seat state parliament (Landtag) but have not formed a formal coalition. In the resolution, the two parliamentary groups call for an immediate ceasefire and the start of negotiations with Russia, alongside the normalisation of economic relations and the immediate lifting of sanctions. Its authors argue that “the energy and economic war being waged against Russia is inflicting enormous losses on German industry, businesses, trade and our citizens”. The AfD and BSW demand a halt to arms deliveries and all financial assistance to Ukraine, with the exception of humanitarian aid. In the longer term, they also want Ukraine to be granted neutral status.
The resolution brings together earlier demands by the AfD and BSW to end German support for Ukraine. However, it also marks the first attempt to advance these demands through the Bundesrat, Germany’s upper house. In practice, the resolution would only be submitted to the Bundesrat by a new AfD-led state government.
Commentary
- Pro-Russian and anti-Ukrainian policies provide common ground for the AfD and BSW. The two parties can therefore be expected to support similar initiatives in the future, even without a formal coalition. In its state election manifesto, the AfD calls for resuming gas imports from Russia, repairing the damaged Nord Stream pipeline, expanding Russian-language teaching and restoring school exchanges with Russia. The BSW also advocates resuming purchases of Russian gas. During the debate in the Landtag, a BSW representative suggested that Kyiv had violated an agreement on ‘Ukraine’s neutrality’ and stressed that “NATO’s eastward enlargement should never have taken place”.
- The decision to convene a special session of the Landtag specifically to discuss policy towards Russia and Ukraine reflects negative public sentiment in Saxony-Anhalt regarding support for Ukraine – a theme that also featured prominently in the campaign ahead of the September state election. Opposition to supporting Ukraine is particularly strong in eastern Germany: according to an INSA poll published on 12 September, 50% of respondents in the former East Germany favour reducing this assistance, compared with 41% in western Germany. An ARD poll published on 6 September found that 57% of Saxony-Anhalt residents, including 92% of AfD voters, support the party’s efforts to halt arms deliveries to Ukraine.
- The state parliament’s decision is political and will not prompt the current state government to submit the initiative to the Bundesrat. On 8 October, the office of the incumbent Minister-President, Sven Schulze (CDU), emphasised that it would decide on the next steps independently. The state government has two months to provide the Landtag with a written response outlining further action. Foreign and defence policy falls within the remit of the federal government. Should the AfD form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, submitting the resolution to the Bundesrat would likely become a priority for the new administration. The election of a new state Minister-President is expected to take place in December this year; the AfD intends to nominate Ulrich Siegmund for the post.

Security costs at Netanyahu's residences top $41 million, quaduple previous prime ministers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:27:31 UTC
20:27:31 KST

Israel's Prime Minister's Office paid 127,432,277 (about $41 million) shekels for security and protection projects at prime ministerial residences between 2023 and October 2026, during Benjamin Netanyahu's current term, more than four times the approximately 29 million shekels (about $9.4 million) paid in the preceding three years, according to newly disclosed government figures.
The figures, released Wednesday by the Prime Minister's Office Freedom of Information Unit following a petition filed by the Givat Mordechai Community Association with the Jerusalem District Court, reveal a sharp increase in security spending at properties under the office's responsibility.
The properties include the official prime ministerial residence on Balfour Street in Jerusalem, Netanyahu's private residence on Gaza Street in Jerusalem, which was designated an alternative official residence, and his private home in Caesarea.
However, the Prime Minister's Office stressed that the figures cover all residences under its responsibility, including official and private properties belonging to serving and former prime ministers. The disclosure does not specify how much was spent at each property.
According to the figures, 10.9 million shekels (about $3.5 million) was paid in 2023, rising to 27.8 million (nearly $9 million) in 2024. Spending then surged to 72.5 million (about $23.4) shekels in 2025, approximately six times the amount paid in 2022. A further 16.2 million shekels (about $5.2 million) was paid between January and October 2026.
By comparison, approximately 29 million shekels was paid during 2020–2022. The two totals cover periods of different lengths, with the latest figures spanning nearly four years and the earlier figures covering three.
The Prime Minister's Office attributed much of the increase since 2024 to changes in the security threat level that required substantial investment in protecting the official residence. The explanation appears to refer, at least in part, to the threat posed by explosive drones following the October 2024 drone strike on Netanyahu's private residence in Caesarea.
The attack highlighted the vulnerability of highly secured locations to aerial threats and prompted renewed scrutiny of security arrangements around the prime minister and his family. Despite releasing the overall figures, the Prime Minister's Office has refused to disclose how much was spent at individual residences, arguing that such information could compromise national security.
The disclosure has renewed scrutiny of Netanyahu's previous criticism of his predecessor, Naftali Bennett, over spending on security arrangements at Bennett's private residence in Ra'anana.
In 2022, Netanyahu shared a television report and accused Bennett of using public funds to renovate his home at a cost of 50 million shekels (about $16 million). "At the expense of Israeli citizens: Bennett renovated his private home in Ra'anana for 50 million shekels. Watch Ayala Hasson's investigation," Netanyahu wrote at the time.
However, the latest government disclosure comes alongside official figures showing that the cost of security and protection work at Bennett's home was approximately half the amount Netanyahu had publicized. According to the State Comptroller, the cost of security work at Bennett's Ra'anana residence totaled approximately 24.9 million shekels (about $8 million). 
During 2021 and 2022, when Bennett and Yair Lapid served as prime ministers for most of the period, approximately 22.7 million shekels ($7.3 million) was paid for security projects across all prime ministerial residences combined. The figures do not necessarily represent the full costs incurred during those years, as some payments for projects undertaken at the time may have been made in subsequent years.
Kobi Eisen, chairman of the Givat Mordechai Community Association, which filed the petition, told the court that the earlier report concerning Bennett had been false and argued that Netanyahu had amplified its claims. "That is why it is critical for the public to know how much money was invested in private homes," Eisen said.
Government: Spending figures could expose security weaknesses
The Security Division of the Prime Minister's Office opposed releasing a breakdown of expenses by property, saying the information could help hostile actors identify vulnerabilities and assess the level of protection at different residences.
"Publishing security expenditures for the prime minister's residences and offices could reveal the extent of the security investment allocated to them and make it possible to draw conclusions about the level of protection and security priorities," the division argued.
It warned that publishing expenses for individual properties could create security risks. According to the division, hostile actors routinely collect publicly available information, including photographs, intelligence obtained through agents and drones, and other sources.
Such information, it argued, could be combined with spending figures to identify preferred targets, potential weaknesses and possible methods of attack. The division stressed that Israel is currently facing a security threat level that is among the highest since the establishment of the state, if not the highest. Under those circumstances, it said, the requested detailed disclosure could not be permitted.
Alon Halva, the Prime Minister's Office deputy director general for security, emergency preparedness, information and cyber affairs, who is considered close to Netanyahu and his wife, also opposed releasing the figures.
Speaking during the court hearing, Halva argued that even the amount allocated to each property could provide valuable intelligence.
An adversary examining the figures alongside information gathered from other sources, he said, could compare the sums invested at residences associated with Lapid, Bennett and Netanyahu and use them to assess their respective levels of protection.
‘A number that reveals nothing’
Eisen rejected the government's arguments, maintaining that disclosing spending totals would not expose actual security arrangements or technical details. "Disclosing quantitative information does not harm security," he told the court. "There is no problem showing how much money was invested in the building on Balfour Street. The information does not allow a third party to know what the money was spent on, only how much was spent."
He argued that the figures were important primarily because they would enable voters to assess the use of public funds. "It is a number that reveals nothing, other than allowing voters to know how much was invested," Eisen said.
He again referred to Netanyahu's earlier criticism of Bennett, arguing that transparency was particularly important given the public controversy surrounding the former prime minister's residence. "The prime minister amplified the false report about Naftali Bennett concerning investments in Bennett's home. That is why it is critical for the public to know how much money was invested in private homes," he said.
Eisen emphasized that his association wanted the information released before the October 27 election. "We want the information to reach voters before voters reach the ballot box," he said. "There is a kind of limbo here. They say the voters should decide, but they are not giving voters the information they need."
Jerusalem District Court Deputy President Judge Arnon Darel ordered the Prime Minister's Office to provide an additional breakdown by Thursday, distinguishing between private and public residences and separating the figures according to periods or governments.
The order represents a further step in the legal dispute over how much information the public should receive about security expenditures at properties used by Israeli prime ministers. The court's next hearing is scheduled for Sunday, October 18, when it is expected to decide whether the more detailed figures should be made public.

2 ships on fire off Romania's Black Sea coast, 7 crew missing
October 15, 2026
Romanian authorities have launched search and rescue operations in the Black Sea in a bid to find seven missing crew from a chemical tanker that caught fire overnight to Thursday.
Another vessel, also a chemical tanker, was also set on fire in the same region some hours earlier, but all its crew is said to be safe.
The fires occurred after Russian drones strayed into Romanian airspace, though Romanian officials have so far not explicitly said the unmanned aircraft caused the blazes.
However, there have been drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships off the coasts of Romanian and neighboring Bulgaria — both NATO members — in the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors lost in those incidents.
What do we know about the ship fires in the Black Sea?
Both ships were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal leading to the Black Sea out of the Danube River when they caught fire.
Romania's naval authority said it launched its search and rescue operation after receiving an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader.
Five of the 12 crew members were said to be safe, while seven were missing.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," Defense Minister Radu Miruta told the Digi24 television channel.
"This is a matter of significant gravity, given that such incidents are occurring in Romanian territorial waters," he said.
The other fire, which broke out earlier, occurred onboard the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J.
Ships often use the canal as a place to anchor in the case of delays caused by weather or congestion.
Growing attacks in the Black Sea
Romania, which shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years during Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
The Danube and its ports are now frequently used by Ukrainian vessels as Ukraine's Black Sea ports come under attack from Russian forces.
Ukrainian ships are also choosing routes in the Black Sea close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.
This comes as shipping in the Black Sea has come under increasing attacks in recent months that have drastically reduced grain transports from both Ukraine and Russia, both major cereal exporters.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Thursday that the EU, of which both his country and Romania are members, will discuss a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea at its ongoing summit in Brussels.
Bulgaria summoned the Russian ambassador over the sinking of a ship off the country's coast on Tuesday following a drone attack.

Private citizens

Water scarcity and costly imports threaten food security in landlocked countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:22:36 UTC
20:22:36 KST

As one of only two doubly landlocked countries globally, Uzbekistan faces unique water and food security challenges.
Almost 57 per cent of people living in the world's 32 landlocked developing countries cannot afford a healthy diet, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Around one in six faces hunger.
Home to nearly 600 million people, these countries face additional obstacles in securing food supplies and reaching international markets. Their dependence on transport routes through neighbouring states can increase costs for farmers, businesses and consumers.
A 2025 UN study quantified that disadvantage. Logistics costs per tonne of imported goods are 75 per cent higher in landlocked developing countries than in transit developing countries – the coastal nations through which exports flow. For exports, the difference is 63 per cent.
The findings provided context for discussions at the Global Technical Forum on Food Security, organised at the beginning of October by the FAO and Uzbekistan's Ministry of Agriculture in Tashkent.
Transport costs affect food security
The impact of geography extends beyond the cost of shipping agricultural products. Food imports, fertiliser and fuel can become more expensive when goods must cross additional borders or travel longer distances.
"The countries that will always be the most affected are the poorest countries, because those are the ones that import food, and their food import costs will increase," Máximo Torero, the FAO's chief economist, told Euronews.
For agricultural exporters, delays also create risks. Fresh fruit and vegetables can lose quality or spoil before reaching buyers, reducing farmers' earnings and increasing losses along supply chains.
Torero also identified climate change and population growth as long-term pressures on food production. He cited disruptions affecting the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, alongside drought-related restrictions on shipping through the Panama Canal, as examples of risks to international agricultural trade.
Uzbekistan: High production, but continued reliance on imports
Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, alongside Liechtenstein. Neither country has direct access to the sea, and all their neighbours are also landlocked.
Agriculture, forestry and fisheries accounted for approximately 19 per cent of Uzbekistan's GDP in 2024, according to the FAO.
Despite its geographical constraints, Uzbekistan has significantly reduced hunger. The FAO estimates that the prevalence of undernourishment has remained below 3 per cent over the past decade, compared with approximately 20 per cent in 2000.
The FAO's July 2026 assessment forecast an above-average cereal harvest of approximately 9 million tonnes, including 7.3 million tonnes of wheat.
Despite that production, Uzbekistan's wheat and wheat flour import requirements are forecast at 4.2 million tonnes for the 2026-2027 marketing year. Demand for high-quality wheat, particularly from neighbouring Kazakhstan, remains significant.
The figures illustrate why domestic agricultural output alone does not eliminate the need for reliable cross-border trade.
"We are telling the world that we have moved from being 'landlocked' to 'land-linked'," Uzbekistan's Agriculture Minister Ibrokhim Abdurakhmonov told Euronews. "But this connectivity does not happen on its own. First and foremost, we need to work together to address our common challenges."
Water management and agricultural innovation
Transport connectivity is only one part of the challenge. Agriculture across Central Asia depends heavily on irrigation, while several countries share limited water resources.
"Our common challenges are particularly visible in Central Asia. First and foremost, there is the issue of water," Abdurakhmonov said.
Uzbekistan is proposing a regional initiative bringing together natural resource management, agricultural research and new technology. The minister also outlined plans to strengthen knowledge-sharing and support the adoption of new farming methods.
The FAO has identified water scarcity, land degradation and climate change among the main challenges facing Uzbek agriculture. Its cooperation programme with Uzbekistan includes initiatives covering digital agriculture, biodiversity and natural resource management.
However, increasing production does not automatically guarantee access to nutritious food.
The FAO's global food security research highlights how processing, transport and distribution costs influence the prices consumers pay. But access to nutritious food also depends on household incomes and the support available when prices rise.
"On food security, I think it's not a standalone goal but it's really part of a larger picture," Sabine Machl, the UN Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan, told Euronews.
She highlighted education, healthcare, social protection and equal opportunities as essential parts of that wider picture. Social protection, in particular, can help vulnerable households maintain access to food when rising prices put pressure on their incomes.

IISc, Samsung open quantum lab to advance research in next-gen technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:22:16 UTC
20:22:16 KST

BENGALURU: The Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and Samsung Semiconductor India Research (SSIR) on Thursday inaugurated a Quantum Research Lab at IISc, aiming to strengthen India's research capabilities in quantum technologies and advanced semiconductors.Supported by Samsung's corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, the lab supports research into quantum devices, cryogenic electronics (electronics operating at extremely low temperatures), and materials that could help develop future technologies.Quantum technologies exploit the unusual behaviour of matter at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles. Unlike conventional computers, which use bits representing zero or one, quantum computers use quantum bits (qubits), which harness quantum effects to perform certain calculations in fundamentally different ways. Building reliable qubits and the systems to control them remains a major challenge.The new facility will focus on qubit characterisation, cryogenic electronics, quantum-device reliability, and single-photon sources and detectors. Single photons are individual particles of light that can carry quantum information, making them important for quantum communication and other applications.Researchers will also investigate two-dimensional (2D) materials, which are extremely thin and can have properties different from their bulk counterparts.
The work includes exploring 2D-material-based quantum devices under cryogenic conditions.A key objective of the collaboration is to make specialised research infrastructure accessible to students and researchers beyond IISc. Such equipment can be expensive to acquire and operate, limiting opportunities for institutions without dedicated facilities. The lab aims to address this gap through structured training and research exposure.The partnership will also connect quantum research with semiconductor skills development through the India Semiconductor Workforce Development Program (ISWDP), which addresses gaps in device physics, process development, modelling, simulation, characterisation and reliability. Selected modules will cover quantum materials and devices, cryogenic electronics and qubit technologies.Prof Mayank Shrivastava, chair of IISc's Department of Electronic Systems Engineering and lead for the two initiatives, said the aim was to build capabilities spanning semiconductor education and advanced research. He said the workforce programme was giving thousands of learners practical exposure to semiconductor workflows, while the new lab was advancing research into 2D-material-based quantum devices, including qubits and single-photon detectors.
Samsung Semiconductor India Research managing director Rajesh Krishnan said semiconductors and quantum were poised to be the next wave of innovation, making talent critical to India's technology ambitions, and industry-academia collaboration could create lasting impact through infrastructure, education and access.IISc director Prof Govindan Rangarajan said Samsung's support had enabled IISc to strengthen frontier quantum research and semiconductor workforce development, complementing its larger role in advancing national capabilities in quantum computing and next-generation semiconductor technologies.The initiative comes as India seeks to expand domestic expertise in semiconductors and quantum technologies. By combining specialised facilities with wider access to training, the collaboration aims to strengthen research while developing talent for these emerging fields.

As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Switzerland plans tougher social media rules to protect minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:21:50 UTC
20:21:50 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Switzerland plans to introduce stricter rules for major communication platforms and search engines to strengthen the protection of minors online, the Federal Council said Wednesday.
Under the proposed legislation, major platforms and search engines, including those powered by artificial intelligence, would be required to assess the risks their services pose to minors and take measures to mitigate them.
Providers would also be prohibited from displaying advertisements to minors based on profiling, which involves analyzing users’ online behavior and personal characteristics.
The Federal Council said the draft legislation had received broad support during the consultation, including from a majority of political parties represented in the Federal Assembly, cantons and national associations.
The proposed bill aims to strengthen users’ rights and increase transparency among major communication platforms and search engines, as “people increasingly rely on” them to access information.
It would also require communication platform providers to establish procedures allowing users to easily report content they suspect is illegal.
The legislation would apply to very large communication platforms and search engines, while smaller services would remain outside its scope.
The Federal Council also said it would consider whether additional measures to protect minors should be included in the legislation.

The selling pressure in global markets intensified after the US monthly inflation rose within expectations by 0.6%, while the annual inflation accelerated above estimates by 3.7%.
While the US inflation hit a five-month high month-on-month, the annual inflation reached its highest in four months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Wednesday.
These developments fueled the US Federal Reserve’s hawkish expectations.
At the same time, gas prices jumped 9.1% over the month, making up more than half of the overall monthly increase of consumer inflation.
The US’ core consumer price index (CPI), excluding energy and food prices, rose 0.3% month-on-month and 2.6% on an annual basis, above estimates.
Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin said the US CPI figures exceeded his expectations and that the producer price index (PPI) to be released on Thursday will help assess the inflation outlook, while refusing to speculate on the Fed’s policy roadmap for this month.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said the September CPI was “discouraging,” while the service inflation was also causing concerns, noting that it remains unclear how the Fed will assess the current situation, faced with a strong economy but high inflation.
Meanwhile, the Fed’s Beige Book showed that price pressures remained and intensified in some regions of the US.
Markets expect the Fed to cut rates this month with a 73% probability, up from 22%, given the recent developments.
Tech stocks tumbled with growing hawkish expectations amid accelerating inflation, coupled with concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) investment profitability, while rising oil prices due to the developments in the Middle East fueled concerns that central banks may need to be tighter on monetary policy.
The US 10-Year Treasury bond yield dropped nine basis points to 5.11%, and the US dollar depreciated 0.2% to 102.1.
December-delivery Brent crude oil declined 1.7% to $104.3 a barrel following reports that US President Donald Trump is considering easing sanctions on ships transporting oil and petroleum products from sanctioned countries like Russia, Iran, and Venezuela.
Gold climbed 1% to $4,145 per ounce as bond yields and the US dollar fell, alongside continued central bank purchases.
At the same time, the global oil demand is expected to fall by 2.5 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter compared to the same period last year, and by an average of 2.6 million barrels per day for the entire 2026, according to the International Energy Agency’s September report.
Some Russian oil refineries were brought back online following repairs, while conditions at the plants improved in recent weeks, Russian deputy prime minister said.
US banks also continued releasing their third-quarter earnings.
Morgan Stanley’s profit and revenue came in better than expected, but its shares closed Wednesday down nearly 3%.
Bank of America saw its third-quarter profit fall 17% to $6.9 billion following a $1.2 billion fine, while its shares lost around 5% and its profit and revenue reports did not meet expectations.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.09%, the S&P 500 declined 1.11%, and the Nasdaq Composite was down 1.88% on Wednesday. American indexes started Thursday on a negative trend.
Meanwhile, European stock markets traded on a mostly positive trend as corporate earnings exceeded expectations.
Dutch semiconductor firm ASML’s shares rose 1.2% after it raised its forward-looking guidance with expectations that the strong AI demand would continue.
Defense firm Renk’s shares jumped 2.7% following a new order worth €130 million ($145.9 million) from tank-maker KNDS.
Chipmaker Infineon closed Wednesday down 1.7% amid an industry-wide selling pressure.
Attention turned to the meetings in Brussels, where EU leaders will address global economic imbalances on Thursday.
In light of these developments, Germany’s DAX 40 rose 0.15%, the UK’s FTSE 100 grew 0.7%, and France’s CAC 40 was up 0.58%, while Italy’s FTSE MIB 30 fell 0.61% on Wednesday. European indexes started Thursday on a negative trend.
Near Thursday’s close, Asian equity markets sharply declined due to a selling pressure on tech stocks.
SK Hynix shares lost 10.2%, Samsung Electronics dropped 8.6%, LG Innotek fell 9.2%, and Kioxia declined 11.3%.

Flydubai hijacking attempt exposes major gaps in Israel's aviation security, experts warn

A bomb scare aboard a Delta Air Lines flight at Ben-Gurion Airport on Tuesday morning prompted a security search that found no explosives, less than two weeks after an attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv exposed serious questions about Israel's aviation security arrangements.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Passengers were evacuated after the Delta flight arrived from New York, and the aircraft was moved to an isolated area for inspection. Authorities found no explosives, and preliminary assessments suggested the anonymous threat might have been a hoax.
The September 30 flydubai incident presented a different and potentially more dangerous threat: An airline employee allegedly attempted to turn the aircraft into a weapon.
According to prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates, a co-pilot aboard flydubai flight FZ1073 attacked the captain with an emergency axe and attempted to seize control of the aircraft. Investigators said he intended to crash the plane into the passenger terminal at Ben-Gurion Airport, causing mass casualties.
The aircraft plunged thousands of feet before the wounded captain, passengers, and other crew members managed to subdue the attacker. Two additional pilots aboard the flight helped bring the aircraft safely to an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Brig.-Gen. (res.) Dr. Mena Bacharach, an international aviation security expert and former senior aviation security official with Israel's Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), said the attack demonstrated the need for additional technological safeguards inside aircraft cockpits.
Bacharach proposed installing remotely activated, Wi-Fi-based cockpit cameras that would allow authorized personnel on the ground to observe what was happening during an emergency. The cameras would remain off during normal operations and activate only after a distress signal had been triggered, potentially allowing ground personnel to assess a crisis and coordinate a response.
Such a system would require careful consideration of operational reliability, secure communications, privacy, and protection against unauthorized access.
“A serious problem needs creative solutions, and there is need for a whole range of them,” aviation commentator Aharon Lapidot told The Media Line. “Any solution, especially the technological ones, brings with it a host of new challenges, such as privacy issues and vulnerability to cyberattacks.”
The suspect, identified as 29-year-old Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, had passed professional and security checks before joining flydubai in January. UAE investigators said he had developed extremist views years earlier and had deliberately pursued a career in aviation to carry out an attack inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States.
The disclosures have intensified scrutiny of how airlines assess their employees and whether existing safeguards adequately address threats originating inside the cockpit.
“In professional terms, this is an ‘insider threat,’ and it forces us to re-examine the fundamental beliefs that aviation security is built on,” Yossi Amrusi, a former senior officer in the Shin Bet security agency and a researcher at the Misgav Institute for National Security and Zionist Strategy, told The Media Line. “It highlights the importance of having additional protection mechanisms in case one of the crew members, not necessarily the pilot, turns out to be a threat.”
Security screening must include ground crews, non-pilot flight personnel
He said security screening must extend beyond pilots to include other flight personnel and ground crews responsible for maintaining and servicing aircraft.
“This is a major earthquake,” Lapidot told The Media Line. “It opens a whole new perspective and a wide range of possibilities for terrorists to carry out attacks.”
UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said on October 9 that the co-pilot's radicalization began in 2017 while he was studying in Australia. Investigators said he had consumed extremist material, adopted beliefs advocating violence, and made preparations for an attack.
The suspect had previously worked for Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc before joining flydubai. According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal, his employment history included concerns about extremist interests that had affected his prospects at those airlines. Flydubai reportedly did not consult his former employers about those concerns before hiring him.
The revelations have raised questions about whether airlines should be required to share more information about employees whose conduct or expressed beliefs have prompted security concerns.
“You can check a person’s history, his training and his professional abilities, but it is much harder to predict his future intentions,” Amrusi told The Media Line.
The incident recalls the March 2015 Germanwings disaster, when co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately flew a passenger aircraft into the French Alps, killing all 150 people aboard.
French investigators subsequently found that Lubitz had experienced serious mental health problems and had concealed information about his condition from his employer.
Although the Germanwings crash was not a terrorist attack, both incidents demonstrate how dangerous it can be when a person entrusted with operating an aircraft deliberately endangers those aboard.
“There are far more terrorists than people with suicidal tendencies who wish to commit suicide while killing other people,” said Lapidot, explaining why the flydubai incident is being viewed as a turning point in the aviation industry.
Bacharach said the flydubai incident exposed weaknesses in Israel's aviation security arrangements that had already been highlighted in a 2024 State Comptroller's report.
The report called for a comprehensive examination of civil aviation security, including flights departing Israel, Israeli aviation operations abroad, and foreign aircraft entering Israeli airspace. It recommended that the National Security Council work with relevant government and security agencies to reassess responsibilities, oversight, and the allocation of resources.
Following the report, the security cabinet ordered an interagency review of security arrangements for international commercial flights to Israel. The National Security Council was tasked with coordinating the work of the Transportation Ministry, Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet, Mossad, and Finance Ministry.
According to subsequent Israeli media reporting, disagreements emerged over which agency should bear responsibility for security checks on foreign airlines and whether the Transportation Ministry had the personnel and resources to carry out the task.
The ministry ultimately retained responsibility, but reporting following the flydubai attack indicated that important screening requirements had not been consistently enforced.
Bacharach said the attempted attack illustrated the need to translate security recommendations into practical safeguards.
“Israel spends billions of dollars on security; it shouldn’t be left to the hands of a brave pilot, courageous civilians and a miracle to thwart attacks,” said Bacharach. “Someone didn’t do their job and fell asleep while on guard.”
Omani co-pilot allowed on flight to Israel despite lack of diplomatic relations
One of the most immediate questions concerned how the Omani co-pilot was allowed to operate a flight to Israel.
Oman does not maintain formal diplomatic relations with Israel. Israeli security regulations restrict the participation of crew members holding citizenship in certain countries on flights to Israel, including countries without diplomatic relations.
According to an internal security directive reported by Israeli media, foreign airlines were responsible for checking crew members against a list of restricted nationalities. However, the Transportation Ministry had not consistently enforced those requirements or verified crew lists.
Following the attempted hijacking, the ministry tightened restrictions on foreign airline crews, barring people holding citizenship in countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel from operating or traveling aboard Israel-bound flights, according to Channel 12.
The change has already affected airline operations.
Israeli media reported that an Ethiopian Airlines cargo flight traveling from Addis Ababa to Tel Aviv was forced to turn back overnight Sunday after Israeli authorities discovered an Indonesian national among the crew.
Indonesia has no diplomatic relations with Israel. According to reports by Channel 12 and The Jerusalem Post, the crew member was a pilot.
Channel 13 reported that the crew list was transmitted to Israeli authorities only after the aircraft departed Ethiopia. The plane subsequently resumed its journey after the crew member was replaced.
The incident illustrated the operational difficulties of enforcing restrictions when authorities do not receive and check information about flight crews before departure.
But Bacharach warned against treating nationality as a sufficient measure of risk.
“The problem is not only pilots from hostile countries,” Bacharach told The Media Line. “With the massive migration waves into Europe in recent years, even a pilot from a country that has relations with Israeli could undergo radicalization.”
Israel has also established a legal framework to collect and analyze passenger and crew information to help identify potential security threats.
A 2023 law provided for the establishment of the National Center for Passenger Data Analysis within the Israel Tax Authority. The legislation authorizes the creation of a database containing passenger and crew information and specifies how authorized agencies may access and use that information.
The legal framework is intended to support aviation security, counterterrorism, border control, and other authorized activities. However, the current operational status of the center, and whether it played any role in screening the flydubai crew, has not been established.
The attempted attack has raised broader questions about whether existing information systems are adequately integrated with airline screening procedures and whether relevant intelligence reaches officials responsible for approving foreign flight crews.
“This isn’t just an Israeli problem,” Amrusi said. “An ‘insider threat’ is relevant to all airlines. A person’s nationality isn’t necessarily the main motivator once someone has decided to use their position in order to target the plane.”
Aviation security has changed significantly since the September 11 attacks, with tighter passenger screening, reinforced cockpit doors, and stricter access controls.
Those measures were largely designed to prevent unauthorized individuals from bringing weapons aboard or gaining control of an aircraft.
The flydubai incident demonstrates the different challenges posed by an authorized crew member who already has access to the cockpit and the aircraft's controls.
“Airlines have to conduct much more thorough and frequent background checks and psychological evaluations,” Lapidot said. “Peer reviews must also be more frequent.”
Such measures could help identify concerning behavior, changes in circumstances, or information unavailable during initial hiring.
Expanded screening would require clearer guidelines on information sharing
But expanded screening raises questions about privacy, employment rights, the reliability of intelligence, and the possibility of unjustified suspicion based on nationality or personal beliefs.
Airlines also operate across numerous jurisdictions, each with different legal requirements governing background checks, professional licensing, and the sharing of security information.
Establishing a coordinated approach would require clearer rules governing what information should be exchanged, who may access it, and what action should follow when a potential warning sign is identified.
Lapidot warned that additional security requirements would also carry financial consequences.
“All of this is going to raise prices for the consumers,” Lapidot added.
Amrusi said screening improvements alone would be insufficient because no system can reliably predict every person's future behavior.
“We need to be honest though - there is no test that can predict with certainty the malicious intentions of a person,” Amrusi said. “Therefore, we need a system that can handle the situation once a person has managed to evade the testing.”
That approach would place greater emphasis on safeguards capable of limiting the damage if an authorized crew member attempts to seize control of an aircraft.
Flydubai suspects Tel Aviv flights, Miri Regev declines resumption of service
The flydubai incident has already produced operational consequences. The airline suspended its Tel Aviv flights following the attack, and Transportation Minister Miri Regev subsequently declined its request to resume service pending further scrutiny of its security procedures.
According to published reports, flydubai has conducted an internal investigation, dismissed several employees, and sought discussions with Israeli authorities about measures needed to restore service.
The case has renewed pressure on governments and airlines to reconsider how they identify potential insider threats and how aircraft can be protected when prevention fails.
Any new safeguards will have to balance security requirements with the realities of international aviation. Yet the questions raised by the attack extend beyond screening technology or the nationality of individual crew members to the effectiveness of coordination among airlines, regulators, and intelligence agencies.
For the passengers aboard flight FZ1073, the existing defenses were insufficient to prevent a violent cockpit attack. Their survival ultimately depended on the wounded captain, other pilots, and passengers who intervened before the aircraft could be brought down.
