October 7 families to hold mass rally demanding state inquiry three days before Israeli elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:16:42 UTC
20:16:42 KST

Just three days before the Knesset elections, the October Council will protest at Hostage Square at 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 24, it announced on the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre.
The rally is “intended to place the demand of the October 7 families – for a full investigation into the failure, the determination of responsibility, and the drawing of lessons – at the center of the public agenda,” the October Council said in a statement.
The rally will be led by bereaved families, former hostages and their families, and residents of the Gaza Envelope, as well as citizens who have been advocating alongside the council for more than two years to demand the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7.
The rally will be attended by the leaders of the political parties who have pledged to establish a state commission of inquiry. Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot; B’Yachad co-leaders Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid; Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman; and Democrats leader Yair Golan are reportedly expected to attend.
The council has marked it as the “last major public event” before the elections.
Hostage families demand establishment of a state commission of inquiry, backed by party leaders
The council is composed of more than 1,500 bereaved families, former hostages, and survivors of the massacre and previously accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s circle of attempting to erase the memory of the October 7 attack.
The council has repeatedly called for the establishment of a state commission of inquiry to investigate the October 7 attack, reportedly asserting that “those who deny its significance should not be allowed to bury the truth”.
The state commission of inquiry has the capacity to conduct comprehensive investigations and make recommendations that are both personal and systemic.
Despite Netanyahu’s repeated pledges that those responsible, himself included, would be held to account, Israel has yet to establish a commission of inquiry into the intelligence, military, and political failures surrounding October 7.
Legislation proposing a coalition-backed, politically appointed commission of inquiry passed its first reading in the Knesset in July 2026. The bill passed with 59 votes in favor, with the opposition boycotting the vote and arguing that the legislation was an attempt to block a genuine investigation by a state commission.
The bill did not complete its final readings before the Knesset dissolved. However, the coalition brought it to a first reading so it could be carried over under the continuity law and resume in the next Knesset.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

EU's Kallas says pressuring Ukraine to surrender is wrong approach to ending war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:16:14 UTC
20:16:14 KST

Melike Pala
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Thursday said pressuring Ukraine to surrender is not the right approach to ending the war with Russia, stressing that pressure should instead be directed at Moscow.
Speaking ahead of a European Council summit in Brussels, Kallas underlined the EU's commitment to supporting Kyiv, arguing that pressure should be directed at Russia rather than Ukraine to end the war.
Asked about the new US agreement with Russia greenlighting diesel fuel sales by Moscow, Kallas said: "We definitely have a different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender. "
"Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that's why Europe is standing by Ukraine," she said.
Kallas said the EU remains committed to maintaining pressure on Russia through sanctions, noting that the bloc is working on its 22nd sanctions package.
She also stressed that decisions concerning frozen Russian assets and the possible lifting of sanctions rests with European countries.
Turning to the broader agenda of the European Council summit, she said EU leaders would discuss competitiveness, energy, economic imbalances, enlargement, and developments in the Middle East.
On the Middle East, Kallas reiterated the EU's role as a security provider in the region and called on member states to deploy additional ships to Operation Aspides, the bloc's naval mission in the Red Sea, to strengthen the escort for commercial vessels through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea.
Kallas also said EU foreign ministers had decided to open up a new mission for Lebanon, while questions remain about security arrangements in southern Lebanon following the end of the mandate for the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL).
On EU enlargement, the bloc’s foreign policy chief warned against bilateralizing the process, arguing that European countries need to work together to strengthen the continent, saying that doing so is “really important.”

Chios airport to close from 15 November to 15 March amid strong local opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:15:48 UTC
20:15:48 KST

Four-month suspension of runway operations at Chios State Airport "Homer" aims to complete works by 28 February 2027 and boost flight safety.
The State Airport of Chios "Homer" will temporarily suspend operations from the evening of Sunday 15 November 2026 until 15 March 2027, as part of works to extend and upgrade the take-off and landing runway, according to an announcement by the Hellenic Civil Aviation Authority (HCAA).
The Authority considers the suspension necessary for the safe execution of the works, which include extending the runway to the north and an overall improvement of the airport's operational infrastructure.
As the HCAA points out, the planning takes into account the particularities of an airport with a limited runway length, the winter weather conditions and the need to ensure smooth air links to the island during the 2027 tourist season.
Shorter timetable for the works
Under the updated schedule, the works in the second and third phase will be completed in four months, instead of the five months foreseen in the original approved timetable.
At the same time, the contractor has pledged to make every effort to speed up the works, with the aim of completing them by 28 February 2027. The HCAA notes that its goal is to limit the runway closure to the shortest possible period.
For the duration of the shutdown, a relevant NOTAM has already been issued so that all parties concerned are informed and can adjust their planning in good time.
What applies to emergency flights
During the works, emergency flights will be able to operate with helicopters, landing and taking off directly to and from the airport apron.
This provision covers, among others, air ambulance transfers, search and rescue missions, firefighting operations, humanitarian and state missions, as well as other flights of national character.
It is noted that at this stage the airport remains operationally available, as the works are still in their first phase. Flights are being served by turboprop aircraft with a limited number of passengers, due to the temporary reduction in the available runway length.
1,799m-long runway once the works are completed
The upgrade provides for the extension of the runway to the north, bringing its total length to 1,799 metres.
The aim is to further enhance operational safety and to enable the airport to serve larger types of aircraft, a development expected to strengthen Chios's air connections and bring benefits both to passengers and to the local economy.
The HCAA calls on passengers, airlines and all stakeholders to take the planned suspension of operations into account when arranging their travel between 15 November 2026 and 15 March 2027.
Reactions from the local community – protests and request for a meeting with the minister
Local organisations on Chios are warning of protest action, including the possibility of shutting down shops to keep the airport open over the holidays, reacting to the plan for an earlier suspension of the island's airport operations.
At the same time, they are requesting a meeting with the Minister of Infrastructure and Transport in order to clarify the timetable for the works and avoid last-minute changes.
Representatives of local bodies express their strong opposition to the prospect of the airport closing on 15 November instead of 15 January, as they say was initially agreed. They describe such a development as a blow to the economic and social life of Chios and call for the original schedule to be respected.
The president of the Chios Chamber of Commerce, Pantelis Legatos, warned of the impact that the interruption of air links will have, especially during the festive period, when many residents have already planned journeys, family visits and medical appointments.
He stressed that the geographical position of Chios, about five nautical miles from the Turkish coast, makes the air link with Athens particularly important for residents' access to health services, as well as for their personal and social needs.
Doubts over completion of the works
Reservations about the timetable were also voiced by the regional governor of the North Aegean, Kostas Moutzouris, who took part via teleconference from Mytilene. He raised questions as to whether the airport will be ready to resume operations before Easter 2027.
At the same time, he underlined the need for a substantive upgrade of the airport's infrastructure, noting that he will take part in the decision-making procedures on the issue.
'No decision without the local community'
The mayor of Chios, Giannis Malafis, stressed the need to maintain the island's air connection during the major festive periods.
The mayor asked for the airport to remain in operation at Christmas, New Year and Easter, while also insisting that any decision on the future of the project should be taken in consultation with local bodies and Chios society.
The timetable for the works remains at the heart of the reactions, with the island's representatives seeking clear answers on the duration of the shutdown and its impact on residents' daily lives and on the local economy.

Poland signs agreement on planned second nuclear plant
Unknown

2026-10-15
11:15:48 UTC

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Poland’s energy ministry has signed an agreement with two state-owned companies, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) and Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE), setting out responsibilities for preparing for the construction of Poland’s planned second nuclear power plant.
“This is an investment in our security, sovereignty and economic development,” declared energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Having our own stable energy sources strengthens Poland’s resilience to crises and reduces dependence on external suppliers.”
❗️ @ME_GOV_PL, @PEJ_PL i @Grupa_PGE podpisały dziś porozumienie określające zasady współpracy przy przygotowaniu budowy drugiej polskiej elektrowni jądrowej 🇵🇱
Polska jest 20. gospodarką świata, ale nasze ambicje sięgają wyżej. Nie będzie silnej, niezależnej gospodarki bez… pic.twitter.com/eQ7zWFEolh
— Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) October 13, 2026
Under the agreement, PEJ, which is also responsible for developing a first nuclear project that is already underway on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, will act as the investor and coordinate the project.
PGE, the country’s largest power producer, will prepare preliminary feasibility studies and analyse potential locations for the plant.
However, a decision on selecting an international partner for the project is not expected to be made until next year. The potential candidates include US company Westinghouse, which is involved in the first nuclear power plant, France’s EDF, and Canada’s AtkinsRéalis.
The second plant was initially envisaged as a joint project with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a South Korean company, under a letter of intent signed in 2022 under Poland’s former government. However, the partnership was never formalised and fell through last year.
Once the new partner has been selected, it will work with PGE to analyse potential sites. The current preferred locations are Bełchatów – home to the largest coal-fired power station in Europe, owned by PGE – and Konin, both in central Poland, because of their existing energy infrastructure and experience in electricity generation.
According to the Polish government’s nuclear strategy – which was last month updated for the first time since 2020 – construction of the second plant is scheduled to begin in 2032, with its first reactor potentially entering service in 2040. That would be one year behind the previously planned schedule.
The government has updated Poland's nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new plan confirming that the first nuclear plant will launch three years later than previously planned, in 2036, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule https://t.co/vgtuSXLDjZ
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 3, 2026
Meanwhile, Poland plans to begin construction of its first nuclear power station in 2028, with the plant beginning operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Together, the two plants are expected to have a combined capacity of up to 9 gigawatts.
The move is part of Poland’s transition away from coal – which still generates around half of electricity, by far the highest proportion in the European Union – and towards cleaner sources of energy, particularly nuclear and renewables.
Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).

Company managing Narva border queue asks city for support after traffic dries up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:15:00 UTC
20:15:00 KST

Company managing Narva border queue asks city for support after traffic dries up
Cross-border vehicle traffic has come to a standstill and the city-owned company is struggling to make ends meet. City officials have not ruled out suspending the company's operations.
Transservis-N, the company that has managed the border crossing queue in Narva, has been struggling financially for two years. In better times, when thousands of vehicles crossed the border, the company paid dividends to the city of Narva. Now it is asking its owner for financial support to stay afloat — €50,000 this year and twice that amount next year. The city of Narva has yet to decide what to do with the company.
"If we shut it down, it will be very difficult to get it up and running again. The buildings will deteriorate and what would we do with the parking lot? We are still finding some use for it today. Cars from Latvia, Lithuania and Finland are parked at the Transservis-N lot, belonging to tourists who cross the border on foot. That brings in some revenue. But the number of Finnish tourists and people crossing the border here in general is steadily declining. We will start discussing this. We may indeed have to make a difficult decision," Narva Mayor Jaan Toots said.
The mayor nevertheless hopes that the border will reopen to vehicle traffic and that the company will not have to close.
Narva's opposition believes there is no point in holding out false hope as border traffic is only likely to decline further during the war, rather than increase. City officials must take this into account. Keeping the company operating solely to provide parking makes little sense.
"These are not even cars belonging to Narva residents and this is certainly not an essential service for us. I think it would make sense to temporarily shut down the company and reestablish it if the border does reopen for some reason. But that can only happen after the war ends," Narva City Council member Katri Raik said.
Narva city officials will decide the fate of Transservis-N as they prepare next year's budget. Vehicle traffic across the border in Narva was suspended in early 2024 when Russia began rebuilding the vehicle terminal at the Ivangorod border crossing. The work is reportedly scheduled to be completed this December.

Another Starlink facility hit by blaze in EU (VIDEO)
A blaze has occurred at a Starlink satellite internet service facility near Bulgaria’s capital Sofia, Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev has said.
The incident follows a fire at a SpaceX station in Poland, which serviced the Ukrainian military, in late September. Ukraine has relied heavily on Starlink during the conflict with Russia for battlefield communications and controlling drones.
Earlier this week, an MP for the opposition Democratic Bulgaria coalition, Ivaylo Mirchev, claimed that masked men had deliberately set a Starlink facility outside Sophia on fire, destroying 11 out of the 17 antennas at the site. He also published a video purporting to have captured the incident.

Radev confirmed that the blaze had happened when he appeared before the Bulgarian parliament on Wednesday, but declined to say if it was a result of an arson attack.
“An investigation is underway. Just a little more patience, and there will be a result,” the prime minister said, urging other government officials against disclosing any details of the probe until it’s concluded. “If the specific findings are revealed, we will not achieve the outcome we are aiming for,” he added.
Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told lawmakers that additional measures to protect Starlink stations and similar facilities across the country will be implemented. However, he stressed that they are private sites and that the primary responsibility for their security lies with their owners.
However, Democratic Bulgaria MP Bozhidar Bozhanov wasted no time waiting for the results of the investigation of the blaze to lash out at Moscow. “Why are you afraid to name Russia? Why don’t you act like Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” he asked Radev.
The prime minister responded by saying that Bozhanov apparently has “a crystal ball and therefore knows who the perpetrator is.”
Tusk previously called the fire at Wola Krobowska outside Warsaw last month “another act of hybrid warfare.” Polish special services coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak said this week that there was “no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” but provided no proof to the accusations. Two Turkish nationals have been arrested in Germany in connection with the incident.
Russia has consistently rejected claims of it engaging in any sabotage activities in Europe. Russian President Vladimir Putin and various officials have said that the so-called “Russian threat” is only being promoted by Western politicians to scare their public, distract people from the mounting problems in their own countries and justify growing military spending.
On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders complained that Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working when drones flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk denied giving any instructions to restrict Kiev’s access to the service, saying that doing so is the prerogative of the American military and US President Donald Trump personally.
The problems occurred as Trump is working to increase pressure on Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for surging global energy prices.
Last month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that allowing Starlink to be used to facilitate Ukrainian strikes deep into Russian territory would be “a very harmful, potentially dangerous and misconceived step.” Moscow has all the means to respond to such actions, he warned.

Voting in Israeli elections begins at diplomatic missions abroad

Ikrame Imane Kouachi
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Voting in Israel’s general elections began Thursday at the country’s diplomatic missions abroad, nearly two weeks ahead of the nationwide vote scheduled for Oct. 27.
The Times of Israel reported that the first votes in Israel’s 2026 elections were cast overnight as polling began at Israeli diplomatic missions around the world.
It said voting for diplomatic mission employees abroad and their family members would last about 30 hours, with each embassy opening its polling station during daytime hours according to the local time of its host country.
According to the daily, 101 polling stations will operate across 99 diplomatic missions, allowing approximately 4,800 eligible voters to cast their ballots.
It noted that overseas voting is restricted to diplomatic envoys, diplomatic staff and their family members.
The Israeli Embassy in Wellington, New Zealand, was the first mission to open for voting, with polling beginning at 9 am local time, corresponding to 11 pm (2000GMT) Wednesday in Israel.
Staff at the Israeli Embassy in Fiji followed, with its polling station opening an hour after voting began in New Zealand.
The last missions scheduled to hold voting are the consulates in San Francisco and Los Angeles in the US, where polling will close at 8 pm local time, corresponding to 6 am (0300GMT) Friday in Israel.
After voting concludes, the ballots will be flown to Israel and then sent to the Knesset, the parliament, for counting, according to the daily.
Opinion polls show that neither the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor the Jewish opposition bloc can independently reach the 61 seats, out of 120, required to form a government.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022, leading a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu also faces charges of corruption, bribery and breach of trust in three cases.
In addition to the domestic corruption trial, Netanyahu has been wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) since 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in the Gaza Strip, where more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s genocidal war since October 2023.

No Kings protest across the US aims to get voters to the polls for midterms
The upcoming No Kings mass demonstrations this weekend aim to mobilise voter turn-out for the upcoming 3 November US midterm elections.
On Saturday 17 October, cities across the US will be holding demonstrations to get Americans to the polls ahead of the 2026 midterm elections–what many see as key to preserving the country's democracy.
"No Kings Vote Early is the next step in reclaiming our power after a year of mass mobilisations," reads a statement on the No Kings website.
"It's a day of non-partisan voter participation, being in community with each other, and making sure every eligible voter has a plan, knows their options and is ready to make their voice count," the statement continues.
The midterms will take place on 3 November. Early voting has already started in multiple states, and many advocates are urging for people to cast their ballots as soon as possible to ensure their vote is secured.
According to polls, Democrats are expected to bring in a blue wave by reclaiming the House and possibly the Senate. US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly accused the Democrats of rigging the elections, has said that he will be sending election monitors to polling sites. He has also suggested sending in the military to the polls, which many critics see as voter intimidation.
The last several months have seen internal debates among protest organisers over whether or not they should continue holding mass demonstrations or focus on voter turnout. This event is brings together both camps.
"Voting early means your vote is locked in and safe, days before anyone else can decide what happens next," reads the demonstration's website. "No matter what the laws look like where you live, preparation is universal."
To date, three No Kings protests have taken place across the US, each having its own theme. The first one, in June 2025, was to compete with Trump’s America 250 concert that was also a celebration of his birthday. The demonstrations were a response to the suggestion that Trump was ruling as a king.
Previous No Kings protests, which serve as an umbrella of multiple coalitions have seen record turnouts, with the last one in March seeing at least 8 million attending nationwide.
"A blue wave could be a result of this mobilisation. They seem to be funneling all of these themes into policy," David Frank, a professor of rhetoric and political communication at the University of Oregon, told The New Arab. "I think it's a wise move by the organisers."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) is campaigning for better public services, stronger community support, and safer streets.
Shen is challenging incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) in the Nov. 28 local elections. The legislator has made childcare, housing, transport, and services for older residents central to his campaign.
Liberty Times reported that Shen unveiled a five-part policy platform called "HEART" in August. The plan aims to improve public spaces, create opportunities, strengthen community support, and make daily life easier for residents.
Shen has proposed more housing for young people and families, additional green spaces, and improvements to aging apartment buildings. He also wants to expand services for older residents and make their homes more accessible, per PTS.
Shen plans to expand childcare support across Taipei's 12 districts. He wants to establish a single contact point where parents can seek advice and assistance for children up to age 18.
He has also proposed four hours of free temporary childcare each week for children under 6, per CNA. Shen said the service would give parents more time to rest and manage daily responsibilities.
On transport, Shen wants safer routes to schools, better bus services, and more bicycle lanes, per Rti. He has also proposed including shared electric scooters in Taiwan's TPASS public transport program.
Shen has also pledged to help young people develop skills and improve their financial security. His proposals include a youth development fund, artificial intelligence training, and support for overseas study and entrepreneurship, per Newtalk.
Shen grew up in Taipei and attended Taipei Municipal Jianguo High School before studying law at National Taiwan University. He later earned a master's degree from the University of Pennsylvania and a doctorate from the University of California, Irvine.
Before entering politics, Shen taught criminology at National Taipei University. He became known for his research into Chinese disinformation and its impact on Taiwan's democracy.
Shen founded Doublethink Lab, which studies disinformation, and helped establish Kuma Academy, which provides civilian emergency preparedness training. He was also involved in human rights advocacy and served as vice chair of the Taiwan Association for Human Rights.
Shen entered the Legislative Yuan in February 2024 as a DPP party-list legislator. He has served on the Foreign and National Defense Committee, focusing on national security and foreign affairs.
His involvement in civil defense has drawn criticism from political opponents. In June, questions arose over Kuma Academy's fundraising, while DPP Secretary-General Hsu Kuo-yung (徐國勇) rejected attempts to link the organization's finances to Shen personally.
The DPP formally nominated Shen for Taipei mayor in May, marking his first mayoral bid. At the nomination event, Shen said he would focus on meeting residents and listening to their concerns rather than following a fixed campaign strategy.

A deep dive into the global spy plane market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:09:50 UTC
21:09:50 KST

A deep dive into the global spy plane market
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
All over the globe – from the Mexican border to Syria to the Sahel – companies are renting out planes equipped with powerful sensors to armies and intelligence services for political missions. The market may be discreet, but it isn’t invisible.
Metrea, Berry Aviation and DEA Aviation aren’t your run-of-the-mill aviation companies. They don’t transport passengers or merchandise; their planes are equipped with powerful intelligence equipment like cameras and radar. These planes are used for "ISR", an acronym for "intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance". ISR missions are meant to detect, identify and then follow targets from the sky.
These days, there is a global market for ISR planes, a trend that began in the early 2000s. When the United States began operations in the Middle East after the attacks on September 11, the army needed to carry out surveillance in both remote and mountainous regions in Afghanistan and within Iraqi cities. Their needs for ISR planes surpassed their capabilities.
The US began calling on companies equipped to provide these services. This practice continues: today, governments employ private planes to patrol and gather intelligence across Africa, the Middle East and along sensitive border zones.
French company CAE Aviation
CAE Aviation is a French company known to be discreet. Registered in Luxembourg, the company has a training and maintenance centre at the aerodrome in Lapalisse, France. It is the leading French company in the field of ISR planes.
The French Ministry of the Armed Forces used a CAE Aviation plane with the registration number F-GYEE on December 7, 2025, when a coup threatened the government of Benin – which reportedly has close links to the French government. This plane was spotted flying over the Benin capital looking for the coup leaders.
Metrea: from Mexico to Africa
On the other side of the Atlantic, the giant aeronautical company Metrea also carries out ISR missions. Some of its planes routinely patrol the border between Mexico and the United States. One of its planes, registered under the number N339CA, can be seen flying in continuous circles characteristic of an ISR mission.
According to online analysts, Metrea planes are also present on the African continent. One plane reportedly landed on October 5, 2026, at the airport in N’Djamena, Chad, after flying through Malaga, Spain. According to the online analyst who runs the X account @fabsenbln, the company isn’t a new actor in the Sahel.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
The company isn’t just involved in the ISR sector. In July 2024, for instance, the company purchased two supply planes from the French government.
Beechcraft King Air: the ‘everything’ plane
For long surveillance flights, one plane surpasses the others: the Beechcraft King Air. This plane is to the skies as the pickup is to the desert. Discreet and capable of operating across a wide range, this easy-to-use plane is popular among private companies specialised in ISR.
The Beechcraft is modular and can easily be equipped with radar to detect convoys and troop movements. Communications antennas that work via satellite can also be installed, making it easier to contact operators on the ground.
The plane is also, importantly, equipped with what is known as an optronic pod, a system fitted with a powerful camera capable of monitoring the ground, both day and night. Some optronic pods can be used to identify a target with a laser for the benefit of guided missiles.
States aren’t the only ones using ISR planes from private fleets. The European agency Frontex relies on companies like CAE Aviation and DEA Aviation to monitor people trying to cross the Mediterranean.

====================================================================================================

EXPLAINER - Why higher oil prices cannot shield Gulf economies from Hormuz shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:03:41 UTC
20:03:41 KST

- Saudi Arabia, UAE also expected to shrink as production and export disruptions outweigh gains from higher prices
- IMF forecasts point to a strong rebound in 2027, but recovery depends on restored production and trade
Gulf economies are expected to shrink sharply this year as long-term disruptions to energy production and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz outweigh the benefits of higher oil and gas prices, according to the International Monetary Fund’s latest forecasts.
The October World Economic Outlook points to particularly severe declines in economies most exposed to interruptions in hydrocarbon output and transport, with Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain facing double-digit contractions.
The deterioration highlights a central feature of the regional shock: higher global energy prices offer limited protection when producers cannot maintain production or deliver exports to customers.
The damage also extends beyond hydrocarbons, as weaker trade, higher costs and uncertainty weigh on business activity and complicate efforts to diversify Gulf economies.
Smaller Gulf producers face steepest declines
The IMF projects Kuwait's economy will contract 16.7% in 2026, while Qatar is expected to shrink 15.6% and Bahrain 11.3%, according to published accounts of the October report.
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are also forecast to contract, although by smaller margins, reflecting differences in economic structure and exposure to disrupted export routes.
Saudi Arabia's economy is projected to shrink 3.3% this year, a sharp reversal from the 1.7% growth forecast in July. The change represents a five-percentage-point downgrade in just three months.
The IMF expects Saudi growth to rebound to 7.9% in 2027, compared with its previous projection of 5.5%, indicating that part of the activity lost this year could return as conditions improve.
The UAE is forecast to contract 3.9% in 2026 before expanding 7.7% next year. Outside the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council, Iraq faces a projected 16% contraction, underlining the broader exposure of regional energy exporters to the disruption.
These figures are projections for annual real economic output, rather than confirmed full-year outcomes, and remain sensitive to the course of the conflict and the restoration of trade.
Outlook deteriorates as disruption persists
The new forecasts mark a substantial deterioration from the IMF's spring assessment.
In April, the fund still projected 2% growth for the Gulf Cooperation Council as a whole in 2026. Its country forecasts included contractions of 8.6% for Qatar, 0.6% for Kuwait and 0.5% for Bahrain.
That earlier outlook assumed a relatively short-lived conflict, with trade resuming and production normalizing by the middle of the year.
The persistence of disruption has therefore undermined a central assumption behind the earlier projections, leaving economies exposed to a longer period of reduced output and impaired logistics.
The geographical differences are important. In its April regional briefing, the IMF highlighted that Oman faced a more limited downgrade because its access to the sea lies outside the Strait of Hormuz.
That distinction illustrates why the availability of alternative export routes can influence economic outcomes alongside the size of financial reserves or the level of global oil prices.
Higher prices cannot replace lost production
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned Gulf finance ministers and central bank governors on Oct. 1 that the regional economy was expected to contract as hydrocarbon production fell sharply and growth outside the sector slowed.
She identified the near closure of Hormuz, disruption in the Red Sea and damage to energy facilities as constraints on exports and production capacity.
Reduced trade, weaker business confidence and rising prices for essential goods were also restricting non-hydrocarbon activity, she said.
For energy producers, the distinction between prices and volumes is critical. A higher price per barrel can support receipts from the oil that is sold, but it does not restore barrels that cannot be produced or shipped.
Real GDP measures production after accounting for price changes. Consequently, an increase in export prices does not automatically prevent an economy from contracting when physical output falls.
This also helps explain why an energy shock can simultaneously raise import costs elsewhere and reduce economic activity in the countries supplying those commodities.
Strong rebound would not erase every loss
The IMF's projections envisage substantial recoveries in several of the hardest-hit economies next year as production, exports and logistics normalize.
Qatar is forecast to grow 18.8% in 2027, Kuwait 17.1% and Bahrain 13.9%. The broader Middle East and Central Asia region is projected to expand 6.3% after contracting 0.3% this year.
However, large percentage rebounds partly reflect the lower starting point created by this year's contractions.
Applying the projected annual changes illustrates the distinction. Kuwait's output would fall from an index of 100 in 2025 to 83.3 in 2026, then recover to approximately 97.5 in 2027. It would therefore remain about 2.5% below its 2025 level despite double-digit growth.
Qatar's projected contraction and rebound would bring output approximately back to its 2025 level. Neither calculation captures the additional production that might have occurred had the disruption never happened.
Financial buffers and logistics shape resilience
Georgieva said government measures and investment in energy and logistics infrastructure had helped contain the wider fallout, including through rerouting supplies and supporting firms and banks.
She nevertheless stressed that financial buffers cannot substitute for physical resilience to trade shocks.
The IMF has highlighted the potential for the GCC Railway and Saudi Landbridge projects to reduce losses from a Hormuz closure by improving alternative transport connections.
Its policy advice calls for temporary, targeted support where needed, while avoiding broad stimulus when the principal constraint is disrupted supply.
As conditions normalize, the fund recommends rebuilding financial buffers and maintaining investment in diversification and economic security.

Russia Keeps Attacking Ukraine’s Frontline but Has No Verified Gains to Show, ISW Says
Russian forces continued offensive operations across several sectors of the frontline on October 13 and 14 but failed to achieve confirmed territorial gains, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
In its October 14 assessment, ISW reported that Russian troops attempted to advance in the Kharkiv, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia regions, although Ukrainian forces prevented confirmed breakthroughs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In northern Kharkiv region, Russian troops continued offensive operations on October 13 and 14 without achieving verified advances. Meanwhile, Russian officials and military bloggers circulated claims that Ukrainian units had been encircled in the northeastern part of the region.
On October 13, Russia's Defense Ministry claimed on the Max social media platform that Russian forces were eliminating allegedly surrounded Ukrainian troops in Mykolaivka, Varvarivka, and Nefedivka, located east of Vovchansk.

Further south, Russian forces launched attacks northeast and southeast of Lyman on October 13 and 14, although ISW reported no confirmed territorial gains. Similar attempts were recorded east of Sloviansk, particularly near Kryva Luka, Mykolaivka, Piskunivka, and Kalenyky, where Russian troops continued offensive operations without making verified progress.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, Russian forces maintained offensive pressure in and around the city throughout October 13 and 14. However, ISW found no evidence of confirmed Russian advances in the area.
Meanwhile, in western Zaporizhzhia region, Russian sources reported continued offensive operations over the same period amid Ukrainian counterattacks. Despite these claims, ISW said it had not observed evidence of Russian territorial gains in this section of the frontline.
The latest assessment follows reports of Ukrainian territorial gains in the Sumy region, where Ukrainian forces recently advanced southeast of Yunakivka, northeast of the city of Sumy.
According to ISW's October 13 assessment, geolocated footage published on October 12 confirmed the Ukrainian advance, marking a verified change in frontline positions in the area.

====================================================================================================

Honeybees deemphasize potential ‘misinformation’ in their waggle dances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:01:38 UTC
20:01:38 KST

When a bee wants to tell its hive mates how to find a scrumptious field of flowers, it wiggles its rear end. A complicated combination of figure eight–like movements known as a waggle dance tells nearby bees what direction to fly in and how far to go. But what happens if a waggling bee is unsure of its directions?
A study published in Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology earlier this year shows that bees amplify their communication based on how certain they are that their information is true. It seems the more confident a bee is in what it’s conveying, the more emphatically it communicates with the hive, says study lead author Karmi Oxman, a behavioral ecologist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
“Confidence is sort of a human-y word, but it’s useful in this context,” Oxman says. Confidence reflects the communicator’s belief in a message’s relevance or reliability, “and the dance is a self-report of the situation in the field.” This extra information also prevents the bee from accidentally misleading the hive.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The experiment started with one bee flying to a specialized feeder. This first bee, also known as the focal bee, was always met with a sugar solution. The researchers then manipulated the scenario by changing what happened after the focal bee returned to the hive and gave directions to the feeder. In the “honest” scenario, the feeder remained full, and all the bees following the directions got a sugary treat. In the “liar” scenario, the feeder was found empty. And in the “unverified” scenario, all the bees were caught before they could return to the hive and report what happened.
When given the chance to communicate the feeder’s location to the hive again in a later experimental stage, the focal bee in the honest scenario tried harder to convince its fellows to visit the sugar source by performing more waggle dance circuits—suggesting the bee could assess the reliability of its own signal. Unverified and “liar” bees did not show that same increase; in fact, unverified bees decreased their recruitment efforts.
“For me, the big takeaway is that bees are not little robots,” says James C. Nieh, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, who was not involved in the study. “They’re getting information from their environment, and that [information] also includes how successful they are in communicating to their nest mates.”
Both Oxman and Nieh say they wonder what other types of communication beyond what we can see—such as chemical signals or vibrations—could be playing a role in waggle dances. Further research into how bees communicate can help with efforts to “maintain the world in a way that they can still thrive,” Nieh says.

The group warned of an escalation in the targeting of Palestinian children through practices including intimidation, arrest, torture, starvation, isolation and denial of health care.
It added that information on the number of children detained from Gaza since the start of the war remains incomplete, particularly amid the presence of thousands of missing people in the enclave, including children, and the continued practice of “enforced disappearance.”
The group said Israel’s administrative detention policy, under which Palestinian detainees are held without charge or a clear timeframe for release, leaves children facing an uncertain future and deprives them of family life and educational stability.
It also said Israeli courts contribute to the continuation of violations against children amid the absence of effective accountability.
Detention conditions
The Palestinian Prisoners Society cited the case of child Walid Khaled Ahmad, who “died in Megiddo Prison in March 2025, amid medical findings at the time indicating severe emaciation and signs of malnutrition and dehydration.”
The group raised questions about accountability for his death, noting that the investigation into the case had been closed.
It also highlighted the case of 15-year-old Mohammed Hamid, who it said developed scabies while detained in Ofer Prison, leading to a deterioration in his health and serious infections affecting vital organs.
Hamid underwent heart surgeries and was admitted to intensive care in critical condition before one of his legs was later amputated, the group said.
It added that Hamid has continued receiving treatment for about three months since Israeli authorities released him following the deterioration of his health, a move the group described as “an evasion of responsibility for his medical care.”
The group called for international action to secure the release of children held arbitrarily, end administrative detention and coercive interrogations, and stop torture, starvation and the denial of medical treatment.
It stressed the need to move beyond documentation and condemnation towards concrete measures that end the violations and bring impunity to an end, saying that “protecting Palestinian children requires firm international intervention to ensure respect for their rights, lives and dignity.”
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza in Israel’s genocidal war, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Israeli army raids and attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their property have also intensified in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since then.

====================================================================================================

Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:00:11 UTC
20:00:11 KST

Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal.
Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office.
The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates.
The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption.
A nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios.
After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.
“We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.”
Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why.
Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme.
Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote.
A free 99-year lease
On 6 February 2024, Dubravka Đukanović, a Serbian conservation professor in her 60s, arrived for a meeting at the presidency, a domed former royal palace. For three years, she had been the director of the country’s institute for the protection of cultural monuments.
The topic was the General Staff building, the former Yugoslav ministry of defence in central Belgrade. The building, an architectural gem seen as an emblem of resistance to the Nazis, was already cherished when Nato forces bombed it in 1999 during its campaign to force Milošević to withdraw from Kosovo, deepening its resonance.
Vučić himself had reaffirmed the General Staff building’s legally protected status in 2016. Now, the president said he wanted Đukanović to rescind it, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting. Some unspecified “foreign investor” was keen on the site.
Under Serbian law, stripping the General Staff building of its protected status was not in Đukanović’s gift. Her institute would have to commission an expert opinion, which would have to conclude that there were good reasons why protected status was no longer merited.
But the president wanted it done. At 6ft 6in and intolerant of dissent, Vučić can be intimidating. His tone towards Đukanović and another heritage official present was unpleasant, the sources said. He told them they were lazy and incompetent. The message was clear: do what I want or resign.
A plausible explanation for Vučić’s forceful intervention came the following month, when an agreement between the Serbian government and Kushner’s real estate company leaked.
Married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka, Kushner had been an influential White House aide during his father-in-law’s first term. Since Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election, Kushner had been concentrating on his investment fund.
By early 2024, Trump was storming to the Republican nomination and was favourite to win the coming election. If Trump took back the White House, Kushner would once more be one of the most influential people on the planet.
The leaked agreement showed the Serbian authorities had granted Kushner’s company a 99-year lease over the General Staff site, free of charge.
Kushner, whose spokesperson said he had been looking at the project since 2021, posted an image of the design on X, professing himself “excited”.
The news was not universally welcomed in Belgrade. “Serbia is not a buffet, and Vučić is not a waiter,” said Aleksandar Jovanović Ćuta, an environmental activist who revealed the agreement. “This is not his private property.”
Yet Vučić’s regime proceeded to sign a contract, dated 13 May 2024 and seen by the Guardian, undertaking that the “cultural heritage designation” of the site would be removed “to the satisfaction” of Kushner’s company.
Comply or resign
The week after the contract was signed, Đukanović was summoned to another meeting. The president was not there this time. Siniša Mali, his finance minister and right-hand man, took charge.
Mali urged Đukanović and Olivera Vučković, Belgrade’s top heritage official, to cancel the General Staff site’s protected status, according to the indictment’s summary of testimony the two women would later give prosecutors. It makes no reference to the earlier meeting with the president but indicates that the subject had previously been broached.
“Mali asked them if they had given it any thought,” the indictment says, “and if they would initiate the procedure to remove the building’s protected status.”
The women refused, “believing that the legal conditions for it were not met”. In that case, Mali told them, repeating his boss’s ultimatum from February, they should resign. They did.
In her resignation letter, which the Guardian has seen, Đukanović wrote that she could not agree “to inappropriate interventions that would permanently destroy all the values of the complex, which testifies to the highest achievements of contemporary Serbian architecture and is of incalculable importance for preserving enduring creative values, the education of future generations, and the strengthening of the cultural identity of the Serbian people”.
Approached by the Guardian, Đukanović and Vučković confirmed the accuracy of this account. Đukanović added: “I prefer not to make any statement on this matter while the court proceedings are ongoing.”
Little was heard of the General Staff plan for months. In November, Trump beat Kamala Harris to win re-election. Ten days later, Vučić’s government announced that the General Staff site had been stripped of its protected status.
Keeping it in the family
One of the first things Trump did upon regaining the presidency was to ditch the pledge he made in his first term that his family business would refrain from doing deals abroad while he was in office.
“The scale of corruption will be orders of magnitude greater than what we saw in the first Trump administration,” Kathleen Clark, a government ethics lawyer at Washington University School of Law, warned at the time. Trump had made it much easier, she said, to buy his favour.
The family business remained officially under the control of his two oldest sons, Don Jr and Eric. In January 2025, four days after their father’s inauguration, Eric spoke about some new projects. The Trumps and the Kushners, New York real estate families united by marriage, had decided to embark on their first venture together: Kushner’s Belgrade hotel and tower would bear the Trump name.
“It’s going to be fun to bring the family together,” Eric told the New York Times. “Serbia is one of the fastest-growing countries in Europe, and we’re incredibly honoured to be there.” Kushner, who had travelled to Belgrade for what Vučić called an “inspiring” meeting with the Serbian leader, added: “Our research showed that the Trump brand would be the best for this market.”
That brand has enjoyed a surge in demand around the world during Trump’s second term, accompanied by allegations that it comes with a quid pro quo.
In Vietnam, Eric was showered with confetti at the groundbreaking ceremony for a £1.5bn golf resort, the permits for which were granted with unusual speed. Then Trump halved Vietnam’s tariffs. The Saudis poured money into Kushner’s fund, and plans emerged for a Trump plaza in Jeddah. Then Trump agreed to sell the kingdom new US fighter jets. A cryptocurrency baron’s company and senior Emiratis cut a lucrative transaction with World Liberty Financial, the digital currency venture Don Jr and Eric founded. Trump gave the crypto baron a pardon and the Emiratis access to restricted US chips.
Asked about such deals last year, Kushner, now a presidential envoy to Russia, Israel and elsewhere, said: “What people call conflicts of interests … I call experience and trusted relationships that we have throughout the world.”
Those who strike up “trusted relationships” with the Trumps, even if there is not an obvious quid pro quo, gain something less tangible but maybe still more valuable: the aura of friendship with a president who is happy to wield his superpower to make or break smaller nations and their leaders.
Vučić has plenty in common with Trump. Both are friendly with Vladimir Putin and contemptuous of the EU – in Vučić’s case, despite his country having applied to join. A shared disdain for Nato may help explain why the one part of the General Staff building’s heritage that the redevelopment pledged to retain was a memorial to the alliance’s “aggression” against Serbia.
And there is a lot that Vučić could use US help with, not least the fate of Kosovo, which he says is still part of Serbia.
Not long after his father returned to office, Don Jr landed in Belgrade. Vučić said that during their meeting he “emphasised the importance of the economic and political relations between Serbia and the USA and stressed the importance of strategic cooperation between the two countries and joint projects in the years to come”. When Don Jr returned the following month, Vučić fed him a choice sucking-pig.
For Vučić, the support of the first family was timely. Days before his regime stripped the General Staff site of its protection, the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, triggered rolling protests against graft. The student organisers’ slogan has become “Serbia or mafia”.
Don Jr’s visit came on the eve of the biggest demonstration in Serbia’s history. He invited Vučić on to his podcast, Triggered, and declared that the Serb ruler’s opponents were “weaponising” the Novi Sad disaster, just as Trump’s had done with the Capitol riots after his 2020 election defeat.
But the protesters maintained their momentum, and began to rally against the Trump tower. In May 2025, Vučić went to the US, hoping to visit Trump at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida members’ club. He got to see Rudy Giuliani, Trump’s disgraced lawyer, but not the president. State media reported this was because Vučić fell ill.
No sooner was Vučić home than police arrested Goran Vasić, the man who had been installed as head of the heritage institute to replace Dubravka Đukanović following her resignation. To achieve the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protected status, prosecutors said, Vasic had forged a supportive expert opinion.
More arrests followed. In December 2025, Vučić’s culture minister was indicted for abuse of office for his alleged part in the General Staff scheme. Within days, Kushner’s company announced the project was off.
Coup or cover-up?
Vučić’s threat of reprisals was not idle.
His allies attacked Đukanović, claiming that she had tried to profit personally from her time as a heritage official. Her deputy, who received a visit from the state security service after she went on television to denounce the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protection, has been accused of unrelated misconduct. The Serbian conservators’ industry body said this had “the obvious aim of discrediting her”. Both are expected to give evidence in the criminal proceedings.
For the specialist unit of organised-crime prosecutors who brought the charges, this is a watershed case. Never before has a serving Serbian minister been indicted.
Vučić accuses the prosecutors of staging a coup. Others, though, fear they are pulling their punches. That concern increased when Nikola Selaković, the indicted culture minister, used a court appearance in April to reveal that, while police were raiding his ministry, he was in his office sipping plum brandy and smoking cigarettes with Mladen Nenadić, the head of the organised-crime prosecutors’ unit. The unit’s spokesperson said there was “no discussion regarding the course of the case”.
“In everything that happened regarding potential investments, I saw a chance for our country and citizens,” said Selaković, who faces three years in prison if convicted.
Vučić has not been charged. Neither has his lieutenant, Mali. Both deny wrongdoing.
The indictment refers to evidence from witnesses who were present at the Vučić meeting in February 2024 but does not mention it, raising questions about the apparent decision to omit what would appear to be a key part of the narrative.
The spokesperson for the organised crime prosecutors’ unit said that it had evidence regarding Vučić’s February 2024 meeting with the heritage officials. Beyond those already indicted, prosecutors were “conducting pretrial proceedings in this case to determine potential criminal liability of other persons as well”, the spokesperson added.
Vučić has stepped down and cannot seek another term but is expected to retain his control over the regime if he is elected prime minister on 25 October. In one of his last acts as president, he issued 49 pardons. Some of the recipients have not been identified and it is not clear whether they include defendants in the General Staff case.
The White House referred questions to the Trumps’ company. Its representative said: “The Trump Organization has no plans to develop any project in Belgrade, was never, at any point, involved in any discussions or negotiations to acquire any site in Belgrade and denies any involvement in or knowledge of the alleged claims.”
Kushner’s spokesperson said: “The suggestion that Jared Kushner pursued the Belgrade project as part of any political arrangement or ‘pay to play’ scheme is categorically false.” Rather, it was “an opportunity to transform a site associated with a painful chapter in Serbia’s history into a symbol of healing and reconciliation, while bringing substantial private investment, jobs and economic opportunity to Belgrade”.
The spokesperson added: “Jared had no involvement in the Serbian government’s internal processes concerning the site’s protected status.”
For all Vučić’s difficulties, the tale of the Trump Tower Belgrade does not appear to have put others off doing business with the first family. Trump retains stakes in dozens of his companies, even if his sons nominally run them. In July, he released his financial disclosure for his first year back at the White House. It showed he had made $2bn.

Kids’ Content Is Deeply Broken. A New Platform Wants to Fix It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.
Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.
Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads, doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.
The company’s cofounder and chief product officer Tanyella Leta tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”
Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”
Launching today, Maka’s programming slate is a mix of licensed content from global studios and independent creators. It features 25 shows in its curated catalog, including Franklin, The Wiggles, Pocoyo, Vida the Vet and Sesame Street. The platform runs on a subscription service, with a $15 monthly plan and a $107 annual plan.
It was during the Covid pandemic that Sheinman and Leta became obsessed with thinking about how to redesign kids' media. The solution? Every episode streamed on Maka is evaluated by child development experts through Imprint, a framework created with researchers at the Yale Child Study Center. The evaluation process, which examines everything from scene cuts to how fast-paced content is, maps adolescent development across seven core domains. It looks for things like emotional regulation, kindness, how child-caregiver relationships are modeled in a story, and how a story might support critical thinking or language development.
AI-generated content has only added a new wrinkle to kids’ entertainment: videos are incoherent, have no plot, or contain outright misinformation, but are packaged to look like learning. Some of it, as WIRED has previously reported, is disturbingly sexualized, featuring gore and other fetishes.
Michael Robb, director of research at the media literacy nonprofit Common Sense Media, says that on a platform like YouTube, slop videos that have the veneer of education sit side by side with carefully designed educational shows. Robb says YouTube and other kids’ streaming platforms have not done enough to distinguish educational content from slop, which has only made filtering content harder for parents. “Platforms have taken steps to reduce kids’ exposure to age-inappropriate content, and that matters. But ‘not inappropriate’ is a very low bar. There’s a big gulf between that and media created intentionally with kids in mind.”
A 2020 study by Common Sense Media on YouTube videos watched by young kids found 75 percent had “weak or no educational value.” Kids also frequently ended up watching ads and content intended for older audiences.
According to its policy for YouTube Kids, which lets parents approve specific content themselves, YouTube excludes videos that are “deceptive, sensational, or clickbait,” but acknowledges that not every video has been manually reviewed. YouTube also makes clear that automated filtering cannot guarantee every video will be appropriate. “There’s a chance that your child will find content that you don't want them to watch,” the company notes in its support docs.
Earlier this year, in an effort to encourage better digital literacy among kids, the American Academy of Pediatrics updated its guidance beyond screen time recommendations, urging children to avoid “AI-generated content,” “AI chatbots,” “short-form videos,” and “highly sensationalized content or clickbait.” The guide prioritized quality content and coviewing with parents rather than passive watching.
Tiffany Munzer, a developmental-behavioral pediatrician and digital media researcher at the University of Michigan, was the lead author on AAP’s “Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents” policy statement, and tells WIRED in an email that the proliferation of low-quality content has led kids to “miss out on important, slower learning opportunities that promote critical thinking, generate new ideas, and practice stretching their attention spans.”
In April, child advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter, signed by more than 200 organizations and individual experts, asking YouTube to address the spread of AI videos on its platforms, saying AI slop “harms children’s development by distorting their sense of reality, overwhelming their learning processes and hijacking their attention.”
A YouTube spokesperson tells WIRED that on YouTube Kids, which is meant for kids 12 and under, AI content is limited to a small set of high-quality channels, and parents have the option to block channels entirely. The platform has stricter standards for content made for younger viewers, the company says.
For Maka’s business model to succeed, its shows will need to entertain and educate kids while also establishing confidence in parents. “The value that parents want is relief, knowing that what their child is seeing has been vetted by child development experts and everything on Maka they can trust is good for their kid,” Sheiman says.
Yalda Uhls, a former film executive at Sony and MGM who is now a researcher at UCLA focusing on how media affects the social learning of young children, worries that as AI revolutionizes kids’ streaming content, people who study child development are being left out of the process. “When I was a studio executive, every story meant for children passed through layers of accountable adults,” she says. “But today, algorithms, anonymous creators, and AI tools shape what kids see, and people who study child development are rarely in the room.”
“The gatekeepers have been replaced by a metric, minutes watched,” Uhls says. “Nobody in that chain is required to ask what a child is actually learning.”
One of Maka’s core features is a timer that parents set at the start of every viewing session to help the child wind down off the screen. As the show concludes, a character Maka developed named Scoot appears on the screen to get the child ready to detach from their device. Features like that are the difference between capturing a child’s attention versus earning it, Sheinman says. “So it becomes less of a moment of tension in a family and a moment that the child is prepared for.”
The founders ultimately want Maka to help change the perception of kids' relationship to screens.
“We’re seeing a really big challenge around the judgment of parents,” says Leta, explaining that one problem with screen time is the demonization of parents who rely on it. “We have all judged parents who bring out the screen on the train or at a restaurant. Let's be real, most parents will reach for the screen at some point. We don't think that they should be judged for that choice.”
Whether any of this will work is unclear. One question at the core of Maka’s mission is whether it can build a successful streaming company without adopting the same incentives that created the problems it is trying to solve.
Robb from Common Sense Media calls competing with YouTube a Herculean task. “YouTube is free and already on the devices within their homes. Moving them away can be tricky,” he says. The real test for Maka, Robb says, “will be whether it can grow with kids and stay sustainable without being pulled back toward the engagement metrics that drive the rest of the industry.”
Leta, one of Maka’s cofounders, admits that it’s easy to be cynical when it comes to children and screens. “But TV also gave us Sesame Street. It gave us Fred Rogers who believed that the space between the child and the screen was sacred ground.”
“One of the dads in our beta told us that with other platforms, when his kid is watching, it feels like ‘a race to the bottom of my kid’s brainstem,’” Leta says. “It doesn't have to be like that.”

LinkedIn shared its 2026 ranking of the best Israeli startups on Wednesday, with the newly unveiled identity security firm Oak, which was launched publicly in July with a $60 million seed investment, leading the ranking.
Greylock Partners, Accel, and CRV led Oak's seed funding, and Shai Morag, who has already founded two cybersecurity companies acquired by market giants such as Palo Alto Networks and Tenable, co-founded the company with Tal Marom.
"Our annual LinkedIn Top Startups list surfaces the 15 emerging Israeli companies growing fast, gaining attention and recruiting top talent right now," said LinkedIn in a statement.
The three-year-old AI development firm doubleAI placed second, AI operating system developer Wonderful placed third, open software platform Kela Technologies was fourth, and business-to-business (B2B) cybersecurity firm Kela Technologies placed fifth.
LinkedIn explained that it identified companies working on pioneering cybersecurity solutions, AI "expert intelligence," and automation of workflows, while only data from LinkedIn was used to develop the ranking.
The full ranking includes Cyera (Private network security), Notch (AI automation), Mate Security (Cybersecurity), Eon (Cloud data protection), Port (Workflow automation), Encore AI (AI data analysis), Limitless Labs (AI for precision manufacturing), Adaptive6 (Spending control), Dream (AI cybersecurity), and FINQ (AI fintech firm).
How is the LinkedIn ranking made?
The professional social networking platform explained that the ranking focused on five sections of data available on LinkedIn: employee growth, engagement, job interest, and attraction of top talent.
It also specified that engagement was measured with "views and follows of company pages by non-employees, as well as non-employees’ views of startup employees’ profiles."
The "job interest" ranking used views of and applications to advertised roles, while the acquisition of top talent was measured by ranking the company's ability to hire workers from LinkedIn’s global Top Companies lists.
LinkedIn also explained that companies included in the ranking were required to be no more than seven years old, privately held, fully independent (and not owned by larger firms), and to have at least 30 employees employed from July 2025 to June 2026.
It also clarified that startups that laid off 10% or more of their workforce during July 1, 2025, and the list’s publication were ineligible for the ranking.

Online ads helped deliver Israeli spyware to devices visiting Al Jazeera, 120,000 websites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:59:33 UTC
19:59:33 KST

Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru, a spyware company blacklisted by the US government, and other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex, and others, according to separate reports from the Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society, and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads, often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods, reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Discover-Tech could identify and track users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads, and it would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Candiru spyware used to compromise Al Jazeera devices
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, such as Gaza and the West Bank, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine - any site - you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Discover-Tech being frozen out of online ad market
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant on the investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that it suspended Discover-Tech from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.
