Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson sentenced to 15 years for child sexual offences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:37:28 UTC
19:37:28 KST

Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years for sexual offences against two women who were children when he abused them, paving what was described as a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”.
The sentence at Newry crown court completed the downfall on Thursday of a former Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader who once dominated unionism in Northern Ireland.
Donaldson, 63, was sentenced to 11 years for rape against complainant B and four years for offences against complainant A, to be served consecutively. He is to remain on the sex offenders register indefinitely.
He had reached the “very height of public office” before a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”, the judge, Paul Ramsey said.
The former Lagan Valley MP had shown no remorse or empathy, he said. “There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort.”
He paid tribute to the victims, who were in court. “It is only through the courage, resourcefulness, and determination of two young women that you’ve been brought to justice in respect of the crimes you committed against them when they were children,” he said.
The head of the Public Prosecution Service’s serious crime unit, Catherine Kierans, lauded the victims’ courage in coming forward to seek justice. “Jeffrey Donaldson held a prominent public position,” she said. “This case shows that sexual abuse can be hidden behind a facade of respectability.”
Donaldson, wearing a blue suit, white shirt and pink tie, showed no emotion and was escorted from the dock by two custody officers. He was returned to Maghaberry prison, where he has been held since his conviction.
He was found guilty in June of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one count of rape, spanning a period from 1985 to 2008. He has denied all wrongdoing and plans to appeal.
Speaking outside court, Det Ch Insp Leah Crothers of the Police Service of Northern Ireland said Donaldson had manipulated his victims and exploited their trust. Police and the criminal justice system had sent a clear message, she said. “No-one is above the law.”
Statements from the complainants, read by Crothers, detailed enduring trauma. Complainant B said the abuse had taken away her ability to trust people. “I stood up many years ago because for me this is about drawing a line in the sand and knowing that the Donaldson’s [sic] can no longer hurt anyone else.”
Complainant A said her childhood had been stolen. “I learned to survive by shutting away my emotions, trusting no one and expecting people to hurt me … I should never have had to become this strong.
“The last few years have been nothing short of a battle … But those responsible do not control me now … The cycle is being broken and it ends with me.”
The DUP said its former leader had committed “vile and disgusting crimes” and expressed sympathy for the complainants. “He deserves every day of the lengthy prison sentence he has to serve following the guilty verdict for preying on innocent child victims.”
The jury in the four-week trial found that Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, aided and abetted his offending. The 60-year-old was deemed unfit to stand trial on mental health grounds and faced a trial of the facts, which tests evidence but does not result in a criminal conviction.
She is due to return to court on 13 November 2026 for a hearing in relation to the conclusion of her case.
The case shredded the reputation of an establishment figure who was knighted and played a key role at Westminster during post-Brexit negotiations over Northern Ireland’s position in the UK.
During the trial Complainant B said she was raped when she was of primary school age and was of secondary school age when Donaldson lifted up her top and fondled her breasts. The jury heard that Donaldson’s wife witnessed part of the latter incident and walked away.
Complainant A said she was of primary school age when Donaldson began to be “physical” with her. She recalled waking up in the night with a sexual feeling and having nightmares about “men doing horrible things to children”.
The trial heard that in the 1990s the victim told a pastor about the abuse, after which Donaldson apologised to her at a Christian centre in County Antrim. Prosecutors also told the jury of a letter Donaldson wrote to Complainant A in 2020 in which he expressed regret for causing “hurt, pain and distress” and asked forgiveness for his “sinful nature”.
At the trial he denied wrongdoing and said the apologies related to other matters.
The prosecutor, Rosemary Walsh, told the trial both victims kept memories “locked away inside” until turning points in adulthood prompted the decision to report the offences to police in 2024.
Until his arrest in March 2024, Donaldson embodied unionist probity. Born into a Presbyterian family in Kilkeel, he married Eleanor in 1987 and served apprenticeships in the Ulster Unionist party before defecting to the DUP in 2004.
Donaldson was knighted for political services in 2016 and became DUP leader in 2021, before resigning in 2024. After his conviction, King Charles stripped him of his knighthood in July.

Three years of protest and repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:35:02 UTC
19:35:02 KST

Breadcrumb
From mass marches to direct action: three years of Palestine protest and repression in Britain
Three years into the Gaza genocide, Britain’s pro-Palestine movement looks very different from when it first filled the streets in 2023.
When Israel first launched its attacks on Gaza, over a million people swarmed the capital.
Demonstrations took place weekly. But as the genocide continued unabated – killing tens of thousands of Palestinians, including thousands of children – protesters started to ask themselves: “What can I do?” Feeling that marching along police-approved routes was no longer enough.
So, attention turned to direct action, which often falls on the wrong side of UK laws.
Businesses linked to Israel's arms industry became primary targets. Activists focused heavily on factories belonging to Elbit Systems, one of Israel's largest arms manufacturer.
In August 2024, activists broke into an Elbit Systems site in Bristol, causing millions of pounds in damage. Months later, in June 2025, activists broke into RAF Brize Norton, spraying red paint into aircraft turbines.
In response, Home Secretary Yvette Cooper moved to proscribe direct action group Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation.
The ban sparked sit-ins and some of the largest acts of mass civil disobedience Britain has seen in years. Thousands of protesters, many of them pensioners, held placards defying the proscription. The demonstrations resulted in hundreds of arrests under anti-terror legislation.
Rather than deterring dissent, the proscription appeared to strengthen it.
The willingness of so many people to risk arrest, prosecution and damage to their livelihoods showed the depth of public anger over Britain's support for Israel's genocide in Gaza.
State efforts to suppress solidarity are nothing new. The Conservatives previously sought to restrict Palestinian flags and many pro-Palestine slogans.
However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has since apologised for Labour's initial response to Gaza. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has also introduced sanctions targeting extremist Israeli settlers and groups, alongside trade restrictions.
Together, these moves suggest a growing recognition of the national and international political costs of supporting Israel's actions in Palestine after years of sustained pressure from activists.
What three years of repression have failed to achieve is the movement's defeat. Despite arrests, suspensions and prison sentences, solidarity with Palestine has endured and even deepened.
People of all ages continue to risk their freedom in pursuit of ending the genocide and securing a free Palestine, demonstrating that state repression has not extinguished the movement, only strengthened its resolve.

The protests mark the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who won a fourth term last year.

“Corruption must be confronted and, as the EU itself has recently reaffirmed, Albania is tackling it as never before,” Rama said.

Türkiye’s first floating production platform set for Black Sea deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:31:48 UTC
19:31:48 KST

This photo shows Osman Gazi, Türkiye's first floating production platform. (AA Photo)
Türkiye’s first floating production platform, Osman Gazi, will be dispatched from Filyos Port in the northern province of Zonguldak to the Black Sea on Oct. 17, according to a statement from the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry.
The Osman Gazi Floating Production Platform is expected to double domestic natural gas output from the Sakarya Gas Field in the Black Sea.
The platform is scheduled to operate in the Black Sea for 20 years and is aimed at increasing daily natural gas production at the Sakarya field to 20 million cubic meters from the current 9.5 million cubic meters.
First unveiled to the public by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in July 2024, the platform is 298.5 meters long, 56 meters wide and 29.5 meters deep. Erdoğan announced on May 27, 2025, that the platform would be named Osman Gazi, and he had seen off the platform from the Dolmabahçe Working Office to Filyos on May 29, 2025.
After undergoing accreditation and certification procedures in Filyos, the platform was also modified to meet the specific requirements of the Sakarya Gas Field.
The platform’s topside consists of 21 separate facilities. Eleven of those facilities were rebuilt in line with the field’s characteristics, including seven manufactured in Turkey and four produced abroad. The remaining ten facilities were modified and integrated into the platform.
With accommodation capacity for 140 personnel, Osman Gazi will operate approximately 170 kilometers offshore after departing Filyos Port on Oct. 17.
The platform will process natural gas and deliver it to Türkiye’s national transmission network.
According to ministry estimates, the platform’s planned daily gas production corresponds to an economic value of about $10 million at current prices and is expected to contribute approximately $3.5 billion annually to the Turkish economy.
Following its deployment, the first gas is expected to be flared from the platform’s flare tower by the end of this year, while production is scheduled to begin in early 2027. The move is expected to complete the second phase of development at the Sakarya Gas Field.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said in a social media post that the platform was ready to head to its mission area in what Türkiye refers to as the “Blue Homeland.”
“On the path toward our goal of full energy independence, Türkiye’s first floating production platform, Osman Gazi, is ready to depart for its duty station in the Blue Homeland,” Bayraktar said.
He added that the project would increase the number of households whose natural gas needs are met through domestic resources from 4 million to 8 million.

"After careful consideration, we have, in mutual agreement, decided to part ways. This decision is necessary and important to us and our future ambitions," Nightwish said in its statement posted on Instagram.
The group said the separation was amicable and wished Jansen success in her future projects.

Nightwish, meanwhile, intends to continue recording music. Helsingin Sanomat reported that the band plans to enter the studio in 2027 to record another album.
The announcement coincides with the group's 30th anniversary. Nightwish formed in 1996 and has become one of Finland's most successful international music exports.
The departure prompted reactions from fans on social media, with some expressing disappointment and others supporting Jansen's decision.
Nightwish has not announced who will replace Jansen as lead vocalist or provided a release date for its planned 2027 album.

MPs move to curb small schools amid cost and curricula concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:30:20 UTC
19:30:20 KST

MPs move to curb small schools amid cost and curricula concerns
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
MPs and the cabinet want to curb the growth of small, independent schools in the Netherlands, after a school linked to the far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD) opened with just four pupils, according to broadcaster NOS.
A 2021 law made it easier to set up state-funded schools based on new educational ideas or on religious or other “worldview” beliefs. Since then, more schools have opened every year, a large share of them Islamic.
The “Renaissance School” in Almere, which opened in August, was approved partly on the basis of market research showing around 350 people were positive about it.
MPs from both coalition and opposition parties said the research amounted to little more than an online survey, and that respondents often did not know what kind of school was planned. It is linked to the far-right FVD party.
Junior education minister Judith Tielen told parliament on Wednesday she would look at whether that part of the law should be tightened or scrapped. She had already written to MPs that keeping so many small schools going was “no longer sustainable”.
Tielen said she saw no reason to intervene at the Renaissance School for now. It must have at least 139 pupils by the start of its fourth school year or close.
The law originally was a VVD initiative, which the FVD voted against it at the time.
The debate comes a year after research by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur found that a number of orthodox Protestant and Islamic schools were teaching messages at odds with democratic values, such as rejecting same-sex relationships or teaching that women should be subordinate to men.
All schools in the Netherlands are legally required to stick to democratic values, including equality and non-discrimination. The schools inspectorate said it would investigate where necessary.

His remarks came during a call with Taiz Gov. Nabil Shamsan to discuss humanitarian conditions, public services and the effect of the siege.

READ: Rights groups warn Houthi siege threatens millions in Yemen’s Taiz

Saudi Arabia has faced attacks in recent days on airports and civilian facilities amid an escalating military confrontation with the Houthis. The escalation began in July following a period of relative calm after a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.

====================================================================================================

Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

As polls indicate Democrats could take back the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the Trump administration. But that may prove to be a difficult task, even with a majority in both chambers of Congress.
In late September, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report on Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency titled “DOGE: Congress and the Public Lack Assurance That Systems and Data Were Protected at Multiple Agencies.” In it, the GAO revealed that multiple executive branch agencies had refused to fully cooperate with investigators about the extent and nature of DOGE’s access to sensitive systems and information. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which DOGE and the Trump administration gutted in the early months of the president’s second term, sent GAO a letter accusing investigators of bias and alleging the report was “misleading.”
The report, just the latest example of the Trump administration seeking to dodge congressional oversight, raises questions about what—if any—avenues the legislature has to enforce accountability, or even access basic information about what the government has been doing.
“In a world where there is no shame, it's hard to think of what Congress can do that doesn't involve some coercion of some kind,” says Emily Berman, a law professor at the University of Houston. “Like withholding money or going to court.”
The GAO serves as Congress’ primary investigative body; its work is most often initiated by requests from Congress, but it is independent and nonpartisan. It does not, however, have the ability to enforce laws or take on prosecution. Federal agencies don’t necessarily have to enact the agency’s suggestions, but they are legally required to cooperate with GAO’s requests for information and auditing.
The GAO and a Democratic congressional aide who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity, though, say that the agencies investigated by the GAO for the DOGE report—the CFPB, the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (VA), the Department of Education, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the Small Business Administration (SBA)—all, in one way or another, refused to cooperate with the investigation.
“We have experienced increased challenges in obtaining information from agencies over the past year and a half,” GAO spokesperson Sarah Kaczmarek says. “As this report demonstrates, when agencies do not provide requested information, it can limit GAO’s ability to provide Congress and the public with assurance that federal programs, systems, and information are appropriately managed and protected.”
As an example, every agency included in the report refused to do so much as name which DOGE operatives they’d played host to—even when that information had already been publicly reported. The CFPB refused to name all six of the DOGE operatives who were detailed to the agency even though, in February 2025, WIRED identified three of them: Nikhil Rajpal, Chris Young, and Gavin Kliger. DOGE members Jeremy Lewin and Jordan Wick were also part of the team at the agency.
According to the report, both the SBA and the VA “did not respond to requests for information needed to determine the access DOGE team members had to their systems.” Previous reporting from WIRED found that the DOGE affiliate at the VA, Sahil Lavingia, sought to use AI to write code for the agency’s systems, and at the SBA, DOGE affiliates Edward “Big Balls” Coristine and Donald Park were granted broad access to the agency’s financial and loan systems.
VA and SBA did not respond to a request for comment.
The Democratic aide says that in addition to the VA and SBA refusing to provide information, several agencies slow-walked their responses to the GAO. The aide says that meeting some resistance within an agency to a GAO investigation is not unheard of, but that responses to the DOGE inquiry represented a “surprising” level of obstruction.
“We did see a little bit of a range in terms of cooperation,” they say. “Normally, an agency might be reluctant to provide as much information as the GAO requests, but then they try to find accommodations. If they can't provide X, they provide Y. If they can't provide Y maybe they could walk investigators through something, or show different things. But there's just a complete lack of willingness to kind of get to yes.”
And it’s not just the agencies named in the DOGE report that have been resistant to congressional efforts to investigate. In a statement to WIRED, Senator Ron Wyden, the Oregon Democrat, says that his office was notified by the GAO that the Commerce Department “is refusing to cooperate with my request with Sen. Welch to investigate the effectiveness of U.S. export controls to address AI-fueled national security risks.”
The Department of Commerce did not respond to a request for comment.
“There is no good reason to deny GAO investigators the access they need to root out corruption and waste in federal programs,” says Wyden.
While the current Republican-led Congress appears to have little interest in using them, there are tools to enforce cooperation with a GAO investigation. The most obvious–and likely–is using their subpoena power, which the Democratic aide says members of Congress are preparing to do. “We are expecting that the administration is gearing up for the [the next Congress] to be hostile,” they say.
If someone refuses to cooperate with a subpoena, Congress can hold them in contempt. “It used to be that if Congress threatened to hold an executive official in contempt of Congress, that was like a huge embarrassment,” says Berman. “And that imposed a lot of pressure on the executive branch to reach some agreement with Congress.” But in recent years this has changed. Since 2012, three different attorneys general have been held in contempt of Congress, with seemingly few repercussions.
This is because without the cooperation of executive branch agencies like the Department of Justice, Congress has little power to enforce a subpoena or hold those who don’t comply in contempt.
Last month, Congress held billionaire Leon Black in contempt for refusing to answer subpoenas to return and testify under oath regarding his connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Whether Black will face any consequences, however, is now out of Congress’ hands—the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia will ultimately decide whether or not to prosecute him.
Without being able to count on the support of agencies nested under the executive branch and staffed by presidential picks, Berman says, today’s Congress now has fewer options than in the past. It could impose fines on those held in contempt; it “can arrest them and put them in their little jail cell in the basement of the Capitol;” or it could file a lawsuit, potentially winding all the way up to the Supreme Court. But any legal case could easily stretch beyond the House’s two-year term, creating “a real problem” for using the courts to enforce accountability, says Berman.
“This is part of a broader shift of power from Congress to the executive branch,” she says. “Over time, the way the law has moved is to give the executive branch more and more power and discretion over decisions within its own branch. So it's had the effect of essentially broadening the scope of what the executive branch can argue they're entitled to keep secret.”
With its own oversight powers limited, Congress is going to have to think of other ways to force the executive branch to cooperate. Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat who serves as the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, told reporters in September that Congress has “the power of the purse” as a way to pressure the executive branch to comply with investigations.
But in order for this power to be effective, Congress would need to change the way it legislates. As it stands, Berman says, the budget is a “blunt tool” because Congress often passes legislation in large omnibus bills. This means that critical funding for regular government operations, or initiatives that have broad bipartisan support, is often bundled along with other allocations for the administration’s priorities. For instance, following the killing of Alex Pretti by two Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents during the Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, Senate Democrats refused to pass an appropriations bill that included funding for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees CBP. What followed was a months-long partial government shutdown. But DHS is also home to the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), meaning that TSA workers went without pay for weeks, and led to massive delays at airports around the country.
Berman says that if Democrats take control of the Senate, they could also put pressure on the administration through refusing to confirm appointments unless the executive branch cooperates with investigations.
But in reality, she says, “there are no good options.”
Maddy Varner contributed reporting.

The Russian Foreign Ministry has proposed forming a network of foreign bloggers and opinion leaders who can convey Russia’s viewpoint to the world, International Organizations Department Director Kirill Logvinov said at a meeting of the Federation Council’s Commission on Information Policy and Media Relations.

Russia detains Swedish citizen as Moscow eyes future prisoner swaps

The FSB arrested the Swedish citizen in Pskov region on terrorism charges and Japanese journalist Yuki Imai on Sakhalin on espionage charges, days after former president Medvedev wrote that Russia may need to “fill up the exchange pool with European and American idiots” to recover Russians abroad.
Russia detained a Swedish national and a Japanese journalist within days of one another as former president Dmitry Medvedev called on Moscow to replenish its "exchange pool" of Western citizens to trade for Russians held abroad.
Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said on Wednesday it arrested the Swedish citizen in the Sebezh district of Pskov region, near the borders with Belarus and Latvia.
He is accused of entering Russia under cover of joining the Russian military while intending to carry out "sabotage and terrorist attacks" on military sites.
The FSB said it established that from February to June the detainee served as commander of a drone section in the 24th separate assault battalion of Ukraine's Aidar unit — a volunteer formation that emerged during Russia's initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014 which the Kremlin has designated a "terrorist organisation," a common domestic classification aimed at Ukrainian units.
He had allegedly admitted to serving in the unit. The FSB said it holds documents confirming his participation in combat against Russian forces, and that he faces charges of illegal border crossing, organising the activities of a terrorist organisation and serving as a mercenary. His name has not been disclosed.
Sweden's government has not commented. Moscow's claims could not be independently verified.
'You have to howl like a wolf'
The second arrest — that of Yuki Imai, a journalist for Japan's Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper — took place on Sakhalin Island as he was preparing to leave the country, the FSB said.
He is accused of gathering information on Russia's defence capabilities at the direction of Japanese intelligence services.
Japan summoned Russia's ambassador in Tokyo Nikolai Nozdrev on Wednesday. Kimitake Nakamura, head of the foreign ministry's European affairs department, lodged a protest both over the arrest and Moscow's decision to announce it without first informing the Japanese government.
Tokyo has demanded consular access to Imai and assurances of humane treatment.
The Committee to Protect Journalists called for his immediate release, warning that journalists "must not be used as a bargaining chip in broader geopolitical disputes."
The organisation estimates that at least 30 journalists are currently held in Russia in connection with their work.
The arrests followed Medvedev's post on Telegram on 9 October calling for Russia to increase its "exchange pool" of foreign nationals it uses to negotiate the release of its citizens deemed useful to the regime.
Writing after the arrest in Montenegro of Mikhail Zvinchuk, a Kremlin propagandist and founder of Rybar — a Telegram channel close to Russia's military and security services — Medvedev said Moscow might need to detain more Western nationals to secure the release of Russians held abroad.
"Now, quite likely, we will have to fill up the exchange pool with European and American idiots in order to pull our own people out," he wrote.
"There is no other way: if you live with wolves, you have to howl like a wolf." Zvinchuk has since been returned to Russia.
Using people as bargaining chips
Russia has for years detained foreign nationals on charges including espionage and drug smuggling, a practice its critics describe as the taking of hostages for exchange.
The most recent large-scale swap took place in August 2024, when 26 people were freed in a multinational exchange: Russia released 16 detainees, and Western countries handed back 10.
Among those Russia released were Wall Street Journal journalist Evan Gershkovich, sentenced to 16 years in a high-security prison on espionage charges, and former US Marine Paul Whelan, convicted on the same charges and given the same sentence.
Germany obtained the release of Rico Krieger, who had been sentenced to death in Belarus, and Patrick Schabel, detained at Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport over cannabis-infused gummy sweets.
Russia received back, among others, Vadim Krasikov, who was serving a life sentence in Germany for the assassination of Georgian national Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in a Berlin park in 2019, Artem and Anna Dulcev, accused of spying in Slovenia under the guise of South American art dealers, and Pablo González aka Pavel Rubtsov, a Russian-born Spanish journalist who had been held in Poland on espionage charges since February 2022.

Kenya confirms second Ebola case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:23:57 UTC

Kenya confirms second Ebola case
Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, with a family member of the country’s first patient testing positive for the virus, the Health Ministry announced on Wednesday. The latest infection brings the total number of confirmed cases to two, including one death.
The new patient, a 39-year-old man, had already been placed in quarantine after being identified as a close contact of the first case. He developed symptoms on Tuesday, including fever, fatigue and joint pain, and was subsequently tested for the virus. The man has been transferred to a designated treatment facility, where he is receiving supportive care.
Health authorities said the two cases are linked and there is currently no evidence that the virus has spread into the wider community.
Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case last week after a man who had lived in DR Congo for seven years died at a Nairobi hospital. According to Health Minister Aden Duale, the patient had fallen ill about a month earlier and traveled through Uganda before flying to Nairobi on October 3, where he was hospitalized and later tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of the virus.
The ministry has identified 128 people who came into contact with the first patient, of whom 113 had been traced as of Tuesday. Among them, 108 are undergoing quarantine in Kenya, with daily health checks over a 21-day period. Another five contacts are outside the country.
Kenya has also banned the repatriation of bodies of people who died from Ebola abroad under new public health regulations introduced on Monday. The rules also impose strict requirements for handling and burying the bodies of Ebola victims to prevent further transmission of the virus.
An Ebola outbreak in DR Congo that began in May shows no signs of abating. According to the latest figures from the Congolese Health Ministry, 9,144 infections and 4,410 deaths had been recorded as of October 12, with the virus spreading across seven provinces. The northeastern province of Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for nearly three-quarters of all confirmed cases.

The face of Taiwanese opera Yang Li-hua reflects on a colorful career
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:22:41 UTC
19:22:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Yang Li-hua (楊麗花), the 82-year-old Taiwanese opera star revered for her roles as young men and imperial heroes, appeared at the Taipei premiere of a documentary about her life on Tuesday.
“Emperor on Stage: Yang Li-hua” (世紀初戀 楊麗花) is a dramatic 108-minute look back at an exceptional life. Though the spotlight is firmly on Yang, the wider picture is of Taiwan’s development and its unique culture over the past 70 years or so.
Directed by Tseng Wen-chen (曾文珍) and filmed over five years, “Emperor on Stage” was co-produced by Public Television Service, Taiwan Television Enterprise, and the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute. Their cooperation has produced a fitting tribute to a cultural icon.
Yang was literally born into the business and says in the documentary that she was inspired to excel by the thought of being better than her mother. On her way to fame, she performed in Taiwanese opera theaters, bars, construction sites, and on the road. She also appeared on radio, television, film, and major stages, including the National Theater and Taipei Arena.
She became one of the nation’s best-known entertainers through her cross-gender “xiaosheng” (小生), or young male, roles. Her televised opera performances became part of daily life for many families.
The documentary combines archival footage with interviews conducted in Taiwan, Singapore, and Malaysia. It also includes images of Yang with performers including Teresa Teng (鄧麗君), Fong Fei-fei (鳳飛飛), and Weng Chien-yu (翁倩玉).
Tseng said the documentary shows how Yang built a connection with audiences across generations. “Yang Li-hua gave them very beautiful, very sweet memories,” she said. “The earliest memory of following an idol actually comes from Yang Li-hua.”
Yang observed that her audiences were loyal and often followed her from one production to the next, but each new work needed to offer something different. She said the stage was her favorite medium because it relied on physical movement and improvisation and allowed direct interaction with audiences.
Yang began performing male roles when she was young. She also recounts in the documentary how her mother beat her as a child for taking off her top like the boys and running around with them. She recalled that when she later played women in contemporary dramas, she had to relearn feminine mannerisms.
The documentary also examines Yang’s family life, friendships, and efforts to pass Taiwanese opera on to younger performers. She said the art form needs to continue developing, but innovation should not come at the expense of its core elements.
“Innovation cannot discard Taiwanese opera’s bones,” Yang said. “Its essential elements — singing and rhyming lyrics — must be preserved, or Taiwanese opera could disappear.”
“What I should do, I will do for Taiwan’s children to see.”
“Emperor on Stage: Yang Li-hua” opens in theaters on Oct. 30.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s indigenous submarine Narwhal conducted its 25th sea trial on Thursday morning as testing continues ahead of planned delivery later this year, per CNA.
Narwhal, the first of eight submarines commissioned by the Department of National Defense’s Navy Command, was built by the Taiwan Shipbuilding Corporation and bears hull number SS-711. It departed Kaohsiung at 7:50 a.m. for its 19th submergence test.
Taiwan Security and Development Association Chair Chi Tung-yun (紀東昀) said the sea trials are entering their final phase, with longer and more complex tests ahead. He said the shipbuilder had reported resolving most system integration problems after repeated adjustments and technical assistance.
The submarine is 70 meters long and has a range of up to 11,000 kilometers. Its top speed is 8 knots (15 kph) on the surface and 17 knots (31.5 kph) underwater. The first submarine had a price tag of NT$49.36 billion (US$1.53 billion), Reuters reported in 2023.
Narwhal can fire US Mark 48 Mod 6 torpedoes, which have a range of up to 50 kilometers and can detonate beneath large vessels, per CNA. It uses a diesel-electric propulsion system.
The defense ministry announced plans in 2014 to build submarines domestically to replace the Navy’s decades-old fleet, with support from countries other than China, after declining several refurbished models. Construction of Narwhal began in November 2020, and it was named and symbolically launched on Sept. 28, 2023.
The submarine left Kaohsiung Harbor for its first surface trial on June 17, 2025. Submergence trials began on Jan. 29 of this year.
Narwhal completed preparatory checks of its sonar, propulsion, and underwater speed log systems on Jan. 26. It began combat systems testing with practice torpedo launches in May and expanded testing to other systems on June 1.

Taiwan seeks 462 extended-range air defense missiles for NASAMS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:21:51 UTC
19:21:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is seeking 462 extended-range missiles for 12 US-made National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS) to strengthen its air defenses and protect critical infrastructure.
The first phase of the procurement includes 123 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile Extended Range (AMRAAM-ER) missiles. The US has yet to announce the exact number for the second phase, but Taiwan hopes to acquire 462 across both phases, per Liberty Times.
The AMRAAM-ER has an effective interception range of up to 50 kilometers and a maximum altitude of about 25 kilometers. Its range is roughly 50% greater than that of the AIM-120C-7 missiles previously used by NASAMS, more than three times that of Taiwan’s land-based Sky Sword II missiles, and more than 10 times that of the Stinger missiles used by Taiwan’s Avenger air defense systems.
A military official told Liberty Times on Thursday that the US Air Force awarded Raytheon a contract in April to prepare for large-scale AMRAAM-ER production. The contract covers foreign military sales to countries including Taiwan, Hungary, and the Netherlands.
Taiwan’s Air Force plans to deploy NASAMS as a distributed network, with centralized command and control and launchers positioned at multiple locations. Each of the 12 systems would have three launch vehicles carrying six missiles apiece, for a combined capacity of 216 ready-to-fire missiles.
If Taiwan acquires all 462 planned missiles and fully loads the launchers, 246 would remain in reserve, Liberty Times reported. Those missiles would be stored in protected facilities for reloading after an initial engagement.
NASAMS has also been deployed in Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks. By February 2025, the systems had made about 900 successful interceptions there, with a reported success rate of 94%, according to Norwegian military figures cited by Euromaidan Press. Nearly 60% of the intercepted targets were cruise missiles.

China, North Korea opens long-delayed bridge to strengthen ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:20:00 UTC
19:20:00 KST

China and North Korea opened a border bridge Thursday after more than a decade of delays, signaling a further strengthening of ties between the neighboring nations.
China's official Xinhua News Agency reported that a ceremony for the launch of the New Yalu River Bridge was held in the morning.
An online video from state media outlet China News Service showed trucks adorned with the national flags of China and North Korea waiting on the bridge, which was also decorated with the flags.
Beijing expected that the four-lane, 3-kilometer (1.8-mile) crossing, which connects the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju, would further promote economic, trade and "people-to-people" exchanges.
During the ceremony, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in a video address that the crossing would become a new landmark symbolizing the two nations' traditional friendship, Xinhua reported.
He hoped both sides would seize the opportunity of the opening to continue to enhance connectivity and explore potential for cooperation in border areas, it said.
"The relations between China and North Korea have entered a new stage, embarking on a new chapter," he was quoted as saying.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song also made a video address, the report added.
The bridge initially was expected to enter use in 2014, when China had apparently completed construction on its side. But the date came with no opening and without North Korea doing corresponding work on its side.
The absence of substantial work in Sinuiju fueled speculation that Pyongyang was wary of becoming more economically dependent on China or displeased with Beijing voting for United Nations resolutions toughening international sanctions on the North over its nuclear program. Some observers suggested North Korea and China also differed over the bridge's location.
The setback over the bridge prompted an unusually sharp report in the Global Times, a newspaper affiliated with the ruling Chinese Communist Party, which quoted Dandong residents expressing frustration over delays in what they had hoped would be an economic boon for their border city.
Observers said the new bridge would likely boost bilateral trade and enhance logistical efficiency gradually.
It is expected to lessen the burden on an aging bridge on the Dandong-Sinuiju route, which handles more than 70% of official trade between the two countries. That decades-old bridge carries a railway line as well as cars and trucks, but vehicle traffic can move only one way at a time.
The South Korean government said last year there were at least 17 active road and rail links across the porous North Korea-China border, which stretches more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles).
The new bridge's launch came about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations. Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about its opening.
China has long been North Korea's biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in past years, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has prioritized Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.
Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve his country's economy and build a front against the United States.
China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea's external trade was with China.

Egyptian villager's chance find reveals giant Ramesses II statue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:19:39 UTC
19:19:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Egyptian villager's chance find uncovers giant Ramesses II statue, earns him trip to Mecca
An Egyptian villager who discovered an ancient stone covered in hieroglyphics outside his home has led archaeologists to uncover the remains of two colossal statues believed to depict the pharaoh Ramesses II, with one originally standing more than eight metres tall.
The discovery was made in Behbeit El-Hagar, a village in Egypt's northern Nile Delta, after Khaled El-Shahat Khalil came across an inscribed stone block while working on a plot of land in front of his house.
Rather than attempting to remove or sell the artefact, Khalil immediately alerted the local antiquities authorities, prompting emergency excavations by Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities.
The excavations uncovered a massive stone head measuring 1.6 metres in height, belonging to a statue of Ramesses II that archaeologists estimate originally stood approximately 8.5 metres tall, including its base.
The pharaoh is depicted wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, symbolising the unification of the two ancient kingdoms under a single ruler.
Archaeologists also discovered part of the statue's back pillar, bearing an inscription of Ramesses II's Horus name, "Hor Ka Nakht Mery Maat", one of the royal names used by ancient Egyptian monarchs.
A second royal statue, measuring approximately 2.4 metres in its surviving portion, was also uncovered and is believed to depict the same pharaoh.
Although the statue is missing its legs, base and part of its upper section, its facial features remain remarkably well preserved. The figure wears the traditional nemes headdress, a striped royal headcloth closely associated with ancient Egyptian kings.
Nearby, archaeologists discovered a 1.3-metre block of pink granite inscribed with two of Ramesses II's royal titles: "Nesu Bity", meaning King of Upper and Lower Egypt, and "Sa Ra", meaning Son of Ra, the ancient Egyptian sun god.
Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, said excavations would continue to establish the relationship between the discoveries and determine whether further archaeological remains lie beneath the site.
The discovery has renewed attention on Behbeit El-Hagar, an important ancient religious centre best known for the remains of a vast temple dedicated to Isis, one of the principal goddesses of ancient Egyptian religion.
Ramesses II, who ruled Egypt for approximately 66 years during the 13th century BC, is among the country's most celebrated pharaohs.
Known as Ramesses the Great, he oversaw an extensive programme of monumental construction, including the temples at Abu Simbel and major additions to the temple complex at Karnak.
His reign was also marked by military campaigns against the Hittite Empire, including the famous Battle of Kadesh, and a subsequent peace treaty regarded as one of the earliest surviving international peace agreements.
The latest discovery could provide further evidence of the pharaoh's monumental building activities in the Nile Delta, a region closely associated with his reign.
Meanwhile, Khalil's decision to report the original discovery has earned him an unusual reward from the Egyptian government.
On Wednesday, Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy travelled to Behbeit El-Hagar alongside Gharbia Governor Alaa Abdel Moaty to personally honour the villager.
Khalil and his wife were presented with certificates of appreciation and rewarded with an Umrah pilgrimage to Mecca, in recognition of his honesty and contribution to preserving Egypt's archaeological heritage.
Fathy insisted that the ceremony take place on Khalil's own land, surrounded by his family and fellow villagers.
The minister praised Khalil's responsible conduct, saying his prompt notification had enabled archaeologists to investigate the site scientifically and safeguard the discoveries.
He also announced that the area would receive greater archaeological attention, with preliminary indications suggesting that further significant discoveries could be awaiting excavation.

‘We expect war to reach the city soon’: Yemenis stockpile as Houthis advance on Taiz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:18:58 UTC
19:18:58 KST

Ali Abdulsamed spent all day waiting and walking. Like many people in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz, he was searching for some food for his family of six. But each time he reached the end of the queue at the grocers, he was greeted with empty shelves. He would go on foot to the next shop, unable to afford the price of petrol, which more than doubled last week.
After visiting more than a dozen stores, Abdulsamed managed to find a 25kg bag of wheat flour – sold at more than twice its usual price. It would have to do, he was lucky to find anything at all.
As Iran-allied Houthi rebels advance and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces closes off routes into the city, conditions in Taiz have become increasingly difficult. Yemen’s third most populous city has found itself besieged from all sides, with its supplies of fuel, food and other basic goods cut off.
The UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Monday that the fighting had denied vital assistance to 800,000 people in Taiz: a city of about 1 million, which already had some of the highest levels of food insecurity in the country.
The speed of the Houthi advance gave people little time to prepare, prompting a sudden rush on stores and driving up the price of goods still left in the city. Crowds have been gathering around grocery stores and gas stations, trying to stock up on the essentials as fears of shortages spread.
“I wasn’t aware that the situation would become difficult so suddenly and that shops would close, but since 3 October, almost all food items have disappeared,” said Abdulsamed, 48. “I don’t have savings to stock up on food for the family, so I resorted to selling my wife’s gold ring.”
He, like many others in Taiz, has stopped driving or even taking buses as petrol and bus fares have become too expensive. To avoid paying, Abdulsamed sometimes walks up to 10km (6 miles) a day.
Abdulsamed works in a mobile repair shop on one of the main streets in the heart of Taiz. Traffic outside used to be constant and the shop was visited by a steady flow of customers. Now, the street is almost empty, save for those few people in Taiz scrambling to find supplies before hurrying home.
The sound of explosions and gunfire echoes throughout the day.
Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast. The renewed offensive interrupted four years of relative calm in Yemen after a UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines in 2022.
The Houthis have moved south at a blistering speed, seizing more than 1,000km of territory over the last month, which gives them control over the Bab al-Mandab strait: a vital shipping lane. They have traded strikes with Saudi Arabia, launching attacks on Riyadh airport, with rebel-controlled Sana’a being hit in return, as the Saudis try to support Yemeni government forces.
Their offensive was halted at Taiz, a city that has never fallen out of Yemeni government control since the country’s civil war began in 2014, and has been a long-sought goal for the rebels. The city sits at the crossroads between the north and the south, and if it should fall to the Houthis, Aden, the seat of Yemen’s government, will be cut off.
So far the Houthis have failed to capture the city. Its rugged terrain is defended by local fighters as well as reinvigorated government forces, who announced a counteroffensive two weeks ago to push back the Houthis.
But those who live in Taiz fear the Houthis cannot be kept at bay for ever. Conversations at home, the mosque and at work are all dominated by the war. The latest news is shared at the dinner table, with out-of-school children asking their parents what will happen next.
“Residents expect the war to reach the city soon, so everyone is stocking food at home, preparing to stay indoors for a long time and ensuring they have all their necessities,” said Abdulsamed.
Life in the once-busy city ground to a halt as fighting drew closer last week. Schools, universities and many public institutions in Taiz closed on 4 October out of concern for the safety of students and employees.
“This is not a time for studying. What we need now is to have enough food and water at home and wait until Taiz overcomes this crisis,” said Rawa, a 35-year-old schoolteacher, who asked to be identified only by her first name.
Rawa spends almost all of her time at home, only leaving to scrounge for supplies. She used to spend her weekend afternoons at a nearby park, but on Sunday, arriving to find it completely deserted, she turned around and went back home.
Even home offers little safety. Rawa’s house is located close to the frontlines in eastern Taiz and the sounds of explosions have been growing closer in recent days. In the past, she would have fled to her ancestral village south of Taiz, as she had done in the past. But now, the road is blocked.
As fighting draws closer, she can do little more than make sure she feels prepared for a long siege. But, with each day, food and basic supplies grow more expensive.
“We are just lucky we can afford [goods] and now have enough food and water at home,” said Rawa.

Just over half of candidates in key US Senate races say they will accept results, others hedge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:16:09 UTC
19:16:09 KST

Just over half of candidates in key US Senate races say they will accept results, others hedge
WASHINGTON, Oct 15 - Just over half of major party candidates in the most competitive US Senate races told Reuters they will accept election results regardless of the outcome, while some signaled a degree of uncertainty less than a month before the November 3 midterms.
Reuters asked Republican and Democratic Senate candidates and their campaigns whether they would accept election results in 13 states that could determine which party controls the upper chamber of Congress in the final years of Donald Trump's presidency.
The news agency also sought their positions on possible election intervention by the Trump administration. Reuters spoke to some candidates in person but conducted most queries via email or text message.
The mixed responses highlight the uncertainty that hangs over the midterms nearly six years after Trump tried to overturn his 2020 election loss to former Democratic President Joe Biden. Ahead of this year’s vote, Trump has made repeated efforts to federalize state-run elections, obtain access to state voter registration rolls and voting records, and accuse Democrats of voter fraud without evidence.
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 seat Senate majority. But Trump's record-low approval rating and high prices for energy and other goods spawned by his tariff policy and the war with Iran have undermined Republicans, even in normally Republican-leaning states, raising Democratic hopes of taking control of the Senate. Democrats are already favored to win the House of Representatives, independent analysts say.
Of the 26 campaigns surveyed, those of nine Democrats, one independent and four Republicans said their candidates would accept results without conditions.
At a time when state and local election officials are preparing for the possibility of intervention by the Trump administration, some Democrats criticized Republican voting restrictions and stressed the need to ensure that all eligible votes are counted, while some Republicans accused Democrats of undermining public trust in elections.
In four contests — Alaska, Iowa, Maine, and New Hampshire — both parties' campaigns said they would accept election outcomes without condition. In five other races — Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Ohio and South Carolina — Democrats signaled acceptance while Republicans offered conditional responses or did not address the question.
At least one campaign did not respond to Reuters queries in the remaining races: North Carolina, Georgia, Minnesota and Texas. The reasons for their reticence were unclear.
OBLITERATING INTERFERENCE
"We fully expect a fair election where every eligible Georgian can feel confident they have had their voices heard," said Ellie Dougherty, campaign spokesperson for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking his second term in Georgia, a central battleground in the administration's push for voter data and election records.
"But if there are credible concerns of interference by the Trump administration, or any entity, we will put the full force of our legal apparatus behind obliterating that interference," Dougherty said in a statement.
The campaign of Republican Mike Collins, Ossoff's election rival, did not respond to repeated Reuters queries seeking comment.
Senator Susan Collins of Maine was the only Republican whose campaign addressed the possibility of intervention in the November election, saying she would "oppose any efforts to undermine the outcome of free and fair elections in Maine and across the country."
Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, one of eight Republican senators who voted to block certification of Biden's 2020 election victory, dismissed the issue of intervention, telling Reuters: "I haven't spent a moment thinking about that, and I just think it's a hypothetical, and I'm not going to go there." But he expressed concern about the integrity of voting nationwide, particularly mail-in voting.
The White House said in a statement that Trump "has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections" and underscored the president's demands for voter ID and proof of citizenship, measures that Congress has not enacted. "Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said.
Election uncertainty among politicians comes at a time when most American voters are confident that their ballots will be accurately counted. Seventy-six percent of registered voters voiced such confidence in a September 30 to October 5 Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll. That was up from 69% in 2022 and driven largely by increased confidence among Republicans.
MARSHALL FACES COMPETITIVE CHALLENGE
Marshall is facing an unexpectedly competitive reelection bid against Democrat Adam Hamilton. The Republican said he is "comfortable with voter integrity in Kansas, because we have a voter ID law." But his campaign did not respond to queries asking specifically whether he would accept the results.
A spokesperson for Hamilton's campaign said the Kansas Democrat "will absolutely accept the results of the election, regardless of who wins in November."
A similar dynamic appeared in Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown's campaign said their candidate would accept the election results.
Brown is running against Republican Senator Jon Husted, a former Ohio secretary of state, who offered a qualified response, telling Reuters that he would accept "any certified election that is run well." Husted cut off a question about possible intervention, saying: "Stop! Stop! ... I have great confidence in the Ohio election system. Stop trying to introduce questions when there aren't any."
Husted added: "The rest of the country does not have a great system."
In North Carolina, a campaign spokesperson for Democratic candidate Roy Cooper cited new state restrictions on voting, saying: "We must make sure every vote is counted and Roy Cooper will accept the results of the election after the lawful counting process is complete."
Cooper is running against Republican Michael Whatley for the seat of retiring Republican Senator Thom Tillis. Whatley, whose campaign did not respond to Reuters queries, helped lead Trump's 2024 effort to challenge state election systems as chairman of the Republican National Committee.
BELIEVE IN DEMOCRACY
In Michigan and Nebraska, Democrats offered outright acceptance of election results, while Republicans deflected the question.
"I believe in democracy. I will accept the results of this election regardless of the results," Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a close race with Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, said in a statement.
A spokesperson for the Rogers campaign responded: "This hypothetical is irrelevant because Mike will win on November 3rd."
Nebraska independent Dan Osborn, who is running against Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, would "yes, absolutely" accept the outcome of the election, according to a campaign spokesperson.
The Ricketts campaign responded: "Nebraska has free and fair elections and voters can be confident in them. Senator Ricketts plans on winning this race."
South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews will accept the results of her contest, according to her campaign.
Her opponent, Republican Senator Darline Graham, who is running as a permanent replacement for her late brother, Lindsey Graham, "is taking nothing for granted this election," according to her campaign spokesperson, who predicted she would win.
In the hotly contested race for Senator John Cornyn's Texas seat, neither the campaign of Democrat James Talarico nor Republican Ken Paxton responded to queries seeking comment. REUTERS

Trump called her an attorney. Now his new press secretary faces a bar complaint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:15:40 UTC
19:15:40 KST

President Donald Trump's new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, is facing mounting scrutiny just days into her appointment, not only over her rocky debut before reporters but also over questions surrounding her professional qualifications as a lawyer. An American watchdog group has filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, asking it to investigate whether Zacharia violated state law by repeatedly presenting herself as an attorney despite no public record showing that she holds a license to practice law in the United States.
The complaint adds to the pressure facing the 41-year-old spokeswoman, who took over from Karoline Leavitt and held her first White House press briefing on October 13. At the center of the controversy is whether Zacharia, who has frequently described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and in professional roles, is legally qualified to use that title.
Campaign for Accountability said Zacharia had identified herself as a lawyer during appearances on Fox News, CNN and the conservative Newsmax network. She also had presented herself as general counsel for a conservative nonprofit organization based in California. The watchdog's executive director, Michelle Kuppersmith, accused Zacharia of repeatedly presenting herself as a lawyer to enhance her professional reputation and credibility, and called on California's legal regulator to investigate whether she had misled the public about her qualifications.
The filing of a complaint does not establish wrongdoing, and there has been no finding that Zacharia violated the law.
‘When I moved to China’
Questions surrounding Zacharia's credentials have become particularly awkward because Trump himself described her as an attorney when announcing her appointment on October 9. Yet journalists searching attorney licensing databases have found no record that she was admitted to practice law in any U.S. state.
During her first White House briefing on Tuesday, Zacharia was asked where she had passed the bar examination. Her answer was brief and raised further questions: "When I moved to China."
In a subsequent statement to AFP, Zacharia said she had practiced international transactional law with the appropriate professional credentials. However, she did not clarify whether she holds a U.S. law license or specify where she had qualified to practice law. The State Bar of California confirmed to American media outlets that it had no record of Zacharia being licensed under either her married name or her maiden name.
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011, but obtaining a law degree does not automatically authorize someone to practice law in the United States. Lawyers generally must also satisfy the licensing requirements of the jurisdiction in which they practice.
Her reference to China raised additional questions because foreign nationals are not permitted to sit for the country's national legal qualification examination, although foreign professionals may perform certain legal work at Chinese law firms. Zacharia has said she worked at a law firm in Beijing after moving to China with her husband.
Speaking to The New York Times, Zacharia said that when she first began appearing on American television news programs, she asked Pepperdine University how she should describe her professional background. According to her account, the university president told her she could use the word lawyer but not attorney, which she understood to refer specifically to someone licensed to practice law.
The distinction, however, is not necessarily recognized in the way Zacharia described it under U.S. professional licensing rules, particularly when someone presents themselves publicly as authorized to provide legal services. Trump used the term attorney when announcing her appointment.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Zacharia had taken California's bar examination after graduating from law school but failed it. California's examination is widely regarded as one of the most demanding in the country.
The White House has defended its new press secretary. Communications Director Steven Cheung described Zacharia as exceptionally capable and highly intelligent, arguing that she was qualified to help communicate the administration's message to the American public.
Former professors have also spoken in her defense. Robert Pushaw, who taught Zacharia at Pepperdine and later attended her wedding, remembered her as a good law student and a genuinely good person. He acknowledged, however, that he could not say whether she was technically licensed as an attorney.
Another former professor, Roger Alford, now at the University of Notre Dame, described Zacharia as a standout student at Pepperdine. Alford, who employed her as a research assistant during law school, urged critics to get to know her before rushing to judgment. At the same time, he acknowledged the unusual nature of a situation in which someone describes themselves as a lawyer without having passed a bar examination.
‘My president, sorry, my husband’
The controversy over Zacharia's qualifications follows a difficult first appearance as White House press secretary on October 13. Her debut briefing lasted just 14 minutes and featured extensive reliance on prepared notes, an unusually brief appearance compared with the press conferences frequently held by her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, some of which lasted nearly an hour.
Zacharia opened by slowly reading from prepared material and took questions from just three media outlets, all generally considered sympathetic to Trump. She appeared to stumble during several exchanges and, at one point, accidentally referred to the president as her husband.
The slip occurred while she was discussing her family and praising her husband, Tyler Zacharia, for helping manage their family life. "First of all, I want to give a huge shoutout to my husband," she began, before explaining that the couple have four children, ages 12, 10, eight and six.
Zacharia said spending evenings with her children was a top priority and that her husband had accompanied her to Washington during a week when the family was celebrating two birthdays. Then came the verbal mix-up.
"My president, sorry, my husband," she said, catching herself and laughing at the mistake.
During the briefing, Zacharia also told reporters that her goal was to amplify Trump's accomplishments, emphasizing that the president was his own most effective spokesman. When she brought the session to an abrupt end, she told journalists they would have an opportunity to ask Trump questions directly on the White House South Lawn before he departed for a campaign event in Alaska.
Critics suggested that Zacharia appeared nervous and had ended the session earlier than originally planned.
Former White House press secretaries weigh in
Zacharia's performance drew criticism from several former White House communications officials. Jen Psaki, who served as press secretary under former President Joe Biden and now works as a television news host, compared the briefing to a sketch from the comedy program Saturday Night Live.
Sarah Matthews, a former deputy White House press secretary during Trump's first administration, was similarly critical. Writing on X, Matthews contrasted Zacharia's debut with the first appearances of former Trump press secretaries Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt.
Matthews argued that regardless of whether people liked McEnany or Leavitt, both had arrived at their first briefings sharply prepared, confident and ready to demonstrate their command of the job. Zacharia's appearance, she said, had been disappointing, pointing to the small number of questions taken, her heavy reliance on notes and her apparent difficulty commanding the briefing room.
Trump, however, offered a sharply different assessment. Asked by reporters about his new press secretary's first appearance, the president praised her performance, saying: "I thought she was very good."
For Zacharia, the immediate challenge now extends beyond improving her performance behind the White House podium. The complaint filed in California has placed her legal qualifications under scrutiny, with the state's bar authorities being asked to determine whether her public descriptions of her professional status crossed a legal line. Whether the complaint results in any formal action remains unclear.

Kremlin Says Russian Diesel Exports Reaching Global Markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

The Kremlin said on Thursday that Russian diesel had begun to reach global markets following an agreement with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump said last week that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices, while Moscow partially lifted its ban on diesel exports from Oct. 10 following the agreement.
"The diesel has started reaching global markets and is expected to have a positive effect on stabilising oil markets, although it will not be enough to fully stabilize them," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a daily conference call.
LSEG data showed on Wednesday that Russia had resumed diesel export loadings from the Baltic port of Primorsk.
According to the shipping data, a tanker carrying around 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel was loaded on Tuesday and was heading towards Morocco.
Under the terms announced by Trump last Friday, Russia agreed to immediately release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel onto global markets, followed by an additional 500,000 metric tons in November.
The initial 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) is less than a day's supply for the U.S. transportation sector alone, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels.
The U.S. Treasury Department issued a license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The deal has sparked pushback from European and Ukrainian officials, who argued that unlocking Russian energy revenues directly fuels the Kremlin’s war effort.
Russia has rejected European criticism of the diesel deal as "cynical," given that Europe continues to buy some Russian oil and liquefied natural gas.
Peskov's comments came a day after Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the diesel supply deal with the U.S. would boost Russia’s economy and include direct exports to the U.S. market.
“Without a doubt, this is a positive signal for our economy,” Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum in Moscow, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
“In accordance with the agreements, supplies will go to world markets, as well as the U.S. directly,” he said.
He added that Russia aims to restore monthly diesel exports to 3.5 million metric tons by the end of 2026, bringing its share of the global market above 10%.
Reuters contributed reporting.

“Without a doubt, this is a positive signal for our economy,” Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum in Moscow, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
“In accordance with the agreements, supplies will go to world markets, as well as the U.S. directly,” he said.
He added that Russia aims to restore monthly diesel exports to 3.5 million metric tons by the end of 2026, bringing its share of the global market above 10%.
Reuters contributed reporting.

What you need to know about Germany’s planned tax on sugary drinks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:14:49 UTC
19:14:49 KST

The German cabinet has approved draft legislation to tax sugar-sweetened drinks in the country from 1 July 2027. The sugar tax is intended to help fund the statutory health insurance system, easing pressure to raise contributions.
The German cabinet has approved draft legislation to tax sugary drinks in Europe’s biggest economy. If passed by the German Bundestag, the tax will take effect on 1 July 2027. The coalition aims to raise revenue for the federal budget while encouraging manufacturers to reduce sugar content and offer healthier products.
The levy is intended to ease pressure on the healthcare system, which faces costs of more than €2 billion every year linked to the high consumption of sugary drinks, which contributes to obesity, diabetes and tooth decay.
According to the federal government, Berlin is using the tax to implement “what associations from the fields of health, science, child protection, and consumer protection have long been demanding.”
The tax is expected to generate additional revenue for the federal government of €690 million in 2027 and €925 million in 2028.
According to the federal government, the revenue would help limit planned cuts to its subsidy to the central health fund, potentially easing pressure to raise people’s health insurance contributions.
Which drinks are subject to the tax, and who is going to pay more?
According to the draft legislation, drinks that would be subject to this tax include those with a total sugar content of 5g per 100ml or more. For drinks containing at least 5g but less than 8g per 100ml, the duty would be €0.26 per litre. At 8g per 100ml or more, it would rise to €0.32 per litre.
The list therefore includes soft drinks, such as Coca-Cola, iced teas, energy drinks, fruit nectars and juice concentrates with added sugar.
Alcoholic drinks and their non-alcoholic versions are not included in the plans. Milk, oat, and rice drinks, as well as pure fruit and vegetable juices, would also be exempt from the tax. Drinks containing sweeteners instead of sugar would also be excluded.
Although manufacturers or wholesalers would pay the tax, the federal government expects shoppers to face price increases of tens of cents for sugary drinks.
Small, independent manufacturers with an annual production volume of up to 70,000 litres would be exempt from this duty. A further exemption for businesses producing up to 1 million litres a year would require European Commission approval under state aid rules.
The tax faced criticism both before and after the coalition reached an agreement. According to German public broadcaster ARD's Tagesschau news service, Hessian Minister-President Boris Rhein (CDU) said the tax would make drinks more expensive and could threaten jobs in the beverage industry.
The US-based Tax Foundation also questioned the health benefits of sugary drink taxes in a report published in 2025. They argued that, "While taxes on sugary drinks do seem to increase their prices, there is no evidence for significant improvement in health outcomes as a result of higher sugary drink prices."
Germany would join several EU countries that already tax sugary drinks, including France, Portugal and Hungary, where a broader public health tax has been in place since 2011.
