The Rada introduced a tax on parcels worth up to €150 — what is changing and what the partners’ money has to do with it
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:14:39 EEST
19:14:39 KST

The Rada introduced a tax on parcels worth up to €150 — what is changing and what the partners’ money has to do with it
Kyiv • UNN
The Rada adopted customs and tax changes: VAT on such parcels will be charged from the first euro. The new rules will take effect no earlier than July 2027.
The Verkhovna Rada amended the Customs Code to abolish the VAT exemption for parcels worth up to €150 sent through foreign marketplaces, thereby adopting tax and customs changes to cancel the tax benefit and impose taxes on such parcels. UNN reports this, citing the parliament’s press service.
Bringing the rules for taxing goods from foreign marketplaces into line with EU standards. Parliament adopted the relevant law (Reg. No. 15460). A total of 249 members of parliament voted in favor
What is changing
The document amends the Customs Code of Ukraine. It updates the rules for taxing imported parcels and abolishes the VAT exemption for shipments worth up to €150. At the same time, non-commercial parcels worth up to €45 will not be taxed.
Previously, the Verkhovna Rada adopted one of the bills (No. 16051-1) to abolish tax exemptions for parcels worth up to €150 sent through foreign marketplaces, namely, to impose VAT on e-commerce and international parcels. The relevant amendments are being introduced into the Tax Code.
Supplement
On September 7, the Cabinet of Ministers approved and submitted to the Verkhovna Rada two related draft laws on taxing small postal and express shipments worth up to €150 ordered through marketplaces. The documents provide for abolishing the tax exemption for parcels worth up to €150.
Draft Law No. 15460 amends the Customs Code of Ukraine (which regulates customs procedures, border clearance rules, and the €150 threshold for import duty).
Under the draft law, VAT would be introduced on imported goods purchased through marketplaces, starting from €0.
Currently, international shipments worth up to €150 are not subject to import VAT or import duty. Under the proposed rules, the threshold itself will remain, but its effect will change: goods worth up to €150 will be exempt only from duty. Thus, VAT at the standard rate of 20% will be charged from the very first euro of the goods’ value.
For shipments worth more than €150, the basis for calculating the duty will change. It will be charged at a rate of 10% of the parcel’s entire invoiced value, rather than only on the amount exceeding €150.
At the same time, private free-of-charge gifts worth up to €45 were expected to remain exempt from taxation. The new rules will not apply to the distance selling of alcohol and tobacco.
Government Draft Law No. 16051, which amends the Tax Code of Ukraine, establishes rules for assessing and paying VAT on e-commerce and parcels; however, the government included in it provisions bringing the rules concerning politically exposed persons (PEPs) into line with the wording agreed with the EU.
Incidentally, on June 9, the Verkhovna Rada adopted in its entirety a draft law (No. 15111-d) on the taxation of digital platforms. On June 11, it was signed by Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk, and on June 12 it was sent to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for signature, and since then the document has been "stuck" with the head of state.
The issue is that, during the second reading, a provision was submitted for the document that provides for changes to the financial monitoring system for politically exposed persons (PEPs). The relevant committee included it in the draft, and the plenary chamber subsequently supported it.
PEPs include current and former senior officials: from members of parliament, ministers, and the president to heads of law enforcement agencies, members of the NBU Board, and ambassadors.
Draft Law No. 16051 provides for excluding heads of structural units of the central office of the National Bank of Ukraine and employees responsible for conducting financial monitoring at a bank in which more than 50 percent of the shares are owned by the state from the list of politically exposed persons.
Under the legislation, banks and other financial companies are required to conduct enhanced financial monitoring of PEPs, their close relatives, and business partners.
PEP status is lifelong. At the same time, enhanced financial monitoring applies throughout a person's tenure in a top position and for 12 months after their dismissal. However, banks and other financial institutions may continue to subject a PEP to enhanced scrutiny if they consider the person to remain high-risk.
The amendments made to the draft law introduce penalties for banks that decide to continue enhanced monitoring of PEP transactions after 12 months have passed since the person left a top position.
According to some members of parliament, this amendment is precisely why Zelenskyy has still not signed the aforementioned draft law.
However, the Verkhovna Rada later adopted an alternative draft law, No. 16051-1, which abolishes the provisions concerning PEPs and establishes that taxes on parcels will be credited to the special fund of the State Budget of Ukraine and allocated to meeting the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Before its second reading, draft law No. 16051-1 also included amendments concerning PEPs, which are intended to unblock the signing of Law No. 15111-d on taxing income from digital platforms.
As members of parliament note , during the vote on tax amendments on October 15, "the amendment concerning PEPs passed." Therefore, this will unblock the signing of the draft law on taxing digital platforms.
"These are the main changes concerning the abolition of the exemption for parcels worth up to €150. Since the tax amendments have already been adopted, it can effectively be said that the authorities have completed the process. However, it will not take effect before July 2027," Yaroslav Zhelezniak, a member of parliament from the tax committee, commented on the adoption of tax and customs amendments concerning parcels.
Connection with funding from partners
The two draft laws concerning the taxation of parcels worth up to €150 are among the four decisions required to unlock EU macro-financial assistance under the Ukraine Support Loan programme. The other two decisions were adopted by parliament the previous day, October 14. The amount in question is €4 billion.
"Let me remind you that, for the €4 billion tranche, the following are needed: a resolution on experts for selecting members of the Accounting Chamber; the assessment law; tax amendments to the law on parcels; customs amendments to the law on parcels; and the amendment concerning PEPs in the tax law on parcels. So the tranche has been unlocked here.... the only problem is that at least another €25 billion is still hanging in the balance and waiting, including for our anti-corruption draft laws.... which the authorities are blocking," Zhelezniak commented.
According to him, this will also help with funding from the IMF.
"The IMF's annual meetings are taking place starting today. So their tranche has also been unlocked. This year they are not in Washington, but in Bangkok (Thailand)," Zhelezniak noted.

Ukrainian cruise missiles hit six Su-34 bombers deep inside Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:14:23 UTC
19:14:23 KST

- Satellite imagery shows a Ukrainian Neptune strike on Russia’s Borisoglebsk air base destroyed four Su-34 bombers and badly damaged two more.
- The Ukrainian Navy said the night attack on Oct. 14–15 also destroyed flight support equipment and caused secondary explosions at the base.
Satellite imagery of Russia’s Borisoglebsk air base shows that a Ukrainian Neptune missile strike destroyed four Su-34 fighter-bombers and badly damaged two more, backing up the Ukrainian Navy’s claim that it hit six of the jets on the night of Oct. 14–15.
The images, published by the Ukrainian aviation monitoring channel AviVector, compare the airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region before and after the attack. Pictures taken on Oct. 13 show six Su-34s parked at the spot that was later struck, while the post-strike imagery shows four of them completely destroyed and two with significant damage. Numerous pro-Russian Telegram channels have also acknowledged the losses.
The Ukrainian Navy said it attacked Borisoglebsk with its Neptune coastal missile system and that the strike hit six Su-34M bombers, the modernized version of the aircraft, and destroyed equipment used to support flight operations. Secondary explosions and a fire followed at the base, the Navy said.
“The destruction of enemy Su-34Ms significantly weakens the enemy’s aviation potential and reduces the intensity of tactical aviation use in the relevant areas of the front,” the Ukrainian Navy said.
The Su-34 is the main aircraft Russia uses to drop heavy guided glide bombs on Ukrainian troop positions and frontline towns. Fitted with wing kits, those bombs can be released tens of kilometers from the target, outside the reach of many Ukrainian short-range air defenses, which makes the bombers themselves a priority target for Kyiv.
Borisoglebsk hosts the 783rd training aviation center, one of the main schools for Russian strike and bomber pilots, along with units of the 105th composite aviation division that fly Su-34, Su-35S and Su-30SM jets, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported. Residents reported a missile alert and a series of explosions in the town on the evening of Oct. 14.
The strike came days after Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation delivered a new batch of Su-34s to the Russian Aerospace Forces.
Ukraine developed the Neptune as an anti-ship missile, and it became widely known after two of them sank the Russian Black Sea Fleet flagship Moskva in April 2022. Ukrainian engineers have since adapted the missile for strikes on land targets, and longer-range versions have hit military sites deep inside Russia.
The Ukrainian Navy said it is still assessing the full results of the attack on Borisoglebsk, including damage to support equipment and infrastructure at the base.

Germany news: Train station alcohol ban comes into force

Germany news: Train station alcohol ban comes into force

Follow our roundup of headlines across Germany for Thursday, October 15.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add DW as a Preferred Source on Google
Bleak forecast for potato harvest and prices after scorching summer
Potato prospects this year are poor after the prolonged hot and dry weather in the summer, according to the government's statistics office Destatis.
"The 2026 potato harvest will be considerably more meager than the previous year, according to forecasts, which will have consequences for the prices of potatoes at various economic levels," Destatis wrote.
In September, Destatis said, potatoes were 11.3% more expensive than in the same month in the previous years. For frozen produce like chips/fries, the difference was less pronounced at 4.7%.
But these figures vastly outstripped both overall year-on-year inflation for September, 3.35%, and particularly the rate of inflation for food and drink products, 0.4%.
Destatis estimated that the 2026 harvest would be almost exactly one-quarter smaller than the previous year — partly because of fewer hectares being used to grow spuds but in larger part because of reduced average yields on the farmed soil in use.
Forecasts predict a yield of around 38.9 metric tons per hectare this year, compared to 46 tons per hectare in 2025.
READ: Hamburg court sentences Iranian agents for plot to attack Jewish leaders
A court in Hamburg has sentenced two men convicted of planning attacks in Germany on behalf of Iran's secret service.
One was given an eight-and-a-half-year prison sentence, while the other was ordered to spend four-and-a-half years behind bars on charges of espionage and attempted murder.
Among others, they were accused of plotting to attack Josef Schuster, the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany and Volker Beck, a Green party politician and president of the German-Israeli society. Beck hailed the verdict online.
Bavaria's Ansbach named 2026 train station of the year
Choo-choo! All aboard the October 15 German rail news express, stopping wherever and whenever the conductor asks politely.
Ansbach train station in northwestern Bavaria, west of Nuremberg, has been named the finest in all the land.
The "Pro Rail Alliance" travel organization's special jury named Ansbach the Bahnhof des Jahres 2026, saying that after a renovation process lasting several years, it now "receives travelers in a light and friendly atmosphere."
They praised its well-lit waiting area, easy accessibilty by car, bike or bus, and ample storage for bicycles. They also noted its practical connection to the wider public transport network.
"Ansbach's bus station can be found right outside the train station building, and so can be reached with the greatest possible ease," the jury wrote.
If you're looking for a reason — other than the now alcohol-free train station, that is — to visit the town of roughly 40,000 people, you'll find it on the historic Castle Road from Heidelberg to Bayreuth. It's near the Frankenhöhe National Park, is home to the Ansbach Residence medieval castle complex, the picturesque Ansbach Court Gardens, an 18th century synagogue, and is also the site of the crypts of the Margrave noble family of Franconia.
Reforms to emergency service response passes Bundestag
The government's planned changes to emergency service response have cleared the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag.
One opposition party, the Greens, also supported the grand coalition's proposals, which are similar to plans that were under discussion in the previous government before it was cut short by early elections in 2025.
Health Minister Carsten Linnemann says the changes aim to ensure that patients receive care quicker, and in the right place.
Its main goal is to help ease the burden for paramedics and emergency first responders, by trying to prevent unncecessary calls to the 112 emergency hotline when a different service might be more appropriate.
Perhaps the main pillar of the plan is to directly network the emergency ambulance phone line 112, with the out-of-hours emergency doctor helpline 116 117 that is designed for less life-or-death medical cases.
Linnemann said the reforms were long overdue and that the reality was still that too many people did not really know who they were supposed to call when, and if in doubt would just call 112.
The reform package also envisages setting up integrated emergency centers, known by the German acronym INZ, that will be open around the clock and will bring doctors and hospital staff and other emergency responders together at one site.
Special emergency centers for children and adolescents will also be set up.
Alcohol ban comes into force at all German train stations
Alcohol bans came into force at all German train stations when the clock struck midnight and Thursday began.
All the roughly 5,700 stations across Germany, including the train platforms themselves, are now booze-free zones.
Pubs, restaurants and other such hospitality businesses at train stations are exceptions to the rule, though, and can still serve alcohol. Consumption of alcohol will also remain legal on many trains, with long distance ones still serving beers and other tipples at their on-board bistros.
Rail operator Deutsche Bahn says the change aims to make train stations safer and cleaner, and more pleasant places to spend time waiting for a (who knows, perhaps delayed) train.
Various misdemeanors and incidents had prompted discussions on alcohol at stations over the years, but two this year in particular brought the issues into sharp focus.
A 26-year-old security staff member for Deutsche Bahn was beaten and kicked by a drunken passenger when trying to check their ticket. During the struggle the train door buckled and opened, and the Bahn employee fell from the train, suffering severe injuries. Earlier in the year, a train conductor was killed when attacked by a man without a valid ticket.
The new rules are part of DB's house rules, rather than being criminal law — meaning that at least in the first instance it is a matter for Bahn security staff to enforce rather than police.
"The alcohol consumption ban applies at stations every day, also on days with major events," Bahn spokeswoman Anja Bröder said when asked about often beer-fueled train usage days, like when football fans flock to Bundesliga games.
Around 40 stations piloted the project for some time prior to its implementation, including some of the largest like Cologne, Munich, Hamburg and Berlin. DB says it has had positive experiences with the early experiments, reporting more peaceful stations with less litter and travelers and employees saying they preferred the atmosphere.
A federal group dedicated to helping the homeless has criticized the measure, however, saying that for homeless people with addiction illnesses, train stations often served as "important, weatherproof and comparatively safe places" to shelter. A spokeswoman also told the Rheinische Post newspaper that if they were driven from sites like train stations, it would be harder for social workers to locate them.
Welcome to our updates
Alla hopp! Another day, another digest of the main news morsels on the menu in fair Deutschland, delectable and perhaps disgusting alike. Thanks for stopping by, Planet Earth.
If you're waiting for a train and frustrated by the delay — hardly an unthinkable scenario in modern Germany — on no account crack open a beer to wile away the time. Starting this Thursday, booze is banned at all of the country's train stations. It's part of a bid to improve behavior, fight littering and in extreme cases protect travelers and staff alike.
Various reform plans should start the parliamentary reading process in the Bundestag, after the Cabinet signed off on them in a Wednesday meeting. These include hikes to tobacco taxes, emergency service reforms, and changes to the federal law on support in education.
The Bundestag will also vote, in what's probably a formality, on extending the military peacekeeping deployments in the Red Sea and in South Sudan into 2027.
Left-leaning coalition negotiations are set to restart in Berlin after hitting a big bump in the road earlier this week.
Essen police are still searching for a prisoner who was violently freed from custody yesterday by two accomplices during a doctor's visit.
And the government stats office is warning of a meager potato harvest and increased prices after the scorching, dry summer.

The aircraft of legendary aviator Amelia Earhart may be found after 89 years of searching
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:10:47 EEST
19:10:47 KST

The aircraft of legendary aviator Amelia Earhart may be found after 89 years of searching
Kyiv • UNN
An American expedition is searching for the Lockheed Electra near Nikumaroro Island. Researchers hope to determine its fate within just a few days.
A group of American researchers believes that within just a few days it may find what remains of legendary aviator Amelia Earhart’s missing aircraft near a remote island in the southern Pacific Ocean. CBS News reports, writes UNN.
Details
The expedition team, led by Steve Schultz of Purdue University and Richard Pettigrew of the Institute for Archaeological Heritage, has begun a thorough search for the Lockheed Electra 10-E aircraft that Earhart may have been flying.
Expedition members are surveying the lagoon off the coast of Nikumaroro Island. They are focusing primarily on an object known as the "Taraia object." It is a visual anomaly that could be seen in aerial photographs as early as 1938, but was first noticed in satellite images in 2020. These satellite images prompted the organization of a new expedition.
Researchers say they may solve the mystery of Amelia Earhart’s missing aircraft within a few days.
Photo: American researchers search for Amelia Earhart’s aircraft on Nikumaroro Island in October 2026. Purdue University.
The search area is so far from civilization that it took the expedition’s 17 members five days at sea to reach it.
Despite this, the team is confident that within a few days it will be able to say whether it has managed to find Earhart’s aircraft.
For reference
Earhart disappeared on July 2, 1937, while attempting to become the first person to fly around the Earth along the equator. Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared after covering 22,000 miles during their expedition.
Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago of the state of Kiribati, located approximately halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island lies about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, which, according to the researchers, was the final point on Earhart and Noonan’s route around the equator.

Kyiv’s envoy to Berlin, Oleksii Makeiev, condemned the outcome, calling the motion the "peak of absurdity.” Local news outlets emphasized that the vote remains non-binding and largely symbolic, as decisions regarding international sanctions and defense assistance fall under the direct authority of German federal leaders and the European Union, as reported by Deutsche Welle.
Previously, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov described Germany’s accusations against Moscow over an attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport as the beginning of a “real war,” as relations between Berlin and Moscow deteriorate following the incident.

Trump Eyes Sanctions Relief for Russian Shadow Fleet as Oil Freight Costs Surge
Unknown

2026-10-15

19:09:20 KST

- Category
- World
Trump Eyes Sanctions Relief for Russian Shadow Fleet as Oil Freight Costs Surge
The administration of US President Donald Trump is considering easing sanctions on vessels associated with the Russian so-called shadow fleet and other sanctioned oil shipments in an effort to reduce record-high global shipping costs, Reuters reported on October 14, citing a US official.
According to the official, discussions are focused on potentially allowing previously sanctioned tankers to transport oil and petroleum products that are not subject to US restrictions, rather than lifting sanctions on Russian or Iranian oil.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed measures are intended to increase the transportation of crude oil and refined petroleum products from the Gulf region, where rising freight rates have complicated global energy shipments.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright reportedly addressed the proposal in a video message to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week, according to energy research firm Energy Aspects.
Wright said the Trump administration was discussing the possibility of relaxing restrictions on shadow fleet vessels to address record shipping costs, which have also weakened demand for US crude oil.
According to Reuters, companies seeking to operate previously sanctioned tankers would need authorization from the US Treasury Department, while the Department of Energy stressed that any easing of restrictions would not enable Russia to increase exports of its oil or petroleum products.
However, analysts at Energy Aspects expressed skepticism that the proposed changes would significantly reduce global freight rates. In a note to clients, the research firm said that lifting restrictions on shadow fleet tankers would be unlikely to substantially increase the number of vessels available for conventional oil transportation, particularly because many of the ships are aging and poorly maintained.
The analysts also noted that most tankers sanctioned over their connections to Russia or Venezuela had continued operating during the previous three months, limiting the potential impact of removing restrictions.
Nevertheless, the proposed measures could facilitate additional oil shipments in the Middle East “could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs,” the strategically important waterway between Iran and Oman, according to Reuters.
The discussions come as the Trump administration has also announced a separate arrangement involving Russian diesel supplies to the United States and international markets. Trump said he had reached an agreement with Russian leader Vladimir Putin following what he described as an “extremely successful discussion” about increasing diesel shipments.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly afterward. He added that Moscow would subsequently provide an additional 3 million tons as quickly as possible, taking into account the condition of Russia's diesel refineries.

Ukraine Takes Out 6 Russian Su-34M Bombers With a Single Airbase Strike, Navy Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

Ukraine Takes Out 6 Russian Su-34M Bombers With a Single Airbase Strike, Navy Says
Ukraine says one Neptune strike wiped out six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers at Borisoglebsk, taking a chunk out of the fleet Russia uses to hammer the front with guided bombs.
Ukraine’s Navy says a Neptune missile strike on Russia’s Borisoglebsk military airfield destroyed six Su-34M fighter-bombers overnight on October 15, potentially dealing a major blow to one of the aircraft fleets Moscow relies on heavily for guided-bomb strikes against Ukrainian troops and frontline cities.
According to the Ukrainian Navy, the strike was carried out with a Neptune coastal missile system against the airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Six Su-34M aircraft were destroyed, along with ground equipment used to support flight operations, while secondary explosions and a fire were recorded across the base.
“On the night of October 15, the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine struck the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region using the Neptune coastal missile system,” the Navy said.
“As a result of the strike, six Su-34M bombers were destroyed. Technical equipment supporting aviation operations was also destroyed, while secondary detonations and a fire were recorded on the airfield grounds. Information is being clarified.”
The Su-34M is a deeply modernized version of Russia’s Su-34 all-weather supersonic fighter-bomber and was developed as an evolution of the aircraft intended to replace the older Su-24M.
The modernization substantially expanded its avionics, reconnaissance capabilities, electronic warfare systems, and range of precision weapons.
The aircraft can carry multiple guided and conventional aerial bombs at the same time, along with various missile types. Russian forces have relied heavily on the Su-34 family to launch glide bombs fitted with UMPK guidance and wing kits, allowing aircraft to strike Ukrainian positions and settlements from well behind the front line.
The Su-34M modernization also introduced improved communications, navigation, weapons-control equipment, and reconnaissance pods designed for electro-optical, electronic, and radar intelligence missions. The aircraft’s two pilots sit side by side inside a heavily armored titanium cockpit.
Its expanded weapons suite includes precision-guided bombs, cruise missiles, and anti-ship weapons, while upgraded electronic warfare and radar systems are intended to improve survivability against air defenses.
Ukraine’s Navy said destroying the aircraft would reduce Russia’s ability to conduct tactical aviation missions in the affected sectors and weaken the fleet used for guided-bomb strikes against Ukrainian forces and communities near the front.
Earlier, a Ukrainian air-defense FPV drone shot down a modernized Russian Mi-28NM attack helicopter in midair.

Domestic violence in France: 111 women killed by a partner or ex in 2025, up 4%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:08:48 UTC
19:08:48 KST

The Interior Ministry has published its 2025 study on violent deaths within couples: 136 deaths, a stark picture of these intimate tragedies and the warning signs that precede them.
In France, police and gendarmerie services recorded 136 violent deaths within couples in 2025, a slight 1% decrease compared with 2024 (138 deaths). On average, one person dies like this every three days.
That is the finding of the National Study on violent deaths within couples, published by the Interior Ministry.
Looking at the breakdown by gender, women remain the main victims of this violence. In 2025, 111 women were killed by their partner or ex-partner, compared with 107 in 2024, a 4% rise. Women account for 82% of all victims.
Conversely, the number of men killed fell by 19% in a year, from 31 in 2024 to 25 in 2025. They make up 18% of the victims.
The report, seen by Euronews, also records 445 attempted homicides, a figure up on 2024, highlighting the scale of the violence suffered daily in people's private lives.
Break-ups and arguments often behind the tragedies
Perpetrators of fatal domestic violence remain overwhelmingly male, representing 82% of those implicated. Among the main triggering factors are arguments, which led to 36 cases and break-ups that were not accepted, involved in 30 cases. Taken together, these two situations account for almost half of the cases studied.
The violence most often takes place in the home, in 76% of cases. Knives and other bladed weapons are the most frequently used (58%), ahead of firearms (34%).
The consequences of this violence also affect children. In 2025, 106 minors lost their father, their mother or both parents as a result of these tragedies. Nine infanticides were also committed in the context of relationship conflict.
One tragic example came in February 2025 in Franconville, in the Val-d'Oise department, when a one-year-old girl was killed by her father, who then took his own life. The couple had a history of domestic violence and were already subject to judicial monitoring.
The consequences of this violence also affect children. In 2025, 106 minors lost their father, their mother or both parents as a result of these tragedies. In addition, nine children were victims of infanticide in the context of marital conflict.
Previous violence before the killings often known to the authorities
The report notes that 37% of women killed had already suffered violence. Of these, 61% had reported the abuse to the police or gendarmerie and, within this group, 88% had already filed a complaint.
Despite these reports, protective measures were very rarely in place at the time of the killings: only one victim had a "grave danger" emergency phone (TGD) and another had an alarm button.
Finally, in 36% of cases, investigators found at least one substance likely to impair judgement, such as alcohol, narcotics or psychotropic medicines, present in the perpetrator or the victim at the time of the events.
Comprehensive law against sexual violence reaches Senate
The fight against sexist and sexual violence was declared a national cause during Emmanuel Macron's first five-year term (2017-2022). Yet it took until this year, following the abduction, rape and murder of 11-year-old Lyhanna and the mobilisation that followed, for a wide-ranging cross-party bill to emerge: the comprehensive bill against sexist and sexual violence.
Backed by eight political groups in the National Assembly, the bill notably provides for a minimum investigative framework to prevent complaints from being closed too quickly, the creation of specialised police units and judicial bodies, as well as an annual compulsory interview at school to better detect violence, from 2032. It also provides for a care pathway for child victims.
On Tuesday, the bill was adopted unanimously by the National Assembly, with 503 votes in favour and none against. It must now be examined by the Senate.

US effort to get Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire collapses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:08:48 UTC
19:08:48 KST

The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it was the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to the sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in his social media post on X, referring to a growing quarrel with the Trump administration. “Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security.”
Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”
Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations.
But the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine.
The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning from Washington of Russian missile strikes for several days this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers also complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines.
The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes that his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said that Ukraine should “get a new president”.
Asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, Zelenskyy said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said.
Musk, the powerful head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a top critic of Zelenskyy in the US.
On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a social media post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.”

Brazil's Bolsonaro racks up endorsements, shaping potential governing bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:06:40 UTC
19:06:40 KST

Brazil’s Bolsonaro racks up endorsements, shaping potential governing bloc
SAO PAULO, Oct 15 - Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has secured the new backing of multiple parties ahead of an election runoff later this month, suggesting his campaign is building momentum and offering an early glimpse of what a governing coalition could look like if he wins.
The right-wing lawmaker, the eldest son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, will face leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the runoff on October 25, after he exceeded expectations in the first-round vote with a slight lead over the incumbent.
Endorsements have since rolled in from a number of center-right and right-wing parties, putting Bolsonaro's coalition on track to hold comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress should he win the presidency. Brazil's Congress is highly fragmented and whoever wins the presidency needs to assemble a congressional coalition in order to advance their legislative agenda.
Support in Congress would increase the chances that Bolsonaro will be able to push through the free-market economic reforms investors are clamoring for. It could also help a potential Bolsonaro government reshape Brazilian institutions like the Supreme Court by confirming new justices and even impeaching sitting ones.
"I am very pleased with this formal support. This is how we are going to rebuild Brazil," Bolsonaro said last week during a press conference with lawmakers and members from allied parties.
The new backers include PP, Uniao Brasil, Republicanos and Podemos, parties that had remained neutral during the first-round campaign. Lawmakers from some of those parties used to hold influential positions in Lula's administration, including cabinet posts.
Bolsonaro also secured the support of three presidential contenders defeated in the first round: former Minas Gerais Governor Romeu Zema, former Goias Governor Ronaldo Caiado and author-psychiatrist Augusto Cury. Zema's Novo party also endorsed Bolsonaro.
The endorsements mark a significant turnaround for the senator, who entered the final stretch of the first-round campaign without formal support from major parties as opinion polls consistently showed him trailing Lula.
If Bolsonaro wins, he would likely need to make concessions to allied parties, as is common in Brasilia and as Lula did in 2023, when nearly half his cabinet posts went to allies.
A rightward shift in Congress after this month’s elections could make those deals less costly.
"If he keeps his campaign promises, his support is likely to be overwhelming," political analyst Antonio Flavio Testa said.
STRENGTH IN NUMBERS
Combined, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable majorities in both chambers.
Bolsonaro highlighted the potential legislative strength during an event last week, saying congressional support would allow his government to "amend the Constitution and restore democracy to this country," a remark criticized by Lula's supporters, who argued it showed a lack of respect for Brazil's democratic institutions.
The candidate later said that he was referring to the passage of constitutional amendments, which demand broad congressional support, adding that interpretations beyond that were speculative.
A strong congressional base could be key to the younger Bolsonaro’s pledge to grant amnesty to his father, who is serving 27 years for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
Testa said the coalition could hold through 2028, when parties are expected to reassess alliances ahead of municipal elections.
But any government turmoil could put it under strain. The elder Bolsonaro shuffled his cabinet several times to shore up support from allied parties as his government came under growing public scrutiny over its handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Lula, meanwhile, has struggled to attract new endorsements ahead of the runoff, having already consolidated support from most center-left and left-wing parties before the first round.
After a bruising first round, Lula is rushing to overhaul his campaign communications to engage millions of Brazilians who did not vote, according to people close to the campaign. REUTERS

Sinelnikov-Murylev, 66, is a senior researcher at the Gaidar Institute for Economic Policy and the former president of the Economic Development Ministry’s Russian Academy of Foreign Trade.
He received state awards and a presidential commendation in 2018 for contributing to Russia’s 2018-24 national development strategy. He also joined the government’s expert council in December 2022.
The Zamoskvoretsky District Court reportedly granted the investigation’s request to place Sinelnikov-Murylev under house arrest for two months.
The 66-year-old economist faces up to 15 years in prison if found guilty of receiving a large-scale bribe.
Specific details on the alleged bribe amount or the involved parties have not been disclosed. The Interfax news agency reported that the case material is available on the court’s website.
This is Sinelniov-Murylev’s second criminal prosecution in recent years. He was arrested in April 2023, and in March 2025 convicted of large-scale embezzlement and abuse of power, receiving a suspended prison sentence of five and a half years.
Sinelnikov-Murylev served as president, or rector, of the Russian Academy of Foreign Trade from 2007 to 2024, continuing there as chief researcher while also holding senior research roles at the Gaidar Institute.
According to RBC, Sinelnikov-Murylev in 2017 ranked third among Russia’s wealthiest university rectors with an annual income of 53.4 million rubles ($638,700 at the current exchange rate). He attributed the earnings primarily to research and teaching activities at the time.

Venezuela’s Maduro due in court over new US torture charge

- The case now includes drug trafficking and torture charges. If convicted on all counts, each faces a mandatory minimum 50 years in prison, with trial set for June 1, 2027.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores are due in US court on Oct 15 to respond to a new indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents.
The additional charges, brought Oct 8, significantly expanded the US criminal case against Maduro, 63, and Flores, 70.
They previously pleaded not guilty to charges that they abused their power to help drug traffickers ship cocaine.
Their lawyers have said they deny the torture charges as well.
Maduro and Flores, captured by the US military in a January raid ordered by US President Donald Trump and flown to New York, are expected to be asked for their pleas on the torture charges at an arraignment starting at 11am EDT before US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in Manhattan federal court.
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s office say Maduro directed officials to torture opposition politicians and military personnel accused of plotting against him to maintain power in the South American country.
In one alleged incident described in the indictment, Maduro in 2014 directed officials to kidnap military personnel to draw information out of them about possible dissidents, and told officials to “squeeze them harder” when some remained defiant.
Flores agreed with the plan in the meeting, and dismissed a suggested alternative plan to glean information by infiltrating the ranks, according to the indictment.
Maduro and Flores are not accused of personally carrying out any acts of torture. Scheduled to go on trial starting on June 1, 2027, they would each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 50 years in prison if convicted on all charges.
Relations between Maduro, a socialist, and the United States were tense during his 13 years in power leading the oil-rich country.
Successive US administrations imposed sanctions on top Venezuelan officials and key state companies, citing alleged human rights violations, corruption and election-rigging.
Maduro accused the United States of seeking his ouster to gain greater control of the South American country’s natural resources.
The pressure campaign culminated with the Jan 3 raid, when the US military captured Maduro and Flores at their Caracas home and brought them to the United States to face drug trafficking charges announced that same day.
Since then, they have been held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.
Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodriguez, has led Venezuela since his capture and has ramped up cooperation with the United States.
Trump has touted Maduro’s capture and the reset of relations with Venezuela as a key foreign policy success heading into the Nov 3 midterm elections in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. REUTERS

Seven subpoenas engulf Nevada election chief in key midterm battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:06:10 UTC
19:06:10 KST

Seven subpoenas engulf Nevada election chief in key midterm battle
Oct 15 - The first Justice Department subpoena demanding voter information caught Democratic Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar off guard. It was June, and his office had been working informally with the FBI on routine election security.
Weeks later, in a July 16 address from the Oval Office, President Donald Trump claimed without evidence that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens had registered to vote, citing an administration review. That review cited Nevada - a key prize in November's fight for control of the US Congress - as one of four states where noncitizen voter registration was widespread.
“We're going to be the target of this," Aguilar recalled telling Republican Governor Joe Lombardo before Trump’s address.
Then three more subpoenas seeking voter data arrived on September 1 and 2.
In total, the Justice Department would deliver seven subpoenas to Aguilar’s office between June 16 and September 2, a public records request shows.
As the Trump administration escalates its efforts to compel states to hand over voter rolls in search of fraud, the federal pressure is shaping a high-stakes rematch for Aguilar's job in Nevada, a top electoral battleground.
As secretary of state, Aguilar is Nevada's chief election officer, responsible for overseeing elections and certifying results among other administrative duties.
The subpoenas have buried Aguilar in paperwork, distracting him from his own reelection campaign against Republican Jim Marchant, who falsely claims the 2020 election was rigged to favor Democrats and whom Aguilar narrowly beat in 2022.
Lombardo has not endorsed either candidate, and did not respond to a request for comment on whom he's supporting.
Trump has framed many of his election-related moves as an effort to help Republicans win seats in a year in which his party is widely expected to lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate. He has claimed without evidence that Democrats want noncitizens to be able to vote because their support would return them to power, a charge rejected by Democrats.
More than 50 election officials and election-law experts see multiple ways the Trump administration could potentially interfere with the 2026 midterms, Reuters reported on Wednesday. They identified potential flashpoints ranging from election-fraud claims and pressure on state officials to seizures of election materials and immigration enforcement near polling sites.
The White House says the administration's goal is to safeguard election integrity and voting security.
AGUILAR KEPT BUSY ANSWERING SUBPOENAS
Aguilar said he considers the flood of subpoenas a deliberate attempt by the Trump administration to weaken his reelection bid and influence who will oversee Nevada's ballots in the 2028 presidential election.
A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency does not confirm or comment on grand jury subpoenas and declined to address Aguilar's assertions about political motivation. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Aguilar said his days were consumed by reassuring worried staff, pushing back on Trump's claims in media appearances, meetings with his personal lawyers and answering the subpoenas. Some donors had withdrawn support because they worried that support could harm their businesses, and his time for fundraising calls has dropped from as many as three hours a day to one a week, he said.
“If they can take me out in ‘26, they have control in ‘28,” said Aguilar, one of only two Democratic incumbent secretaries of state running in battleground states this cycle. “It’s absolutely intentional,” he told Reuters in an interview.
No other Democratic secretary of state - including in Arizona, the other battleground state where the incumbent is up for reelection - is known to have received any subpoenas, according to the Democratic Association of Secretaries of State and other secretaries in key swing states.
Unlike in states like Arizona where counties have more power, Nevada's elections process gives the secretary of state more control in administering elections, Aguilar and other secretaries of state said.
NO EVIDENCE OF WIDESPREAD VOTER FRAUD
Marchant welcomed the federal spotlight, arguing it would lead voters to question Aguilar's stewardship.
"People are so tired of not trusting their election system," Marchant said in an interview, claiming without evidence that Aguilar has overseen elections rife with fraud.
Aguilar dismisses such assertions.
He pointed out that it was already illegal for noncitizens to vote in Nevada, as is true in all states for federal and state elections. His office had also investigated Trump's claims and has not found evidence that any of the people flagged by his administration were noncitizens, he said.
Nevada, whose voter base is roughly 30% Latino, narrowly swung toward Trump in 2024 by 46,000 votes.
Louis Jacobson, a senior columnist with the politics website Sabato’s Crystal Ball, moved the race toward Aguilar in September, writing that Marchant's election denialism likely won't be warmly received in a Democratic-friendly political environment.
Still, Jacobson told Reuters the Justice Department's focus could cause some voters to stay away from Aguilar if they think he's administered fraudulent elections. It could also elevate him as a defender against Washington overreach.
TRUMP'S PRESSURE CAMPAIGN
The Trump administration has intensified a campaign to exert control over state elections, even as it struggles in court. The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to provide voter data and has lost 26 of those cases, including against Nevada.
The Department of Homeland Security has claimed as many as 16,000 noncitizens are on Nevada's rolls, an effort Aguilar says is designed to intimidate Latino voters who may worry federal immigration agents could seek to detain them at polls.
In meetings, DHS officials told Nevada election officials it had thus far confirmed only 185 such cases, according to emails and a video seen by Reuters. Nevada officials, however, said in the emails their records indicated all 185 were citizens and that DHS had provided nothing substantive to suggest otherwise.
A DHS spokesperson said officials have since found that at least 2,000 names on the initial list of 16,000 were those of noncitizens. DHS said it had given Nevada enough information to parse the list on their own, but Aguilar said the agency had not yet provided the state with credible evidence.
Aguilar said the accusations were meant to exhaust his office and erode public trust.
"This whole series of events is like lasagna," he said. "You keep adding on layers of threats and pulling our resources to respond."
THE PRICE OF DEFIANCE
The pressure has followed Aguilar home and across the state. Publicly, he has tried to project optimism and calm.
Aguilar recalled when he served as general counsel to tennis great Andre Agassi's business interests. Agassi had coaches and advisers around him, he said, but when a match began, he alone stepped onto the court.
Aguilar said he does not feel as isolated as Agassi did on those occasions, but as Nevada's top election official, he is the final decision-maker and the public face of the state's election system.
His initial concern about the subpoenas has now turned into defiance.
"Bring it," he said. They "don’t scare me." REUTERS

Israeli firm used online ads to run vast spy operation, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:05:59 UTC
19:05:59 KST

Israeli firm used online ads to run vast spy operation, researchers say
- Israeli firm Discover-Tech used online ads to spy on users and help hack devices, researchers said. Its ads reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps.
- The reports said Discover-Tech helped Candiru and other Israeli surveillance firms use ad platforms from Google, Comcast and Yandex. Ads could track users, extract phone numbers and plant spyware.
- Google, IAB Europe and Comcast have now cut ties with Discover-Tech after policy breaches. The case raises wider fears that ad tech is a national security threat.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Oct 15.
Its services gave Israel’s Candiru – a spyware company blacklisted by the US government – as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia’s Yandex and others, according to separate reports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
“The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat,” Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. “For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.”
Discover-Tech’s online ads — often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods — reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said.
Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users’ devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech’s overall volume.
Malicious ads shown in hundreds of sensitive networks
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements — called cookie matching — allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
“Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech,” Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and e-mails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters’ attempts to reach Candiru’s owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech’s ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025.
The watchdog said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in “hundreds of networks in sensitive categories”, including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court.
He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm’s ads.
“You go to almost any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country,” he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments.
Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organisations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech’s users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Measures against Discover-Tech taken
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant’s investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms “for systematically violating our policies”.
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an e-mail that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform “following recent activity”, Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat.
Earlier in 2026, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers.
Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices. REUTERS

In 2025, Ukraine unveiled an upgraded version of the missile, which had already demonstrated a range of 1,000 kilometers (620 miles). In March 2025, President Volodymyr Zelensky said the system had successfully completed testing and would be deployed for combat use.
The Su-34M is a heavily modernized, upgraded variant of the baseline Su-34 fighter-bomber. The Russian Su-34 is a Russian medium-range fighter-bomber. Ukrainian forces have targeted the warplanes in attacks on Russian military airfields and have reported downing the jets on several occasions.

19:01:45 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Protecting seabirds and restoring native vegetation could help low-lying tropical atoll islands withstand rising sea levels by boosting coral reef growth and reducing erosion, a new study has found.
An international team analyzed ecological data from 28 atoll islands in the Indian and Pacific oceans to examine how nutrients from seabirds affect the islands and surrounding coral reefs, influencing their ability to adapt to climate change-driven sea-level rise, according to a statement from the University of Auckland released Thursday.
By looking at seabird census data, the researchers estimated the amount of "energy" seabirds bring from the open ocean back to each of the small atoll islands and how the nutrients, deposited in seabirds' droppings, influence the islands and surrounding marine ecosystems, according to the study published in Science Advances.
The study found that reefs in lagoons around islands free of invasive rats, which support abundant seabird populations, grew 1.8 times faster than reefs around rat-infested islands. Ocean-facing reefs grew 2.5 times faster around rat-free islands.
Seabird droppings transfer nutrients from the open ocean to islands and surrounding ecosystems, boosting coral growth and sediment production that helps build or maintain islands and reduce erosion as sea levels rise, the study found.
The researchers said that replacing abandoned coconut plantations with natural vegetation and restoring seabird populations by eradicating invasive rats could be key to the survival of low-lying islands. ■

Nepal explores disaster financing mechanism in wake of devastating floods
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:01:30 CST
19:01:30 KST

KATHMANDU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Nepal and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the lending arm of the World Bank Group, signed a mandate agreement to explore the development of a catastrophe bond to help Nepal access funds quickly in case of a major earthquake, the global development financier said on Thursday.
"The agreement marks the beginning of a collaboration to assess how capital markets can support Nepal's broader disaster risk management strategy," said the World Bank in a statement.
This initiative is part of the World Bank Group's established catastrophe bond program, which helps countries access international capital markets to transfer disaster risk and secure financial protection against natural hazards.
Payouts rely on objective physical triggers, such as an earthquake's magnitude or a storm's wind speed within a designated geographical grid, rather than lengthy post-disaster damage assessments. This ensures rapid liquidity for emergency relief.
As one of the world's most disaster-prone countries, Nepal is working to better prepare for, withstand, and recover from future natural disasters through a combination of risk reduction, preparedness, and financial protection measures.
The two sides signed the agreement in the wake of devastating mudslides and floods on Aug. 26 that have so far claimed nearly 1,500 lives while over 5,000 are unaccounted for. The disaster also swept away communities, houses, hydropower facilities, bridges, roads and other infrastructure.
The estimated physical damage was 1.66 billion U.S. dollars, according to the World Bank's Global Rapid Post-Disaster Damage Estimation report. ■

TOKYO, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested in parliament on Wednesday that the wording concerning the Three Non-Nuclear Principles could be revised in the country's three key security documents, which the government plans to update by the end of this year, the Nikkei newspaper reported Thursday.
Responding to a question from Komeito party lawmaker Shinichi Isa at a House of Representatives Budget Committee session, Takaichi said the Japanese government is still upholding the Three Non-Nuclear Principles, but added that, as work on revising the three security documents is under way, there is "still room for discussion" regarding the specific wording on the principles.

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Ancient, modern canals connect and create opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:01:21 CST
19:01:21 KST

NANNING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- From a viewing platform above the ship lock at the Madao Junction in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, foreign delegates watched as water filled one of the world's largest inland lock chambers.
The structure is designed to raise or lower vessels to overcome a maximum water-level difference of 29.6 meters. It is part of the newly opened Pinglu Canal, a 134.2-km waterway linking the Xijiang River system in southern China with the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
For many of the delegates attending the World Canals Conference 2026 that concludes Thursday, the scale was simply striking.
Edith Bronder, an expert on China's canals who has studied waterways in China and overseas, said she had encountered no comparable project elsewhere. Sharon Leighton, president of Inland Waterways International (IWI), called the canal "history in the making."
Their visit on Monday is part of the conference agenda. The four-day gathering has brought together representatives from canal cities, universities, research institutions and waterway organizations in more than 20 countries and regions.
Themed "Innovation and Perseverance: A Crucial Choice," the event places two Guangxi waterways at the center of its discussions: the 2,200-year-old Lingqu Canal and the Pinglu Canal, which opened to shipping last month.
"Canals are not simply artifacts of the past," Leighton said at the opening ceremony of the conference. "They are living infrastructure, living landscapes and influential heritage assets."
Weng Xiaobing, an official with the Water Transport Bureau of China's Ministry of Transport, said the country's water transport sector is at a critical point in its shift from large-scale infrastructure construction toward a greater focus on quality, efficiency, integration and innovation.
That transition is visible in Guangxi, where a waterway built over 2,200 years ago now shares the conference agenda with the country's newest river-to-sea canal.
Completed in 214 B.C. under Emperor Qinshihuang, the Lingqu Canal was originally built to carry provisions for the Qin army during its military campaign in southern China. By linking the Xiangjiang and Lijiang rivers, the 36.4-km canal opened a navigable route between the Yangtze and Pearl River systems.
Though roads and railways replaced the canal as a major freight route, Lingqu still supports irrigation, local water supplies and tourism. Restoration work has repaired historic structures, improved sewage collection and helped secure dry-season water supplies.
The Lingqu scenic area received more than 1 million tourist visits in 2025, according to local authorities.
The Pinglu Canal tackles a longstanding challenge: getting cargo from inland production centers to the coast despite mountains and winding river routes.
Built at an estimated cost of 72.7 billion yuan (10.8 billion U.S. dollars), the canal provides parts of southwestern China with a more direct route to domestic and overseas markets. It shortens the journey to the sea by more than 560 km compared with routes through neighboring Guangdong, and official estimates suggest logistics costs could be slashed by 18 to 30 percent.
Last month, Nanning Port, previously an inland river port with no direct waterway link to the Beibu Gulf, handled 668,400 tonnes of cargo, up 145 percent year on year, as shipments began using the new canal, port authorities said.
Other supporting infrastructure is also expanding. A railway spur serving the industrial complex near Nanning Port is under construction. Designed to handle 3.2 million tonnes of cargo annually, it is scheduled for completion in August 2027, according to Beibu Gulf Port Group.
"The Pinglu Canal introduces a new chapter in the long story of populations using waterways to connect and create opportunity," said Leighton, the IWI president. "It incorporates the engineering, knowledge and technology of our era and is carefully designed to ensure tangible benefits for generations to come." ■

The secrets of Hohle Fels cave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

Hohle Fels cave in southern Germany has been a place of great interest to archaeologists since it was first excavated in 1870. Discoveries at the site date back as far as 43,000 years and include some of the earliest figurative art and oldest musical instruments ever unearthed. As the Hohle Fels excavation leader Nicholas Conard discusses in this short video, such discoveries point to complex Ice Age cultures built on myths, beliefs and rituals – that is to say, societies that were in many ways not so different from our own. In particular, Conard turns to the recent discovery of two tiny ivory birds at the site to explore why he believes a sophisticated symbolic culture may have given humans an evolutionary advantage over other hominins, including Neanderthals.

European Union countries immobilised some €210 billion ($235.73 billion) of Russian central bank assets after Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Around €185 billion of this is held in Brussels-based central securities depository Euroclear.

Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:00:36 UTC
19:00:36 KST

A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.
