Psilocybin appears to strengthen this optical illusion, but LSD microdoses do not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

New research indicates that very low doses of LSD can make the world look blurrier, more colorful, and more dynamic to participants, even without causing full hallucinogenic trips. However, the drug did not appear to change how strongly people experienced a visual illusion that depends on the surrounding scene. The findings were published in Neuroscience of Consciousness.
To make sense of what we see, the visual cortex, the brain region at the back of the head that processes sight, takes the surrounding scene into account. One result is an illusion called contrast surround suppression: a striped pattern looks fainter, or lower in contrast, when it is surrounded by a bold, high-contrast pattern. Scientists think this happens partly because activity in brain cells responding to the surround dampens the response of cells responding to the center.
Classic psychedelics such as LSD and psilocybin produce their effects mainly by activating a type of serotonin receptor, a chemical docking site on brain cells. A study covered by PsyPost in 2022, which analyzed more than 6,000 written accounts of psychedelic trips, linked descriptions of altered sensory perception to areas of the visual cortex rich in serotonin receptors.
Previous experiments suggest that psychedelics can change how strongly the brain relies on visual context. For example, a 2019 study of mice showed that a psychedelic drug reduced surround suppression in the visual cortex.
In humans, however, the effect might go the other direction. A small 2024 pilot study of six volunteers found that a high dose of psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, made a similar contrast illusion stronger, and that people with more intense visual effects showed bigger changes.
Adding to this evidence, a 2025 study found that low to moderate doses of psilocybin made people more susceptible to the Ebbinghaus illusion, in which a circle looks larger or smaller depending on the size of the circles around it. Together, these findings suggest that psilocybin can change how the human brain uses surrounding visual context.
Some people take very small amounts of psychedelics, known as microdoses, in hopes of boosting their mood or creativity. However, a second study covered by PsyPost in 2022 found that repeated LSD microdoses did not reliably improve mood or cognitive performance compared with a placebo, though the higher dose produced small increases in feelings of vigor. The new study tests whether these very low doses might still objectively alter basic visual perception.
The research, led by Lucca Jaeckel, a doctoral student at the Translational Psychiatry Lab at the University of Basel’s Department of Psychiatry, aimed to test whether a low dose of a different psychedelic, LSD, would produce changes like those seen with psilocybin. “There are different theories about how psychedelic drugs cause altered visual perception,” Jaeckel told PsyPost.
“A few studies, two of which investigated psilocybin in humans, have shown alterations in a neural phenomenon called surround suppression, where brain responses to a stimulus at some location in the visual field are suppressed by stimulation in the surrounding area,” he explained. “One way to study surround suppression is through studying visual illusions. The previous studies showed that psilocybin could enhance the illusory amplification of perceived stimulus size and the illusory suppression of stimulus contrast, which are both linked with these surround suppression mechanisms.”
“We wanted to see if LSD microdoses (10 and 20 μg) affect these processes in the same way as psilocybin, using a contrast discrimination task in healthy human participants,” Jaeckel said.
The researchers conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, analyzing data from 31 healthy adults who completed at least two sessions. Each participant was scheduled for three testing sessions at least a week apart, receiving a placebo in one, 10 micrograms of LSD in another, and 20 micrograms in the third. Neither the participants nor the researchers knew which substance was given on which day until the study concluded. The participants averaged 28 years old, and about half had used psychedelics before.
Four hours after taking the dose, the participants completed a visual contrast task on a computer. On each of 100 trials, they saw two circular patches of drifting light and dark stripes for one second. One patch sat in the center of the screen inside a ring of high-contrast stripes, while the other appeared off to the side with no ring.
The participants pressed a key to indicate which patch looked higher in contrast. Because the surrounding ring creates a suppressing illusion, people typically underestimate the contrast of the center patch.
Throughout the testing days, participants also filled out detailed questionnaires about their subjective experiences. They rated how they felt on sliding scales, answering questions about whether their vision seemed sharper or blurrier, brighter or darker, more or less saturated with color, and static or dynamic. They also rated broader psychological feelings, such as whether they felt a sense of boundary dissolution or visionary changes.
These subjective measures were examined in exploratory analyses, meaning they were not part of the plan the researchers registered in advance. On a 100-point scale, ratings of “any drug effect” rose by about 17 points at 20 micrograms and about 5 points at 10 micrograms. The 20-microgram dose also produced a mildly altered state of consciousness, with higher scores for visionary changes, oceanic boundlessness (pleasant feelings such as bliss and insightfulness), and reduced alertness. These increases were small, amounting to roughly 2 to 5 percent of each scale’s maximum.
Visually, participants reported that 20 micrograms made colors look more saturated, made the world seem more dynamic, as if things were in motion, and made their vision blurrier. Even the 10-microgram dose made vision slightly blurrier than placebo, while brightness ratings did not change. These shifts were modest, between about 3 and 7 points on a scale running 50 points in either direction from “normal.”
At the end of each session, participants guessed which treatment they had received. They identified the placebo and the 20-microgram dose at better-than-chance rates, but not the 10-microgram dose.
“There is considerable disagreement as to what dose of a psychedelic constitutes a microdose,” Jaeckel noted. “We used doses of 10 and 20 μg which are often considered microdoses.”
“Some people would argue a microdose is a dose that does not noticeably affect conscious state,” he explained. “Interestingly, our 10 μg dose was not identified as an active dose beyond chance level, yet we could show a small effect of that low dose on subjective visual perception.”
Despite these subjective changes in how the world looked, the objective task results told a different story. Of the 93 completed sessions, 68 sessions from 24 participants met the researchers’ quality criteria; most of the rest were excluded because the responses suggested participants had misunderstood or could not perform the task. In the remaining data, the task reliably produced the illusion, but LSD did not measurably change its strength. A statistical analysis designed to weigh evidence for and against an effect strongly favored no effect of the drug.
The researchers also checked whether participants who reported the biggest changes in their visual perception at 20 micrograms showed bigger changes on the task. They found no correlation, unlike the 2024 psilocybin pilot study, which had linked more intense visual effects to stronger suppression. This suggests that, at these doses, the conscious feeling of altered vision can occur without changes in the brain’s early, automatic filtering of visual contrast.
“Unlike psilocybin, LSD did not affect spatial context-related contrast perception as would be expected from altered surround suppression. At the same time, we did find subjective alterations to visual perception,” Jaeckel said. “This indicates that alterations in surround suppression are not necessary for the perceptual alterations induced by LSD. Nevertheless, it may be that psychedelics affect surround suppression at higher doses where this may affect visual perception.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Because participants could often tell when they had received the 20-microgram dose or the placebo, expectations may have inflated their subjective ratings. The authors argue that expectations alone are unlikely to explain the visual effects, noting that some sources describe low-dose psychedelics as making vision sharper, the opposite of the blurriness participants reported.
The authors suggest the most likely reason for the lack of an objective effect is the low dose. Based on a direct comparison study, 20 micrograms of LSD is roughly equivalent to 4 milligrams of psilocybin, far below the 25-milligram dose used in the 2024 contrast study and slightly below the 5-milligram dose that affected the size illusion in the 2025 study.
Low doses of LSD may change conscious perception without being strong enough to shift early visual processing. LSD also acts on dopamine receptors in ways psilocybin does not, and the authors speculate that these effects, which may emerge later in the drug’s time course, could have counteracted any change in surround suppression.
There are a few other things to keep in mind regarding the study design. The contrast task was administered four hours after the participants took the drug, past the absolute peak of the drug’s effects. Additionally, participants were asked to avoid caffeine before and during sessions, because caffeine can itself influence brain activity measures and surround suppression. For regular caffeine users, withdrawal or fatigue four hours into the session may have made it harder to maintain focus.
Future studies could build on these findings by testing higher doses of LSD to see if the contrast illusion eventually shifts, or by testing participants earlier in the drug’s timeline. For now, the evidence indicates that while low doses of LSD can make the world seem more colorful, blurry, and dynamic, they did not measurably change how the brain handles this contrast illusion.
“This is the first publication from a larger study investigating how LSD affects how different kinds of context are used toward making choices about perceptual stimuli,” Jaeckel told PsyPost. “So there’ll be more data coming out soon.”
One of the study’s co-authors, Matthias Liechti, serves as a consultant for Mind Medicine, a company developing LSD-based treatments, and Lykos Therapeutics.
The study, “Low-dose lysergic acid diethylamide alters subjective visual perception but not visual contrast surround suppression,” was authored by Lucca F. Jaeckel, Deborah Logvinski, Mika Kanana, Felix Müller, Nicolai Rohner, Anna M. Becker, Matthias E. Liechti, and Philipp Sterzer.

Demining coalition hands Ukraine new Inguar armored vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

- Ukraine’s Support Forces received a new batch of equipment from the Lithuania- and Iceland-led Demining Capability Coalition, including Ukrainian-made Inguar-3 armored vehicles.
- The Inguar-3 is a Kyiv-built MRAP rated to withstand 7.62 mm armor-piercing rounds, 155 mm shell fragments and an 8 kg mine blast.
Ukraine’s Support Forces, the branch that runs the military’s engineering and demining units, have received another batch of equipment from the international Demining Capability Coalition led by Lithuania and Iceland, including Ukrainian-built Inguar-3 mine-resistant armored vehicles.
The Support Forces Command announced the handover on Oct. 15 but did not list the full contents of the delivery or the number of vehicles. Maj. Gen. Dmytro Herega, the command’s commander, thanked partners for their steady support and said engineering units need reliable equipment to carry out both combat and humanitarian demining.
The Inguar-3 is a mine-resistant ambush protected vehicle, or MRAP, designed and built by Kyiv-based Inguar Defence on its own chassis rather than an adapted commercial truck. The manufacturer rates its steel and aluminum armor to STANAG 4569 Level 3, the NATO standard covering protection against 7.62 mm armor-piercing rounds, fragments from a 155 mm shell bursting 60 meters (about 200 feet) away, and an 8 kg (18-pound) mine blast under the hull. A 356-horsepower Deutz diesel and an Allison automatic gearbox drive the vehicle, which also has central tire inflation and run-flat inserts so crews can keep moving after a puncture.
Before entering service, the Inguar-3 covered about 10,000 km (6,200 miles) of trials, including combat testing with the National Guard’s Azov brigade in the Serebryansky Forest, and won its first orders from Ukrainian military customers in early 2025, The Defense Post reported. Inguar Defence later took the vehicle to the Eurosatory 2026 exhibition in Paris.
For deminers, a vehicle with that level of protection matters because sapper teams often work close to the front line, where they face mines along routes as well as artillery and drone strikes while moving between clearance sites.
Lithuania launched the Demining Capability Coalition in 2023 and invited Iceland to co-lead it, and the group now includes 23 member countries along with observers and partner organizations. Member states paid about 150 million euros ($168 million) into the coalition fund in 2024–2026, and the coalition used that money to buy and send Ukraine 89 million euros ($100 million) worth of equipment, the Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence said in June. Separately, Ukraine has received 608 million euros ($681 million) in donated demining equipment from countries including Germany, Lithuania, Finland and Denmark.
The coalition’s purchases have ranged from mine detectors and explosive ordnance disposal kits to trucks, ambulances, mine rollers and electronic warfare systems. At its June meeting in Lviv, the group handed over trucks, MRAP armored vehicles and minibuses bought with the fund.
Lithuanian officials describe Ukraine as the most heavily mine-contaminated country in the world, and the coalition plans to spend at least 165 million euros ($185 million) in 2026 on equipment, machinery and specialist training for Ukrainian demining units.

Press review: Ukraine, EU push peace away and US blacks out Kiev's missile sight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Ukraine and the EU continue to show that they are not peace-minded; the US is no longer warning Kiev about Russian missile attacks; and Germany’s authorities face mounting pressure over the Nord Stream blast investigation. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Ukraine, EU keep peace off the table
The course of action pursued by Kiev and its European allies is doing little to bring talks on Ukraine any closer. The European Union is discussing a new package of sanctions on Moscow and may try to undermine the recently agreed diesel deal between Russia and the United States, moves that Moscow sees as contradicting its claims that it is ready to join peace talks, Izvestia writes.
There is no basis for negotiations with Britain, Germany and France at this point as they seem content to speak to Moscow through a series of ultimatums and meaningless sanction packages, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told the newspaper.
The EU is set to continue its policy of maximum military and diplomatic support for Kiev, regardless of the cost. Besides, European elites will keep strengthening ties between Ukraine and the EU in various ways, European studies expert Mikhail Kucherov noted.
Meanwhile, efforts to settle the Ukraine conflict remain at a standstill. It's worth noting that the US appears to have adopted a different approach than Europe, resuming partial pressure on the Kiev regime. First, media reports surfaced that Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing with the Ukrainian armed forces, followed by reports from the Ukrainian military of disruptions and restrictions affecting satellite internet services.
Oleg Karpovich, department head at the Diplomatic Academy of the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, pointed out that this pressure on Kiev was aimed primarily at ending strikes on Russian oil refineries and stabilizing diesel prices. Still, the parties remain too far apart to reach a settlement. The US has repeatedly flip-flopped on who it supports, but this has never led to any long-term solutions, the expert stressed.
If Russia and the US develop a joint peace plan, the EU is unlikely to accept it because the bloc’s interests are now totally opposed to those of Moscow, Kucherov said. Europe may instead seek to strengthen the Coalition of the Willing and draw up its own peace initiative.
A shift toward a really effective settlement process would require the US to put pressure on its allies in Europe. It’s the Europeans that are showing no willingness to engage in dialogue with Russia, seeking to increase support for Kiev and prevent the normalization of relations between Moscow and Washington.
Kommersant: US no longer warning Kiev about Russian missile attacks
Kiev hasn't received any US data on Russian ballistic missile launches for at least two days, the Ukrainian authorities claim. On October 14, Ukraine also reported disruptions to Starlink services, Kommersant writes.
Reports emerged on October 9 that the United States could suspend weapons supplies and intelligence sharing with Ukraine unless Kiev halted strikes on Russian refineries. On October 12, the Ukrainian armed forces reported that they had not received US early-warning data on ballistic missile attacks. As a result, air raid sirens in Kiev were not activated until after the strike. The next day, the same thing happened.
Ilya Kramnik, a research fellow with the Center for North American Studies at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, explained that the early-warning data in question allows air defense systems to be readied by identifying the direction of the attack and its potential targets.
"If early-warning data is unavailable, enemy missiles can be detected only once they enter the range of air defense radars, which significantly complicates defensive operations. Radars must remain on permanently, which increases the risk of their being destroyed. Besides, continuous operation wears those systems down," the expert said. This will further aggravate Ukraine’s already existing air defense problems, he added.
Talking about Starlink disruptions, Kramnik said they will affect the Ukrainian army’s strike capabilities. A speed limit of 160 km/h means that Kiev will not be able to use Starlink terminals on drones. This would reduce Ukraine’s ability to strike targets within its 1991 borders, Kramnik explained, as Starlink services are not available in Russian territory.
"This is a fairly powerful way to hint at the need to accept certain conditions for participating in the peace process. However, it remains to be seen if this works as intended," the expert concluded.
Media: German authorities face mounting pressure over Nord Stream blast investigation
The Alternative for Germany party plans to send further inquiries to the German government regarding the investigation into the explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines, a Bundestag member told Izvestia. Meanwhile, the trial of the first defendant in the case has begun in Hamburg. According to the prosecution, the act of sabotage was carried out on orders from Kiev.
The trial has drawn unprecedented attention for several reasons. First, the case concerns one of the largest acts of international sabotage in modern history. Second, the defendant is a citizen of Ukraine, a country that Berlin has been actively supporting for several years, by providing both funds and weapons.
However, even if evidence is found of government involvement in the attack, Germany is unlikely to change its policy on assistance to Kiev, said Fyodor Basov, a senior researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations. In his view, the attack against the Nord Stream pipelines could be classified as an act of self-defense. Still, the trial has just begun, and it is too early to assess its potential political consequences, the expert added.
The German authorities have found themselves in a difficult situation. Acknowledging Ukraine's involvement in the attack would confirm Moscow’s assertion that the Kiev leadership poses a security threat to all of Europe. On the other hand, concealing the investigation’s findings would undermine Germany’s key principles of the rule of law and judicial transparency, Denis Denisov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, pointed out. As long as Berlin tries to sit on the fence, its official policy toward Kiev will not change.
Nevertheless, European authorities will eventually have to choose which way to go, Denisov said. They will have to officially acknowledge that Ukraine is to blame for undermining the competitiveness of European manufacturers and creating systemic energy security problems for Europe. Alternatively, European politicians could once again turn a blind eye to the issue, disregarding the enormous damage inflicted on their own citizens, the political scientist emphasized. The latter scenario could trigger a further collapse in the approval ratings of Germany’s ruling coalition.
The case is of great political importance for Berlin, and there are serious doubts about whether the court will be able to remain impartial, Rossiyskaya Gazeta notes. Earlier, the court barred the pipeline operators, Nord Stream AG and Nord Stream 2 AG, from taking part in the proceedings. Even Germans don’t believe that the truth will emerge. Experts doubt the trial will establish that the attack was authorized by government officials.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Houthi attacks threaten to trigger another global economic shock
Yemeni Houthis are threatening further attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities, while strikes on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue. Attacks on the Middle East’s largest oil producer will further hurt the global outlook, Nezavisimaya Gazeta writes.
Saudi Arabia’s economy is important both for the region and the entire world, which is why the current developments could affect everyone, without exaggeration, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned. "If further strikes target oil pipelines, processing facilities or export terminals, it will become harder to offset supply shortfalls. This could drive fuel prices and transportation costs up, accelerate global inflation, and slow the global economy," Freedom Global analyst Vladimir Chernov specified.
As for Russia, the International Energy Agency estimates that the country’s total oil export revenues rose by $3.58 billion in September amid increasing global oil prices. However, these gains may turn out to be short-lived. "A prolonged crisis will weaken global demand. In the current situation, Russia may benefit from a temporary increase in prices but it would be wrong to view further tensions as a beneficial factor," Chernov said.
Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure have given Russia a short-term windfall, agrees Oleg Abelev, head of analytics at the Ricom Trust investment company. However, the advantages are being offset by discounts, sanctions, Ukrainian strikes and structural economic problems, the expert added.
Meanwhile, Finam analyst Nikolay Dudchenko does not rule out that Houthi strikes could trigger a further escalation of violence and draw the United States into the conflict. "If the Americans intervene, US ships and facilities in the Red Sea region could come under attack, which would also keep oil prices high," the expert said.
Izvestia: Logistics issues cloud Russian food export prospects
Russia’s agricultural trade gained significant momentum in the January to August period of 2026, with food exports rising faster than imports. However, the increase stems largely from favorable global prices, while serious damage to export terminals sustained at the end of the summer raises questions about whether the current trend will persist, Izvestia writes.
According to the World Bank, average food prices were 6.7% higher in the first eight months of the year compared to 2025. That said, the rise in dollar-denominated revenues does not necessarily mean a corresponding increase in actual export volumes, Alexander Firanchuk, leading researcher at the Presidential Academy’s Laboratory of International Trade of the Presidential Academy, observed.
Southern Russia’s transport infrastructure suffered a serious blow at the end of the summer. Darya Snitko, head of Gazprombank’s Department for Economic Forecasting, confirms that agricultural exports have declined considerably since August due to disruptions to shipping through Black Sea ports.
The disruption of the usual and cheapest sea route is forcing traders and producers to look for alternatives. Shipments are being redirected to rail transport and ports on the Baltic and Caspian seas. The forced redirection of flows is increasing transportation costs and reducing profits, even amid high global prices. Food exports are unlikely to return to previous levels until port operations in the country's south are fully restored and shipment processes normalize, Firanchuk said.
In short, Russia’s agricultural sector is currently in a state of uncertainty. On the one hand, rising fertilizer and energy prices driven by the Middle East crisis have prepared the global market for high-priced Russian exports. But on the other hand, damage to port infrastructure presents an obstacle that cannot be fixed through financial measures alone. Russia’s ability to resume profitable food exports will depend largely on how quickly Black Sea terminals are restored and whether transport companies can optimize more expensive alternative delivery routes.

The ladder of knowledge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
20 minute listen
On the evening of 8 September 1930, the German mathematician David Hilbert stepped up to a microphone in Königsberg and addressed his countrymen by radio. He was 68, recently retired, and at the height of his fame. The talk was a defence of pure reason, delivered in the city of Immanuel Kant, and it ended with two phrases that would later be carved on his tombstone: Wir müssen wissen. Wir werden wissen. We must know. We shall know.
Are certain questions closed to the human mind? Are there truths about the world that we can never know? Hilbert thought that, at least within mathematics, this could not be the case. For him, mathematics was a game played with symbols: one could fix the right axioms as rules of the game and every mathematical problem could be solved. He was wrong.
The day before his Königsberg address, at a small academic meeting in the same city, a 24-year-old Austrian named Kurt Gödel had quietly announced that no such system for arithmetic could exist. Whatever reasonable set of rules you fix, something true must lie beyond them and thus beyond our knowledge. We can’t know. We won’t know. Gödel’s results, known as the Incompleteness Theorems, are landmark achievements of 20th-century logic. Recent work in philosophy and mathematics has begun to illuminate the gap they opened, and with it something deeper about the foundations of knowledge itself. The story begins in the same city, but two centuries earlier.
When Kant remembered a book by David Hume he’d read years earlier, he was woken from what he called his ‘dogmatic slumber’. Kant had believed that pure reasoning could teach us every absolute truth about the world, but Hume had asked a question that that stumped him: what reason do we actually have to believe that the future will resemble the past? We may have seen the Sun rise a thousand times, but how do we know it will rise tomorrow? The belief that the future will resemble the past is, Hume argued, merely a kind of habit. Kant couldn’t answer Hume’s challenge and was silenced for a decade.
For Hume, proving a theorem was like unpacking a suitcase to find an outfit. Kant could not leave it there
When Kant finally broke his silence with the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), he offered a radical answer. We can know the world only as it appears to our minds, and that is where our science sits; the noumenal world – the Ding an sich (the ‘thing-in-itself’) – simply lies beyond our reach. Causation is not something we discover in the world, but something the mind supplies for experience to be coherent at all. When we watch a cat push a glass off a table, we don’t see a bare sequence of motions and then infer, by some metaphysical principle, that the push caused the fall. No: we see the push as causing the fall. The causal structure is not a hypothesis we add to the experience; it is part of how the experience comes to us in the first place. It is in our minds already.
So far, so good: Kant has met Hume’s challenge, and the workings of science are intelligible: we are structuring our experiences. But the work is not done, for there remains mathematics, the very language in which the sciences are framed. Hume was content that arithmetic and algebra are merely the unpacking of definitions; that proving a theorem is like unpacking a suitcase to find an outfit. Kant could not leave it there. If mathematics were only such unpacking, how could it underwrite the sciences? Either the sciences tell us nothing new about the world, or something has gone missing from the account.
Does one unpack ‘add 7 and 5’ to find ‘12’? Kant thought not. Rather, one constructs 12 from 7 and 5 in the mind. More than a century later, a young Dutch mathematician called L E J Brouwer, following Kant’s thought, argued that, if the mathematician’s work consists in such mental constructions, then one cannot assume any statement is either true or false. That was controversial: to strip the mathematician of that assumption, Hilbert retorted, would be like ‘proscribing … to the boxer the use of his fists’.
Gottlob Frege, working in the late 19th century, found Kant’s account of mathematics intolerable for different reasons: arithmetic, he claimed, is not psychological. The numbers exist whether anyone counts them or not. He set about reducing arithmetic to pure logic, grounded in the mind-independent categories of True and False. The project consumed two decades of his life and produced some of the most consequential advances in the philosophy of language and mathematics in history. It is widely regarded as having sparked the modern discipline of logic. And yet, as the second volume of his masterwork, the Grundgesetze der Arithmetik, sat at the printer in 1902, the foundations cracked. The British philosopher Bertrand Russell sent Frege a letter pointing out an inconsistency at the heart of the system. A melancholy note in his diary later summed up his defeat: ‘My efforts to become clear about what is meant by number have resulted in failure.’
Russell had been wrestling with the foundations of mathematics for some years before his letter. It was only after meeting the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano at the International Congress of Philosophy in 1900 that he acquired the tools to attempt the problem. In place of Frege’s edifice, Russell set out to build his own, together with his colleague Alfred North Whitehead. Principia Mathematica appeared in three massive volumes between 1910 and 1913: all of mathematics, grounded in pure logic.
Mathematics carries what’s already there without adding anything, as plumbing moves water without supplying any
Russell’s student Ludwig Wittgenstein spent the war in the Austro-Hungarian artillery, volunteering again and again for the most exposed posts he could find – an observation position under fire on the Eastern Front, from which he was decorated for bravery at least three times. He carried notebooks. In them, between bombardments, he worked the Frege-Russell philosophy into a complete account of how language touches the world: the world is made of facts, a sentence is a picture of a fact, and whatever can be said at all can be said clearly. He finished the manuscript in an Italian prisoner-of-war camp in 1918 and sent it to Russell from the camp. Wittgenstein took himself to have solved the problems of philosophy, gave away his inherited fortune, and left to teach primary school in the Austrian mountains.
The Tractatus became the manifesto of a group of philosophers in Vienna including Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap and Otto Neurath, who called their position logical positivism. A statement is meaningful only if there is some way of settling whether it is true. Analytic statements are settled by unfolding the definitions of the words involved: for example, ‘All bachelors are unmarried’ is true because a bachelor is, by definition, an unmarried man. Synthetic statements are claims about the world, and are settled by – in principle – going out and looking: ‘It rained in Vienna on 3 June 1929’ is false because one could have observed that the sky over the Ringstrasse stayed clear that day. Anything else is grammar without content.
The Vienna Circle, as they became known, claimed that mathematics is analytic and science is synthetic. The function of mathematics is to extract information from scientific claims: it carries what is already there without adding anything, the way plumbing moves water without supplying any. If the Vienna Circle were right, then Kant’s and Brouwer’s restrictions on scientific and mathematical knowledge were entirely unnecessary. If.
By 1929, after almost three decades of labours by Hilbert, Russell, Frege, Wittgenstein, the Vienna Circle and Brouwer, among others, the foundations of mathematics looked very nearly finished. One beam remained that would lock the whole frame together. In the plenary addresses for the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris in 1900, Hilbert had set out 23 problems that would define the next century of the subject. The second problem was this: prove that arithmetic is consistent – that is, no chain of reasoning from the axioms, however long, would yield a contradiction. The beam would not go in.
While studying physics at the University of Vienna in the 1920s, Gödel had attended Schlick’s seminar on Russell, which drew him into the problems of logic and, by way of them, into Hilbert’s programme. His PhD in 1929 showed that the standard system of first-order logic is complete – every logically valid statement can, in principle, be derived from the axioms of logic. It was the result Hilbert wanted, though for pure logic rather than mathematics. A year later, he turned to the natural next step: the consistency of arithmetic, Hilbert’s second problem.
What he announced at the Königsberg meeting the day before Hilbert’s radio address, no one had expected. Taking Principia Mathematica as the articulation of mathematics within logic, Gödel showed that there were true mathematical statements that cannot be proved using the resources of Principia Mathematica alone. Among them is the statement ‘Principia Mathematica is consistent.’ The trick at the heart of the proof is to encode statements about the system within the system itself – a move with the same vertiginous quality as Russell’s letter to Frege. But where Russell’s letter had killed a system, Gödel’s theorem killed a programme.
The one-time prophet of the Vienna Circle left nothing of its philosophy standing
His argument was so general that it applied to any reasonable system for arithmetic. Hilbert’s dream of an axiomatic system capturing all of mathematics – or even just arithmetic – was over.
The response in Vienna was disbelief, then dismay. The Circle had built its philosophy on the assumption that mathematics was analytic; Gödel had shown it wasn’t as simple as that. Carnap struggled for years to absorb the result. Wittgenstein dismissed it, but was already repudiating the Tractatus himself. Meaning, he came to argue, lay not in matching picture to reality but simply in how people discourse in public. The one-time prophet of the Circle left nothing of its philosophy standing.
Hilbert never publicly conceded that Gödel’s result doomed his programme. He died in 1943; his colleagues had by then been murdered or exiled by the Nazis. His tombstone in Göttingen bears the words he had spoken into the Königsberg microphone: Wir müssen wissen. Wir werden wissen. We must know. We shall know.
And Gödel? After the Anschluss, he escaped Vienna for Princeton, where he continued to make extraordinary contributions to logic while taking long walks with his close friend Albert Einstein. At his American citizenship exam in 1947, asked by the judge whether a regime like the Nazis’ could arise in the United States, he began to explain a logical loophole he had found in the Constitution that would permit exactly that. The judge cut him off and moved the proceedings swiftly to their conclusion. (We still don’t know what loophole he found.)
The orthodox response was to keep the truth and give up the proof. There is a realm of mathematical fact, standing independent of us, and axiomatic systems reach only part of it; incompleteness measures the distance between what is so and what we can show. Its most committed advocate was Gödel himself. However, two problems come with the realm. First, with logical positivism in ruins, Kant’s problem returns: if mathematical truth is independent of the mind, how can it structure sciences that exist within the mind? Second, the realm is posited chiefly to spare us two unwelcome alternatives – psychologism on one side, Brouwer’s restrictions on the other. Avoiding two conclusions is not an argument for a third.
In 1973, the British philosopher Michael Dummett was invited to deliver the annual philosophical lecture at the British Academy. He took as his subject ‘The Justification of Deduction’ – how to justify the ordinary practices of mathematicians without helping oneself to the assumption that their subject matter exists in a realm of its own. The problem, he told his audience, was perhaps ‘one of the most fundamental and intractable problems … in all philosophy’.
Dummett was the great Frege scholar of the 20th century; his Frege: Philosophy of Language (1973) brought an otherwise obscure figure to the forefront of the discipline. The book had been years in the writing, but in 1964, with the manuscript all but finished, Dummett put down his pen. He conceived it his duty, he explains in the preface, to involve himself ‘actively in opposition to the racism which was becoming more and more manifest in English life.’ When he returned to the manuscript several years later, a previously suppressed fragment of Frege’s Nachlass (ie, his literary estate) had surfaced, revealing the philosopher as a ‘virulent racist’ with ‘extreme Right-wing political opinions’. Once his book was finally published, Dummett recorded the bitter irony, and reflected that he had learned something dark about how a mind he revered could harbour views he despised.
Our linguistic practices – the ways in which we are prepared to assert, justify and infer – determine logic
What Dummett took from Frege’s work on logic was that the problems of mathematics are, at heart, problems of language. Where things had gone wrong, he thought, was that Frege had grounded his account in a mind-independent notion of truth. ‘In this respect (and in this respect alone),’ Dummett wrote, ‘Frege’s new approach to logic was retrograde.’ For Frege, logic answered to truth: the rules were good because they preserved something already fixed. Dummett turned this around.
Following Wittgenstein’s later thinking, Dummett argued ‘a theory of meaning is a theory of understanding.’ And understanding, he insisted, must be manifestable: whatever a competent speaker knows in knowing what a sentence means must be something she can, in principle, display in her use of language. In The Logical Basis of Metaphysics (1991), Dummett gave this account of language, logic and reality its most sustained form. Our linguistic practices – the ways in which we are prepared to assert, justify and infer – determine logic. Logic, in turn, determines what counts as a fact, what counts as truth, and ultimately what we are entitled to regard as real.
Consider how a child learns the word ‘red’. We do not begin by telling her about light of a certain wavelength, or the metaphysics of colour properties, or the conditions that would make ‘this is red’ true. We point at things. We correct her when she calls a ripe tomato green; we approve when she calls a fire engine red. Over time, she comes to use the word as we do – and at that point, she understands it. There is no further fact, hidden behind the practice, in which her understanding consists. The understanding is the practice, competently exercised.
Dummett died in 2011, having been knighted in 1999 for ‘services to philosophy and to racial justice’. He is remembered as one of the most significant British philosophers of the previous century. Yet for all its power, his programme remained a prospectus: he set out what a theory of language, logic and reality must achieve, but he never completed one.
In 2005, Tor Sandqvist, a doctoral student at Uppsala University, submitted a thesis that took up Dummett’s challenge: to justify the ordinary practices of mathematicians without any appeal to truth. Where Dummett had given the conditions a solution must satisfy, Sandqvist gave a solution. He produced a precise mathematical justification of deduction as mathematicians actually use it, grounded entirely in practices of assertion. The boxer’s fists were untied.
It was rediscovered a decade later in the Department of Computer Science at University College London, where a group of logicians recognised what Sandqvist had actually built, and developed it into a full framework on a par with the orthodox truth-conditional view. The framework now stands equal to the truth-based account, analogous to the situation after Gödel’s PhD thesis. What about mathematics? The UCL team have recently shown that the Dummett-Sandqvist framework gives a way to understand what Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems are about, and it is not the limits of knowledge.
If meaning comes from practices of assertion, then our concepts are settled only as far as our practices have settled them. A system of definitions is a kind of constitution that determines something. The US Constitution, for example, is meant to enshrine a form of democracy. But what a constitution defines answers to how it is amended.
An amendment can betray what a constitution defines. But it can also unfold it
Principia Mathematica is a constitution for arithmetic. To read it as a constitution is to assume it is consistent; otherwise, it would be nonsense. So, when we amend it by asserting that ‘Principia Mathematica is consistent,’ we are not changing the subject: the new axiom says aloud only what the practice already did. Gödel’s theorems apply afresh to the enlarged constitution: the amended system has its own unprovable truth, its own consistency it cannot certify. No amendment is the last; each faithful extension opens room for the next. To grasp a concept like arithmetic is not to survey a finished structure; it is to hold a principle for going on: a rule for laying the next stretch of line, not a map of where the line ends. Dummett called this openness indefinite extensibility.
Faithful is the word doing the work, because not every amendment is. Gödel claimed the US Constitution could deliver a dictatorship. That does not make dictatorship a form of democracy. Whatever loophole he had in mind, it would have contradicted the practices the Constitution already enshrined. An amendment can betray what a constitution defines. But it can also unfold it, drawing out what the founding commitments demanded all along. Only the second kind is what Dummett has in mind.
The constitution of our language is our current practice for public discourse. As it is extensible in this way, what we claim as ‘true’ is not a fixed structure with a ceiling we are forever failing to reach, but something that can change. Gödel’s verdict never applied to mathematics, but only to some edition of the constitution. Within the Sandqvist system, we can attend to the extension systematically. Hilbert’s words outlive his programme: Wir werden wissen. We shall know. Not because the answers are waiting at the end of a ladder, but because truth goes exactly as far as we have built the rungs.

‘Nightmare Scenario’: Zero-Click Spyware Is Infecting Phones via Targeted Ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

On Thursday, researchers from The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto revealed a worst-case scenario found in the wild: spyware silently infecting targets as they browse past ads in their daily digital lives.
Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.
Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk.
“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”
The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.
“The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.
During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.)
“The ability to push individualized, arbitrary content at specific users is a hallmark of the modern online ads ecosystem, and is perfectly suited to the mercenary spyware industry,” Marczak says. “Until this architecture changes, or ad companies get serious about customer vetting, we’re going to keep seeing this kind of abuse.”
Emails and messages sent to Discover-Tech and its CEO by WIRED did not receive a response before publication. Integrity Partners, which is believed to own Candiru’s assets, following sanctions by the US government in 2021, also did not respond to requests for comment.
Google, which operates one of the world’s largest advertising businesses, terminated Discover-Tech’s registration after collaborating with Citizen Lab and researchers from the cybersecurity firm Confiant and confirming a spyware link. “Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies,” a Google spokesperson says. “We also set up Safe Browsing warnings to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group.”
The European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), an ad industry body, confirmed to WIRED that it has suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list, known as the GVL. The company was suspended by IAB Europe following an audit of its policies, it says. “Further confirmation of the findings regarding spyware could also justify a definitive expulsion from the GVL,” a spokesperson for IAB Europe says.
A spokesperson for Beeswax, an online advertising industry company owned by Comcast, says in a statement: “Beeswax removed Discovery-Tech from our platform following recent activity and independent validation by a third-party security specialist. We maintain a zero-tolerance policy for malicious advertising.”
Often when you see ads online or in apps, they’re displayed following a complex process known as real-time bidding—essentially an automated auction where advertisers place bids to show you specific ads. The milliseconds-long process can result in advertisers collecting huge volumes of data about your device, your location, and browsing history, plus a whole lot more. The process has been a privacy nightmare for years, with murky data brokers selling people’s personal information, and law enforcement agencies and hostile nations buying it to track or target people.
The Citizen Lab researchers say that Discover-Tech operates an advertising platform, Controlium, that can allow its users to “de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices” once an ad appears. Overall, the researchers estimate that millions of devices were directed to Candiru’s servers, where they could be profiled. By analyzing ad-bidding records that were publicly exposed on the Discover-Tech website, the Citizen Lab researchers say, ads linked to the firm with attacker script tags were shown in more than 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June this year. Multiple apps, the researchers say, displayed more than a million ads linked to Discover-Tech.
The firm’s ads weren’t necessarily all weaponized to potentially distribute spyware, but the researchers say that, in general, they have seen Discover-Tech ad impressions on government and national-security-linked networks around the world. These include NATO and United Nations networks, as well as lawmaking bodies in Europe, critical infrastructure providers in Australia, plus armed forces and government agencies in Norway and Sweden.
Previous zero-click targeted ad campaigns that distribute spyware have rarely surfaced publicly, but the Citizen Lab researchers say this is likely a symptom of ad infrastructure being so extensively trusted and incorporated in all aspects of digital life without specific oversight.
“The network logs from Al Jazeera were key in understanding the ad-based nature of that attack,” Marczak says. “If a user’s personal device were targeted, say, while they were connected to their home Wi-Fi or mobile data, there’s not going to be the same level of network monitoring there. So I think the lack of prior reporting is probably mainly a visibility issue: Defenders have to be in the right place at the right time, looking at the right data.”
Speaking generally about threats that can result from the sheer ubiquity of the digital ad ecosystem, Jason Kint, CEO of the digital media trade organization Digital Content Next (WIRED parent company Condé Nast is a member), says these kinds of attacks are both plausible and damaging.
“Although rare and sophisticated, I wouldn’t be entirely surprised to learn about zero-click attacks through ads,” Kint says. “Anything that goes directly against users’ expectations or lowers the trust in the open web is deeply concerning.”

Ida-Viru County's only psychiatric hospital closes doors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:58:00 UTC
18:58:00 KST

Ida-Viru County's only psychiatric hospital closes doors
Ida-Viru County's only psychiatric hospital specializing in mental health treatment is closing due to a shortage of specialists.
Ahtme Hospital will continue providing inpatient mental health treatment services to Ida-Viru Central Hospital until next spring. According to Ahtme Hospital's chief physician, Georgi Belotserkovski, the main reason for the closure is a staff shortage. The first major change came a year ago when the hospital stopped accepting emergency patients.
"People will no longer receive proper treatment because not everyone can travel to Tartu or Tallinn. As a result, people's health will deteriorate, potentially leading to undesirable consequences. The population is also aging, meaning the number of age-related mental disorders is increasing, so there is a growing need for care," Belotserkovski said.
Ida-Viru Central Hospital is looking for solutions to the potential problems. It has increased its inpatient capacity, but this will not help all patients.
"They will not be left to fend for themselves, as has been suggested in the media. No, we will not abandon them. But it will take some more time before we can announce definitive solutions," said Ida-Viru Central Hospital's chief physician, Pille Letjuka.
Ida-Viru Central Hospital had planned for years to take over inpatient psychiatric services from Ahtme Hospital, but ultimately abandoned plans to build a new facility for patients with mental disorders.
"One reason was that we did not receive the funding we had initially been promised. The second reason is that even if we had received the funding and completed the new building, we would have no one to staff it," Letjuka said.
More than 5,000 patient consultations took place at Ahtme Psychiatric Hospital last year. Following the hospital's closure, there are plans to convert the facility into a nursing home.

Russia discussing additional phase for Bangladesh nuclear plant – Rosatom CEO

Unknown Publisher

Russia discussing additional phase for Bangladesh nuclear plant – Rosatom CEO
Russia is in discussions with Bangladesh to build a new phase of high-capacity units at the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant near Dhaka, Rosatom CEO Aleksey Likhachev said on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum.
Rooppur, built in collaboration with state-owned Rosatom, is the South Asian country’s first nuclear plant. Its first unit is on track to be connected to the national power grid by the end of November.
”We are primarily talking about a possible additional phase of large units,” Likhachev told reporters. “Although our Bangladeshi friends are also discussing small-capacity units and a research reactor with us, the main trend for future development, in my view, is increasing the capacity of the Rooppur NPP.”
He said Bangladesh has asked for proposals from Rosatom for “small nuclear power plants and floating nuclear power plants.”
The Rooppur plant comprises two Russian-designed reactors with a combined capacity of 2,400 megawatts. Moscow is financing $11.9 billion in state loans for the project, which is estimated to cost up to $12.8 billion.
Rosatom expects to begin commissioning the second unit of the Rooppur plant next year, Likhachev said. The first unit attained criticality – where a self-sustaining chain reaction occurs – on Sunday.
Russia is providing equipment, nuclear fuel, and engineering assistance for the project, and the plant is expected to meet up to 12% of Bangladesh’s electricity demand when completed.

CSTO peacekeepers practice repelling enemy attack on humanitarian convoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:57:19 UTC
18:57:19 KST

MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) peacekeepers have repelled an attack by a simulated enemy on a convoy carrying humanitarian aid as part of the Indestructible Brotherhood 2026 exercise in Belarus, Vladislav Shchegrikovich, press secretary for the CSTO Joint Staff, reported.
"At the Losvido training ground in the Republic of Belarus, during the Indestructible Brotherhood 2026 command and staff exercise involving CSTO peacekeeping forces, peacekeeping units repelled an attack by a simulated enemy on a convoy carrying humanitarian aid. The exercise focused on organizing the safe transit of vehicles and ensuring the unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid to the population. Particular attention was paid to the escorting of humanitarian cargoes, which required coordinated action among various units and the use of specialized equipment," the statement reads.
According to the exercise scenario, a simulated sabotage and reconnaissance group attacked the humanitarian convoy while it was in transit. "Motorized rifle units from a Central Military District formation, supported by BTR-82A armored personnel carriers, practiced repelling an attack using the standard weapons of their combat vehicles and AK-12 assault rifles. The BTR-82A crews used 30mm 2A72 automatic cannons and coaxial 7.62mm PKTM machine guns to provide fire support for the motorized rifle units and suppress the simulated enemy’s firing positions," Shchegrikovich reported.
"Mobile reserve groups were promptly deployed to provide fire support, successfully eliminating the remnants of a sabotage and reconnaissance group. "A damaged armored personnel carrier was successfully recovered by repair units using a REM-KL wheeled repair and recovery vehicle, which underscored the readiness of the collective forces to handle complex tasks in the field," he said.
The CSTO press secretary noted that during this phase of the exercise, the peacekeepers demonstrated determination and professionalism, while an electronic warfare (EW) system successfully neutralized several explosive devices, thereby minimizing casualties. "Although one vehicle sustained damage, the rest of the convoy quickly moved out of the line of fire and continued its advance," he added.
He pointed out that the movement of the mixed convoy was carried out under heavy, reinforced protection. "The airspace was monitored by a pair of Mi-35 helicopters providing air cover. The route was scouted using an unmanned aerial vehicle. To protect the convoy, a security detail was organized, comprising armored personnel carriers, a mobile fire support group, and electronic warfare systems," he noted.
Shchegrikovich emphasized that an electronic warfare system mounted on an all-terrain vehicle played a key role in ensuring security. "The automated electronic warfare system, capable of operating at a range of up to 500 meters, effectively suppresses radio emission sources--a capability that is critical for preventing the detonation of radio-controlled explosive devices," the press secretary said.
About the exercise
On October 11, the CSTO command and staff exercises Indestructible Brotherhood 2026 and Barrier 2026 began in Belarus. They involve over 1,500 military personnel and 300 pieces of weaponry, military hardware, and specialized equipment. Taking part in the exercises are troop contingents (Collective Forces) from the CSTO member states: Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan. These include military contingents, units of internal affairs bodies and national guard, as well as task groups of the CSTO Joint Staff and Secretariat. The Russian military contingent is primarily composed of units from a combined arms army of the Central Military District.

Estonia continues to maintain a Russian gas pipeline that crosses Võru County, allowing Russia to use it to supply the Königsberg region, reports ERR News.
The 22-kilometer-long section of the pipeline consists of two pipes, each 70 centimeters in diameter, which run from Russia through the southeastern corner of Estonian territory, continuing through Latvia and Lithuania toward Königsberg. This section is owned by Elering, the Estonian electricity and gas transmission system operator. Under an existing agreement, Russia uses it as an alternative supply route for Königsberg—for instance, in the event that the pipeline running directly through Lithuania or the floating terminal in Königsberg becomes inoperative. Russia requires the gas to operate power plants in the Königsberg region, which has become an energy-isolated enclave following the Baltic states' disconnection from the Russian electricity grid.
In July 2023, half a terawatt-hour of Russian natural gas—an amount equivalent to approximately 15% of Estonia's annual consumption—was transported through the pipeline. An equal volume of natural gas passed through Estonia again in the autumn of 2024.
The newspaper Eesti Ekspress reported that none of the politicians responsible for the sector in recent years had been aware of the agreement regarding the Russian gas pipeline.

Chinese automakers’ share continues to grow in European market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:55:16 UTC
18:55:16 KST

Yunus Turk and Emir Yildirim
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The rise in sales of Chinese electric and hybrid cars is reshaping the EU’s competitiveness in the bloc’s auto sector and trade balance with China, according to a recent report.
The European auto sector is experiencing structural changes due to ramping competition from Chinese manufacturers, a recent report from Allianz Trade showed.
Chinese automakers’ share in the EU rose from 2% to nearly 10% in recent years, while their sales across the continent exceeded 1 million units for the first time.
Chinese brands make up 16% of all electric vehicle (EV) market and 26% of the plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) market in Europe.
The European auto market grew 5% year-on-year in January-August, while the sales of fully electric cars surged 45%, accounting for 22% of new car registrations, matching gas cars.
Fully electric cars made up 30% of new car sales in France and 26% in Germany, while this rate was below 10% in Italy and Spain.
At the 2026 Paris Auto Show, Chinese brands’ share among participants rose from 23% in 2024 to 50% this year, while the share of European brands dropped from 68% to 39% over the same period.
 
Competitive price point
Chinese carmakers offer competitive prices, advanced technologies, and a growing after-sales service network, which have helped cement their prominence in the European market.
The EU used to run an automotive trade surplus with China, reaching €20 billion ($22.4 billion), but this trend reversed and the bloc started posting a trade deficit instead.
The EU’s auto exports to China declined over the past two years, while Chinese electric and hybrid car exports to the bloc doubled in the first half of this year, totaling $14.2 billion, while hybrid car shipments alone surged by a whopping 206%.
Chinese carmakers continued to grow in the European market despite the EU’s tariffs of up to 35% on Chinese-made EVs, as the manufacturers moved towards hybrid models in the face of these trade barriers.
The market share of three major German automakers declined in both Europe and China since 2021, while the added value that these manufacturers generated in Europe dropped by 30-45% in the first half of this year compared to 2021-2022.
German automakers could face additional losses of around €3 billion ($3.4 billion) in added value if they lose an additional three percentage points of market share in both markets by 2030, the report showed.
Chinese battery production capacity in Europe could rise from 15% to 37% by 2030 based on announced investment projects, while this rate could hit 45% if projects that have not yet been finalized are implemented.
Europe ran a battery trade deficit of €47 billion ($52.7 billion) in 2025 and €57 billion ($64 billion) as per annualized data as of July this year.
The report urged investments in battery technology, software, and semiconductors to be increased to ensure that the European auto sector can maintain its competitive edge.

Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:52:00 UTC
18:52:00 KST

Why Brazil's elections matter for the planet
October 15, 2026
Few national elections carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.
Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant.
Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.
"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.
"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."
Amazon rainforest: One of nature's most powerful defenses
The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.
For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation.
During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.
"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank Climate Analytics.
Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.
Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.
Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.
Pitting environment against the economy
Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.
"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest,'" said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Center at London-based think tank Chatham House.
"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.
Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.
"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.
More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.
"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.
In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.
No straightforward climate success story for Brazil
A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.
But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.
Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".
"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.
The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians climate is not high on their list of priorities.
"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.
"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.
Edited by: Tamsin Walker

Russia has nearly completed construction of a new base for launching jet-powered drones - Reuters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:51:35 EEST
18:51:35 KST

Russia has nearly completed construction of a new base for launching jet-powered drones - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
In Russia’s Rostov region, Russia has nearly completed construction of a base with eight launch pads. The facility is intended for Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones.
Russia has built a large-scale facility for launching jet-powered drones in the Rostov region near Ukraine in just six weeks. According to Reuters, the base will have at least eight launch sites and is intended, among other things, to launch Russia’s latest Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones, UNN writes.
Details
According to commercial satellite imagery provided by Planet Labs and Airbus, a site in the Rostov region in southwestern Russia that was an empty field on August 31 had by Wednesday been transformed into a large complex covering approximately 126 football fields.
The construction coincided with an increase in Russia’s use of jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine, which is finding it increasingly difficult to intercept the faster aircraft capable of reaching speeds of up to 600 km/h.
The full-scale war has been ongoing for a fifth year, and Kyiv expects Russia to further intensify its attacks with jet-powered drones and missiles this winter.
Mike Monnik, the founder and CEO of the private intelligence company DroneSec, said that the facility shown in the satellite imagery could be used to launch the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models — Russia’s newest jet-powered drones.
According to Monnik, eight sites with launch rails capable of launching such drones can be seen on the western edge of the complex. This would supplement Russia’s existing network of at least 11 fixed launch sites used for attacks on Ukraine.
The speed of construction … demonstrates how easily Russia can rapidly deploy already-established offensive capabilities
According to him, the facility appears to be almost complete, and it will probably take several weeks, if not less, before it is fully operational.
It covers an area of approximately 0.9 square kilometers and is located about 3.5 km from Russia’s Millerovo air base, home to the 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment.
According to DroneSec’s assessment, the new site is likely within the coverage zone of air defenses provided by systems at the air base. This makes Ukraine’s attempts to strike the new facility more difficult.
Reuters’ analysis indicates that launch rails have already been installed at two of the eight launch sites. Construction of the rails was ongoing at two more sites. Other construction work could also be observed from satellites over three days this week.

Albania’s leader defies calls to resign as student protesters rampage in capital
TIRANA, Oct 15 - Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Thursday rejected calls to resign as thousands of student-led protesters smashed windows and fought running battles with riot police firing water cannon and tear gas in the capital.
Protesters voiced anger about perceived corruption, the cost and quality of education and a deal to sell off parts of its pristine southern coastline to a luxury resort development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
They demanded Rama's resignation, saying no one had listened to their concerns during a summer of largely peaceful protests over the development.
In a written statement to Reuters, Rama rejected calls to quit.
"My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward. The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership," he said.
RAMA CONDEMNS ATTACKS ON PUBLIC PROPERTY
A student who gave her name as Kiara said the cost of living, poor job prospects, and alleged corruption were the main issues.
"Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption. You can only find work in your field if you know a guy who knows a guy," she said, her face covered by a mask, like many on the streets on Thursday.
The protests, now in their third day, mark the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who won a fourth term last year, with EU membership at the centre of his campaign. Parliament cancelled its session as the violence erupted again nearby.
Rama, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss the rising cost of education, but added: "Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate demands of students."
Tirana's streets were littered with burned out garbage bins, shattered bus stops and broken traffic lights.
Wafts of tear gas drifted across the centre. Protesters hurled stones at police, who used water cannon to push protesters back. In the central Skanderbeg Square, police hit fleeing protesters with batons as tourists looked on.
PROTESTER SAYS THEY ARE NOT BEING HEARD
"This government is corrupted, led and governed by a corrupt prime minister," protester Lulzim Tanushi, a lawyer, said. "Since Rama came to power he has abused and ruined people's lives and that is why people are showing their anger — when they were not heard before."
The protests follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by the plans to build the resort, which has faced legal challenges.
Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was wrongfully sold for development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors for drug trafficking, charges his lawyer denied.
Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute.
AIMING FOR EU ENTRY AS SOON AS 2028
Albania's image has been tarnished over the years by corruption scandals and political analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking, complicating its efforts to join the EU.
Along with Montenegro, Albania is currently leading the accession process among Balkan countries and is aiming for entry as early as 2028.
"Corruption must be confronted and, as the EU itself has recently reaffirmed, Albania is tackling it as never before," Rama said to Reuters.
"Perhaps some forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to succeed as a forerunner for EU membership. But I will not allow violence to derail Albania's European future."
A European Union mission to Albania in a statement on X said: "Constructive dialogue is the only way forward."
The unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education. REUTERS

Levine acknowledged that his earlier pledge was partly intended to counter calls for the city to support the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) protest movement targeting Israeli goods.
