Kazakh scientists set to reveal mystery of ancient silver headdress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:49:29 UTC
18:49:29 KST

Kazakh scientists set to reveal mystery of ancient silver headdress
Researchers from the Margulan University are carrying out a detailed study of a unique ancient silver headdress discovered in 1959 and preserved at the Pavlodar Regional Local History Museum, Qazinform News Agency cites the Science Ministry.
Specialists from the University's Institute of Archaeological Research are using X-ray fluorescence analysis to examine the artifact. The technique allows scientists to determine the metal's composition, investigate manufacturing methods, and gain new insights into the headdress's possible origins.
According to museum curator Yelena Tusheva, the artifact holds significant historical and scientific value and has remained one of the museum's most important exhibits for decades.
Preliminary findings indicate that the headdress is composed of approximately 97% silver. Researchers believe the results will help them better understand ancient metal-processing and purification technologies used in its production.
The next stage of the project will focus on identifying the manufacturing techniques that enabled craftsmen to create such a delicate and fragile object.
One of the key questions for researchers is how the artifact has survived for so long. In the climatic conditions of Eurasia, silver objects often deteriorate over time. Yet the headdress has remained remarkably well preserved, despite some of its components being only a few millimeters thick.
Scientists note that the discovery is unique not only because of its exceptionally fine craftsmanship, but also because no comparable artifacts from the same period have been found in Kazakhstan or neighboring regions.
Future research will seek to determine the artifact's origin. If sufficient data become available, specialists hope to identify the original silver source used in its manufacture.
The study is being carried out as part of a scientific cooperation project between the Margulan University and the Pavlodar Regional Local History Museum.
It should be noted, archaeologists uncovered six structures and a well-preserved coin at Kesken-Kuyuk, an early medieval settlement in the Kazaly district, Kyzylorda region.

IMF warns attacks on Saudi Arabia could hurt global economy after strike on Aramco headquarters

09:48:00 UTC

Aramco's headquarters has been hit, flights are suspended and oil prices are rising. The IMF warns that the economic fallout from attacks on Saudi Arabia could be felt worldwide.
The International Monetary Fund warned on Wednesday that attacks on Saudi Arabia could hurt economies worldwide, after a strike damaged oil giant Aramco's headquarters.
IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva pointed to Saudi Arabia’s economic importance.
“In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere,” she said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said an administrative building at Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran was hit on Tuesday evening, causing a limited fire. It said there were no deaths or injuries.
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility. The group has also attacked Saudi airports during renewed fighting with a Saudi-led coalition.
The building's top three floors, including chief executive Amin Nasser's office, were badly damaged, a person with direct knowledge told Reuters.
Two sources said operations at the complex were continuing as normal, although some employees had been told to work from home. Another said some work had moved to offices abroad.
Aramco oversees its oil rigs, refineries, export terminals and pipelines from a centre at its headquarters. The company had not responded to the news agency's request for comment.
Oil prices rose on Wednesday, with Brent crude trading above $106 a barrel. Aramco's shares fell 0.5% in early trading.
Air travel has also been disrupted. Lufthansa has suspended flights to Riyadh up to and including 18 November, according to its latest advisory.
Saudi Arabia plans to let executives join its Future Investment Initiative conference online after attacks on Riyadh airport, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the plans. The event is due to take place later this month.
Recovery depends on shipping
Saudi Arabia's economy was already under pressure from the Iran war and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The IMF expects it to shrink by 3.3% this year, before growing by 7.9% in 2027.
The fund published those forecasts on Tuesday, but had prepared them before Saturday's deadly attack on Riyadh airport.
The recovery forecast assumes the Strait of Hormuz will gradually reopen from March 2027, with shipping returning to pre-war conditions by October.
Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline carries oil to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. The IMF said this had reduced the economic damage compared with some neighbouring countries.
Georgieva said the kingdom’s efforts to develop businesses outside oil had also helped protect its economy from the war’s impact.
She warned that poorer countries that depend on imported energy were among the hardest hit by rising costs. She urged governments to help people facing higher food and energy bills.

Setback for TikTok as EU court adviser backs gatekeeper label

Setback for TikTok as EU court adviser backs gatekeeper label
- EU court adviser Andrea Biondi said TikTok should lose its challenge to the “gatekeeper” label under the Digital Markets Act.
- He backed the lower court, saying other social networks do not prove TikTok is not an “important gateway”.
- The case is the first DMA test at the EU’s top court and could shape how Europe limits Big Tech, with fines up to 10% of global turnover.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – An adviser to Europe’s highest court recommended on Oct 15 that TikTok lose its challenge to its “gatekeeper” status under landmark EU rules, backing regulators in a closely watched test of the bloc’s efforts to curb Big Tech’s power.
The case, the first involving the EU’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) to reach the Court of Justice of the European Union, is being closely watched by technology companies seeking clues on whether Europe’s courts will reinforce or limit regulators’ efforts to boost competition and expand consumer choice.
ByteDance’s TikTok is challenging its designation as a gatekeeper under the DMA, a status that subjects companies to a strict set of obligations aimed at preventing anti-competitive practices.
A lower tribunal rejected TikTok’s challenge in 2024. Other companies designated as gatekeepers include Alphabet’s Google, Meta Platforms, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft and Booking.com.
“The Court should dismiss the action brought by ByteDance (TikTok) against the decision of the Commission designating it as a gatekeeper under the Digital Markets Act,” Advocate General Andrea Biondi said in his opinion.
He endorsed the lower court’s ruling.
“The General Court did not make the errors of law alleged by ByteDance in rejecting those arguments. In particular, the fact that users also use other social networks does not, in itself, show that TikTok is not an important gateway,” Biondi said.
The judges, who are expected to rule in the coming months, follow such non-binding opinions in around four out of five cases.
TikTok did not immediately respond to an e-mailed request for comment.
The DMA imposes a range of obligations on designated gatekeepers, with breaches potentially attracting fines of up to 10% of a company’s annual global turnover.
Meta is also challenging the designation of gatekeeper for its Messenger and Marketplace services. REUTERS

Syria arrests Ali Kayali, chief suspect in 2013 Baniyas massacre
Unknown

Mohammad Sio
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
- Kayali has also been implicated in 2013 twin bombings in Reyhanli, Hatay, in southern Türkiye, which killed dozens of people
Syrian intelligence authorities have arrested Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, the chief suspect in the 2013 Baniyas massacre, as he was trying to flee across the border, state media reported Thursday.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) said the General Intelligence Directorate detained Kayali, who is accused of playing a leading role in the May 2013 massacre in the coastal city of Baniyas.
The report did not specify where the arrest took place or which border Kayali was attempting to cross.
Kayali, a former militia leader loyal to Syria’s then-leader Bashar al-Assad, has long been accused of involvement in the mass killings of civilians in Baniyas and the nearby village of al-Bayda in western Syria during the early years of the country's uprising.
His arrest came less than two weeks after Syrian counterterrorism authorities detained Jamal Trabulsi, his former deputy in the pro-Assad Syrian Resistance militia, on Oct. 4.
Syrian authorities have accused Trabulsi of taking part in military operations alongside forces loyal to Assad, including the 2013 massacres in Baniyas and al-Bayda.
On May 2, 2013, Syrian regime forces and allied militias stormed the village of al-Bayda in the Tartus province, killing hundreds of civilians.
Survivors said regime forces carried out mass executions, burned homes, and killed women and children during the assault.
Kayali has also been implicated in the May 2013 twin bombings in Reyhanli, in Türkiye's southern Hatay province, which killed dozens of people.
Following Assad's ouster in December 2024, Syrian authorities have intensified efforts to arrest former regime officials and militia commanders accused of committing crimes against civilians during the country's civil war.

Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X/Twitter that Starshield - the military version of Starlink - was owned and controlled by the US government, which decided on any limits on speed.
Zelensky has said that Ukrainian military officials were warned by their US counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
In the FT interview, Zelensky said the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, but he dismissed the idea that failures of the Starlink satellite system might have been caused by a fault.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he told the FT.
Zelensky demands US interceptors in exchange for halting strikes on refineries
Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, he told the newspaper he could only agree if, in return, he was given more US-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the “minimum” that would be acceptable.
"We didn't destroy any relationship," he said, claiming it wasn't up to him to repair US-Ukraine relations.
Ukraine claims to have damaged six Russian military aircraft
Ukraine's military said on Thursday it had damaged six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region.
In a Telegram statement, Ukraine's military general staff said it had confirmed damage of varying degrees to all six aircraft.
The Su-34M is a large fighter-bomber, costing tens of millions of US dollars apiece and frequently used by Russia to drop devastating glide bombs onto Ukrainian cities near the frontline.
Ukraine said on Telegram that it used its Neptune coastal missile system in the attack.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield reports.
Kremlin condemns Ukraine refinery strikes as ceasefire violation
The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts, after a Ukrainian drone struck a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia did not perceive that Ukraine had ever complied with an energy ceasefire announced last week by Trump. Ukraine says it paused such strikes for three days but resumed them after Russia continued to attack its own energy sector.

Netanyahu vs Bar: Who called who is fascinating, but both ignored writing on the wall - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:45:31 UTC
18:45:31 KST

The latest broadside from former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) director Ronen Bar against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu includes some fascinating new details and discussion.
The most focus has been on whether Bar had Netanyahu's phone number and whether the prime minister in the past has always taken Bar's calls or sometimes ignored them.
These are great anecdotes, and the fight over them shows the depth of miscommunication and enmity between the men; The Jerusalem Post will unpack them to explain what they really mean.
But the main point from the start is that all of this is a sideshow.
Netanyahu wants the debate to focus on the night before the invasion, but that is a straw man.
The October 7 disaster was a decade or more in the making, especially with contributions of failures by both the political leadership and the entire defense establishment after the 2021 war with Hamas and during the internal Israeli fight over the judicial overhaul.
The phone call that wasn't
More on that in a moment, after explaining the phone drama.
Presidents and prime ministers do not have their phones attached to their brains while they sleep.
For that reason, national security staff are nearby and designated to receive middle-of-the-night calls to wake them if needed.
In Netanyahu's case, I already reported in my new book, IN THE WAR ROOM, that a Shin Bet official, under Bar's orders, called Netanyahu's wake-up staff at 6:13 a.m., 16 minutes before the invasion started.
The head of the wake-up staff, Netanyahu's personally selected military secretary, Maj. Gen. Avi Gil, Netanyahu's personally selected military secretary, decided not to wake him up.
This is not the fault of the Shin Bet.
Gil was Netanyahu's personal appointee to make these exact decisions for him: when to wake him up in the middle of the night.
In that sense, Bar did not need to complain that Netanyahu did not give him his personal phone number, because Netanyahu would not have picked up such a call while sleeping.
Bar's unnecessary attack on this issue was made because of Netanyahu's unnecessary defense: they did not call me on October 7.
No one called Netanyahu personally because the procedure was to call his staff, which was done.
In that sense, it is somewhat disturbing that Netanyahu withheld contact information from the Shin Bet chief, and it could show he never trusted him because Bar was appointed by Naftali Bennett.
When push comes to shove, who is responsible for October 7?
But it is immaterial to who is responsible for October 7.
Netanyahu, the IDF, the Shin Bet, and all officials in their positions going back 10-15 years are responsible because they all participated in propagating the idea that Hamas was contained and deterred.
They neither pushed to see whether cutting a peace deal with Fatah in the West bank would sufficiently weaken Hamas to cause it to be less of a threat, nor did they attack Hamas in a stronger way to topple it militarily (or assassinate its top leaders), nor did they leave enough soldiers on the border to defend against a ground invasion which they were sure would never come.
These were the true October 7 failures of Netanyahu, the IDF, and the Shin Bet.
Add on that all of them misread the 2021 war as an Israeli win, when Hamas chief Yahya Sinwar viewed it as a validation of his strategy to ignite a multi-front war against Israel.
Moreover, add to that that they all mishandled the judicial overhaul internal fight in a way that led to the country being viewed as more vulnerable to attack by Hamas.
Relations between Netanyahu and top defense establishment figures were so bad in July 2023 that he refused to receive certain critical intelligence briefings, lest they expose him to various potential criticisms after the fact.
At the end of the day, whatever happened on the eve of October 6-7 was a tiny part of the story; whether Netanyahu gave his cell phone number to Bar or not does not impact the bottom line, and the person who the prime minister chose to decide whether to wake him up decided not to because he, like everyone else in Israel, could not imagine that Hamas would actually do what they did a short while later.

Crime on the rise in Switzerland driven by fraud and property offences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:42:33 UTC
18:42:33 KST

Crime rising in Switzerland driven by fraud and property offences
Crime in Switzerland rose between 2022 and 2025, both according to police statistics and in terms of unreported cases.
The increase is particularly evident in property offences and fraud. At the same time fewer and fewer people feel safe. This is the finding of a study published today by the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW) and the University of St Gallen (HSG).
According to the study, entitled Crime Survey 2025, an increasing number of people are falling victim to crime. For almost all the offences examined, a greater number of respondents reported having been victims compared with the last survey in 2022. The most striking increase relates to fraud: over the course of a year, 15.9% of respondents were affected, compared with 8.4% in 2022.
+ Swiss crime fell in 2025 but homicides and serious violence rose
At the same time, reporting rates have remained virtually unchanged. “This means that the rise in recorded crime is not primarily attributable to a greater willingness to report offences,” says Dirk Baier, co-leader of the Crime Survey project and professor at the ZHAW. Sexual offences are an exception to the general trend, as no increase in the victimisation rate was observed for these offences.
Meanwhile, feelings of insecurity in the face of crime are on the rise. Some 83.1% of the sample – comprising 13,500 people aged between 16 and 80 living throughout Switzerland – feel fairly or very safe after dark in their neighbourhood, a figure down from 87.6% in 2022.
The proportion of people who have been afraid of becoming victims of a crime on the street in the last twelve months has increased. Furthermore, more respondents consider the police presence in public spaces to be insufficient: 37.9%, compared with 28.9% in 2022. Trust in the police, however, remains high.
Overall, the researchers do not regard the decline in the sense of security and the fear of crime as dramatic. “We must take this development seriously, without over-dramatising it. Despite the decline in the sense of safety, the population continues to perceive Switzerland as a safe country,” says Nora Markwalder, co-director of the project and professor at the HSG.
A supplementary report examines domestic violence. Overall, the proportion of people who have experienced at least one form of domestic violence over a five-year period has not changed significantly compared with 2022. Women remain significantly more affected than men: 5.4% of women and 2.2% of men report such experiences.
“The fact that women are affected by domestic violence at a significantly higher rate than men is evident not only from official statistics but also from unreported cases,” notes Baier. “The findings therefore underline the importance of further preventive measures against violence against women.” Among the individual forms of violence examined, only domestic hate crimes show a statistically significant increase compared with 2022.

Niger slams France over expulsion of security agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:41:33 UTC
18:41:33 KST

Niger slams France over expulsion of security agents
Niger has condemned France’s expulsion of two embassy security officers and their families, including a man who the authorities said was left paraplegic after being stabbed during a mission carried out with French forces more than a decade ago.
Justice Minister Alio Daouda described the decision as a “serious and unacceptable act of ingratitude” in a government statement broadcast on national television on Tuesday. He accused Paris of circumventing its own courts to remove one of the men.
The officer, Abdoul-Razak Ibrahim Moussa Toro, was stabbed in the spine during a mission in 2014 in Diffa, southeastern Niger, and evacuated to France for treatment, according to the statement. The minister said French partners financed the operation and provided fuel, logistics, and allowances.
“This is how France thanks those who served alongside it,” Daouda said. “It solicits men, recruits them and finances them. Then, when they fall, it throws them out with their families,” he added.
Toro challenged an order to leave France, but the authorities declared him persona non grata on September 16 before the court ruled, the minister said. His family, including his children, were given 48 hours to leave. They departed on September 19.
Six days later, the Versailles Administrative Court annulled the original departure order and instructed the French Foreign Ministry to reconsider his situation, according to Daouda. “This is not an administrative error. It is a deliberate violation of the rule of law,” he said.
A French diplomatic source told AFP that the two men were intelligence agents whose presence was no longer justified because bilateral cooperation had ended. Le Monde reported, citing a Nigerien source, that one was suspected of monitoring opposition figures in France. The French Foreign Ministry has yet to publicly comment.
Relations between Niger and France have deteriorated since Niamey’s current leadership took power in a military coup that ousted President Mohamed Bazoum in July 2023. France deployed troops in Niger as part of a wider campaign against Islamist insurgents in the Sahel. Its intervention began in Mali in 2013 and expanded through Operation Barkhane in 2014, with the stated aim of combating armed groups and supporting regional forces. Despite years of French operations, the insurgency spread, fueling resentment toward Paris and demands for its troops to leave.
Since 2020, a wave of military coups has reshaped politics across the Sahel region in Africa, toppling civilian governments in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.
France, once the region’s dominant external power, has steadily lost influence amid rising anti-French sentiment and deep frustration over insecurity, economic stagnation, and foreign interference. The former colonial power was forced to withdraw troops from Mali in 2022, Burkina Faso in 2023, Niger later that year, and Chad in early 2025.
About 4,500 soldiers had been deployed under Operation Barkhane, France’s largest overseas mission, across Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Chad – a campaign that the military governments in Bamako, Niamey, and Ouagadougou have said only permitted Islamist insurgents to expand their activities.
The three West African states have established the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and withdrawn from the International Organization of Francophone Nations (OIF) operating in Francophone countries, many of them former French colonies. The AES has forged new alliances, including with Russia, which its leaders hail as a more reliable economic and security partner.
In August 2023, Niamey ordered French Ambassador Sylvain Itte to leave amid a standoff over France’s refusal to recognize the military leadership.
Last month, Niger accused France of inciting an August 29 mutiny in which soldiers attacked Niamey’s international airport, the adjoining Air Base 101, and the presidential palace. The authorities said loyalist forces backed by Russia’s Africa Corps regained control of the base. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot rejected the allegations as “pure fantasies.”

Syrian court sentences two to death over torture, killings during 2025 coastal massacre
Two men have been sentenced to death and several others handed prison terms over the deadly violence that swept Syria's coastal region in March 2025, when more than 1,400 people were killed amid widespread attacks on civilians.
The sentences were handed down on Thursday by a military criminal court in Aleppo as part of ongoing proceedings against suspects accused of involvement in the violence, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
The rulings included death sentences for Al-Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali, a 20-year prison sentence for Mohammad Bakour, and a 12-year sentence for Maher Othman.
The court sentenced Bakour to 20 years in prison after convicting him of intentional murder, while Ammar Abdul Aal received a three-year sentence for torture, SANA reported.
The court also convicted Captain Mustafa Shannan and Khaled Muhaimid, both members of the Defence Ministry's 54th Division, of complicity in torture and sentenced them to two years in prison.
Abdul Raouf Bakrjan and Mohammad Zarzouri were acquitted, while Mahmoud Shaheen, another Defence Ministry member, received a two-month prison sentence for assault.
In a separate case linked to the massacre in Syria's coastal region, Ismail and Ali were sentenced to death after being convicted of offences involving acts intended to incite civil war and sectarian fighting, as well as leading armed groups formed to attack government forces.
Othman was sentenced to 12 years in prison after being convicted of complicity in the same offences.
The latest rulings form part of ongoing judicial proceedings aimed at holding those responsible for the March 2025 massacre to account.
The unrest involved armed clashes, military operations and widespread abuses against civilians, prompting calls for justice and accountability for perpetrators regardless of their affiliations.
On 17 September 2026, the military criminal court in Aleppo issued earlier verdicts against defendants involved in the same events, including death sentences, life imprisonment and 20-year prison terms, alongside the acquittal of one defendant.
The trials have attracted considerable attention as a major test of Syria's efforts to address abuses committed during the coastal violence.
Syrian authorities face the challenge of establishing individual criminal responsibility and ensuring that those implicated in abuses are held accountable through transparent judicial proceedings.
The violence erupted in Syria's coastal region in March 2025, beginning with attacks by armed groups linked to the former Assad regime against security and military positions.
The attacks were followed by military operations during which widespread violations against civilians, particularly from the Alawi community, were reported.
A national fact-finding committee investigating the coastal massacre previously documented the deaths of 1,426 people, including 90 women, and identified 563 suspects allegedly involved in abuses committed by different parties.

Finnish court cuts Simon Ekpa’s terrorism sentence to four years
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:37:49 EEST
18:37:49 KST

A Finnish appeals court has reduced the prison sentence of Nigerian-born separatist leader Simon Ekpa from six to four years while upholding his convictions for terrorism offences linked to armed groups operating in southeastern Nigeria.
The East Finland Court of Appeal delivered its ruling on Thursday, finding that Ekpa, 41, had participated in the activities of a terrorist group and publicly incited criminal acts for terrorist purposes.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The court upheld the findings of a district court that convicted Ekpa in September 2025 but reduced his sentence after examining the circumstances surrounding the conflict in Nigeria.
The appeals court accepted the prosecution's evidence concerning Ekpa's involvement in armed separatist activities between 2021 and 2024.
Ekpa, who lives in Lahti, Finland, directed several armed groups seeking independence for Biafra, a region in southeastern Nigeria.
Members of these groups carried out attacks against Nigerian police stations, government buildings and military checkpoints as part of their campaign for an independent state.
During his appeal, Ekpa argued that southeastern Nigeria was experiencing an internal armed conflict and that international humanitarian law, rather than Finnish terrorism legislation, should govern his actions.
He submitted evidence concerning the organisation of armed groups, their weapons and the Nigerian government's military operations.
The appeals court examined whether the fighting met the legal threshold for an internal armed conflict, drawing comparisons with international tribunal assessments of the Balkan wars.
Judges acknowledged that the weapons and equipment used by Nigerian government forces and the armed groups under Ekpa's command indicated conditions resembling an internal armed conflict.
They nevertheless concluded that the intensity and frequency of fighting did not meet the threshold required under international case law.
The court found that attacks occurred intermittently, primarily targeting police stations and road checkpoints.
It also found insufficient evidence that Ekpa's forces possessed the operational capacity to sustain prolonged military campaigns.
The absence of reports documenting substantial civilian displacement from the affected areas further weakened the argument that the conflict amounted to a civil war.
Despite rejecting Ekpa's central defence, the court determined that the circumstances surrounding his offences resembled situations involving civil war, self-defence and necessity.
The court considered those circumstances sufficient to justify reducing the prison term while maintaining the terrorism convictions.
Ekpa has remained in custody since November 2024.
He moved from Nigeria to Finland in 2007 as an athlete and later became involved in Finnish local politics with the National Coalition Party. He subsequently served on a regional public transport committee.
The appeals court ruling is not yet final. Ekpa and the prosecution have the option of seeking permission to appeal to Finland's Supreme Court.

No more ‘gifts’ to Ukraine – Slovak PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:37:35 UTC
18:37:35 KST

No more ‘gifts’ to Ukraine – Slovak PM
Ukraine will never repay the billions of euros lent to it by the EU to keep it afloat in the conflict with Russia, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said. Slovakia is refusing to partake in another massive financing package for Kiev.
Speaking in Brussels on Wednesday, Fico noted that the existing €90 billion ($101 billion) EU loan package had already proved insufficient. The sum was intended to meet Ukraine’s needs in 2026–2027, with €60 billion allocated to the military and €30 billion to budget support. Under the agreement, Ukraine is required to repay the loan only after receiving Russian reparations – something that Moscow has categorically ruled out.
Fico said that the EU is now considering another loan, stressing that while Slovakia would not prevent other EU countries from providing additional funding, it would seek an opt-out for itself.
“By all means, give money to Ukraine, but the Slovak Republic will not participate in this mechanism. These are not loans; they are gifts. Ukraine will never pay back any of this money,” he stressed.
The prime minister suggested the EU summit could produce a political commitment to decide on another multi-billion-euro loan in December. He warned against tying participation in the scheme to negotiations over the bloc’s 2028–2034 budget, insisting that Slovakia would once again seek an opt-out.
Under Fico, Slovakia has remained skeptical of Ukraine assistance as well as the country’s push to join NATO, and has halted government weapons shipments while consistently calling for peace talks.
Fico’s remarks come after Ukraine’s revelation in August of an unexpected $27 billion defense funding shortfall, reportedly catching European officials off guard. Many are said to doubt whether Kiev is overstating its needs.
Brussels refused to validate the figure, subsequently rejecting Kiev’s request to bring forward funding earmarked for 2027. Instead, it is demanding progress on reforms – including those meant to tackle rampant corruption – to unlock assistance already available.
Earlier this month, Vladimir Zelensky announced that Ukraine would be able to cover its budget deficit through austerity measures and spending reallocations. A Ukrainian government source told RBC-Ukraine that some funding would be found by cutting weapons expenditures. Kiev’s European backers had also agreed to work toward arranging for weapons production while shifting payments into January, the outlet reported.

A Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, Ukraine’s largest painting, in the section depicting the future. Its artist spent nearly two years creating it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:36:59 UTC
18:36:59 KST

Debris from a Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, a painting that set a national record in Ukraine, the Korsaks Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, where the artwork was exhibited, reported on 14 October. A fire destroyed part of the painting’s final section, titled The Future, according to the statement.
Russian drones continue to attack Ukraine. Overnight into 15 October alone, Ukrainian air defense forces downed or suppressed 536 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). In recent days, Lutsk, a city in northwestern Ukraine, has been among the cities damaged by Russian attacks. Russian UAV attacks set fire to an oil depot, a wholesale warehouse, and a shopping center. At the museum, located on the shopping center’s premises, the fire damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, which covers a canvas of more than 2,000 square meters.
Russian attack damages museum in Lutsk
A fire broke out at the Adrenalin City shopping and entertainment complex, where the museum is located, Suspilne Lutsk reported. The blaze damaged the last of the painting’s six sections, according to the report.
“By destroying art and culture, they are also trying to destroy Ukrainians,” Tetiana Repnytska, director of the Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, told Suspilne Lutsk.
Museum staff also had to evacuate more than 300 works by Ukrainian artist Emma Andiievska, which were exhibited alongside Cosmogony, Oles Tomakh, the museum’s chief curator, told Suspilne Lutsk. Some works could not be removed in time, resulting in shattered glass. However, the museum’s other exhibition halls were unaffected, the chief curator said.
The museum is weighing whether to fully restore the damaged fragment or keep the fire’s traces as a reminder of the war, and will decide after consulting the artist, Petro Antyp, and restoration specialists, it said. Repnytska told Suspilne Lutsk that the painting’s authors could also create a new section.
“Despite the shelling, we will continue to develop contemporary Ukrainian art and preserve it,” the museum director said.
Cosmogony—Ukraine’s largest painting
Artist Petro Antyp began working on the painting in November 2022, Suspilne Lutsk reported, and it took almost two years to complete, according to the museum’s website. The painting covers an area of 2,086 square meters.
In September 2024, the project set a national record as Ukraine’s largest painting.
The artwork explores the evolution of the universe, Earth, nature, humanity, society, culture, and science. Its six sections combine myths, legends, scientific theories, and symbols from different cultures, according to the museum’s website.
The project extends beyond the canvas, as the museum presents a multimedia performance that combines light, sound, and art.
Civilians killed and injured in Russia’s latest attack on Lutsk
Around noon on 14 October, a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone attacked Lutsk. Drone debris damaged a wholesale goods warehouse and a residential building, Roman Romaniuk, acting head of the Volyn Regional Military Administration, told Suspilne.
Falling drone debris sparked a large fire at the Yevrohurt wholesale warehouse. A nine-story residential building on Sobornosti Avenue was also damaged, Romaniuk later reported on social media.
Six people were killed in the strike on the warehouse: five were found at the scene, and another person died in the hospital. Eleven more people were injured, Romaniuk said.
Two other people, including a child, were injured in the residential building. Twelve people remained hospitalized, one of whom was in serious condition, according to the report.

Ethiopian forces expand control in Tigray as militia claims heavy Eritrean losses
Unknown

Andrew Wasike 
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Ethiopian government forces and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters have expanded their control across northern Tigray, entering the historic city of Aksum, as the pro-government militia claimed Eritrean troops suffered heavy losses and retreated toward the border.
Solomon Hailemariam, spokesperson for the TPF, claimed Thursday that Eritrean forces had sustained significant casualties during the fighting.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected the claims as false in comments to local media. The extent of the reported losses could not be independently verified.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an independent conflict-monitoring organization, documented Ethiopian government forces and TPF fighters entering the historic city of Aksum, while rival Tigrayan fighters remained in surrounding mountainous areas.
ACLED also reported Eritrean troops withdrawing across the border through Zalambessa following advances by Ethiopian forces and their allies into several strategic towns.
The organization documented Ethiopian tanks and heavy weapons moving toward the Eritrean border Tuesday, raising concerns about a possible confrontation between the neighboring countries.
Eritrea has denied accusations that its forces entered Tigray to support armed opposition groups, accusing Ethiopia of threatening its sovereignty.
The developments come amid growing international pressure to prevent further fighting. On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio discussed the tensions with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and called for de-escalation.
“The Secretary emphasized that the region cannot tolerate more conflict,” the US State Department said.
The TPF supports Ethiopia’s federal government in its campaign against rival Tigrayan forces linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
The renewed fighting threatens the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended a two-year war in Tigray. Ethiopia and Eritrea, allies during that conflict, have since fallen out over regional security and Addis Ababa’s pursuit of access to the Red Sea.

‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:35:01 UTC
18:35:01 KST

‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel
Balkan countries’ ties with Israel reflect domestic politics, defence deals and strategic interests rather than a united regional position.
Throughout Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Europe’s position has, to an extent, been aligned.
Outliers such as Spain and the Republic of Ireland have long been more vocal in condemning Israel, but overall, the shift from unconditional solidarity with Israel to concern over its conduct has taken hold in much of the continent.
Across the Balkans, divergent policies towards Israel reflect domestic calculations, transactional diplomacy, and unresolved identity politics rather than a shared vision for the Middle East, according to experts.
“The Balkan countries have almost no common positions at all, and so it’s not surprising their positions towards Israel and Gaza are all over the map,” Marko Prelec, analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “Each country goes its own way.”
Prelec noted that while there is genuine revulsion towards Israeli policy in Gaza and sympathy for Palestinians – particularly among Bosnian Muslims – most countries in the region take their positions based on unrelated interests.
Florian Bieber, professor of Southeast European history and politics at Austria’s University of Graz, said regional consensus is nearly impossible.
“The position towards Israel is strongly shaped by domestic politics and also national narratives, which makes a regional or even a country-specific position unlikely,” Bieber told Al Jazeera.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: Differences from one entity to another
Nowhere is this fragmentation more evident than in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the war in Gaza has deepened existing ethno-national divisions.
Bosniak political representatives and much of the public in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina have expressed strong solidarity with Palestinians, while leaders in Republika Srpska have been openly pro-Israel, and some Croat political figures have also adopted a more sympathetic tone towards Israel.
“Bosniak solidarity with Palestinians is often seen not just through an ideological lens, but also from the perspective of war and being a victim of Serb nationalist aggression, comparing the Palestinian experience with the Bosniak experience in the 1990s,” Bieber explained.
Conversely, leaders in the Serb-majority entity, Republika Srpska, led by former President Milorad Dodik, have openly embraced Israel.
Foreign policy analyst and journalist Bosko Jaksic told Al Jazeera that for Dodik, “The enemy of my enemy is my friend – Jews and Orthodox Serbs against Muslims. This religious and ethnic factor allows him to maintain an Israeli connection parallel to his closeness with Russia, while simultaneously performing a new American flip by glorifying [US President] Donald Trump.”
Prelec added that Bosnian Serb outreach to Israel and specifically Likud, the ruling Israeli party, represents “an attempt to find allies for its internationally unpopular flirtation with separatism, and an indirect way to strengthen ties with parts of the MAGA [Make America Great Again] movement and the Trump administration”.
Serbia: Arms sales and multi-vector balancing
In Serbia, the approach to Israel blends defence economics with foreign policy.
Despite historically friendly relations with Palestine and voting in favour of Palestinian membership in international bodies, Belgrade has exported ammunition and arms to Israel since October 2023.
The relationship has also moved beyond exports. In September, Serbia opened an Israeli-linked drone assembly plant, underlining the growing practical dimension of bilateral defence cooperation.
Vuk Vuksanovic, lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Serbia’s defence industry “has not been particularly picky when it comes to its customers, and the desire for profit has been one of the factors”.
However, he emphasised broader geopolitical ambitions.
“In the past three years, there has been a tilt towards Israel regarding security cooperation, while diplomatically Serbia tries to be cautious in multilateral institutions due to its ties with the wider Islamic world,” he said.
Vuksanovic noted that Belgrade views Israel as a partner to “acquire the protection of Israeli lobby groups and access to the Trump administration in the US”, especially as the Serbian government faces domestic political opposition.
Meanwhile, Jaksic warned of the international risks involved.
“Due to the significant increase in ammunition exports to Israel during the war in Gaza, Serbia risks being accused of complicity in genocide,” he said. “Beyond financial calculations, the Serbian president attempts to use closeness with his ideological, authoritarian, and nationalist ally, [Israeli Prime Minister] Benjamin Netanyahu, to get closer to Trump.”
Kosovo, Albania, and the Washington anchor
For Kosovo and Albania, foreign policy regarding Israel remains anchored to security alliances with Washington.
Under the 2020 Washington Agreement, Kosovo recognised Israel in exchange for Israeli recognition of Kosovo’s independence, subsequently opening its embassy in Jerusalem. Serbia, which had pledged in 2020 to move its embassy to Jerusalem, ultimately did not do so.
Pristina opened its Jerusalem embassy “defying the stance of the wider international community”, said Jaksic.
“Israel’s growing influence in the Western Balkans is evident,” he noted. “That includes investments, and in the case of Serbia, especially military cooperation. This absolutely does not exclude personal attempts to buy political impunity from American sanctions, or to ease diplomatic pressure.”
In neighbouring Albania, Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government has preserved warm political ties with Israel.
Driven partly by operational defence needs, Albania deepened cooperation with Israeli cybersecurity companies after cyberattacks, while aligning broader diplomacy with Washington and Brussels.
Executive rifts and ideological turnarounds
In Croatia, foreign policy on Gaza has been paralysed by a sharp executive rift between conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic and President Zoran Milanovic of the Social Democratic Party.
Plenkovic’s government has followed a cautious, mainstream European Union approach, while Milanovic has openly condemned Israel’s military conduct in Gaza, labelling it disproportionate and creating a public fracture in the country’s foreign policy leadership.
Further north in Slovenia, there are ideological shifts.
The previous centre-left government adopted firm measures against Israel – such as an arms embargo, a ban on imports from illegal settlements, and a ban on the entry of top officials like Netanyahu – as well as recognising Palestinian statehood.
Conservative forces under Prime Minister Janez Jansa have sought to reverse these policies.
“In Slovenia, we can see the classic left-right division where populist and far-right parties support Israel because of Netanyahu as a similar political actor,” said Bieber. “They recognise him as ideologically aligned, which helps reinforce their view of Islam as a threat, fitting their own narratives.”
Quiet alignment and strategic alliances
Smaller NATO members like Montenegro and North Macedonia have chosen a path of quiet alignment.
Both adhere to standard EU and NATO statements, calling for ceasefires and humanitarian aid while carefully avoiding high-profile bilateral disputes or bold independent diplomatic initiatives.
Further east, Romania and Bulgaria maintain a cautious tone that sometimes leans towards Israel. Grounded in historic bilateral relations and deep strategic defence partnerships with the United States, Bucharest and Sofia balance carefully worded statements at the United Nations with ongoing military and intelligence coordination.
Meanwhile, in Greece, consecutive governments in Athens have maintained a robust strategic military and energy partnership with Israel; Athens recently signed a $3.5bn missile deal with Israel. Originally forged alongside Cyprus to balance regional maritime rivalries in the Eastern Mediterranean, this alliance has held firm despite significant domestic public backlash and protests over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
Ultimately, the disparate responses across the Balkans demonstrate that Middle Eastern policy in the region is rarely about the Middle East itself.
Whether driven by defence profits, constitutional rivalries, or the search for political backing in Washington, regional actors continue to view Israel almost exclusively through a transactional lens.

Taipei election primer: Chiang Wan-an’s record and re-election bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:33:11 UTC
18:33:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) is seeking a second term, campaigning on education measures and development projects as his lead over DPP challenger Puma Shen (沈伯洋) narrows.
Chiang has highlighted the Taipei Dome, MRT expansion and Nvidia’s planned Taiwan headquarters in his re-election campaign, per CNA. His campaign headquarters is scheduled to open on Oct. 26.
Born and raised in Taipei, Chiang graduated from National Chengchi University and earned a law degree from the University of Pennsylvania. He worked as a lawyer in the US before returning to Taiwan to establish a law practice.
Chiang entered politics in 2015, defeating incumbent KMT Legislator Lo Shu-lei (羅淑蕾) in the party’s primary for Taipei’s third legislative district. He won the seat in 2016 and served two terms, focusing on social welfare and domestic issues, per CNA.
In 2019, Chiang broke with the KMT’s legislative caucus to support key provisions legalizing same-sex marriage, per Ettoday. He later called for discussions on transforming Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall.
Chiang resigned from the legislature in 2022 to run for mayor. He won a three-way race with 575,590 votes, or 42.29%, returning the KMT to Taipei City Hall after eight years.
His administration introduced a city-funded weekly milk program for schoolchildren and later expanded it to junior high schools, reaching about 289,000 students. The city also announced free lunches for elementary and junior high school students at public and private schools starting in the 2026 academic year.
Chiang has proposed smaller classes, more teacher training, and improved school facilities. These measures form part of his campaign’s emphasis on support for families and children.
The long-delayed Taipei Dome opened in 2023, during Chiang’s first year in office, after years of construction disputes. It has since hosted sporting events and concerts.
Chiang has also promoted MRT expansion and urban renewal, including redevelopment of the aging South Airport housing complex in Taipei’s Zhongzheng District. Responding to criticism that his administration lacks new ideas, he has pointed to progress on projects that have faced delays.
Chiang has proposed relocating Taipei Songshan Airport and turning its 300-hectare site into an AI technology hub, per CNA. The plan has raised concerns over national defense, emergency medical flights, and transport to outlying islands, but Chiang said alternative arrangements could address these issues.
The city signed a land-rights agreement with Nvidia in February for the company’s planned Taiwan headquarters at the Beitou-Shilin Technology Park.
An April city government survey found 69.1% of respondents satisfied with Chiang’s performance. A TVBS poll in May put satisfaction at 59%.
His administration faced criticism over its handling of a sexual abuse case at a private preschool. Although the first complaint was filed before Chiang took office, parents and opposition lawmakers criticized city agencies for their response to warnings during his tenure, per Liberty Times. Chiang apologized in July 2024 and promised stronger oversight.
An Oct. 8 TVBS poll put Chiang ahead of Shen by 49% to 41%, compared with a 28-percentage-point lead in May. Chiang has said he will continue focusing on city affairs while seeking another four years in office.

Breadcrumb
Three years of Gaza genocide: how Palestine activism reshaped British universities
Police intervention. Disciplinary action. British campuses have become a key battleground in the movement for Palestine.
In the three years since the start of the genocide in Gaza, as streets across the world filled with Palestinian flags and thousands of protesters, another front in the struggle against the Israeli state and its crimes against Palestinians came into focus: British universities.
Specifically, the institutions’ material support for the Zionist entity, which is carried out through research collaborations and investments in technology and arms manufacturers.
Over the last three years, students mobilised and reclaimed campuses through rallies, teach-ins, occupations of buildings and encampments where pockets of Palestine were created and sustained by students’ and staff.
This collective action was soon met with increased suppression. We have seen multiple cases of disciplinary action taken against students and police have regularly been invited on campuses to dissuade further activism.
But despite feeling the full weight of their management, students remained steadfast.
They become bolder and more resolved in refusing to water down their words or politics, drawing inspiration from the Palestinian National Thawabet, the core principles of the Palestinian struggle - including the right of return, resistance, and opposition to normalisation with the Israeli state.
Young people today are not afraid to name Zionism and settler colonialism as the enemy, and British imperialism as the underlying cause. Rather than conceding by presenting liberal campaigns that don’t challenge the current world order, they have become explicit about the overall demand for Palestine’s liberation from the river to the sea.
Students and academics recognise the increasing repression in academic institutions for what it is: another tool through which universities continue to provide political and ideological cover for the Zionist entity and, ultimately, a distraction.
With the normalisation of Israel’s genocide since 2023, Students have responded by proactively building collective movements on campuses and consolidating their knowledge in national student conferences with the Palestinian Youth Movement.
From running successful rectorship campaigns, to shutting down the London Defence Conference, to unprecedented massive graduation walkouts, students are proving that their actions since 2023 have not been episodic mobilisations, but organised deliberate steps towards a long-term vision that only culminates in the isolation of Zionism in academic spaces.

Drone attacks also prompted officials to cancel classes at schools and kindergartens in Ryazan’s Oktyabrsky district, where the refinery is located, and parts of the Sovetsky district.

The facility was last attacked on Sept. 6, following which it halted operations.
Musk Tells Zelensky to ‘Go’ as Ukraine Questions US Support
Military airfield targeted in Voronezh Oblast
Also overnight, Ukrainian forces reportedly struck a military airfield in Borisoglebsk, in Russia’s Voronezh region.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Supernova+ and Exilenova+ published eyewitness footage showing the reported strike and a glow from a fire.
According to reports circulated by Ukrainian monitoring channels, the airfield was targeted with Neptune missiles, damaging six Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers. The claims have not been independently verified.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev confirmed an attack on the region, saying air defenses had destroyed 33 drones and “several jet-powered aerial targets.”
Falling debris damaged outbuildings at several private homes and one vehicle, but caused no casualties, Gusev said. He did not mention the reported strike on the military airfield.
Russia’s defense ministry claimed that its air defenses had intercepted 166 drones over 14 regions overnight, including the Moscow, Ryazan, Voronezh, and Rostov regions.

The non-governmental organization that the Israeli army arrested six children overnight in the towns of Sa'ir and Al-Shuyukh in the Hebron governorate of the occupied West Bank.
Monitoring and documentation indicate that “more than 2,000 children have been arrested since the start of the genocide on October 2023, while at least 350 remain in detention under harsh conditions,” it said.

It added that information on the number of children detained from the Gaza Strip since the start of the war remains unclear, particularly amid the presence of thousands of missing people in the enclave, including children, and the continued practice of “enforced disappearance.”

Detention conditions

approximately 23.5 billion euros in new measures to support

(DBP) that Premier Giorgia Meloni's government sent to European
Commission and the Italian parliament on Thursday.

billion euros for next year, with the banks and insurance

industry will also help cover the spending.

purchasing power—with a particular focus on the most vulnerable—
and support for businesses and investment at the heart of its
budgetary policy," the DBP reads.

national escape clause allowing a country to run extra deficit
to finance increased spending on defence and energy security.

year to enable Italy to emerge from its excessive-deficit

====================================================================================================

Austria students resist school headscarf ban over targeting Muslims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:29:00 UTC
18:29:00 KST

A headscarf ban for girls under 14 has triggered widespread protests across Austria as the new school year begins, with dozens of students refusing to comply in classrooms and on the streets.
Austria's conservative-led government has insisted the ban, introduced Sept. 1, promotes gender equality and protects Muslim girls from "segregation and oppression."
But critics argue it disproportionately targets Muslims, infringes upon religious freedom and is forcing young girls to dress in a way that makes them feel uncomfortable.
Since the ban took effect, education authorities across Austria have held 127 meetings with parents and filed 52 reports over alleged breaches of the law, according to the Education Ministry.
Opponents of the ban have also held protests across the country, with several hundred people gathering each time.
At a demonstration in Vienna, Zehra, 37, who did not want to give her last name, said her two daughters, ages 9 and 13, were "sad and angry" about the ban.
"We raise our children by telling them, 'You can decide who you want to be' – and this law is the exact opposite," she said.
Seham, 12, said she felt "afraid" to remove her headscarf at school "because I'd worn it for two years and it felt like a part of me."
After discussions with school leaders, she said she was allowed to cover her hair with an alternative non-traditional head covering, but would still "rather wear the full headscarf."
Roughly 8% of Austria's 9 million residents are Muslim, according to 2021 government statistics.
They suffer the highest rates of racism and discrimination against Muslims in the European Union, according to a 2024 report by Europe's FRA rights agency.
In the 2024 elections, the far-right Freedom Party won for the first time even though it failed to form a government. The anti-immigration party continues to top voter opinion polls.
The new law is Austria's second attempt to restrict headscarves in schools after a coalition between the conservatives and the Freedom Party introduced a ban for primary school students in 2019.
That law was overturned by the constitutional court on the grounds that a regulation targeting only Muslims was incompatible with religious neutrality.
The Islamic Religious Community in Austria, which is supporting legal action against the new headscarf ban, said it had received about 70 reports from families about difficulties during its implementation.
"A law that was justified as protecting children's welfare is putting precisely those children under pressure at school," the group said in a statement.
The constitutional court confirmed to Agence France-Presse (AFP) that it had received a legal complaint about the law and a decision is expected in the first half of 2027.
When girls refuse to comply with the law, schools are required to hold a series of discussions with students and their parents before cases are referred to education authorities.
Ultimately, parents who continue to ignore the ban can be fined.
In a statement sent to AFP, Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr said the fact there had only been 127 meetings so far showed "that the vast majority of pupils and parents are cooperative."
"In addition, the figures show that the discussions held with the parents concerned in the event of a violation are, for the most part, successful," he added.
Education authorities in Vienna said that "on the basis of the discussions held so far, the impression has emerged that the girls wish to wear the headscarf of their own accord."
Sandy, 12, said she began wearing a headscarf about a year ago because "I place a lot of importance on my religion and I want to be able to live it."
A teacher who has worked with two affected girls in the capital told AFP there was no sign they were being forced to wear headscarves.
The girls had spent weeks adapting to the new rules and searching for acceptable alternatives to headscarves, said the teacher, who wished to remain anonymous. "It is very uncomfortable for them."

Davos rejects 21 temporary construction projects for WEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:27:49 UTC
18:27:49 KST

Davos rejects 21 temporary construction projects for WEF
The Davos local government has set a cap of 125 on temporary construction projects for the 2027 World Economic Forum (WEF) Annual Meeting. According to a press release, a total of 190 planning applications were submitted. Some 146 projects fall within the quota, while 21 projects have now been refused.
The Kleine Landrat – that is, the executive body in Davos – reviewed the 146 projects. According to a statement issued on Wednesday, 21 of the projects did not meet the requirements. “No planning permission will be granted for these projects. This leaves 125 applications for which planning permission, subject to quotas, has been granted.”
+ Switzerland renews support for WEF for 2025-2027
During the annual WEF meetings, many temporary structures are erected and existing premises are repurposed. In recent years, the number of such construction projects has risen steadily. Consequently, the Davos local government has decided to introduce an upper limit for the first time for the 2027 annual meeting.
Increased traffic and a shortage of accommodation
The Davos local government wrote in April that “the temporary construction projects attract a large number of additional guests and require staff to run them”. As a result, traffic increases and the already existing shortage of accommodation is further exacerbated.
“Security is also increasingly compromised, as systematic checks – such as those relating to fire safety – require ever more staff resources.” Despite special efforts, it is not possible to review an unlimited number of projects with the necessary care within a short timeframe.
The projects were assessed using a points-based system. In the first stage, the completeness of the application, the end users and the date of submission are evaluated. Penalty points are also awarded if projects have been fined in previous years due to misconduct.
In the event of a tie, the applications are analysed in a second stage with regard to sustainability and innovation, the use of public land, and the space required for guests. If there is still a tie after the second round of assessment, the decision is made by drawing lots.

====================================================================================================

El Niño vs climate change: Which had more influence over the powerful Hurricane Polo?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:27:18 UTC
18:27:18 KST

El Niño turbocharged the Pacific hurricane – but climate change had an even greater impact, scientists find.
A new study finds that climate change and El Niño combined to rev up last month's explosively intensifying Hurricane Polo, which was the longest-lasting Category 5 storm ever to churn in the Pacific.
Global warming caused by the burning of coal, oil and gas was the bigger of the two culprits, adding nearly 10 kph to its already monstrous strength, according to a joint study published on 14 October by scientists from World Weather Attribution and Climate Central. El Niño contributed a bit less, about 8 kph, a study co-author said.
Climate change made the conditions that fuelled the hurricane 23 times more likely, while El Niño – the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific – made it 14 times more likely, the study found. It all has to do with the 31.2°C waters that were as much as 2°C warmer than normal, the study said.
This year, with a super strong El Niño, has set records for strength and longevity of Pacific storms. Polo set the record for time spent at Category 5 in the Pacific at two-and-a-half days.
'El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse'
“El Niño and climate change both made this hurricane stronger than it would have otherwise been, but the effect of climate change is even bigger than the one of El Niño,” says climate scientist and study co-author Friederike Otto, who coordinates the international science team behind World Weather Attribution.
“El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse. That means that now every hurricane that will occur in the East Pacific has at least this climate change signal making it stronger. And as long as we keep burning fossil fuels, that will only get bigger,” Otto adds.
Researchers found that without climate change and El Niño, Polo would have been a monster storm anyway. But every bit of additional wind speed can dramatically increase the damage.
Decoding Polo's rapid strengthening
While Hurricane Polo ultimately weakened considerably before it hit a sparsely populated part of Mexico, scientists remain fascinated by how it turbocharged from a tropical storm to a top-of-the-chart Category 5 hurricane in about 24 hours.
The study puts the different atmospheric dangers in perspective, says Kristina Dahl, a climate scientist and vice president of science at Climate Central, a science and journalism nonprofit out of New Jersey.
“It’s a powerful reminder that even though El Niño right now is shifting hazards around the globe and changing where it’s flooding and getting dry, the really dominant signal behind all of this remains climate change,” she says.
The study looked at the warm water that fuels storms, using a measure of how strong they can get. But the study didn't focus on the upper level wind shear where El Niño has a huge footprint. El Niño usually increases those storm-decapitating high altitude winds in the Atlantic. However, in the Pacific because of changes in wind patterns, El Niño decreases the winds that weaken storms.
The two sets of researchers measured conditions slightly differently and used different techniques but came to the same general conclusion, making them more confident in the result. However, the rapid study has not had time to be peer-reviewed, which is the gold standard of science.
To calculate the impact of climate change on Polo, both teams used the scientifically accepted method of comparing what happened in our warmer real world to a hypothetical world that hasn't warmed by 1.4°C since pre-industrial times.
How El Niño and climate change interact
Study co-author Daniel Gilford, a Climate Central scientist, says the process they looked at was similar to cars on a road. Wind shear from El Niño can be a red light, as it is in the Atlantic, or a green light, as it is in the Pacific. In the Pacific that green light says go, and then the water warmed by both climate change and El Niño acts like a driver flooring the accelerator.
University at Albany atmospheric scientist Brian Tang, who wasn't part of the study, says he was initially surprised that the research found climate change to be the bigger influence on Polo, “given how extreme this El Niño is, but from a long-term standpoint, perhaps the result isn’t as surprising as it might seem.”
But three other outside scientists – Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections, University of Pennsylvania's Michael Mann and North Carolina State University's Carl Schreck – say they believe the study underestimates how much climate change has added to Polo's strength. Masters points to Gilford's own 2024 study that found climate change added 30 kph to hurricanes in the Atlantic from 2019 to 2023.
Gilford acknowledges that Thursday's report could be underestimating climate change's impact a bit, but says he was factoring in other conditions and being conservative.

According to data from the Bulgarian publication Maritime.bg, a distress signal from the vessel was received at around 20:00 on October 14. There were 17 crew members on board from Syria, India, and Iran. According to preliminary data, none of the crew members were injured.
It is noted that following reports of the incident, the Romanian Agency for Life Saving at Sea (ARSVOM) dispatched the rescue vessel SAR Apollo to the tanker.
According to Maritime.bg, the YARA J is currently proceeding under its own power to the port of Constanța.
The Romanian public broadcaster specifies that the tanker had arrived from Turkey and was scheduled to enter the Sulina Canal. At the time of the incident, the vessel was stationary in the area, awaiting favorable weather conditions for passage.
In turn, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bulgaria expressed solidarity with Romania regarding the fire on board the tanker Yara J in the Black Sea.
"The recurring incidents affecting commercial shipping in the region are a matter of deep concern," the Bulgarian MFA reported on the social platform X.
The ministry emphasized that under circumstances where details are still being clarified, coordination between Bulgaria and Romania is essential to guarantee the safe passage of merchant vessels in the Black Sea.
The Bulgarian MFA also added that this issue will be one of the key priorities during upcoming discussions in the European Council.
As reported, Romanian President Nicușor Dan and Iliyana Yotova agreed on close cooperation between Romania and Bulgaria to introduce more effective countermeasures against drones within the EU and NATO following drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea near the Bulgarian coast.
According to him, during a telephone conversation, the parties also discussed other incidents affecting shipping and infrastructure in Romanian waters.
Earlier, on October 5, Romanian media reported that the Turkish vessel Royad Mammadov, carrying a cargo of grain and previously calling at the Ukrainian port of Izmail, was struck by a drone in the Black Sea near Peskerash oil platform, after which a fire broke out on board and the vessel sank; two people died, while 11 crew members were rescued.
Also on October 12, near the Bulgarian coast, the merchant vessel Chelsea 3, sailing under the flag of Malta and registered in the port of Odesa, was attacked by three aerial drones.
On October 6, in the same area, two merchant vessels were struck by aerial and maritime drones in the exclusive economic zone of Bulgaria in the Black Sea, approximately 70 nautical miles east of Byala. The vessel ALFA WATAN, sailing under the flag of Togo, sank, and its crew of 12 Syrian citizens went missing. Another vessel, ABLE, flying the flag of Palau, sustained damage, after which a fire broke out on board.

US weighs relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers, days after freeing Russian diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:25:14 UTC
18:25:14 KST

The Trump administration is weighing looser sanctions on shadow fleet tankers that have hauled oil from Russia, Iran, and Venezuela, a US official said on 14 October, Reuters reported. An industry research group expects the change to do little for freight rates.
With Reuters calling high fuel prices a risk for Trump before the 3 November midterms, Washington has already eased sanctions on Russian oil and diesel this year and is now looking at the ships blacklisted for hauling sanctioned cargoes. In March, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a waiver on Russian oil at sea would bring Moscow no significant financial benefit, yet Russia’s seaborne oil income jumped by $890 million in the week to 15 March, Bloomberg data showed.
“Legal oil” on blacklisted ships
The talks center on letting “legal oil” sail on previously sanctioned vessels, the official said. Only crude or fuel free of US sanctions would qualify, not Russian or Iranian oil. Washington wants more crude and refined products moving out of the Gulf, the official added. Companies would need US Treasury approval to use the ships.
Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles
Research group Energy Aspects said US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh, tied the easing to record freight rates. Those rates hit records after the Iran and Ukraine wars drove up inflation and left US crude too costly for Asian refiners, Reuters said. Energy Aspects itself expects the easing to do little for freight rates, since most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have kept trading for the past three months.
The Energy Department said any relief would do nothing to help Russia ship its oil or refined products. Treasury referred questions to the Energy Department. Yet Reuters noted that both departments could face pressure to let these vessels carry Russian diesel, given Trump’s push to get it onto world markets fast.
Britain is pushing the other way. UK finance minister John Healey urged counterparts at International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok on 15 October to keep tough sanctions on Russia, “especially a tighter ban on shipping services” that keep Putin’s shadow fleet operating.
Diesel license criticism and an unconfirmed ceasefire
On 9 October, the US Treasury issued a license clearing Russian-origin diesel trade until 7 April 2027. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters it was a weak decision unworthy of Ukraine’s partners. Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chuck Schumer, and Elizabeth Warren called it a “total betrayal of Ukraine.” Republican Senator Thom Tillis said there is “a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law.”
“He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow
Trump then pressed Kyiv to spare Russian refineries and declared an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October. A White House official told Axios it covers only oil refineries. Neither side confirmed a similar announcement Trump made in mid-September, AAP reported.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on 13 October that contacts on the ceasefire were continuing and referred further questions to Trump, Russian newspaper Vedomosti reported. He claimed the diesel deal was “a very mutually beneficial item of Russian-American cooperation” that serves the interests of Russia, the US, and world energy markets, Russian newspaper Kommersant reported.

Finland's appeal court cuts Simon Ekpa's terrorism sentence to four years
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:25:13 EEST
18:25:13 KST

The Court of Appeal has upheld the decision by Päijät-Häme District Court last year to find Simon Ekpa guilty of terrorism-related charges.
However, the appeal court reduced the amount of time Ekpa will spend behind bars from six years to four.
Ekpa, who moved to Finland from his native Nigeria in 2007, was found by the district court to have participated in a terrorist organisation and to have publicly incited crimes for terrorist purposes.
The charges related to Ekpa's alleged activities aimed at re-establishing an independent state in the Biafra region of southeastern Nigeria, which was briefly independent in the late 1960s.
In its verdict, the district court said that Ekpa had used his significant social media following to stoke tensions in the region between August 2021 and November 2024.
Ekpa appealed this ruling, and although the Court of Appeal found him guilty of the same offences, it reduced the severity of his sentence because it took into consideration the circumstances surrounding his actions — noting that the current situation in the Biafra region closely resembled, but did not meet the definition of, a civil war.
Ekpa had argued in court that, because of the political turmoil in Biafra, his involvement was not carried out with terrorist intent.
The prosecutor in the case had also lodged an appeal against the district court's decision, arguing the amount of prison time did not reflect the seriousness of Ekpa's offences.
The 41-year-old Ekpa is a long-term resident of Lahti and once served on the city's council, representing the National Coalition Party.
The court of appeal's verdict is not final, meaning it can be appealed to a higher court.

Eisenkot pledges to end Hamas rule within 18 months if he wins election race
Former IDF chief accuses Netanyahu of failing to turn battlefield gains into lasting security; Likud questions his ability to act alongside potential political partners
Gadi Eisenkot sought to put Netanyahu’s wartime record at the center of the election campaign, promising that a government under his leadership would end Hamas rule in Gaza within 18 months.
Speaking near the Gaza border, the former military chief and leader of Yashar! with Eisenkot accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of squandering the opportunities created by Israeli troops. Likud responded by questioning whether Eisenkot’s potential political alliances would prevent him from acting against Hamas.
“How will you topple Hamas without getting permission from your partners, Mansour and Tibi?” the party said, referring to Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi.
Eisenkot’s pledge combined a deadline with two possible routes: implementing President Donald Trump’s proposed framework, which he said Netanyahu’s government had accepted, or using military force.
“Within 18 months of my taking office as prime minister, Hamas will no longer rule the Gaza Strip,” he said. “We will bring about the destruction of Hamas’s military wing.”
His central argument was that Israel’s military successes had not produced the political and security outcomes needed to prevent another war. Three years after the October 7 massacre, he said, Hamas remained in control of Gaza, was acquiring weapons and was rebuilding its fighting capacity.
“As long as Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power, Hamas will remain in power,” Eisenkot said.
The criticism extended beyond Gaza. Eisenkot argued that the government had failed to turn battlefield achievements in Iran and Lebanon into the strategic results Netanyahu himself had promised. He accused the prime minister of yielding to coalition demands and draft evaders while presenting himself to voters as an uncompromising leader.
The speech builds on a dispute that began while Eisenkot was inside Netanyahu’s government. He served as an observer in the small war cabinet established after the October 7, 2023, attack, before leaving the government alongside Benny Gantz in June 2024 over what they described as Netanyahu’s failure to develop a strategy for the Gaza war.
Eisenkot, who led the IDF from 2015 to 2019, is now presenting that military experience as a qualification for national leadership. In his address, he said he had the knowledge needed to oversee the military, Mossad and Shin Bet.
He also pledged to establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7, arguing that investigating the failures and implementing its findings were essential to preventing another disaster.
“We must not accept the notion that such failures are an inevitable fate,” he said. “There is a way to prevent the next disaster.”
