Türkiye’s budget posts 532 billion lira deficit in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:22:18 UTC
18:22:18 KST

Türkiye’s central government budget posted a deficit of 532 billion Turkish Liras in September, according to data released by the Treasury and Finance Ministry on Oct. 15.
Budget revenues rose 22.7 percent year-on-year to 1.25 trillion liras in September, while expenditures increased 34.1 percent to 1.79 trillion liras.
Non-interest expenditures climbed 39.1 percent from a year earlier to 1.52 trillion liras, while interest payments increased 11.2 percent to 263 billion liras.
The primary deficit was 269.2 billion liras in September, marking a 269 percent increase from the same month last year.
In the January-September period, budget revenues increased 34.5 percent year-on-year to 12.1 trillion liras, while expenditures rose 36.4 percent to 13.9 trillion liras.
As a result, the central government budget recorded a deficit of 1.84 trillion liras in the first nine months of the year.
The primary surplus for the January-September period fell 7.7 percent from a year earlier to 410.8 billion liras.

Mental health at work starts by breaking the taboo, EU agency says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:21:16 UTC
18:21:16 KST

Nearly half of European workers face mental health risks on the job, yet the subject remains taboo.
Health and safety is the backbone of working life. However, as workplaces and working practices evolve, new challenges emerge while old ones remain unsolved.
Against a backdrop of staff shortages and ageing populations, Europe’s workforce is battling poor mental health; however, the issue is still not being recognised at workplaces, William Cockburn, EU-OSHA executive director, told Euronews.
“Whether we're asking employers or workers, they identify a reluctance to speak openly about mental health issues as the … main obstacle to actually taking action,” he said.
Many EU employees say their jobs are hurting their mental health. Nearly half of workers (45%) face risks to their mental health on the job, according to the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA).
“We see psychosocial risks at the workplace, for example, long working hours, highly intense work, emotionally demanding tasks … and we link that to increased impact on workers’ health,” Cockburn said.
Around 44% of workers report severe time pressure or overload. According to the European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), work-related depression costs the EU more than €100 billion a year, when absenteeism, reduced productivity, and healthcare and wider social costs are combined.
Despite the burden these conditions place on employers, Cockburn said a reluctance to talk and persistent stigma among workers are slowing action.
So, what can be done about it?
For Cockburn, mental health issues “need to be addressed like physical health issues at work”.
The approach, he noted, is to assess the risks first and then adapt whatever is needed to minimise harm.
“We identify hazards like long working hours, like adverse relationships at work … to an extreme you can go to bullying and harassment, violence or threats of violence,” he added.
Workers should be part of the conversation
While many see mental health as a personal issue, Esther Lynch, general secretary of the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), argues that prevention should focus on the workplace rather than on the individual affected.
“We don't wait until people have a finger chopped off before we put guardrails in place,” Lynch said. “We do a risk assessment and say what's the risk associated with the way this work is carried out and then we put the guardrails in place”.
To achieve this, experts agree, workers must be part of the conversation. Yet only 45% say they are consulted about the stressful aspects of their jobs, according to EU-OSHA.
“Worker participation is a legal obligation under European law, but it's also a key success factor for successful interventions in health and safety at work,” said Cockburn.
This week, the European Commission launched the Healthy Workplaces campaign, an initiative to help employers prevent, assess and manage psychosocial risks at work. One of its aims is to overcome this reluctance to speak about mental health struggles.
“When we invest in building and keeping healthy working environments, we improve not only people's well-being, we reduce sick leave and staff turnover; we improve performance, and we don't put pressure on our health systems,” said Roxana Mînzatu, executive vice-president for social rights and jobs, at the campaign’s launch on Tuesday. “It’s a win-win for everyone.”

Startup’s laser turns Rheinmetall autonomous cargo vehicle into drone killer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:20:36 UTC
18:20:36 KST

- Aurelius Systems is displaying its Archimedes autonomous counter-drone laser on an American Rheinmetall unmanned ground vehicle at AUSA 2026.
- The startup raised $40 million in August and says Archimedes can defeat small and medium drones at more than a kilometer.
Aurelius Systems is showing its Archimedes autonomous laser weapon mounted on an American Rheinmetall unmanned ground vehicle at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting in Washington this week, where the two companies are pitching mobile laser defense against small drones to U.S. Army buyers.
The San Francisco-based startup said in a post on X that Archimedes is on display in motion at the Rheinmetall booth through the end of the show, as part of the companies’ partnership to bring counter-drone lasers to uncrewed combat vehicles.
Archimedes is a lightweight turret that combines a high-power laser with machine vision and radar, and Aurelius says it can find, track and burn down a drone on its own without an operator initiating each engagement. The system is aimed at Group 1 and Group 2 drones, the small and medium-size types that include commercial quadcopters and many of the one-way attack drones used in Ukraine, and the company says it can defeat them at more than a kilometer.
The two firms announced their partnership in July. According to Tectonic, Archimedes is being integrated first on the Ox, the unmanned ground vehicle American Rheinmetall has entered in the U.S. Army’s Ground Optionally Autonomous Transport competition for a vehicle that hauls supplies and equipment over rough terrain. With a laser on board, a cargo-carrying vehicle can defend itself against drones during resupply runs, a role Rheinmetall has described as protection for autonomous logistics missions.
Aurelius first showed the laser on a Rheinmetall vehicle at the Reindustrialize 2026 conference in Detroit in June, in a display built with American Rheinmetall and electric vehicle startup Harbinger.
In August, the company raised a $40 million Series A round co-led by Draper Associates and KAS Venture Partners to scale up Archimedes production. During the Pentagon’s T-REX 26-2 experimentation event, the laser downed more than 20 quadcopters and more than five drones supplied by the U.S. Army, Tectonic reported, and at the U.S. Army’s Operation Jailbreak exercise at Fort Carson, Colorado, Aurelius linked Archimedes with Anduril’s Lattice software and the Army’s Forward Area Air Defense command and control system, which ties sensors and shooters together.
Lasers appeal to militaries because each shot costs only the electricity needed to fire it, compared with tens of thousands of dollars or more for a missile interceptor, and Aurelius says it builds Archimedes largely from commercially available parts to keep the system’s own price down.

Ukrainian parliament passes key bill on international parcel taxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:20:00 UTC
18:20:00 KST

Editor's note: The story has been updated to include comments from Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
Ukraine's parliament passed a bill on taxing e-commerce and international parcels on Oct. 15, meeting a condition linked to international financial assistance after missing earlier deadlines.
The bill passed its final vote with 252 lawmakers in favour after facing criticism from some lawmakers. Parliament had previously failed to advance the bill and sent it back for revision.
Its adoption is linked to Ukraine receiving the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) tranche of around $700 million and the EU tranche of 3.7 billion euros ($4.1 billion) in macro-financial assistance.
The parliament repeatedly failed to pass some of the conditions set by Ukraine's partners throughout 2026, amid widespread unpopularity of the changes. Most toxic was a package of new taxes, including a tax on small imported parcels, and a tax on income received from digital platforms, such as Uber.
The legislation introduces the value-added tax (VAT) on international parcels worth up to 150 euros ($168), which are currently tax-exempt. Lawmakers also backed new customs regulations for international mail and express shipments.
The changes could take effect on July 1, 2027, but only after a separate government decision.
In recent days, parliament has advanced several key bills tied to Western aid, as $29.5 billion in budget funding at stake if lawmakers and the government fail to meet the required conditions.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said he hoped lawmakers would maintain the pace of passing bills.
"The results of this plenary week give us all reason to be optimistic, but there is still a lot of work ahead," Koretskyi wrote on social media.
"We count on the same constructive cooperation in the coming plenary weeks to ensure that all necessary decisions are adopted on time and Ukraine receives the full amount of international financial aid."

Slovakia's populist, Moscow-friendly leader framed this outreach as part of Bratislava's foreign "policy toward all four cardinal directions."
Fico noted that the upcoming Slovak-Ukrainian talks will be the fourth meeting of this format, with the last one held in the eastern Slovak city of Kosice last October.
The negotiations are to focus on expanding border crossings, providing humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, and establishing a school for Ukrainian children in Bratislava.
Fico last visited Ukraine in September 2025 for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky. He was also scheduled to attend the inaugural Carpathian summit on Sept. 18 in Ukraine's Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast, but ultimately skipped the event for health reasons.
Speaking to Slovak lawmakers before his departure for the European Council, Fico said that EU leaders are set to hold talks on a potential next loan for Ukraine and said Bratislava would not take part.
Fico's government has declined to participate in the EU's 90-billion-euro ($101 billion) loan for Kyiv adopted in April, but has not blocked it either and has voiced support for Ukraine's accession talks.
At the same time, the Slovak leader has consistently criticized energy sanctions against Russia and military aid to Ukraine, cutting off arms deliveries from Slovak army stocks. He was the only EU leader to visit the Russian capital for the May 9 Victory Day celebrations in 2025 and this year, meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Fico agreed with Putin on restarting the intergovernmental commission during the May celebrations in 2025, the Slovak newspaper Sme reported.
The last meeting of the commission, focused on economic and scientific cooperation between the two countries, was held in November 2021, months before the start of the all-out war in Ukraine.
The Slovak leader did not provide further details about the upcoming talks with the Russian side.

Australia introduces digital safety bill allowing users to switch off social media algorithms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:18:20 UTC
18:18:20 KST

Faisal Mahmud
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Australia introduced legislation Thursday requiring social media platforms to let users switch off algorithm-driven recommendations, as part of sweeping measures aimed at strengthening online safety.
The Digital Duty of Care Bill 2026 would require technology companies to proactively prevent online harms rather than respond after they occur.
According to a statement published on Communications Minister Anika Wells’ official website, Australians aged over 16 would be able to choose between algorithmically recommended content as their primary feed or accounts they follow.
The proposed law would establish minimum safety standards for social media platforms, gaming services, applications and artificial intelligence chatbots.
Platforms would also be required to protect users under 18 from harmful content, including material promoting eating disorders, dangerous stunts, criminal behavior and hostility toward women.
The legislation would empower Australia's eSafety Commissioner to remove AI-powered nudification services and reduce response deadlines for cyberbullying and online abuse complaints from 48 to 24 hours.
Companies violating the requirements could face penalties of up to $109.2 million Australian dollars ($75 million).
Professional news content and entertainment media would be exempt from the proposed provisions.
"The Digital Duty of Care is the next step in our world-leading online safety laws," Wells said.
"It will set basic safety standards for the digital services we use every day, just as we have for food, cars and kids’ toys," she added.
The bill was introduced in the House of Representatives and must pass both houses of Parliament, including the Senate, before becoming law. 
The proposal follows Australia's landmark restrictions on social media access for children under 16, part of Canberra's broader efforts to regulate digital platforms.

Tallinn tram driver: TLT doesn't train staff enough or review incidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:18:00 UTC
18:18:00 KST

Tallinn tram driver: TLT doesn't train staff enough or review incidents
A Tallinn tram department employee says drivers aren't given enough training or information about serious incidents, contradicting the transport company's public position.
The claim follows ERR's report on a father separated from his child by closing tram doors. Tallinn Transport (TLT) head Kaido Padar rejects the criticism, saying each incident gets reviewed.
The source, who asked to remain anonymous, contacted ERR this week following the father and child incident. They said the public is left with the impression from Padar's comments that driver training is continuous and systematic. However, daily experience tells a different story.
"We would also like to know: who is actually responsible today for the professional training of tram drivers, what does it consist of, how much practical instruction takes place, and how is its quality checked?" the source said.
"There are also growing questions among drivers about how new drivers are prepared, what the role of instructors is, on what basis people are selected for those positions, and whether professional requirements are still the priority," they added.
The source cited another incident from late February this year. In this case, one tram ran into another on Lubja tänav. Five people were injured, there was significant material damage, and tram traffic was disrupted for several hours.
"That serious accident has not, to my knowledge, been analysed together with the collective of tram drivers. The causes and circumstances of the accident remain unknown to employees," the source said. They added that TLT staff have still not been told what should be done to avoid similar accidents.
"Analysing such cases together should be an important part of tram driver refresher training. Unfortunately, that practice has, to my knowledge, disappeared."
The source said one more similar incident involving children and adults separated by closing doors occurred in the past week alone, as well as the one reported — which suggests no lesson has been taken from the earlier case.
Padar rejected this criticism, saying incidents are analysed and conclusions drawn from each one.
"When there are incidents, we always improve our system. There is always something to take from each case. The relevant group manager has spoken to the tram drivers and asked them to be even more attentive," Padar said, referring to the response to the father and child case.
He also said responsibility rests partly with passengers when boarding and departing from trams. "We have discussed how to make it clear to passengers, for example through a campaign, that you go to the doors before the stop, not when the stop has arrived and the doors are starting to close."
Padar said TLT has added the topic of door closing to its customer service training program, with the first session held on Tuesday. He said procedures include an apology process, and that the control center sends drivers reminders during the day.
Padar said unsuitable people don't get to be tram drivers, and that the training lasts months, and the bulk of applicants do not get selected. "We last hired people a year and a half ago. Tram driver training lasts four to six months. We had 92 candidates then, out of whom we selected 15 tram drivers."
"The tram driver's job is very prestigious and we have no vacancies there. It isn't a case of simply walking in and doing it," he noted.
He said a further recruitment round is likely next autumn since some drivers are approaching retirement.
Padar added internal matters cannot always be discussed openly because he cannot share personal data. "If our person is at fault, has done something wrong, or the matter is borderline, I'm not going to start whipping them in front of the organization. The easiest thing is to dismiss someone, but I repeat: if someone in our organization has erred, it goes to the employment contract termination committee; if there has been an accident, the accident committee reviews it."
Responding to the criticism, Padar said anyone inside the organization with questions should go to their direct manager and ask for additional training or a better understanding.
He added that there is room for improvement in Tallinn's public transport organization. "Can it be better? It can always be better. Can training be even better? Training can always be better," Padar confirmed.
ERR reported that the incident involving a family on a Tallinn tram brought similar stories to light on social media, with drivers accused of a lack of due care. TLT says it receives around 270 complaints a month, but that these mostly concern sticking to schedules.
As well as the two recent incidents where minors got separated from the caregivers accompanying them on the tram, and February's accident on Lubja, several other incidents have been reported. In March this year, a dog was left outside a tram with its leash caught in the doors, after which the driver physically and verbally assaulted a passenger who pulled the emergency brake to avert the worst; the driver was fired. In March 2025, a man on the tracks was killed by an approaching tram on Peterburi tee, with footage showing the driver had been watching a video on a smartphone just before the collision.

Dronten wreckage identified as British WWII bomber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:17:59 UTC
18:17:59 KST

Dronten wreckage identified as British WWII bomber
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Aircraft wreckage uncovered four years ago in Dronten has been identified as a British WWII bomber, according to local officials.
Discovered in what is now the Van Veldhuizenbos forest in Dronten, the aircraft is said to be a British Avro Lancaster Mk III that was shot down by German forces on the night of September 27-28, 1943, while attempting to target Hanover, Germany.
The aircraft, run by the Canadian 405 Pathfinder Squadron stationed near Cambridge, England, crashed into what was then the Ijsselmeer.
The plane was carrying seven crew members – four Canadians, one Australian, and two Britons – whose bodies were never recovered. But human remains were found in 1959 and buried in the Jonkerbos War Cemetery in Nijmegen.
Additional human remains were discovered and are now being examined by the Ministry of Defence’s Recovery and Identification Service to see if they belong to the slain crew members.
“Behind every plane wreck lies a human story,” said Dronten mayor Jean Paul Gebben, who said the aircraft’s identification was of great historical significance.
Some of the recovered wreckage will be loaned to museums and foundations.
The government estimates that some 5,500 aircraft were lost over the Netherlands during the Second World War. Annually, a maximum of three aircraft recovery operations are carried out in the country, with the costs mostly covered by the national government.

‘Switzerland is a partial member of the EU,’ says historian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:16:12 UTC
18:16:12 KST

‘Switzerland is a partial member of the EU,’ says historian
Switzerland has historically been shaped by the major powers around it and is far from being an independent country that can rely solely on itself, says historian André Holenstein.
The Senate has completed its review of the package of agreements (known as Bilaterals III) with the European Union (EU), and the issue is now heading over to the House of Representatives. The conservative camp, led by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, uses rhetoric that emphasises Switzerland’s independence in the face of “diktats from Brussels” and “foreign judges”, warns against “submission to Europe,” and denounces “interference by European institutions.”
Historian André Holenstein believes this idea of an independent Switzerland that can rely only on itself makes no historical sense. In his view, the debate over the agreements with the EU “suffers from a biased perception”.
More
Swiss senators flex muscles over EU treaty package
“Switzerland – both the old Confederation and modern Switzerland – is a country caught between, on the one hand, openness, especially in trade, towards the world and towards Europe, a Switzerland open to the world through migration flows; and on the other hand, a very rigid mental image of isolationism, the idea that we are a country that has always survived on its own resources and strength,” he told the public broadcaster RTS.
The co-author of the book Die Souveränität der Schweiz in Europa (Switzerland’s Sovereignty in Europe) points out that Switzerland is, in fact, already highly integrated in the EU.
“Through a series of democratic votes, Switzerland has decided to integrate itself into the European Union’s common market [Switzerland is, notably, a founding member of the European Free Trade Association or EFTA]. We are a partial member of the European Union,” Holenstein argued.
Shaped by foreign powers
The historian therefore considers it logical that this proximity comes with certain obligations: “If we want to be part of this common market, of course we are obliged to follow the rules under which it was established. It’s quite simple in principle. So to speak of a colonial contract or a contract of submission is to refuse to see what is at stake.”
More
Why Switzerland stays out of the European Union
Holenstein goes further. In his book Mitten in Europa (In the Middle of Europe), he shows that Switzerland is a nation shaped by the will of foreign powers and that it has never been sovereign.
“What happened between 1798 and 1848 was absolutely decisive in the formation of modern Switzerland,” he said. “Before that, under the Ancien Régime, we were a Helvetic body – a Confederation composed of 13 small republics whose primary common interest was to avoid becoming a nation in order to preserve as much autonomy as possible.”
These 50 years were marked by numerous political crises, including wars between the cantons and interference by neighbouring great powers. “Foreign powers played a major role in helping Switzerland become what it was by 1848,” said Holenstein.
He cites the example of the French invasion and the creation of the Helvetic Republic in 1798. “This marked the end of many vital and essential elements of the Ancien Régime,” he explained. “There would never again be subject territories. From that point on, in principle, the former subject territories would be equal to the former cantons.”
Buffer state
“Next, it is important to recall that it was Napoleon who, in 1803, created six new cantons, including Vaud, Ticino, Thurgau, and St Gallen,” he added. “These cantons owe their cantonal sovereignty and their status as full-fledged cantons of the Confederation to Napoleon, not to the Confederates.”
Holenstein also points out that the Congress of Vienna in 1815 was pivotal in establishing Swiss neutrality.
More
The Swiss-EU bilateral treaty updates, explained
“Here again, it was the foreign powers that, in a sense, recognised Switzerland’s independence. They reasoned that this small country, situated in the middle of the continent, served – through its neutrality – a new European security architecture. Switzerland acted as a buffer state separating France and the former Austrian Empire, thereby making a major contribution to European peace and security.”
“All of this serves to remind us just how significant a role foreign influence played in this transition from 1798 to 1848, during which Switzerland took a long time to find its new form and its new role,” Holenstein concluded.

Norway’s Kongsberg to Make Anti-Drone Cannon Turrets in Poland From 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:16:11 UTC
18:16:11 KST

- Category
- World
Norway’s Kongsberg to Make Anti-Drone Cannon Turrets in Poland From 2028
Norwegian defense manufacturer Kongsberg is preparing to build a production facility for anti-drone hardware in Poland to support the domestic SAN air defense network.
The agreement is expected to be signed by the end of the year, with construction starting immediately afterward, Defense Express reported on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The total financial commitment stands at 200 million Polish zlotys ($51 million), equivalent to €45 million ($50.2 million), with operations expected to launch in 2028.
Integrating production facilities within Poland aims to streamline supply chains for the country's national defense architecture. The plant will produce Kongsberg PROTECTOR weapon stations equipped with 30mm cannons, which serve as core modules for the SAN counter-drone system.
Establishing localized manufacturing addresses prior concerns regarding reliance on external components, helping to ensure greater domestic control over military hardware while creating economic value within the country.
The SAN air defense network relies on a combination of defensive platforms. Alongside 30mm cannon turrets, the network incorporates 12.7mm machine gun mounts, self-propelled 35mm SA-35 anti-aircraft systems, electronic warfare units, APKWS precision rockets, and Merops interceptor drones. These capabilities are configured onto Legwan all-terrain vehicles and Jelcz heavy trucks, as reported by Defense Express.
Polish armed forces have ordered 18 batteries of the system, comprising 18 command platoons and 52 firing platoons to expand protection against unmanned aerial threats. Neighboring Slovakia has also indicated interest in the platform through regional defense cooperation frameworks.
Cannon and machine gun turrets offer a cost-effective countermeasure compared to traditional surface-to-air missiles, despite functional constraints regarding operational ceiling and maximum engagement range.
Previously, Poland signed a major defense contract valued at approximately $4.2 billion with a consortium of PGZ and Kongsberg to acquire the SAN anti-drone system.
The contract, which was scheduled for delivery between 2026 and 2028, included 18 batteries, 18 command platoons, and 52 fire platoons capable of autonomously detecting, classifying, and neutralizing drones.

Herzog flies over Turkey despite ban on Israeli state planes, joins summit alongside Iranian representative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:16:06 UTC
18:16:06 KST

Israeli President Isaac Herzog arrived in Azerbaijan for an international summit attended by representatives of countries that have no diplomatic relations with Israel, including Iran, after taking an unusual flight through Turkish airspace despite Ankara's ban on Israeli government aircraft.
Among those attending were the emir of Qatar, Kuwait's deputy foreign minister, the ambassadors to Azerbaijan of Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Pakistan, Malaysia and Indonesia, Bangladesh's acting foreign minister and Iran's deputy foreign minister. When Herzog addressed the summit, the representatives of Iran, Turkey, Kuwait, Pakistan and the Palestinian Authority left the hall. The emir of Qatar remained, as did representatives of Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Central Asian countries.
Herzog landed in Baku on Wednesday aboard a commercial Azerbaijan Airlines flight, allowing him to reach the Azerbaijani capital without taking a longer route over the Black Sea, which his team considered potentially dangerous because of the war between Russia and Ukraine.
The flight also provided an unexpected workaround to Turkey's restrictions on Israeli official aircraft, which have previously disrupted visits by senior Israeli leaders to Azerbaijan.
Herzog arrived for a day-and-a-half visit to participate in the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), an international forum dedicated to strengthening cooperation and relations among Asian countries.
Alongside the Israeli president, the summit includes representatives from several countries that do not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, including Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Malaysia and Indonesia. An Iranian representative is also attending.
According to a report by Middle East Eye, flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 and footage from Herzog's welcoming ceremony in Baku indicate that the Israeli president traveled on Azerbaijan Airlines flight J222. The flight departed Ben-Gurion Airport at 11:35 a.m. Wednesday, crossed Turkish airspace and landed in Baku at 3:40 p.m. local time.
Images from the welcoming ceremony showed Herzog arriving on an Azerbaijan Airlines Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner, matching the aircraft type recorded for the flight.
The president's team reportedly chose the commercial flight rather than a longer alternative route through Greece, Bulgaria and the Black Sea. The alternative raised security concerns because of continuing attacks on vessels in the Black Sea amid the Russia-Ukraine war.
Turkey has barred Israeli government aircraft from using its airspace, but commercial flights operated by Israeli and foreign airlines are still permitted to pass through the country on routes to and from Israel.
According to Middle East Eye, an official familiar with the matter said Azerbaijan had not informed Ankara that Herzog was aboard the flight.
"Naturally, Turkey cannot get the passenger manifest for every airliner just passing through the airspace," the Turkish official said. The official added that Israel had stopped submitting requests to use Turkish airspace because it was already familiar with Ankara's position.
Turkey's restrictions have previously interfered with Israeli diplomatic travel. In May 2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu postponed a planned visit to Baku, with reports at the time citing Ankara's refusal to allow Israel's official Wing of Zion aircraft to pass through Turkish airspace. Netanyahu's office cited developments in Gaza and Syria and a demanding political and security schedule.
Herzog himself canceled a planned visit to the COP29 climate conference in Azerbaijan in November 2024, amid reports that Turkey had refused permission for the Israeli state aircraft to cross its territory. This time, Wing of Zion was unavailable because of maintenance work, and Herzog traveled aboard the Azerbaijani aircraft instead. The President's Office declined to comment on the flight details.
The unusual journey also attracted attention because of the name of the aircraft carrying Herzog. Social media users identified the Azerbaijani plane as "Shusha," a name associated with the Shusha Declaration, a 2021 agreement between Azerbaijan and Turkey strengthening their strategic and defense cooperation following the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.
Some commentators interpreted the choice of aircraft as a further symbolic jab by Baku at Ankara, although there has been no confirmation that the aircraft was selected for that reason.
The diplomatic symbolism extended to the summit itself. Herzog met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev ahead of the gathering, which brings together countries with sharply differing positions on Israel and the wider Middle East.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan did not attend the summit, with Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan representing Ankara instead. Some reports suggested Erdogan's absence may have been connected to Herzog's participation, although this has not been officially confirmed. The meeting comes at a sensitive moment in relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan, two close regional allies.
Azerbaijan's recent school dress-code restrictions, which have prevented some students and teachers wearing Islamic headscarves from entering classrooms, have triggered protests and a public dispute involving political figures in both countries.
The restrictions have become another source of friction between Ankara and Baku, adding a further dimension to Herzog's appearance at the international gathering. On Thursday morning, as voting opened at Israeli diplomatic missions around the world ahead of the October 27 election, Herzog visited the Israeli Embassy in Baku alongside Israel's ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ronen Krausz.
"This is a very important moment during my state visit here to Azerbaijan," Herzog said. "I have the opportunity to see how the election process begins and how voting is actually conducted at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad, here at the embassy in Baku."
The president encouraged Israelis to participate in the democratic process and emphasized the importance of the upcoming election after a difficult period for the country.
"These elections are a celebration of democracy in Israel and at its embassies abroad," he said. "I call on all Israeli citizens to exercise their right to vote and, of course, to influence Israel's future."
Herzog also appealed for restraint amid political tensions surrounding the election campaign. "These are very important elections after a difficult period for the State of Israel, and the main thing I want to say to every Israeli citizen is that elections are not a civil war," he said.
"On the contrary, they are the genuine democratic process through which we influence our lives and determine the direction our country takes."

Croatia pumps the brakes on Montenegro’s EU membership bid

Croatia pumps the brakes on Montenegro’s EU membership bid
Zagreb is pressing Podgorica to resolve long-standing disputes over war crimes, compensation and border demarcation before wrapping up EU accession talks.
Croatia's Prime Minister Andrej Plenković attends a press conference after work sessions at the MED9 summit in Split on October 7, 2026. | Marko Perkov/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Montenegro as the EU’s 28th member by 2028? Not so fast, says Croatia, the bloc’s most recent member.
Ahead of a debate on enlargement among EU leaders at Thursday’s summit, Croatia — which joined the bloc in 2013 — is among the countries raising concerns about Montenegro’s accession bid.
Speaking to POLITICO at a pre-summit meeting of the European People’s Party, Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said Zagreb had been “extremely constructive” but pointed to unresolved issues under negotiating Chapter 23 (Judiciary and Fundamental Rights) and Chapter 31 (Foreign, Security and Defence Policy), some of which date back decades.
Advertisement
“Some have been on the agenda for the last two years [with] no progress whatsoever,” he said, urging Montenegro to make headway. “We will ask our colleagues to help them to make progress, if there’s an objective to conclude the negotiations.”
Croatia’s concerns are laid out in an orientation paper, obtained by POLITICO, in which Zagreb insists it supports Montenegro’s EU membership ambitions while identifying several outstanding disputes that need to be resolved.
“Croatia seeks to facilitate Montenegro’s accession, not obstruct it,” the paper reads. Several of the unresolved issues stem from Montenegro’s involvement in the military aggression against Croatia in the 1990s, including attacks on Dubrovnik and the occupation of parts of Croatian territory, according to the document.
Among Zagreb’s demands is compensation for Croatian nationals detained at the Morinj camp, where more than 300 Croatians were held between October 1991 and August 1992, following the occupation of part of the Dubrovnik region by Serbian and Montenegrin forces.
Croatia is also calling for the preservation and permanent display of a memorial plaque at the former detention camp, as well as the renaming of a municipal swimming pool in Kotor dedicated to Zoran Gopčević, a former international water polo player who, according to the document, served as a guard at Morinj in 1991 and 1992.
Other outstanding demands include the prosecution of war crimes committed during Croatia’s War of Independence and further talks on the delimitation of the border between the two countries.
Despite those disputes, Croatia has so far consented to Montenegro’s progress in accession negotiations. The country has provisionally closed 21 of its 33 negotiating chapters, making it the frontrunner in the EU’s enlargement process.

Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for children

Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for children
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Routine vaccinations are free of charge and available at healthcare facilities.
50,000 doses of the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine have arrived in Ukraine for free vaccination of children in accordance with the Immunization Schedule. This was reported by the Public Health Center of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Ukraine receives these vaccines as part of cooperation between the Ministry of Health and the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (Gavi). The partnership agreement between the Global Alliance and Ukraine was signed at the end of 2024. Under the agreement, Gavi finances part of the vaccines supporting the national immunization program, in accordance with the national Immunization Development Strategy through 2030
According to the available information, במסגרת this partnership, UNICEF procures and delivers the vaccines to the country, while the Public Health Center of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine coordinates their distribution to regional disease control and prevention centers (DCCs). The vaccines have now reached healthcare facilities, which will ensure the continuity of routine immunization for children.
Where a child can be vaccinated
To vaccinate a child, you should contact your family doctor, pediatrician or the nearest healthcare facility. The Public Health Center emphasizes that vaccination under the National Immunization Schedule is free of charge.
If a child has missed any routine vaccinations, you should contact a doctor as soon as possible; the doctor will draw up an individual catch-up schedule
Why these infections are dangerous
Measles is a contagious infectious disease that can lead to serious complications, from pneumonia to encephalitis (inflammation of the brain) and even death. In pregnant women, measles can cause premature labor or miscarriage.
Mumps is one of the most common and contagious infections in the world, and can cause a number of severe complications, such as orchitis in men (inflammation of the testicle, which can lead to infertility), acute pancreatitis, meningitis and deafness.
Rubella is an infectious viral disease that can lead to miscarriage or congenital malformations in the child in pregnant women.
Vaccination is the most effective protection against these diseases.

Artemis III Scientist Shares What to Expect From NASA’s Next Lunar Mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

For years, NASA hoped to bring humans back to the moon’s surface, and Artemis III was going to be the mission to accomplish this feat. That will no longer be the case.
Following the successful Artemis II flyby last April, the program’s schedule was revised. According to the most recent announcements, the next mission will have to wait until 2028, and while the new plans are admittedly less spectacular than a lunar landing, they’re hardly dispensable.
In 2027, NASA plans to test in Earth orbit whether the Orion capsule can safely rendezvous and operate with commercial lunar landing systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin before attempting those same maneuvers around the moon. WIRED en Español spoke with Barbara Cohen, a scientist on the Artemis III project, to better understand this upcoming mission—the conversation ranging from the role humans still play in the face of increasingly capable robots and sensors to what we can learn about the solar system’s violent past from traces preserved on the moon.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
JORGE GARAY: What should people expect from Artemis III, and why does this mission matter even if it won’t land astronauts on the moon?
BARBARA COHEN: Artemis III is an Earth-orbiting mission. That’s the one that’s coming up next. We will send the Orion capsule to Earth’s orbit with the people in it. Blue Origin and SpaceX are the companies that are making the lunar landers, so each one of those companies will make a test article. It won’t be the full lunar lander, but those companies will send their version of the test article into Earth’s orbit to meet up with Orion. This is to make sure that Orion can meet with the lunar landers, so that when they do go to lunar orbit, they can do that safely.
Where does science fit into the Artemis program, and what have you learned so far about how astronauts can contribute scientifically?
The Artemis missions, just to be clear, are not science missions. They’re exploration for a lot of different reasons. We do that for technology development. We do that for inspiration. And we try to get the science that we can from the opportunity. And so we still work really hard to identify unique science opportunities that exist because the mission exists.
One of the things on Artemis III we’re doing is like a dress rehearsal for bringing samples back from the moon. When we land on the moon and start to bring samples back, those samples change as soon as you take them out of their natural environment. We try to make sure that they change as little as possible, but they are going to change.
You have to bring them back and put them into curation so that scientists can study them. We want to understand every step along the way: What could be changing the samples, how the samples could be reacting, especially to the environment around them. So we’ll have our crew deploy these witness materials—pieces of aluminum foil, pieces of Teflon, maybe pieces of ceramic. They’re very clean surfaces, very small pieces, maybe the size of a quarter or a nickel. And the team will be opening those up and exposing them to the crew cabin throughout their flight. That’ll give us a feel for how the humans change the environment around them.
With the capabilities of probes and other robotic tools today, what is the purpose of sending human astronauts into space?
If you just want to take pictures, you do that with robotic assets. Robots can take pictures. They do that all the time. We have lots of pictures in the area. We also have, on the International Space Station, a way for us to ask, “Please take a picture of this. Please take a picture of that.” That’s not what we did with Artemis II, and that’s not what we’re trying to do with Artemis III or Artemis IV, V, VI. With the Artemis missions, we’re trying to use the humans to their best capability, and what the humans are really good at is seeing a wide scene, zooming in on details very naturally, and then trying to interpret what they’re seeing and take the next step.
We don’t know everything about the moon. To learn more, we need to literally go on the surface and figure out what’s there and where to go next. So some of this is trying to train—not just the crew onboard—but the flight directors and the science team and the engineers. We all need to work together to enable humans to do what they do best.
We also give the crew science prompts. We say, “What do you think is happening in this scene? There’s something like a storm or an algal bloom or a fire. What do you see? How do you see the scene changing? What do you think that means? What do you think is causing that change? What do you think is going to happen next? If you could do anything, what would you do next?” That helps us understand what they’re looking at, which is not just taking pictures. It’s making observations, making understanding, making inferences with their brains. That’s what humans are really good at. That’s what we’ll be asking them to do.
From a science point of view, we learned a lot about how crew really wants to use their powers of observation, and how we should participate in the observations and train them in the science that we want them to do. We also had the ability to include science directly in flight. On Artemis II, we had our science officer talk directly to crew. That was a new thing that we’ll be carrying forward to Artemis III and beyond.
When humans return to the lunar surface, what scientific questions would you most like Artemis to help answer?
I have a personal opinion. My personal scientific interest is how old craters on the moon are. If you look at the moon—with binoculars or a small telescope, or even in pictures—you see that it is covered in craters. In fact, we call it saturated, because every crater that forms does so on another crater. The whole surface is covered in craters. The Earth is not, but I promise you that for every crater that formed on the moon, there was a crater that formed on Earth.
The moon doesn’t get hit more than the Earth, but we have a lot of water. We have erosion on our continents. Our continents move around. They get subducted. We get new land that forms. All of those processes on the Earth erase craters. And so, if we want to know what was hitting the Earth in the past—and I promise you that things were hitting the Earth—we can’t find that evidence on the Earth anymore. We’ve erased it. So we have to go to the moon to figure that out.
There was a period in time when the solar system was forming—4.5 billion years ago, 4 billion years ago. Humans weren’t around. Life hadn’t arisen on Earth yet. We think that the solar system was very dynamic, and there were a lot of impacts happening, a lot of material being exchanged. So there were a lot of craters—big, big craters, basin-size craters, craters the size of continents. They really disrupted the moon, and they would have disrupted the Earth as well. Like I said, we don’t have any evidence of that because we don’t have any rocks from that time anymore. But it’s really worth knowing. Did we disrupt the Earth several times? How did life get going? How did we get nutrients? How did material move around the solar system? That evidence is preserved on the moon.
There is a big crater called the South Pole-Aitken Basin. It’s on the lunar far side, but it intersects the South Pole of the moon, where we expect humans to be going. It would be my personal desire that humans could collect pieces of that big crater, and we could understand when it formed and what it did to the moon and what was happening in the solar system at that time.
Artemis III won’t do that just yet. Lunar touchdown is currently expected as part of Artemis IV, which is expected to take off in early 2028. Before then, the upcoming third mission will have to demonstrate something far less spectacular, but crucial for the program’s future: That the spacecraft, procedures, and the people who will one day carry out these missions can work together safely.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

NATO state seeks to shut down Russian gas pipeline – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

18:13:37 KST

NATO state seeks to shut down Russian gas pipeline – media
The Estonian government reportedly plans to seek neighboring Latvia’s cooperation in shutting down a gas pipeline that serves as a backup supply route to Kaliningrad Region, the Russian exclave that Western officials recently called a strategic vulnerability for Moscow.
The government of Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal was surprised to learn that local operator Elering was maintaining the pipeline in working condition, Eesti Ekspress reported on Wednesday. Tallinn now intends to work with Riga to close the route, the outlet said.
The Estonian section of the pipeline consists of two parallel pipes, each 70 centimeters in diameter, running just 22 km through Voru County in the southeast of the country. The connection is clearly marked on a pipeline map published on Elering’s website. According to Eesti Ekspress, it was last used in fall 2024.
Michal reportedly hopes to persuade the Latvian government to close a valve and physically prevent gas from flowing through the connection. If Riga refuses, Tallinn could impose sanctions on Russian gas transit, potentially creating legal complications for Latvia and Lithuania, through which the backup route passes before reaching Kaliningrad Region. Estonian Energy Minister Erkki Keldo told Eesti Ekspress he feared Moscow would exploit such a move to publicly criticize Tallinn.
Officials in several NATO members, including Estonia, have recently described Kaliningrad Region as a Russian vulnerability due to its geographic position. Moscow has warned that any escalation where the US-led military bloc threatened Russia’s territorial integrity, including that of its westernmost region, could result in a nuclear war.
Kaliningrad’s principal overland gas supply route is the Minsk-Vilnius-Kaunas-Kaliningrad pipeline, which first entered service in 1985 and has an annual capacity of 2.5 billion cubic meters. Russia’s Gazprom renewed its transit agreement with Lithuania’s Amber Grid in 2025, securing the arrangement through the end of 2030.
Nevertheless, Moscow has long considered the Baltic states unreliable transit partners, fearing they could cut off supplies for political reasons. In 2019, Gazprom commissioned an LNG receiving terminal near Kaliningrad, complementing the region’s underground gas storage facilities. The maritime supply system uses the Marshal Vasilevskiy, an LNG carrier equipped to regasify its cargo.
Originally intended as insurance against geopolitical disruptions, the more expensive maritime route was activated last year as Western sanctions targeting Russian gas made deliveries from Leningrad Region to the isolated Russian territory commercially viable. In an emergency, the LNG system has sufficient capacity to meet Kaliningrad Region’s entire gas demand, which the regional government said totaled 2.24 billion cubic meters last year.

Zelenskyy: 850 Shaheds came as Starlink limits hit defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:11:10 UTC
18:11:10 KST

- Zelenskyy said Russia launched over 850 Shaheds between Oct. 14 and 9 a.m. Oct. 15, during a SpaceX speed cap on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals.
- The 160 km/h Starshield limit, imposed overnight Oct. 13–14, cripples interceptor drones needed against Russian jet-powered Shaheds flying up to 600 km/h.
Russia launched more than 850 Shahed attack drones at Ukraine in roughly a day and a half, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 15, an onslaught that came as a new speed cap on SpaceX’s Starlink network curtailed the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to shoot them down.
Zelenskyy said the count covered the period from the start of Oct. 14 until 9 a.m. on Oct. 15. He said attacks came in constant waves and that Ukrainian airspace was not free of drones for a single hour. Russian strikes killed three people in Kropyvnytskyi and three more in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukrainian media reported.
“From the start of yesterday until 9 a.m. today, there have already been more than 850 Shaheds, and this is precisely at a time of an artificial speed restriction on our defensive capabilities. Some of the Shaheds were shot down. But unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits,” Zelenskyy said, in remarks translated from Ukrainian.
The restriction he referred to took effect overnight on Oct. 13–14, when SpaceX capped Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukraine’s armed forces, at 160 km/h (about 100 mph) for terminals in motion. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said SpaceX imposed the limit unilaterally and without warning, and that any terminal moving faster than that loses its connection, disrupting interceptor and mid-range drone missions as well as frontline reconnaissance, logistics and signal relays.
Under the cap, the restriction falls most heavily on Ukraine’s air defense. Russia’s jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones can fly at up to 600 km/h (about 370 mph), so interceptors that must chase them down need far more speed than 160 km/h. Starlink has been blocked over Russian territory since February 2026 under a whitelist of approved terminals, and Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian targets rely on other communications. The capped terminals instead serve tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles operating over Ukraine and the occupied territories, which means the limit cuts into Ukraine’s defense.
Service was later restored below the 160 km/h threshold, and Mykhailo Fedorov said attack and interceptor drones should be able to fly again, while adding that Ukraine now needs the Starshield speed limit removed altogether.
Elon Musk said on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the U.S. president, the Associated Press reported, while the White House told Kyiv it does not control SpaceX, according to Axios. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times on Oct. 15 that the restriction was a deliberate decision on the American side rather than a technical fault, though he said he did not know whether SpaceX or the U.S. government made the call.
Zelenskyy also accused Moscow of escalating its strikes after seeing sanctions eased and attempts to pressure Kyiv, and urged Americans to side with Ukraine’s defense instead of the aggressor.
The Defense Ministry said it is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners and is setting up backup communication channels, but neither SpaceX nor the U.S. Department of War has said whether or when the 160 km/h cap will be lifted.

He made the remarks to journalists on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in Bangkok, Ukrinform reports, citing Reuters.

According to the German official, these expectations are linked, among other things, to the need to explain to the German public the substantial amount of aid provided to Ukraine amid cuts in Germany’s budget spending.
Klingbeil said he was holding talks with international partners to secure continued funding for Ukraine. In particular, Australia and South Korea reaffirmed their commitments to continuing support during meetings in Bangkok on Thursday.
“One has to say that this is a different kind of commitment from that of us Europeans, who are geographically much closer," Klingbeil said. "But both made very clear that their support for Ukraine will continue,” the German minister said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Prime Minister of Ukraine Sergii Koretskyi said Ukraine’s need for external budget financing next year exceeds $52 billion.

Labour MPs urge Healey to raise taxes on slot machines
Rob Davies
Nearly 90 Labour MPs have urged the Chancellor, John Healey, to ignore the gambling sector’s warnings about job losses and double the tax on high street slot machines at his inaugural budget later this month.
Campaigners say raising “machine games duty” (MGD) from 20% to 40% could raise £460m to fund public services and reduce the harm caused by 24-hour slots venues.
In a letter sent on Thursday, 88 Labour MPs – nearly a quarter of the party’s backbenchers – demanded that “those who profit most from products associated with the greatest harm should be taxed at a higher rate”.
Their main target is “Category B3” slot machines, which allow punters to place rapid fire stakes of £2 every 2.5 seconds, for a chance of a £500 jackpot. Fruit machines in pubs, which are usually Category C, should be exempt, they said.
There were 49,094 B3 machines in Great Britain as of June 2024, racking up annual takings of nearly £2bn according to Gambling Commission figures. Each terminal took an average of £40,127 during that year, more than the median UK salary.
The MPs cited evidence from the regulator that players of these machines are “among the groups most likely to contact gambling help services, that those with gambling problems play gaming machines more frequently than those with fewer problems, and that problem gamblers spend relatively more time and money on machines.”
The Guardian has previously exposed how so-called adult gaming centres (AGCs), known by some in the industry as “slot farms” have exploited vulnerable gamblers and taken advantage of lax planning laws to flood high streets with the machines in the UK’s poorest areas.
The machines “depend on repeated local losses, often in communities least able to afford them” according to the letter, led by Alex Ballinger MP.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is understood to be supportive of measures that would crack down on AGCs, having been a vocal critic of them as Mayor of Greater Manchester.
Earlier this week the bosses of firms including Ladbrokes and Paddy Power signed a last-ditch letter to Healey, predicting that doubling MGD could trigger up to 1,470 betting shop closures, 34 casino closures and 15,900 job losses.
Signatories included Britain’s largest taxpayer, Fred Done, whose family have earned £105m in dividends from their gambling business since 2022.

SYDNEY, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have launched a new study to examine whether cervical cancer can be detected through a non-invasive blood test.
Led by the University of Queensland (UQ), the CLARITY cervical cancer study at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital will investigate the potential of blood biomarkers in the screening, monitoring and management of cervical cancer, according to a UQ statement released recently.
"The project has the potential to improve early detection, treatment responses and post-treatment surveillance, as well as support more personalized treatment approaches for women with cervical cancer," said Andreas Obermair, chief investigator at UQ's Queensland Center for Gynecological Cancer Research.
Despite advances in prevention and treatment, including the Gardasil vaccine, cervical cancer continues to impose significant physical, emotional and financial burdens on women worldwide, Obermair noted.
A reliable, non-invasive test could offer "a more accessible and acceptable alternative" to current cervical screening methods, particularly for women facing cultural, systemic or personal barriers to screening, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and culturally diverse communities, he said. ■

LANZHOU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's C919 passenger jet has carried more than 8.4 million passengers and served 27 cities since entering commercial service, Shen Bo, president of the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC), said Thursday.
Speaking at an industry conference in Dunhuang, northwest China's Gansu Province, Shen said COMAC has also continued to expand the regional aviation network served by its C909 aircraft, a regional jet designed for short- and medium-haul routes.
The C909 has safely carried more than 41 million passengers since entering commercial service, Shen said, adding that the aircraft is providing travelers with more convenient options.
Wang Changshun, chairman of the China Air Transport Association, said China's regional aviation fleet has been rapidly transforming in recent years, with domestic aircraft accounting for a substantially larger share.
The C919 is accelerating its scale-up in commercial operations, while the C909 has become a mainstay of the regional aviation market, contributing to the high-quality development of China's regional aviation sector, he said.
The C919 is the first trunk jetliner independently developed by China in accordance with international airworthiness standards and with independent intellectual property rights.
The baseline model is designed for 158 to 192 passengers and a range of 4,075 to 5,555 kilometers. It completed its first commercial flight in May 2023. After successful operations on multiple domestic routes, the aircraft completed its first scheduled international commercial passenger flight in August this year.
The C909, formerly known as the ARJ21, entered commercial service in 2016. According to COMAC, it is suitable for regional airports or sub-hub airports to build route networks and supplement transport capacity for hub airports.
China's civil aviation market continued to expand in 2025, carrying 770 million passenger trips, up 5.5 percent year on year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China.
The country's latest five-year plan for civil aviation development from 2026-2030 calls for improving transport infrastructure, efficiency and services as well as fostering independent innovation and industrial integration. It sets a 2030 goal of reaching world-class standards in aviation safety, service capacity and infrastructure. ■

UK Pledges $23M for Chornobyl Repairs Amid Support Strains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:08:45 UTC
18:08:45 KST

Britain pledged £17 million ($23 million) on Thursday, Oct. 15 toward repairs to the protective shelter and ventilation system at the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, as far-right parties question continued aid to Kyiv and Ukraine’s military faces disruption to satellite communications.
The UK government said the funding will help restore the shelter’s confinement and ventilation functions. The contribution is part of an international program coordinated by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), working with Ukraine and G7 donors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, it is not the full cost of the repairs. The EBRD has estimated that the work could exceed €500 million ($585 million).
Why Chornobyl’s shelter needs repairs
The New Safe Confinement is a 35-story arch built over reactor No. 4 to contain radioactive material and allow engineers to dismantle the remains of the reactor and the original sarcophagus. The €2.1 billion ($2.5 billion) structure was designed to last 100 years and was constructed with contributions from 45 countries.
A Russian drone struck the plant on Feb. 14, 2025, punching a hole through its roof and igniting a fire in the cladding. The fire smoldered inside its layers for two weeks before it was extinguished. The strike damaged the ventilation system and the structure’s seal, allowing moist air to enter and raising the risk of corrosion in the steel arch.
In May, the EBRD said that radiation was not escaping the confinement, but warned that corrosion could undermine the structure if repairs are delayed. Engineers also face difficult working conditions: the site’s radiation levels limit how long workers can remain inside.
Musk Tells Zelensky to ‘Go’ as Ukraine Questions US Support
The extent of the damage is still being assessed, and the final repair estimate could change. More detail on the damage to the confinement and the repair work shows why the British contribution is one part of a much larger funding effort.
The UK has previously donated €8 million ($9 million) to the International Chornobyl Cooperation Account, which supports nuclear safety at the site. It announced another £54 million ($72 million) in winter support last week, including £20 million ($26 million) for energy assistance. The government says Britain has provided nearly £25 billion ($33 billion) in total support to Ukraine.
During a meeting in London, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told President Volodymyr Zelensky that Britain was “behind you and that will not change,” The Guardian reported.
Far-right parties challenge continued aid
The pledge comes as European support for Ukraine faces political pressure.
Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally party and a potential contender in the 2027 presidential election, said France “cannot keep financing Ukraine,” citing the country’s economic situation. Le Pen has said she would end French financial aid to Kyiv if elected, while leaving military assistance and training open.
Her comments raise questions about future French policy, but do not signal an immediate change in France’s current support. The Guardian said current polling predicts Le Pen could win next year’s vote. Her position also comes as European governments debate how to finance further support for Ukraine.
In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany and the leftist BSW party backed a motion in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament calling for Berlin to end military support for Ukraine. The measure is symbolic: state parliaments do not set Germany’s foreign policy, so it does not change the federal government’s aid. It does, however, show how opposition to military assistance is entering regional political debate.
Europe has no immediate Starlink alternative
The political debate coincides with a disruption to military satellite connections. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials said restrictions had affected Starshield terminals, the military-grade service associated with SpaceX’s satellite network. Some units reported losing connections while moving at speeds ranging from about 72 to 161 kilometers per hour (45 to 100 miles per hour), according to Ukrainian defense ministry sources.
The disruption affected drone missions, including interception and medium-range strike operations, as well as frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relays. Ukraine’s defense ministry said it was gathering reports from units, contacting the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners, and checking backup communications channels. The cause of the restrictions had not been established. The timing added to concerns over strained US-Ukraine relations, but did not prove the restrictions were politically motivated.
Reuters reported that Europe has no ready-made satellite system Ukrainian soldiers could attach to drones as an immediate replacement. Eutelsat’s OneWeb network does provide connectivity in Ukraine through partners, but consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp said its terminals’ capacity, weight, size, and power requirements make them less suitable for frontline use.
Starlink and OneWeb terminals also use different technology, meaning Ukraine could not simply connect existing Starlink equipment to OneWeb – thousands of terminals would need to be replaced.
Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Ukrainian defense technology company Buntar Aerospace, told Reuters the disruption showed that users “can’t rely solely on one solution that can be switched off.” European governments and companies are working on longer-term options, but those plans do not offer a quick fix. The dependence extends beyond communications. Ukraine and European countries rely on US satellite systems for early warnings of ballistic missile attacks.

The number of electric cars registered in Türkiye rose to 486,359 as of the end of September 2026, up from just 80,043 in 2023 and 14,552 in 2022, according to motor vehicle data released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) on Oct. 15.
At the same time, hybrid vehicle ownership climbed to 915,892, highlighting the country’s accelerating shift toward alternative-fuel vehicles.
The data showed a sharp increase in EV and hybrid cars over recent years, while the share of diesel and LPG-powered vehicles continued to decline. EVs accounted for 2.7 percent of all registered cars in September, compared with 0.5 percent in 2023 and just 0.1 percent in 2022. Hybrid cars represented 5.1 percent of the fleet, up from 1.5 percent three years earlier.
Diesel cars, once the dominant fuel type, made up 32 percent of all registered automobiles at the end of September, down from a peak of 38.3 percent in 2020. At the same time, gasoline-powered vehicles increased their share of the fleet to 31 percent, while remaining below the levels seen in the mid-2000s, when they accounted for more than two-thirds of all passenger cars.
According to TÜİK, 18.12 million automobiles were registered in traffic as of the end of September.
The total number of registered motor vehicles in Türkiye increased 6.2 percent year-on-year in September to 35.07 million.
Automobiles accounted for 51.7 percent of all registered vehicles, followed by motorcycles at 21.9 percent, pickup trucks at 14.2 percent, tractors at 6.7 percent, trucks at 3 percent, minibuses at 1.6 percent and buses at 0.6 percent.
Among passenger cars newly registered in September, Renault held the largest share at 16.1 percent. TOGG ranked second with 9.8 percent, followed by Hyundai with 8.6 percent, Volkswagen with 7.1 percent and Toyota with 6.8 percent.
Other major brands included Mercedes-Benz with 5.3 percent, Skoda with 5 percent, Kia with 4.5 percent, Peugeot with 3.7 percent, Nissan with 3.3 percent, Opel, Fiat and Tesla with 2.7 percent each.
In the January-September period, the number of newly registered vehicles fell 14.5 percent year-on-year to 1.5 million, said TÜİK.

Children are being left behind in the Ebola disease response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:03:32 UTC
18:03:32 KST

- The Ebola disease outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo is disproportionately impacting children, with the youngest children facing the highest risk of death.
- Children are also being left behind in the research of innovative medical tools.
- Ongoing and future studies on Bundibugyo virus, the virus driving this outbreak, must include children.
Children are paying a devastating price in the Ebola disease outbreak unfolding in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). While children face a higher risk of death from Ebola than adults, they also represent a significant proportion of the people affected by the current outbreak.
According to Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières’ (MSF’s) epidemiological research centre, nearly one in four confirmed Ebola cases in North Kivu province is a child. MSF is deeply concerned by the disproportionate impact of the disease on children and calls for more attention to their specific vulnerabilities, in both the medical and research response.
While Ebola remains a deadly disease for all age groups, the youngest children face the highest risk of death. In North Kivu, children have been particularly affected by the current outbreak: 24% of confirmed cases are among children under five years of age, compared with 13% in Ituri province, while infants under one year old account for 13% of cases, compared with 6% in Ituri.
At the Ebola treatment centre (ETC) in Butembo, North Kivu, MSF teams have observed that the case fatality rate among children was particularly high. Between June and September 2026, 24 out of 30 children – most of whom were under the age of five – died from the Bundibugyo virus in this ETC alone. The rapid progression of the disease in communities and limited access to specialised care at health facility level are contributing to such alarmingly high fatality rates.
“General health facilities often lack the specialised expertise, equipment, and infection prevention and control measures needed to identify and safely manage suspected cases,” explains Stéphanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for MSF in Butembo. “Most of the paediatric cases admitted in our ETC in Butembo, North Kivu, over the summer, had already been hospitalised for other illnesses in several facilities during the days or weeks before their admission. Their family members did not have Ebola themselves, and it is highly likely that these children contracted the disease inside healthcare facilities.”
Most of the paediatric cases admitted in our ETC in Butembo, North Kivu, over the summer, had already been hospitalised for other illnesses in several facilities during the days or weeks before their admission.
Stéphanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for MSF in Butembo
Strengthening infection prevention and control measures in health facilities, ensuring the availability of personal protective equipment, and reinforcing the training of healthcare workers in non-Ebola health centres across at-risk areas are critical to maintaining essential services while preventing healthcare-associated transmission.
While efforts have been made to reduce the emotional toll of isolation on children in ETCs, including the creation of visibility areas where parents can see and communicate with their hospitalised children, being admitted to an ETC remains a deeply distressing experience for young patients. Children may be too young to understand their situation or meet their own basic needs.
To help address this situation, MSF has recruited and trained caregivers who provide daily support and comfort to children inside several MSF-supported ETCs while wearing full personal protective equipment. These caregivers come from diverse backgrounds, including, but not limited to, being Ebola survivors. Today, 13 caregivers are supporting children at the Kitatumba ETC in Butembo. While far from a perfect solution, this initiative provides essential human contact and emotional support for children facing the outbreak.
“On top of enormous challenges caring for young patients, medical facilities are dealing with a lack of paediatric dosing guidance, and limited availability of child-friendly formulations of investigational medicines,” says Dr Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF. “A child-centred approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts.”
A child-centred approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts.
Dr Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF
Children have been disproportionately affected by the current outbreak, yet they are left behind when it comes to access to innovative medical tools. Historically, children are often excluded from clinical research or included only after significant delays, creating dangerous gaps in evidence and access to potentially lifesaving interventions.
“Treatments, vaccines, and other preventive tools should be evaluated for use in children from the outset of research efforts and made available to them without delay,” says Dr Manangama. “Yet in the current outbreak, children are still being left behind, with very limited access to vaccination trials and campaigns, as well as the latest therapeutic innovations despite bearing a significant burden of disease.” 
“Children cannot continue to wait for data generated in adults before benefiting from advances in Ebola care and prevention,” says Dr Manangama.
MSF urges national authorities, research institutions, pharmaceutical developers, and international funders to prioritise the inclusion of children in all ongoing and future Bundibugyo virus studies. Ensuring equitable access to research and new medical tools, including vaccines, is essential to reducing preventable deaths and improving outcomes for one of the most vulnerable groups.
The impact of the outbreak on children extends beyond Ebola infection itself. Disruptions to essential health services can rapidly increase risks from vaccine-preventable diseases, malnutrition, and other common childhood illnesses. Preserving routine immunisation, nutrition programmes, and access to general healthcare must therefore be considered a core component of the outbreak response, not an afterthought.
Note to editors:
Treatment: One ongoing study, EBO-PEP, is evaluating an oral antiviral drug, obeldesivir, to prevent Ebola infection after high-risk exposure. If proven effective, the treatment could provide a practical way to protect people who have recently been in contact with an Ebola patient. While the trial is expected to expand eligibility to include some children, those under 20 kilograms remain excluded because an appropriate paediatric formulation is not yet available.
For the youngest children, the current alternative involves a 10-day course of intravenous treatment, an approach that is particularly difficult to implement in outbreak settings and can be especially challenging for young patients and their caregivers. More information here: An urgent opportunity to ensure children's access to oral post-exposure prophylaxis trials for Bundibugyo virus disease - The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health.
Vaccination: While the results of ongoing trials evaluating vaccines specifically designed for the Bundibugyo virus are not expected for several months, ERVEBO® is an immediately available option. Its safety profile is well established, it is approved for use in children aged one year and older, and health authorities in DRC have extensive experience using it in outbreak settings. Emerging evidence also suggests that it may offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus, although the degree of protection remains to be clarified. In areas at high risk of Ebola transmission, vaccinating contacts of confirmed cases, including children over one year of age, could help prevent severe illness and save lives.
