Charity buys new drone interceptors to hunt Russia’s jet Shaheds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:03:28 UTC
18:03:28 KST

- Come Back Alive delivered 80 experimental interceptor drones built to hunt jet-powered Shaheds, buying them for 13.6 million hryvnias donated by OKKO.
- The foundation says it has contracted several hundred experimental counter-drone systems since September, with the best performers set for refinement and possible serial production.
Ukrainian charity Come Back Alive has handed frontline units 80 new interceptor drones designed to bring down Russia’s jet-powered Shahed attack drones, also known as Geran-4, paying 13.6 million hryvnias, roughly $302,000 or about $3,800 per drone, with money donated by Ukrainian fuel station chain OKKO.
The foundation announced the delivery in a post on X on Oct. 15, describing the drones as test samples that troops will now evaluate in combat. It did not name the manufacturer or give the interceptors’ speed, range or warhead, and photos released with the announcement show rows of white, four-rotor drones with stubby wings packed in crates.
Come Back Alive said this is not the first batch of jet-Shahed interceptors it has sent to the front, only the first it has made public. Since September, the foundation has contracted several hundred experimental counter-drone systems from different manufacturers under its Dronopad program, with the best performers sent back for refinement and some later moving into serial production.
The charity said it followed the same approach with interceptors built to stop older piston-engine Shaheds, which have since become a standard part of Ukraine’s air defense against Russian long-range drone attacks.
“We think ahead: we analyze the prospects for rapidly scaling up production, retraining pilots and the possibility of an uninterrupted supply of the necessary components,” the Dronopad team said, in a statement translated from Ukrainian.
Russia has been shifting its drone attacks toward faster jet-powered models in the Geran family, its domestically built version of the Iranian Shahed. The newer Geran-4 and Geran-5 can fly at up to 600 km/h (about 370 mph), several times faster than the propeller-driven Shahed-136, and Russia launched nearly 800 jet-powered drones at Ukraine over four days in late August, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. On Sept. 15, Zelensky said Ukraine had successfully tested another interceptor against jet-powered Shaheds, while acknowledging that some aspects of controlling it still needed work.
Interceptor drones that cost a few thousand dollars have become one of Ukraine’s main answers to Russia’s mass drone raids, since firing a surface-to-air missile worth hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars at each attacker is not sustainable. Catching a jet-powered drone is harder because the interceptor needs much higher speed and a shorter reaction time to close on its target.
Founded in 2014, Come Back Alive is one of Ukraine’s largest charities supplying the armed forces and is licensed to buy military equipment directly for frontline units.

The irony of OpenAI crying foul over spying
A company that owes much of its existence – and enormous valuation – to stealing other people’s work is now up in arms about people trying to steal from it.
Americans can rest easy – for the moment, at least. The fine folks at the Federal Bureau of Investigation have thwarted a major national security threat.
On October 9, the FBI arrested 35-year-old engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen employed at the California-based artificial intelligence company OpenAI, which makes the chatbot ChatGPT and describes its corporate mission as ensuring that “artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity”.
A press release from the United States Department of Justice said that Alfozan was accused of installing a “surreptitious audio recording device” in an executive conference room at the OpenAI offices in San Francisco.
The statement quoted Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton’s assessment that “this serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative”. (For those who have not yet got the memo, US President Donald Trump recently decreed that the term “artificial intelligence” be changed to “super intelligence” or “SI.”)
FBI director Kash Patel concurred that “protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security”, and assured everyone that the FBI would continue doing its part “to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge”.
So much for the separation of corporation and state in the world’s self-appointed greatest democracy.
The covert device was reported to have been concealed in toilet paper and attached to the back of a television monitor. The Gizmodo website has noted with amusement that, despite being cast as a “sophisticated” spying apparatus, the device in question can in fact be easily ordered online “for the low low price of $13.99”.
If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in jail and a fine of $250,000.
Now, some of you may still be asking what the big deal is – and why the US government is acting like it’s 1950 and the Soviets are stealing our nuclear secrets.
The spectacle becomes all the more curious when we consider that the company up in arms over the alleged attempted theft of its technology owes much of its existence – and massive valuation – to stealing stuff from people.
The day before Alfozan’s arrest, USA Today and several other newspapers sued OpenAI in a Manhattan federal court for copyright infringement and the unauthorised use of hundreds of thousands of news articles and other materials to develop ChatGPT.
And back in July, various US media outlets including the New York Times and the New York Daily News requested that a federal judge impose sanctions on OpenAI for “hiding and destroying evidence showing how ChatGPT was trained on stolen journalism”, as attorney Steven Lieberman put it.
The moral of the story, perhaps, is that when OpenAI steals things it’s to “benefit all of humanity” – but when a 35-year-old Saudi engineer does it, it’s a national security crisis.
In case we were not already bored to tears hearing about national security, US Attorney General Todd Blanche took to X on Tuesday to preach that the “theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security”, necessitating continued “swift action … to protect American innovation and safeguard our nation”.
Of course, many Americans might wonder why “innovation” gets such special treatment when they themselves are so often on the receiving end of government abuse. The frequency with which US police officers murder unarmed Black people, for instance, would seem to indicate that there are far more literal threats to the nation’s security than a $14 device hidden in toilet paper.
But human security is of no interest to a corporatocracy increasingly dominated by AI, an industry that thrives on putting people out of jobs and that is deeply entwined in a number of sordid developments at home and abroad. Among them is mass surveillance, which combines AI-assisted violations of civil liberties and constitutional protections with good old police state “innovation”.
To that end, a bunch of US cops have taken advantage of new AI-powered technology, such as automated licence plate readers, to stalk their exes. Then there is the matter of the FBI and other government agencies buying up data en masse from tech companies in a bid to keep tabs, Big Brother-style, on everyone’s personal information at all times.
It makes you think twice about the sudden concern for “spying” in the Alfozan case.
As for threats to other people’s national security, OpenAI and like-minded tech companies that do business with the Pentagon have been complicit in recent US aggression – from Venezuela to Iran – as the US pursues its strategy for “Accelerating America’s Military AI Dominance” (concocted before Trump mandated the renaming of AI as SI).
Israel, too, has exploited OpenAI technology, among other US-made goodies, to conduct its contemporary apocalyptic exercises in the Middle East. Last year, the Associated Press news agency (AP) revealed that US tech giants had “quietly empowered Israel to track and kill many more alleged militants more quickly in Gaza and Lebanon through a sharp spike in artificial intelligence and computing services”.
The AP report went on to note that “the number of civilians killed has also soared, fueling fears that these tools are contributing to the deaths of innocent people”.
But while it might be news to the AP, that is unfortunately how a genocide works.
And as the US goes to war for AI dominance while the tech giants bank on a post-human world, one can’t help but feel that the toilet paper was a nice touch, indeed.

The proposed amount is EUR 12.80 below the maximum possible minimum wage of EUR 672.80, previously announced by Minister of Labour and Social Policy Natalia Efremova.
If approved, the minimum wage will increase by EUR 39.80, or 6.4%, from EUR 620.20 in 2026. The minimum hourly wage will be EUR 3.98. The public consultation period will last two weeks, until October 28.

“The final decision on the minimum wage will be taken within the next two weeks, when all the budget parameters will be agreed. My ambition is to get as close as possible to the upper limit of €672,” Social Minister Natalia Efremova said in Svishtov.
She added that the monthly allowance for a child with the highest degree of disability would rise by more than €100, family allowances for children by 16–19%, one-off childbirth grants by more than 56%, and the benefit paid during the second year of maternity leave by around 13%.

The policing of Muslim women&#8217;s bodies, from West Asia to Europe and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:01:03 UTC
18:01:03 KST

There is something profoundly vile about discriminating against women and policing their bodies in the name of secularism. Dictating what a woman should or should not wear is fundamentally at odds with freedom of choice. When institutions use their authority to compel women to dress according to a particular vision of society, secularism begins to resemble the very authoritarianism it claims to oppose.
The question has never been whether women should wear the hijab. The question is why everyone seems to believe they have a say in the matter.
As I write this, in October 2026, Azerbaijan is witnessing protests following new school clothing restrictions that have resulted in hijabi students and teachers being denied entry to some schools. The government’s amendment, approved in September, prohibits clothing deemed inconsistent with the principle of secularism, indirectly restricting the wearing of the Muslim headscarf. Women are now being forced to choose between their religious beliefs and their access to education or employment.
But what kind of freedom requires a woman to abandon part of her religious identity before she can enter a classroom? What does secularism achieve when its application excludes the very people it claims to liberate?
The language of secularism often obscures the power relations at work. Rather than allowing religion to remain a matter of personal conviction, the state assumes the authority to determine which expressions of religion are acceptable in public. The woman’s body becomes the site on which the state performs its commitment to a particular national identity. Her clothing is no longer simply clothing. It becomes a political problem to be managed, regulated and, ultimately, removed from the public sphere.
This is not to suggest that secularism necessarily requires such restrictions. A secular state can protect the right to practice a religion while refusing to impose religious doctrine on its population. The contradiction emerges when secularism is interpreted as a mandate to make religious women less visibly religious. And Azerbaijan is hardly the only place where women’s clothing has become a battleground.
The freedom to wear the hijab, and the freedom not to
If the justification for banning the hijab is women’s liberation, what are we to make of Iran, where women have faced state enforcement of compulsory veiling? How can a politics that claims to liberate women through unveiling coexist with a politics that claims to protect them through veiling, while both deny women the authority to decide for themselves?
These systems are not identical, and their histories, institutions and methods of enforcement differ. Yet what they share is a troubling premise that women’s bodies are legitimate objects of state intervention, and that women cannot be trusted to make their own decisions about how they appear in public.
A woman who chooses to wear the hijab is not necessarily oppressed. A woman who chooses not to wear it is not necessarily liberated. Clothing alone cannot tell us whether a woman is acting under coercion, religious conviction, personal preference, cultural attachment or some combination of these.
The insistence that it can tell us more about the observer than the woman herself.
Freedom of choice cannot be conditional on making the choice that the state approves of. If a woman is compelled to veil, her autonomy is violated. If she is compelled to unveil, her autonomy is violated too. Defending one freedom while dismissing the other is not a consistent defence of women’s rights.
It is also worth asking why the language of women’s liberation so readily becomes a justification for excluding women from public life. When a student is denied access to education because she wears a headscarf, or a teacher is prevented from entering her workplace, the consequences are not abstract. The woman loses access to institutions, opportunities and their livelihoods. The supposed liberation takes the very form of exclusion.
READ: Hamas marks Al-Aqsa Intifada anniversary, urges Arab, Muslim support for Palestinians
Who gets to be modest?
The policing of Muslim women’s bodies does not always come from the state. Sometimes it comes from a restaurant door, a private beach, a dress code or the unspoken expectations of a particular social class.
In Egypt, investigations have documented cases of hijabi women being denied entry to upscale restaurants and other venues. A 2022 BBC News Arabic investigation found that 11 of 15 venues contacted during its reporting said women wearing the hijab were not permitted entry.
In Lebanon, allegations of hijab-based exclusion at private beach resorts have continued to generate public debate. In June 2026, a visitor reported being denied entry to Nowhere Beach because her friend wore a hijab, prompting renewed criticism of discriminatory admission policies.
These incidents reveal another dimension of the problem. The woman who covers her hair or wears a full-coverage swimsuit is not always being asked to conform to religious expectations. She is sometimes being asked to conform to an entirely different aesthetic: one that treats visible expressions of Muslim identity as incompatible with leisure, luxury, modernity or even social prestige.
This is where the policing of women’s clothing intersects with class and racialisation. Certain spaces cultivate an image of exclusivity by deciding which bodies belong in them and which bodies disrupt the atmosphere they are trying to sell. A headscarf can become a marker through which women are judged as insufficiently fashionable, insufficiently modern or somehow out of place, even in societies where Muslim women are part of everyday public life.
The contradiction becomes especially striking when we consider the attention given to celebrities who wear full-coverage swimwear. In June 2026, photographs of Anne Hathaway wearing a full-body swimsuit in Saint-Tropez prompted comparisons between the praise directed at her choice and the restrictions faced by Muslim women who wear similar swimming suits. There is nothing wrong with celebrating Hathaway’s clothing choice. But it is the double standard through which one woman’s covered body becomes a symbol of skincare, practicality or personal style, while another woman’s covered body is treated as evidence of backwardness.
The same garment can be fashionable on one woman and politically threatening on another. Its meaning is assigned according to who wears it, how she is perceived and what her body represents to the people looking at her.
The racialisation of Muslim identity
The policing of Muslim women’s bodies also raises questions about the relationship between religion, ethnicity and national identity.
Consider Azerbaijan. The country is predominantly Muslim, yet its official commitment to secularism has become central to the controversy over the visibility of religious clothing in schools. The current dispute raises a broader question about what forms of identity are permitted to appear in public and under what conditions.
I find myself wondering whether the discomfort with the hijab is also, in some contexts, a discomfort with the visible presence of an identity that is treated as foreign, even when it belongs to the people being asked to conceal it. In some political imaginaries, Muslimness and Arabness are conflated, despite the fact that most Muslims worldwide are not Arab and that Arab identity is not synonymous with Islam.
This conflation has consequences. It allows Muslim women to be racialised through their clothing, their bodies turned into symbols of a cultural identity that others wish to regulate, distance themselves from or erase.
It also makes the relationship between domestic exclusion and foreign policy worth examining. Azerbaijan’s restrictions on hijab in schools and its military relationship with Israel are distinct political matters; establishing a direct causal connection between them would require further evidence. But their coexistence raises questions about how national identity, Muslim visibility and solidarity with Palestinians are understood within the same political landscape.
The question is not whether these policies have a single motive. It is whether the boundaries drawn around acceptable Muslim identity at home can be examined alongside the state’s political and military relationships abroad.
The same scrutiny should extend to Europe, where secularism has frequently been invoked in debates over Muslim women’s clothing. France, in particular, has made the hijab a recurring site of political conflict. In September 2026, French National Rally MP Julien Odoul shared an AI-altered image of a Muslim woman’s photograph that removed her hijab and changed her clothes, captioning it “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE!”
There is something deeply revealing about invoking freedom while digitally altering a woman’s appearance, without her consent, to remove the very thing that makes her religious identity visible. It is a contradiction that deserves to be taken seriously.
When a politician uses AI technology to manufacture an unveiled version of a Muslim woman and presents that image as an expression of freedom, whose freedom is being represented? The woman’s, or the politician’s desire to see her differently?
The incident demonstrates how the demand to unveil can move beyond legislation and into the realm of public humiliation. A woman’s image becomes material for someone else’s political performance and agenda. Her consent is displaced by an assumption that her body would be better, freer or more acceptable if only it looked different.
READ: US Muslim group urges White House, Congress to demand release of American teen held by Israel
I am a hijabi, and my life is not smaller
I want to bring this discussion back to the everyday lives of the women who are so frequently discussed but so rarely allowed to define themselves.
I write this as a hijabi woman who travels. Wearing the hijab has not prevented me from hiking, swimming, travelling or pursuing the things I want to do. Across professions and walks of life, hijabi women are doctors, nurses, teachers, dancers, researchers, business owners, chief executives, politicians, employees and students. They occupy public space, develop expertise, build careers, create art and participate in the world around them.
Their lives are not adequately described by the fabric they wear.
I am not suggesting that every hijabi woman experiences the same freedoms, or that the hijab is never imposed on anyone. Some women experience family pressure, social coercion or state enforcement. Others choose to wear it freely. Some women change their minds over the course of their lives. Their experiences are not interchangeable, and none of them should have to prove that she is sufficiently independent before her rights are respected.
What I reject is the assumption that the hijab itself is proof of a woman’s oppression, or that removing it is necessarily proof of her liberation.
As a hijabi, I do not want my life reduced to a debate over whether the way I dress is acceptable to someone else other than myself. I do not want my ability to study, work, travel, swim or enter a public space to depend on whether another person approves of my appearance. I do not want to be treated as a political symbol before I am recognised as a person.
And I should not have to demonstrate how much I can accomplish while wearing the hijab to deserve that freedom in the first place.
The right to autonomy does not have to be earned through productivity. A woman who wants to become a doctor and a woman who wants a quiet life deserve the same respect. A woman who wears the hijab and a woman who removes it deserve the same freedom to participate in society without coercion or discrimination.
It is unacceptable that people are still discriminated against because of their headwear or skin color. We must reject these outdated prejudices and judge everyone by their character and actions—not their appearance.
A meaningful commitment to women’s freedom must resist that premise wherever it appears. It must oppose compulsory veiling without turning that opposition into a justification for compulsory unveiling. It must defend secularism without confusing it with the removal of religion from public life. And it must challenge discrimination against Muslim women without assuming that all Muslim women share the same beliefs, experiences or relationship with the hijab.
Secularism, if it is to mean anything in a plural society, should protect the freedom to practise any religion and any belief, and the freedom not to practise it too. It should not require women to erase visible expressions of their beliefs to gain access to education, employment or public life.
Women’s liberation cannot be measured by how closely women’s bodies conform to someone else’s preferred image of freedom.
A woman should not have to remove her hijab to enter a classroom, put it on to satisfy a religious authority, change her swimsuit to gain access to a beach or watch strangers digitally alter her appearance to make a political point.
She should be able to decide for herself.
That is what freedom of choice means. Not the freedom to choose what we approve of, but the freedom to make choices that belong to us, even when others disagree.
And if we truly believe in that freedom, we must be prepared to defend it even when a woman’s choice is not the one we would make for ourselves.

====================================================================================================

‘Like selling wolves from Yellowstone’: how protected US sharks are being sold off to foreign aquariums
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:00:14 UTC
18:00:14 KST

Shortly after 12.45pm, what remains of a 300-metre line goes taut. Somewhere beneath the murky green surface of Delaware Bay, on the eastern US coast, a sand tiger shark has taken the bait of a mackerel chunk. Marine researchers at the University of Delaware haul the line towards a small boat as the shark’s grey-brown outline emerges.
It is a large animal: 225cm (7ft) long with a 90cm girth. Its mouth hangs open, revealing rows of jagged teeth. The researchers work quickly, measuring the shark, recording its sex, and taking blood and muscle samples. A tag is then fastened beneath its dorsal fin, through its thick sandpapery skin.
The mature male seems to watch them as they work. Then it is lowered back into the bay. With a powerful flick of its tail, it disappears almost as quickly as it arrived.
Several thousand miles away, sand tiger sharks collected from these same waters circle tanks in Abu Dhabi, moving among artificial reefs and through blue-lit tunnels in the desert city’s aquariums, where visitors pay up to $100 (£75) for day passes. They will never return to Delaware Bay.
Tagging sand tigers – a species of concern that is prohibited from being caught in US waters – offers clues about the lives of these fish, which are critically endangered globally.
However, in recent years, the bay – a US habitat of particular concern between the states of Delaware and New Jersey – has become a hotspot for private collection of specimens for the global aquarium trade.
A recent study by marine researchers from the University of Delaware, Delaware State University and the University of Rhode Island shows that, since 2018, the number of sand tiger sharks collected from Delaware Bay for public display has risen sharply, from two that year to 40 in 2023. In total, 80 of the sharks were taken from Delaware waters for aquariums between 2018 and 2024.
The study, citing data from Delaware’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control (DNREC) shows that nearly all the sand tiger sharks collected from Delaware Bay were sent overseas: the highest numbers went to China and the United Arab Emirates, while others went to South Korea and Thailand. Some were sent to other countries – including Turkey, Scotland, Israel, Italy, France and Uzbekistan – with a few remaining in the US.
“This [private collecting of sand tiger sharks] is like going into Yellowstone [national park] and catching wolves and then selling them to zoos in France or in the Middle East,” says Brad Wetherbee, a shark researcher at University of Rhode Island who co-wrote the study.
“[These countries] used to have sand tigers. They could just go out in their own waters and catch them and collect them, but their populations are so low they can’t do that any more.”
The US has spent decades restricting the killing of sand tiger sharks, yet in recent years, through a regulatory maze of federal and state permits, private collecting companies can legally remove these protected sharks from the wild for public display. A shark that an angler would be required to release after catching can instead be transported thousands of miles and placed in a foreign aquarium, with private companies profiting from the trade.
“How can we say these people [private collectors] can remove them and functionally harvest them, whereas these ones [recreational anglers] can’t?” says Aaron Carlisle, an associate professor from the University of Delaware’s school of marine science and another of the study’s authors. “If our concern is sustainability, we need to know what is the impact of removal.”
Sand tigers, despite their fearsome appearance, are non-aggressive and docile. They have one of the lowest reproductive rates of any shark species, reaching sexual maturity at about six to 10 years old, depending on sex, and producing just one or two pups every two to three years.
Once widespread across subtropical and temperate coastal waters, the species has declined across much of its range. Populations in parts of south-east Asia, west Africa and the Arabian Sea have fallen to critically low levels, largely because of overfishing, including bycatch, and habitat degradation. In some regions, they are believed to have been wiped out entirely.
The north-west Atlantic is one of the few regions where the species’ populations are not critically endangered, largely due to federal and state protections. Yet the population has never had a formal assessment, and how healthy it actually is remains difficult to determine.
One private company has accounted for most of the recent collection in Delaware Bay. Dynasty Marine, a Florida-based supplier of live marine animals to aquariums and research institutions worldwide that drew bipartisan outrage in Florida in 2025 after legally netting a manta ray for SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, began collecting sand tigers in Delaware in 2021.
A spokesperson for Delaware state’s department of natural resources and environmental control (DNREC) says the company has “ramped up collection in the following years”.
Records reviewed by the Guardian show that Dynasty Marine collected 71 sharks between 2022 and 2024. The study also records 35 sand tiger harvest requests in 2025, with most destined for China.
Recipients of the sharks caught between 2022 and 2024 included SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, Dubai Aquarium and Underwater Zoo, Sea Life Busan in South Korea, Aquaria Phuket in Thailand and Guangzhou Ocean World in China.
Dynasty Marine was asked to comment on the number of sand tigers it collects a year but did not respond. In a statement to the Guardian, it said: “Every collection we conduct is done in full compliance with all applicable federal and state permits and regulations.
“The animals we collect are cared for to the highest standards and go on to live in human care, where they play a vital role in educating millions of people each year about marine life and the importance of ocean conservation.”
The company says it supports “numerous marine conservation, science and education initiatives”, including shark research, manatee rehabilitation and coral restoration efforts.
Private companies seeking to collect sand tigers for public display must first obtain an exempted fishing permit from the US National Marine Fisheries Service (known as Noaa Fisheries). If the collection takes place in Delaware waters, the permit holder must then obtain a scientific collecting permit from DNREC.
Noaa Fisheries says it reviews applications for capture of the sharks on a “case-by-case basis”.
“We have an overall scientifically based annual quota for all shark research and public display,” says John Chu, a Noaa Fisheries spokesperson. “We consider that overall quota when issuing public display permits.”
The state follows the federal lead in granting permits. The DNREC says Noaa Fisheries’ approval is “evidence enough for the state to believe that removal of the permitted number of individual sharks is sustainable”.
However, scientists argue that, without knowing the population’s size or trend, it is difficult to determine what impact removing sharks for display in an aquarium may have.
The concern is heightened by the size of many sand tigers collected in Delaware. Many are large juveniles or near-mature adults that could soon reproduce if left in the wild.
The DNREC says the recent increase in collections is “an emerging concern”, but says it would be up to the federal government to act on that. It says an assessment on the number of sand tiger sharks in the area would “lend context” to a permit request from a private collection company.
This uncertainty extends to what happens to the sharks after they leave Delaware Bay. Neither the DNREC or Noaa Fisheries record the sharks’ final status, including whether those animals become sick or die, though the DNREC says it intends to change this.
Dewayne Fox, an assistant fisheries professor at Delaware State University who also worked on the study, says the issue is not just whether the collections are sustainable, but also who benefits from a population protected in US waters.
“We have protected the habitat and yet we are going to allow some out-of-state company to come in, catch these animals and then ship them all the way around the world and make money,” he says. “Everybody else is benefiting from our conservation success.”

Unions Are the Key to America’s Cost of Living Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:00:03 UTC
18:00:03 KST

Ask an everyday working American, and they’ll likely tell you there’s something fundamentally wrong with our economy. Across industries, big cities, and small towns, working people are struggling. Their paychecks aren’t stretching far enough. They stress over every expense and struggle to cover rent and electric bills, let alone take their families to dinner once in a while. Meanwhile, our research shows that top CEOs gave themselves massive raises in 2025 and now make well over 300 times what typical workers are paid.
As everything gets more and more expensive, we believe there is a powerful solution: unions.
Union contracts raise pay for workers. A new report from the Economic Policy Institute shows that tripling union membership in this country would deliver a 14.5% raise to the median worker—more than $7,700 a year or the equivalent of 7.5 extra weeks of pay annually. This adds up to nearly $270,000 over a 35-year career. Unions can also be powerful tools for combating racial pay discrimination; the new report shows tripling union membership would narrow the racial wage gap by more than a third.
Tripling union density wouldn’t only benefit union members. Nonunion workers would also see large raises, because strong unions lift standards across the economy. All told, EPI estimates that tripling union membership would shift $1.2 trillion of wealth in the economy to working people every year, reversing a third of the rise in inequality since 1979. And because union workers can win better benefits like health insurance, tripling union membership would also provide health care to 6.8 million more Americans. It’s what the labor movement calls the union difference: higher wages, access to health care, retirement security, paid time off and sick leave, and dignity on the job.
An economy where 30% of workers are union members isn’t a pipe dreamーit’s part of our own history. After New Deal policies of the 1930s and 40s secured workers’ legal rights, union membership soared. In the 1950s, union membership was above 30%, and working people saw huge gains. Wages grew, and racial wage gaps shrank.
A fundamental promise of a union is that the workers will share in the profit they create—and as soon as wealthy executives and shareholders saw their bottom lines under threat, they went to work attacking that progress.
Anti-union court rulings and so-called “right-to-work” state laws have broken the labor law that once protected workers. Relentless and retaliatory union-busting has created significant risks for unionizing, with corporations spending more than $1.5 billion a year to stop workers from exercising their fundamental right to organize. And the Trump Administration has weakened worker protections at the Department of Labor and prevented the government agency charged with protecting workers’ rights to organize and bargain collectively from operating for nearly all of 2025, closing off workers’ avenue for justice.
But workers are fighting back, and seeing real results. There is more organizing happening on the ground than at any point in our lifetimes. Workers are organizing at manufacturing plants, in newsrooms, in technology, in hospitals, on college campuses, and construction sites. They’re changing the game with historic contracts in women’s sports. They’re organizing in “right-to-work” states in the South and are being led by women, communities of color, and young workers.
The results are in the numbers. Nearly half a million workers unionized in 2025 alone, and the number of workers in unions is at a 16-year high. Public-sector employees increased their unionization rates to 36.4% in 2025, and the number of private-sector workers covered by union contracts increased by close to a quarter million, including in industries such as health care, retail, construction, and education. Union representation among federal workers actually grew in the last year, reaching 31.1%, despite the Trump Administration stripping union rights from more than one million of those workers.
The recent spike in worker organizing coincides with a sharp rise in public approval of unions, and there are millions of nonunion workers in the United States who say they would join a union tomorrow if given the opportunity.
Still, we know that union membership remains well below the level needed to unlock the full potential of worker power and raise pay standards across the economy. Even as we make essential progress, we’re still at about one-third of that 1950s high. The reality is that organizing alone can’t fix a system stacked against us.
It’s clear to us that we must use this momentum to win key legislation that makes it easier for Americans to organize—and we have a roadmap in Congress to get there. We believe the Protecting the Right to Organize Act would restore worker protections eroded by legal loopholes and impose real penalties on companies that violate labor laws. Part of the legislation passed the House earlier this summer with bipartisan support. Another bill, the Public Service Freedom to Negotiate Act, would guarantee for the first time that every public-sector worker in the country has the right to bargain collectively.
Alongside these necessary labor law reforms, Congress can pursue bold new proposals, like requiring collective bargaining at companies where CEOs are paid at least 100 times more than typical workers, or guaranteeing newly unionized workers a cost-of-living raise.
These are big fights. But they are fights we can win. That means ensuring our elected leaders will stand with workers, not billionaires, and pass pro-worker legislation. It means continuing to organize, even when the bosses and billionaires try to stand in the way. Together, we can build a better economy for working people by strengthening workers’ rights to organize and bargain collectively. Because the research proves what workers have always known: It's better in a union.

Over $600 Million in Polymarket Election Trades Took Place After Races Ended
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.
Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.
This summer, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.
Even odder? “Nearly all of it—about $284 million—came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with each other,” says former Polymarket trader Chris Park, who now runs the prediction-market forensic analysis firm MSR Decode.
Such a high volume of seemingly pointless back-and-forth transactions has raised eyebrows among experts. “It's obviously some form of volume manipulation,” says Rajiv Sethi, a Barnard College economics professor who researches prediction markets.
When asked about these markets, Shana Bautista, Polymarket’s head of global intelligence and investigations, told WIRED that the team “immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading.” Polymarket did not respond to follow-up questions about why the accounts were able to trade such a high amount of volume before it took action.
The timing of these trades made things even weirder. Polymarket’s rules stipulated that the Ethiopia market would be resolved in October after the prime minister was formally appointed and sworn in, which meant that it stayed open for several months after Ahmed’s victory was all but a foregone conclusion. For 123 days after the election, bursts of seemingly irrational trading continued, prompting Polymarket users to leave comments like “THIS NOT RESOLVED?” and “fuckkkk.”
Sethi calls the phenomenon a “zombie market,” where people can buy and trade on events that have already taken place or are no longer happening.
Another market about a 2024 election in Romania facilitated what Sethi described as “even more dramatic” trading anomalies. The initial election was called off due to fears about foreign interference. A new race was held several months later, but instead of closing the original market in the meantime, Polymarket kept it running alongside the new option.
It was during this period that Sethi first noticed something weird appeared to be happening with the older market. An algorithm Sethi and his colleagues created to flag potential wash trading on Polymarket identified nearly all of the volume as suspicious. “99.6 percent of volume in this market for certain weeks has been wash trading,” Sethi says.
Wash trading is a type of market manipulation in which accounts repeatedly buy and sell assets to create the illusion of heavy trading activity, when in reality, money is simply moving back and forth. It’s banned on regulated financial exchanges in the United States and is specifically prohibited in Polymarket’s terms of service. An earlier study conducted by Sethi and colleagues found evidence of widespread wash trading on Polymarket’s offshore platform.
Wash trading could explain what happened with the Ethiopian and Romanian political markets, but because the identities of the traders is unknown, uncertainty remains. “What appears to be wash trading isn't always wash trading,” says Sethi.
MSR Decode ran an analysis of the Ethiopian market for WIRED, which found that the most likely explanation for the anomalous trading is “activity farming,” which is when people try to artificially inflate their trading volumes. The firm suspects that traders may have been interested in boosting their volume because they believed that they could benefit if Polymarket launched a cryptocurrency token. In 2025, Polymarket chief marketing officer Matthew Modabber told the hosts of a crypto-themed podcast that there “would be a token” but did not provide specifics. Sethi also finds it plausible that traders could be motivated by potential “token allocation” to higher-volume accounts.
This type of behavior has been observed before in the cryptocurrency industry. “These are textbook examples on how market participants farm a potential airdrop,” says Andre Guettler, the director of Ulm University’s Institute of Strategic Management and Finance, who researches the structure of prediction markets.
When MSR Decode analyzed the Ethiopian election market, it found that it was highly unlikely that the trading volume could be attributed to sophisticated traders using algorithms to eke out profits. It analyzed over 38,000 “trade loops” that took place after the election (instances where individual wallets bought and sold to each other in quick succession) and found that over 98 percent resulted in neither side losing or gaining money. The median time that the accounts held onto the contracts they purchased before selling them again was nine seconds.
These types of unusual trading patterns are not a new phenomenon on Polymarket. Earlier this year, Barron’s reported that much of the activity on markets predicting the 2028 US presidential election centered on unlikely candidates such as Elon Musk and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, neither of whom is eligible to run because they were born outside of the country.
Both Polymarket and its chief rival, Kalshi, have been publicly scrutinized for unusual market activity in recent months. Furor over suspicious activity on its recently launched perpetual futures market for cryptocurrency grew so intense on X that Kalshi published a blog post denying allegations of wash trading on it. (Sethi agrees with Kalshi that the allegations were unfounded. He argues that the unusual volume could instead be explained by Kalshi’s incentives for market makers, which create opportunities for other traders to profit from small price discrepancies.)
Polymarket recently raised an over $1 billion round of funding led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The company is now valued at an estimated $21 billion, and earlier this summer, it announced that its annualized revenue was now over $1 billion. Polymarket’s explosive growth is often measured in volume traded, since it’s a metric that can point to how active users are.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets in the United States, declined to comment on whether it is looking into these election trades. The CFTC previously investigated a number of suspected instances of market manipulation on Polymarket, including several exclusively reported by WIRED, but they usually involved potential insider trading rather than wash trading or other suspicious activity.
In the past, the agency has issued hefty fines for wash trading in other sectors. “It seems to me that the CFTC would want to know about weird activity in a very large market,” a former CFTC employee tells WIRED.

Anthropic revenue jumps 46% to $16.8bn as AI firm eyes record $2 trillion IPO valuation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:57:53 UTC
17:57:53 KST

AI developer Anthropic grew its sales by about 46% to $16.8 billion (€15bn) last quarter and turned an adjusted profit, it told investors on Wednesday, weeks before a November stock market debut that could value it at up to $2 trillion (€1.79bn).
Anthropic, the San Francisco-based developer of the Claude AI models, generated $16.8 billion (€15bn) in revenue between July and September, up about 46% from $11.5 billion (€10.3bn) in the previous three months, and posted an adjusted profit.
It presented the figures to investors at its headquarters on Wednesday, according to Bloomberg citing people familiar with the matter, weeks before a planned initial public offering in November that could value the company at up to $2 trillion (€1.79bn).
The company told investors it was profitable for a second straight quarter on an adjusted basis, a measure that strips out certain costs. On the same basis, it had positive free cash flow, meaning it brought in more cash than it spent, and an operating margin of 11%, the share of revenue left after running costs.
Each dollar it spent on computing power brought in $1.70 of revenue in the quarter, but growth is slowing.
Revenue had more than doubled from the first to the second quarter, and the latest figures fell short of some investors’ hopes cited by the Financial Times.
Annualised revenue, which projects recent sales over a full year, is now reportedly expected to end 2026 below $100 billion (€89.5bn), short of the more than $100 billion (€89.5bn) several backers had previously anticipated.
For instance, research firm SemiAnalysis puts the current figure at about $74 billion (€66.2bn), compared with some $65 billion (€58.1bn) in late July.
Record IPO in sight
Anthropic filed confidentially for an IPO with US regulators in June and has yet to publish its full prospectus.
It is aiming to list in November, once the US midterm elections are over, at a valuation of as much as $2 trillion (€1.79bn), with US investment banks Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley reportedly leading the deal.
That would top the roughly $1.8 trillion (€1.6tn) at which SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and satellite company, priced its record-breaking IPO in June, and be about double the $965 billion (€863bn) valuation at which Anthropic raised $65 billion (€58.1bn) from private investors in May.
On standard accounting measures, Anthropic lost $42 billion (€37.5bn) in 2025 on revenue of $4.6 billion (€4.1bn), according to a draft prospectus reported last month, largely because of $34 billion (€30.4bn) in accounting charges linked to past fundraising.
Race with OpenAI
Rival OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, was approaching $50 billion (€44.7bn) in annualised revenue at the end of September, although the two count revenue differently, so the figures are not like for like.
OpenAI is not expected to list on public markets before 2027, but competition in the sector remains fierce.
Anthropic had appeared to lose ground to OpenAI in recent months due to the release of the Astra model by Sam Altman's firm, while much cheaper Chinese models posed a risk to its revenue.
Anthropic could start marketing its shares to investors as soon as the week of 9 November, according to Bloomberg, further citing people familiar with the matter.

U.S. Army’s sled air defense idea gets industry backers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

17:57:35 KST

- MSI Defense Solutions says its Self-Loading Equipment Deck appeared on several partners’ displays at AUSA 2026, including General Dynamics Land Systems.
- The U.S. Army has asked industry for a self-loading deck air defense package for light infantry vehicles, targeting fielding in 2027 to 2029.
Mooresville, North Carolina-based MSI Defense Solutions says its Self-Loading Equipment Deck, a removable mission pallet that can carry weapons and sensors on and off vehicles, appeared on several partner companies’ displays at this week’s Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting in Washington, including one built by General Dynamics Land Systems.
In a series of LinkedIn posts during the show, MSI described the SLED as part of its Common Deck family, a modular base meant to let partners integrate mission systems faster across different vehicles. The company did not say which General Dynamics Land Systems capability was mounted on its deck, how many other partners used it at the show, or whether any of the configurations are under contract.
“Our SLED (Self-Loading Equipment Deck), part of the Common Deck family, provides a modular foundation for integrating mission systems across different platforms and requirements,” MSI Defense Solutions said.
The idea behind a self-loading deck is that a small crew can lift a complete weapon or sensor package off one vehicle and onto another, or onto the ground, without a forklift or crane. Partner company 3SL, which showed an air defense version called the EAGLS SLED at the AUSA Global Force symposium in Huntsville in March, said that design lets three or four soldiers swap mission payloads in the field.
In a March 2026 request for information for Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense Increment 4, the U.S. Army said it wants an air defense package for light infantry built on a self-loading equipment deck that can ride on vehicles such as the Infantry Squad Vehicle and the uncrewed Robotic Combat Vehicle. The service specified that the deck must keep working independently once removed and that the carrier vehicle must return to full functionality without it, with fielding targeted for 2027 to 2029.
MSI, which moved from motorsports engineering into defense work in 2008, already sells an air defense system that fits that requirement’s description. Its EAGLS package uses laser-guided 70 mm rockets fitted with BAE Systems’ APKWS guidance kits to shoot down drones, and the company says on its website that it has delivered six EAGLS systems and fielded APKWS-equipped platforms to UK special operations forces and Ukrainian marines.
During the same week, MSI said in a separate post that it held talks with representatives from Kosovo about how its modular platforms and weapons integration work could support that country’s emerging defense requirements, though it did not describe any specific proposal.

Rada abolishes VAT exemption for parcels valued up to EUR 150
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:57:14 EEST
17:57:14 KST

The Verkhovna Rada, on its third attempt, has adopted at second reading and in general bill No. 16051-1 on amendments to the Tax Code regarding the taxation of e-commerce transactions with VAT, which abolishes the tax exemption for international postal shipments valued up to EUR 150.
As reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, deputies began reviewing amendments to the bill on Wednesday, October 14, with the vote taking place on Thursday, October 15. The decision to adopt the document in general was supported by 252 MPs against the required minimum of 226 votes, with three voting against.
During preparations for the second reading, deputies submitted 1,935 amendments. The second edition of bill No. 16051-1 was amended during the vote to include a provision on the lifetime status of former politically exposed persons (PEPs), establishing at least 12 months of enhanced oversight following resignation, coupled with individual risk assessments by banks. This measure is intended to help unblock the signing by President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy of another law—No. 15111-d on taxing income from digital platforms (adopted in June of this year as a structural benchmark under the IMF program).
During Thursday's voting, the Rada rejected amendments concerning the presumption of innocence for businesses regarding the cancellation of advance payments on corporate income tax for retail fuel traders, as well as provisions concerning the placement, installation, assembly, and construction of wind power plants in the Carpathian mountainous areas.
However, an amendment to reduce the personal income tax (PIT) rate on apartment rentals from 18% to 5% was supported on the floor.
Implementing the provisions of the law alongside Customs Code amendments (bill No. 15460) is a condition for Ukraine to receive the third tranche under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) program, totaling approximately $0.7 billion, and the second tranche of macro-financial assistance from the European Union of EUR 3.7 billion under the Ukraine Loan facility of EUR 90 billion. Under the updated IMF memorandum, Ukraine was required to adopt this law by July 2026, while the original timeline was the end of March alongside other tax norms, though this structural benchmark was missed.
The law introduces special VAT taxation rules for remote sales of goods (excluding excisable goods) imported into Ukraine via international postal and express shipments addressed to individuals valued up to EUR 150, making e-commerce interface operators or their intermediaries responsible for calculating and remitting the tax.
At the same time, VAT exemptions are preserved for small non-commercial consignments valued up to EUR 45 sent between individuals free of charge, as well as for goods in unaccompanied baggage valued up to EUR 150 and security and defense goods (energy equipment and supplies for the defense forces).
Prior to the first reading, presenting the document, Minister of Finance of Ukraine Serhiy Marchenko noted that implementing these norms will generate an additional estimated UAH 10 billion annually for the state budget.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada adopted the respective bills in the first reading on September 16, 2026, following previous unsuccessful attempts.
During the consideration of the documents, Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko stated that the provisions of the laws will begin to apply from July 1, 2027, following the technical implementation of automated tax payments by international marketplaces.

Can Europe step in as Ukraine struggles with Starlink and US satellite data?
- Ukraine faced Starlink and US warning gaps as Russian missile threats continued. Zelensky said partners gave no alert for a second night.
- Europe has no quick replacement for Starlink or US missile warning systems. Experts said OneWeb is not suited to frontline use and terminals would need replacing.
- Officials warned Europe is too dependent on American space power. The EU plans IRIS², but it is years away, so countries want their own capabilities.
AI generated
KYIV – As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer any ready-made alternatives.
Ukrainian officials said on Oct 14 the functioning of Starlink’s military-grade service Starshield had been interrupted when terminals were moving at high speed, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defence.
Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that, for the second night running, Ukraine had received no warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.
The reasons for the difficulties were not immediately clear but followed another souring of relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukraine, after Trump announced a deal to waive sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Zelensky to be replaced.
Trump said on Oct 13 that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, which operates Starlink, said the US government controlled that system’s speeds.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on the social media platform X, using the acronym for president of the United States.
Musk has been a close political ally of Trump.
European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelensky.
But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
“That is fairly unique and… what basically that can detect is the heat generated by missiles as they’re launched,” said Marc DeVore, an associate fellow at think tank Chatham House. “There is nothing equivalent in Europe.”
No simple Starlink swop for Ukraine, Europe
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Oct 14 following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
But Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, said Eutelsat’s OneWeb network was not well suited to wartime use.
“Its current constellation remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” he said.
“Capacity and performance constraints, combined with the cost, weight, bulk and power consumption of its user terminals, limit its suitability for frontline applications.”
A spokesperson for Eutelsat told Reuters that the company continued to provide connectivity services in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit networks with its partners.
It declined to comment further “given the sensitive nature of the situation”.
Von der Ropp also said switching networks would require replacing thousands of terminals, as Starlink and Starshield terminals use proprietary technology and could not simply connect to OneWeb.
Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Ukrainian defence technology startup Buntar Aerospace, said the sudden interruption to Starshield services “highlights to almost every end user both in Ukraine and abroad you can’t rely solely on one solution that can be switched off”.
“You need to have some kind of sovereign capabilities,” he added, so that “you are not subject to somebody’s mood today”.
Fears of over-reliance on US defence technology have grown in Europe in recent years, as Trump has threatened to quit the NATO military alliance just as European leaders see Russia posing the greatest threat to the continent in decades.
European Defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a conference hosted by Politico in Brussels on Oct 14 that the continent was “quite dependent on American space capabilities”.
“The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities,” he added, mentioning the European Union’s planned satellite constellation IRIS² and urging European countries to work together.
But that project is years from becoming operational even if everything goes according to plan, causing frustration among European government officials. Germany is developing its own military satellite constellation. REUTERS

Russia builds major new drone attack base in six weeks, satellite images show

Russia builds major new drone attack base in six weeks, satellite images show
- Russia has nearly finished a new jet-drone base in Rostov in six weeks, showing a rapid expansion of its attack power near Ukraine.
- Satellite images show the site could launch Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones, with eight launch platforms and a possible capacity of 100 drones in 24 hours.
- Experts say the faster drones are harder for Ukraine and NATO to stop, creating a strategic risk as Russia plans more winter attacks.
AI generated
LONDON - Russia has nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones in just six weeks, according to defence experts and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, in the latest expansion of its attack capability close to Ukraine.
The site in what was an empty field in Russia’s south-western Rostov region on Aug 31 had become a complex facility the size of around 126 soccer pitches by Oct 14, commercial imagery provided by Planet Labs and Airbus showed.
The construction coincides with a surge in the use of Russian jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine, which is struggling to intercept the faster weapons that can travel at speeds of up to 600km.
With the full-scale war well into its fifth year, Kyiv expects Russia to further escalate jet drone and missile attacks this winter.
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, said the site in the imagery would be capable of launching the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, Russia’s newest types of jet-powered drone.
He said the western edge of the facility showed eight platforms for launch rails capable of firing those drones, adding to an existing Russian network of at least 11 fixed launch sites used for drone attacks on Ukraine.
“The speed of construction... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly,” Monnik said.
The site, he added, looked very close to completion and it will be “probably a matter of weeks before (it is) fully operational, if not earlier.”
A challenge for NATO
The construction of the facility coincides with worsening relations between Russia and the NATO military alliance.
European governments accuse Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyber attacks against them, while Russia warned in September it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Kaliningrad exclave.
Monnik said the combination of industrial production of jet-powered drones, their increasing sophistication and the relative lack of comprehensive counter-drone defences in many NATO countries were a challenge for the West.
“This ability to rapidly field an ability to launch large-scale attacks using UAS (unmanned aerial systems) poses a strategic vulnerability for NATO countries,” he said.
Monnik said the facility may have the potential to fire 100 jet-powered drones or more in 24 hours, although Russia normally fires them in small numbers throughout the day.
It would also depend on factors like available supplies and objectives.
Rob Jordan, programme director at the London-based RUSI think-tank, said the concrete pads and two possible takeoff rails shown in the imagery looked consistent with launch tracks for Russian Geran drones.
“This level of construction in this short a time is impressive,” he said. “This shows the relative faith Russia is putting in its deep strike capability – possibly to the detriment of its conventional land forces.”
Russia’s defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the facility and on its jet-powered drone programme more broadly.
Use of jet drones surges
Military analysts say Russia has shifted its drone production capabilities to jet-powered models as Ukraine has struggled to counter them.
Russia increased its use of jet-powered drones roughly six-fold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data reported by Reuters in September.
Kyiv and the surrounding region were targeted most heavily, the data showed.
The jet drones pose a problem because they are too fast for the interceptor drones designed by Ukraine to cheaply intercept their slower, piston-powered predecessors.
Kyiv is now scrambling to devise a solution.
Overhead imagery of the new facility taken on Aug 31 pictured a few vehicles in a field but no sign of construction.
Imagery taken the following morning showed that work had begun.
The site, which occupies an area of around 0.9sq km, lies about 3.5km from Russia’s Millerovo air base, home to the 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment.
According to DroneSec, the new launch site likely sits within the air defence “bubble” provided by systems at the airbase, making Ukrainian attempts to target the new facility more difficult.
Of the eight launch platforms, two already had rails on them, a Reuters analysis showed.
Rails were being constructed on two other pads as well, while other construction work was visible from space over the course of three days this week. REUTERS

Ukraine’s Navy says it hit six Su-34 bombers at a Russian airbase with Neptune missiles—the jets that drop glide bombs on Ukrainian towns (updated)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:54:21 UTC
17:54:21 KST

Ukraine’s Navy hit six Su-34M bombers at Russia’s Borisoglebsk military airfield in Voronezh Oblast with Neptune missiles overnight into 15 October, the Navy said. Residents filmed a large fire at the base after a missile alert, and the Navy’s count has not been independently confirmed. The facility is about 400 km from the frontline.
Glide bombs are now central to how Russia’s army fights, used to pin down Ukrainian defenders, including drone teams, before small infantry groups move in. They also hit frontline cities and the civilians who live in them.
Six bombers and flight equipment hit, the Navy says
The Neptune coastal missile system also hit technical equipment that supports flights, the Navy said. It recorded secondary detonations and a fire on the airfield and said details were still being clarified.
The Su-34M can carry several guided and high-explosive aerial bombs at once, along with missiles, the Navy noted. It called the jet one of Russia’s key tools for glide-bomb strikes on Ukrainian positions and frontline towns. In September, a Ukrainian Neptune missile reached a Russian warship at its own pier.
Fire over the airfield late on 14 October
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev declared a missile alert across the region shortly before 22:00 local time on 14 October. Within an hour, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported explosions and a fire, preliminarily at the Borisoglebsk airfield. It later wrote that the airfield had come under missile attack and a fire was burning there. Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ posted footage from the town showing the blaze.
On the morning of 15 October, Gusev claimed that 33 drones and several jet-powered aerial targets had been downed over the oblast overnight. He did not mention the airfield.
A base Ukraine has hit before
The airfield hosts the 783rd training aviation center and units of the 105th composite aviation division of Russia’s Aerospace Forces, which flies Su-34, Su-35S, and Su-30SM jets, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported. In summer 2026, it had no permanently based combat jets, and Russia used it mainly as a stopover to refuel and rearm aircraft striking Ukraine, the outlet said, citing satellite observation.
Ukrainian drones hit the airfield overnight on 8 July, starting a fire, and satellite images later showed its fuel and lubricants depot destroyed. Drones also attacked the base’s pilot training center in July 2025.
The same night, Ryazan Oblast Governor Pavel Malkov reported a fire at an oil refinery in Ryazan. It came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was resuming strikes on Russian refineries.
Update: Satellite imagery confirms the strike
New satellite images show damage at Borisoglebsk airbase and six Su-34 bombers positioned in the affected area two days earlier, although the extent of the aircraft losses remains unconfirmed.
The monitoring channel Exilenova+ reports that 4 airframes were completely destroyed, while 2 others sustained significant damage.

Jaisingh said she was representing a woman who had been “very badly” treated by a police officer. Jaisingh sought a blanket direction in the matter, while Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, said the issue should be considered after the police submitted its report. The court had granted the Centre an extension until Thursday to respond to these pleas, as well as a batch of petitions challenging alleged police detentions.The petitions also raise allegations of attacks and assaults on children and peaceful protesters by certain goons, who were allegedly garlanded by supporters after being granted bail just a day after their arrest.Mehta said the apologies tendered by the authorities before the court were in keeping with the procedure followed in contempt proceedings. The Delhi High Court is scheduled to hear a plea seeking interim protection from arrest on Friday.

Judge blocks sanctions against two US-based human rights orgs. over working with ICC against Israel

A United States federal judge temporarily blocked US President Donald Trump's administration from sanctioning two US-based human rights organizations on Tuesday for working with the International Criminal Court (ICC) in its investigations into alleged Israeli war crimes in the Gaza Strip.
In his order, US Judge Jesse M. Furman cited a 2025 case in which two law professors filed a lawsuit challenging Trump's executive order imposing sanctions on the ICC.
Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN) and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG) sued the Trump administration in July over these ICC sanctions. At the time, they argued that the order "unconstitutionally restrict [s] Americans from seeking justice on Palestine at the ICC and working with human rights defenders designated solely for calling on the ICC to investigate Israeli and American nationals."
Furman said that DAWN and TAAG raised a similar challenge in their lawsuit against the two law professors, in which the court had decided that the order “violated those plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights because it constituted a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and did not survive strict scrutiny."
However, Furman rejected the plaintiffs' request to declare the 2025 executive order as "facially unconstitutional."
US State Department says ICC poses 'intolerable threat' to US sovereignty
A US State Department spokesperson told The Guardian that, while they could not comment on pending litigation, “The Trump administration has been clear: the ICC poses an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.”
Omar Shakir, DAWN's executive director, celebrated the courtroom victory, saying that the court had "put the brakes" on the Trump administration's efforts to "shield from justice the Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide and their US backers.
"The court ruling makes clear that the law does not permit barring Americans from advocating for justice at the ICC or working with human rights defenders that this administration sanctioned solely for calling for justice for US and Israeli war crimes," Shakir added.
TAAG's Anna Marie Stenberg also responded to the court decision, saying that the judge had "affirmed important First Amendment protections," and that it was a "significant victory, but our work is far from over."
Trump administration sanctions ICC after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the ICC on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday's move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.

A commander in one of the Basij’s female units was killed in an attack on Wednesday in Mehrestan, a border county in Iran’s Sistan and Baluchestan province, Iranian state media reported. The woman was identified as Afsaneh Aqila.

In a separate incident in the same province, the Islamic Republic News Agency reported that security officer Mohsen Shahriyari was killed while confronting a “terrorist group.”
Sardar Mohammadreza Eshaqi, the province’s police commander, issued a statement following the killings, describing Aqila as “a woman of faith, courage, and sacrifice.”
“I condemn this terrorist act and offer my condolences and congratulations on the martyrdom of these individuals to their comrades, the honorable people of Mehrestan, and the Basij community of Sistan and Baluchestan province,” Eshaqi said.
Iranian People's Fighters Front claims responsibility for six attacks
Attacks targeting members of the IRGC and other security forces in the province appear to have increased in recent weeks. The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported earlier this week that at least 94 people were killed and 33 wounded in 63 armed incidents across southeastern Iran between March 31 and October 10.
The People’s Fighters Front has claimed responsibility for only six of the incidents documented by HRANA. Responsibility for the remaining incidents remains unknown.
Security expert Roger Macmillan told The Jerusalem Post that anti-regime attacks have increased since the Sunni group Jaysh al-Adl merged with the PFF. He said there had been significant anger toward the IRGC over its “systematic arrest and torture of their people, many of whom don't even speak Farsi, and were forced into signing false documents, which have seen them convicted of alleged terrorist attacks, and then executed.”

The Iran-backed Shia group is composed primarily of Afghan Hazara refugees and migrants and is funded and trained by the IRGC.
Iranian regime seeking to project strength, public support for Basij
The attacks come as the regime seeks to project an image of strength, cohesion, and public support for the Basij. The Islamic Republic has released numerous images from its Janfada (self-sacrifice) training exercises, prominently featuring women training with guns and drones. Janfada spokesperson Sasan Zare claimed that more than 500,000 women registered within 100 minutes of registration opening for the “National Resistance” battalions, filling the first 1,000 units.
Despite the alleged masses who have registered for the self-sacrifice training, the Iran Human Rights Monitor has reported the regime is using violent criminals to fill its ranks, offering conditional release to those willing to suppress protests and signs of dissent.
Basing its report on testimonies received from inmates, their families, informed sources within prisons, and field reports from human rights groups, criminals convicted of general, violent, or drug offenses were offered repentance forms in August and September and granted bail after they registered with the Basij.
Although reports of personnel shortages in the Basij and IRGC predate the recent attacks, Macmillan suggested that financial desperation could drive people to enlist despite the risk of assassination.
