Could Israeli technology aid Saudi Arabia's struggles to stop Houthi missile attacks? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:52:20 UTC
17:52:20 KST

Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 8, 10, and 11 killed at least 16 people. The deadliest strike, on October 10, killed 12 people and injured 309 others. On October 13, another attack damaged an administrative building at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. Saudi forces have intercepted numerous incoming weapons, but others have reached their targets despite the billions of dollars the kingdom has spent on air defenses.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Why are missiles and drones still getting through, and could Israeli technology help Saudi Arabia stop them?
Israel has spent decades developing defenses against different types of aerial threats. Some have already been supplied to the United Arab Emirates. In May, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help defend the UAE against Iranian attacks.
There have also been reports of Saudi-Israeli discussions about sharing intelligence through American military channels. Neither government has confirmed such an arrangement, but it raises the possibility of cooperation that would have been politically difficult to imagine only a few years ago.
Why are Saudi defenses struggling?
Saudi Arabia operates American-made Patriot missile batteries and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), which is designed to intercept ballistic missiles at high altitude. The kingdom’s first THAAD battery became operational in July 2025, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
These systems provide substantial protection, but the Houthis have weapons designed to exploit different weaknesses.
Ballistic missiles climb high into the atmosphere before descending at high speed toward their targets. Cruise missiles fly more like pilotless aircraft, sometimes close enough to the ground to escape radar detection until late in their flight. Drones can be smaller, slower, and much less expensive than the missiles used to shoot them down.
A defender facing multiple weapon types at once must identify each threat, choose the right interceptor, and respond before the weapons reach their targets.
A 2020 study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, The Missile War in Yemen, documented the Houthis’ growing arsenal of missiles and drones, developed with Iranian assistance, and their repeated attacks on Saudi territory.
The Houthis have since improved their capabilities. Regional officials told the Associated Press that investigators believe drones were launched ahead of cruise and ballistic missiles during the recent attack on Riyadh’s airport. If confirmed, the sequence would suggest an attempt to stretch Saudi defenses by presenting several threats in quick succession.
The kingdom has faced similar problems before.
After the September 2019 attacks on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities, Washington Institute for Near East Policy researchers Michael Knights and Conor Hiney examined gaps in Saudi radar coverage and weaknesses in the coordination of its defenses.
The weapons appeared to approach from the north, while much of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture was oriented toward threats from the east. Low-flying missiles and drones could take advantage of radar blind spots created by terrain, the curvature of the Earth, and the limitations of individual sensors.
The researchers recommended better coordination among existing radars, command systems, and interceptors, rather than relying solely on additional missile batteries.
Saudi Arabia’s geography presents another problem. The kingdom covers nearly 2.15 million square kilometers, approximately 78 times the combined land area of Israel and the West Bank. Its cities, airports, refineries, oil fields, military bases, and ports are scattered across enormous distances.
Israel’s much smaller geographic area lets some defensive systems cover several population centers or installations. Saudi Arabia needs far more widely distributed equipment, even though large stretches of sparsely populated desert do not require the same protection as major cities or oil facilities.
Cost is another concern. An inexpensive drone can force defenders to fire an interceptor worth hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars.
Dr. Sidharth Kaushal of Britain’s Royal United Services Institute discussed the depletion of Gulf interceptor stocks and the difficulty of replacing them quickly in an April 2026 BBC interview. The Financial Times reported this week that Saudi Arabia was struggling with interceptor shortages and ongoing gaps in radar coverage.
Interception does not always prevent casualties. On October 13, debris from intercepted cruise missiles injured four people and damaged 15 homes in Riyadh, according to Saudi Civil Defense.
Which Israeli systems could help?
Israel’s air defenses rely on several systems that operate at different ranges and altitudes. Iron Dome is the best known, but other Israeli weapons may be better suited to some of the threats Saudi Arabia faces.
Iron Dome was developed to intercept short-range rockets. Its radar tracks incoming projectiles and calculates where they are likely to land, allowing the system to focus on threats to populated areas or key installations.
Upgrades have expanded its ability to engage drones and cruise missiles. Iron Dome batteries could protect individual Saudi sites, but their coverage is too limited to defend much of the kingdom’s territory.
David’s Sling, developed jointly by Israel and the United States, is designed to intercept cruise missiles, certain ballistic missiles, aircraft, and drones. Tests conducted in February 2026 included improvements intended to address newer aerial threats.
Arrow 2 and Arrow 3 are intended mainly for ballistic missiles. Arrow 3 can intercept suitable targets outside the atmosphere, before they descend toward the ground. Israel has used Arrow-family defenses against missiles launched from Iran and Yemen.
Such systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ballistic-missile defenses, but they would not solve the problem of detecting and intercepting a small drone approaching an airport at low altitude.
Two less familiar Israeli products could be especially useful for defending individual installations.
Rafael’s mobile SPYDER system is designed to engage aircraft, drones, and cruise missiles. Israel Aerospace Industries manufactures Barak MX, which uses different interceptors against aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, and some ballistic threats.
Either could potentially complement Saudi Arabia’s existing defenses around oil facilities, airports, or military bases, provided the equipment could be integrated into the kingdom’s command and radar networks.
Iron Beam offers a different approach. Instead of firing an interceptor missile, it uses a powerful laser to destroy certain short-range threats. Israel delivered its first operational system to the military in December 2025.
The attraction is partly financial: Firing a laser can cost far less than using a missile against a relatively inexpensive drone.
Its limitations are substantial, particularly in Saudi Arabia. Lasers need a clear line of sight, and dust, haze, clouds, and distance can reduce their effectiveness. They cannot replace longer-range defenses against ballistic missiles.
Israel also operates C-Dome, a naval adaptation of Iron Dome that could help protect ships and offshore installations.
Which systems would be most useful to Saudi Arabia would depend on the targets it wanted to protect, the weapons it expected to face, and the equipment it already possessed.
How has Israel helped defend the UAE?
The United Arab Emirates offers the clearest example of Israeli air defense technology being used by an Arab country.
After Houthi attacks on Abu Dhabi in early 2022, Israeli defense sources told Breaking Defense that an agreement to supply Rafael’s SPYDER system was nearing completion. The publication subsequently reported that an Israeli-made Barak air defense system had been deployed in the UAE, although the precise model was not identified.
The two countries had established diplomatic relations under the 2020 Abraham Accords, removing a major obstacle to military purchases.
Their cooperation reportedly expanded during the 2026 war involving Iran.
On May 12, Huckabee publicly confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help operate them in the Emirates, according to the defense publication Janes.
The Financial Times reported that Israel had supplied additional equipment, including a version of Iron Beam, surveillance technology, and real-time intelligence about Iranian missile launches.
Those details have not all been independently confirmed. An October study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies discussed the reported laser and surveillance deployments but did not independently verify that they took place. Janes also noted that Huckabee’s remarks did not confirm those specific transfers.
There is no public accounting of how many incoming weapons were intercepted by Israeli systems operating in the UAE.
Still, the deployment of Iron Dome batteries and personnel establishes that the Israeli-Emirati defense relationship has moved beyond ordinary equipment sales. That experience may offer lessons for Saudi Arabia, although Riyadh has not normalized relations with Israel.
Could Saudi Arabia obtain Israeli assistance without normalizing relations?
Intelligence sharing would probably be easier to arrange than a weapons sale.
Information about missile launches and flight paths could potentially be relayed through American military channels, giving Saudi crews more time to prepare an interception without requiring Israeli launchers or personnel on Saudi territory.
Regional arrangements already support this kind of cooperation. In January 2026, US Central Command announced the establishment of a multinational air- and missile-defense coordination cell at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. It aims to improve information sharing, joint planning, and coordination among regional military partners.
Israeli media reports suggest that Saudi-Israeli intelligence cooperation may already be taking place.
In September, The Jerusalem Post reported, citing a regional diplomat, that the two countries had discussed intelligence assistance through US Central Command. Ynet and Israel Hayom also reported, citing diplomatic and security sources, that Israeli intelligence was reaching Saudi Arabia through American channels.
Neither government has publicly confirmed those accounts, and it is unclear what information, if any, is being shared.
The Media Line reported in September that senior military commanders from Israel, Saudi Arabia, and six other Middle Eastern countries had attended a US-organized security meeting in Germany. US Central Command confirmed the gathering, but it did not establish a formal military alliance.
Saudi political analyst Abdulaziz Alshaabani warned against assuming that such contacts would lead to open military cooperation.
“Any intelligence coordination would likely remain limited and pragmatic, while Riyadh continues to rely primarily on its own security mechanisms and broader regional frameworks,” Alshaabani told The Media Line.
Purchasing Israeli missile defenses would raise additional problems.
Israel would have to authorize the export, and Saudi Arabia would need arrangements for training, maintenance, software, spare parts, and replacement interceptors. Some Israeli systems would also require American approval because of US involvement in their development.
Germany’s purchase of Arrow 3, for example, required Washington’s consent.
Political considerations could be harder to overcome than the technical requirements.
Saudi Arabia has repeatedly insisted that diplomatic relations with Israel depend on the establishment of a Palestinian state. Its Foreign Ministry reiterated in February 2025 that it would not normalize relations without an independent Palestinian state with east Jerusalem as its capital.
A publicly acknowledged purchase of Israeli weapons would be considerably more difficult for Riyadh to explain than intelligence cooperation conducted through American military channels.
Saudi Arabia has not publicly announced an agreement to purchase Israeli missile defense systems, nor has it officially confirmed that negotiations for such a deal are underway.
Would Israeli technology solve the problem?
Israeli missile defense systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s defenses, but acquiring and deploying them would take time.
Saudi Arabia would need its own launchers, radars, trained crews, and interceptor supplies. Iron Dome batteries stationed in Israel are too far away to protect Riyadh. Any new equipment would also have to operate alongside the kingdom’s existing Patriot and THAAD systems.
Israel has its own shortages to consider after prolonged fighting with Iran and the Houthis. Its military needs to replenish interceptor stocks, which could limit the equipment available for export.
Saudi Arabia is also seeking assistance from established defense partners, including the US, Britain, France, Turkey, and Pakistan. Those relationships offer alternatives without the political complications of buying weapons from Israel.
Protecting civilians remains important even when interception fails. Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent attacks after September 29, leaving residents without official alerts before the deadly airport strikes. Warnings later resumed, including alerts issued by Saudi Civil Defense for Riyadh and Al-Kharj on October 14.
For Saudi Arabia, earlier warning of incoming attacks may be more immediately useful than new missile batteries. Better intelligence could help its existing defenses respond sooner, while new equipment would require procurement, deployment, and training.
A Saudi purchase of Israeli missile defenses would be a much bigger step, requiring decisions in Riyadh, Jerusalem, and possibly Washington. In the meantime, Saudi forces must defend widely separated cities and installations against missiles and drones that can approach from different directions, often with little warning.

Romanian ground drone that fights fires gets military role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:46:37 UTC
17:46:37 KST

- Maximus Labs released new Max1 footage and says the unmanned ground vehicle is deployed in a military theater of operations, without naming the user.
- The company now describes a fully Romanian supply chain, after telling The Defence Blog in August that Max1 uses American communications gear and NVIDIA processors.
Romanian company Maximus Labs has released new footage of its Max1 unmanned ground vehicle and now says the tracked machine is deployed in a military theater of operations, although it has not named the armed force using it or where.
Chief executive Alexandru Radulescu made the claim in a LinkedIn post accompanying the images, writing that Max1 has been operating for years across multiple countries, fights fires, works in mines and tunnels, and is “set to become the backbone of the army.” He did not identify which army, how many vehicles are in service, or whether any government has signed a purchase contract.
“Max1 is the result of 14 years of research, a multi-role, dual-use UGV (Unmanned Ground Vehicle) built for high-risk missions,” Radulescu wrote.
The post also took aim at rivals, describing Max1 as a working machine that does not dance or perform martial arts, and that needs no operators in haptic suits hidden behind the scenes, an apparent reference to the humanoid machines that have appeared in recent technology demonstrations.
Radulescu said the vehicle, its remote weapon station and a low-altitude radar are all built in Romania on a fully national supply chain, with 70% to 80% of components made in the company’s own Romanian factory. That description differs from what Maximus Labs told The Defence Blog in August, when it said Max1 was produced entirely within the European Union except for American-made communications equipment and NVIDIA Jetson processing modules. Romanian business outlet Economica.net reported at the time that Max1 was being built under a French license in cooperation with state arms maker Romarm and the ICI research institute.
The company has made several claims about Max1’s use that have not been independently confirmed. In August, Maximus Labs told The Defence Blog the vehicle was NATO-approved and operational in the United States, France and Poland, with further testing in Romania, the United Kingdom, Germany, India and Morocco. It did not provide documentation for those statements.
Built around a modular chassis, Max1 is meant to switch between roles by changing its payload. According to the company, it carries up to 850 kg (1,874 pounds), withstands temperatures up to 500 degrees Celsius (932 degrees Fahrenheit), and runs for more than four hours on dual sodium-ion batteries at a top speed of 16 km/h (9.9 mph). Defense modules listed by Maximus Labs include remote weapon stations with 12.7 mm machine guns or grenade launchers, along with low-altitude radar and electronic warfare equipment. Logistics options range from casualty evacuation kits to mine-clearing attachments.
The company says Max1 uses an NVIDIA Jetson Orin module for functions such as follow-me and return-to-home, and that a weapon-equipped version can detect and track targets autonomously at about 5 km (3.1 miles). Firing still requires authorization from a human operator, Maximus Labs said.
Romania, which borders Ukraine and has had Russian drone debris land on its territory since 2022, has been expanding domestic defense production, but the Romanian Ministry of National Defense has not announced any order for Max1.

UK threatens to ban Eritreans over returns policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:45:43 UTC
17:45:43 KST

Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agrees to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals, Shabana Mahmood has warned.
VIPs and officials from the east African country have already been stripped of fast-track access to UK visas after their government refused to cooperate with the return of its nationals, the home secretary said.
The warning comes after Eritrea abruptly withdrew returns cooperation earlier this year, the Home Office said.
Refugee organisations have warned that the UK should not get drawn into rejecting applicants for asylum from Eritrea because it is a war-torn country and the UK usually accepts the vast majority of applicants, who are often escaping famine and conflict.
Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals.
Mahmood said: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.
“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.
“I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”
The move follows similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025.
Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February.
In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum.
Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans.
Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality.
After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers.
India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions.
Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total.
About 84% are successful on first application and more will be successful on appeal, she said.
“There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.”
Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”.
The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.”
UN experts say that the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation.
“There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said when launching a report this year into the human rights situation.
“Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved.
“The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.”
Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record.
“It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.”
Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support.
“It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”

Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:45:00 UTC
17:45:00 KST

How China came to dominate consumer technology
October 15, 2026
Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?
At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.
The main culprit? Chinese competition.
GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.
Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.
"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.
China's growing tech lead
GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.
Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.
"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."
This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.
BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.
So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?
Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.
Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.
Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.
While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.
"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."
Privacy and security concerns persist
Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.
A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.
Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.
"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.
Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."
"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.
Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.
In addition to privacy concerns, Chinese consumer tech firms have come under scrutiny over espionage and other risks, most recently regarding connected devices like EVs.
Is a new trade war brewing?
In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.
A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.
"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.
European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.
Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.
"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.
"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."
Can Western companies compete?
As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.
Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.
"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.
To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.
"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.
"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

Iraq devalues dinar to ease cash crunch, leaving traders in limbo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:44:58 UTC
17:44:58 KST

Iraq devalues dinar to ease cash crunch, leaving traders in limbo
The government hopes a weaker dinar will help pay salaries, but traders face rising import costs and uncertainty.
Baghdad, Iraq – Sitting anxiously in his small office in Jameela market, one of Baghdad’s main wholesale markets, food trader Hamza al-Rudayni is waiting to see what the coming days will bring.
A decision by the Iraqi government to devalue the country’s currency, the dinar, against the US dollar has left traders like him facing sudden losses and uncertainty over the prices they should charge for their goods.
“I don’t know what to do,” al-Rudayni told Al Jazeera after the devaluation reduced the dollar value of his dinar holdings, leaving him with less money to purchase imported goods.
“All I know is I woke up a few days ago to discover that I had lost 25 million Iraqi dinars (roughly $16,500 at the new exchange rate) because of this decision, while larger merchants lost billions,” he said.
Al-Rudayni entered the wholesale trade market last year after losing his previous job at a private Iraqi bank that he says was sanctioned by the United States Treasury. He sold his car and used his savings to start trading with a larger merchant before recently launching his own business.
With exchange-rate fluctuations making prices unpredictable, al-Rudayni said he and many other traders have chosen to suspend buying and selling until the situation stabilises.
“Market activity has ground to a halt,” al-Rudayni said. “Traders buy goods in dollars but sell them in dinars, as regulations prohibit them from selling in dollars.”
That is the root of the problem for traders: A weaker dinar means they have to pay more in local currency for goods imported in dollars, while making it harder to determine the right price they should charge customers for goods they already have in stock.
Why devalue?
On October 7, the Iraqi government introduced a new official exchange rate against the US dollar, in an attempt to ease a financial crisis triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran and the disruption of oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the war, Iraq exported around 3.5 million barrels of oil per day through the Strait of Hormuz, accounting for 90 percent of Iraq’s government revenue.
The Central Bank of Iraq decision set the rate at 1,520 dinars per US dollar for cash sales to the public. It was previously set at 1,320 dinars per dollar.
Devaluing the Iraqi dinar by almost 15 percent against the dollar allows the government to receive more local currency for every dollar of oil revenue it converts, helping it cover public spending, including government employee salaries.
“It is my decision and I am responsible for it,” Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said during a meeting with parliamentary leaders on Thursday.
“I was facing three challenging options to cover salaries and other mandatory expenditures,” al-Zaidi added. “The first is to cut salaries by 35 percent … the second is to pay the salaries every 45 days … while the third is to resort to foreign loans.”
Al-Zaidi, a former banker, also said that his government had inherited public debt exceeding 208 trillion Iraqi dinars ($139bn at the new rate) when it took office in May. He said the government needed approximately 10 trillion dinars ($6.7bn) each month to cover salaries and other essential expenditure.
A shortage of liquidity
The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz had caused a severe financial squeeze for the Iraqi government.
Although the situation has eased somewhat in recent weeks after Iraq’s oil exports partially recovered, they have yet to return to their pre-war levels.
Mudher Mohammed Salih, the Iraqi prime minister’s financial adviser, said in August that the Central Bank of Iraq’s foreign currency reserves had declined from $106bn to approximately $80bn.
To make up for the loss of revenue, the Iraqi government has also turned to borrowing from domestic banks to cover salaries and other expenses.
A Finance Ministry official told Al Jazeera that ensuring salaries were paid on time remained the government’s main priority, describing this issue as a matter of domestic economic stability.
“Our hands are tied regarding the revenue and how to maintain enough money to ensure that we can pay the salaries,” the official, who asked to remain anonymous because he was not authorised to speak publicly, said.
Economists have warned that while adjusting the exchange rate could ease some immediate fiscal pressures, it would not address the deeper weaknesses in Iraq’s economy.
“Nothing in economics is sacred, including the exchange rate,” said Nabil al-Marsoumi, professor of economics at Al Maaqal University in Basra. “It can be adjusted, but only after all other options have been exhausted.”
“In any case, the exchange rate shouldn’t be used as a cover-up for failures in the state’s economic and fiscal policies,” he added.

"Six hours is absurd" — Patients describe long night-time waits on Finland's A&E wards
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:43:32 EEST
17:43:32 KST

Patients seeking care at an accident and emergency (A&E) ward during the night in Finland face average waiting times of between five and six hours.
That's according to information obtained by Yle from several regional healthcare authorities, otherwise known as wellbeing services counties, about the average waiting times during the month of August.
The data reveals that patients who arrive between 10pm in the evening and 7am in the morning could spend an average of up to six and a half hours waiting to receive treatment.
The worst waiting times during August were found to be in Turku, where they averaged 6 hours and 29 minutes, while the shortest were in Jyväskylä, at 4 hours and 49 minutes.
Based on the information Yle received from the wellbeing services counties, the situation regarding waiting times during the night appears to have remained almost unchanged for several years.
Patients want quicker care
Yle visited the A&E ward at Jorvi hospital in Espoo — where the wait for night-time care (6 hours and 4 minutes) was among the longest in the country in August — to speak to patients about the waiting times.
Marcos Wichert, a Brazilian who has lived in Espoo for six years, injured his arm while dismantling a trampoline in his yard. He told Yle that he suspects his arm is broken, but at the time of his interview he had been waiting to see a doctor for more than two hours without any pain medication.
"I thought I'd get help faster," he said.
Espoo resident Heini Nurmi was also surprised by the length of the waiting time at Jorvi.
She told Yle that she came to the emergency room with chest pains just before 10pm.
"I can't wait five and a half hours, which is the estimated visit duration shown on the screen in the waiting room. I need to go to my children," she said, adding that the absolute maximum length for an emergency room visit should be four hours.
"Six hours is an absurd amount of time to wait for urgent care," Nurmi noted.
Chief Physician: Situation challenging but improving
Kimmo Suojanen, regional chief physician responsible for the Jorvi emergency room, told Yle that only a small proportion of the hours a patient spends in a waiting room is wasted time — as much of the care takes place out of the patient's sight.
"For example, X-rays are being analysed, specialists are being consulted, or blood test results are being awaited," Suojanen said.
He added that the conditions of patients arriving at night are often more demanding to treat than those arriving during the day, so treating them requires several time-consuming examinations and procedures.
This naturally lengthens waiting times, Suojanen noted, adding further that the situation at Jorvi has improved considerably compared to a number of years ago, when waiting times of up to 10 hours were possible.
"There are far fewer completely unreasonable waiting times than just a few years ago," he said.
Maaret Castrén, former chief of operations at HUS and professor emerita of emergency medicine, meanwhile noted that studies have shown the detrimental impact lengthy waiting times can have on patients, particularly elderly people.
"This hasn't been taken seriously in Finland, even though we, as representatives of emergency medicine, have said that patients should be moved on from the emergency room within four hours," she said, adding that hospitals should focus on shortening waiting times in the emergency room as a matter of priority.
"This should be a priority for the entire hospital, not just a goal for the emergency department," Castrén said.
Castrén is currently serving as a member of parliament for the governing National Coalition Party, and she also intends to stand as a candidate in next spring's elections. In this article, she comments on the topic based on her previous professional experience.
Leaving in frustration
Yle caught up with the interviewees — Marcos Wichert and Heini Nurmi — before they left Jorvi to hear how long they had to wait.
Wichert left around midnight, meaning his visit lasted four hours and 40 minutes. An X-ray revealed that his arm was not broken, but it remained swollen and sore.
Nurmi meanwhile grew increasingly frustrated with the waiting time and opted to go home after an hour and a half — despite not seeing a nurse or doctor during that time.
The next day, she told Yle that her chest pains had eased and she would not require medical attention, at least for the time being.

Police urge Ahold to file a report over cybersecurity breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:42:43 UTC
17:42:43 KST

Police urge Ahold to file a report over cybersecurity breach
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch police and the Public Prosecutors Office have asked Ahold Delhaize, the parent company of Albert Heijn, to file a report on what the company is still calling a “cybersecurity incident”.
“There is currently no criminal investigation into the incident,” the police said in a press release issued on Wednesday. “Police and the OM have been in contact with Ahold Delhaize. The company has been invited to file a report.”
“In order to successfully track down and prosecute, it is crucial to always get information from victims as quickly as possible.”
Although Ahold did report the incident, which began on Sunday night, to the National Cyber Security Centre as required by law, a criminal investigation can’t be started without a formal police report.
The company says it will “work with all relevant authorities”, but it gave no explanation as to why it hasn’t filed a report and said it is not currently making any further statements.
The incident hit other Ahold chains Etos and Gall & Gall, leading the company to shut down several of its IT systems that has continued to make online shopping and deliveries impossible.
Sector insiders told the Financieele Dagblad, on condition of anonymity, that the crisis is costing Ahold Delhaize “tens of millions” of euros a day. Ahold told the paper it was too early to say what the financial impact would be.
Fresh produce took a particularly hard hit, with the supermarkets’ fruit and vegetable sections very low on stock.
Albert Heijn said on Thursday that its distribution centres are running again, but its website and delivery services are still not operating, meaning customers still can’t place orders online or via app. Deliveries of fresh products were also said to be resuming as of Thursday night, while delivery of non-perishable products has been fully restored.
“This is a positive step forward in the recovery of our supply chain,” said the company. “The investigation into the nature and cause of the cybersecurity incident is ongoing. At this time, there is no indication that any customer or employee data has been involved in the incident.”
Bad actors
“We can no longer see cybercrime as a collection of separate crimes, but as a criminal ecosystem,” said a police statement. “Behind almost every attack lies a chain of cooperating perpetrators, resources and criminal services that reinforce each other: a criminal supply chain.”
Several foreign servers are known to be used in the attack, including in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that’s where the attacks are coming from as traffic can be routed through other countries.
Ahold supermarkets in Belgium (Delhaize) and the US (Stop & Shop and Food Lion) have also been affected.
The Albert Heijn incident came on the same weekend as a separate cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets in France.

The hijab issue and spontaneous protests in Azerbaijan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:41:02 UTC
17:41:02 KST

The recent wave of protests against hijab restrictions in the Republic of Azerbaijan—sparked by Cabinet Ministers decree regarding school uniforms—has become the starting point for on-the-ground demonstrations and the initial focal points of spontaneous domestic unrest.
The first signs of public protest emerged after officials at School No. 9 in the Jalilabad district barred girls wearing the hijab from entering classrooms; these protests quickly spread to other cities, including Baku. Subsequently, Azerbaijani authorities defended the Ministry of Science and Education’s decree of September 21, 2026—which prohibits any attire inconsistent with the "principle of secular public education"—asserting that it aligns with the country's secular constitution. Although the specific phrase "hijab ban" does not appear in the text of the decree, it declares any attire inconsistent with the official uniform to be unauthorized—a clause effectively amounting to a ban on the hijab. In this context, the following points are significant:
1.Public protests against the hijab ban in the Republic of Azerbaijan have been entirely spontaneous and represent a natural reaction to the violation of fundamental civil rights. In this context, even teachers and students who do not wear the hijab stepped forward; in a spontaneous social movement, they demonstrated their solidarity with the expelled schoolgirls by participating in marches and class boycotts. Religious communities and Islamic activists within Azerbaijan also viewed the Ministry of Education’s anti-hijab decree as a clear violation of the constitution, freedom of belief, and the right to education. Meanwhile, figures and media outlets close to the Azerbaijani government have attempted to portray this spontaneous movement as alleged foreign ideological interference by Turkey and Iran, using it as a pretext to crack down on hijab advocates. This is despite the fact that there is no evidence of Iranian or Turkish involvement in the matter; the primary cause of the protests and unrest was the Azerbaijani Ministry of Education's anti-hijab decree.
2. Efforts by Zionist media, as well as officials and media outlets aligned with Israel, to accuse Turkey and Iran of interfering in Azerbaijan's internal affairs and inciting protesters are seen as reflecting Tel Aviv's strategy to undermine Baku's relations with its two key neighbors and to discredit the spontaneous actions taken by the Azerbaijani people against the hijab ban.
Many political and media analysts believe that Israel is the force behind the scenes—or at least the primary beneficiary—of this situation. Friendly relations between Baku, Ankara, and Tehran have long been a source of concern for Israel; media outlets aligned with the Zionist regime aim to weaken Azerbaijan's regional ties with its Muslim neighbors by highlighting anti-Islamic stances in Azerbaijan and deliberately pitting Baku against Muslim public opinion in Turkey and Iran. Some also view Israel's approach as part of a broader scenario aimed at steering the Republic of Azerbaijan toward a strictly secular identity aligned with Tel Aviv's strategic interests in the Caucasus.
3. There is no doubt that the entirely spontaneous popular movement opposing the ban on the hijab in schools occurred without foreign interference; while the country's Muslims welcome moral support from Muslim nations, they oppose any action that would highlight foreign involvement in this event—a stance that demonstrates the political maturity of Muslim political parties and groups. Furthermore, the secular constitution of the Republic of Azerbaijan recognizes the freedom of worship for followers of various religions, including Islam, as a fundamental right of citizenship.
Accordingly, reason dictates that the country's authorities—by upholding the constitution, adhering to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and observing the standards of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation—should not oppose the hijab itself, which is a religious ruling and a fundamental tenet of Islam, nor should they further position themselves in opposition to the people.

EXPLAINER - Argentina’s Milei faces fresh congressional battle over economic deregulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:40:51 UTC
17:40:51 KST

Argentina’s President Javier Milei faces a renewed showdown with Congress over his sweeping economic deregulation decree as opposition lawmakers seek to overturn the measure following a Supreme Court ruling that temporarily reinstated restrictions on foreign ownership of rural land.
The dispute centers on Decree of Necessity and Urgency 70/2023, known as DNU 70/2023, which Milei signed shortly after taking office in December 2023. The measure introduced extensive changes to Argentina’s legal and economic framework, including the repeal of a law restricting foreign ownership of rural land.
The latest judicial decision has complicated the parliamentary debate ahead of a special session called by opposition lawmakers for Thursday.
The governing party has scheduled a separate session for Oct. 21 as both sides pursue different approaches to land ownership rules and the broader decree.
Milei signed DNU 70/2023, titled “Bases for the Reconstruction of the Argentine Economy,” on Dec. 20, 2023. It was published in Argentina’s Official Gazette the following day.
The decree’s preamble describes Argentina as facing a severe economic and social crisis and argues that urgent structural reforms are needed. It identifies excessive regulation and state intervention as obstacles to economic activity and investment.
Article 2 states that the government will promote an economic system based on free decisions, competition, private property and the constitutional principles of the free movement of goods, services and labor.
The decree changes or repeals provisions across numerous sectors, including foreign trade, agriculture, labor relations, health care, housing rentals and commercial activity. The government presented it as part of a broader effort to reduce state intervention, deregulate the economy and encourage private investment.
One of its most controversial provisions is Article 154, which repeals Law 26,737, known as the Rural Land Law. Enacted in 2011, the law established limits on foreign ownership of rural property.
The government argued that these restrictions constrained property rights and investment in agriculture. Opponents questioned whether such a significant change should have been introduced through an emergency decree rather than ordinary legislation.
Argentina’s Constitution allows presidents to issue decrees of necessity and urgency under exceptional circumstances, subject to specific restrictions and congressional review.
The breadth of DNU 70/2023 has raised questions about the extent to which the executive can modify existing laws without ordinary legislative approval.
Argentina’s Rural Land Law established restrictions on foreign ownership to limit land concentration and protect national interests linked to territory and natural resources.
The law set a general ceiling of 15% for foreign ownership of rural land at the national, provincial and departmental levels.
It also stipulated that no single foreign nationality could account for more than 30% of the permitted foreign-owned share.
In addition, the legislation limited a single foreign owner to 1,000 hectares in Argentina’s core agricultural zone, or an equivalent area elsewhere, depending on the location. It also restricted foreign ownership of certain properties involving significant bodies of water and areas near international borders.
Supporters of the law argue that these safeguards protect Argentina’s territorial interests, agricultural resources and control over strategically important areas.
They also warn about land concentration and the potential consequences for local communities and access to natural resources.
The government and supporters of deregulation argue that removing the restrictions could attract foreign capital, facilitate agricultural investment and expand productive activity.
The debate therefore concerns not only who can purchase farmland but also how Argentina balances investment opportunities with safeguards involving land, water resources and border areas.
The issue had already become contentious during congressional discussions over a separate bill concerning private property.
According to Argentine fact-checking organization Chequeado, the government later proposed allowing foreign ownership of up to 25% of rural land at the provincial level rather than eliminating all restrictions.
The proposal retained a provincial ceiling while allowing greater room for foreign ownership within individual departments or municipalities.
The government ultimately withdrew the chapter concerning land restrictions after failing to secure sufficient support, highlighting the political difficulties of changing the rules through ordinary legislation.
The legal battle over the repeal took a new turn with two Supreme Court decisions on Sept. 29 and Oct. 9.
Although both concerned challenges to the repeal, they involved separate proceedings and different legal arguments.
On Sept. 29, the Supreme Court overturned an earlier ruling by the Federal Court of Appeals in La Plata that had declared the repeal unconstitutional. The case had been brought by the Center for Malvinas Islands War Veterans, known as CECIM.
The Supreme Court rejected the claim because it found that CECIM lacked the legal standing required to bring the case.
The ruling did not determine whether Milei could constitutionally repeal the Rural Land Law through an emergency decree.
The decision removed that particular judicial obstacle, leaving the repeal in effect at that stage.
The situation changed on Oct. 9, when the Supreme Court temporarily suspended the effects of Article 154 in a separate proceeding involving the environmental organization Arbol de Pie and other claimants, including former senator and Río Negro provincial legislator María Magdalena Odarda.
The claimants raised different legal arguments, including concerns related to environmental protection.
The court sent the case back to the Federal Court in Bariloche, where a judge must determine whether the claimants have legal standing and consider their request for precautionary relief.
In the meantime, the Supreme Court provisionally suspended the repeal provision to prevent potential irreparable harm while the proceedings continue. The measure temporarily restored the Rural Land Law’s restrictions but did not resolve whether repealing the law through DNU 70/2023 was constitutional.
The decision was not unanimous. Justice Carlos Rosenkrantz opposed the interim suspension, arguing that the Supreme Court lacked the authority to issue such a measure before the lower court had ruled on the request.
The distinction between the two rulings is central to the dispute. The September decision concerned the legal standing of one claimant, while the October ruling provided interim relief in a separate case. Neither constituted a final decision on the constitutionality of repealing the law through the decree.
Opposition lawmakers have called a special session of the Chamber of Deputies for Oct. 15 to seek rejection of DNU 70/2023. Their initiative extends beyond the Rural Land Law, targeting the entire decree and its changes across numerous sectors of Argentina’s economy.
The Senate rejected the decree in March 2024, but the Chamber of Deputies has not voted on it. A rejection by the lower house would complete the parliamentary process required to overturn the measure under Argentina’s current legal framework.
Under Law 26,122, Congress reviews decrees of necessity and urgency through a specific procedure.
The Permanent Bicameral Committee examines each decree and submits its conclusions to both chambers.
Lawmakers cannot amend individual articles through this review mechanism. Each chamber must accept or reject the decree as a whole. Its formal rejection by both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate results in its repeal while preserving rights acquired during its validity.
This creates a political dilemma for lawmakers who oppose the repeal of the Rural Land Law but support other provisions of DNU 70/2023. Rejecting the decree would also reverse its other reforms, making the vote a broader judgment on Milei’s economic program.
The opposition must secure sufficient support to open the session and then obtain the votes needed to reject the decree.
Negotiations with provincial and centrist blocs are particularly important, as some lawmakers may oppose the removal of foreign land ownership restrictions while remaining reluctant to reverse the government’s wider economic reforms.
The Supreme Court’s temporary suspension of Article 154 adds another consideration to those negotiations. However, the court has not ruled on the broader legal status of the decree or the scope of presidential emergency powers.
The governing party has called a separate session for Oct. 21, with proposals concerning private property and other policy issues on the agenda. The government can also seek changes to land ownership rules through ordinary legislation, subject to congressional debate and voting.
The confrontation highlights competing views on foreign investment, national control of rural land and the limits of presidential emergency powers.
For Milei’s government, deregulation is a central component of its economic program intended to reduce state intervention and encourage investment. Opponents argue that restrictions on foreign land ownership protect national interests, natural resources and strategically important territory.
The dispute also underscores the role of Argentina’s legislative and judicial branches in checking executive power. The Supreme Court’s interim measure has temporarily restored the land restrictions without settling the constitutional challenge, while Congress faces a separate decision on the decree as a whole.
The Oct. 15 and Oct. 21 sessions will provide the next opportunities for lawmakers to advance their competing strategies. Their outcomes remain uncertain as of Oct. 13.
Ultimately, the dispute will test the reach of Milei’s deregulation agenda and Congress’s ability to scrutinize presidential decrees. The future of the Rural Land Law will depend on the ongoing judicial proceedings and decisions by lawmakers.

Chiang takes Songshan Airport relocation plan to Cabinet

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said Thursday that the Taipei City Government had not proposed relocating Songshan Airport in the past four years, describing the plan as a significant shift in Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) position.
Chiang attended Thursday’s Cabinet meeting to discuss the relocation proposal, calling it a crucial step toward developing northern Taiwan’s high-tech sector, TTV reported. He said his administration was willing to work with the central government to advance the plan.
Democratic Progressive Party Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) said Taipei had never discussed the issue with the central government, NOWnews reported. He also urged Taoyuan Mayor Chang San-cheng (張善政) to reconsider whether Taoyuan International Airport could accommodate the air traffic currently handled by Songshan, noting that the planned third runway was not designed for that purpose.
Lee outlined the Cabinet’s concerns, noting that Songshan serves as a backup when Taoyuan International Airport cannot accommodate air traffic, UDN reported. Asked how Chiang proposed replacing Songshan’s functions, Lee said the mayor had suggested that medical evacuations could be reorganized or handled through alternative arrangements.
Lee also cited Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰), saying Chiang’s position differed significantly from the one he held four years ago, NOWnews reported. She asked the Taipei City Government to provide records of relevant discussions and meetings involving Chiang.
Chang and Taichung Deputy Mayor Cheng Chao-hsin (鄭照新) also attended the Cabinet meeting. Chang backed Chiang’s proposal, noting that while Songshan remains important for national defense and emergency response, its future as a commercial airport is constrained by its limited size and a ban on operations between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m., UDN reported.
Chang proposed establishing a formal platform for discussions among local governments. He also called for transportation links to Taoyuan International Airport to be included in discussions of the relocation proposal, saying increased air traffic would require greater ground transportation capacity to move passengers.
Chang added that Taoyuan Metro’s signaling system was no longer commercially available, warning that this could become a bottleneck for potential changes or upgrades.
Meanwhile, Cheng cited the relocation of Taichung Airport as a possible reference for Taipei, ETtoday reported. He said cross-party cooperation under former President Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁) had enabled Taichung to secure a dedicated conference venue.
Cheng also called on the central government to expand its proposed Taichung International Airport upgrade, saying the plan should target annual capacity of 10 million passengers rather than 3.69 million.
After Thursday’s Cabinet meeting, Chiang presented an official document showing that the city government had proposed relocating Songshan Airport as early as 2023, FTNN reported. Civil Aviation Administration Deputy Director Yang Kuo-feng (楊國峯) acknowledged that the Taipei City Government had “written some words” on the issue in 2023.
The Taipei City Government also rejected claims that it had never proposed relocating the airport, citing its formal response on Aug. 8, 2023, to an inquiry from the National Development Council, UDN reported. The city said it had repeatedly asked the central government to include relocation in future plans for Songshan Airport.

Taipei opens Nangang Bus Station East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:40:30 UTC
17:40:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei’s Nangang Bus Station East opened Thursday, taking over 12 intercity bus routes from the former West Station at a facility designed to improve passenger services and strengthen transport connections in eastern Taipei.
Taipei Deputy Mayor Lee Tai-hsing (李泰興) attended the opening ceremony and said the station would strengthen Nangang’s role as a transportation hub while supporting development along the area’s technology and biotechnology corridors, per CNA.
The routes serve Keelung, Taoyuan, Yilan, Hualien, and Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, providing connections for commuters and travelers.
The station was developed under a build-operate-transfer arrangement involving Shin Kong Life Insurance. The building includes a bus terminal on its lower floors, a transfer passage connecting to Nangang Railway Station, and commercial office space on its upper floors.
According to the Public Transportation Office, the station has nine passenger platforms and four additional platforms for dispatching buses. Its larger waiting hall and improved internal layout are intended to ease congestion during peak periods and improve bus movements.
The first and second floors serve as the intercity bus terminal, while the third floor provides transfer access and supporting facilities. Floors four through 19 are designated for offices, which officials expect could generate 3,000 to 4,000 jobs, per CNA.
The new facility also incorporates provisions for green transport. The city said space and utility infrastructure are reserved for charging facilities as intercity bus operators move toward electrification. The station has also received candidate certificates for green-building, smart-building, and low-carbon-building standards.
Lee said the opening follows the September completion of a connecting road to the National Biotechnology Research Park, further improving access to Nangang’s industrial and commercial areas.
The former West Station site has been returned to Taiwan Railways.

The case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors: how prolonging the trial could help the accused avoid responsibility
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:40:25 EEST
17:40:25 KST

The case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors: how prolonging the trial could help the accused avoid responsibility
Kyiv • UNN
In the case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, five consecutive court hearings have been postponed. Against the backdrop of systematic delays in considering the case, the risk of the statute of limitations expiring is growing. Lawyer Rostyslav Kravets explained how the court can counteract the delaying of proceedings and what consequences deliberate evasion could have for the accused.
The criminal case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors is once again on hold: the court was forced to postpone five hearings in a row. Each such postponement brings the case closer to the expiration of the statute of limitations, after which the defendants may avoid criminal liability. UNN looked into whether the court has mechanisms to counteract the delaying of proceedings.
The Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa continues hearing the criminal case against private Odrex clinic doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, who are accused of improper performance of their professional duties while treating businessman Adnan Kivan at the clinic. However, instead of conducting a consistent examination of the evidence, the trial is being interrupted with increasing frequency by motions from the defense.
In the past two weeks alone, the court postponed five hearings in a row. Thus, the hearings scheduled for October 9 and 13 did not take place because of a motion by the lawyer for the accused, Maryna Bielotserkovska. Subsequently, the court postponed three hearings at once, scheduled for October 14, 15, and 16. This time, the reason was a motion by the accused, Vitalii Rusakov, who, according to UNN sources, is on sick leave.
The situation with the postponements became more acute back in September. At that time, the court scheduled 13 hearings, expecting to expedite consideration of the criminal case. However, only six took place. More than half did not take place because of motions from the defense.
Such delays may have serious legal consequences. The doctors are accused under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, which provides for up to two years of imprisonment. Under Article 49 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, the statute of limitations for such an offense is three years. Adnan Kivan died in October 2024, so in the absence of circumstances that suspend or interrupt the running of the limitation period, the issue of its expiration may arise as early as 2027. This means that, under certain conditions, the accused may be released from criminal liability. Even if the court finds the doctors guilty, the expiration of the limitation period may serve as grounds for releasing them from the sentence imposed.
Can the court stop the case from being delayed?
As lawyer Rostyslav Kravets explained in a comment to UNN , criminal procedural legislation provides mechanisms for responding to systematic failures by defense lawyers to appear. In particular, the court may initiate a disciplinary review of the lawyers’ actions and, where there are legal grounds, apply other procedural measures.
If we are talking about cases in which a lawyer systematically fails to appear at court hearings, the court has several mechanisms for responding. First, it may send a relevant referral to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar concerning the possible bringing of the lawyer to disciplinary liability. Second, where the grounds provided by law exist, the court may impose a monetary penalty on the lawyer. In addition, in cases stipulated by law, the court may appoint a defense lawyer through the system of free legal aid to participate in a specific procedural action. At the same time, such replacement must take into account the accused’s right to defense and must not create risks for his procedural interests
In the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors, presiding judge Viktor Chaplytskyi has already used one of these mechanisms. He found the reasons for the accused’s lawyers’ failures to appear unjustified and sent the relevant information to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar. The commission must now assess whether the defense lawyers’ actions contain signs of a disciplinary offense.
At the same time, contacting the disciplinary commission in itself does not guarantee that subsequent hearings will take place without delays. The court must ensure a balance between the accused’s right to adequate defense and the need to hear the criminal case within a reasonable time.
Changing lawyers as another possible way to delay the proceedings
According to Rostyslav Kravets, the abuse of the right to change defense attorneys poses a particular danger. This concerns situations in which defendants may systematically engage new lawyers so that they can submit motions to adjourn hearings to review the case materials.
Another problem is the systematic replacement of defense attorneys by defendants. Such changes may lead to repeated motions requesting time to review the case materials, adjournments of hearings, and other procedural delays. As a result, court proceedings may last for years while the statutes of limitations expire
According to the lawyer, establishing the real reasons for the procedural actions of the defense is of fundamental importance in such situations.
In such cases, it is crucial to establish whether there were objective reasons for changing defense attorneys and adjourning hearings, or whether the relevant motions were submitted formally and systematically, despite the court having already expressed its position on them
The expiration of the statute of limitations is not an acquittal
At the same time, exemption from criminal liability due to the expiration of the statute of limitations does not mean that the defendants have been acquitted. Closing a case on this ground is not a rehabilitating decision and does not establish innocence.
If Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska are confident of their innocence and want to prove it in court, the law allows them to object to the dismissal of the case due to the expiration of the statute of limitations. In that case, the trial must continue under the general procedure. This will give the defendants an opportunity to defend their names and professional reputations and obtain a final court decision concerning the charges brought against them.
Reminder
According to the investigation, the improper performance of professional duties by medical personnel while treating businessman Adnan Kivan could have led to postoperative complications and sepsis, which, against the backdrop of his oncological illness, could have caused his death. The court must provide the final assessment of the evidence and the question of their culpability.

Taiwan chip equipment suppliers eye gains as ASML weighs 2028 expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:40:15 UTC
17:40:15 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese semiconductor equipment suppliers could benefit from growing industry demand as Dutch firm ASML considers expanding production capacity in 2028, CTEE reported Thursday.
ASML develops and manufactures photolithography machines, which chipmakers use to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. CEO Christophe Fouquet said customers had raised their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts.
Some customers are also interested in placing orders for 2029 and beyond, pointing to sustained demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Taiwanese suppliers including Foxsemicon Integrated Technology Inc., Gudeng Precision Industrial Co., and Marketech International Corp. could benefit from the broader industry outlook.
Foxsemicon specializes in precision components, equipment module assembly, and system integration. Its contract manufacturing business, which accounts for about 87% of total revenue, is best known for producing etching and thin-film deposition equipment, according to Yahoo Stocks.
Strong industry demand has extended Foxsemicon’s order visibility from three to six months to six to nine months. Foxsemicon has also entered the optical inspection equipment market this year, with the product line becoming the fastest-growing segment of its contract manufacturing business.
Gudeng specializes in photomask and carrier solutions used to protect, transport, and store materials during front-end semiconductor manufacturing. Its extreme ultraviolet (EUV) pods protect 6-inch photomasks as they move between processing stations, according to Gudeng and DigiTimes.
Photomasks transfer circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers. As chipmakers adopt EUV lithography to manufacture 2-nanometer and more advanced chips, demand for protective pods and related handling and storage equipment is expected to grow.
Marketech provides semiconductor equipment agency services, system integration, and fab engineering services. Its major engineering projects include TSMC facilities in Taiwan and the US, with order visibility extending through 2028, according to FTV.
Yuanta Securities Investment Consulting said Marketech’s outstanding orders totaled NT$134.7 billion (US$4.2 billion) as of August, a record high. About 80% came from fab engineering projects, while equipment contract manufacturing and agency services accounted for the remaining 20%, supporting further revenue growth over the next two years.
Semiconductor equipment plays a critical role in the development of smart devices, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence. From wafer fabrication to final packaging, these machines perform the precise operations needed to manufacture chips, according to Sinotrade.
Front-end equipment is used to form nanoscale transistors on silicon wafers and build multiple layers of interconnects that carry electrical signals. Key tools include lithography systems and thin-film deposition equipment, which must operate reliably under demanding conditions, including high temperatures and vacuum environments, to maintain high manufacturing yields.
Back-end equipment focuses on wafer dicing, chip bonding, packaging, and testing. Automated systems, including probe cards and burn-in testers, help identify defects and verify that chips operate reliably.

Lai urges Micron to negotiate with Taiwanese workers as bonus dispute escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:40:11 UTC
17:40:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Thursday urged Micron Technology and its Taiwanese workers to resume talks over a bonus dispute, as unions pressed the US chipmaker for a clearer share of its profits.
Lai made the appeal at the opening of a new Micron advanced assembly and testing facility in Taichung, Reuters reported. A strike remains possible.
The president called on labor and management to negotiate in good faith, saying stronger communication would help build consensus and benefit both employees and the company. “Fish help water, water help fish,” he was quoted as saying by Nownews.
Lai praised Micron’s commitment to Taiwan and said he hoped the company would continue expanding its investment. He added that Micron had secured government support for research and development in high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, a type of advanced memory increasingly used in artificial intelligence systems.
Micron employs about 15,000 workers in Taiwan and has invested more than NT$1.6 trillion (US$49.4 billion), UDN reported earlier this month, citing the company. The nation is a major manufacturing center for dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, and HBM chips used in AI servers.
The labor dispute centers on the company’s bonus scheme and calls for a more concrete profit-sharing proposal. Unions representing employees at Micron’s Taoyuan and Taichung operations have urged management to provide a clearer arrangement for sharing the company’s financial gains with workers, CNA reported.
The Taoyuan union said its members had authorized a strike after a vote, escalating the dispute. Mediation between the union and management ended without agreement in September, while negotiations involving the Taichung union have continued.
CNA reported that the unions are encouraging employees to take a day off on Monday to attend a rally in Taipei. They have said the demonstration is not a strike, although the strike authorization leaves open the possibility of further industrial action.
Micron President and Chief Operating Officer Manish Bhatia did not address the labor dispute in his remarks at Thursday’s opening ceremony, instead emphasizing strong demand for advanced memory chips.
“We have already sold out all the capacity for 2027 that this factory will build and we expect high-bandwidth memory to grow faster than the rest of the DRAM industry all the way through 2028,” Reuters reported Bhatia as saying.
Micron’s remarks highlight the growing importance of memory chips to the global AI industry, while the dispute underscores the challenge Taiwan’s semiconductor sector faces as companies expand production and workers seek compensation that reflects the industry’s growth.

Typhoon Champi forms near Guam, Taiwan impact uncertain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:40:10 UTC
17:40:10 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tropical Depression TD33 strengthened into Typhoon Champi at 2 p.m. Thursday east of Guam and was moving west-northwest, according to the Central Weather Administration (CWA).
CWA forecaster Hsieh Pei-yun (謝佩芸) said the storm was still more than 4,200 kilometers from Taiwan. It was expected to remain far away even five days later, and forecasters needed more time to determine whether it could approach Taiwan’s coast, UDN reported.
Meteorologist Wu Der-rong (吳德榮) said the storm had the potential to strengthen into a severe typhoon. European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts model simulations indicated a track mainly over water south of Japan, followed by a pronounced turn to the northeast. Other models showed widely divergent paths, highlighting considerable uncertainty.
WeatherRisk meteorologist Wu Sheng-yu (吳聖宇) forecast that Champi would generally move northwest along the edge of a high-pressure system while gradually strengthening and expanding. He said the storm could reach severe typhoon strength by Monday or Tuesday, with its radius potentially growing to 280 kilometers or more, per UDN.
Wu said the typhoon could continue moving northwest toward waters southeast of Taiwan before slowing and turning north as a Pacific high-pressure system retreats. The storm could then pass near the Ryukyu Islands before continuing toward Japan, although its turning point and distance from Taiwan remain uncertain.
Wu assessed the likelihood of a direct hit on Taiwan as low. However, if the storm turns north closer to Taiwan, its outer circulation could affect weather and sea conditions around the island from next Thursday through Saturday.
People planning outdoor activities or travel over the long holiday weekend should monitor weather updates and take precautions, he said.
