Estonian PM: The faster Russian refineries are blown to smithereens, the better
Estonia continues to insist that Russian oil refineries and energy facilities should be destroyed because they fund Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: Prime Minister of Estonia Kristen Michal ahead of a European Council meeting on 15 October, as reported by European Pravda's Brussels correspondent

"We rely on them. And also sometimes even good friends need a remind[er of] what is right," the Estonian minister said.
Michal mentioned that Estonia shares a border with Russia and has the support of the three nuclear powers within NATO: the US, UK and France.

They all came. Help came from NATO… So, basing on that, I must say that NATO is working well and the US is a partner in NATO. Trump has assured us and everybody else last time in Ankara that he is following NATO and also Article 5."

Nearly one in three civilian Ukrainians has PTSD or complex PTSD – T&F
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:18:27 EEST
17:18:27 KST

A national survey of Ukrainian residents showed that 31.2% of respondents met the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or complex PTSD (CPTSD), according to the results of a study published by British academic publisher Taylor & Francis Group in the European Journal of Psychotraumatology.
"High rates of both lifetime and war-related trauma were documented. The national prevalence of ICD-11 PTSD was 25.2%, with an additional 6.0% of respondents meeting criteria for ICD-11 CPTSD, yielding a combined prevalence rate of 31.2%," the publication says.
The collected data reflects the state of mental health at the time of the survey rather than the dynamics of symptom changes over time. The article material was received by the publisher in 2025.
Factors associated with a higher likelihood of developing PTSD or CPTSD included female sex, older age, lower education level, prior military service, forced displacement due to war, as well as a higher number of lifetime traumatic events and war-related stressors.
Loneliness was the only factor specifically associated with CPTSD rather than PTSD.
Study co-author, clinical psychologist Emma Facer-Irwin, noted that the fact that PTSD occurred much more frequently than CPTSD may indicate that psychological responses to an ongoing war do not always fit neatly into models developed in post-conflict settings. "When the threat remains current and unpredictable, the ways of experiencing and adapting to traumatic stress may differ, representing an important area for future research," she indicated.
Lead author of the study, lecturer and researcher in forensic mental health at King's College London (KCL), Deirdre MacManus, noted that the vast majority of those surveyed experienced multiple traumatic events during their lifetimes, and many were also directly affected by the ongoing war through forced displacement, loss of loved ones, destruction of their communities, or anxiety for family members, with many Ukrainians continuing to face stressors in daily life. "Despite this, many Ukrainians continue to live and adapt under extraordinarily difficult circumstances," she noted.
Study co-author, professor at the Department of Social Sciences at the Kyiv School of Economics Volodymyr Kulyk, noted that PTSD and CPTSD affect not only veterans or people who were near active combat zones. "These disorders are also common among other population categories severely affected by the war—including internally displaced persons, people who have experienced missile and drone attacks on their cities and towns far from the front line, as well as those caring for injured or traumatized individuals," he stressed.
According to Kulyk, further research will be necessary to understand how the psychological impact of war evolves among the general population as the conflict continues.
In addition to specialists from KCL and the Kyiv School of Economics, the research team included scientists from George Washington University, the University of Manchester, the Centre for East European and International Studies (ZOiS), and Combat Stress—a leading British charity caring for veterans' mental health. The study was initiated by the research network "Conflict and Cooperation in Eastern Europe" (KonKoop), led by Professor Gwendolyn Sasse (ZOiS), and funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space.
The study was conducted via telephone interviews based on a random sample of 2,504 respondents in government-controlled areas of Ukraine. The relationships between the type and number of lifetime and war trauma exposures and PTSD/CPTSD status were examined using a series of logistic regression models adjusting for age and sex. The sample is representative by age, sex, marital status, education level, macro-region, language, and ethnicity.
Prior to field work, questionnaires were pre-tested on an approximately representative sub-sample (n = 20) of the target group (adults residing in urban and rural settlements of Kyiv and nine regions of Ukraine). During data collection, interviewers had the opportunity to ask questions and consult with a psychologist regarding complex cases. The average duration of an interview was 27 minutes.

European Prosecutor's Office will not keep Estonia in the loop in Datasel proceedings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:18:00 UTC
17:18:00 KST

European Prosecutor's Office will not keep Estonia in the loop in Datasel proceedings
The European Public Prosecutor's Office said it would not comment on the ongoing investigation involving Datasel to the Riigikogu's Anti-Corruption Select Committee.
Anastassia Kovalenko-Kõlvart (Center), chair of the Riigikogu Anti-Corruption Select Committee, expressed a desire to meet with the European delegated prosecutor leading the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) criminal investigation involving the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) and Datasel.
European Chief Prosecutor Laura Kövesi responded that, under the current regulation, only the European chief prosecutor may be heard before a member state's parliament. They "may be replaced by one of the deputy European chief prosecutors" and such hearings may only be held to discuss "the general activities of the EPPO."
Kövesi explained that, as a rule, the EPPO does not comment on ongoing investigations or disclose details about them.
"This is to avoid jeopardizing any ongoing proceedings and their outcomes. When we are able to share information about an investigation, we do so on our own initiative. I would also remind you that our jurisdiction is mandatory, meaning that we must act on every lead that falls within our remit. I assure you that we do so diligently," Kövesi said.
The EPPO is responsible for investigating, prosecuting and bringing to trial crimes affecting the European Union's financial interests. Its jurisdiction includes fraud involving EU budget expenditures where the estimated potential damage exceeds €10,000, as well as fraud affecting EU budget revenue, such as cross-border value-added tax fraud where the estimated potential damage exceeds €10 million.
Kövesi stressed that the EPPO fully respects the presumption of innocence and does not take political considerations into account when carrying out its duties.
"In all our investigations, we are obliged to seek all types of evidence, both incriminating and exculpatory, either on our own initiative (motu proprio) or at the request of the defense."
In 2024, RKIK signed contracts worth approximately €70 million to purchase ammunition from Datasel S.R.L., an Italian-registered company owned by Indian businessmen.
RKIK made advance payments totaling approximately €60 million, but the ammunition delivered did not meet the agency's requirements, according to RKIK. Datasel denies any quality issues.
In September, the EPPO launched an investigation into the transactions.
The procurement involving Datasel was funded not by Estonian taxpayers but by the European Peace Facility. This funding came from a European-level mechanism backed in part by proceeds from frozen Russian assets.

"Therefore, I would like this diesel deal to serve as an example of how sensible politicians can not only just remove sanctions, but look for windows of opportunity allowing for the gradual normalization of relations," he said.

CBA season preview: Reforms fuel title race, reignite relegation battle
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:15:59 CST
17:15:59 KST

by sportswriter Cao Yibo
BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 2026-27 Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) season tips off on Friday, with changes to the competition format, a reshuffled title race and expanded opportunities for young players set to shape the campaign.
The league's 32nd season will see promotion and relegation return after more than two decades, the regular season expand to 46 rounds and foreign-player registration limits tightened. Beyond the regular season, the CBA Club Cup and the Chinese Basketball Development League (CBDL) will also provide additional opportunities for competition and player development.
REFORMS RAISE STAKES FOR CLUBS
The 2026-27 CBA regular season will feature 460 games across 46 rounds, up from 420 last season. The playoffs will return to a 3-5-5-7 format, replacing last season's 3-3-5-7 system. The round of 12 will remain a best-of-three series, while the quarterfinals and semifinals will be played in a best-of-five format, followed by a best-of-seven final.
The most notable structural change this season is the return of promotion and relegation, which was abandoned after the 2003-04 season.
The bottom two CBA teams after the regular season will face the top two sides from the National Basketball League (NBL) in home-and-away playoffs in April 2027. Winners must still pass salary-cap compliance checks and a subsequent admission assessment to register for the following CBA season.
Overseas-player regulations have also been tightened. Each club may register up to three overseas players at a time, down from four last season, with a season-long registration limit of six players, compared with eight previously. The salary cap will also shift from a fixed seasonal limit to a tiered system linked to a team's progress through the season.
The changes are expected to encourage more selective recruitment and give domestic players greater responsibility, but whether they lead to more competitive games and better development opportunities for Chinese players will be one of the season's central questions.
OFFSEASON RESHUFFLE SETS UP COMPETITIVE TITLE RACE
A series of offseason moves has reshaped the title race, with the Shanghai Sharks seeking to defend their crown and the Beijing Ducks, Shanxi Loongs, Zhejiang Lions and Guangdong Southern Tigers among the clubs looking to challenge.
Shanghai enters the season with much of its domestic core intact, including Zhang Zhenlin, Li Hongquan and Liu Zheng, while retaining last season's Finals MVP Brandon Goodwin. Former NBA All-Star D'Angelo Russell and NBA champion JaVale McGee have joined the squad, adding considerable experience and new offensive options.
Head coach Lu Wei, however, has stressed that last season's title cannot guarantee future success. "Since the final buzzer, the championship has already turned the page," he said, adding that the team must start over and approach each game with full commitment. How quickly Russell adapts to the CBA and fits into the team could be decisive in Shanghai's bid to defend the crown.
The Ducks are also looking to take the next step after reaching the semifinals last season. The club has brought in Barry Brown Jr., JaKarr Sampson and Lindy Waters III. Former Chinese national team coach Li Nan, who replaced Chinese basketball Hall of Famer Xu Limin, has called for a more forceful approach, particularly in defense and rebounding. "Results in competitive sport are not achieved by talk; they are fought for," he said at the team's season launch.
The Lions, meanwhile, will rely on continuity among key players Hu Jinqiu, Sun Minghui and Zhu Junlong, but must compensate for the departures of several domestic rotation players, including Zhao Jiaren and Lin Bingsheng. The club retained American scorer Rayjon Tucker, added Cameroon international Landry Nnoko and brought veteran Dezmine Wells back into the fold.
Shanxi, Zhejiang's opponent in the season opener, has made substantial changes after finishing 10th in the regular season and reaching the quarterfinals. The team retained import Hamidou Diallo and added Lindell Wigginton and Petr Cornelie. Domestic recruits Zhao Jiaren, Wang Junjie and Xie Zhijie are expected to strengthen the team's wing and backcourt rotations. A coaching change, with former assistant Vytautas Buzas taking charge, adds another variable as Shanxi seeks to build on its playoff run.
Eleven-time champion Guangdong has reinforced its overseas-player group with the additions of veteran guard Kyle Fogg and center Udoka Azubuike, alongside Croatian forward Luka Bozic. The availability of shooting guard Edmond Sumner, who has been dealing with a hand injury, could affect the team's early-season options.
The Beijing Royal Fighters, who narrowly missed the playoffs last season, have also undergone a significant rebuild. The Royal Fighters have appointed a new coaching staff led by head coach Charalampos Markopoulos, brought back forward Wang Shaojie and added Zhao Jiayi. Guard Grant Riller remains with the team and is joined by Harry Giles and Javonte Cooke. The club has set its sights on returning to the playoffs and challenging for a top-eight finish, although the new lineup will need time to build chemistry.
CLUB CUP AND YOUTH LEAGUE BROADEN STAGE
The CBA's competition structure will extend beyond the regular season. The third CBA Club Cup will return during the league's window periods, with 24 teams taking part: all 20 CBA clubs and four NBL teams. Group-stage games will be held in Wuhan, Yantai, Yinchuan and Qionghai, with the finals in Nanning. The expanded field and regional venues are intended to bring professional basketball to more cities and broaden the league's reach.
The CBDL will also expand, with all 20 CBA clubs fielding teams made up of players aged 18 to 24 from club rosters and youth squads. The league will feature 292 games across preliminary and final stages, providing young players with more opportunities to gain competitive experience.
The 2027 CBA All-Star Weekend will take place in Xi'an, Shaanxi Province, from March 5 to 7, marking the first time the event has been held in northwest China.
At the season launch, Chinese Basketball Association president Guo Zhenming said the national team's results still fell short of expectations.
"The league is the national team's most fundamental talent base and competitive platform. The two are closely linked and share the same destiny," he said. ■

First World War Soldier of the West Yorkshire Regiment Buried in France more than a century after his death
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:15:33 BST
17:15:33 KST

First World War Soldier of the West Yorkshire Regiment Buried in France more than a century after his death
An unknown soldier of the West Yorkshire Regiment, discovered near the Thiepval Memorial on the Somme, has been given a peaceful burial more than 100 years after his death.
More than a century after his death in the First World War, the remains of a man of the West Yorkshire Regiment were laid to rest today (14 October 2026) with full military honours at the Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s (CWGC) Serre Road Cemetery No.2 in France.
In the winter of 2025 – 2026 human remains were discovered on the edge of a freshly ploughed field about a kilometre south of the Thiepval Memorial. Since the remains had been disturbed by a plough, it was impossible to fully understand the context of the find and to relate the artefacts to the soldier conclusively. However, a shoulder title found near the remains indicated possible service with the West Yorkshire Regiment, and this was strengthened by the presence of a belt with the letters WYR marked on it, also found near the casualty. An entrenching tool issued prior to July 1916 and first-issue webbing gave some clues as to when this soldier might have been equipped, but there was no clue as to his personal identity.
The recovery location was immediately adjacent to the Leipzig Redoubt, and records of the West Yorkshire Regiment show that various battalions were tasked with capturing Thiepval including the Leipzig Salient on the 1st July 1916, and remained in the line in this area until 17 July, before revisiting the area again in August of the same year.
Research showed that more than 1000 men of the West Yorkshire Regiment are named on the Thiepval Memorial, having died in the period 1 July 1916 – 31 August 1916. A further 745 men of the same regiment died on other dates from September 1915 to March 1918, and also remain missing.
With such an extensive list of potential candidates, and nothing in the way of artefactual evidence to point to his identity it proved impossible to identify the man. Nonetheless, he gave his life in the service of his country, fighting for freedom and peace. Whilst his identity remains known only to God, today he was buried by a party from the Royal Yorkshire Regiment – his military family, with full military honours.
The service was organised by the JCCC and supported by serving soldiers of the Royal Yorkshire Regiment, as well as staff from the CWGC.

Eight US states sue OpenAI over ChatGPT safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

17:14:43 KST

Eight US states sue OpenAI over ChatGPT safety
Eight US states have filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI, with Iowa accusing the company of misleading parents about ChatGPT’s safety and exposing children to harm, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent, citing the Iowa Attorney General’s Office.
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird announced the lawsuit at a press conference on October 14, alleging violations of the state’s Consumer Fraud Act.
Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana have also brought individual cases in their respective state courts, according to the announcement, which described the states involved as a bipartisan group.
“My lawsuit is about protecting our kids and holding OpenAI accountable under our state law,” Bird said.
The Iowa attorney general’s office alleges that OpenAI portrayed ChatGPT as a tool that prioritizes safety while failing to adequately protect vulnerable users, particularly children.
According to the announcement, the chatbot has provided dangerous medical advice and encouraged users to harm themselves or others. The office also alleges that its agreeable responses and simulated compassion can foster unhealthy emotional relationships.
Bird’s office further cited research that it said linked ChatGPT use to impaired critical thinking, reinforced paranoia and delusions, and unhealthy behaviors. These assertions are allegations presented by the attorney general’s office, rather than findings established by a court.
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers and West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey joined Bird at the press conference.
The Iowa lawsuit seeks to require OpenAI to comply with the Consumer Fraud Act, halt activities the state considers dangerous and protect the rights of affected residents.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that OpenAI had confirmed that its artificial intelligence agents unexpectedly interacted with websites operated by the US Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission, while a separate incident involving the Education Department remained under investigation.

China and North Korea open New Yalu River Bridge after 12-year delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:13:28 UTC
17:13:28 KST

The 3,026-metre, four-lane New Yalu River Bridge links the Chinese border city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea. Hundreds of people gathered in Dandong on Thursday to watch as lorries began crossing in both directions, some decorated with Chinese and North Korean flags and flowers.
Completed in 2014, the bridge had stood unused for 12 years because connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side were not finished. Its official opening marks a significant step in efforts to revive trade between the two countries after years of strained relations and pandemic-era border restrictions.
The crossing is expected to ease freight transport and reduce reliance on the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge nearby, which has carried much of the cross-border traffic since 1943. Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, estimated that the new crossing could triple or quadruple cargo traffic, particularly shipments of heavy machinery and construction materials.
China remains North Korea's largest trading partner and a crucial economic ally. Residents in Dandong hope the new link will bring more business and improve living standards across the border, although North Korea has yet to resume issuing tourist visas to Chinese visitors.

Pan Am-inspired cruise set to launch in 2027 to mark airline’s 100th anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:12:14 UTC
17:12:14 KST

The 28-day cruise will trace some of the former airline’s historic routes through the Caribbean and Central America.
Ever dreamed of travelling with Pan Am? While flying with the former airline isn’t a possibility, Holland America Line is offering up the next best thing.
Next year, the cruise line will be hosting a Pan Am 100th Anniversary Legendary Voyage, complete with talks from aviation historians, Pan Am-inspired dining experiences, and a recreation of the Clipper Club, the private airport lounges the brand was known for.
The 28-day cruise will set sail from Miami in Florida on 30 October 2027, and will retrace parts of the Pan Am’s historic routes through the Caribbean and Central America.
“Pan Am helped redefine what it meant to travel, turning the journey into an experience filled with discovery, connection and a sense of occasion,” Paul Grigsby, vice president of itinerary planning and deployment for Holland America Line, said.
“With this cruise, we’re bringing that era to life while merging elements of Pan Am’s storied history with Holland America Line’s signature experiences, giving guests a chance to see how the legacies of two travel brands come together in ways that feel authentic to both, from the ship to the destinations along the way.”
What to expect on board
Airline food today leaves a lot to be desired (at least if you’re in economy class, that is), but the same cannot be said for the plates on Pan Am.
Guests on the cruise will be able to try special menus that might once have appeared on board, including cocktail de crevettes, with jumbo shrimp, boiled egg, asparagus and Louis dressing; broiled filet mignon Maître d’Hôtel; and soufflé grand marnier with crème anglaise.
Cocktails, too, will be themed, with the Pan Am featuring white rum, Campari, orgeat, lemon juice and egg white, and the Clipper, with rum, Dolin Blanc and grenadine garnished with a lemon twist.
The programme will also include talks giving an insight into the airline’s culture and history from people including Linda Freire, the chair and co-founder of the Pan Am Museum Foundation, and David Kliman, a former Pan Am pilot.
As for land-based activities, passengers will visit destinations including Cartagena in Colombia, Colón in Panama, St. John’s in Antigua, and Port of Spain in Trinidad & Tobago for Pan Am-inspired excursions.
Other Pan Am revivals
Late last year, JP Hospitality announced it would be reviving the Pan Am brand for a collection of airport hotels.
The brand plans to open in locations across Europe including Amsterdam, Berlin, Brussels, Copenhagen, Geneva, Lisbon, London, Oslo, Madrid, Milan, Munich, Paris, Stockholm and Vienna, as well as cities around the globe such as Dubai, Bangkok, New York, Tokyo and Sydney.
Pan Am Hotels already operates a suite and lounge in Berlin, which have a mid-century design.

Riga City Council approves ambitious Central Market renovation plans worth over 22 million euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:10:43 UTC
17:10:43 KST

Riga City Council has approved a proposal for the development of Riga Central Market, paving the way for long-term cooperation with the municipal company Rīgas nami and investments exceeding 22 million euros in the development, preservation and renovation of the market’s historic pavilions, surrounding territory and infrastructure.
Riga Deputy Mayor Edvards Ratnieks described the decision as historic, saying it would turn long-awaited plans to renovate Riga Central Market into reality and transform it into a modern marketplace that meets 21st-century standards. At its meeting, Riga City Council decided to extend the management and maintenance agreement with Rīgas nami until 24 April 2067.
At the same time, the municipal company was assigned specific obligations concerning investment, infrastructure improvements, the restoration of historic buildings and the implementation of new development projects, Riga City Council announced. “We want to see Riga Central Market become one of Riga’s jewels. With this historic and long-awaited decision, development is no longer just an idea – it now has specific funding, deadlines and tasks that Rīgas nami must deliver,” Ratnieks said. “We have chosen an approach that allows the market’s renovation to move forward without using municipal budget funds, instead attracting financing from other sources. At the same time, Rīgas nami will continue actively seeking investors, including by presenting the Riga Central Market development project at international exhibitions as one of Riga’s most significant investment opportunities,” the deputy mayor added.
Rīgas nami must secure 21.2 million euros in investment for the development, preservation and restoration of Riga Central Market’s pavilions and surrounding territory. The financing is expected to come from the company’s own resources, European Union funds and programmes, loans and other financial instruments. No additional funding from the municipal budget is planned for this purpose.
In addition to these investments, Rīgas nami has committed to carrying out essential structural safety improvements at the former Meat Pavilion.
 The preliminary cost of these works is estimated at 1.385 million euros. The project will include restoring the basement’s load-bearing structures and the metal support structures of the pavilion’s roof. The procurement procedure must be completed by the end of 2026, while construction work must be finished by July 2027.
“It is particularly important that we are providing not only funding for infrastructure but also a clear path towards attracting private investment,” Ratnieks said. “The former Meat Pavilion is one of the buildings that must be given a new lease of life while preserving its historical value. By May 2027, we plan to announce an auction for lease rights to attract a long-term tenant and investor who will renovate and develop the pavilion,” he explained.
The former Meat Pavilion is expected to become a publicly accessible, multifunctional facility that complements the Central Market’s existing offerings. Its redevelopment must preserve the building’s cultural and historical significance. To establish a unified vision for Riga Central Market’s future, Rīgas nami will be required to organise an architecture and design competition within six months. The competition, titled Development of the Architectural and Design Concept for Riga Central Market, will help determine a coherent approach to renovating the pavilions and surrounding public spaces.
The market’s future development will be guided by several key principles, including providing high-quality, sustainable food products;
 creating green and accessible public spaces; supporting cultural activities and creative industries; encouraging local entrepreneurship and ensuring transparent and professional management.
Ratnieks said Rīgas nami has also been instructed to prepare an indicative five-year schedule of development works and investments, identifying planned activities and their estimated costs. The company will also work with potential investors to attract financing and implement development projects.
According to Rīgas nami, the long-term development programme aims to restore Riga Central Market’s historic pavilions by its 100th anniversary in 2030. The plans also seek to improve working conditions for traders and create a more convenient and attractive market for Riga residents and visitors. Renovation work will vary between the pavilions, with approximately 19 million euros earmarked for their restoration.
The planned changes include Fish Pavilion where extensive renovation will be carried out while maintaining the sale of fish and seafood products. In former Vegetable Pavilion the building will be adapted for the sale of meat products. In Gastronomy Pavilion renovation work will prepare the pavilion for the sale of dairy products and groceries and in Former Dairy Pavilion the building will be developed into a food service and dining area.
Structural safety improvements will also be carried out at the former Meat Pavilion.
 By summer 2027, the pavilion’s basement load-bearing structures and roof-supporting metal structures are expected to be restored.
An auction for the pavilion’s lease rights will be announced by May 2027 to attract a long-term tenant responsible for its renovation and development.
The building is intended to become a publicly accessible, multifunctional destination while retaining its cultural and historical value. Improvements are also planned for the shared infrastructure of the market pavilions, including the restoration of facades, lighting, waterproofing and external utility networks. The pavilions’ extensive basement areas are also expected to be adapted for civil protection purposes. At least 3.5 million euros will be allocated to the development of public outdoor spaces.
The work will be implemented gradually, with efforts made to ensure that market operations continue throughout the construction period. The renovation of outdoor areas and pavilions will also include arrangements for the sale of fruit and vegetables.
An international architecture and design competition organised by Rīgas nami will help establish a unified vision for the development of the market’s pavilions and surrounding territory.
 The competition results are expected to support the harmonious development of Riga Central Market according to consistent design principles. The investment programme will be financed through Rīgas nami resources, European Union funds and programmes, loans and other financial instruments. The programme is intended to proceed without municipal co-financing.
In addition, Rīgas nami plans further investments in the coming years in the development of its Spīķeri buildings, parking facilities and commercial activities.
The newly approved plans build on renovation work already underway at Riga Central Market.
Since Rīgas nami took over the market’s management in 2023, more than 4.4 million euros has been invested in development and urgent improvements. Completed projects include the restoration of the former Vegetable Pavilion’s roof, metal roof structures and basement. The metal roof structures of the Dairy Pavilion have also been reinforced, alongside other measures aimed at preserving the historic buildings.
Since opening in 1930, Riga Central Market has been one of the largest markets in Europe. The site covers a total land area of 9.9 hectares, of which 6.7 hectares are officially designated as market territory. Riga Central Market is a cultural monument of national significance and forms part of Riga’s historic centre, which is included on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Israel blocks building of Trump peace board Gaza military base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:07:04 UTC
17:07:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel blocks construction of Trump peace board military base in Gaza
Israel is blocking the construction of a military base in the Gaza Strip intended to house international troops under US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, delaying a key component of plans to stabilise and rebuild the Palestinian territory following Israel's genocidal war, according to a report by The Guardian.
The British newspaper reported on Wednesday that Israeli authorities had refused to allow contractors and construction vehicles into Gaza, more than two months after the US-led body awarded its first construction contract for the territory.
In early August, the Board of Peace, established following the October 2025 ceasefire and chaired by Trump, awarded Louisiana-based Arkel International a contract to construct a fortified military outpost capable of accommodating 150 international troops.
The troops were intended to form the advance contingent of an international stabilisation force tasked with providing security for reconstruction efforts.
However, a source with direct knowledge of the project told The Guardian that Israel has continued to prevent work from beginning.
"Israel won't open the border," the source said.
The proposed base would cover an area of approximately 10,000 square metres, measuring 100 metres by 100 metres, on land previously used by the now-defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF).
The controversial US-backed aid organisation operated in Gaza between May and October 2025, distributing humanitarian assistance under the protection of private security contractors.
According to the report, the new military facility would accommodate rotating deployments of 150 armed troops drawn from a larger contingent of 500 personnel already sent from Morocco and Kosovo.
Israel's refusal to authorise construction threatens to derail the wider Board of Peace programme, with the international stabilisation force considered essential to securing reconstruction sites and allowing equipment and basic services into Gaza.
"You can't get in without [an international stabilization force (ISF)]. You can't rebuild," the source told The Guardian.
"There's no security. There's no deliveries of construction equipment. You can't even start putting utilities. You can't start putting in basic life-support facilities you know because without the ISF you can't go in."
The source said the Board of Peace believes the Israeli government may allow the project to proceed after the country's parliamentary elections, scheduled for 27 October.
The Israeli government, military and Board of Peace have declined to comment on the reported obstruction.
Gaza reconstruction plans face further delays
The latest setback comes as the Trump-led body seeks to implement an ambitious reconstruction programme for Gaza, much of which has been devastated by Israel's military offensive.
On 23 September, the Board of Peace unveiled a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan, described as the first stage of a broader reconstruction effort expected to cost approximately $71 billion over the next decade.
The announcement followed discussions involving the commander of the international stabilisation force, General Jasper Jeffers, board members and other stakeholders.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and US envoy Steve Witkoff sit on the board's executive committee, while Trump has been designated its chair for life.
The initiative has attracted criticism over its governance structure and proposals for Gaza's future, including plans presented by Kushner envisioning luxury waterfront developments and high-rise buildings in the devastated territory.

Two ships ablaze off Romanian Black Sea coast, 7 sailors missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:06:08 UTC
17:06:08 KST

Two ships ablaze off Romanian Black Sea coast, 7 sailors missing
BUCHAREST, Oct 15 - Rescuers were searching for seven missing crew on Thursday from one of two chemical tankers that caught fire overnight just outside Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea, after Russian drones strayed into national airspace, Romanian officials said.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, but declined to say whether they were Russian.
"Two air drones hit them," Dan told reporters in Brussels ahead of a summit of EU leaders, adding only a few hours had elapsed since the strikes and Romania was waiting for more information.
"There will be a reaction from the Romanian state," he added.
The two ships hit overnight were both anchored in the Black Sea near the mouth of the Sulina canal leading into the Danube River, a major shipping route used by Ukraine as Russia has attacked Ukraine's own Black Sea ports. One was in Romanian waters, the other just outside.
The incidents follow drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring fellow NATO member Bulgaria over the past 10 days. At least 23 sailors were lost from those strikes, which took place just outside NATO's territorial waters.
SEARCH FOR MISSING SAILORS
Romania's naval authority said it received an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader. Seven of its 12 crew were missing and 5 were rescued. The ship was hit 13 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, one mile outside Romanian waters.
The interior ministry said it had sent two Black Hawk helicopters to the search and rescue mission, as well as two ships with medical staff on board.
"At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves," it said in a statement.
Late on Wednesday, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J also caught fire, 8-10 miles southeast of Sulina, inside national waters. Romanian authorities initially said it was not clear whether it had been attacked. All its crew were safe.
INCREASING ATTACKS ON BLACK SEA SHIPPING
Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube. It has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years.
Both Wine Trader and Yara J caught fire near the mouth of the Danube River's Sulina Canal leading to the Black Sea, where ships often anchor waiting to pass because of delays from weather and congestion. Both ships were empty of cargo.
Increasing attacks on Black Sea shipping connected with the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months have threatened to cause a global food crisis, as both countries are major exporters of grain, as is Romania.
"We're looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu told a security conference in Warsaw earlier this week.
"It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence."
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said EU leaders would discuss on Thursday a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea. Dan and Radev will meet NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte later on Thursday.
Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube River ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania. For its part, Ukraine has targeted Russian ships near the mouth of the Don River in the Azov Sea. REUTERS

Japan will suspend operations at a nuclear reactor in the country’s northeast around Saturday after detecting a leak of water containing a small amount of radioactive material, the plant’s operator said Thursday.
Tohoku Electric Power Co. said the No. 2 reactor at the Onagawa nuclear power plant in Miyagi Prefecture would be shut down to inspect and replace faulty components, according to Kyodo News.
The company said a small amount of radioactive material was detected in the leaking water, but all contaminated water had been collected.
No abnormal radiation levels were detected in the surrounding environment, it added.
The operator estimated that approximately 0.2 metric tons of water had been leaking every hour.
Water levels in a drainage sump had been rising since July, prompting an investigation that identified a leaking valve.
The company said inspections, repairs and preparations for restarting the reactor would take approximately 10 days.
The Onagawa reactor became the first in eastern Japan to resume operations after the devastating 2011 earthquake and tsunami triggered the Fukushima nuclear disaster.
The reactor was briefly shut down in November 2024, just days after restarting, because of equipment problems. It resumed operations later that month following repairs.
The 2011 disaster forced Japan to suspend nuclear operations nationwide and introduce stricter safety requirements before allowing reactors to restart.

Estonia would allow criminal proceeds to be confiscated without a conviction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:05:00 UTC
17:05:00 KST

Estonia would allow criminal proceeds to be confiscated without a conviction
Estonia plans to work with other European Union countries to amend legislation to allow assets obtained through criminal activity to be confiscated even without a criminal conviction.
It was about six years ago that the Supreme Court ruled to permanently terminate criminal proceedings against Edgar Savisaar who had been accused of corruption. The court found that Savisaar was so seriously ill that even if convicted, he would be unable to serve a sentence.
Similarly, no one was convicted in the lengthy Port of Tallinn corruption trial. In that case, the court ruled that the alleged corruption offenses had passed the statute of limitations.
Under a plan agreed upon by European Union member states, it would in the future be possible to confiscate assets belonging to individuals or companies even without a criminal conviction, provided a court determines that the assets are of criminal origin.
This would be possible, for example, if a suspect becomes seriously ill, evades proceedings or the statute of limitations on the offense has expired.
So far, only a small proportion of criminal proceeds have been successfully confiscated, both in Estonia and across Europe more broadly. In large-scale fraud cases, for example, it may be possible to clearly establish that assets were obtained illegally, while proving the precise role of each participant is more difficult.
"If these assets were obtained through criminal activity, terminating the proceedings would essentially mean that the criminal proceeds would remain in the hands of those who committed the offenses, allowing them to profit from their crimes. The process involves proving where the assets came from and establishing that they are of criminal origin, meaning they were obtained as a result of a crime. Once that has been proven, the assets can be confiscated," explained Andreas Kangur, head of the Penal Law and Procedure Division at the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs.
The European Convention on Human Rights states that everyone charged with a criminal offense is presumed innocent until proven guilty according to law. The same principle is enshrined in Estonia's Constitution.
Kangur also emphasized that confiscating criminal assets in this way must not involve labeling someone a criminal, even implicitly.
"The European Court of Human Rights has ruled on such cases and found that, as long as someone is not explicitly labeled a criminal, confiscation without a criminal conviction does not violate the presumption of innocence under the European Convention on Human Rights," Kangur said.
Chief State Prosecutor Alar Lehesmets said that confiscating assets without a criminal conviction is far from unprecedented.
"Many European countries have had such measures in place for a long time, including the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Sweden has had a similar provision for several years. Estonia is by no means breaking new ground here. On the contrary, we are actually lagging behind and are only now taking steps to combat crime that more progressive countries have already taken," Lehesmets said.
Estonia is therefore moving in step with other European Union member states in adopting the so-called asset recovery and confiscation directive. In fact, Estonia is already running behind schedule, as member states agreed to adopt the legislation by the end of November.
"Drafting this legislation has not been easy for us. Some of the measures that, as I understand it, have become fairly widely accepted in many European countries still seem quite radical to us," Kangur said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Mirjam Mäekivi

Unprecedented rainfall triggers flash floods in Istanbul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:00:33 UTC
17:00:33 KST

A spell of exceptionally intense precipitation across Türkiye’s Marmara region has broken historic meteorological records, delivering an unprecedented volume of rainfall to the metropolis of Istanbul within a remarkably brief window.
The storm generated localised rainfall figures rarely witnessed in the region's recorded climate history.
Meteorological measuring stations across the Marmara basin recorded extreme cloudbursts that shattered seasonal averages. In several Istanbul districts, precipitation levels exceeded 100 to 130 millimetres per square metre within just a few hours — a volume equivalent to nearly two months' worth of average autumn rainfall hitting the ground at once.
The sudden volume of water overwhelmed municipal drainage networks, causing underpasses, underground passages, and low-lying ground-floor properties to submerge rapidly.
While the entire Marmara region experienced heavy precipitation, Istanbul bore the brunt of the storm's impact, with several neighbourhoods experiencing critical damage.
In response to the escalating situation, central authorities in Ankara deployed state resources to coordinate emergency management and relief operations across the Marmara region.
The Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD) was immediately mobilised to direct field operations, dispatching high-capacity water evacuation pumps, search and rescue personnel, and amphibious vehicles to support Istanbul's emergency teams.
National meteorological authorities issued high-level weather alerts urging citizens to avoid unnecessary travel and remain indoors as municipal teams worked around the clock to clear debris and pump out submerged infrastructure.

LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:00:25 UTC
17:00:25 KST

Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.
More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.
The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.
The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.
Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”
Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.
Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.
The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.
While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.
Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.
“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”
She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.
The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.
LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.
The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.
The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.
There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.
In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

Inside Nepal’s unending cycle of avalanches, floods and landslides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:00:05 UTC
17:00:05 KST

Inside Nepal’s unending cycle of avalanches, floods and landslides
Experts warn such events could become an ‘annual occurrence’ and urge the government to rethink its development model
The rock-ice avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border that opened the floodgates in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26 killed more than 1,450 people, with nearly 6,000 others still missing. It was followed by a massive landslide after parts of a mountain collapsed into a river in the Mustang region in late September.
And on Sunday, another rock-ice avalanche flooded the Budhi Gandaki River – which joins the Trishuli downstream – in central Nepal’s Gorkha district, with concrete-like slush swallowing houses, bridges and trekking trails, though no casualties were reported.
“To have two similar events, nearby and in one year, is unprecedented in Nepal,” said John Pomeroy, director of the Centre for Hydrology at Canada’s University of Saskatchewan, who has been following the events.
“While climate change did not directly trigger these catastrophes, the thawing of frozen ground, melt of glaciers, increased lubrication of frozen materials from rapid snowmelt and rainfall all destabilised the high mountains and created the preconditions that permitted these events to form.”

Boxer ruled out of cavalry role as variants shelved
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:59:29 BST
16:59:29 KST

Armoured mortar, repair and recovery, and mounted close combat overwatch capabilities are no longer being pursued within the Mechanised Infantry Vehicle programme, and Boxer will not be used in the armoured cavalry role at all, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what elements had been cut from the programme as part of the funding removal and budget reprioritisation recorded in the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s Major Projects Annual Report for 2025 to 2026, which logged £1,858.38 million coming out. He separately asked how many of each Boxer variant would go to the armoured cavalry role and how many to mechanised infantry.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “As part of reprioritisation within the Military Strategic Headquarters, the Armoured Mortar, Repair and Recovery and Mounted Close Combat Overwatch capabilities of the Mechanised Infantry Vehicle programme are no longer being pursued.
“The Army is considering how the underlying capability requirements will be addressed.”
On the cavalry question, Pollard said: “Boxer vehicles will not be used in the Armoured Cavalry role. Boxer will form the spine of the Mechanised Infantry force. Under current plans, Boxer is being fielded in supporting roles across 3rd (UK) Division, including Command and Control, Specialist Troop Carrier and Medical functions. Detailed fielding plans and vehicle allocations remain subject to refinement.”
The requirement survives the first decision even though the Boxer-based route to meeting it does not, which leaves the Army to find another way. In practice that means an existing vehicle takes the task on, a separate procurement follows, or the capability thins.
Each of the shelved functions does a job the mechanised infantry brigades still need done. Armoured mortar gives a battlegroup indirect fire of its own, able to move with the vehicles it supports and put rounds down without waiting on artillery allocated at a higher level. Repair and recovery keeps a wheeled armoured fleet running and drags disabled vehicles off the battlefield, which matters because a vehicle of Boxer’s weight that loses mobility cannot be moved by anything smaller than a purpose-built recovery variant. Mounted close combat overwatch is the anti-armour role, carrying a missile system that lets the infantry hold tanks at a distance.
Armoured cavalry is the reconnaissance and screening job the Army is equipping with Ajax, the tracked family built by General Dynamics Land Systems UK and fitted with a stabilised 40mm cased telescoped cannon. Ajax carries the sensors and the gun for that work, while Boxer is wheeled, has no turret on the British variants ordered so far, and is built to carry infantry and the things infantry need. Ruling it out of the role closes off a line of speculation that has followed the vehicle since Britain rejoined the programme.
Boxer is a modular design built around a common drive module onto which different mission modules are fitted, the feature that was supposed to make adding variants straightforward. Britain rejoined the programme in 2018, having left it in 2003, and the order has grown past six hundred vehicles across infantry carrier, specialist carrier, command and ambulance types, built under licence by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford and WFEL at Stockport.

White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia did not pass a US bar exam, despite President Donald Trump describing her as an attorney when announcing her appointment, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.
Zacharia took the California bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011 but failed, a person with direct knowledge of the matter told the WSJ. At the time, she was preparing for her wedding and a move to China, the person added.
Questions about her credentials emerged after searches of attorney directories in California, Texas, and Washington, DC, under both her married and maiden name produced no listings.
Zacharia has claimed she is a lawyer on multiple occasions. When reporters asked her on Tuesday which state’s bar exam she had passed, she replied: “When I moved to China.”
Her LinkedIn profile currently lists her as having a Juris Doctor degree. Notably, if she did not pass the bar exam and has not been licensed, she is not a lawyer by definition.
Fox News also identified her as an attorney at least 18 times when she appeared as a commentator on several different programs. The network did not respond to the WSJ’s request for comment.
Zacharia has also called herself an attorney on other podcasts, news broadcasts, and media appearances.
In a statement, she said: “I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.”
Zacharia joined Beijing's Zhong Lun Law Firm in 2011
Zacharia moved to Beijing in the summer of 2011 and joined the international practice team at Zhong Lun Law Firm. A source familiar with her employment told the WSJ that she was among four international associates who drafted agreements for multimillion-dollar cross-border transactions and communicated with American and multinational clients operating in China.
Another source with direct knowledge of the matter said lawyers later advised Zacharia that her law degree and international transaction experience qualified her to provide legal analysis.
Her LinkedIn profile also lists a position as general counsel at Fix California, the nonprofit founded by Trump administration official Richard Grenell, from January 2024 to March 2025. General counsel positions usually involve serving as an organization's in-house lawyer, meaning Zacharia would have had to practice law, though she is not licensed to do so.
Acting as an organization’s attorney in California without a license would be a misdemeanor.
Someone familiar with her work there said she coordinated the organization’s outside lawyers and served as their point of contact.

'Spain's hallmark in Vatican': The Spanish medical science behind Pope Francis' lung operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:55:07 UTC
16:55:07 KST

Thoracic surgeon Diego González Rivas, based in A Coruña, Spain, developed the Uniportal VATS technique, a minimally invasive procedure using a single incision, which was used in the pontiff's surgery.
Pope Leo XIV's lung operation at Rome's Gemelli Hospital has thrown the spotlight on the contribution of Spanish science to thoracic surgery. The procedure, carried out to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung, used the Uniportal VATS technique developed by Spanish surgeon Diego González Rivas.
"The Pope has already been operated on; he is on the ward with hardly any pain and recovering very well," the surgeon said in a video released on social media. "The most interesting thing, and the reason why I feel deeply proud, is that he was operated on using our Uniportal VATS technique."
González Rivas, who graduated in medicine and surgery from the University of Santiago de Compostela, explained that this is a technique developed in A Coruña in 2010 and that since then "it has been spreading around the globe, reaching 146 countries so far".
The doctor expressed his satisfaction at the use of the technique he devised and at the fact that the operation was performed by the Gemelli team, with whose staff he said he has a close relationship. "Spain's hallmark at the Vatican," the physician concluded proudly.
The 71-year-old pontiff underwent surgery on Tuesday, in an operation lasting around 90 minutes which, according to the Vatican, went smoothly and as planned. Leo XIV spent a "calm" night and woke up normally, while doctors await test results to determine whether the cancer has spread.
What the Uniportal VATS technique involves
Uniportal VATS is a minimally invasive thoracic surgery technique that allows surgeons to operate through a single small incision of between 3 and 5 centimetres. A video camera, which guides the operation, and specialised surgical instruments are introduced through this opening.
This method makes it possible to carry out complex procedures, such as removing part of a lung, as well as lung or pleural biopsies. Its main advantages include reduced post-operative pain, a shorter hospital stay and faster recovery.
However, its use requires thoracic surgeons with experience both in minimally invasive techniques and in conventional surgery, capable of dealing with possible complications during the operation and in the post-operative period.

In 2025, 27 people were killed and 10 injured when a five-story building collapsed in the impoverished area of Lyari in the southern city of Karachi.

====================================================================================================

EIB seeks cross-border projects to boost Central Asia’s economic development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:52:29 UTC
16:52:29 KST

The European Investment Bank is seeking to expand cross-border investments in Central Asia, while requiring projects to meet environmental standards and offer benefits for both regional economies and European industry.
The European Investment Bank (EIB) is looking to expand its financing of cross-border infrastructure projects in Central Asia as it seeks to support economic development across the region.
“We would be, of course, very much interested not only in financing the individual country projects, but if there was a cross-country project, it would be even more interesting for us because we would also see a potential for development of the whole region,” EIB Vice-President Marek Mora told Euronews during his visit to Astana.
Interstate hydropower plant
One of the most prominent examples of interstate cooperation that the EIB supports in Central Asia is the construction of the Kambar-Ata-1 hydropower plant in the Kyrgyz mountains.
The project is being jointly developed by Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and the EIB allocated €900 million to the three countries for water management projects and the construction of energy grids.
The plant, which is expected to be completed around 2035, will be able to generate 5.6 billion kWh of electricity per year. It will greatly contribute to energy security in the region.
According to Mora, Europe could also benefit from this project.
“We heard some ideas about energy or electricity interconnector between Kazakhstan under the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, which could then further continue to Europe,” he said.
The water management aspect of this project is important too. The power plant is being built on the biggest river in Kyrgyzstan — the Naryn River. The Naryn merges with the Kara Darya River in Uzbekistan to form the Syr Darya River.
The Syr Darya flows through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan and empties into the Aral Sea. For both countries, it is one of the major rivers supplying water to agricultural land and providing drinking water.
The power plant will regulate the seasonal flow of the Naryn River, storing water during periods of snow and glacier melt and releasing it during the dry months. This will provide a more stable and predictable flow of water into the Syr Darya River.
Kazakhstan could build industries around transit routes
Transport projects are also of great interest to the EIB. The bank recognises the importance of Central Asia’s role as a transport corridor between Asia and Europe.
Mora highlighted that Kazakhstan has potential beyond being a transit country.
“We have a firm conviction that Kazakhstan does not have only potential as a transit country. We think that around this whole transit industry, there could be its own industry built around it, be it logistics, be it services," Mora said.
When it comes to transport investments, there is already a €150 million loan to KazAvtoZhol, Kazakhstan's national road management operator, to improve roads.
The project covers key transport routes in Kazakhstan, including access roads to international border crossings, the Caspian route, corridors to China, the southern transit route, and important interregional highways.
There is a similar €200mn loan to the Development Bank of Kazakhstan, aimed at both transport and energy.
"And this was even then enlarged by a letter of intent to increase this amount by €120 million,” Mora added.
What does a project need to secure EIB funding?
But projects need a lot of preparation to qualify for financing, says the EIB vice-president. They have to be predictable, have clear objectives and methods, and follow transparent procurement rules before the bank is ready to put money on the table.
“There are two groups of conditions, which a project would need to fulfil if we were ready to finance it. One is the already mentioned environmental and social standards, to which we put a lot of attention,” said Mora.
This means projects linked to the coal industry, coal technologies or gas technologies are excluded from the list of potential investment opportunities. The bank is more interested in green technologies, such as the autonomous truck project, which Mora discussed with Kazakh Minister of Transport Nurlan Sauranbayev during his visit.
“We had a very good meeting today with the minister of transport. He mentioned to us one of the possible future projects: that Kazakhstan would build special roads for autonomous trucks, which could cross Kazakhstan. And these trucks could be even electric and maybe of European origin,” Mora explained.
The second condition for the EIB to finance a project is a "win-win situation".
“A win for Kazakhstan, but also a win for the European economy or the European industry. We would like to see that if we finance a project in Kazakhstan, that, of course, it's there to support the Kazakh industry. But if possible, if there was a European content, it's really something we would be very much interested in,” Mora noted.
At the same time, he highlighted that the general development of the region is one of the bank's priorities.
“I think water management is, I would say, a global public good. So, the better we do in Kazakhstan, the better we contribute to the world management of this resource, which will become more scarce in future everywhere. And it's already quite scarce in Kazakhstan,” he said.
In June, the EIB opened a representative office in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, highlighting the strategic importance of the region.

Syria’s state-owned petroleum company said Thursday that a pipeline transporting oil products from the coastal city of Baniyas to the central province of Homs was damaged, prompting emergency measures and repair work.
Oday al-Satouf, director of the Syrian Petroleum Company’s media office, told the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) that a hole had been discovered in the pipeline in the Hadida area.
Emergency crews immediately isolated the affected section and secured the surrounding area, while firefighting teams, excavation crews and technical specialists were mobilized to respond to the incident, he said.
Al-Satouf said valves on both sides of the damaged section were shut off to isolate the pipeline.
Technical crews began repairing the damage, while other teams continued to monitor the site and implement necessary safety measures, he added.
The company did not specify the cause or extent of the damage or whether the incident had disrupted fuel supplies.
Similar incidents involving damage and suspected sabotage to oil and gas pipelines have been reported in Syria in recent months.
More than a week earlier, the Syrian Petroleum Company said an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in northeastern Hasakah province was damaged in a sabotage attack, adding that authorities had arrested those responsible.
In late September, a fire blamed on sabotage struck a gas pipeline in eastern Syria, disrupting supplies from the Jbessa gas plant to power stations.
A separate explosion in August also damaged a gas export pipeline in Hasakah, temporarily halting supplies, according to the company.
Syria has been working to restore its energy infrastructure and increase domestic oil production, including resuming operations at oil fields in northeastern Hasakah province to supply refineries in Homs and Baniyas.
In January, the company announced plans to transport crude oil from newly recovered fields to the two refineries as part of efforts to revive the country’s energy sector.

As AI agents take on more work, companies may need fewer software accounts, potentially challenging traditional software-as-a-service providers that charge customers according to the number of users, Cheng said.
The discussions reflected a broader shift in the AI industry toward combining software capabilities with industry-specific applications. Forum participants said Taiwan could provide an environment for international partnerships to reach global markets.

EU leaders heading for mighty clash over EU's next long-term budget - snap analysis
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
One other thing that is clear from this morning’s doorstep statements: leaders are heading for a mighty clash over the EU’s next long-term budget.
Agreeing the EU seven-year budget is always a fraught negotiating exercise, which pits a group of “frugals”, such as Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, who oppose a bigger budget, against a larger group in southern and eastern Europe, who want to maintain the EU’s traditional spending on agriculture and regional funding.
European Council president António Costa wanted a deal by the end of the year to ensure that the next long-term budget (2028-35) would be ready on time – and avoid getting caught in the crossfire of major elections next year in France, Poland and Italy.
That timing is in doubt, as the EU’s frugals (who prefer to be called “modernisers”) reiterated this morning they are in no hurry.
Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson said he expected tense talks today.
“We are not reaching agreement this month, not next month. I don’t know even if it’s possible to reach an agreement before the end of the year. I think we are not in a hurry, honestly. We need to have a budget that could combine the modernisation, the resources for Ukraine and of course the traditional things as well. But all the titles [areas of spending] need to be decreased to be able to reach an agreement.”
Friedrich Merz said he expected the “very, very difficult” talks to run into December (11:05) but privately Germany has made it clear it is ready to see the talks go into next year unless there are massive cuts to the current proposal.
In the other camp is Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who described the current proposal as “insufficient” to face the bloc’s challenges, adding that his government would fight to expand it. But with Spain due to hold elections in November, the Socialist leader may not be around to make that argument.
The latest draft summit conclusions call for only a “timely agreement” rather than setting a deadline “by the end of the year”, as in an earlier version.
The European Commission’s €2tn (£1.7tn) budget proposal, which aims to increase spending on defence, border security and research, has already been trimmed by €140bn by Ireland, who as holders of the rotating presidency were tasked with finding a common ground by October.
But almost nobody is happy. The frugal camp thinks the cuts, which target defence and research, are in the wrong places, while the self-styled “friends of cohesion” think there is too much scrimping on the EU’s traditional priorities, such as regional development funds.
France, which does not belong in either camp, but faces acute budget pressures, wants to see the EU agree to new common taxes in order to fund a budget that allows increased spending on new priorities such as defence and maintain the traditional ones, such as farm subsidies.
While the Commission has floated EU taxes on big companies, tobacco and e-waste, member states cannot agree on any of the options.
And the whole budget has to be agreed … by unanimity.

Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson also offered his backing for Ukraine, as he criticised Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia.
“We very much regret this agreement on diesel. It’s obviously not a very big part, but still, it’s in the wrong direction. And every step now to help the Russians to increase their the financing of the war is a bad sign.
So we very much stick to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s view on this.”
This 'senseless war of aggression' only continues because of Putin, Dutch PM says
EU leaders are now arriving for the European Council summit in Brussels and understandably they get asked about the latest situation in Ukraine.
Dutch PM Rob Jetten offered his strong backing for Ukraine and president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying “there is only one reason why this senseless war of aggression is continuing, and that’s because Putin chooses to do so.”
“He is the one that can end this war by starting negotiations for just and lasting peace. And as long as he doesn’t, the Ukrainians will have to defend themselves and defend European values, and we stand shoulder to shoulder with the Ukrainians.”
He urged other leaders “to do more financially, militarily, and non-militarily, because a lot of European countries are lagging behind in the support for Ukraine.”
“So let’s step up our game and make sure that they can win this senseless war.”
Starlink satellite restrictions highlight Europe's dependency on US technology
As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer any ready-made alternatives, Reuters reported.
European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelenskyy. But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Wednesday following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
Morning opening: Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions
Billionaire tech mogul Elon Musk has suggested that the US government could be behind the decision to restrict the speed of SpaceX’s satellite-technology used by Ukraine’s military.
In a post of X, he appeared to suggest the Trump administration was behind the move, which Ukraine says restricts its ability to use key defensive weapons.
Musk said:
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
In further posts overnight, reacting to Zelenskyy’s comments on his relationship with Donald Trump, Musk went further and appeared to suggest Zelenskyy should leave the post, saying it’s “time to go.”
In a TV interview with Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s decisions and worried about “losing a strong partner,” playing a critical role across Ukraine’s defence.
For what it’s worth, Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The issue is likely to come up again today and tomorrow as EU leaders meet in Brussels for key political talks on the future.
With today’s discussions focused on the bloc’s internal matters, including the EU’s next budget, Ukraine is expected to come up on Friday when Zelenskyy joins other leaders in Brussels. But the ongoing crisis in Ukraine’s relations with the US risks overshadowing the entire meeting.
