Lithuanian trade unions oppose president’s plan to limit migrant workers’ permits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:48:00 UTC
16:48:00 KST

Eight organisations representing Lithuania’s trade unions are urging politicians to reject President Gitanas Nausėda’s proposed restrictions on migrant workers, warning that the measures could increase workers’ dependence on employers and make it harder for them to defend their rights.
The proposed system would allow foreign workers to stay in Lithuania on fixed-term work permits and require them to leave the country for at least six months after completing two years of employment, the Lithuanian Trade Union Confederation said Thursday. It would also not allow them to bring their families to Lithuania.
“The greatest concern is that the proposed system could further tie a foreigner’s right to work and live in Lithuania to a specific employer,” the confederation said in a statement. “In such a case, it would be difficult for a worker to change jobs even if they faced unpaid wages, poor working conditions or other violations.”
Trade union leaders argued that Lithuania should focus on improving working conditions and wages to attract and retain workers rather than making their residence status dependent on their employers.
“If Lithuania lacks workers, we must first ask why we are unable to attract and retain them. Perhaps the problem is not a shortage of workers but the working conditions on offer?” confederation chairwoman Dalia Jakutavičė said.
“Lithuanian businesses must compete on wages, working conditions and productivity, not on workers’ dependence on their employers,” she added.
The eight organisations are calling on the presidential office, government and parliament to reassess the proposal and focus on measures that would help companies recruit staff while increasing employment opportunities for Lithuanian citizens.
“We cannot create two labour markets, one in which people can freely choose their jobs and another in which that possibility is restricted,” Jakutavičė said.
The parliament, Seimas, approved Nausėda’s proposals in principle in mid-July. The president’s office says the changes are intended to improve migration management while addressing labour shortages in the Lithuanian economy.
Under the proposed model, fixed-term permits would primarily apply to foreign nationals who intend to work in Lithuania temporarily rather than settle there, including long-haul truck drivers and construction workers. The system would streamline entry and application procedures to help employers recruit workers more quickly when they cannot find suitable staff locally.
After two years of employment, workers covered by the scheme would have to leave Lithuania for at least six months. Highly skilled workers from outside the European Union would not be subject to the same restrictions.
The presidential office has also argued that the model would help prevent family reunification from accelerating growth in the migrant population.

They were followed by Ambassador Maya Yaron and her staff in Fiji, who voted for the first time in the country's history, and then by the Israeli Embassy in Canberra, Australia, headed by Ambassador Hillel Newman.
Overseas voting will conclude Friday at 6 a.m. Israel time on the U.S. West Coast, at Israel's diplomatic missions in San Francisco and Los Angeles.
In total, more than 4,800 diplomats, state representatives and their family members are eligible to vote at 101 polling stations across 99 Israeli diplomatic missions worldwide. The largest number of voters is expected at the Israeli mission in New York, while the smallest will be at the embassy in Kathmandu, Nepal.
All ballots will be flown to Israel by diplomatic mail as part of a complex logistical operation coordinated by the Foreign Ministry and the Central Elections Committee. The ballots will then be transferred to the Knesset, where they will be counted as double-envelope ballots alongside votes cast by soldiers.
On Thursday morning, as voting opened at Israeli missions abroad, President Isaac Herzog visited the Israeli Embassy in Baku, accompanied by Israel's ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ronen Krausz.
"This is a very important moment during my state visit here to Azerbaijan," Herzog said. "I have the opportunity to see how the election process begins and how voting is actually conducted at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad, here at the embassy in Baku."
"These elections are a celebration of democracy in Israel and at its embassies abroad," the president continued. "I call on all Israeli citizens to exercise their right to vote and, of course, to influence Israel's future.
"These are very important elections after a difficult period for the State of Israel, and the main thing I want to say to every Israeli citizen is that elections are not a civil war. On the contrary, they are the genuine democratic process through which we influence our lives and determine the direction our country takes."

Analysts expect UK inflation to rise towards the end of the year as higher oil and gas prices feed through to household bills, with little sign of an end to the Middle East war.
"We still expect the coming rise in inflation to dampen growth, but the economy is more robust than we thought," Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said.
GDP in the three months to the end of August grew 0.7%, the ONS noted.
Liz McKeown, ONS director of economic statistics, said that "computer programming was once again the largest contributor to growth in the three months to August".
The boom in the artificial intelligence sector had also helped drive growth in July.
"There is a bit of a divergence going on within the economy, with businesses performing well (partly due to AI-related spending) while households are becoming more circumspect," Dales said.
Samuel Edwards, head of client portfolio management at financial solutions firm Ebury, sent his comments on the update in a client note to Euronews. He noted how the IMF's gloomier outlook for 2027 suggests the UK is far from out of the woods.
“Rising energy prices linked to the ongoing Iran conflict risk reigniting inflation, potentially forcing the Bank of England to raise interest rates further and piling more pressure on households and businesses.
“With confidence already fragile, the prospect of further tax rises in the Autumn Budget could see consumers rein in spending and businesses put investment on ice.
“Against this backdrop, businesses must strengthen their financial resilience – keeping operations lean, maintaining access to finance and using effective FX hedging to limit exposure to further volatility,” Edwards added.

UFO-shaped futuro house brings radical 1960s vision of prefab living to the market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:45:03 UTC
16:45:03 KST

UFO-shaped futuro house brings radical 1960s vision of prefab living to the market
listed for sale in idyllwild, california, the rare dwelling designed by matti suuronen reflects a 1960s vision of portable living, when prefabrication and lightweight materials promised new ways to inhabit remote landscapes.
[FEATURED]
UFO-shaped residence in california hits the market for $1.5 million
A UFO-shaped Futuro house in Idyllwild, California, is on the market for $1.495 million. Designed by Finnish architect Matti Suuronen, the prefabricated dwelling was conceived as a portable ski cabin that could be transported by helicopter and installed in remote locations. With fewer than 100 Futuros built, the property offers a rare surviving example of a Space Age experiment in portable living.
Its elliptical yellow fiberglass shell, circular windows and aircraft-style entrance reflect a period when space exploration and advances in synthetic materials fascinated designers, leading them to imagine radically different ways of living.
the Matti Suuronen-designed house is designed to go anywhere
Listed by Desert Sotheby’s International Realty, the UFO-shaped dwelling is owned by historic preservationist and former Obama administration appointee Milford Wayne Donaldson and his wife, Laurie Donaldson. Known as the Donaldson Futuro, the house is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, preserving an experimental approach to residential architecture that emerged from the technological optimism of the late 1960s.
Suuronen developed the Futuro around the idea of a lightweight, prefabricated dwelling that could be adapted to different landscapes. The structure comprises modular components that can be bolted together on-site, while its design allows the house to be dismantled and reassembled or transported by helicopter. Made from fiberglass-reinforced polyester plastic with polyurethane insulation, the Futuro was intended to be quick to install and heat, even in cold environments. Its original concept required only four concrete piers to support the structure, reducing the need for extensive foundations and conventional construction.
Measuring approximately 8 meters in diameter and 4 meters in height, the Donaldson Futuro contains 73.7 square meters of interior space. The dwelling weighs approximately 5,398 kg and sits on a 0.23-hectare property in the San Jacinto Mountains near Idyllwild.
why the Futuro never became the house of the future
Developed during a period of confidence in industrial production and new materials, the Futuro proposed an alternative to the conventional house. Its prefabricated components suggested that a dwelling could be manufactured, transported and installed with relative ease, rather than built from the ground up on a permanent site. Yet the design struggled to gain widespread acceptance. Its unconventional appearance and plastic construction met resistance from some communities, while zoning restrictions and difficulties securing financing presented additional obstacles. The 1973 oil crisis also drove up the cost of producing synthetic materials, undermining the economic premise of plastic architecture.
Fewer than 100 Futuros were built, according to the structure’s published history. What began as an attempt to make a portable retreat accessible through industrial production instead became a limited architectural experiment, with surviving examples now valued for their rarity and cultural significance.
The Donaldson Futuro has undergone extensive restoration, retaining the integrity of its original 1969 design, materials and workmanship. Its inclusion on the National Register of Historic Places recognizes its place within the history of experimental residential architecture. The property’s current status reveals a tension at the heart of the Futuro’s original proposition. Conceived as a transportable dwelling that could occupy a range of landscapes, it now stands as a rare, carefully preserved artifact of a particular vision of the future. Listed for $1.5 million, the house is a collector’s property, reflecting how architectural experiments that fail to achieve widespread adoption can acquire a new kind of value through scarcity, preservation and historical recognition.
project info:
name: Donaldson Futuro
architect: Matti Suuronen
location: 52895 Big Rock Road, Idyllwild, California, USA
area: 73.7 sq m (793 sq ft)

China launches eight AI computing satellites among 10 sent into orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:43:07 UTC
16:43:07 KST

China has successfully launched 10 satellites aboard a Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket, including eight designed to advance artificial intelligence computing capabilities in orbit, state-run Xinhua News Agency reported on Wednesday.
The rocket lifted off at 7.40 pm local time (1140 GMT) from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwestern China, placing all 10 satellites into their designated orbits, according to Xinhua.
Eight of the satellites belong to the second group of the Star Compute project, developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company ADAspace.
Designed to operate in dawn-dusk orbits, the satellites carry high-performance computing systems, laser communication equipment and low-light cameras.
They will test technologies including 10,000-watt liquid-cooling systems, large deployable cooling structures, space-based laser communication networks and the training of AI foundation models directly in orbit.
ADAspace said the mission would accelerate technological development and commercial applications of space-based computing.
Plans for orbital AI network
The company aims to establish an orbital AI infrastructure network comprising 2,800 computing satellites.
The first group of 12 satellites was launched in May 2025. In January, ADAspace announced that it had deployed Alibaba’s Qwen3 AI model aboard its orbital computing network, enabling AI processing directly in space.
The company plans to establish a 1,000-satellite network by 2030 and complete the larger constellation by 2035.

Nestlé sued in US over arsenic in baby food
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:43:04 UTC
16:43:04 KST

Nestlé sued in US over arsenic in baby food
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has brought legal proceedings against Nestlé and its US subsidiary, Gerber Products, for misleading parents about the presence of toxic heavy metals in Gerber baby food.
Gerber claimed that its products were safe, rigorously tested and recommended by paediatricians. However, the company’s own tests revealed dangerous levels of arsenic and lead.
Between 2017 and 2019, Gerber used 67 batches of rice flour containing more than nine times the concentration of arsenic permitted by the federal government in bottled water, the Texas Attorney General said in a statement released on Wednesday.
Its carrots contained up to 17 times the permitted cadmium limit in bottled water. Its sweet potatoes contained nearly 10 times the permitted lead limit. “Gerber rarely carried out mercury tests. For most of this period, the company tested certain ingredients rather than the finished baby food products,” said Paxton.
+ Does infant formula have too many ingredients?
In 2021, the Alaska State Laboratory also detected two samples of Gerber rice cereal with arsenic levels exceeding the federal limit. “Gerber issued no recalls or warnings and continued to sell its products. Gerber has recalled products due to the presence of plastic and choking hazards, but never because of heavy metals,” notes the Attorney General.
According to him, these metals are neurotoxins. Federal health agencies rank arsenic, lead and mercury as the first, second and third most potentially harmful substances to human health, respectively. Moreover, in medical toxicology, there is no established safe threshold for lead or inorganic arsenic in infants, below which they would be completely harmless.
‘Broken’ promises
The subsidiary of the Vevey-based giant Nestlé had promised parents that its baby food was safe and subject to rigorous testing. “Yet its own analyses have revealed the presence of toxic metals. When a company makes promises regarding baby food, I hold it accountable and ensure it keeps them,” emphasised Paxton.
Gerber has since been displaying the test results via a QR code on its labels. “However, the heavy metal content of the food has remained unchanged, as have the safety claims on the front of the packaging,” adds the lawyer, who has brought a legal action under the Texas Unfair Trade Practices Act (DTPA).
When contacted by AWP, Nestlé was not immediately available for comment.
This is not the first scandal involving the Vaud-based group’s baby food products. Earlier this year, it issued a series of recalls of infant formula contaminated with the toxin cereulide. In early January, this recall affected 31 countries and accounted for less than 0.5% of the group’s turnover. Since then, around 60 countries have been affected, with reports of ill babies increasing, particularly in Belgium and the United Kingdom, and three suspected deaths of infants who had drunk the recalled milk being investigated in France.

Sally Rooney forced to withdraw sale of books in UK due to support for Palestine Action

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:40:09 UTC
16:40:09 KST

The best-selling author of “Conversations With Friends” and “Normal People” is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.
Sally Rooney, the celebrated and best-selling Irish author behind “Conversations With Friends”, “Normal People” and “Intermezzo”, has said that she can no longer sell books in the UK.
Rooney said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale because of her public support for the organisation Palestine Action, meaning she could no longer receive royalties from UK sales.
Rooney’s publisher Faber said: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.”
"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," the British publisher said, adding that it would continue to sell her work in other countries and regions.
The UK banned Palestine Action last year, with the UK government previously warning Rooney that her support could fall foul of terrorism laws. The "terrorist" organization is not banned in Ireland, where Rooney lives.
Thousands of people have protested against the ban and been detained, while rights groups condemning the ban as criminalizing dissent. More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned in July 2025.
Palestine Action's stated goal on its website is to end "global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime."
In a statement, Rooney said: “‘In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland."
“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”
Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action, said: “Sally Rooney being unable to publish her work in the UK marks a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action … [She] took a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced. She has refused to compromise her convictions, even at considerable personal and professional cost.”
Ammori added: “Her work should be celebrated and widely available , not driven off the shelves of British bookshops because she refuses to be complicit in the suppression of solidarity with the Palestinian people. No author should have to choose between their principles and their freedom to publish.”

Sources told the paper that Eric van der Burg, the VVD junior home affairs minister, will soon present targets for cutting staff numbers, although estimates are not yet known.
Experts told the Telegraaf the rise in civil servants, which went from 140,000 in 2021 to 170,000 last year, that things are not improving. One said the government is being stifled with ever more rules and subsidies.
Policy officials in particular, who have almost doubled to 20,000 in the past decade, are putting needless pressure on the government, one analyst said.
Insiders said using AI could save an extra €200 million in both 2028 and 2029. A further €200 million has been planned for the interior ministry’s budget for the following year, rising to €1 billion a year from 2035.
Van der Burg is reported to be partly following the thinking of an advisory committee on the future of the civil service, which is due to present conclusions this year.
Ahead of a meeting with MPs, the committee said digitalisation and AI can make government more efficient, but only if the build-up of rules and checks is also tackled.
Government economist Jos Blank wrote that the state had been underperforming for decades, and that a constant stream of new rules, subsidies and mergers was making public services worse.
Former senior civil servant Roel Bekker criticised growing “policy overload” and called for the number of policy officials to be cut by 20% to 30%.

‘High likelihood of attack’: Israel set to extend home front emergency past election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:37:44 UTC
16:37:44 KST

The Israeli government is expected to approve an extension of the nationwide special home front situation until November 3, keeping the emergency declaration in effect through the October 27 Knesset election amid security assessments warning of a continued high likelihood of an attack on the civilian population.
Defense Minister Israel Katz has requested the extension, which would prolong the declaration beyond its current October 20 expiration date. Government Secretary Yossi Fuchs circulated the proposal to ministers Thursday for approval in an urgent telephone vote.
According to the explanatory document accompanying the proposal, security officials believe there is still a "high likelihood" of an attack targeting civilians, particularly because of continued uncertainty surrounding the security situation with Iran and Lebanon.
The document also states that the need for any further extension will be reviewed before the new expiration date, based on an updated security assessment.
The government's decision will require approval from the Knesset's Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee.
Katz first declared a special home front situation across Israel on February 28, 2026, when Operation Roaring Lion against Iran began. The declaration has since been extended repeatedly through government decisions, most recently on October 6, when ministers approved its continuation until October 20.
Under Israeli law, a special home front situation grants the IDF's Home Front Command additional powers to issue emergency instructions to civilians, including restrictions on educational activities and public gatherings.
However, no such restrictions are currently in effect, meaning the proposed extension would preserve the authorities' ability to impose them if the security situation deteriorates rather than immediately introducing new limitations on daily life.
The extension would also mean that the nationwide emergency declaration remains in force on election day, as Israel prepares to vote amid continued concerns about possible attacks on the civilian population.
The Defense Ministry's legal adviser, attorney Mor Yamin-Bartal, determined that there is no legal obstacle to approving the proposal.
She acknowledged that repeatedly extending an emergency declaration that has remained in force since February could raise legal difficulties, but emphasized the urgency and necessity of the measure.

UK economy grows 0.1% in August, defying contraction forecast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:34:34 UTC
16:34:34 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The UK economy grew 0.1% month-on-month in August, beating market expectations of a 0.1% contraction, according to Office for National Statistics data released Thursday.
Growth slowed from an unrevised 0.4% in July, while June's expansion was revised up to 0.4% from 0.3%.
Production output rose 0.8% in August, driving the monthly increase in gross domestic product (GDP), while services showed no growth and construction output fell 0.2%.
Manufacturing expanded 1.2%, with nine of its 13 subsectors recording growth. Pharmaceutical production rose 5.1%, providing the largest contribution to the manufacturing increase, followed by transport equipment, which grew 1.8%.
Mining and quarrying output increased 1.4%, while electricity and gas supply edged up 0.1%.
Within services, gains in wholesale and retail trade and professional, scientific and technical activities were offset by weakness elsewhere, including administrative and support services.
Consumer-facing services declined 0.3%, following a 0.1% fall in July. Sports, amusement and recreation activities dropped 7.1%, while food and beverage services fell 2.7%.
Construction output contracted for a fourth consecutive month, with new work falling 0.7%. Private housing new work declined 1.9%, contributing most to the monthly decrease.
 
3-month growth accelerates
GDP expanded 0.7% in the three months to August compared with the preceding three months, accelerating from 0.5% growth in the three months to July.
This marked the eighth consecutive increase on a rolling three-month basis.
Services grew 0.9%, providing the only positive contribution among the three main sectors. Production fell 0.2%, while construction declined 1%.
Professional, scientific and technical activities, alongside information and communication, supported services growth, with both subsectors expanding 2.8%.
The economy grew 2.1% compared with August last year. Over the three months to August, GDP was 1.8% higher than a year earlier.

Auckland FC's Sam Cosgrove clashes with reporter over A-League Men suspension loophole
In short:
Auckland FC's Sam Cosgrove has responded angrily after being asked about the club using a suspension loophole to allow him to play the A-League Men season opener.
Cosgrove served a two-game ban in New Zealand's reserves league for a red card in an August Intercontinental Cup game.
What's next?
The defending champions will begin their A-League campaign at home to Melbourne City on Saturday.
Auckland FC striker Sam Cosgrove has blown up over questions about using a "loophole" to serve out a suspension before the A-League Men season.
Cosgrove was handed a two-game ban after being sent off in the closing stages of Auckland's 1-0 FIFA Intercontinental Cup loss to Saudi side Al-Ahli in August.
Auckland are allowed to play A-League professionals in their reserves side under New Zealand Football's participation agreement and competition regulations.
That includes up to two 23-year-old non-citizens for each match-day squad.
The clause opened the door for the 29-year-old Englishman to serve out his ban in Auckland's recent New Zealand National League fixtures against Wellington Olympic and Miramar Rangers.
In a fiery exchange on Thursday, Cosgrove could not recall the two matches and was bemused when asked if he had any unease or embarrassment over using the "loophole".
"Embarrassment?" he shot back at a reporter.
"Why would the club not push to have a player available and use every power that they have?"
Cosgrove bagged 11 goals in his debut season with Auckland, securing the men's competition golden boot along the way to the club's first championship.
"It doesn't matter, does it? I have technically [served my ban]. I've missed two NPL matches," Cosgrove said.
"If you pick up a suspension in the A-League, you have to serve it in the A-League.
"So technically, in that case, I should be missing the next few Intercontinental Cups, but I'm not."
The media conference ended abruptly before the reporter repeated his claim that Cosgrove had not actually served the ban.
"What are you doing here then? Bugger off, if you're going to talk shit," the striker replied.
An Auckland FC minder stated that FIFA, Football Australia and Football New Zealand were "fine" with the way the ban was served.
"You know what football's like in this country, mate? We f***ing work hard to get it good. You bring it down with shit like that," Cosgrove said, prompting a chuckle from the reporter.
"What are you laughing for? We'll just f*** you off. You won't get back here again."
In a podcast episode posted on Tuesday, Cosgrove said he was relieved when news of the rule's workaround became public so he could "finally stop lying about it".
"It was a poor challenge in oppressive heat and late in the game, but the two-game suspension was a little bit harsh," he told The Unused Subs podcast.
"We were trying to get that reduced, and the power of lawyers and legal teams these days, they managed to find a way to sign me up with the Auckland reserves."
The defending champions will begin their A-League campaign at home to Melbourne City on Saturday, before an away trip to face Western Sydney Wanderers on October 24.

Ministry of Culture drops plan to slash county library funding
Minister of Culture Heidy Purga told Kuku Radio that a previously planned cut in state funding for public libraries next year has now been scrapped.

Last week, Ministry of Culture library adviser Ülle Talihärm told ERR that €1.77 million had been earmarked for public library acquisitions in 2027, compared with €1.87 million last year. "The decrease is linked to the 10 percent budget cut spread across multiple years in the state budget," Talihärm said.

The Finnish Interior Ministry will distribute around 3.5 million printed emergency preparedness guides to households and businesses across the country, broadcaster Yle reported Thursday.
The guide is expected to outline how people should prepare for disruptions and crisis situations, while also addressing the current threat posed by drones.

Photos: Ülle Madise meets Alexander Stubb in Helsinki on 2nd foreign trip

Unknown Publisher

Photos: Ülle Madise meets Alexander Stubb in Helsinki on 2nd foreign trip
Newly inaugurated Estonian President Ülle Madise met Finnish President Alexander Stubb in Helsinki on Wednesday to discuss European security and Nordic-Baltic cooperation.
This was Madise's second official foreign trip since being sworn in at the start of the week.
She said a stronger Europe strengthens NATO, and welcomed Finland's move to halt issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens.
"Finland is Estonia's close friend and a reliable ally. Our security depends on allies we can trust, and on being worthy of their trust ourselves," Madise said. She noted there is something in the bond between Estonia and Finland that both peoples understand the same way, given their two languages are closely related.
"We know what that word means. It is a wonderful word in both Finnish and Estonian," she said.
On European security, Madise stressed that a stronger Europe strengthens NATO.
"Europe must take greater responsibility for its own defense and turn investments into means of defending people. This also helps keep the United States engaged. A strong political will and readiness to respond to hybrid threats are also needed," Madise said.
She welcomed Finland's initiative to stop issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens entirely, and stressed the need to prevent Russian fighters from entering the Schengen area.
She agreed with Stubb that international law primarily protects small and medium-sized countries. "A rules- and obligations-based international order is ultimately beneficial to most countries and to every person," she went on.
Madise reiterated that Estonia stands firmly with Ukraine. "Ukrainians have the right to live freely in their own country, and that right is defended by the UN Charter and the Helsinki Final Act. We do not recognize borders changed by force. A just and lasting peace must allow people to rebuild their lives without fear of losing their homes again."
The Estonian president stressed that it is Ukraine that gets to decide its own future, and that Europe must be at the table when its security is at stake. She also reaffirmed Estonia's support for Ukraine's progress towards the EU and an open path to NATO membership.
Madise's first official foreign visit as head of state took place on Tuesday, when she met Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs in Riga.

Switzerland’s open AI model could help guard the web – or empower its attackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:32:03 UTC
16:32:03 KST

Switzerland’s open AI model could help guard the web – or empower its attackers
As AI agents launch faster and more autonomous cyberattacks, defenders increasingly need equally powerful AI systems to keep up. Open models like Switzerland’s Apertus could level the playing field – but their capabilities can end up in the hands of anyone, even criminals.
The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) models – software programs capable of acting autonomously to achieve a goal – has disrupted the traditional balance between attack and defence in cyberspace.
OpenAI’s agents, developed by the company behind ChatGPT, have demonstrated this in recent weeks by hacking dozensExternal link of corporate and government websites around the world. Among the targets were Hugging Face, the platform that hosts millions of open AI models (including Switzerland’s Apertus) and Australia’s healthcare system. These agents displayed what OpenAI itself described as behaviour “misaligned” with developers’ instructions.
For humans, responding to attacks at the speed of AI is virtually impossible. “The most advanced AI systems can perform thousands of actions per minute,” says Andrei Kucharavy, a professor at the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Western Switzerland and security lead for Apertus, Switzerland’s fully open AI model.
The OpenAI hacking incidents were stopped before they led to serious consequences. But Maxime Stauffer, director of the Geneva-based Simon Institute for Longterm Governance, expects such episodes to become more frequent and harder to manage. “Swarms of AI agents could target critical infrastructure such as schools, hospitals and energy systems, or even entire countries, intentionally or accidentally,” he says. Stauffer also points to the risk of AI being used to develop biological weapons, a concern highlighted by recent attemptsExternal link blocked by US company Anthropic.
Defenders may not have access to equally powerful tools. Systems with the most advanced cyber capabilities, such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, are available only to a select few. Open models could help rebalance this asymmetry, according to Kucharavy.
Apertus, for instance, can identify vulnerabilities, suggest patches and analyse attack logs to reconstruct an incident, although it was not designed for cybersecurity and still has considerable limitations, Kucharavy says. Some experts fear that the same defensive capabilities in widely accessible open models could also be used maliciously on a much larger scale.
>> Read more about the development, and limits, of Switzerland’s AI model Apertus:
More
One year on, has Swiss AI model Apertus lived up to the hype?
If AI agents attacked a hospital
The Hugging Face case is emblematic. When several OpenAI agents penetrated its systems, the platform tried to use some of the world’s most powerful AI models to understand what was happening – without success.
“The frontier models [the most advanced AI models] automatically blocked all of our requests for security reasons. And so we had to fall back to deploying open-source models to understand what was happening,” Lewis Tunstall, an engineer at Hugging Face, told Swissinfo.
AI models can be developed and released with different levels of openness:
Open source: The model’s trained parameters, or “weights”, training code and information about the training data are publicly available, allowing others to inspect, modify and reproduce it. Examples include Apertus and OLMo.
Open weight: The model’s weights are publicly released and can be downloaded and adapted, but the full training code and datasets are not necessarily disclosed. Examples include Meta’s Llama and Alibaba’s Qwen.
Closed/proprietary: The model’s weights, training code and datasets are not publicly released. This is the case for most commercial models, including OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude.
Tunstall says the OpenAI agents behaved unusually compared with a typical hacker. They were not trying to take control of the infrastructure, but rather to find datasets containing answers to the security tests on which they were being evaluated.
“It was a little bit like a student who really, really wants to get a good score on their exam and, instead of studying, thinks: maybe I can just hack into the teacher’s laptop and get the answers,” Tunstall explains.
OpenAI later confirmed that the agents had escaped the protected environment the company had created for the test. But what would have happened if they had attacked a hospital instead?
“It would have been truly disastrous,” says Tunstall. The agents could potentially have gained access to large amounts of personal and sensitive data. This is also why, according to Tunstall, open AI models can be particularly useful: data does not need to be sent to companies such as OpenAI or Anthropic because the models can be adapted or controlled locally.
“None of your sensitive data leaves your infrastructure. It just stays totally in-house.”
For similar reasons, key sectors in Switzerland such as finance are also increasingly interested in open models, says Nino Antulov-Fantulin, a lecturer at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology ETH Zurich and an expert in machine learning for finance.
“Financial institutions are afraid of just using closed models and sending sensitive information to servers that are far away from Switzerland or to external providers. They want to control where the model is hosted,” says Fantulin.
Open models are getting more powerful – and cannot be recalled
The problem, however, is that open models can also be used for malicious purposes.
This is one of Stauffer’s biggest concerns. In his view, the development of open-source models is largely beneficial for now, but in future, risks could outweigh benefits, especially if AI companies further restrict access to their frontier systems. Open models fill the gap but their large-scale spread and the possibility of removing their safeguards may increase the likelihood of malicious use.
“If you have an extremely powerful capability, but no one has access to it and it remains under control, then the risk is almost zero. But if everyone has access to it, then the risk is likely higher,” says Stauffer.
As open models grow more capable, Stauffer believes it may become important to have a way of withdrawing them if they prove too powerful or dangerous, something that isn’t currently possible.
Some research points to similar concerns. A studyExternal link led by researchers at Stanford and Princeton universities similarly identified broad accessibility, modifiability and the inability for the original developers to recall weights – the numerical parameters learned by the model during training – or monitor their use as features that can increase both the benefits and risks of open models.
And a recent paperExternal link by the UK AI Security Institute found that open models modified to remove safeguards provided substantially more helpful for criminal activity than models with safeguards in place. Neither study, however, concludes that open AI models are inherently more dangerous.
‘Control and legislation’ are needed
Kucharavy acknowledges that open models carry risks and can be abused. “AI models are dual-use technologies. They can be used to do good as well as to do harm,” he says. But he believes their risks are far more controllable precisely because of their openness.
It is no coincidence, Kucharavy argues, that the recent incidents involved closed labs. “The main problem is the lack of supervision of the frontier labs,” he says, calling for greater oversight and transparency for all AI development centres, whether public or private, open or closed.
“What we really need is control and legislation governing what all AI developers are doing.”
The lack of oversight and rules highlights another major issue in the industry: the concentration of power in the hands of a small number of actors, mainly based in Silicon Valley. For digital ethics expert Nathalie Klauser, this imbalance of power is an even greater concern than whether AI models are open or closed.
“A handful of large technology companies set the rules for AI themselves, with almost no external accountability,” says Klauser, who argues that international regulation is needed.
Attempts in this direction, however, remain fragmented and slow. In the US, one of the leading powers in AI development, President Donald Trump has opposed broad AI regulation and praisedExternal link industry “self-policing”. Switzerland has adopted a somewhat similar approach, abandoning the idea of comprehensive AI legislation in favour of sector-specific legal changes and non-binding measures.
In the current geopolitical context, Switzerland – as a neutral country, a European hub for Big Tech and a country known for its good offices – has a growing political responsibility to help broker an international agreement on AI, Klauser argues.
Lawmakers from all six Swiss parliamentary groups see the upcoming Geneva AI Summit in June 2027 as a major opportunity for the country to do so. They have urgedExternal link the government to leverage the event to push for minimum international standards on extreme AI risks.

Vase by Picasso’s daughter turns up at Flemish charity shop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:31:30 UTC
16:31:30 KST

A vase by Picasso’s daughter, Paloma Picasso, has been discovered at the charity shop in Bornem (Antwerp Province). The vintage vase dates from the 1990s and was used at the time to promote Paloma’s perfume. It is not clear how much it is worth. The vase will be auctioned via the charity shop’s website.
Christina, a member of staff at the Bornem charity shop, discovered the vase amongst the items that had been donated. “At first she thought it was a tourist trinket of little value, but when she took a closer look at the vase, she realised it was a vintage vase belonging to Pablo Picasso’s daughter, Paloma,” says Ann Doran of the social enterprise, which runs the charity shop in Bornem.
Paloma’s perfume
It is a vintage Greek vase featuring an image of the Minotaur – a monster, half-man, half-bull, from Greek mythology. “A matt ceramic vase that was used in the 1990s as promotional material for the launch of Paloma’s perfume, called ‘Minotaure’.”
The charity shop does not know how many were produced. “It is certainly a limited edition, even though they are copies of an original piece. It is a unique vintage find.”
Authentic piece
How does the charity shop know that a piece is authentic? “Our staff are trained by experts,” says Doran. “We work with art historian and auction expert Marcel Brouwer. Thanks to his tips and tricks, we’re able to recognise special pieces.”
“We’ve already sent Brouwer some photos; he’s certain it’s an authentic Paloma vase, but he’s coming here in a week’s time to examine it in person,” says Doran.
In the meantime, the vase has been set aside. The charity shop cannot estimate how much it is worth. It will be auctioned via the charity shop’s website.
It is also not known who brought the vase in, but it is not as though that person can now come and reclaim it. “What’s done is done,” says Doran with a laugh. She hopes the vase will fetch a tidy sum.

Switzerland’s top trade official says gifts to Trump ‘were for the American people’
The gifts presented in November 2025 by Swiss businessmen to US President Donald Trump were not intended personally for the then 79-year-old, but for the American people.
This was stated by Helene Budliger Artieda, Director of the Swiss Secretariat for Economics Affairs (SECO), who clarified that this was a private-sector initiative.
“The gifts are duly registered at the White House and, if all goes well, will end up in a presidential library,” the outgoing State Secretary (who has tendered her resignation, effective at the end of March 2027) said today in an interview with Bloomberg TV on the sidelines of an economic forum in New Delhi.
In the midst of the tariff dispute, a delegation of Swiss business leaders had travelled to the US to negotiate with the president over tariffs. During the meeting, Trump was presented with a Rolex table clock and an engraved gold ingot, with a combined value of around CHF100,000 ($120,580).
According to Budliger Artieda, these were “serious businesspeople” who had certainly carried out legal checks beforehand. “I am convinced that everything was done in accordance with the law,” she said. The delegation included, among others, Partners Group co-founder Alfred Gantner, Rolex CEO Jean-Frédéric Dufour and Richemont chairman Johann Rupert.
More
Is offering a Rolex to a foreign official considered bribery under Swiss law?
Meanwhile, the visit in question continues to spark debate in Switzerland. The House of Representatives Control Committee has announced that it intends to examine the federal authorities’ handling of US tariffs. A report on the topic is expected to be finalised by the end of the year.
Meanwhile, Budliger Artieda has expressed satisfaction with the current state of play in the negotiations on trade barriers between Switzerland and the United States. Since November 2025, when the two countries were able to announce a reduction in US tariffs from 39% to 15%, the US has complied with the agreement.
Ultimately, Bern is seeking above all certainty and “calmer waters” in trade relations, following the turbulent period that ensued after Trump’s announcement of customs tariffs on so-called “Liberation Day” in April 2025. “Otherwise, it is very difficult for Swiss exporters,” the former ambassador observed. Talks on a legally binding agreement are, however, still ongoing, she concluded.

Since Trump returned to power, Washington’s support for Ukraine has fluctuated alongside his unexpected social media remarks, which have often taken Moscow and Kiev by surprise.
Trump last week unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” that was never publicly confirmed, and Moscow continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
But after a wave of renewed Russian strikes on facilities on Oct. 14, Zelensky told the FT: “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done.”

Since Russia launched its invasion in 2022, Ukraine has faced repeated strikes on its power infrastructure and gradually expanded what it says are retaliatory strikes into Russian territory, including on refineries.
Trump criticized the attacks, especially after he struck a surprise diesel deal with Moscow and ordered Ukraine to stop targeting Russian refineries.
Zelensky said Ukraine paused the strikes for several days, despite Russian claims, denied by Kiev, that Ukraine attempted to target refineries during that period.
Despite complying, Zelensky said Ukraine saw its access to key U.S. military capabilities and intelligence restricted.
Starshield, the satellite network built on Starlink and used by militaries, was slowed over on Oct. 14.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” Zelensky told the FT.
He also warned of a “dangerous” cutting off of intelligence sharing with Kiev, which relies heavily on early warnings to protect its cities from Russian air attacks.
Fears that Washington could curb intelligence cooperation had already surfaced after a public clash between Trump and Zelensky early in Trump’s presidency.
The Ukrainian presidency has since worked to smooth relations with Washington, trying to adapt to Trump’s fluctuating stances.
In the interview, Zelensky made a pointed comment about the relationship between Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelensky also urged the United States not to stand with the aggressor on Oct. 15, calling for “honesty.”

Catching Fog: How Architecture Collects Water from the Air
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Where rivers, reservoirs, and rainfall can no longer be relied upon consistently, water is increasingly being sought in the atmosphere. Fog, atmospheric humidity, and condensation each offer different ways of collecting it. When architecture begins to collect water from the air, surfaces, structures, and open spaces become part of the water system.
According to UNICEF, Jordan's National Water Strategy estimates that each person has access to only about 61 cubic meters of renewable water per year, far below the 500 cubic meters commonly used as a threshold for absolute water scarcity. Around half of the population receives piped water only once a week, while groundwater is being extracted faster than many aquifers can naturally recharge.
Atmospheric water harvesting encompasses several different technologies. Fog consists of suspended droplets that can be intercepted by mesh; dew forms when a surface cools below the dew point; and humidity can be extracted through sorption or condensation processes. Each requires different climatic conditions and produces different quantities of water. A critical review of atmospheric water harvesting for building façades identifies these as distinct approaches and finds that their integration into architecture remains constrained by technology readiness and manufacturing costs.
Related Article
Warka Water and Arturo Vittori Create Integrated Village for the Rainforest Community in Cameroon
Columbia GSAPP's Water Urbanism: Amman explored these possibilities in Jordan. Developed around Jordan's water crisis and refugee conditions, the studio proposed interventions that combined water collection with shade, sanitation, gathering, and productive landscapes. At the Al-Hadalat site, shelter clusters of refugees were proposed around fog towers capable of collecting an estimated 800 to 2,000 liters of water per day, alongside smaller shaded fog structures projected to collect around 500 liters. These figures are design projections rather than measured operational results.
Built from palm wood and mesh knitted from discarded ration sacks, the structure would intercept fog while using its exposure to moving air to provide shade and a place for congregation. Water would travel through the structure into underground storage before being distributed to showers, sanitation, and productive landscapes. Wastewater would move through constructed wetlands and return to the agricultural system.
Reservoirs, treatment plants and distribution networks operate largely outside the architectural experience of the city. Fog harvesting requires infrastructure to remain uncovered to the atmosphere. The collector must occupy space, remain exposed and respond directly to atmospheric conditions. Designing the collector as shade, shelter, or public space gives it another use.
Any such system still has to contend with the unpredictability of the atmosphere. Morocco provides an example where fog harvesting has moved beyond the speculative drawing into an operational water system. At Sidi Ifni, on the Atlantic coast, fog is collected at Boutmezguida mountain, approximately 35 meters inland from the coast, and channelled into a wider system serving local communities. A 2024 assessment of the project describes it as the world's largest fog-collection project and evaluates its water output, water quality and community participation.
The project's output varies substantially across the year. Over four years, annual average collection ranged between 1.6 and 6 liters per square metre per day. During the fog season, March and April produced an average of 8.5 liters per square metre per day, while the highest monthly figure recorded was 21 liters per square meter per day in April 2021. Fog occurred throughout the year, but its frequency varied, making storage and supplementary supply important to the system.
Collection is only one component of the system. Water has to be captured, stored, treated, and distributed. The community also has to participate in maintaining and using the infrastructure. The researchers identify fog-yield variability and groundwater pollution among the project's principal challenges, warning that relying on fog as the sole source could result in inconsistent water availability.
Research into atmospheric water harvesting on building façades suggests that the envelope could become an active collection surface. Orientation, surface area, material properties and exposure to air all become environmental design variables. Sorption-based systems, in particular, have been identified as promising for integration into building envelopes, although current research still identifies low technology-readiness and manufacturing costs as significant barriers.
A water-harvesting façade would sit between interior and exterior while also responding to air movement and collecting water from the surrounding atmosphere. Roofs could become condensation surfaces. Screens could become fog collectors. Courtyards could incorporate collection and storage. Structures could also provide shade where their collection systems need to remain exposed.
Architecture cannot design the atmosphere itself. It can orient a collector toward prevailing fog, increase its surface area, provide storage and reduce dependence on distant infrastructure. It cannot guarantee that fog will arrive. In practice, atmospheric water would need to operate alongside storage, treatment and conventional supply systems.
At Al-Hadalat, the fog tower combines collection with shade and gathering space. At Sidi Ifni, collection forms part of a larger system of storage, treatment and distribution. At the building scale, façades can collect water while continuing to control heat, light and air.
Architecture has always responded to the atmosphere: keeping rain out, tempering heat, admitting daylight and directing air. Atmospheric water harvesting adds another task: collecting water from the same atmospheric conditions buildings already respond to. Atmospheric water harvesting works as part of a wider water network. It adds another source to that network, one whose performance depends on climate, exposure, storage, and maintenance.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. Kallas: Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries constitute self-defence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:29:20 UTC
16:29:20 KST

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries are legitimate, as Kyiv vows to resume them despite Trump’s energy ceasefire.
The EU's High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, has defended Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries as a legitimate means of ending Russia’s war of aggression, saying the quickest way to stop them is to end the war.
“If we look at international law, it is clear that [hitting refineries] is in defence of Ukraine because that is where the funding comes from for this war to kill Ukrainian people every day,” she told Euronews in an exclusive interview.
The remarks come after US President Donald Trump announced a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel amid a global energy crunch, followed by an “energy ceasefire” under which Russia and Ukraine would stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure.
“If we look at the big picture, the majority of the financing for this war comes from oil. And that is why Ukraine is also targeting them [the refineries], while Russia is targeting the energy infrastructure inside Ukraine, to cause as much suffering for the Ukrainian people in the upcoming winter,” she said.
Kallas stressed, however, that the war has a clear aggressor and a victim, and that the US should join Europeans in pressuring Russia rather than Ukraine, since the EU will continue to support Kyiv, which has not surrendered.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, accusing Washington of suspending intelligence-sharing and disrupting Starlink satellite internet services amid intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine.
"The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done," Zelenskyy told the Financial Times in an interview published just hours before the EU summit.
Ukraine has significantly intensified its campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, striking 12 major refineries in September alone, according to Ukraine's Defence Ministry.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), only five of Russia's 32 major refineries had escaped Ukrainian drone attacks by late August, with some facilities struck as many as 15 times since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine had halted strikes on Russian energy facilities for three days at Washington's request, while Moscow continued attacking Ukrainian infrastructure and killing civilians.
According to Zelenskyy, US officials also warned their Ukrainian counterparts that intelligence-sharing would be suspended unless Kyiv stopped its strikes, although the subsequent disruption was presented as a technical problem.
He also rejected suggestions that interruptions to Starlink services were accidental.
"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelenskyy said.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, responded with thinly veiled sarcasm, effectively suggesting that no energy ceasefire was yet in place.
"What was announced? What are the boundaries of the energy ceasefire? What does it mean? Was any of this specified?" Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov asked on Wednesday.
"That is why work in this direction is continuing," he added.

Russia-US diesel deal could set precedent for suspension or removal of sanctions

MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. The Russian-American agreement on diesel fuel supplies could become a promising precedent for how sanctions might be lifted or suspended, provided the United States is economically and politically interested in it, Russian presidential commissioner for the protection of entrepreneurs' rights, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP) Alexander Shokhin told TASS.
"There was an old Soviet-era ditty, which said: ‘A friend and I worked together on a diesel engine’, and I wouldn't want our Russian-American deal to end the same way that that ditty does. However, I think that this is a very promising story because it turns out that when there appears a genuine economic or political interest, including domestic political interest, in the case of the American side, sanctions can be lifted or suspended. This is a good example for a country like Germany, where we see that Alternative for Germany is gaining votes not merely because of its opposition to excessively lenient migration policy, but tariffs are rising, prices are climbing, the industrial sector is faltering, and some industries have shut down entirely," Shokhin said in his first interview after being appointed business ombudsman.
In European Union countries, the automotive industry is currently surviving only because they're now producing weapons, he noted.
"Therefore, they are probably behaving so aggressively toward Russia in the case of Ukraine as well. And, fundamentally, one can only hope that [US President Donald] Trump manages to retain at least the Senate, perhaps by ensuring that diesel prices in the United States do not rise," Shokhin said, adding that logistics and transport flows are road-based in the US, and large trucks require diesel fuel.
"Therefore, it’s not a bad example, and the pragmatism of Trump and the American administration could prove contagious here," he concluded.

Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:25:18 UTC
16:25:18 KST

Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, ending a three-day pause it held at Washington’s request, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times in an interview published on 15 October. Russia kept bombing Ukraine’s energy system throughout the pause, while Kyiv lost US missile warnings and its Starlink service slowed. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would halt energy strikes again only in exchange for more US air defense.
Ukraine's deep-strike campaign targets the Russian oil industry, which fuels Russia's army in Ukraine and earns the export revenue funding the war. Striking the plants that turn Russian crude into fuel, 12 of them hit in September alone, is one of the few levers Kyiv controls on Moscow’s war income. US President Donald Trump has blamed those strikes for higher US fuel prices, which most analysts attribute to the Iran war, and Washington has threatened to withhold intelligence, and reportedly weapons, unless Kyiv gives it up. Each step Washington takes toward Moscow, from fuel waivers to talk of frozen assets, widens the gap Europe and Ukraine must fill, while Russia gains revenue and time to keep striking.
A pause that bought nothing
Zelenskyy said he stopped the refinery strikes for three days to meet US wishes, but Russia kept hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and killing civilians. During the pause, Ukraine received no US warnings of ballistic missile launches, he said. Starlink also slowed across the country, hampering front-line operations and mid-range strikes on Russian military targets, he added.
Russia used those days to fire 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukraine’s grid overnight into 14 October, leaving at least 600,000 people without power. “We hold energy ceasefire from our side,” Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan on 14 October. Of the Starlink slowdown, he added: “I’m sure that they knew what they did.”
The price of another pause
Ukraine could again stop hitting Russian energy only if it receives more US interceptors for its Patriot systems, Zelenskyy told the FT. He warned that a halt could simply invite more US-Russia deals that feed Russia’s war machine, and predicted the next one would involve gas.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government”: Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, is behind cut hitting Ukraine
US intelligence officials had warned Ukraine’s embassy in Washington that a new strike on Russia’s energy facilities would end all intelligence sharing at once, The Washington Post reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. Washington has not fully cut it off, but the threat stands, the person said. Trump said on 13 October that the US was still sharing intelligence.
Washington’s other moves toward Moscow
A senior US official told Axios the administration had nothing to do with the Starlink limits, which Elon Musk had blamed on the US military. The administration is also considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers, which have carried oil from Russia, Iran, and Venezuela, so the blacklisted vessels could haul non-sanctioned cargo, a US official told Reuters. The US Energy Department said the move would not help Russia ship its oil or fuel.
Washington eased sanctions on Russian oil this spring, after which Russia’s oil income jumped $890 million in a week, and it extended that waiver despite telling allies it would not. US envoys also proposed unfreezing part of Russia’s frozen assets to lure Moscow back to talks, an idea European officials rejected, the Financial Times reported.

Anika Wells opens door to lawsuits against big tech companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:23:50 UTC
16:23:50 KST

Anika Wells opens door to Australians suing big tech under new online safety laws
In short:
Labor is weighing up stronger legal avenues for people harmed by online platforms as it tries to secure parliamentary support for its digital safety laws.
Despite concessions aimed at addressing concerns about censorship and press freedom, the Coalition remains firmly opposed.
What's next?
A Senate inquiry will scrutinise the legislation as the Greens push for tougher penalties and greater powers for individuals to sue tech companies.
Labor is open to giving Australians the right to sue tech companies for online harms under new digital safety laws and has questioned why the Coalition would "deal themselves out" of talks.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said the federal government would contemplate a Greens proposal to give individuals the right to take legal action against the platforms as she pushed back on claims the digital duty of care could be misused for political censorship.
Labor has scrapped proposed controversial ministerial powers to designate additional harms and bolstered protections for journalistic content, but the Coalition remains opposed to the bill.
The government has added three harm categories, including the creation of fake nude material, to the proposal, which has been sent to a Senate inquiry due to report back before parliament rises at the end of November.
In an address to the National Press Club today, Ms Wells said the duty was "not a stepping stone for regulating misinformation and disinformation".
"If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the Moon landing was fake, they can continue to do so without restriction," she said.
Earlier, Ms Wells introduced the legislation to parliament that would require online services to take reasonable steps to protect underage users from harmful content and features, while platforms would have to limit adults' exposure to "serious harms".
The bill would also pave the way for regulation to give Australians over the age of 16 the option to turn off algorithmic recommendations on their social media feeds.
Coalition calls bill a 'dog's breakfast'
Ms Wells said she was "confident" Labor could get the bill through the Senate, describing the Coalition's hostility to the proposal as "puzzling" given its past support of online safety measures.
"It's on them to explain why they would want to deal themselves out of a law that is either the next logical step in a proud bipartisan history of online safety or, if this is so reprehensible, but they know that the Greens are supportive of the principles [and] want to see it amended, why they would deal themselves out of anything that might improve the bill," she said.
Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson said the bill was a "dog's breakfast" and took issue with what she described as "vague" definitions of harms.
"We think this is a dangerous step in the wrong direction and this bill cannot be supported," she said.
The Coalition has repeatedly warned the bill would limit free speech and enable government control of what people could see and say online.
But one of Senator Henderson's complaints about the latest draft was the broad exemption for material in the "public interest" to be published.
"What does material in the public interest mean?" she said.
Wells dismisses 'sock puppet' criticism
The bill would allow the eSafety Commissioner and accredited researchers to set up fake "sock puppet" accounts to observe and test whether online platforms were complying with their duties.
The regulator would be required to develop policies in consultation with the Australian Federal Police and report annually on their use, while university researchers would have to obtain ethics approval.
But the Senator Henderson suggested the fake accounts would be allowed to "crawl" the internet and gain unchecked access to real users.
Ms Wells said there was "absolutely nothing of the sort" permitted in the bill.
"I don't know how to be more emphatic," she said.
"It doesn't exist. It is not possible."
Ms Wells said it was not "tenable" to argue the independent regulator would be "trying to spread government propaganda" rather than shut down pro-terror or eating disorder content going to young Australians.
Greens seek tougher penalties, right to sue
Ms Wells signalled that Labor would consider a proposal put forward by the Greens that would allow private citizens to sue tech companies, including, potentially, through class action lawsuits.
"I think it's fair to say that our eSafety Commissioner does a marvellous join at enforcement and compliance, but it's a huge burden, and private right of action allows people to share that burden," she said.
With eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant due to finish her second term this year, Ms Wells left the door open to restructuring the independent agency to spread the workload among multiple commissioners.
"It's certainly one solution I am considering at the moment, given the resourcing required for the digital duty of care and the value that … is rising sharply in complaints and people seeking recourse," she said.
Greens Communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said she still wanted the bill strengthened to put "the fear of god" into big tech companies and demanded penalties be tied to social media platforms' global revenue.
"We are sick and tired, as Australians and as consumers, of big tech running our lives," she said.
"We're sick and tired of having material shoved into our children's feeds that is dangerous and harmful."
Small businesses face 'minimal' impact
Under the digital duty of care all online platforms and websites would be required to undertake an annual risk assessment, including small businesses.
Small Business Minister Anne Aly said there would be further regulatory guidance provided to those impacted by the duty, noting the average business website did not carry many safety risks.
"Providers of low-risk services, like websites and applications run by small businesses, will have minimal obligations," she said.
Teach Us Consent founder and chief executive Chanel Contos said she welcomed the duty and its provisions that would allow Australians to switch off their algorithmically recommended content.
"Opt-in doesn't ban algorithms — it makes them optional," she said.
"Nothing about this stops people, organisations or businesses reaching audiences through algorithmic feeds. It just means people get to choose that feed, rather than have it forced on them."
Minderoo Foundation chief executive John Hartman also welcomed the bill and its expanded definition of seriously harmful conduct, which now included protections against image-based sexual abuse, explicit threats of physical violence and material that promoted gender-based violence.
"The bill is also a much-needed step when it comes to protecting women and children, who experience disproportionate harms in the online world," he said.
"That harm includes violence, misogyny and inappropriate material on social media and dating apps."

====================================================================================================

Across China: When yak milk meets coffee on China's Tibetan plateau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:23:33 CST
16:23:33 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Gonbu never developed a taste for coffee, and that remains true to this day.
But that hasn't stopped the 30-year-old Tibetan from opening a restaurant that serves coffee with a local twist: yak milk, highland barley and butter.
Growing up on the grasslands of southwest China's Sichuan Province, Gonbu spent his childhood days riding horses and herding yaks. He had never even heard of coffee.
Today, he is bringing the flavors of his childhood to visitors in the ancient town of Songpan, hoping to ignite interest in the nomadic culture behind them.
Gonbu runs a Tibetan restaurant in the town, which has a history spanning over 1,000 years. Located in Songpan County, where the average elevation exceeds 3,000 meters, the town was once a trading hub between southwestern and northwestern China. There, traders exchanged horses, medicinal herbs, and animal hides for tea and grain.
Born in Caoyuan Village in Songpan's Maoergai Township, he later studied Tibetan-Chinese translation at Northwest Minzu University in Lanzhou, where he tried coffee for the first time.
He was drawn to the atmosphere of coffee shops -- "somewhere you can read a book or just sit for a while," as he put it.
He found similar places in other cities and wondered why the grasslands couldn't have one, too.
In 2019, Gonbu returned to Maoergai and opened a small reading lounge serving coffee. "Young people on the grasslands also need somewhere to relax and learn about the outside world," he said.
Over the next five years, he traveled to learn coffee-making and Tibetan cooking while studying how restaurants operated in cities.
He kept thinking about Songpan's ancient town. The county is a gateway to the UNESCO World Heritage sites of Jiuzhai Valley and Huanglong, and the town now has more than 10 businesses established by returning college graduates.
In late 2024, Gonbu opened the restaurant, hoping to offer visitors a fresh perspective on Tibetan cuisine and nomadic life.
Inside, sheepskins are draped over the chairs, and ingredients are sourced from the plateau whenever possible. Traditional Tibetan dishes share the menu with coffee made from barley, yak milk, butter and yak yogurt.
By day, customers eat, drink coffee and read. In the evening, traditional ethnic music alternates with modern folk songs.
Gonbu wants the restaurant to offer more than just food and entertainment. He teaches his staff to make coffee and has filled the restaurant with books.
Of his 18 employees, 12 come from Maoergai. Their average age is just 22 to 23.
One is 18-year-old Tsering Drolkar. Had she not come to the ancient town, she said, she would probably be herding yaks at home. Collecting medicinal herbs can sometimes bring in good money.
"I just want to go out and see more of the world," she said. Since arriving, she has learned to make coffee, played the guitar for the first time and encountered unfamiliar foods.
At 11, she traveled beyond the grasslands for the first time, visiting her father's hometown of Mianyang in Sichuan. Before the trip, she had heard stories of watermelons, bananas and other fruits rarely seen back home.
Today, leaving the remote highlands is easier. Nine decades ago, crossing them was a struggle for survival.
In 1935, the Communist Party of China-led Red Army entered northwest Sichuan during the Long March, a roughly 12,500-kilometer military odyssey from 1934 to 1936. The soldiers crossed the marshy grasslands of what are now Songpan, Hongyuan, Ruoergai and surrounding areas.
In his book "The Long March: The Untold Story," American journalist and author Harrison Salisbury described the area as "untouched for 3,000 years." With its swamps, extreme cold and low oxygen levels, the treacherous terrain claimed the lives of many soldiers.
This year marks the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victory. Gonbu's grandparents lived through that era and passed down stories of the Red Army.
"With transportation being so convenient today, it's really hard to imagine what they went through back then," he said.
On Aug. 30, 2024, a new section of the Sichuan-Qinghai railway opened, bringing bullet train services to Songpan. From Huanglong-Jiuzhai station, a short drive from the ancient town, the fastest trains reach Chengdu in about one hour and 40 minutes.
Near the station stands a memorial park commemorating the Long March. A statue depicts a Red Army soldier raising a rifle and flowers. Nearby, modern trains speed past.
The grasslands are now drawing more visitors. Songpan County received 10.64 million tourist visits in 2025, up 15.53 percent year on year, with total tourism spending reaching 31.81 billion yuan (about 4.73 billion U.S. dollars).
Visitors now come for more than scenery. They ride horses, hike, watch the stars or stop for coffee in the ancient town. The shift toward experiencing local life reflects the growing popularity of immersive tourism in China.
The outline of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), released in March, calls for closer integration of culture and tourism and a wider range of high-quality tourism offerings.
For Gonbu, a cup of yak milk coffee is only a starting point. If customers wonder where the milk comes from, he hopes to take them to Maoergai to see the yaks, pastures and people who produce it.
He plans to build a ranch there with a reading lounge, bringing together food, tourism and herding life.
"Tradition and modernity, the countryside and the city -- they can all come together in a place like this," he said. ■
