Wallace & Gromit maker Aardman falls short of return to profit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

Don’t break out the celebratory Wensleydale just yet. Aardman, the British animation studio behind the cheese-loving inventor Wallace and his beloved dog Gromit, has fallen short of a target to get back in the black, its accounts show.
The employee-owned business was aiming to record a small profit in 2025 after two years of consecutive losses but was hit by production delays and a “challenging market” in children’s content.
So although its revenues jumped 8% to £20.4m last year, it was in the red to the tune of £1.1m, albeit an improvement on the previous year’s £4.1m loss.
Aardman, which also produces the popular Shaun the Sheep series, said the timing of some “significant” deals and weaker income in some parts of the business had hurt its bottom line.
It will be hoping for a boost from new projects, such as a recently opened exhibition at Lightroom in London that explores its 54-year history, as well as a third Shaun the Sheep film, which was released last month.
And the famously silent Gromit will soon be getting a voice, with this month’s audiobook of his autobiography read by the actor Martin Freeman.
In 2024 the studio launched a five-year business plan, which involved more investment in its intellectual property and cutting back costs.
Since then it has enjoyed the success of Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl, which broke viewing records over Christmas in 2024 as the most watched animated film broadcast on British television since 2002.
The film won two Baftas and received an Oscar nomination for best animated feature film.
Aardman said in its annual accounts that it had undertaken a further strategic review in early 2026 as it looked for ways to manage inflationary cost pressures, which resulted in “several redundancies”.
Its headcount for the 2025 financial year had already shrunk from 297 to 230 people, with permanent staff falling from 128 to 110.
The studio also recognised artificial intelligence as a principal risk and uncertainty to its business. It wrote that AI and generative AI were “reshaping parts of the creative industries, creating opportunities to improve workflows and support innovation while also raising important legal, ethical and authorship issues”.
It said it was vital this technology was developed and used responsibly and selectively, but only in ways that “support and celebrate human creativity and craft rather than replace it”.
Peter Lord and David Sproxton co-founded the studio in the early 1970s in Bristol. They began animating as teenagers, selling their first short – starring a superhero called Aardman – to the BBC’s Vision On in 1972.
They created Morph for the children’s programme Take Hart in 1977. The studio began appealing to adult audiences through Channel 4’s Conversation Pieces series, and its animators, including Nick Park, went on to make Wallace & Gromit.
Aardman became employee-owned in 2018, with Lord and Sproxton transferring majority ownership to staff to safeguard the company’s independence. The pair were knighted earlier this year.

UK goods trade deficit narrows to $26.2B in August, below expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:00:07 UTC
16:00:07 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The UK's goods trade deficit stood at £19.8 billion ($26.2 billion) in August, below market expectations of £21.9 billion, as imports fell more than exports, official figures showed Thursday.
The deficit, excluding precious metals, narrowed by £200 million from July, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Goods imports decreased 2.3% month-on-month to £54.2 billion, while exports fell 3.1% to £34.4 billion.
Imports from non-EU countries dropped 6.3% to £25.6 billion, driven primarily by lower purchases of machinery and transport equipment following a record increase in July. Aircraft imports from the US and ship imports from China declined.
Imports from the EU rose 1.6% to £28.6 billion, supported by higher purchases of German aircraft and pharmaceutical products, alongside refined oil from the Netherlands.
Goods exports to the EU fell 7.3% to £15.8 billion, reflecting declines in machinery and transport equipment, manufactured materials, fuels and chemicals.
Lower aircraft exports to the Netherlands and reduced crude oil shipments to Germany, Poland and Italy contributed to the fall.
Exports to non-EU countries increased 0.9% to £18.6 billion, supported by higher shipments of inorganic chemicals to the US.
After adjusting for inflation, total goods imports fell 2.5%, while exports declined 2.8%.
 
3-month trade deficit widens
The total goods and services trade deficit widened by £1.4 billion to £8 billion ($10.6 billion) in the three months to August compared with the three months to May.
The goods deficit increased by £2.5 billion to £59.1 billion, partly offset by a £1.1 billion rise in the estimated services surplus to £51.1 billion.
Early estimates for August showed services exports increased 0.4% from July, while imports rose 0.2%.

Details

The use of a MOAB in the conflict with Iran would mark a new stage of escalation. At the same time, according to the publication, sources familiar with discussions of the military plans have expressed doubts about whether this weapon would help achieve the strategic goals of U.S. President Donald Trump or change the balance of power in the war.

Although some administration officials have characterized the war as effectively won, Trump has been more cautious in his latest statements, not declaring victory and saying that the U.S. still has unfinished business in the country
At the same time, over the past several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various courses of action regarding Iran.

For Kallas, the central issue is that Russia must end its war of aggression, which would also bring an end to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries.
“If we look at the big picture, the majority of the financing for this war comes from oil. And that is why Ukraine is also targeting them [the refineries], while Russia is targeting the energy infrastructure inside Ukraine, to cause as much suffering as possible to the Ukrainian people in the upcoming winter,” she said.
Kallas insisted that international pressure should be directed at Russia to end its invasion, rather than at Ukraine to accept Moscow’s demands – a position she said Europe had consistently maintained.
“If we did this together with the US, then the message to Russia would be clear: stop this war, and all your worries when it comes to oil refineries and whatnot will also stop,” she said.
Asked whether a wave of elections in key EU countries, including the prospect of Marine Le Pen becoming French president, signalled waning support for Ukraine, Kallas acknowledged that public attitudes had shifted over four years of war.
However, she said Europe needed to present a united front for its foreign policy to be effective.
“This is what the Russians are actually playing at: that the Europeans will get tired and then they will get what they want. And what I want to stress is that their appetite will then grow,” Kallas said.

====================================================================================================

Inflation is significantly higher in Lithuania. What does this mean for monetary policy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:54:16 UTC
15:54:16 KST

Annual inflation in Lithuania is currently significantly higher than the euro area average. According to preliminary estimates, inflation in September 2026 stood at 3.8% in the euro area and 6.1% in Lithuania. This gap naturally raises questions: what does it tell us about the state of Lithuania’s economy, and what does it mean in the context of the euro area’s single monetary policy?
The inflation gap between Lithuania and the euro area alone is not enough to draw conclusions about the monetary policy stance. First, we need to understand the factors driving this difference.
Commentary by Tomas Reichenbachas, Principal Economist at the Monetary Policy Division of the Economics Department, Bank of Lithuania
The ECB’s monetary policy focuses on price stability across the euro area
It is important to remember the European Central Bank’s (ECB) objective. The ECB does not aim to keep inflation at exactly 2% in every euro area country at all times. Its objective is to stabilise inflation at 2% across the euro area over the medium term. When making decisions, the ECB assesses not only the current inflation rate but also the inflation outlook, underlying inflation dynamics and how monetary policy is transmitted to the economy. As Lithuania is a highly open economy and most of its exports go to other euro area countries, stability across the euro area is very important to us.
Within a single currency area, inflation rates can naturally vary between countries. These differences reflect economic structures, positions in the economic cycle and the various factors driving price changes. In one country, inflation may be driven more strongly by rising wages and service prices; in another, by changes in energy prices or taxes.
Forecasts suggest that inflation should decline
It is important to assess not only the current inflation gap but also how inflation will evolve. The Bank of Lithuania forecasts that average annual inflation will fall from around 5.1% in 2026 to 3.1% in 2027 and 2.6% in 2028. The Eurosystem also projects that euro area inflation, expected to average around 3% in 2026, will subsequently decline to 2.1% in 2028.
If these forecasts materialise, the current large inflation gap between Lithuania and the euro area will gradually narrow. This is one reason why the ECB focuses on medium-term inflation developments rather than a single month’s figure.
Country-specific and temporary factors account for a substantial share of Lithuania’s inflation
Not all of Lithuania’s current inflation is the result of excessive domestic demand. Energy prices have become one of the main drivers of price growth this year, particularly fuel prices pushed up by more expensive oil. Increases in indirect taxes—excise duties—at the beginning of the year are also adding to inflation in Lithuania. The Bank of Lithuania estimates that their impact will account for around one-fifth of this year’s average inflation.
Funds withdrawn from second-pillar pension funds have provided an additional, but considerably smaller, boost to demand. The Bank of Lithuania estimates that their impact on inflation in 2026 will amount to around 0.2 percentage points.
The key point is that the effects of both the tax changes and withdrawals from second-pillar pension funds are largely temporary. As these effects fade, inflation should decline. Adjusting for these specific factors, the inflation gap between Lithuania and the euro area would be considerably smaller.
Under normal conditions, Lithuania’s inflation may be slightly higher
There is another reason why Lithuania’s inflation should not be compared mechanically with the euro area average. Lithuania is still catching up with wealthier European countries. Our labour productivity, wages and price levels are converging with those of Western Europe, so a somewhat higher inflation rate is a natural part of this process.¹
This does not in itself mean that higher inflation should be regarded as normal over an extended period. However, if wages and living standards in Lithuania continue to approach those in Germany, the Netherlands and other wealthier euro area countries, price levels will also converge.
As labour productivity and wages rise, so do the prices of local services that cannot, or cannot easily, be provided from abroad, such as restaurants, repairs, hairdressing, healthcare and other professional services. In other words, part of Lithuania’s higher inflation may be a natural consequence of economic convergence.
However, higher inflation cannot be ignored
None of this means that higher inflation in Lithuania can simply be dismissed. It may also signal an overheating economy.
If service prices and wages continued to rise rapidly in Lithuania after energy prices had stabilised and tax effects had faded, if wage growth significantly outpaced productivity growth for a prolonged period, if lending expanded rapidly and domestic demand exceeded the economy’s capacity, this would be a clearer sign of mounting domestic inflationary pressures and differences between Lithuania’s cyclical position and that of the euro area as a whole.
Wages in Lithuania are indeed currently rising rapidly: the Bank of Lithuania forecasts wage growth of around 9.4% in 2026. Service price inflation, labour costs, lending and domestic demand therefore need to be monitored closely.
Even in such circumstances, however, monetary policy is not the only tool available. Within a single currency area, national economic policies play an important role in addressing country-specific imbalances. If Lithuania’s economy is overheating, the country can pursue a less expansionary fiscal policy and exercise greater caution when increasing permanent public expenditure. The Bank of Lithuania can also apply macroprudential measures if it identifies risks of excessive credit growth or overheating in the real estate market.
What matters most is what causes the inflation gap
When assessing inflation in Lithuania, the central question should therefore not be “Why is inflation in Lithuania different from the euro area average?” but “What exactly is driving this difference?”
How much is attributable to energy, how much to taxes and temporary boosts to demand, how much to wage and price convergence, and how much to genuinely excessive domestic demand?
Lithuania’s annual inflation rate of 6.1% is a signal that requires serious analysis. However, the inflation gap itself does not reveal its causes. Country-specific and temporary factors account for a significant share of Lithuania’s current inflation, while part of the gap may be linked to economic convergence. At the same time, it is important to monitor whether higher inflation is becoming a sign of more persistent domestic price pressures.
¹ The Bank of Lithuania’s 2024 study, “Anatomy of inflationary shock in Lithuania: causes, effects and implications”, estimates that in 2022, when Lithuania’s price level was still around 26% below the euro area average, price convergence may have contributed to inflation being around 0.5–0.9 percentage points higher. The median model estimate suggested that “equilibrium” inflation in Lithuania could have been around 2.6%, compared with 2% in the euro area. As Lithuania’s price level approaches the euro area average, this gap gradually narrows.

Tallinn French Lyceum struggling with leaky sports hall roof
The Tallinn French Lyceum's sports hall began leaking even before it opened, but the leak has now become so severe that the school has suspended use of the building for several days.
The Tallinn French Lyceum's sports hall was officially opened in October 2018. Principal Peter Pedak told ERR that the building had actually begun leaking even before it opened.
"Water has never come in as heavily as it is now, but there have been leaks before," Pedak acknowledged.
According to Pedak, the current, more serious leak is likely caused by a blockage in the rainwater drainage system. However, a camera inspection scheduled for Wednesday should help determine whether that is the case. The school closed the sports hall on Tuesday and Wednesday to investigate the problem.
The principal noted that the sports hall's roof also serves as a walkable surface and is partially covered by a flower bed.
"We are not entirely sure how well it is waterproofed," Pedak admitted. "In short, we first need to establish what is causing the leaks and then draw up a plan with the school's governing authority, the Tallinn Education Department. We have been in close contact with them on this issue and I hope that, now that the situation has become truly critical, we can get the building repaired more quickly."
However, leaks are not the relatively new sports hall's only problem, as there are also cracks in its ceiling. Asked whether these were construction defects, Pedak said that was a more complicated issue. He explained that the cracks are located above the panels and are generally not considered to pose an immediate danger.
The school does not have funding in its budget for major construction work. While the lyceum is commissioning the camera inspection itself, any major repairs, should they prove necessary, would be the responsibility of the Education Department. What happens next will depend on the inspection results. Once the causes of the rainwater entering the building have been identified, a repair plan can be drawn up and the costs estimated.
The principal hopes the building can continue to be used in the near future. The current closure for a few days will not disrupt physical education classes, as these are being held outdoors anyway until the fall break.
Tallinn Education Department spokesperson Sille Tiitsmaa said the sports hall's current problem is water accumulating on the roof and leaking into the building. She said this was caused by a blocked drainage system that prevents rainwater from draining off the roof quickly enough.
Tiitsmaa confirmed that the Education Department has been in close contact with the school and has supported its efforts to resolve the problem.
"At present, there is no reason to plan more extensive renovations of the sports hall or a roof replacement as the problem is caused by a blockage in the drainage system, which is currently being addressed," Tiitsmaa added.

First swans return to Bruges’ canal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:48:22 UTC
15:48:22 KST

The first swans are back in Bruges. The swans at 't Stil Ende waterway had to be moved away during the summer because blue-green algae caused the water quality to deteriorate, but they have now returned. Swans from other Bruges’ canals will remain in the enclosure for the time being. The city is continuing to monitor the water quality of its waterways.
The number of blue-green algae in Bruges’ canals is gradually decreasing. The lab provides a weekly update, enabling the city to continue monitoring water quality. “It is the water quality that determines when the swans can return safely. We monitor the test results weekly and assess the situation at each location. The welfare of the animals is always our top priority,” says alderman Franky Demon.
“We are keeping the swans in their familiar location for as long as possible. If their health or welfare is at risk, we will take the necessary measures. Thanks to targeted monitoring and good care, all the swans are doing well.”
Removed earlier than last year
The city also took measures last year. In 2025, the swans at Wijngaardplein were able to remain where they were, but they were kept on dry land for around two weeks with fresh drinking water. In August 2025, the city removed a family of swans from the vicinity of the Carmers Bridge, the Potterierei and the Sint-Annarei because the water quality was inadequate.
In October 2025, these swans were allowed to return after spending around two months in the enclosure. The swans from Stil Ende spent the same amount of time in the enclosure this year, but the city had to remove them earlier. The long spell of warm weather early in the year encouraged the growth of blue-green algae and put pressure on water quality.
Number of swans on the rise
Bruges now has a total of 59 swans. In the swan enclosure, the city is still looking after 22 adult swans and eight newly purchased young swans for the Wijngaardplein. In addition, there are two swans from the children’s farm and seven swans from the Potterierei.
A few months ago, the number of swans fell below 52. According to a persistent legend, the city must maintain at least 52 swans on its waters. With the purchase of eight young swans, the total now stands at 59 once again.
According to Demon, the city did not buy the swans to uphold the legend. “The purchase is part of the routine management of the swan population in our city,” he says.

From Morocco to South Africa, Israel election watched closely across Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:46:52 UTC
15:46:52 KST

From Morocco to South Africa, Israel election watched closely across Africa
October 27 vote could test whether Israel’s ties with African countries withstand the fallout from the war on Gaza.
Lagos, Nigeria – As Israelis prepare to vote on October 27, African governments from Pretoria to Rabat are weighing what the result could mean for their own foreign and domestic policies.
The war on Gaza has exposed sharp differences across the continent, with some governments pursuing diplomatic measures against Israel while others maintain commercial and security ties.
Recent polling has shown a closely contested race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads and a bloc of Jewish-led opposition parties.
Neither is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, with a protracted period of coalition talks expected to follow the vote.
The next government’s approach to Gaza and the Palestinian question could influence Israel’s efforts to preserve and expand its partnerships across the continent.
Israel’s relationships across Africa are shaped by competing priorities. While the Gaza war has intensified diplomatic pressure and public opposition in many countries, security needs, commercial interests and longstanding bilateral partnerships continue to influence government decisions.
Diplomatic strain vs closer ties
Since the war began in October 2023, South Africa has emerged as one of Israel’s most vocal critics in Africa. Its government brought a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention. Israel rejects the allegations. The court’s so-called provisional measures in 2024, including an order for Israel to take action to prevent acts of genocide, are not a final ruling on whether genocide has occurred.
In November 2023, South Africa’s National Assembly adopted a motion calling on the government to close the Israeli embassy and suspend diplomatic relations. The motion did not itself implement those measures, but it underscored the strength of political opposition to Israel’s military campaign.
Other African governments have taken different approaches that reflect national political priorities and foreign policy calculations rather than a single continental position.
Chad recalled its ambassador to Israel in November 2023, while some countries have maintained relations despite criticism of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.
Morocco offers a contrasting example. It restored relations with Israel in 2020 under a US-backed arrangement linked to Washington’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. Despite public demonstrations opposing normalisation, Rabat has continued to pursue closer ties.
On September 16, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita met in New York at a trilateral summit hosted by US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz. The three countries reaffirmed plans to upgrade diplomatic relations, elevate their respective missions to embassies and appoint ambassadors.
They also agreed to conclude investment protection and double taxation agreements by the end of this year, expand flights to include Moroccan airlines and arrange reciprocal high-level visits in the coming months. These were announced commitments, rather than confirmation that the changes had already been implemented.
For Idowu Johnson, associate professor of international relations at the University of Ibadan, the diversity of African states makes it difficult to predict a uniform response to Israel’s election.
“Africa’s heterogeneity means individual states have handled relations with Israel separately. Since the October 7, 2023 attacks, African criticism has focused on Israel’s denial of Palestinian statehood.
“The October 27 election will therefore be pivotal, as a new government’s stance on the Palestinian cause will shape how far Africa cooperates on agriculture, trade, security and technology, guided by self-determination and international law as well as bilateral interests,” Johnson said.
Israel’s relationship with the African Union (AU) also reflects these divisions. In 2021, the AU Commission chairperson accredited Israel’s representative to the organisation, prompting objections from member states.
In February 2022, the AU Assembly established a committee of heads of state and government to consult on Israel’s observer status. The dispute continued into 2023, when the AU moved to suspend Israel’s accreditation pending further consideration.
The disagreement has reflected wider divisions over Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and the organisation’s approach to the conflict.
A new Israeli government could seek to ease those tensions, but any change would depend on its policies as well as the positions of AU member states.
Security ties may outlast diplomatic tensions
Security cooperation has been a significant part of Israel’s relationships with some African governments. Israeli companies have pursued defence and security contracts involving equipment, surveillance technology and training.
But the nature and scale of those relationships vary by country and claims about particular agreements or technologies should be tied to documented cases rather than treated as evidence of a uniform Israeli security presence across the continent.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo offers a recent example of efforts to deepen cooperation. Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi visited Israel on August 31 and September 1, meeting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog. Discussions covered security, defence, agriculture, infrastructure, energy and high technology. Both sides expressed a desire to strengthen their strategic partnership and expand cooperation across several sectors.
The visit followed memorandums of understanding signed on July 27. Congolese officials said the visit would review those agreements and explore further Israeli investment, including opportunities linked to the Lobito Corridor. The meetings demonstrate the potential scope of bilateral cooperation, but do not establish that a specific new security contract has been concluded.
For governments confronting armed groups, insecurity can create incentives to seek equipment, intelligence and training from foreign partners. Yet the importance of Israeli cooperation differs between countries and diplomatic tensions will not necessarily have the same effect on every security relationship.
The limits of Israel’s diplomatic outreach were also evident after it recognised Somaliland as an independent state on December 26, last year, the first country to do so. Somalia and other critics rejected the move, arguing that it undermined Somalia’s territorial integrity. The decision triggered demonstrations in Somalia and Somaliland.
Speaking to Al Jazeera this month, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said Somalia will not accept Israeli presence in the country “under any circumstances”. He added that Israel was planning to establish a naval base in Berbera and use the city’s airport, adding that its real aim was to get closer to the Gulf states and Iran.
According to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project (ACLED), 110 demonstrations directly linked to Israel’s Somaliland recognition had been recorded by the time of its February 2026 Africa overview. Only seven supported the move, all in Somaliland; the others opposed it. The figures cover demonstrations linked to that particular decision, not all African views of Israel, and should not be treated as a continent-wide measure of public opinion.
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an Africa analyst at the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute, argues that public opposition can constrain governments even when they see strategic value in maintaining ties.
“The strongest constraint, however, may come from African publics rather than governments: the Somaliland recognition drew widespread opposition, the African Union and many governments reaffirmed Somalia’s territorial integrity, and ACLED logged 110 related demonstrations, only seven in support.
“Depending on its approach, the next Israeli government could therefore either deepen strategic cooperation in Morocco, Sudan and the Red Sea, or face a legitimacy problem if it continues policies seen as tied to the Gaza war, widening the gap between state-level cooperation and public sentiment,” Ibrahim told Al Jazeera.
The Somaliland episode shows how a diplomatic move can provoke opposition when it is perceived to challenge a core principle of sovereignty.
It does not, by itself, establish that African governments will abandon security agreements with Israel. The consequences will depend on the countries involved, the terms of their cooperation and the domestic political costs of maintaining them.
Trade, agritech and the contest for influence
Trade and development cooperation offer Israel another route to maintaining relationships in Africa. Israeli firms and officials have pursued partnerships in areas including agriculture, irrigation, water management, health and technology.
Such cooperation can offer practical benefits to governments seeking investment and technical expertise, but commercial ties do not necessarily translate into public support for Israel’s policies.
Zambia illustrates Israel’s efforts to deepen bilateral engagement. Israel opened a resident embassy in Lusaka in August last year, after a 52-year absence. Agriculture, water management, health, education and technology have been identified as potential areas for closer cooperation. The move formed part of Israel’s broader effort to strengthen its engagement with African countries.
Some analysts have interpreted Israel’s renewed engagement with Zambia as an attempt to cultivate partners who could counterbalance South Africa’s influence in the region. That remains an interpretation, not an established explanation for the relationship.
Zambia has its own reasons for seeking investment and cooperation, particularly in agriculture, water management and technology; closer bilateral ties alone do not prove that countering South Africa is Israel’s objective.
Professor Iwebunor Okwechime, of Obafemi Awolowo University, points to the historical roots of South Africa’s position towards Israel.
“If we trace the stance South Africa took, it goes back to the apartheid era, when Israel backed the apartheid regime and refused to support the struggle against the minority government. This historical context is important for understanding South Africa-Israel relations today,” Okwechime told Al Jazeera.
For African governments, the challenge will be to balance security and commercial interests against public opposition, commitments to Palestinian rights and positions on international law. For Israel, the upcoming election will test whether a new government can ease diplomatic tensions across Africa without fundamentally changing the policies that have fuelled them.
As Okwechime told Al Jazeera, “There won’t be a radical change in sentiments regardless of the government in power”.

On Wednesday, Deputy Defence Minister Karolis Aleksa said more than 45% of the planned defence budget had already been spent, with spending progressing faster than at the same point last year.
Lithuania’s defence budget stands at 4.8 billion euros in 2026, equivalent to 5.38% of GDP.
The government plans to increase defence funding by 36 million euros next year, bringing it to a level equivalent to 5% of GDP.

How to Turn an Attic Into Usable Living Space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

What happens to the space beneath a roof? In many houses, the answer is simple: it becomes an attic, a storage space, or a largely unused volume between the upper floor and the roof. Yet the same space can become a bedroom, home office, playroom, or additional living area if the roof and the room beneath it are considered together.
This potential matters in both existing buildings and residential architecture. Converting an attic can add usable space without extending the building's footprint, while designing a new house with a usable roof space in mind can make it more adaptable over time. The question is therefore not only how to convert an attic, but how to recognize the architectural potential of underused space created by a sloped roof.
The VELUX Design Guide approaches this through the relationship between roof geometry, daylight, ventilation, views, and indoor climate. Its guidance considers how to coordinate these factors to make spaces beneath the roof comfortable and efficient.
Making Better Use of Existing Attics
Many existing attics were never intended to be occupied, making them an overlooked opportunity for adding usable space within an existing building. A cold attic, for example, may sit above the insulated upper floor as an unheated and largely unused volume. Converting it into living accommodation means bringing that space into the building's environmental and structural strategy: insulation, ventilation, access, headroom, roof structure, and existing services all need to be reconsidered. Issues such as condensation, moisture, or heat loss may need to be addressed along the way, but the same interventions can also improve the performance of the existing building while unlocking space that was previously underused.
The gable roof is one of the clearest examples. Two sloping planes meet at a ridge, helping shed rain and snow while creating a triangular volume above the upper floor. Whether that volume becomes useful depends on its proportions: roof pitch, ridge height, knee-wall height, structural depth, and access all affect how much of it can actually be occupied. Roof pitch is particularly important. A steeper roof generally creates more usable height, while the lower areas beneath the eaves can still accommodate functions such as storage, seating, or beds.
Designing Attics for Future Use in New Homes
An attic conversion can make use of space within the building envelope rather than extending the building outward. The VELUX Room to Grow: The case for easily convertible attic design in new homes research frames this as an opportunity to provide additional living space while making better use of the land already allocated to new homes.
An analysis of approximately 669,000 homes built in England between 2020 and 2024 estimated that around 530,000—roughly 80 percent—could feasibly support attic rooms meeting minimum space standards. The assessment considered roof pitch, eaves, stairs, and a minimum space standard of 6.51 m², and found that steeper roof pitches increased conversion viability.
Existing buildings require architects to work with what is already there. New construction offers a different opportunity: the roof can be designed with future occupation in mind. A house doesn't necessarily need a fully finished attic when it is completed. Instead, the roof space can be made conversion-ready. The staircase position, structural arrangement, roof pitch, insulation, services, and available headroom can all be coordinated so the space can accommodate another use later.
The Room to Grow research estimates that the average uplift in floor area from a viable attic room can be around 31% for detached homes. Its wider argument is that adaptable roof spaces can accommodate changing household needs while using the land allocated to new homes more efficiently.
Once an attic becomes habitable, its sloping geometry should inform the room rather than feel like an inconvenience. This is why the VELUX Design Guide recommends thinking "in section, not just in plan." A floor plan shows the available footprint, but a section reveals where someone can stand, how furniture fits beneath the slope, and how daylight can reach deeper into the room.
Bringing Light, Air and Views Indoors
To make the volume comfortable to occupy, different criteria should be considered. Roof windows, such as those by VELUX, can contribute daylight, ventilation, and views; however, their effectiveness depends on how they relate to the room, roof geometry, and planned use. Daylight is particularly important beneath a sloped roof because roof windows can bring natural light deeper into the plan than vertical façade windows, potentially helping distribute daylight more evenly throughout the room. EN 17037, the European Standard for daylight in buildings, defines target illuminance levels of 300, 500, and 750 lux and provides methods for assessing daylight provision across a space.
Natural ventilation uses wind pressure and temperature differences to move air through a building, improving indoor air quality and humidity control while reducing reliance on mechanical cooling. In an attic, openings at different heights can take advantage of warm air naturally rising. Thanks to their elevated position, roof windows can support natural ventilation by allowing warm air to rise and escape, helping improve indoor airflow. However, two windows on opposite sides can support cross-ventilation, while openings at different heights can use the stack effect as warm air rises. Combining both approaches can help move air through the space more effectively. Their position also affects the view. Drawing on the principles of the European standard EN 17037 for views to the outside, the VELUX Design Guide recommends positioning the lower edge of roof windows approximately 95 to 110 centimeters above the floor to provide views from a seated position. It also emphasizes the importance of views that include different layers of the surrounding environment, ideally encompassing the sky, horizon, and ground.
The value of an attic ultimately lies in more than the floor area it adds. For existing buildings, it can unlock space already within the building envelope; for new housing, designing the roof with future conversion in mind can preserve options as household needs change. In both cases, the architectural challenge is to connect roof geometry with height, furniture, daylight, ventilation, views, and thermal conditions, making what might otherwise be leftover volume into usable, adaptable space.

- Category

Ukraine’s TENCORE and Canada’s Dominion Dynamics to Produce TerMIT UGVs for NATO Allies
Ukrainian defense company TENCORE has partnered with Canada’s Dominion Dynamics to produce its TerMIT unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) in Canada, starting in 2027, Militarnyi reported on October 14.
The companies signed a memorandum of understanding at the AUSA 2026 international defense exhibition in Washington, DC, with plans to supply these robotic systems to both Ukrainian forces and NATO partners.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the partnership, TENCORE will transfer technology and train Canadian specialists to enable full-scale serial production, scheduled to begin in 2027.
In turn, Dominion Dynamics will integrate its AuraNet command, control, and navigation hardware-software suite into the platform. The Canadian firm will also develop a specialized modification of TerMIT tailored for operations in extreme Arctic conditions.
“Partnership with Canada provides us with a scalable manufacturing base, resilient supply chains, and a reliable energy grid to launch this cycle alongside allies who require combat-proven solutions,” said Roman Tkachenko, co-founder of TENCORE, Militarnyi reported.
The base version of the TerMIT UGV is designed for battlefield cargo transport. It features an operational range of up to 40 km, speeds reaching 15 km/h, and ballistic protection designed to maintain logistical support under fire.
On July 9, 2026, building on Ukraine's rapid integration of robotic systems on the frontline, defense company TENCORE introduced AI KIT—an artificial intelligence software suite designed to enhance the autonomy of its TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles.
The technology aimed to reduce operator strain and improve combat efficiency by removing the need for constant manual control. The system featured a hands-free navigation mode, an automatic 180-degree return function in signal-loss zones, and predefined failsafes to keep the platform operating safely under heavy electronic jamming.

EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:43:00 UTC
15:43:00 KST

EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget
October 15, 2026
European Union leaders are to meet in Brussels on Thursday for two days of talks that will focus on some of the major economic challenges facing the bloc, including competition from China.
The meeting is also likely to see some heated debate over the bloc's budget for the years 2028 to 2034, with the usual divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients.
On Friday, leaders are set to discuss further support for Ukraine as it faces a full-scale Russian invasion, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy due to attend.
Here are the main topics on the agenda:
Chinese competition in focus
The leaders are expected to discuss ways to remedy the bloc's massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.
The meeting comes less than a week after the bloc's executive body, the European Commission, reached an agreement with Beijing to curb imports of hybrid cars from China.
The EU has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field.
Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.
Ahead of the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for new EU measures to counter any actions leading to market distortion.
The leaders will, however, also be looking at soaring energy prices within the bloc as another factor weighing on its competitiveness.
Divisive EU budget
The bloc's next seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 is also set to be another controversial issue on the agenda, ahead of a special summit set for November to try to reach agreement.
Discussions on the budget, which requires unanimous approval, are often intense, with divisions between wealthier states and those that rely on EU cohesion funds.
The talks at the summit are not expected to bring any breakthrough, but leaders are hoping to reach a compromise by the end of the year.
Pressure to finalize the budget is growing ahead of elections next year in several member states that could make it even more difficult to reach a deal acceptable to all.
Ukraine support
The EU leaders are expected to turn their attention to the situation in Ukraine on Friday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy invited to join the meeting.
He is likely to urge the bloc to up its support for Kyiv as Russia intensifies its strikes ahead of winter, killing dozens of civilians.
European aid is taking on ever more importance as the US under President Donald Trump continues its ambivalent path with regard to the conflict, as reflected in a recent deal securing Russian diesel imports despite international sanctions.
Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukrainian leader.

Unemployment remains at 4%, 408,000 out of work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:42:15 UTC
15:42:15 KST

Unemployment remains at 4%, 408,000 out of work
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Over 408,000 people were out of work in September, national statistics office CBS said on Thursday.
The number of jobless people rose by an average of 5,000 a month over the past three months. The number of people in paid work stayed level.
Unemployment returned to 4% in July after dipping slightly in June. A year ago, 409,000 people were out of work, also 4% of the workforce.
The recent rise is mainly down to fewer unemployed people finding work rather than people losing their jobs.
Benefits agency UWV was paying out 197,100 unemployment benefits at the end of September. The UWV figures are not directly comparable with the CBS total, which counts everyone without paid work who is actively looking for a job.
A further 3.2 million people aged 15 to 75 are not counted as part of the workforce because they have not recently looked for work or cannot start straight away. Most are retired or unable to work because of illness or disability.

06:41:45 UTC

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fears a military campaign against Iran in the two weeks before the election could undermine Likud’s chances of remaining in power, sources familiar with the matter told Maariv on Thursday.
Internal Likud assessments have fueled optimism that the rival blocs could finish tied or that Netanyahu’s bloc could secure a majority. Netanyahu, however, fears a security escalation could change the electoral picture.
A message conveyed from Jerusalem to Washington in recent days indicated that Israel would prefer military action against Iran to begin after the October 27 Knesset election, the sources said.
In private discussions, Netanyahu has raised two main considerations against launching a campaign at this stage, according to the sources: the difficulty of postponing the election and the potential toll of Iranian retaliation on Israel’s home front.
“These are precisely the scenes we cannot afford to see. A country in shelters, missile strikes, destroyed buildings, wounded people and, God forbid, deaths - that is what could lead to a victory for Eisenkot and his partners,” a senior Likud official said, adding that the remarks reflect Netanyahu’s position.
Likud fears that missile fire, casualties, and prolonged disruption to daily life would shift the public agenda in the final days before the election.
According to assessments published in the US, renewed strikes against Iran could prompt the launch of hundreds of ballistic missiles at Israel. A strike shortly before the election could also raise questions about its motives and timing.
Could renewed war with Iran cause elections to be postponed?
Netanyahu considers postponing the election because of a security emergency impractical, the sources said.
Section 9A of Basic Law: The Knesset requires the support of 80 MKs to pass legislation extending the Knesset’s term, along with special circumstances that prevent the election from taking place as scheduled. Likud officials believe they cannot secure the necessary support from the opposition.
The possibility of postponing the election also arose in security discussions between Israel and the US. IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke with US Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman Gen. Dan Caine about the possibility of renewed fighting within three weeks, Axios reported. Their discussions included the possibility that such a campaign would lead to Israel’s election being postponed.
Likud’s optimism rests on internal assessments, while public polling presents a mixed picture. Polls published in recent days have shown substantial differences between polling firms, with some placing Netanyahu’s bloc well short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
Senior Likud officials believe the bloc can improve its position before the election and want to avoid an escalation that could undermine those efforts.
Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot recently said he was unaware of any critical development that would justify immediate joint US-Israeli action against Iran. He stressed, however, that he has not had access to the latest intelligence since leaving the war cabinet.
The position attributed to Netanyahu in private contradicts briefings and assessments suggesting he favors a strike before the election because he believes another campaign would benefit him politically.
Netanyahu, Trump reportedly discuss resuming Iran war
Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump have spoken several times over the past two weeks, with the possibility of renewed strikes against Iran coming up in their conversations, according to several sources.
The White House denied that the two had discussed resuming the war.
Israeli officials believe the denial was intended to distance Israel from the American debate over a strike on Iran and avoid reinforcing claims that Netanyahu influences Trump’s decisions. The officials said the White House recognizes that such claims could damage Trump politically at home.
The Prime Minister’s Office said Netanyahu maintains regular contact with Trump but did not comment on the substance of their conversations.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran remain high. Trump said on October 8 that the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, but subsequently renewed his threats.
At a campaign rally in Alaska over the past day, Trump threatened to deal Iran a heavy blow and said he had grown tired of its conduct.
According to a US report, the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command to complete preparations for renewed, extensive military operations against Iran.
The operational assessment in Israel, however, is that Trump has yet to make a final decision to attack and that no date has been set for action in the immediate future.
Military preparations continue amid reports that Iran is strengthening defenses around strategic facilities and restoring capabilities damaged in the previous campaign.
Washington and Tehran are also continuing diplomatic contacts through regional mediators over Iran’s nuclear program, shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz, and a possible agreement to prevent further escalation. The talks have yet to produce a breakthrough.
“Trump is Trump. With him, everything can turn around and change very quickly,” the sources said. “We do not control the situation, but the message has certainly been conveyed to him. As far as we are concerned, we would prefer quiet on the security front until October 27.”

Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers – a problem for Moscow and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:41:34 UTC
15:41:34 KST

Ukrainian strikes on data centers within Russian territory are aimed at disrupting military planning and communications, but they have also had an impact on other areas—Russians are complaining about longer wait times for dinners ordered via apps, reports Politico.
Kyiv’s drone strikes on Yandex data centers in Sasovo, Kaluga, and Vladimir caused disruptions for thousands of businesses and households that rely on Yandex’s cloud infrastructure—including e-commerce platforms, digital payment systems, and apps for food delivery and taxi services. On the 14th of October, Ukrainian forces struck a Sberbank data center in the Saratov region, though a company official stated that no operational disruptions occurred.
Following the strikes on the data centers, Kyiv pointed out that Moscow has repeatedly attacked its digital infrastructure. A high-ranking official familiar with the operation remarked that the Ukrainians wanted to show that two can play at this game.
These attacks and counter-attacks highlight a new front line in the war: the infrastructure that sustains digital economies. Attacks on facilities that provide computing power are comparable to attacks on power plants that supply electricity, heating, and fuel for both military and civilian needs. Such strikes can weaken an adversary's ability to wage war while simultaneously bringing daily life to a standstill. Experts have noted that restoring Russian data centers will be exceptionally costly, as it requires rare raw materials that must be imported. Oleg Shakirov, a researcher specializing in cyber policy and international security, stated that replacing equipment destroyed in large-scale strikes would be difficult; he pointed out that most of the hardware must be imported—a challenging task due to both high global demand and the sanctions imposed on Russia. He added that
 the full extent of the damage remains unknown, though the fact that two data centers remain offline suggests it is significant.
Researcher Joseph Jarnacki warned that the normalization of strikes against data centers could lead to new and dangerous consequences. He told *Politico* that such attacks pose a major risk at a time when the world is becoming increasingly reliant on digital services. Data centers have also come into focus in other recent armed conflicts. In the context of the conflict between Iran and the US and Israel, drones from Tehran attacked three Amazon facilities located in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. Because data centers can serve both civilian and military purposes, the legal status of such attacks is complex. Kubo Mačák, an expert in international humanitarian law, stated that for data centers to qualify as military objectives, two conditions must be met: they must be used in military operations, and their destruction must offer a clear military advantage. If they store military intelligence or are used to power military artificial intelligence tools, they may be classified as military targets.
Following attacks on Yandex data centers, users on the platform X reported a sharp decline in bot activity—including among accounts associated with pro-Russian narratives, support for Donald Trump, or the German far-right party Alternative for Germany. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seized on these reports to suggest that the strikes had rendered the social media landscape less toxic. Mačák stated that 
the use of data centers to operate troll farms or bots—aimed at influencing elections in other countries—does not constitute sufficient grounds for strikes.
 In other words, the researcher argues that the mere hosting of propaganda bots does not, in itself, render data centers a legitimate military target.
The dilemma of "dual-use" infrastructure has frequently been raised in the context of attacks on energy infrastructure—a recurring feature of the war in Ukraine. On the 10th of October, Trump urged Ukraine to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing that such actions drive up fuel prices. He has called on both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure; however, the status of any potential "energy truce" remains unclear.

Rooms with a view: The highest hotel in France just opened in the Pyrenees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:41:00 UTC
15:41:00 KST

Featuring 16 double rooms with panoramic views, the Hôtellerie des Laquets is connected to Pic du Midi via a private cable car.
There are rooms with a view, and then there’s this: The highest hotel in France, located some 2,620 metres above sea level.
Found in the French Pyrenees, the Hôtellerie des Laquets was originally built between 1930 and 1933.
Having been closed for more than 30 years, the renovated property reopened its doors to guests in late September.
The original hotel building has been kept, with furnishings paying homage to Pyrenean alpine culture, while the new wing is pure minimalist Nordic chic.
Featuring 16 double rooms, all of which offer panoramic views, you can reach the hotel by taking a cable car from La Mongie to the summit of the Pic du Midi, before taking a private cable car down to the property below.
The views aren’t the only thing set to impress, either, as the hotel’s restaurant will feature a menu from chef Stéphane Tournié, who earned a Michelin star at Les Jardins de l'Opéra in Toulouse.
Hôtellerie des Laquets overtakes Refuge de Solaise, which lies at 2,551 metres above sea level in the Alps, for the title of France's highest hotel.
The highest hotel in Europe overall is Glacier Hotel Grawand, is 3,212 metres above sea level in Val Senales in South Tyrol, Italy.
What to expect at Hôtellerie des Laquets
The Hôtellerie des Laquets is located within the Pic du Midi International Dark Sky Reserve, meaning it’s a brilliant option for stargazing, with unobstructed views of the Milky Ways sans light pollution.
At the summit, you can learn all about the science behind the observatory at Espace Expériences du Pic du Midi, before heading to the planetarium for an immersive show ahead of the real show that evening.
Pic du Midi is also home to a 12m-long footbridge that juts out into the mountainscape, offering fantastic photo opportunities.
From December this year, the hotel’s spa area will open, complete with sauna and steam rooms.

Politico reports details that Slovakia-Russia meetings suspended after 2022 are to resume
Slovakia and Russia are set to resume meetings of an intergovernmental commission which were suspended following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with energy supplies, nuclear fuel and the treatment of Russian athletes among the key issues.
Source: Brussels-based politics and policy news organisation Politico, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The intergovernmental commission, which deals with economic, scientific and technical cooperation issues, has been inactive since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its last meeting was held in Bratislava on 12 November 2021.
Politico obtained a note from the Russian government written by Russia's Science Minister Valery Falkov, who is on the EU sanctions list. The document states that Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár agreed during a video call on 20 August to hold a meeting of the Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission in Moscow.
Prime Minister Robert Fico said on 14 October that the meeting was scheduled for 25 November. The Russian note, dated 10 September, had initially proposed a different date: 26-27 October.
Asked about the possible agenda for the commission meeting, Slovakia's Foreign Ministry referred Politico to Blanár's public statements following the 20 August call.
"We pursue a policy in all directions and maintain dialogue with all countries that are interested in pragmatic cooperation with us for the benefit of the Slovak Republic's national interests," Blanár said at the time.
According to the Russian document, during the August video conference Blanár expressed Slovakia's opposition to the EU's gradual phase-out of Russian gas imports and asked for the issue of supplies to be discussed at the meeting in Moscow. Slovak representatives also stressed the importance of continuing Russian oil deliveries through the Druzhba pipeline and welcomed regular supplies of nuclear fuel for Slovak power plants.
The agenda for next month's meeting extends beyond energy cooperation. The two sides plan to discuss setting up working groups on culture, tourism, agriculture and environmental protection as well as the status of the Russian Centre of Science and Culture in Bratislava.
Blanár also expressed disagreement with what the note described as "discrimination against Russian athletes" at international competitions, saying the issue would be discussed at the commission meeting.
Background:
- Fico recently said he does not want war to come to Slovakia "because of some Article 5" of NATO.
- Fico also accused the West of having "needlessly added fuel to the fire" for more than four years in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war, thereby supposedly provoking a conflict between Russia and NATO.

Can a European Security Council help the EU fight Russia’s hybrid attacks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:35:30 UTC
15:35:30 KST

The EU wants a faster political response to sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. Experts say the proposed Security Council could help, but only partly.
Sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, disinformation, and drones in restricted airspace. Russia’s hybrid campaign against Europe no longer looks like isolated incidents. The EU is now rethinking its response.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the hybrid threats facing Europe are “less and less hybrid and less and less threats”. Her State of the Union address introduced a new idea, the European Security Council.
From resilience to deterrence
For Ionela Ciolan, a research officer at the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies, the challenge is clear. Russian hybrid warfare today, she says, means the “weaponisation of everything,” from attacks on critical infrastructure and election interference to targeted arson and the instrumentalisation of energy.
The EU’s response has so far leaned on resilience and coordination. Its Hybrid Toolbox, activated in June 2024, bundles cyber, sanctions, diplomatic, and support measures. It created a dedicated Russia hybrid sanctions regime, with first listings in December 2024, and rapid response teams, first deployed in Moldova in 2025.
Analysts now see a shift. Faster public attribution to Russia, more talk of imposing costs on Moscow, and viewing incidents as parts of one campaign. Parliament adopted a report in September calling for a more proactive approach by 470 votes to 129.
Gaps remain, sanctions need unanimity, intelligence is fragmented between capitals, and there is no consensus on when sabotage merits a collective military response.
What is on the table
The proposal has three linked parts: a standing leaders’ forum, an Emergency Security Protocol, and a funding instrument for shared capabilities such as air defence. The protocol is the most relevant for hybrid threats. Von der Leyen described it as Europe’s answer to NATO’s Article 4, letting any member state convene all 27 governments when it feels its security is threatened.
The Commission is reportedly considering inviting partners such as the UK, Norway, Ukraine, and Canada. No formal legislative proposal has been tabled, and no legal basis, voting system, budget, or launch date has been agreed.
Luigi Scazzieri, a senior policy analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies, is blunt about what it would be. In von der Leyen’s version, the Council is essentially a dedicated European Council meeting with invited partners. “This is not a decision-making body per se,” he says.
That means it cannot cut through the disagreements that slow EU responses. Scazzieri argues its worth lies elsewhere: “The key value […] is not necessarily speed, but it’s more the cross-policy coherence.” He says it would help the EU think more strategically about its toolbox, from sanctions to spending, while NATO keeps collective defence.
Critics, he acknowledges, will say Europe already has plenty of forums, including the European Political Community.
The threshold problem
The harder question is when a hybrid attack becomes graver. Ciolan points to the EU’s mutual assistance clause, Article 42.7, and the debate over operationalising it for hybrid attacks.
“A cyberattack that shuts down hospitals or sabotage that disables a power grid could have consequences comparable to a conventional military attack,” she says. Moscow, she adds, thrives on the grey area: “Russia exploits ambiguity to complicate attribution and delay a collective response.”
Her conclusion is that Europe needs common rules: “Europeans therefore need a shared framework for assessing these attacks, and must be able to respond to hostile actions even when they remain below the threshold of armed aggression.”
In her view, a Security Council and an Emergency Security Protocol could help member states “move more quickly from national reactions to a common European response, bringing together military and non-military instruments.” The decision to invoke Article 42.7 would stay with the state under attack.
A hedge against Washington?
Steven Blockmans, deputy director at the International Centre for Defence and Security in Tallinn, says the idea was revived by doubts about US commitment to NATO’s Article 5. The concept dates back to a 2018 proposal by Angela Merkel and Emmanuel Macron. He sees a Council as a fallback if the North Atlantic Council were blocked, whether by Washington or another ally. He links its new momentum to the Greenland crisis and says Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius has pushed the idea for more than a year.
Blockmans argues the body would need teeth to be credible. “It would boost the legitimacy of a European Security Council if its governance had decision-making procedures,” he says, giving national parliaments a democratic backstop and linking it to NATO-compatible command structures and a dedicated budget.
That, he says, is an ideal that would take years of treaty drafting. But if the situation demands it, “an informal construct could well be created tomorrow, if push comes to shove.”
So is the European Security Council a tool against hybrid attacks? From what we know so far, only partly. As proposed, it would improve coordination and give leaders a regular space to discuss security with partners. The Emergency Security Protocol could provide an earlier political entry point for incidents below the armed attack threshold. But experts agree that the underlying obstacles lie in national politics.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,559,230 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:35:17 UTC
15:35:17 KST

Russia has lost 1,559,230 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 15.
The number includes 1,880 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,414 tanks, 25,537 armored combat vehicles, 163,324 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,233 artillery systems, 2,216 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,707 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,955 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

EU leaders enter crunch talks on energy, China and the budget
Unknown

06:34:45 UTC
15:34:45 KST

Good morning from Brussels, where EU leaders are about to kick off a two-day summit. On their menu today: soaring energy prices, China trade ties and the showdown over the EU’s next long-term budget. Let’s dive in.
But first, some breaking news: The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has just told Europe Today that the US-Russia diesel deal is a “gift to Putin”, while defending Ukraine’s right to hit Russian oil refineries.
“The core issue is that Russia should stop this war,” Kallas said. “If we look at the big picture, the majority of the financing of this war comes from oil.”
Asked by our EU editor Maria Tadeo if Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was right in saying that he would continue strikes on Russian oil refineries, Kallas said: “Yes, if we look at international law, it is clear that it is in defence of Ukraine.” Watch.
Summit primer: EU leaders will in just over an hour kick-off a two-day summit with a discussion on energy prices, which have been skyrocketing amid hostilities in the Middle East, my colleague Jorge Liboreiro writes. Oil remains above $100 per barrel despite a coordinated G7 release, with the International Energy Agency (IEA) warning Wednesday that Europe could face renewed wholesale diesel price rises in the coming weeks.
The Italian and Greek leaders have urged Brussels to relax EU fiscal rules to allow governments to use "temporary and targeted measures" to bring down prices. But more fiscally conservative states warn that loosening the rules risks compounding Europe’s already high deficits and fuelling more market volatility.
Then, China: Leaders are then expected to address the ballooning trade deficit with China, a week after EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič struck a preliminary deal to curb imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles into the EU and facilitate access to rare earths.
But there’s a sense that more needs to be done. France and Germany have found rare common ground on the issue, pitching a "kill switch" that would cut off China's access to the EU market if the deficit remained unsustainable.
Leaders will have to carefully calibrate how to further balance the lopsided trading relationship without jeopardising the progress made in recent days by floating further measures.
Money talks: The summit’s most contentious moment will come later this afternoon when the EU’s next seven-year budget is put on the table. The talks are shaping up to be painstakingly difficult, as two opposing camps – the frugals on the one hand and supporters of a bigger budget on the other – remain at loggerheads.
European Council President António Costa wants a deal by the end of the year to ensure the complex legislative work can be fully completed before January 2028. But a compromise proposal brokered by Ireland has made both sides unhappy.
The clash of opinions and the unwillingness to compromise bode ill for Costa's ambition to have a unanimous deal in December. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's shock decision to call snap elections adds yet another layer of uncertainty.
"I don't think there will be blood on the walls, but it's important in these sorts of negotiations that leaders feel where the contradictions are," another senior diplomat said. "We are not in a hurry. We need a good deal. We don’t feel any time pressure."
Jorge has more details in this must-read preview. You can also follow our rolling coverage, with all the behind-the-scenes intel, on our live blog.
Zelenskyy ‘betrayed’: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who will join the summit tomorrow, said on Wednesday that his country is losing a key ally in the US and admitted feeling “betrayed” by Donald Trump, as relations between Kyiv and Washington hit a new low, my colleague Sasha Vakulina reports.
Asked by British broadcaster Piers Morgan whether Ukraine is losing American support, Zelenskyy replied: “Yeah, but not because of us. We can't be weak.”
“It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” he said. Asked whether he felt betrayed, Zelenskyy answered: “Really, yes,” although he stressed that the situation was more complicated than his personal feelings.
US eyes frozen assets: Meanwhile, the FT also reports that US negotiators have proposed that European countries unfreeze some of Russia’s immobilised state assets and transfer them to a financial vehicle controlled by Washington as a means of unblocking stalled peace talks
The plan is reported to have been floated during talks in Miami last week, and rejected outright by European delegates. Oversight over the immobilised assets gives Europe crucial leverage, and the prospect of channelling them directly as a loan to Ukraine will be raised during tomorrow’s talks here in Brussels. The FT has more.
Starlink disruptions: Zelenskyy also last night described the disruption to Ukraine's Starlink connectivity as a “big mistake”, warning that “people will die” unless the service is restored. Ukrainian military operations were disrupted on Wednesday by unstable Starlink connections and speed restrictions, according to Ukrainian military units.
Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov confirmed a speed limit of around 160 km/h on the military-grade Starshield service, which is built on Starlink. The disruption also affected drone operations, including interceptors used to defend against Russian aerial attacks.
By the end of the day, service had reportedly stabilised, although the speed limit remained in place. Questions remained over who had imposed the restrictions in the first place and who had authorised the subsequent improvement.
Former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov publicly thanked Elon Musk as connectivity improved. But the SpaceX chief executive pointed to President Donald Trump as the ultimate authority, saying Starshield systems were controlled by the US government and decisions on restrictions rested with the American military and, ultimately, the president himself.
France’s Marine Le Pen lashes out at the European Commission, says France cannot keep financing Ukraine
French far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen used a visit to Brussels on Wednesday to lash out at the European Commission, saying she wants to strip powers from the EU and cap France’s net contribution to the bloc’s budget at €5 billion a year.
“Being pro-France does not mean being anti-Europe,” she told reporters during a press conference organised after a meeting of the far-right Patriots for Europe group.
“[The Commission] is like the frog that puffs itself up to seem bigger than the ox,” she said.
Crucially, the far-right leader – whose National Rally party is riding high in the polls ahead of next April’s presidential ballot – also said France could not keep on financing Ukraine due to the “perilous” state of the French economy. A U.S. watchdog organization filed a lawsuit on Wednesday alleging that the current role of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as one of the administration’s leading envoys is unlawful and creates numerous risks of conflicts of interest. NBC News reports, writes UNN.
Details
Kushner wields enormous influence on the international stage "without receiving Senate confirmation or filing any declaration of financial income and assets," according to a lawsuit filed by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW).
Kushner "has not undergone the proper vetting to perform his government duties and is evading transparency requirements intended to ensure that he uses his authority in the interests of the American people, rather than for his own benefit," the lawsuit states.
The plaintiffs are seeking to have Kushner removed from his position or, at a minimum, ordered to file financial disclosures.
The lawsuit cites numerous overlapping interests in Kushner’s diplomatic and commercial activities.
He represents the United States in the most high-profile international conflicts, including participating in the country’s efforts to end the wars between Israel and Hamas, Ukraine and Russia, as well as the United States and Iran. He holds direct negotiations with foreign leaders
"At the same time, Kushner is a private businessman. He runs an investment firm that manages more than $6 billion in assets. Approximately 99% of these assets belong to foreign investors, including sovereign wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. The company has significant investments abroad, including in Israel," the lawsuit states. In the plaintiffs’ view, all of this "creates an elevated risk of financial conflicts of interest."
The lawsuit also emphasizes that "declining a salary and official title does not change the real nature of Kushner’s role: he exercises significant executive authority and has done so continuously for most of Trump’s second presidential term. And this in no way exempts him from the constitutional restrictions set out in the Appointments Clause or from the obligation to file public financial disclosures under the ethics law."
The plaintiffs are seeking to bar Kushner from holding public office without Senate confirmation. The lawsuit also states that, if he is a private citizen, "his exercise of government authority would violate the doctrine against the impermissible delegation of powers to private persons, which prohibits transferring government power to private entities."
