A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:20 UTC
13:00:20 KST

On 10 June 2026, the government of Peru made a decision that it knew would hurt one of the world’s major fishing industries. It stopped all anchoveta fishing boats from going out to sea, suspending the fishing season. At first the order was temporary, but in mid-August, the suspension turned into a total closure. This was no easy call. For one thing, it was a brutal blow to the Peruvian economy.
Peruvian anchovies – the scientific name is Engraulis ringens – are not the salty, punch-packing little fillets in a puttanesca sauce or caesar salad dressing. That is a different species – Engraulis encrasicolus – which is smaller, tastier and found mostly in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Only a small part of Peru’s anchoveta catch is eaten in fish form. The rest – more than 90% – is immediately processed as fishmeal and fish oil, packed in sacks and barrels, and shipped to fish, shellfish and seaweed farms, factory farms and nutritional supplement producers around the world.
The vast majority of the anchoveta industry is concentrated off the coast of north-central Peru, and it is hard to overstate how economically significant this fish is. By weight, Peruvian anchoveta have made up about a 10th of the entire global commercial fishing catch since 1970, more than any other fish. Some years, the anchoveta catch is worth close to $3bn and directly employs almost 50,000 people, close to a quarter of a million if you include indirect jobs. The Peruvian central bank is forecasting a 30.7% contraction for the fishing sector and about 78,000 job losses in 2026, and another 44,000 in 2027.
The ripples will be felt far beyond Peru’s borders. The country is by a long way the world’s most important exporter of fishmeal – a crucial input to aquaculture and livestock agriculture virtually everywhere – and prices are skyrocketing as a result. This anchoveta closure will have a direct impact on jobs, food supplies and supermarket prices the world over. Peru’s then minister of production, César Quispe Luján, defended the decision as the only one possible: “The government has the responsibility to manage marine resources based on scientific criteria, timeliness and a long-term vision. When there is a need to strengthen conservation measures, it is necessary to act with prudence and responsibility to ensure the sustainability of the fishery.”
When the June suspension was announced, the fishing boats had already been back in port for weeks. At the start of the season, in early April, Peru’s ministry of production had set a total allowable catch of 1.9m tonnes. But in May, it closed the fishery for 15 days, with only 24% of the quota harvested. When the closure was extended to a full shutdown, there were even hints there would be no second fishing season this autumn. The main concern of the Instituto del Mar del Perú, which recommended the closure, was the risks already posed by this year’s El Niño, and a fear of what is to come.
We are heading into what global climate models forecast as the most severe El Niño since the 1880s, the earliest for which we have accurate records. The super El Niño that is developing “may end up the strongest by a truly mind-blowing margin,” said climatologist Zeke Hausfather in July. Peru’s anchoveta population was already down before the suspension of fishing. We cannot know how the anchoveta would have fared in the absence of El Niño, but we know that its presence makes things considerably more volatile. The warmer waters produced by El Niño threaten the plankton on which anchoveta feed, which in turn threatens the anchoveta population.
The oceans, which cover 71% of the Earth’s surface, are among the most gloriously alive parts of the Earth. While there are vast oceanic deserts, there are also marine versions of the Amazon basin and the Okavango Delta. These rich zones are the result of a host of wonderful contingencies: the shape of the continents, the force of gravity, the chemistry of the ocean and the crazy network of ocean currents.
Most years, the Humboldt current, which flows north along the west coast of Chile and Peru, produces the most fertile fishing grounds on Earth. The current generates massive upwellings of deep colder waters that bring nutrients up from the depths, creating some of the most biologically productive zones in the ocean. This extraordinary biological abundance astounded the first Europeans who witnessed it. Islands piled tens of metres deep with the guano of innumerable birds feeding on sea life; the ocean boiling with million-tonne anchovy and sardine shoals; tuna, bonito and mackerel virtually leaping from the water. By comparison, today’s Humboldt current system is much impoverished – industrialised extraction has taken its toll – but even so, it remains exceptionally productive. Intensive commercial fishing continues, and the most intensive of all is for Peruvian anchoveta, 6in (15cm) flashes of big-eyed, blue-backed silver.
In an average year, Peru produces 20% of the world’s fishmeal. But that word “average” obscures the extraordinary volatility of the anchoveta catch in the decades since the fishery was fully commercialised after the second world war. In 1970, Peru landed more than 12m tonnes of anchoveta. In 1973, the catch fell by 88%. The shock of this stock collapse was so existential for Peru that the military dictatorship introduced the first regulatory regime for the anchoveta fishery. In 1984, the catch plummeted again, to less than 100,000 tonnes, a fraction of what it had been 15 years earlier. The catch recovered in 2000 to about 9.6m tonnes, but has declined since then. Recent annual catches have been in the 2m-4m tonne range.
Overfishing has played a crucial role in this ecological and economic rollercoaster ride. But the crazy seesaw of the anchoveta fishery is not merely a tale of rapacious industrial extraction, but of how overfishing combines with the bouts of accelerated oceanic warming driven by El Niño, which always hit Peruvian coastal waters especially hard.
El Niño (“the little boy”) is the name that fishermen four centuries ago gave periods of unusually warm water off the coast of western South America. It is so named because the episodes usually reach their peak towards Christmas.
Like most oceanic and atmospheric dynamics, both El Niño and the anchoveta fishery are partly born of the fact that the Earth is a spinning ball, turning upon an axis that runs through the middle of the planet from pole to pole. Since the ball is rotating at a fixed rate, different latitudes on its surface spin at different speeds: in the span of one Earth day, places near the equator have a lot more distance to cover to get all the way around than places near the poles, so they rotate faster. Vancouver, the city where I live, is moving around Earth’s axis at 1,100km an hour. If you are reading this in London, you are a little bit closer to the north pole, so spinning a little slower (1,042km/h), but if you are in Jakarta, near the equator, you are whirling about at 1,665km/h. Had someone granted Patsy Cline her wish to Stop the World and Let Me Off, she would have shot out of Nashville at 1,350km/h.
If everything on the Earth’s surface just stayed where it was relative to everything else, things might be fairly straightforward, but that is not how it works. While the terrestrial parts of the Earth spin at a constant rate and in the same direction, the parts of it that are fluid – its molten core, the atmosphere and the oceans – can move at different speeds and in different directions. Often, from our perspective on the surface, it seems as though the fluid parts are somehow moving against the direction of spin. The easterly trade winds of the tropics, for example, which have carried ships across the oceans for as long as we have sailed the seas, are the result of atmospheric patterns shaped by the planet’s eastward rotation, and the higher rotational speeds around the equator. From one perspective, you might even say these “winds” are something of an illusion: it’s not the air that’s blowing past us, but we who are racing through the slower moving air.
Among the most fundamental fluid dynamics resulting from the Earth’s spin are the patterns of circulation of the oceans. These include the planet’s five massive oceanic gyres: two each (north and south of the equator) in the Atlantic and Pacific, and one in the Indian Ocean. These gyres are great circular systems of currents that span each ocean from coast to coast and from the poles almost all the way to the equator, and they too are partly created by the Earth’s roundness and rotation.
The gyres in both hemispheres are like vast oceanic gears spinning in opposite directions: the northern gyres rotate clockwise, while the southern gyres turn anticlockwise. In the Atlantic and Pacific, they meet at the equator, driving wind and water westwards. Along the eastern side of all these gigantic rotating marine gears, cold waters are moving from the poles toward the equator: the Humboldt current is the South Pacific’s version of this process. As these currents push up against the oceans’ eastern coastlines they are driven towards the surface, bringing nutrient-rich cold water to the pelagic zone. In non-El Niño or “neutral” years, the Humboldt current runs all the way up to the seas off northern Peru, where the anchoveta and everything else feast.
During El Niño events, the trade winds weaken and atmospheric pressure builds up over the coasts of Asia. As a result, the higher-temperature water spreads eastwards. With milder El Niño events, it reaches into the central Pacific, south of Hawaii, but in stronger phases it piles up off equatorial South America. Warmer water, much less hospitable to anchoveta, is driven south along the coast into the Humboldt current system, sometimes as far as Lima, Peru, 12 degrees south of the equator. There it sits at the surface, pushing the colder water into the depths and severely limiting the upwelling flows that bring nutrients to the upper layers of the ocean.
For the anchoveta and everything above it in the food web, the result is a disaster. The warm surface waters have the devastating double effect of shrinking the area of the ocean in which the anchoveta find suitable habitat, and robbing them of their main food source, the plankton that depend on the nutrients carried by upwelling. Anchoveta populations shrink, sometimes dramatically; birds starve, predators higher up the food chain that rely on anchoveta scatter or die; and there are a lot fewer fish for the fishing fleet to catch.
Every massive crash in the anchoveta fishery is the consequence of a severe El Niño event hitting already intensely exploited stocks. The climate crisis increases ocean temperatures and acidification, all of which is bad for most marine life, anchoveta included, and further exacerbates the situation by intensifying El Niño.
In its latest report on the state of the world’s marine fisheries in 2025, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization deemed more than a third to be overfished, meaning harvests exceed the rate of reproduction. Though the report classifies most of the anchoveta stocks in Peru as “maximally sustainably fished”, it is worth remembering that calling a fishery sustainable does not take account of the fact that populations are at historically low levels – and, since the onset of industrial fishing, are more vulnerable than ever before.
As with many other shrinking natural resources, what brought us to this point is a combination of increasingly efficient technology and too little regulation for too long. In the case of anchoveta, as regulation has increased, so too has fishing technology adapted itself to the behaviour of the fish. The anchoveta disperse at night to feed, but during the day, when predators like tuna can easily see them, they form large shoals or “schools”. Schooling, when vast numbers of fish mass together in a huge ball, evolved as a strategy to minimise predation. Schooling protects the bulk of the shoal by sacrificing those unlucky enough to end up on the outside edges.
The problem, at least from an anchoveta’s perspective, is that this behaviour evolved before they ran into humans and our modern fishing gear. From the deck of a fishing boat, a school is an enormous swarm of fish conveniently clustered in a tight space near the sea’s surface. Huge fishing vessels can pull anchoveta from the water in enormous volumes. When a boat finds a shoal, it circles the fish while dropping a long float line from its stern. From the float line, which can be as much as 600 metres long, hangs a 50-metre net. Once the net is set in a ring around the shoal, a cable at the bottom edge is pulled tight, and the lower reaches of the net close like the mouth of a drawstring purse, capturing the shoal in what is now a massive mesh bag full of fish. The boats have enormous holds, some as large as 800 cubic metres (equivalent to about 12 40ft-long shipping containers), and can bring millions of anchoveta to port for processing.
Schooling behaviour presents a challenge to scientists monitoring fish populations, because it means anchoveta are not evenly dispersed across their habitat, but massed together in great fish balls. We might catch a lot of them, but we can’t assume there are a lot more fish out there.
A further cause for alarm, and not just for commercial fisheries, is that in the web of predatory relationships, anchoveta are a crucial link between plankton and larger animals: the anchoveta feed on plankton, their population flourishes, which provides food for scores of predator species higher up the food chain, including humans. When anchoveta numbers plummet, it is a potential catastrophe for the whole ecosystem and those who depend on it. When this happened to the Black Sea anchovy late in the 20th century, phytoplankton populations exploded, depleting oxygen levels in the water and threatening an already fragile marine ecosystem, and the other commercial fisheries that depended on it.
The anchoveta matter in all these economic and ecological ways, but they also epitomise a widespread problem in our extractive age: in ecosystems around the world, we are pushing species into conditions of such fragility that we are no longer in control of the situation. Even if we slow or even stop destroying habitat or harvesting, things are now so precarious that “natural” environmental variability could tip them over the edge.
Anchoveta have proven resilient in the face of remarkable levels of environmental variation, from extreme El Niño events to the frenzied overfishing of decades past, but the prognosis isn’t good: research suggests that ocean warming and its effects will lead to a decrease in the amount of anchoveta in the ocean of between 8% and 14% per decade across the 21st century. As sea surface temperatures rise, and salinity and oxygen levels change, the anchoveta’s territorial range shifts, as does the stock’s fertility, spawning seasons and the distribution of the population across different life stages (a crucial consideration in fisheries, because it is imperative to avoid catching fish that are too young to reproduce). All of this is unfolding against the background of ongoing climate heating at a planetary scale, to which El Niño introduces additional and increasing stresses.
This year’s closure of the anchoveta fishery before the quota was reached came as a surprise to some in the industry, but it is not the first time it has happened. Just last year, Peru set the first season quota at 3m tonnes, but when scientists noted the juvenile population – the younger fish yet to reach reproductive age – was especially at risk, the government called the fleet off the water with just 2.5m tonnes landed. “The sustainable extraction of anchovy is a strategic priority for the country,” Jesús Barrientos, the vice minister of fisheries and aquaculture, said at the time.
The anchoveta harvest limit is usually binding: the fleet generally catches its allowance, or very near to it, by the time the season closes. Getting so close to the limit may seem like a bad thing, but it is taken as an indicator of success. A lot of what we know about fish populations is based on industry data about where, when and how many fish are captured, and how old those fish are. However, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing are estimated to be as large as a fifth of the legal commercial harvest worldwide. For that very reason, the Peruvian government polices all commercial fisheries very tightly: in 2024 alone it undertook 163,000 inspections, and confiscated 1,000 tonnes of illegally harvested anchoveta.
If all these efforts work out as planned, then when a fishery hits the quota in a fishing season, it means (at least in theory) that the industry is accurately reporting their operations, the stock assessment was more or less correct, and the regulators and inspectors are doing their jobs. The alternative – a quota that is never reached – might at first glance seem better, but would be very bad news if the whole fleet was out there and couldn’t find enough fish to meet the allowance. This has happened before, most famously during what fisheries expert Dean Bavington calls the “managed annihilation” of Atlantic cod. For centuries, cod had made Newfoundland’s Grand Banks one of the planet’s most productive fisheries. By the time the fishery collapsed completely in the early 1990s, the absurdly high quota didn’t matter because the boats couldn’t find anywhere near enough fish to meet it. The oceans had been emptied; the cod were gone.
In contrast to Newfoundland, Peru’s fisheries managers decided to protect the anchoveta population, despite pressure from an industry that has a lot of sway with the government and is increasingly concentrated in the hands of massive corporations, foreign and domestic. (In November 2024, the Canadian conglomerate Cooke Incorporated paid $1bn for Copeinca, the largest anchoveta firm in Peru. Cooke now controls a sixth of Peru’s anchoveta fishery, and a fifth of its meal and oil processing.) Corporate power like that doesn’t take massive revenue losses lying down. When the government delayed the start of the fishing season in 2023, the CEO of an anchoveta conglomerate moaned that regulators were “lost in a sea of ignorance”, creating an existential crisis for an industry that was “fighting to survive”. At that point, the ministry budged a little, and temporarily reopened the fishery. This year, it held firm: “Sustainability takes precedence over any short-term decision,” Juan Carlos Requejo, the minister of production, said in mid-August.
The stakes are enormous. Peru’s fisheries sector contracted by almost 75% in June and July, and fishmeal production is plummeting just as prices have skyrocketed to almost $3,500 a tonne, more than twice what they were at the same time last year. The same is true of all the fisheries for high-value species that prey on anchoveta: the bonito, jack mackerel and the rest of the bigger torpedo-shaped beauties that bring in premium prices.
The privatisation of the Peruvian anchoveta fishery began in 1992 and culminated in the introduction of a vessel quota system under the guidance of the World Bank in 2009. The creation of private property rights in the fishery has had complex repercussions, not least the increasing marginalisation and impoverishment of tens of thousands of smaller-scale fishers and their communities. Almost all the anchoveta catch is controlled by a collection of wealthy boat owners and big firms with close ties to the state.
Monitoring is continuous, sophisticated and data-driven. The idea is to operate a sensitive, real-time regulatory regime based on the assumption that there is no longer any such thing as “normal” – and there isn’t. Every day of the anchoveta season, Peru’s ministry of production pays close attention to scientists’ advice and is ready to step in, not just to end the season altogether but to make tweaks on the fly, for example ordering temporary closures of local fishing zones.
In August, the ministry declared a national fisheries and aquaculture emergency, which included launching a marine survey, Operation Eureka LXXVIII, to undertake an intensive stock assessment coordinated with the largest vessel owners. The outcome has not yet been officially announced, but in early October, Diario de Chimbote, the newspaper of Peru’s main fishing port (one of the largest in the world), reported that 2026’s second season will be cancelled entirely: the water is too warm, forcing the anchoveta in deeper and closer to shore, and the risks to juveniles are too great. Though this decision has not been confirmed, if it goes ahead, the closure is expected to cost Peru’s economy about $1.4bn. As Jessica Luna, president of Peru’s National Fisheries Society, an industry organisation, put it, the sector is “in the ICU”.
Prior to these most recent calamities, many industry observers have noted that by some measures, Peru’s management of fish populations is a remarkable success story, all the more impressive in light of the way that multinational capital often gets what it wants in similar situations. In the past 20 years, the see-sawing catch numbers that plagued the industry for so long have declined considerably. But so too have average harvests, and the trend is decidedly downward. In the midst of what has been called a “Godzilla” El Niño, it is worth reconsidering what counts as success in a world in which crisis has become normal. Is the goal just a slightly slower road to the same destination?
So far, despite everything, the anchoveta keep coming back, albeit in drastically diminished numbers compared with a few decades ago. It does sometimes seem as though they can survive whatever we throw at them, and their persistence can easily be mistaken for indestructibility. But there are limits to the robustness of any species or natural system. The fact that we don’t know where those limits are doesn’t mean they aren’t there, and as we push the anchoveta, and so much of the planet, we inevitably press upon fragilities we never knew were there, sometimes because until very recently they probably weren’t. Many of our leaders would have us believe that we can continue as before, but we have never been here before, and we need to proceed with modesty and care. Often, you only recognise a threshold once you have crossed it.

Architecture Between Land and Water: Design Lessons from the Bayou
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

A bayou is a slow-moving body of water, typically a creek or river that winds through low, flat terrain in a broader wetland landscape. Found throughout the Gulf Coast, bayous are distinct from swamps, which contain forested wetlands characterized by standing water, and from marshes, where tall grasses and herbaceous plants grow in saturated soils. The currents of a bayou landscape support biodiverse ecosystems of plants, trees, insects, birds, and fish, while the shifting water levels, saturated ground, humid air, heavy rainfall, and long, hot summers create a blurry environment between land and water, wet and dry, interior and exterior.
Communities have inhabited bayou environments for thousands of years, and the architectural language within them reflects generations of adaptation to unique environmental and hydrological conditions. Buildings are elevated above wet, flood-prone grounds with steep roofs and deep overhangs to shed rain and provide shade, while porches, courtyards, breezeways, and tall interior spaces move air through occupied spaces. Certain aesthetic characteristics, like earth-toned materials or broad front porches, will recur throughout the region, but beneath these elements lies a more consequential architectural logic. Bayou architecture patterns historically accommodate this variability, negotiating water, heat, humidity, and airflow through the way buildings meet the ground, shape their envelopes, and organize the spaces between inside and outside.
From Houston, often referred to as the Bayou City, to New Orleans and the landscapes of southern Louisiana, the following lessons demonstrate how accumulated local knowledge continues to inform contemporary design in the twenty-first century. As architects design for places where established climatic conditions are becoming less predictable, these projects offer a perspective on architecture with a careful observation of place and respond through adaptation. Foundations, roofs, envelopes, landscapes, and social spaces become part of an environmental strategy, revealing how vernacular knowledge translates into contemporary architecture and how buildings respond to the landscapes they inhabit.
How to Touch the Ground
In bayou environments, the ground is not a reliable foundation. High water tables, poorly drained soils, periodic inundation, and the movement of water through the landscape leave the ground saturated for extended periods, while storms and seasonal flooding raise the water beyond its ordinary limits. The first architectural question is how to touch the ground.
Across the region, buildings respond by rising above it. Slender piers and stilts allow water and air to pass beneath a structure, while more substantial columns, raised foundations, and elevated plinths keep occupied spaces above anticipated flood levels. The appropriate approach depends on soil conditions, flood exposure, building scale, and program, but the underlying principle remains the same. The foundation is treated as a negotiated edge between architecture and a landscape whose conditions are expected to change seasonally.
How to Move Air
In a hot, humid climate, an essential component of interior comfort will depend on creating sustained air movement. Courtyards, deep porches, breezeways, and other shaded thresholds extend the building outward while drawing air deeper inside. When oriented and proportioned for the scale of the building, courtyards encourage cross-ventilation through adjacent rooms and allow warm air to rise through the open space above, while vegetation and shade reduce solar exposure within the interior courtyard surfaces. Openings in the building envelope positioned across from one another strengthen air movement, allowing prevailing breezes to pass through the building through skylights, open doors or windows, and courtyards.
Deep porches perform a complementary role in drawing air movement. By shading walls and windows from direct sun, they reduce the amount of heat absorbed by the building envelope, while their depth protects doors and operable windows from rainfall, allowing them to stay open through rainy weather conditions. Porches, whether they wrap the entire building or frame the primary entrances, create a thicker, more adaptable boundary threshold between inside and outside, one that tempers sun, rain, and moving air. In the bayou, the edge of a building is an inhabitable space that helps the architecture adjust to changing conditions throughout the day and across the seasons.
How to Shed Water
In a landscape defined by frequent, intense rainfall, the roof is one of a building's most consequential environmental systems. Vernacular builders across the bayou region respond with pitched roofs and deep overhangs that move water quickly away from interior spaces while shading the walls below and protecting openings from sun and rain. The dogtrot house offers a clear example of a single pitched roof that extends across two enclosed volumes and the open breezeway between them, sheltering the passage from rainfall while creating a shaded corridor through the center of the home where air can circulate.
Contemporary architects continue this logic, using shed roofs, folded planes, butterfly forms, and clustered gables to direct rainfall, collect water, frame views of the surrounding landscape, and extend protective canopies over the porches below. Not every building in a wet climate requires the same roof form, but the movement of water is essential to shape the form and orientation throughout the design process. Roof geometry, overhangs, gutters, drainage, and collection systems work together to determine where water falls and how it returns to the ground. In this way, the roof gives architectural expression to environmental forces, turning practical decisions of managing rainfall into the building's identity.
How to Design with Moisture
In the persistent humidity of the bayou, materials and wall assemblies must release moisture, allowing walls, roofs, and other exposed surfaces to dry before prolonged dampness leads to mold or corrosion. Traditional builders relied on durable and decay-resistant materials, such as cypress, brick, and stucco, while contemporary projects expand this palette with metal cladding, fiber cement, and other materials selected for their ability to withstand repeated exposure to moisture. Ventilated rainscreens extend this logic into the construction of the wall, creating a drained and ventilated cavity behind the exterior cladding where water escapes and air circulates.
Shutters, louvers, jalousie windows, transoms, and screens are tools of operable assemblies that create adjustable layers between occupied spaces and the exterior, allowing buildings to admit breezes when conditions are favorable, reduce solar exposure during the hottest times of the day, and provide protection when storms arrive. Contemporary construction balances operability with the demands of moisture control, airtightness, and mechanical conditioning. The designers in this environment create a building envelope that is capable of responding to humid conditions.
How to Design for Heat
In the bayou climate, heat and humidity reinforce one another, making the control of solar heat gain essential to maintaining comfortable interior spaces. Light-colored exterior walls and reflective roofing materials reduce the amount of solar energy absorbed by the building envelope, while shade from deep eaves, porches, vegetation, and adjacent structures limit direct exposure in the interior spaces. These strategies are relatively simple, but they effectively reduce the thermal burden placed on occupants and mechanical cooling systems during the long, hot summers that characterize the region. Inside, tall ceilings increase the volume of space above occupants and allow warmer air to collect above, while clerestories, transoms, and high operable vents pull warm air outside. Even in compact floor plans, additional height creates a sense of openness while contributing to a more responsive interior.
How to Work with the Landscape
Site orientation reduces solar exposure, captures prevailing breezes, and determines interior daylight, but in cities and towns, existing street grids, neighboring structures, and zoning setbacks may limit the freedom to position a building. Even within restrictions, openings should be aligned with local wind patterns, western exposures should be shaded by trees, galleries, and deep eaves, and courtyards should be used to bring light and air into urban footprints. In a bayou environment, the site is part of a larger hydrological system. Permeable surfaces, bioswales, rain gardens, planted buffers, and areas designed to temporarily hold water will slow runoff and reduce the volume of water entering drainage systems. At a larger scale, preserving existing vegetation and maintaining connections to natural drainage patterns ensures a project participates in the hydrology of its surroundings.
How to Center Social Life
Perhaps the most compelling lesson of bayou architecture is that some of its most comfortable spaces are rarely found in the entirely enclosed, interior spaces. Deep porches, shaded courtyards, covered galleries, and dogtrot passages occupy the threshold between a controlled interior and the exposed landscape, offering long hours of shade and access to moving air. Their social value is inseparable from their environmental performance. Shade, airflow, and protection from rain make longer periods of occupation possible, while their position at the edge of the building creates opportunities for interaction that more clearly divided interior and exterior spaces may not provide. Climate-responsive design shapes how and how long people gather together, turning environmental infrastructure into social infrastructure.
Lessons from Architecture in the Bayou
The lessons of the bayou carry new weight in the contemporary practice because the landscape that shaped them is changing. Sea level rise, subsidence, coastal land loss, and increasing flood exposure alter the conditions under which communities across the Gulf Coast build and rebuild. Buildings rise above uncertain ground, envelopes open and close, landscapes hold or slow water, and air movement makes extreme climates more comfortable.
A changing climate exposes the limits of adaptation at the scale of an individual building. Architecture alone cannot indefinitely compensate for changing coastlines, subsiding land, disappearing wetlands, or increasing flood risk. Designing for the bayou asks architects to design beyond the building's boundary toward the larger systems that make inhabitation possible. The local knowledge embedded in bayou architecture is not a collection of historical solutions to reproduce, but a way of design-thinking to expand upon. Its larger lessons are of responsiveness and observation. In the bayou and far beyond it, place-based design considers the comfort, health, safety, and identity of future landscapes.

Europe’s debt map flips: Belgium borrows like Greece as France pays more than Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:57:13 UTC
12:57:13 KST

Eurozone treasuries are preparing record bond sales for 2027 just as the IMF warns that borrowing costs have hit a two-decade high.
Imagine an investor who fell asleep in the summer of 2012, at the height of the euro crisis, and woke up this morning. He would remember a simple map. In the north, a core of countries that borrowed cheaply, with Germany at the centre. In the south, a periphery of debtors – Greece, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Ireland – that paid dearly for the privilege of staying in the single currency. Fourteen years later, that map no longer describes the eurozone.
Belgium, home to the European Union institutions, now borrows for ten years at 4.29%. Greece, bailed out three times, pays 4.35%, almost the same rate. Portugal, rescued in 2011, pays less than Spain. Ireland, rescued in 2010, pays almost the same as the Netherlands. And France, which he remembered as part of the core, pays more than Italy.
The old periphery has moved north. That is the backdrop against which eurozone governments are about to ask investors for more money than ever before.
What moved the border
Bond yields are the interest rates a government pays to borrow. They rise when investors think a country will need more money than it can comfortably repay, and they fall when it proves the opposite. Greece has spent a decade proving the opposite.
In 2025, Athens ran a budget surplus of 1.7% of gross domestic product (GDP), and its debt, though still the highest in Europe, fell by more than nine percentage points of GDP in a single year.
“For years, when markets talked about sovereign risk in Europe, the focus was usually on the periphery,” Ken Egan, head of European sovereign credit at the rating agency KBRA, told Euronews.
Over the past decade, he said, those countries have followed more prudent fiscal policy, improved their primary balances, extended debt maturities, collected taxes better through digitalisation and rebuilt their banks.
“That has helped smooth refinancing risks and put debt on a much firmer path than 10 or 15 years ago.”
Belgium went the other way. Its deficit widened to 5.2% of GDP last year, larger than France’s 5.1% in the same year, and its debt rose above 109% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, and investors noticed.
“The traditional core has changed as well, but in a different direction,” Egan said.
“In some cases there is less clarity around the policy path, more political uncertainty, rising structural spending pressures and much higher refinancing costs than governments had become used to during the low-rate period.”
France’s position on the map is defined by one figure above all: the state spends 57.2% of everything the economy produces, the highest share in the G20. Debt has reached €3.6 trillion, or 119% of GDP, up from 98.2% before the pandemic.
The bill due in 2027
On 29 September, the French Treasury set out how much it will need to borrow next year: €340 billion in medium- and long-term bonds, a record, equal to about 11% of GDP and up from €310 billion this year.
Much of it is not new spending but old debt coming back for refinancing, as bonds issued during the pandemic and the energy crisis mature.
Every euro of that debt is being renewed at a higher price.
France has paid an average interest rate of 3.55% on medium- and long-term bonds issued so far this year, up from 3.14% last year. Its annual interest bill is forecast to rise from €62.6 billion in 2026 to €72.9 billion in 2027, roughly a fifth of what the state collected in revenue last year.
That last number is the one investors now read first.
“Markets are looking much more closely at the fiscal story, and not just at how much governments are borrowing, but what they are borrowing for,” Egan said.
“Borrowing that supports investment and future growth is one thing; borrowing mainly to cover a rising interest bill is viewed quite differently.”
Germany is issuing a record €512 billion of securities this year, but to pay for defence and infrastructure, which is the kind of borrowing markets forgive.
Italy and Spain will each refinance several hundred billion.
And the IMF, in its latest World Economic Outlook, pointed to a detail that makes every government more exposed: in the G7 and Spain, nearly 30% of public debt now matures within a year, so a change in interest rates reaches the budget within months rather than decades.
Why sovereign yields keep rising
Between February and September, the average 10-year yield across the G7 rose by more than a full percentage point to its highest level in nearly two decades, the IMF’s fiscal chief Rodrigo Valdés and his deputy Era Dabla-Norris wrote this week.
The oil shock, persistent inflation and the money pouring into artificial intelligence all played a part. But at the centre, they wrote, are fiscal fundamentals: investors demand more to lend for ten years to governments that keep spending more than they collect.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has added to the cost, raising its deposit rate twice this year to 2.50% to contain inflation.
The German 10-year yield, the floor for the whole eurozone, has climbed from 2.64% in February to 3.45%. France’s has risen twice as fast and briefly touched 5% in early October, the widest gap with Germany since 2012.
The danger, Egan said, is that the market itself becomes part of the problem.
“A political headline or weak budget can push the curve higher, refinancing becomes more expensive, fiscal space narrows, and the market then has another reason to demand a higher premium.”
That loop turns faster than it used to, because the buyers have changed.
For a decade the ECB bought government bonds with newly created money; now it lets them run off.
“There is less natural long-duration demand in the market, with central banks stepping back, pension demand changing and more of the marginal buying coming from price-sensitive investors,” Egan said. Higher energy prices, he added, make it worse by “weakening growth while keeping inflation and rates higher”.
The IMF describes the result in one sentence: in a growing number of countries, the interest rate on new debt is now higher than the growth rate of the economy.
When that happens, debt rises on its own unless the government runs a surplus before interest.
Most of Europe does not. “The more countries wait, the more painful the adjustment becomes,” the Fund wrote.
Is this 2012 again?
Not yet, says Lombard Odier. The Swiss bank’s investment office argues that markets are “pricing uncertainty rather than the conditions for a new sovereign debt crisis”. France’s interest payments remain affordable, at slightly above 2% of GDP, half Italy’s.
Its current account deficit is small, and it does not depend on foreign money the way Portugal, Spain and Greece did in 2012, when they imported capital worth 7% to 12% of their economies every year.
The bank’s forecast is dull rather than dramatic: French spreads stay wide until a credible budget passes parliament, probably not before the May 2027 presidential election, and the euro drifts lower, to $1.09.
Clara Raposo, vice-governor of the Banco de Portugal, offered a different warning this month.
Sovereign bond markets, she said, have become more sensitive to inflation, fiscal doubts and geopolitics, and shocks now spread faster from one country to another, amplified by funds that sell first and ask questions later.
“Trust may be intangible, but its economic consequences are real,” Raposo said.
Your debt, my inflation
The transmission is not only financial.
A randomised experiment with German firms in the Bundesbank’s panel, which surveys roughly 7,000 firms, published by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) earlier this year, found that half of them think the ECB will hold back on rate rises to protect weaker treasuries.
When researchers showed them a pessimistic forecast for the average debt-to-GDP ratio of France, Italy and Spain, the firms raised their expectations for German inflation three years ahead by 1.4 percentage points among those who distrust the ECB.
Fiscal stress in one member state, in other words, can raise inflation expectations in another, and the channel is trust.
In 2012, the question was whether the periphery could pay. In 2027, the question is who, exactly, the periphery is.

U.S. inflation accelerates in September amid high prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:54 CST
12:54:54 KST

WASHINGTON, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- U.S. inflation accelerated in September, according to data released Wednesday by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) jumped a hefty 3.7 percent year on year, exceeding Wall Street estimates of 3.6 percent and rising from the previous month's 3.4 percent.
Headline inflation increased by 0.6 percent month on month, driven primarily by a 9.1 percent surge in gasoline prices, according to the data.
Core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, also ticked up, climbing 2.6 percent over the last 12 months.
Price increases for shelter, car repairs and medical services rose at a time when Americans have been reeling from price hikes since inflation took hold in 2021.
Some experts noted that inflation is ramping up rather than tamping down.
Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua, "Inflation is getting higher, not lower and it's in the core, not just energy ... If you're the Fed looking to hit a 2 percent target, you're going the wrong way."
The news caused markets to drop on Wednesday, on fears that a rate cut is even further off than investors had expected. Some experts said the Fed would have to raise rates to get inflation down.
Gary Hufbauer, a nonresident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said "the outlook is for continued high PCE inflation, near 4 percent. To push the rate down, the Fed needs to increase the policy rate to near 5 percent."
Meanwhile, the midterm elections are just around the corner and Republicans are expected to take the brunt of voters' blame for high prices.
Some experts noted that inflation remains a risk to the GOP, the party in power.
Brookings Institution Senior Fellow Darrell West said "inflation remains painfully high and that poses serious risks for Republicans in November."
However, even if Democrats grab control of Congress, prices are unlikely to come down this year.
While halting the Iran war could bring down energy prices, addressing underlying inflation would require significant interest rate hikes, an unlikely move by the Fed given concerns that aggressive tightening could trigger an economic downturn. ■

8 U.S. states sue OpenAI over alleged ChatGPT safety risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:42 CST
12:54:42 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Attorneys general from eight U.S. states filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday, accusing the artificial intelligence company of endangering children through its ChatGPT chatbot and misleading consumers about the product's safety.
The lawsuits were filed independently in state courts by Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana, as part of a coordinated bipartisan legal effort.
According to statements released by the state attorneys general and court filings, OpenAI allegedly designed ChatGPT to be overly agreeable and to simulate human compassion, encouraging users to develop trust in the chatbot and spend more time interacting with it.
The lawsuits allege that ChatGPT can reinforce delusional thinking, provide dangerous medical advice and, in some instances, encourage users to harm themselves or others.
The states accuse OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT's safety while failing to adequately disclose known risks, in alleged violation of state consumer protection laws.
The lawsuits seek court orders requiring OpenAI to modify ChatGPT's operations and strengthen user protections, as well as civil penalties and damages.
Some of the legal demands also seek to restrict the development of self-improving AI models unless their alignment with human values can be demonstrated.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had implemented age-specific safety measures, including parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections.
The company would continue working with experts to strengthen safeguards and cooperate with states on developing AI policies applicable to the broader industry, Pusateri said.
The coordinated legal action follows a lawsuit filed by Florida's attorney general in June over alleged safety risks associated with ChatGPT. ■

CHANGCHUN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The flame lantern was carried into the Changchun History and Culture Museum on Wednesday morning, past a crowd gathered in the cold. It had come from Turin, Italy, where the flame was kindled on October 8 at the birthplace of the Universiade.
Its destination was Changchun, capital of northeast China's Jilin Province and co-host with neighboring Jilin City of the 2027 Winter Universiade.
Inside, 12 people waited to pass the lantern from hand to hand. They were chosen not for fame but for their work in the city, including a firefighter, a delivery courier, a student, a pilot, a police officer, a bank clerk, an insurance claims worker and a WorldSkills award winner. Organizers said the selection was intended to show that the flame belongs to everyone who helps build the city.
The last of the 12 to receive the lantern was Zhou Yang, a three-time Olympic short track speed skating champion. She then passed it to Changchun Mayor Gu Gang.
"The flame is very warm," Zhou said. "It represents athletes' burning dreams. The weather is cold today, so it feels warm. But it traveled thousands of miles from Turin to Changchun. This lantern is a heavy honor."
Zhou competed at the 2007 Asian Winter Games in Changchun and the 2009 Harbin Winter Universiade, where she won the 1,500m title. She said the Universiade gave her confidence ahead of the 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics, where she won two gold medals.
"For me, it's a kind of inheritance," she said of going from competitor to flame bearer. "When I was a competitor, I received the baton from my predecessors. Now I've become a passer."
Among the 12 was Nilava Darya, a Belarusian sophomore majoring in Chinese language education at Jilin International Studies University, who will volunteer at the Games.
"I feel very excited and proud to witness and participate in this flame event," she said. "I welcome young people from all over the world to Changchun."
Darya said Changchun is quieter than other Chinese cities she has visited, and warmer. "I can say it's my second hometown," she said.
In the audience was 90-year-old Gao Xiangchen, who learned to skate as a child and took up figure skating at 65. He continued until he was 83, when his family persuaded him to stop.
"I'm so excited that a world-class winter sports event like the Universiade will be held in Changchun," he said. "I will definitely go watch in person. My favorite sport is figure skating."
His daughter, Gao Yan, was a volunteer at the 11th National Winter Games in 2008 and a torchbearer for the 2008 Beijing Olympics. She said the arrival of the flame symbolized both sportsmanship and Changchun's ice and snow culture.
The flame was collected in Turin, where the first Summer Universiade was held in 1959. Since 2018, Turin has been home to FISU's "Flame of Knowledge," and the flame for each Universiade is kindled there before being taken to the host city.
"The lighting of the 'Flame of Knowledge' in Turin always represents a strong link between the birthplace of the Universiade and the future host," said FISU President Leonz Eder, who attended the collection ceremony.
The 33rd Winter Universiade will run from January 15 to 25, 2027. It will be the first Winter Universiade held in China since Harbin in 2009, following the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics and the 2025 Harbin Asian Winter Games.
Changchun 2027 will feature 97 events across 12 sports. Freestyle skiing will be the only snow sport staged in both host cities. All competition venues are existing facilities being upgraded, while 8,100 volunteer candidates have been recruited.
Nan Chunhua, an executive with the Games' large-scale activities department, was a member of the team that traveled to Turin for the collection ceremony. She said the flame's journey served as a bridge between the two cities.
"When the flame was successfully introduced into the lantern, I was very excited and moved," she said. "This flame carries the hard work of the entire preparation team and the good wishes of the world for the Changchun Universiade."
After the lantern was passed among the 12 representatives, it was used to light the Games' torch, named "Jixiang," or "Auspicious Soaring." Jilin provincial governor Hu Yuting then lit the cauldron, "Zhuxue Yangyan," which translates roughly as "Chasing Snow, Raising Flame."
For Zhou, the message was simple.
"I hope China's sports, especially winter sports, will get better and better," she said. "I hope athletes coming to Changchun will feel the warmth of the people here." ■

Australia's unemployment rate rises to 4.7 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:29 CST
12:54:29 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Australia's unemployment rate rose to 4.7 percent in September, as employment fell and more people became unemployed, official statistics showed on Thursday.
The number of employed people fell by 39,000, while the number of unemployed people increased by 9,000, Sean Crick, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) head of labor statistics, said in a statement.
The employment-to-population ratio fell 0.3 percentage points to 63.6 percent, while the participation rate fell 0.2 percentage points to 66.8 percent, Crick said.
The underemployment rate, which measures people who want and are available to work more hours, rose 0.1 percentage points to 6.3 percent, according to the latest data.
Part-time hours worked fell 1.5 percent in September, while full-time hours increased 0.4 percent, Crick said.
On a trend basis, which the ABS recommends for assessing underlying labor market conditions, the trend unemployment rate remained at 4.6 percent. Trend employment grew by 0.1 percent, while hours worked remained steady in trend terms in September, statistics showed.
Annual growth in employment and hours worked stood at 1.2 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, the ABS said. ■

Zaporozhye NPP has enough fuel for backup generators — spokesperson

12:50:46 KST

MELITOPOL, October 15. /TASS/. The Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) has enough fuel for its backup generators if they are needed, ZNNP’s Spokesperson Yevgenia Yashina told TASS.
"The Zaporozhye NPP has a supply of diesel fuel to feed the backup diesel generators if necessary. How many days this supply will last depends on the equipment's operating mode, the number of generators operating simultaneously, and the load on them. Fuel consumption can vary significantly depending on the current power supply configuration and the plant's needs," she said, adding that this is why it would be impossible to say how long the ZNPP will be able to operate autonomously using diesel generators.
Diesel generators supply the ZNPP with electricity, in particular to cool the reactors, when external power is lost.
Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev said earlier that during the period of escalation, the ZNPP lost external power 26 times. Meanwhile, Yashina told TASS that the situation regarding logistics and the delivery of cargoes to the ZNPP, including diesel fuel for backup generators, remains extremely difficult due to ongoing attacks by Ukrainian troops on the roads leading to the facility and on transport vehicles.
On October 9, International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi expressed concern over the lack of diesel fuel supplies to the ZNPP. According to him, reserves’ depletion adds to the risk of nuclear safety problems when another external power outage occurs.

Milei made the appeal on Wednesday at a Hispanic Heritage gala in Washington, where a Hispanic association gave him an award, ahead of November’s vote.
Conservatives, he said, “cannot give an inch in our reconquest of the hemisphere”, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).
Milei flew into the US capital on Wednesday for meetings with investors and the gala. He is due to address the US Chamber of Commerce on Thursday.
Milei’s lifeline
Trump firmly backed Milei a year ago, when his government also faced crucial legislative elections. He has called Milei his “favorite president”.
That backing, together with a currency swap agreement with the US Treasury, helped Milei to success in those polls, analysts have argued.
The centrepiece of the package, announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, was a $20bn swap with Argentina’s central bank, in which the US exchanged dollars for pesos. The swap came shortly after Milei’s party lost a key provincial election.
Trump made clear at the time that the support hinged on a Milei victory. “I’m with this man because his philosophy is correct,” he said ahead of a White House lunch with the Argentine leader. “If he wins, we’re staying with him. And if he doesn’t win, we’re gone.”
Trump also warned that the US would not be “generous” if Milei lost. The remarks unsettled Argentine markets, with the main stock index giving up earlier gains and falling about 2 percent, The Associated Press reported.

From resources to technology: What Kazakhstan-Belgium talks in Astana revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:42:51 UTC
12:42:51 KST

From resources to technology: What Kazakhstan-Belgium talks in Astana revealed
At the invitation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Kazakhstan hosted King Philippe of the Belgians and Queen Mathilde on their first state visit to the country. The occasion made history as the first visit by a reigning Belgian monarch to Central Asia. Its significance extended far beyond protocol: the visit opened a new chapter in relations, reinforcing Astana’s role as Europe’s strategic partner in energy, critical minerals, transport and innovation. A Qazinform News Agency correspondent examines the opportunities the visit presents and the additional political momentum it brings to established ties.
“L’union fait la force”
Belgium has firmly established itself as one of Kazakhstan’s key economic partners. In 2025, it became the country’s fifth-largest investor, while total Belgian investment over the past two decades exceeded $15.2 billion. Bilateral trade also continues to show steady momentum, reaching $582.8 million in 2025. These figures confirm that cooperation is developing beyond raw materials into areas where technological and logistical expertise matters.
The history of Kazakhstan-Belgium relations also includes memorable milestones that add cultural and symbolic context. Belgian astronaut Frank De Winne travelled into orbit from Baikonur twice, writing Kazakhstan into Europe’s shared space history and making the cosmodrome part of the collective memory of cooperation.
This is why Belgium’s national motto, “L’union fait la force,” meaning “Unity is strength,” resonates so naturally with the Kazakh saying “Birlik bar zherde tirlik bar,” or “Where there is unity, there is life.” The shared values expressed in these sayings provide a foundation for friendship and a new phase of cooperation. The monarch’s historic visit reinforced Kazakhstan’s status as a reliable European partner and opened a new chapter in relations between the two countries.
“Europe is undergoing a major realignment in its relations with Central Asia, and the Belgian monarch’s visit clearly confirmed this process. Brussels openly declared its intention to diversify its partnerships and strengthen ties with Kazakhstan as Central Asia’s largest economy. The Middle Corridor, digitalization, artificial intelligence, education and medicine are increasingly prominent on the European agenda. This broadening range of interests is making our country a leader in the regional architecture and a key hub through which Europe builds its dialogue with Central Asia. King Philippe’s visit therefore became a kind of test of Europe’s renewed interest in Kazakhstan. The monarch, as the saying goes, is paving the way for further technology and business contracts,” says political scientist Boris Polomarchuk.
From Caspian ports to digital hubs
Kazakhstan can indeed offer much more today than raw materials alone. This includes access to the Middle Corridor, digital solutions, artificial intelligence projects, and educational and medical initiatives. Europe understands the considerable value of a stable and predictable partner it can rely on for long-term projects during a period of geopolitical uncertainty.
The business component of the royal couple’s visit therefore demonstrated that the focus was on concrete agreements capable of changing the nature of bilateral cooperation.
An equally important outcome was the agreement on developing transport and logistics infrastructure. Its focus is the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, where Kazakhstan intends to draw on the experience of the Port of Antwerp-Bruges, one of Europe’s largest logistics hubs. Discussions during the visit addressed establishing a direct partnership between Antwerp-Bruges and Kazakhstan’s ports of Aktau and Kuryk, including the introduction of smart port technologies and specialist training.
According to Boris Polomarchuk, a distinct strategic rationale is now taking shape around the Middle Corridor. It is more than a transport route; it is part of a broader European strategy to diversify trade routes between Europe and Asia.
“The connections look impressive: Kazakhstan’s ports of Aktau and Kuryk, access to the Caspian Sea, then the Caucasus and Türkiye, and from there to Europe, including Antwerp, one of the world’s largest logistics hubs. This creates a potential Eurasian supply chain in which Kazakhstan plays a key role,” the expert says.
When agreements are endorsed at the highest level, they send a signal to businesses. As the expert emphasizes, the involvement of European companies in this route accelerates integration.
In critical minerals, the parties agreed to move from raw materials trade towards establishing joint processing facilities. Kazakhstan produces 18 of the 34 critical raw materials identified by the EU, while Belgium has expertise in the chemical industry and metallurgy. Joint projects in metal processing and industrial component manufacturing will help build resilient production chains for the European market and strengthen Kazakhstan’s position as a supplier of both resources and finished products.
“The transition from predominantly raw materials trade to joint production with higher added value appears promising. This includes metal processing, industrial component manufacturing and the development of resilient production chains for the European market,” comments Alisher Abdrashev, a leading expert in the Department of European and American Studies at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan.
The political scientist considers the agreements reached on industrial cooperation and investment another important outcome of the visit.
“The presence in Kazakhstan of Belgian companies such as Jan De Nul, Sarens and Ahlers Logistics already provides a foundation for expanding cooperation. The most promising areas are infrastructure construction, mechanical engineering, petrochemicals, industrial equipment manufacturing and the introduction of modern engineering solutions. Priority should be given to projects involving local production, the training of Kazakh specialists and technology transfer,” says Alisher Abdrashev.
A separate set of agreements covers digitalization and innovation. In the future, this cooperation could also extend to the space sector, where Belgium’s expertise in satellite technologies complements Kazakhstan’s capabilities in space infrastructure.
“Astana and Brussels have complementary capabilities in AI, industrial automation, cybersecurity and the digital management of urban infrastructure. In September 2026, discussions addressed the possibility of establishing a partnership between the Belgian technology hub The Beacon and Astana Hub. Its practical value lies in implementing joint technology projects, startup exchanges and the introduction of digital solutions in industry and logistics,” the expert says.
Science creates the future, culture builds trust
However, financial and technological contracts gain real substance only when supported by a strong foundation in science and education. More than ten agreements were also signed with universities in Antwerp, Ghent, Hasselt, Leuven, Howest and Mons at the Kazakhstan-Belgium Rectors’ Forum, “Artificial Intelligence: Higher Education and Scientific Research.”
These agreements establish a sustainable academic platform, provide access to European research networks and create conditions for training specialists capable of working on an equal footing with their European colleagues.
Cooperation in science and education is particularly significant. A joint AI Math Lab is being established at the Alem.AI international center under the EU’s Horizon Europe program.
The humanitarian dimension of King Philippe’s visit to Kazakhstan offered important confirmation that bilateral relations extend beyond economics and politics. The rectors’ forum demonstrated that university cooperation is moving beyond a simple student exchange model. The focus today is on establishing joint laboratories, research groups and international projects, promoting academic mobility for both students and faculty, and training specialists to a new standard.
“Culture was long considered secondary, yet it creates the trust that diplomatic notes cannot secure. The exhibition of Belgian modernist James Ensor in Astana and a contemporary dance project in Almaty became symbols of the connection between heritage and modernity. Cultural diplomacy creates a space where societies begin to discover one another directly, without politicians acting as intermediaries,” says Boris Polomarchuk.
The cultural and humanitarian program of the royal couple’s visit to Kazakhstan took on particular significance during their visit to the National Center for Children’s Rehabilitation in Astana. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde learned about the institution’s work in providing comprehensive medical, psychological, educational and social support to children with various developmental disorders.
Queen Mathilde showed sincere interest in these initiatives. She spoke with children and their parents, listened attentively to medical specialists and took part in the center’s interactive program.

The royal couple’s visit outlined a broad portfolio of agreements, ranging from agricultural technologies and logistics to science and digital innovation. Their practical value lies in Kazakhstan gaining both investment and expertise that will remain within the country, supporting long-term development and translating Europe’s attention into concrete strategic partnership projects.
The Astana leg of the visit demonstrated Kazakhstan and Belgium’s determination to broaden the economic foundation of their relations. Resources and trade flows, technology, scientific expertise and production are central to the agreements. The extent to which this approach changes the structure of the partnership will be demonstrated by the projects that follow the agreements reached at the highest level.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan could begin exporting pineapples to the US as early as February 2027, with administrative preparations complete and final import rules still pending from US authorities, Agriculture Minister Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said Wednesday.
The US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) published a proposal outlining import requirements for Taiwanese pineapples in the Federal Register on March 3, per SET News. The public comment period has ended, but the US has yet to publish final rules.
Chen told reporters before a Legislative Yuan Economics Committee meeting that he hoped the US would finalize the requirements before Taiwan’s peak pineapple season, which runs from February through May. Initial shipments would primarily consist of the golden diamond variety, which accounts for more than 90% of Taiwan’s pineapple production.
Under the proposed rules, Taiwanese pineapples would be eligible for export after passing phytosanitary inspections, being confirmed free of pests of concern to the US, and receiving a phytosanitary certificate, SET News reported. The requirements would not mandate irradiation, vapor heat treatment, or removal of the fruit’s crown.
The proposal would allow pineapple varieties in the Cayenne group, including golden diamond and mango pineapples. The Agriculture Ministry plans to continue encouraging farmers to grow mango pineapples because they are better suited to storage and transportation.
According to the Agriculture Ministry’s latest statistics, Taiwan exported 15,700 metric tons of pineapples to Japan this year, per UDN. Shipments to Canada, South Korea, and Australia rose by nearly 409%, 171%, and 29%, respectively, while Taiwan also expanded into markets including New Zealand, Singapore, and Malaysia.

Bay watch with first approval for 5 mainland yachts

Unknown Publisher

03:38:53 UTC
12:38:53 KST

Five yachts from the Greater Bay Area have received approval to enter Hong Kong waters as a new scheme facilitating such cross-border visits takes effect on Friday, according to Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat.
The scheme allows yacht masters across the border to sit for accreditation exams up north without needing to travel to Hong Kong and authorises mainland organisations to conduct the assessments.
Visiting yacht owners and masters can submit pre-arrival vetting information online, doing away with the need to do so with a visit to a district marine office.
Visiting yachts can berth freely at five designated anchorage areas: Stanley, Tai Tam and Repulse bays as well as Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung and Tai O.
Speaking on an RTHK radio programme on Thursday, Wong stressed that there was currently no need to cap daily yacht visits from the mainland.
“Across the five anchorage areas, we can accommodate up to 115 yachts measuring 40 metres in length," he said.
"So we believe we have sufficient berthing space for yachts to dock smoothly where they want. That’s why we really don't see any need for a quota for now.”
Wong noted that around 300 mainland yacht masters had completed the training and passed accreditation to operate in Hong Kong waters so far.
To ensure safety, he said, the department has set up a monitoring system to track the yachts.
The system will alert vessels if their automatic identification system malfunctions or if they accidentally enter restricted waters.
Wong added that patrols and enforcement action would also be strengthened in the designated anchorages for visiting yachts.

Healthy corals help bleached neighbours regain colour: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:32:00 UTC
12:32:00 KST

Healthy corals help bleached neighbours regain colour: Study
- Stanford scientists found healthy corals can help bleached corals recover when they touch for three to five days. The study was published in Science Advances on Oct 14.
- The effect comes from healthy symbionts moving between corals through fused tissue, creating a “nutrient highway”. Bleached corals were not a lost cause.
- The method only worked with the same genet, and mixed pairings caused stinging cells. Researchers now want to scale the idea by reintroducing symbionts to reefs.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The world’s coral reefs face an existential threat from rising seawater temperatures that trigger widespread bleaching, a problem driven by climate change and compounded by 2026’s intense El Nino phenomenon.
But a new lab study by scientists at Stanford University finds that simply placing healthy, colourful coral in contact with their bleached counterparts is enough to bring the dying ones back from the brink – a finding that could eventually pave the way for real-world interventions if it can be scaled.
“It’s stunning,” lead author Daniel Collins told AFP about the outcome of the experiments, recalling the “eureka moment” when he first saw positive results and rushed to his PhD supervisor’s office to share the news.
The paper was published on Oct 14 in the journal Science Advances.
Coral reef recovery is a highly active area of research, with efforts ranging from using artificial nurseries to rescue reefs to finding and cultivating more heat-tolerant species.
Bleached corals had been largely written off because of their high mortality rate, said Collins – though the new work instead demonstrates they “really shouldn’t be thought of as a lost cause”.
The Stanford team ran a series of tests with pairs of cauliflower corals, finding five days of contact between healthy and bleached fragments was all it took for the latter to mount a spectacular recovery, at which point they could be safely pried apart.
The key to the success of the method – which the team informally dubbed “helping hands” – is the transfer of healthy photosynthetic algae, also known as symbionts, from which corals derive their colour.
Corals are marine invertebrates made up of hundreds to thousands of tiny, soft-bodied organisms called polyps.
They have a mutualistic relationship with symbionts, which produce the vast majority of food the corals require, in return for shelter, as well as water and the carbon dioxide they need to photosynthesise.
But in times of heat stress, algae can produce toxins, forcing their hosts to expel them.
Collins said the idea for the experiment came from two sources.
The first was a study that showed plastic waste in the ocean can promote disease in corals by transferring harmful pathogens, which made him wonder whether it would be possible to flip that mechanism on its head with a health-promoting transfer.
The second was a happy accident observed by Stephen Palumbi, the study’s senior author, also at Stanford, who noticed in his lab that a healthy coral and bleached coral had tipped over and were touching each other, and the bleached coral had started to recover.
The scaling challenge
The experiments revealed important constraints.
Three days of contact was the minimum required for a bleached coral to begin to recover, and five ensured full recovery.
They also had to be in direct contact – a few millimetres apart, and nothing significant happened.
A major limitation was that the process worked only when the two corals shared the same genetic background, or “genet”.
Mixed-genet pairings resulted in the corals deploying stinging cells, a hostile response that can be likened to organ rejection in humans.
Powerful laser microscopy revealed the mechanism: After a day or two of contact, the corals’ tissues began fusing, creating a “nutrient highway” between the pair.
The biggest challenge will be translating an exciting lab finding into a real-world solution.
“We likely will not be touching corals to one another on reefs,” said Collins, noting the sheer size of reefs tends to preclude this option.
However, it is possible to extract healthy symbionts and culture them – and the team is now thinking about ways to re-introduce them en masse to bleached coral.
This also has the benefit of side-stepping the genetic mismatch problem, which applies to the corals, not the symbionts. AFP

OpenAI bugging suspect allegedly booked one-way trip to Saudi Arabia
Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan was due to fly to Saudi Arabia on October 12, US prosecutors say in a court filing.
The Saudi national accused of bugging OpenAI’s headquarters booked a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia before his arrest, US prosecutors have alleged.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, had been scheduled to fly to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member on October 12, prosecutors said in a court filing unsealed on Wednesday.
The FBI arrested Alfozan, who worked at OpenAI for about 15 months until his termination last week, on October 9, after OpenAI personnel reported the discovery of a hidden listening device in a conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters.
Alfozan, 35, has been charged with “using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications”.
The offence carries a maximum punishment of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
Prosecutors disclosed the alleged flight booking to a judge on October 8 in a motion seeking to seal the criminal complaint against Alfozan, arguing he had the “means – and will have an incentive – to flee” the United States.
William Pernik, Alfozan’s lawyer, said he and his client planned to contest the criminal allegations and his client’s ongoing detention in court.
“We trust that the American justice system will treat our client fairly, despite the narrative painted in the media at this time,” Pernik told Al Jazeera.
“Our client is a well regarded professional with long standing ties to the community,” Pernik added.
“He is presumed innocent and is entitled to fair treatment and due process of law. The emphasis on his national origin and therefore suggestions of lack of trustworthiness or flight risk harken back to dark chapters of our nation’s history that we intend to fight fully.”
Alfozan’s arrest has shone a spotlight on concerns that frontier tech firms are a target for spying and industrial espionage amid the global race to gain an upper hand in AI.
Before joining OpenAI in July last year, Alfozan worked as a systems engineer at Meta and interned at Microsoft, according to a LinkedIn profile in his name.
Alfozan is also listed as a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Riyadh-based venture capital firm whose other partners include Prince Khalid bin Bader al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family.
In a statement announcing Alfozan’s appointment in February 2025, Raed Ventures described the engineer as “a seasoned professional with extensive experience in tech startups” and said his role would involve “identifying promising investment opportunities and supporting startups on their journey toward growth and success”.
