White House spokesperson Katie Zacharia’s law career faces scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
01:35:40 UTC
10:35:40 KST

White House spokesperson Katie Zacharia’s law career faces scrutiny
Katie Zacharia has repeatedly claimed to be a lawyer, but critics question if she passed the bar exam to be licensed.
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary under United States President Donald Trump, has drawn increasing criticism over claims about her professional background.
On Wednesday, a public accountability nonprofit filed a complaint with the State Bar of California over Zacharia’s repeated claims that she was a lawyer.
If made falsely, such a claim is a crime in the state. According to Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile, she received a degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, but critics have questioned whether she received a licence to practise law, as she has suggested.
“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the head of the Washington, DC-based Campaign for Accountability, said in a statement. “Yet it seems it was all a lie.”
Her organisation filed the complaint with California’s bar office, a regulatory agency that oversees the licensing of lawyers.
“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” Kuppersmith said.
“The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”
Zacharia, a commentator who has appeared frequently on Fox News and Newsmax, began her term as White House press secretary on Tuesday.
In a news briefing that day, she seemed to falter and speak haltingly, sometimes having to repeat herself.
Her appearance was brief, lasting under 15 minutes. She spent much of her time at the podium thanking Trump for the opportunity and reading from a prepared statement.
“I have wanted to work for him for a very long time,” Zacharia said.
Later, she joined Trump outside the White House to speak further with reporters. When asked where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied, “When I moved to China.”
The response was an apparent reference to a three-year stint in which she claims she worked at a law firm in Beijing.
A biography on the website for the pro-Trump women’s organisation Trumpettes USA Inc says she “served as outside counsel” for the World Bank and International Finance Corporation while in Beijing.
Her LinkedIn profile, meanwhile, indicates Zacharia served as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. More recently, from 2024 to 2025, it lists her as general counsel for Fix California, a voter rights group started by a Trump administration official.
On her Instagram profile, Zacharia describes herself as a “Wife, Mom, & Lawyer”.
But Zacharia’s assertion that she passed the bar in China has fuelled media scrutiny. China’s equivalent of the bar exam, the notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination, can only be taken by Chinese citizens.
China has, on rare occasion, allowed foreigners to practise law in the country if they have several years of experience in their home countries first.
But that does not appear to be the case for Zacharia. According to media reports, Zacharia has not been found to be licensed as a lawyer in any state in the US.
In a statement to The Associated Press, Zacharia responded to the scrutiny by saying, “I practice international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.”
Since Trump’s return to office for a second term, Zacharia has spent several months as a communications adviser at the Department of Homeland Security.
Since June, she has also worked as the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns the Truth Social platform.

Trump suggests those who leak government information should ‘be shot’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

Trump suggests those who leak government information should ‘be shot’
The US president has long been unhappy with inside information about his administration being leaked to the media.
United States President Donald Trump has suggested that those who leak information to the news media should be shot as punishment.
Trump made the remarks at a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, as he urged supporters to vote in the November 3 midterm elections.
“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump told the crowd. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”
Trump made the statement in an apparent reference to Operation Midnight Hammer, which saw the US launch a surprise attack on Iran in June 2025 during the 12-day war between Israel and Iran.
In the aftermath of the attack, several media outlets published findings from a preliminary report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency.
That report – which had not yet been released to the public – indicated that Iran was able to move some of its enriched uranium away from the sites the US had bombed.
It also suggested that the extent of the damage to Iran’s nuclear facilities was more modest than what Trump had asserted.
Trump, however, appeared to signal that the timing of the US attacks was among the leaked information. He accused the news media of putting military members in danger, calling out The New York Times and CNN in particular.
“They leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving,” Trump said, claiming he had to reschedule the bombing campaign two days later as a result.
“Somebody leaked. Some sleaze-bag, they ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail.”
Trump has long had an adversarial relationship with the news media, and he has previously called for harsh punishment against any official who passes on confidential information to news outlets.
After parts of the Defense Intelligence Agency report became public, he blamed lawmakers in the Democratic Party for its release.
“The Democrats are the ones who leaked the information on the PERFECT FLIGHT to the Nuclear Sites in Iran,” Trump wrote on social media at the time. “They should be prosecuted!”
Under Trump, the White House has taken aggressive action to track down the source of leaks.
Staff in his administration, as well as officers in the military, have also been asked to take polygraph tests.
Journalists at several news outlets, including The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal, have also received subpoenas aimed at determining the sources of internal information made public.
The newspapers had reported on stories such as a botched Navy SEALs raid in North Korea and how Trump ignored internal Pentagon warnings against launching the Iran war.
Last year, the Department of Defense demanded that journalists who wished to access the Pentagon sign an agreement not to publish unauthorised material.
Much of the Pentagon press corps refused to agree, and a federal court struck down many of the new demands made on journalists at the department.
Trump has long raged against leakers, going back to his first term as president from 2017 to 2021.
Former White House official Alyssa Farah Griffin told a podcast in 2024 that Trump had called for leakers to be executed, after media outlets reported that he had taken shelter in a White House bunker during racial justice protests in 2020.
Trump appeared to reprise that sentiment in his speech to Arizona voters on Wednesday, less than three weeks before the November 3 midterms.
“Leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly,” Trump said. “To me, they are the scum of the earth.”

NEW DELHI: CJP members Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka have been sent to five days of judicial custody, while Ajinkya Shinde has been bound down, after 14 party members allegedly trespassed into Jantar Mantar, which is no longer a designated protest venue, and obstructed cops on duty. Bound down means an individual has to appear before an IO whenever called and inform cops before leaving the city.Police said the action was prompted by repeated alleged violations of law and concerns that accused could again disturb public peace.‘Concerns they were likely to breach peace’Police also feared that they could instigate others. DCP (New Delhi) Sachin Sharma said, “Police personnel deployed at the spot intervened and attempted to stop them. However, the protesters allegedly obstructed police personnel in the discharge of their official duties.” Subsequently, all the persons were bound down in the respective case as per law.The DCP said that in view of their alleged repeated attempts to disturb peace and violate the law, Ranka, Das, and Shinde were arrested under relevant preventive provisions.
“Their alleged attempts to instigate others via social media to engage in similar unlawful activities were also taken into consideration,” he added.The three were produced before the special executive magistrate, where proceedings under Sections 126 (security for keeping peace in other cases) and 170 (arrest to prevent commission of cognisable offences) of the BNSS were initiated. Police also submitted videos of CJP representatives jumping a gate and unfurling the flag at Jantar Mantar Tuesday. The court, considering the kalandra (preventive legal measure) details, in view of their repeated violations of law and serious apprehension that if released on bail, they will again violate law and instigate others, remanded Das and Ranka to five days of judicial custody. Special executive magistrate Mahesh Kumar Meena held that their conduct after being released earlier after executing personal and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each for maintaining peace and good behaviour showed they were likely to breach “peace and tranquillity”. The magistrate had directed them to “keep peace in the area for a period of one year from the date of order”. Their lawyer, Abhisht Hela, argued that an executive magistrate had no power to order judicial custody and said he would approach Delhi High Court.
Shinde was released on personal bond and surety of Rs 5,000. However, he was “bound down to maintain peace and good behaviour for six months”. Under Section 141 of BNSS, a magistrate can order the arrest and detention of a person found to have breached a peace bond executed under Section 136 for the remainder of the bond period. The matter has been listed for further inquiry on Oct 19.The FIR invokes sections 223, which deals with disobedience of an order duly promulgated by a public servant, 332 (house-trespass in order to commit an offence) and 61 (2) (criminal conspiracy) of BNS at Connaught Place police station.The second FIR was registered under sections 221 (obstructing public servant in discharge of his public functions), 115 (voluntarily causing hurt), 132 (assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty), 121 (voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty) and 3 (5) (common intention) of BNS at Parliament Street police station.

Ship catches fire in Romania’s waters amid rising attacks in the Black Sea
Authorities are investigating whether drones may have been involved in the latest incident.
A ship anchored in Romania’s territorial waters has caught fire and the crew has been evacuated, Romanian authorities said.
The incident comes amid growing concerns over hybrid attacks in the Black Sea involving Russia.

Multiple drones breached Romanian airspace on Wednesday near its border with Ukraine.
On Tuesday, two ships were hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.

Earlier shipping attacks

Some see incursions by Russian drones into eastern European airspace as a test of NATO and the European Union’s defences and response capabilities.
Romania, a NATO member, shares a land border with Ukraine. Since the Russia-Ukraine war started, drones have breached its airspace while mines floating in the Black Sea threaten key trade and energy routes.
Last Wednesday, Bulgaria’s President Iliana Iotova said she would invite Romania and Turkiye to consultations on ensuring the security of merchant ships in the Black Sea.

Conroy targets 'rot' in Defence after $15.6m bungle unmasked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
01:19:37 UTC
10:19:37 KST

Defence hit by $15.6m in missile contract blunders as Conroy targets 'rot'
In short:
Defence files have unmasked more than $15.6 million in unauthorised contractor payments within Australia's flagship missile program.
The government has conceded the errors and is using the compliance failures to justify greater oversight of spending.
What's next?
The program, known as Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance (GWEO) Group, will be folded into the new Defence Delivery Agency starting in July 2027.
Defence officials behind Australia's flagship missile program racked up at least $15.6 million in financial and procurement blunders, a freedom of information document shows, including paying out $13.3 million before securing basic legal sign-off.
The defence file exposes a pattern of basic accounting and administrative failures within the Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Group (GWEO), the $36 billion initiative designed to manufacture and stockpile advanced weapons and ammunition on Australian soil.
The federal government acknowledged the errors exposed in the document, with Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy telling the ABC: "We agree the rot has to stop."
The defence document shows the administrative errors included two payments of $8.1 million and $5.2 million, which were made in June 2023.
Officials paid out the money to cover contract price hikes before getting the mandatory legal approval required to increase the contract's value.
A further four transactions broke basic rules when staff went out to market to get quotes before getting required sign-off from their managers.
In another instance, officials broke spending rules on a $631,365 order by approving a bill that was higher than the allowed spending limit, then mistakenly filing the paperwork in Australian dollars instead of the foreign currency, distorting the exchange rate used.
The money represents a tiny fraction of the multi-billion-dollar defence procurement budget but it raises concerns about how the funds are handled.
There is no suggestion any of the money was lost, but Defence records make it clear the funds were spent "contrary to Defence procurement policy".
More breaches redacted from document
An unknown number of additional breaches and their costs were redacted from the document.
However, "yes" boxes confirm corrective action was required on at least eight additional occasions.
The paperwork also highlights broader procedural lapses across the program, including an August 2025 breach where staff relied on outdated spending rules, missing a policy change that dropped the manager sign-off threshold from $200,000 to $80,000.
The errors were only identified when a new contract management team conducted a review of previous transactions.
"The personnel involved in processing the escalation payment are no longer within the Contract Management Team," the Defence document said, explaining the current team reviewed the arrangement, identified the non-compliance, and formally reported it.
Officials ultimately granted retrospective approval to the $13.3 million in payments on July 10, 2025, about two years after the cash went out the door.
Mr Conroy used the ABC's revelations to justify the Albanese government's creation of the newly minted Defence Delivery Group to improve oversight, enforce tighter controls on contracts and get "more bang for the buck for taxpayers".
He also laid blame at the feet of the former Liberal government.
"The management of this contract, a legacy of the former government that outsourced important work to a legion of consultants and contractors, was just not good enough," he said.
"We agree the rot has to stop. That's why since coming to office, we have acted to ensure that the management of this contract is now done by Defence public servants.
"That's why we have ramped up investment in GWEO and made it a priority, which includes greater oversight of management of this contract."
The FOI document shows the unauthorised price-hike payments occurred in June 2023, more than a year after the Albanese government first took office.
Greens want accountability
Greens leader David Shoebridge, who is also the party's spokesperson on defence, said the issue highlighted deep issues with defence procurement.
"GWEO is one of the government's big-ticket items on defence spending. Questions need to be asked about who was held to account here," he said.
"The documents only say the 'personnel involved' have been moved on.
"In most cases in Defence, 'moved on' is code for promoted away from a problem.
"What is 100 per cent clear is that no-one in a leadership position has even been held to account."
A Defence spokesperson told the ABC the department took issues of non-compliance and transparency seriously.
"[It has] demonstrated this through proactive referrals, stronger controls, and increased oversight," they said.
Audit office looks into domestic munitions
The internal disclosures come amid an extensive, two-part investigation by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) into Defence's domestic munitions contracts.
The national audit body first exposed severe probity gaps and sole-sourcing failures in June 2024, before handing down a damning second report in July 2026 that criticised the GWEO enterprise for delivering "limited assurance" on value-for-money.
The government has committed between $26 billion and $36 billion over the next decade under the Integrated Investment Program to accelerate the GWEO enterprise.
GWEO is among the divisions set to be consolidated into the new Defence Delivery Agency, which will manage Australia's $56 billion annual defence spending from July 2027.
The initiative aims to curb costly project blowouts on major military assets.

Starlink, meanwhile, plays a crucial role in Ukraine’s defense against Russian Shahed drones, including interceptor drones that use satellite communications to reach incoming targets.

US lawmakers condemn restrictions as potentially aiding Russia
The tightening of Ukraine’s satellite communications access drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, with lawmakers questioning the consequences of limiting critical defensive capabilities during active Russian attacks.
The Congressional Ukraine Caucus, whose co-chairs include Democratic Representatives Marcy Kaptur and Mike Quigley and Republican Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson, issued a joint warning.
“We are alarmed by reports from Ukraine that US intelligence and Starlink support are being withheld, putting innocent civilians and American citizens in Ukraine at the mercy of Russian attacks,” the lawmakers said.
The caucus said Washington must continue providing intelligence to protect civilians and stressed that US allies pay for Ukraine’s Starlink access.
“Restrictions that put civilians in harm’s way are unconscionable and will not be accepted by Congress,” the lawmakers declared.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina also publicly challenged Musk, warning that intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself could be construed as helping a mass murderer.
Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska criticized the administration’s handling of intelligence-sharing and Starlink access, arguing that reducing such support effectively aided Russia’s invasion and its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Their objections underscored concern among Ukraine’s Republican supporters that the restrictions could weaken Kyiv’s defensive capabilities at a critical moment.
Democratic lawmakers also raised questions about the humanitarian and strategic consequences of restricting systems on which Ukrainian troops and civilians depend.

In an official statement, Hoyer said that if Trump administration officials were involved, it would represent a “heinous act of betrayal” of Ukraine and a fellow democracy under attack.

Musk responded by distinguishing between commercial Starlink and Starshield, the military-grade satellite service.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk wrote on X.
He said decisions about operational limits were ultimately made by the US military and the president.
Musk maintained that commercial Starlink service could be used for civilian and defensive purposes but should not support offensive military operations.
A senior US official, however, told Axios that the Trump administration had not been involved in imposing the restrictions. Ukrainian officials remained suspicious that the move was connected to Washington’s pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil facilities.
The conflicting accounts left unanswered who authorized the restrictions, and why they were introduced without warning.
Partial restoration leaves Ukrainian interceptors at risk
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov reported Wednesday evening that Starlink connectivity was being restored at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), although restrictions on the military-grade Starshield system remained in place.
Two Ukrainian officials told RFE/RL that connectivity had improved at speeds below that threshold, but the limits continued to complicate efforts to intercept Russia’s increasingly frequent jet-powered drones.
One Ukrainian source said the operating speed would need to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour) to effectively counter the faster Russian drones.

What I Learned From a Year of Interviewing a Thai Sex Worker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:53:00 UTC
09:53:00 KST

When I started interviewing a Thai sex worker named Ying for my recent book, I was initially looking for something far different from what I eventually wrote. I wanted sleaze: something raw and stimulating. I had wanted to write about a harlot, someone immoral, for whom money took precedence over all. I had expected to write about their greed, their lack of morals and the hypocrisy that arose from an industry surrounding a deeply religious society.
My assumptions were both critical and ignorant. In every way, I had already decided on the book I was going to write without attempting to understand the mechanics or psychology behind them. What I have since learned is about choices, and how few meaningful ones there were for someone caught between family obligation, economic status, and religion. What I learned was about the life of a tortured soul, fighting to make the best of what she had.
Ying had spent most of her adult life selling sex for a living, starting when she was 19 years of age. Like many girls around her, she had dreamed of a better life – one that seemed impossible for someone born into poverty with little education. Ying grew up in Thailand’s mostly agrarian northeast. She arrived in Bangkok at the age of 17, and began work in a restaurant, where she faced long hours and poor earnings with no hope of advancement. Alongside this, she became involved in sex work, present in every nook and cranny of Bangkok. As Ying told me, “There was no choice. It was the only way to earn enough for myself and my family.”
Of course, Ying knew what she was doing. She wasn’t coerced or forced. But still the question remains: what else was available to her? The economics of her situation were inescapable. Ying was earning 6,000 baht per month at a restaurant in the early 2000s. At her peak in the sex industry, she was making close to 80,000 baht each month. Her mother back home in Isan sold food by the road, making less than 200 baht per day. Her father was an odd-job laborer earning even less. For a family like hers, the difference was colossal.
Decades of research into Thailand’s illegal sex industry have long identified economic privation as a leading cause of entry into the trade, which offers substantially superior earnings than the agricultural, domestic, or other poorly paid forms of work available to women who come from rural provinces. Those findings do not apply to every woman in the sex industry, but they help us understand how seemingly voluntary decisions may be constrained in practice.
Another thing became clearer through the interviews. Customers were not buying sex; they were buying a performance. Ying had to convince customers she was interested in them. To make each man feel desirable. To fulfill their every desire, no matter how detestable. Each customer was its own enterprise, and she had to remember their every eccentricity in order to encourage their return. As the industry moved online through the years, women had to improve their skill sets, to understand how to digitally market themselves. To master the psychology of attraction, and the manner in which to exercise it. Ying explained, “You have to make every man like you, or he won’t come back.”
What further surprised me was the power the customer held, even after he had paid and left. The digital world brought private encounters into the public sphere: a displeased customer could affect a woman’s future earnings by becoming an online critic, capable of influencing the market value of her services. The strength of a single review could make or break the personal enterprise she had set up for herself.
Beyond performance, Ying’s experience of sex work also revealed many personal boundaries were up for sale. Many men refused to use condoms; others demanded violent or depraved acts. Blowjob bars in particular distinguish themselves by the absence of condoms. This is an easy boundary to maintain when a sex worker is first starting out, fresh and attractive. But that balance shifts rapidly when they remain in the industry for too long, presenting them with a hard economic decision: refuse the money, or accept a greater health risk. For Ying, ageing and increasing competition intensified those decisions; she described how quickly such considerations become typical when rooted in the industry. The same market that had rewarded her youth gradually made it more costly for her to protect herself.
Her account also revealed the darker experiences of rape and abuse. In one disturbing revelation, she recounted how she was heavily intoxicated, unable to defend herself, while men around her used her sexually. Yet, when pressed on her emotions during that encounter, she seemed more bothered by her boyfriend’s inability or refusal to protect her, rather than the assault itself, a reaction I found difficult to grasp. What affected me was how nonchalant she was in recalling these experiences. It made me question if her career in sex work had created an unavoidable overlap, where consent and violation had become intertwined with her professional need to please every man she came across.
The money Ying earned was not always spent on herself. One of the recurring themes in our interviews was the importance of family responsibility and karma – and how both of these contributed to her decision to enter the sex industry. According to her strict religious upbringing, filial piety is a source of merit that can help to expunge past transgressions and ensure a positive reincarnation. Parents give their children a life, food, and protection. Children repay this debt by sending money home – something that is a moral and religious responsibility.
The same Buddhist moral universe that rejects any immoral behavior now expects a diametrically opposed sacrifice in the name of filial piety, a devastating contradiction I had struggled to understand.
Years later, that contradiction became painfully obvious when even cervical cancer could not keep Ying from returning to sex work. Her family had already structured their lives around her regular financial sacrifices and were reliant on her. She said, “There was no other job at my age that could pay so much.” Nobody forced her back after her hysterectomy. There was no trafficker waiting at her door, no one imposing their will upon her. She did it because she had no other option.
I started out with a plan to write a book about the colorful life of a sex worker. In the end, I was writing about a human being – one of us – trying her best, imperfectly and relentlessly, to survive. I now understand how morality can appear from a distance and how simple any choice can be when proper alternatives exist. And really, given those circumstances, would we have done anything so very different?

SC: Cops can’t seek digital footprints for roving probe

NEW DELHI: SC has said police cannot direct social media platforms under IT Act to share an accused’s digital footprints for periods well before the crime he is being probed for, in an order that is likely to become a precedent for protection of privacy, reports Dhananjay Mahapatra.“Information and Technology Act provisions cannot be misused by police to launch a roving and fishing inquiry by obtaining personal data of an accused in breach of right to privacy,” said SC quashing a Ghaziabad Police order asking ‘X’ to furnish digital footprints of journalist Abhishek Upadhyay since June 1 when he was accused of a road rage incident in Aug 18.Cops must apply principles of proportionality, says SCA bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi said: “Police must apply the prin-ciples of proportionality while taking steps to investigate a crime and can resort to seeking digital footprints only after recording that alternative methods to obtain information about a crime has proved inadequate”. The court also kept in operation its interim order pro-tecting the journalist from arrest as long as he cooperated with the investigators.
Upadhyay, through senior advocate Pradeep Rai, said he had carried out a journalistic investigation into theft of donations at Ayodhya Ram Temple and was first to publish a news article on his digital platform on June 7. The real intent behind the cooked-up FIR of Aug 18 was to seek information from June 1 to identify the sources who informed him about pilferage of donations by devotees, Rai argued.
Ghaziabad Police commissioner had informed the court that police searched for the petitioner for three days in connection with the road rage case, in which he is accused of hurling caste slurs at the complainant bike rider, and when he was untraceable, police sought details of digital footprint from ‘X’.
SC said the commissioner’s explanation and the order seeking digital footprint details appear to be at variance for the purpose of investigation of the road rage case.“Police can surely look for digital footprints if the crime was committed with long planning and conspiracy, but not in such cases where questions of privacy and right to act as a journalist are involved,” said the bench.Rai with advocate Anoop P Awasthi complained to the court that the journalist’s vehicle, which was seized after the FIR against him, has not been returned. The bench directed Ghaziabad Police to return the vehicle to the petitioner within two days.The bench cautioned Ghaziabad Police against using any of the private and personal information related to the petitioner it has obtained from ‘X’.

Unemployment rate remains at 4.7pc in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:50:22 UTC
09:50:22 KST

Unemployment remains at 4.7pc in September with interest rate hike possible
In short:
The unemployment rate held at 4.7 per cent in September after the August result was revised up from 4.6 per cent.
The participation rate slipped to 66.8 per cent, down 0.2 percentage points.
What's next?
Some economists still expect another interest rate hike this year.
Australia's unemployment rate remained at 4.7 per cent in September, after August's jobless rate was revised upwards.
It means the national unemployment rate remains at its highest level in the post-COVID era, in seasonally adjusted terms.
An estimated 39,300 fewer Australians were in work last month, and the number of officially unemployed people increased by 8,900.
The participation rate, which is the proportion of people in work or actively looking for work, also fell, to 66.8 per cent from 67 per cent.
It means the average unemployment rate in the September quarter was 4.63 per cent, well above (and ahead of) the Reserve Bank's forecast of 4.5 per cent for the December quarter this year.
The Bureau of Statistics data show that, in trend terms, things remained steady last month.
The trend unemployment rate remained at 4.6 per cent (with no upward revision), the participation rate held at 66.9 per cent, hours worked remained steady, and the employment-to-population ratio held at 63.8 per cent.
Unemployment will keep rising
Tom Kennedy from JP Morgan said the unemployment rate had now increased by 0.6 percentage points since the RBA started lifting interest rates in February.
He said outside of the COVID-19-related volatility, it was the largest nine-month increase in more than a decade.
"The deterioration is also more pronounced than the RBA had forecast back in August, with the Statement on Monetary Policy projecting an unemployment rate of 4.5 per cent by year-end," he said.
"Importantly, it's too early to see any effect from the RBA's September rate hike, which we think will weigh on both GDP growth and labour demand in coming quarters."
Oxford Economics Australia economist Oscar Guth said unemployment would keep rising over the next 12 months.
He expects the unemployment rate to exceed 4.8 per cent late in 2027 as the lagged effects of oil price shocks and tighter monetary policy continue to affect the labour market.
BDO chief economist Anders Magnusson said the RBA's restrictive monetary policy and slow economic growth were beginning to flow more clearly into the labour market.
"The result suggests that the labour market is moving further in the direction the Reserve Bank has been seeking," he said.
RBA November meeting is still 'live'
Despite the clear signs that labour market conditions are still loosening, some economists think the RBA may soon lift rates again.
EY senior economist Paula Gadsby said today's data had not changed the monetary policy outlook.
"Given persistent price pressures across the economy, we continue to expect at least one rate hike before the end of the year, potentially as soon as Melbourne Cup Day," she said.
CBA economist Ashwin Clarke said next month's RBA Monetary Policy Board meeting would be closely watched.
"The data suggests the labour market continues to gradually loosen," he said.
"On the margin, this supports our expectation that the RBA will hold interest rates steady at its November meeting, though risks remain firmly tilted to the upside and the meeting is live."
Westpac's economics team still expect a rate hike in November.
David Bassanese, BetaShares chief economist, said he also thought the RBA would lift rates in November, but that decision would hinge on an "all-important inflation reading" later this month.
But Tom Kennedy said he thought rates would probably be on hold for a while.
"While price pressures are still elevated and the RBA remains focused on inflation, the steady increase in the jobless rate, in our view, argues for a period of policy stability and we expect rates on hold from here," he said.

Air Force May Buy Land for 120 New Sentinel ICBM Silos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:46:59 UTC
09:46:59 KST

The Air Force may wind up buying land to build 120 new intercontinental ballistic missile silos as part of its revamped infrastructure approach for the new Sentinel ICBM.
The service revealed that and other new details about its Sentinel plans as it announced the start of an environmental impact analysis meant to supplement the program’s original review, which was completed in 2023.
The environmental impact statement released in March 2023 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the Air Force’s effort to replace the aging Minuteman III with the Sentinel across three bases in the western U.S.: F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo.; Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.; and Minot Air Force Base, N.D. But much has changed since that EIS—in early 2024, critical cost and schedule overruns for Sentinel triggered a notice to Congress and a Pentagon review under the Nunn-McCurdy Act.
The program’s issues are not caused by the missile, but rather by the massive infrastructure and civil engineering work needed to build the systems it requires, officials say. The Air Force had hoped to reuse much of the infrastructure that supported Minuteman, but analysis showed much of it was too old or too expensive to upgrade.
Eventually, Pentagon leaders certified the Sentinel program to continue. But in an effort to control costs, Air Force officials decided in spring 2025 it would be more effective to build entirely new silos instead of reusing the old ones. There are 450 active Minuteman silos, which the Air Force plans to replace on a one-for-one basis.
At the time, a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the new silos would be “predominantly Air Force-owned real estate, which means reusing the existing missile sites but not the 55-year-old silos.”
A new website associated with the supplemental environmental impact analysis, launched Oct. 9, states that just over a quarter of the sites could be on land not currently owned by the Air Force, with the service considering:
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 30 new launch silo sites around F.E. Warren
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 30 new launch silo sites around Malmstrom
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 60 new launch silo sites around Minot
Additionally, the service said it is evaluating old sites at Malmstrom formerly operated by the 564th Missile Squadron, now inactive, to reuse for up to 60 new launch silo sites.
The Air Force is planning to buy up to 12 acres per silo, according to the supplemental EIS website.
Launch Centers
Silos aren’t the only ICBM infrastructure getting a refresh in the Air Force’s latest plan for Sentinel.
Currently there are 45 missile alert facilities across the three bases where Airmen stay on watch 24/7. The original plan for Sentinel called for building new “launch centers” to command and control the ICBMs at 24 of those facilities and razing the rest.
The new EIS website states that the Air Force will reutilize Missile Alert Facility sites for Launch Centers “where feasible,” but at Minot specifically, officials are considering “construction of new launch center sites in previously undeveloped areas,” the website states. Each Launch Center would have a footprint of up to 16 acres.
Another new consideration is the construction of a “purpose-built Operations Group Facility” at Malmstrom.
Timeline
Now that the Air Force has announced its plans to craft a supplemental EIS, there is a 30-day public “scoping” period where federal, state, and local agencies, interested organizations, and members of the public can all provide comments on the proposed actions.
After that, the service will release a draft of its supplemental EIS, and there will be another window for public comments. The Air Force plans to release its draft by fall 2027.
A final supplemental EIS is scheduled for release in spring 2028, after which the Secretary of the Air Force can sign a Record of Decision, clearing the way for the acquisition of land and construction.
After that, it will be several more years before Sentinel is in the ground—the current Air Force estimate is for the new missile to reach initial operational capability by the early 2030s.
For now, though, the Air Force and contractor Northrop Grumman are already building a prototype silo for Sentinel at Northrop’s Promontory, Utah, facilities.

US Space Force electromagnetic weapons played key role in Venezuela, Iran operations - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:37:39 UTC
09:37:39 KST

US Space Force electromagnetic weapons played a crucial role in US military operations in Venezuela and Iran, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.
The WSJ was granted access to a US Space Force base in Colorado, where it was shown some of the Pentagon's space warfare capabilities, including systems designed to disrupt enemy satellites and detect threats to the US military.
Among the weapons demonstrated was Meadowlands, an offensive system that can jam enemy satellites and disrupt their communications.
According to the WSJ, these satellites are used for surveillance, communications, and navigation.
Meadowlands often operates alongside a defensive system known as Bounty Hunter, which scans the electromagnetic spectrum to detect and locate potential threats to US forces, the report explained. Commanders can then pinpoint the location of a specific threat and order a defensive strike.
Transportable jamming system used by US Space Force
The US Space Force has also accelerated the deployment of a newer jamming system known as the Remote Modular Terminal. The equipment can be packed into a container and transported to locations around the world, allowing US personnel to deploy electronic warfare capabilities quickly.
Over the past year, US Space Force soldiers, known as Guardians, have transported and deployed these systems to support US military operations in both Venezuela and Iran.
According to the WSJ, “In a sign of how important space systems are, Iran repeatedly targeted US space capabilities, including satellite communications terminals, to try to degrade those advantages.
“Satellites help the US detect missile launches, guide weapons, and get a clear picture of the battlefield,” taking high-resolution imagery from above.
Tech.-Sgt. Joshua Lomax, who helped counter threats during operations in Venezuela before being deployed to defend against threats from Iran, described the pressure of preparing for the missions.
“The threat is real,” Lomax told the WSJ.
He recalled having just 72 hours to pack the equipment in Venezuela, load it onto an aircraft, and depart for Iran.
“It was incredibly intense,” he told the WSJ. “Everybody was head on a swivel.”
Importance of electromagnetic waves in modern warfare
The US Space Force also highlighted the importance of electromagnetic waves, which travel at different wavelengths and frequencies and underpin many of the technologies used in modern warfare. These systems connect military assets ranging from submarines and drones to radar installations.
According to US Space Forces’ Combat Forces Command, led by Lt.-Gen. Greggory Gagnon, a key mission for the US is to dominate the electromagnetic spectrum.
“That thing you never see is incredibly important in warfare,” he said. “If we can dominate the spectrum, we can keep our systems, our satellites, our ships, our planes, all connected and working more effectively, but we can also disrupt the adversary’s ability to do it.”

US considers easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels to cut freight rates, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:36:54 UTC
09:36:54 KST

The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.
The discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow Republicans in the US Senate.
Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine.
The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington, rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures.
The goal is to get more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was talking about easing the sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to cut record freight rates that have cut into demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group.
Bits of the talk were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available.
Companies seeking to use the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department to use the vessels, the official said.
The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia to move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy.
But Trump's push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels.
The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment.
High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7.
Tanker freight rates soar to record highs
Tanker freight rates have soared to record highs as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America.
Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East.
Lifting the sanctions on the tankers that are mostly old and not well maintained is "unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months," it said in the note.
Easing the restrictions "could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs," in the waterway between Iran and Oman.
Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said.

Israel blocks Gaza base for Trump's Board of Peace as election nears, Guardian reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:30:48 UTC
09:30:48 KST

Israel is blocking construction of a military outpost in the Gaza Strip intended to serve as a base for an international stabilization force operating under U.S. President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, The Guardian reported Wednesday, citing a person with direct knowledge of the project.
According to the British newspaper, the Board of Peace awarded its first Gaza construction contract in early August to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company tasked with building a fortified compound for approximately 150 international troops.
More than two months later, construction has yet to begin because Israel has not authorized contractors or construction vehicles to enter the territory, the source said.
"Israel won't open the border," the source told The Guardian.
The newspaper said a Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment, while the Israeli government and IDF did not respond to requests for comment.
A military base holding up Gaza reconstruction
The proposed compound would measure approximately 100 by 100 meters and be built on a site formerly used by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), the now-defunct aid distribution operation that delivered humanitarian supplies through private contractors.
The facility is intended to accommodate rotating deployments of 150 armed international troops, drawn from a larger contingent of approximately 500 personnel dispatched from Morocco and Kosovo, according to the report.
The troops would form part of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), a multinational security mission planned to operate in Gaza under the Board of Peace.
But the source warned that the absence of the military base is preventing the broader reconstruction program from moving forward.
Without the stabilization force on the ground, there would be no security arrangements to enable construction crews to enter, deliver equipment, install utilities or establish basic infrastructure, the source explained.
The delay therefore threatens far more than the construction of a single military facility. It could prevent the launch of the initial reconstruction projects planned for southern Gaza.
Is Israel's election behind the delay?
The source told The Guardian that officials involved in the Board of Peace believe Israel will allow construction to proceed after the country's October 27 election.
That assessment raises questions about whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government is reluctant to permit the start of Gaza reconstruction during the election campaign.
However, the report did not establish that electoral considerations were the reason Israeli authorities had withheld the necessary approvals.
The delay comes despite Israel having already approved the Board of Peace's entry into Gaza and the launch of a limited reconstruction initiative.
In July, Israel's security cabinet approved a pilot program to restore basic services in the territory, with the first stage expected to take place in Rafah, in southern Gaza.
The initiative is intended to lay the groundwork for a broader international effort to stabilize the territory and begin rebuilding infrastructure damaged during the war.
Countries expected to contribute troops to the stabilization force include Uganda, Morocco, Kosovo and Kazakhstan. Discussions have also been held with Albania, Vietnam and Georgia about possible participation.
Temporary housing and a Palestinian administration
Beyond the military outpost, the reconstruction initiative calls for temporary housing facilities in Rafah to accommodate Palestinian residents.
Under the reported plans, Palestinians seeking to move into the designated areas would undergo extensive security screening intended to prevent individuals affiliated with Hamas or connected to the terrorist organization from entering.
The pilot area would be the first in Gaza administered by the Palestinian technocratic body known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
The committee would operate with the backing of the international stabilization force, which is intended to provide security for the reconstruction effort and support the establishment of civilian administration.
The arrangements form part of Trump's broader postwar framework for Gaza, which places the Board of Peace at the center of efforts to stabilize and reconstruct the territory.
For now, however, the plan remains dependent on Israeli authorization to move the first contractors and equipment into Gaza.
According to the source cited by The Guardian, officials involved in the initiative expect that approval may come only after Israelis go to the polls on October 27, leaving the first phase of the reconstruction effort on hold.

2026-10-15
08:25:04 CST
09:25:04 KST

QUITO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Ecuador is set to shore up its electric system to ensure service during the critical months of the El Nino weather phenomenon, forecast to run from late November through February, President Daniel Noboa said Wednesday.
"We are facing a very harsh weather situation, especially along the coast, though highland areas are also being affected," Noboa said in an interview with Radio Centro in the central city of Ambato.
According to Noboa, adverse weather conditions have led to an increase in disruptions in electricity, with incidents climbing from an average of "20-odd" times per day in a normal year to between 60 and 70 currently.
The government has added more than 400 megawatts of electricity generation capacity by granting permits and providing support to the private sector, with the goal of strengthening the system's capacity, he said.
The announcement comes amid Ecuador's dry season, marked by a lack of rainfall in the southern part of the country, home to the reservoirs that supply the Paute Hydroelectric Complex of the National Interconnected System.
The complex is the country's largest hydroelectric system and supplies about 35 percent of national electricity demand.
Currently, large industries in Ecuador are facing up to 72 hours of power cuts a week due to the dry season, a measure intended to reduce consumption and ease pressure on the national electrical system.
In 2024, the country went through an unprecedented energy crisis, with power outages lasting up to 14 hours a day that affected households, businesses and industries.
Ecuador was hit with extreme weather from El Nino in 1982-1983 and 1997-1998, including torrential rains and flooding, particularly in the coastal region. ■

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as Bukele model embraced across Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:24:03 UTC
09:24:03 KST

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as Bukele model embraced across Latin America
President Laura Fernandez says mega-prison is part of ‘tough-on-crime model’ embraced by her government.
Costa Rica has announced the opening of a new mega-prison amid near-record homicide levels and growing organised crime, as countries across the region embrace police crackdowns that have proven popular but often weaken key civil liberties.
President Laura Fernandez opened the High-Containment Centre Against Organised Crime, or CACCO, on Wednesday. The prison will have capacity for 5,100 people, equivalent to about 20 percent of the country’s current prison population.
“The CACCO will force criminals to face a new model – a tough-on-crime model. Costa Rica will become a global benchmark for prison security,” Fernandez said during an inauguration ceremony.
Candidates across Latin America have embraced mega-prisons, seeking to replicate the policies of Nayib Bukele, the president of El Salvador, who has won widespread popularity through a campaign of mass arrests and the suspension of basic rights in the name of combating crime.
Costa Rica, long spared from high levels of violent crime compared with its neighbours, saw a record-setting 905 homicides in 2023, followed by 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025.
Analysts say that is partly due to increased fighting between criminal groups over lucrative drug routes.
The first transfers to Costa Rica’s new mega-prison will take place at the end of October, with Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar saying the facility will help the government reassert control over the prison system and diminish infiltration by organised crime.
Right-wing leaders in other Latin American countries have also sought to replicate the mega-prison model.
Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, inaugurated in July, has announced plans to tour El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), in anticipation of creating a similar facility in her country. CECOT can hold about 40,000 people.
In Colombia, meanwhile, newly elected leader Abelardo de la Espriella campaigned for the presidency, in part, on a pledge to build 10 mega-prisons. He took office in August.
Brazil, the largest country in Latin America, is currently in the midst of its own presidential election, and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has advanced to the final round of the vote. His platform also includes building five mega-prisons, citing the Salvadoran model.
El Salvador first imposed a “state of exception” under Bukele in 2022, expanding police and military powers.
That emergency declaration has been credited with a sharp drop in that country’s homicides, but rights groups say it has led to severe rights abuses and has been weaponised against critics of the government.
The “state of exception” has also resulted in mass arrests and mass trials, with rulings delivered against hundreds of defendants at a time. Some defendants have been detained without charge.
While the Bukele administration frequently touts its success in dismantling the gangs, the government has continuously extended the state of exception since it was first imposed.
Critics have warned that conditions inside mega-prisons are often poor, with imprisoned people facing overcrowding, due process violations and alleged torture in facilities like CECOT.

Israel may be left out of global climate summit in Turkey amid security fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:22:43 UTC
09:22:43 KST

A total of 197 countries are expected to participate in the global climate summit in Turkey next month. Unfortunately, Israel will likely not be among them, due to a combination of security concerns and diplomatic isolation.
The Ministry of Environmental Protection said it had submitted a request to security officials on behalf of both the ministry and the Foreign Ministry, but noted: "At this stage, approval for the joint delegation's departure has not yet been granted. However, the matter is currently being reconsidered, and no final decision has been made."
'It's more of a political conference'
The summit is an annual gathering of countries that are parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This year's agenda will include a review of national emissions reduction targets and mark a decade since the Paris Agreement, aimed at limiting global warming, entered into force.
Asked how important Israeli participation is, Prof. Colin Price, head of Tel Aviv University's Climate Initiative, said: "It's more of a political conference, which is why it's important for us to be there, just as we participate in the United Nations even though we don't have much influence. But being there matters. This year, the situation is apparently different. The fact that the conference is being held in Turkey is preventing many people from attending.
The Ministry of Environmental Protection barely functions these days, so there's less interest. It's a combination of security concerns and a lack of interest on the government's part. So we won't be there, although there may be private-sector representatives.
"Scientists working and conducting research in the climate field don't feel that there's any boycott or that the current situation is affecting international cooperation, including conferences," he added. "I think there's much less politics at the scientific level. I served as a reviewer for one of the chapters of an Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report."
At the same time, Price warned that the private sector could suffer from Israel's absence.
"There's no exposure, no networking and no investment. Four years ago, there were far more foreign investors in companies. I'm involved in a startup, and over the past year or two, investors have stopped responding. They simply don't answer our emails. There's much less foreign investment in climate tech [innovative technologies designed to address climate change]. If we don't attend the summit, we miss out on those connections and meetings."
Udi Avni, co-country director of Greenpeace Israel, also expressed concern over Israel's likely absence from the event.
"Against the backdrop of extreme climate events around the world, Israel's participation in the summit is essential," he said. "The absence of official representation harms the national interest and the Israeli public. If this were Eurovision, things would look and sound very different. The government should be doing everything in its power to demand that the host country guarantee the Israeli delegation's safety or ask the United Nations to relocate the summit. Turkey was chosen as the host nearly a year ago.
"Unlike Eurovision, the climate summit produces technical but important decisions on issues such as renewable energy transition targets, environmental regulations and funding for green technologies. These decisions directly affect the quality of life of all Israelis, the cost of living and the economy, national security and our ability to cope with the consequences of the climate crisis, including wildfires and drought."
Avni added that "the summit is also an opportunity to promote Israeli technologies and international cooperation that could help improve Israel's diplomatic standing by supporting key demands on the agenda, including a rapid, just and adequately funded transition away from fossil fuels, the development of an ambitious national roadmap for phasing out fossil fuels and support for the 'polluter pays' principle by taxing the windfall profits of energy corporations to finance climate compensation funds."
'Another blow to the environment'
Dr. Avner Gross, Head of the Climate Change Research Laboratory at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, said: "The climate crisis is one of the greatest challenges facing humanity, and it will be with us from now on. To address it, we need the entire global community, including Israel. One way to have an impact and be part of the effort is to participate in the international climate summit, which nearly every country in the world attends. Israel's absence would signal a further withdrawal from the global dialogue, potentially harming the country academically and economically."
Mor Gilboa, CEO of Zalul, an Israeli environmental organization focused on protecting marine and freshwater ecosystems, said Israel's failure to attend the summit would be another blow to environmental and climate efforts in a region that urgently needs cooperation to better protect and manage the resources shared by Mediterranean countries.
"It is deeply regrettable that political tensions and security threats will likely prevent Israel from participating in the summit," Gilboa said. "The climate crisis will not wait for political circumstances to change. In reality, it continues to worsen and even adds further tensions to an already strained political situation."

US rejects recommendation for ICE body cams to be automatically activated

US rejects recommendation for ICE body cams to be automatically activated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration has rejected a government watchdog’s recommendation that US immigration officials should use technology that would automatically activate body-worn cameras when an officer pulls their weapon or sets off a car siren.
Automatic activation of body-worn cameras was one of a number of recommendations outlined in a report released on Oct 14 by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an independent nonpartisan watchdog agency for Congress.
The recommendation comes as US agencies face mounting scrutiny over enforcement tactics used in an immigration crackdown that has included fatal shootings of two US citizens in Minneapolis, raising questions about officers’ accountability.
The GAO report said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection “should improve body-worn camera programme management”, adding that CBP and ICE have not updated their programme plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively.
Covering the period from February 2025 until September 2026, the report recommended that ICE implement additional controls to make sure that cameras are activated.
“We maintain that additional controls, such as automated camera activation, would provide greater assurance that body-worn cameras meet ICE’s desired results for transparency, accountability, and public trust,” the GAO said in the report.
The Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, said in comments cited in the report that it did not agree with the recommendation, citing what it said were privacy and operational risks.
For ICE, automatic activation risked the possibility of inadvertent or false activations during routine movement, the DHS said in the report.
DHS also said in the report that inadvertent or false activations could result in the unauthorised recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims, or the recording of bystanders engaged in free speech activities in areas where camera use is restricted.
ICE has been the face of President Donald Trump’s deportation drive, which he says aims to improve domestic security.
Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
Responding to the GAO report’s publication, a DHS spokesperson said on Oct 14 ICE had acquired devices to equip all officers and agents with body cameras.
“Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon,” the spokesperson said. REUTERS

As Indonesian Fires Continue, Singapore Records Highest Air Pollution Reading Since 2015
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:19:00 UTC
09:19:00 KST

Air pollution readings in some parts of Singapore yesterday spiked to their highest levels in more than a decade, as Indonesia came under increased pressure for its failure to contain the wildfires that have caused a dramatic decline in air quality across the region.
Hourly PM2.5 readings rose across all regions of Singapore yesterday afternoon, with the reading in the west of the island climbing to 288 micrograms per cubic meter. The reading, which is in the National Environmental Agency (NEA)’s “very high” range, was the highest recorded since 2015, Channel News Asia reported.
PM2.5 readings were in the “high” range in the south, east, and central regions of the country, while the reading in the north was in the “elevated” range.
With readings entering the “very high” range, the government also began the phased distribution of N95 masks to vulnerable segments of the population, and temporarily closed all outdoor and non-air-conditioned sports facilities in western Singapore.
Indonesia is currently battling the most intense wildfire season in 11 years, which has been exacerbated by an unusually severe dry season linked to a global El Niño weather pattern. The fires, which are concentrated mostly on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, have created a haze that has affected much of maritime Southeast Asia, forcing school closures and impacting the health of tens of millions of people.
The government of Timor-Leste, which borders Indonesia, said in a statement yesterday that it was suspending face-to-face learning activities for three days starting from October 15 “due to contamination by pollutant particles from wildfires in neighboring regions or countries.” This comes after the Malaysian government last week ordered the closure of schools across peninsular Malaysia, including in the capital Kuala Lumpur, due to the worsening haze.
In Indonesia, authorities said more than 280,000 respiratory problems have been recorded in affected regions since August 18. In the province of Central Kalimantan, the country’s ISPU air pollution index yesterday exceeded 1,200, four times higher than the “hazardous” level of 300.
While some fires naturally occur during the annual dry season, many are caused by agricultural burn-off on monoculture plantations, such as palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar, that are controlled by powerful Indonesian conglomerates. The country’s Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said last month that most of the fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra had been deliberately set by individuals or companies, and pledged to investigate and punish those responsible.
As I noted earlier this week, the crisis has highlighted the inadequacy of regional mechanisms for combating transboundary haze. Malaysia this week announced that it would raise the issue with Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers ahead of the bloc’s summit in the Philippines next month.
For now, however, the region is reliant on the actions of the Indonesian government, which has been subject to increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires. In addition to a wave of complaints from Singaporean and Malaysian social media users, the frustration is now breaking into the political realm. Andrew Chen Kah Eng, the head of the Johor state branch of Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan coalition, said on Monday that Indonesia “must be held accountable” for its failure to contain the wildfires.
“Indonesian spokespeople need to stop being indifferent and unapologetic to all ASEAN countries affected, including its own people, by human-induced haze pollution,” he said. “Allowing toxic haze containing PM2.5 fine particles to pollute the air of neighboring countries is unacceptable.”
The following day, Malaysian lawmaker Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman called on Southeast Asian governments to lodge formal diplomatic protests with their Indonesian counterparts, suggesting that Malaysian and Singaporean banks cut off financing to Indonesian companies linked to land burning. “You need to treat them like an outcast in the region,” he said.
On Tuesday, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto ordered the mobilization of additional resources to combat the wildfires, which are particularly difficult to control due to the fact that many are in geographically remote areas and are burning on areas of dried peatland, where fires can smolder for weeks underground.
“This is a top priority for us. We must resolve it immediately,” Prabowo told a meeting with the relevant Indonesian authorities, according to a government statement.
Even if it is successful, without continuing action to control the activities of powerful agri-business interests, the region will continue to be subject to the choking externalities of Indonesia’s dysfunctional political economy.

Israel's largest Hasidic sect threatens to withhold 30,000 votes in election feud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:18:54 UTC
09:18:54 KST

Less than two weeks before Israel's October 27 election, the country's largest Hasidic movement is threatening to withhold its support from United Torah Judaism (UTJ), potentially costing the ultra-Orthodox alliance some 30,000 votes as an internal power struggle threatens to spill over into the ballot box.
The Gur Hasidic movement, which traditionally holds the most senior position within the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael faction and its representation in the broader UTJ alliance, has yet to begin encouraging its followers to vote. The silence has drawn criticism from within the party, particularly as other ultra-Orthodox communities intensify their election campaigns.
In Hamodia, the newspaper affiliated with Gur, there has been no reference to the election and no public instruction from the movement's spiritual leader, Rabbi Yaakov Aryeh Alter, urging followers to support the party.
The absence is especially unusual so close to election day. In previous campaigns, calls to vote for UTJ were prominently featured in the newspaper weeks before Israelis went to the polls.
Initially, Gur officials dismissed the need for an early campaign, arguing that "the rebbe will tell people on election day whom to vote for, and they will listen."
But the continued silence now appears to reflect a deeper dispute over the balance of power within the ultra-Orthodox political alliance.
The split threatening 30,000 votes
The crisis began just hours before the deadline for submitting candidate lists, when lawmaker Meir Porush, representing the Shlomei Emunim faction, and Elyakim Stark, the representative of the Belz Hasidic movement, broke away from Agudat Yisrael.
The two established a separate party, Homat Torat Yisrael, while remaining within the broader United Torah Judaism electoral alliance.
The move effectively freed them from the authority of Agudat Yisrael's institutions, particularly its Council of Torah Sages, the senior rabbinical body that guides the party's decisions.
Porush and Stark occupy the fourth and sixth positions, respectively, on the joint UTJ candidate list.
In Gur, leaders are now considering withholding an official call for their followers to vote, a move that could reduce the number of seats won by the alliance and prevent Stark from entering the Knesset.
"Goldknopf will get in anyway. Our representative is number two on the list, so his seat is secure," a Gur source said, referring to Yitzhak Goldknopf, the movement's senior political representative.
Gur has approximately 30,000 eligible voters, whose support could translate into roughly one to one-and-a-half Knesset seats.
"If Gur gives its mandate or mandate and a half to the party, it will bring Elyakim Stark into the Knesset, even though he is not loyal to the council and has left Agudat Yisrael," the source added.
The calculation is straightforward: Gur's own representative is placed high enough on the list that his election is considered secure, while Stark, in sixth place, could lose his seat if the alliance wins fewer mandates.
Negotiations before election day
Gur representatives are currently engaged in negotiations aimed at securing an agreement on the distribution of positions within the alliance before the election.
If those negotiations fail, the movement could maintain its current position and refrain from encouraging its followers to vote, potentially depriving UTJ of tens of thousands of ballots.
Agudat Yisrael is seeking understandings with Degel HaTorah, the Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox faction that forms the other major component of UTJ, regarding the standing of Porush and Stark.
It is also demanding that Degel HaTorah refrain from negotiating separately with Homat Torat Yisrael in future elections until the breakaway faction returns to Agudat Yisrael and again accepts its organizational framework.
Agudat Yisrael did not respond to a request for comment.
Another concern within Gur is that a last-minute voting instruction from the rebbe could carry less weight among some followers than the traditional campaign appeals issued well in advance of election day.
Nevertheless, the prevailing expectation within the movement is that its leadership will ultimately instruct followers to vote for UTJ, whose ballot designation is the Hebrew letter gimel, as it has in previous elections.
Before that happens, however, Gur officials want an agreement on the allocation of political positions to prevent the dispute from continuing after the election.
The internal struggle has also been fueled by the leadership change within the Belz Hasidic movement.
The Belz rebbe appointed Stark, a powerful figure within the community, as its new representative on the UTJ list, replacing veteran lawmaker Yisrael Eichler.
Eichler has served in the Knesset almost continuously since 2003 and currently holds the position of deputy communications minister. He previously chaired the Knesset's Labor and Welfare Committee and served as a deputy Knesset speaker.
With election day approaching, the dispute has left one of Israel's most influential ultra-Orthodox voting blocs without its customary campaign instructions, while negotiations continue over whether its 30,000 voters will be mobilized to support the joint list.

Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
Victims’ groups, however, have denounced the ruling as ‘selective’ justice that exonerates a former government head.
A Mexican judge has closed the case against Francisco Garduno, former head of the country’s immigration agency, for crimes related to the 2023 fire at a Ciudad Juarez detention centre that killed 40 migrants and injured 30 others.
The incident was the deadliest event ever to occur at a Mexican immigration centre, and critics said it exposed the shortcomings and irregularities in the country’s detention system.
Garduno faced trial for the crimes of abuse of public office and dereliction of duty after footage from the fire showed guards had failed to respond to cries for help.
On Tuesday, Judge Victor Manlio Hernandez Calderon ruled that Garduno had fulfilled the court-mandated measures required to address the damage. But victims rejected that decision and announced they would appeal.
“Yesterday, corruption and the impunity of politicians protected by power won again,” the Foundation for Justice, one of the NGOs representing some of the victims, wrote on social media on Wednesday.
The victims have also compared the judge’s decision to close the criminal case to a de facto exoneration for Garduno.
In their view, the ruling “confirms that justice in Mexico is selective” and denies the victims “full reparations” and concrete guarantees that such an event will not be repeated.
Miguel Zenteno, one of the foundation’s lawyers, noted that the ruling is not yet final because it will be appealed and because another injunction is pending against the court-mandated reparations, which critics say failed to meet the standards for serious events.
On March 27, 2023, some 70 men were crammed into a locked dormitory with no ventilation and barely any water at the Ciudad Juarez immigration detention centre, on the border with El Paso, Texas.
As night fell, a small group set fire to some mattresses in protest, and within seconds, smoke engulfed the entire area.
Security cameras recorded the guards leaving the area despite cries for help. They made no attempt to open the gates of the dormitory. Only the women, held in another cell, were released. Most of the victims were Central Americans and Venezuelans.
Garduno, a former prison guard and current official at the Ministry of Education, led the National Migration Institute (INM) starting in 2019 and continued in the role until 2025 despite the fire.
The judge had previously ordered Garduno to compensate the families, provide them with free specialised medical care, issue a public apology, provide human rights training to migration personnel and guarantee that the events would not be repeated.
Zenteno acknowledged that the measures were implemented only partially because Garduno did not pay the damages as stipulated by the legal process.
Instead, Zenteno pointed out that the funds came from the INM, and the payments did not fully compensate the families. Furthermore, he added, the victims were not even informed how to access free medical services, and the apology “was a mere formality, not substantive”.
In addition to Garduno, prosecutors accused another former director of the institute of the same crimes.
Six immigration agents – including a military officer and a private security guard – and the two migrants accused of starting the fire are charged with homicide and assault. Most of the officials remain free pending trial.

Russia-US diesel deal already having positive effect – Putin aide to RT (VIDEO)

Dmitriev argued that the immediate market response demonstrated the economic benefits of cooperation and the costs of maintaining sanctions against Moscow.

Israeli guards shoot Palestinian prisoners with rubber bullets, causing severe wounds

Unknown Publisher
