Australia is the monster that turns World Cup dreams to nightmares
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:37:28 UTC
07:37:28 KST

Fri, 18 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Tigers 0, Raiders 6
analysis
Australia's dominance looms over the women's Rugby League World Cup
Almost a decade ago, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was the last day before everything changed.
Australia's cracking 23-16 win over New Zealand in 2017 didn't just deliver the team its first-ever World Cup final victory on home soil; it was the last major match before the women's game was transformed forever.
The following season, the interstate series moved under the NRL banner, the first NRLW season kicked off, and women's rugby league began to take giant strides.
A few players from that watershed moment are still around for this year's Rugby League World Cup, which begins tomorrow in Parramatta, when Australia plays Samoa.
Isabelle Kelly, Kezie Apps and Simaima Taufa are still wearing green and gold; Zahara Temara has switched to New Zealand and will play for the Kiwi Ferns in their tournament opener against Fiji on Sunday alongside Raecene McGregor and Apii Nicholls.
These six exist in a different world from the one they came from, one where the players are now faster, stronger, fitter and more skilful; where pathways have improved, and player numbers have exploded; and where the game has evolved to the point where this should be the last World Cup held simultaneously with the men's tournament because the product is strong enough to stand alone.
But the issue heading into the tournament is at the top end of the product, because Australia's dominance has become one of the growing pains the game must endure as everyone else tries to catch up.
Since that win in 2017, the Jillaroos have won 15 of 16 matches. They have not conceded more than two tries in a game since 2018.
In the last World Cup, they won their five matches by a cumulative scoreline of 312-12, including a 54-4 massacre of New Zealand in the final.
The last time they played England, they won 90-4, and those four points mark the only try they've conceded to a team other than New Zealand in their past 16 games.
They won the Pacific Championship last year, scoring 110 points and conceding just 12 across three matches, with the Kiwi Ferns copping a 40-8 belting in the final.
State of Origin regulars like Jesse Southwell and Abbi Church, both overlooked for the match against Samoa, can't make this team. A living legend like Ali Brigginshaw can't even make the squad.
The Jillaroos have nine players from this year's NRLW Dally M Team of the Year. In Tamika Upton, Olivia Kernick, Tarryn Aiken, Isabelle Kelly and Jess Sergis, they have the best player, forward, halfback and centres in the world.
They are, without question, the best women's rugby league team ever, and they are so much better than everyone else that anything less than a dominant run to the final and a thumping victory at Lang Park will feel like a departure from a predestined fate.
Other teams have improved. New Zealand, which handed Australia its sole loss in recent years in 2023 and went down by just six points in one game last year, has risen highest with the tide.
As the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, they could rise higher still, and their squad for this year's tournament should put them in contention for the final.
Samoa is another side that has improved and could still get better. The Fetu have benefited from the injection of diaspora players like Taliah Fuimaono, Evania Isa'ako and Amber Hall, plus fresh faces like Queensland Origin flyer Destiny Mino-Sinapati and reigning NRLW rookie of the year Mercedez Taulelei-Siala.
They are a vision of what is possible for the expansion of women's rugby league and beneficiaries of the improved pathways leading to the NRLW.
It will take time, because we are talking about change that can take a decade or more to become apparent, but the benefits are there for all to see in the men's game.
The women's game is on the same path; they're just not as far along. This is a brave, dangerous side with a real future, one which is easy to see unfolding before us.
One day a team like Samoa might be able to give the World Cup a real shake. But not these days.
The Samoans are currently 53.5-point underdogs against the Jillaroos in tomorrow night's match. They lost to them 60-0 in the corresponding clash last year.
Even that was nothing compared to the 90-4 belting England copped in Las Vegas last year, an eye-popping result that showed just how lopsided things had become.
The English will get a chance at revenge in Perth next week, and they're a much better side than the one that travelled to Nevada.
Roosters backrower Jasmin Strange is a welcome addition, and they have a core of NRLW players, including North Queensland's Fran Goldthorp, Canberra forward Hollie-Mae Dodd and clever Newcastle playmaker Georgia Roche.
If they can keep things respectable against the Jillaroos, that will be progress.
That gap can close as more top-level talent filters through the ranks, for England and everybody else.
But it will take time to run the Jillaroos down. And because the women's game is semi-professional, it's unlikely to happen as rapidly as it has in the men's game, meaning progress could take a decade or more.
Until then, there is no choice but to keep going.
Every nation will have a moment. Some will have more than one because there will be glories outside of absolute victory. Fiji will make its World Cup debut and Papua New Guinea will look to continue its steady progress of recent years.
A semi-final berth would be a major achievement for Samoa and a place in the final would be a shot in the arm for the game in England, so their group-stage clash is the pick of the early tournament matches.
The Kiwi Ferns will fancy their chances of an ambush should they meet Australia in the final, given the Jillaroos will have had a soft run in. They will point out that they are the one in 15-1, and perhaps they will be right.
But at the end lurks Australia, the monster at the end of the dream that turns it into a nightmare. And, just under a decade since the rest of history began, the truth of the pain it is about to inflict is simple.
This is the best collection of players ever assembled in women's rugby league, and if they are at any point over the next month beaten, it will be one of the biggest upsets the game has known.

Lawyers for man shot by ICE in New York City say agent did not identify himself

Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York City said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.
The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers”.
The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal’s release, said he had picked up his son from school and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.
“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way,” Belgal’s lawyers wrote. “Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”
New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.
The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.
A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.
Whatever happened next didn’t appear on the NYPD’s security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal’s damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.
Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.
DHS didn’t comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal’s lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.
Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and now has impaired hearing.
The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.

A phone message seeking comment was left on Wednesday with a representative for Omar.
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The justice department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s fifth district, including Minneapolis. She is part of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

CBI said it is investigating into the roles of all persons involved
New Delhi: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) Wednesday said it has seized Indian assets worth Rs 2,033 crore belonging to Reliance Power Ltd (RPL), an entity of the Reliance Anil Ambani Group, under Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), for the alleged siphoning of assets worth an equivalent amount to tax havens of British Virgin Islands (BVI) and Cayman Islands.The attached assets include bank balances of RPL and its shareholding in Sasan Power Limited. "The Headquarter Investigation Unit has seized assets worth ₹2,032.81 crore in India belonging to RPL, which are equivalent to the foreign exchange held outside India in contravention of FEMA," ED said. ED has already attached assets worth thousands of crores of the Anil Ambani group, including his residences in Mumbai, in multiple money laundering cases involving over Rs 40,000 crore.ED said its investigation into findings of Sebi, pertaining to write-offs/provisions aggregating ₹2,101.46 crore made by RPL in its books of account, had revealed that "these write-offs were related to overseas investments and advances made to companies in the British Virgin Islands (BVI) and the Cayman Islands".In a statement released to BSE and NSE Tuesday, RPL said the ED order of seizure of assets "relates to foreign currency convertible bonds issued in 2006, i.e.
20 years ago, and the related overseas investment made in 2008, i.e. 18 years ago, in a subsidiary in Singapore with all applicable approvals. The seizure primarily pertains to the shares held by the company in its wholly owned subsidiary Sasan Power Ltd, which are already pledged in favour of Power Finance Corporation Ltd (a govt undertaking) under security arrangements for more than 10 years, as well as certain bank balances of the company".ED had conducted related searches in March and seized "several pieces of incriminating evidence", recording statements of several persons. "Investigation has revealed that Reliance Natural Resources Ltd (since merged with RPL) raised $300 million through foreign currency convertible bonds in 2006. Of this, $275 million was invested in its wholly owned Singapore subsidiary Reliance Natural Resources (Singapore) Pte Ltd (RNRL-S)."RNRL-S placed these funds on deposit with Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA, Geneva. The deposits were used as collateral for loans extended to entities incorporated in the British Virgin Islands. The investigation found that the BVI entities were controlled and managed from India by the Reliance Anil Ambani Group (RAAG) through front persons, who acted as per the group's directions," ED said.
Further, the loan proceeds were utilised for varied purposes, including temporary round-tripping of funds to India through foreign entities based in Mauritius, the central agency said, adding that this was done to benefit the RAAG."The BVI entities failed to repay the loans extended by Deutsche Bank. As part of cover-up, documents were fabricated to show that RNRL-S and Indonesian subsidiaries of RPL had made advances to these BVI entities for apparently genuine business purposes. During investigation, it was found this documentation was backdated and prepared in order to project these transactions as genuine business transactions," ED said. Further investigation is in progress.

Ukraine accuses US of aiding Russia by withholding strike warnings and slowing Starlink

Ukraine has accused the United States of indirectly aiding Russia by failing to provide early warnings of incoming Russian missile strikes and restricting Starlink satellite internet systems vital to Kiev's battlefield drone operations.
The diplomatic fallout follows two consecutive nights of ballistic missile attacks against the capital, Kiev, where air-raid sirens failed to sound before impacts occurred, killing 15 people nationwide and damaging power plants in Kharkiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy, and Chernihiv.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced the intelligence blackout as "completely unjust", warning that Moscow showed "ostentatious disrespect towards the United States" by breaching a supposed energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy also appealed directly to US billionaire Elon Musk to restore full connectivity for Starlink terminals.
In an interview with British journalist Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on."
He also responded affirmatively when asked if he felt "betrayed" following Washington’s diesel pact with Moscow: "It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side."
Starlink restrictions
Ukrainian defence officials reported that satellite terminals were throttled when drones exceeded 160 km/h—and in some instances 80 km/h—crippling the military's ability to intercept Shahed drones or target Russian-held positions.
Musk stated that any disruptions were the direct responsibility of the US government rather than SpaceX, drawing a clear distinction between civilian Starlink equipment and military Starshield hardware.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote on X, referring to Trump.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov subsequently noted that connectivity up to 160 km/h was being restored, though he insisted that "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defence."
Meanwhile, in Moscow, Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev confirmed that contracts to supply diesel to the US would be finalised within days.

Trump says ‘leakers should be shot’ at Arizona rally, days after approving firing-squad execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:15:45 UTC
07:15:45 KST

US President Donald Trump called for severe punishment of those who leak classified military information, days after authorizing the execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at a Texas military base.
Trump, who was campaigning in Bullhead City, Arizona, on Wednesday as part of an intensive nationwide tour ahead of the November midterm elections, recalled the story of an intelligence leak that he claimed had forced him to postpone the June 2025 American strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities, carried out by B-2 stealth bombers during Operation Midnight Hammer.
He continued, stating that people who leak sensitive military information should be shot, delivering the remarks just days after approving the execution by firing squad of Hasan, the former US Army officer convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
“Now leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly,” Trump told the crowd.
He then escalated his criticism, declaring: “The leakers are the scum of the earth.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans last week to livestream the execution, scheduled for December 3, with a military firing squad expected to carry out the sentence. The proposal has drawn criticism and sparked debate across the US.
Trump subsequently indicated that he would make the final decision on whether the execution would be broadcast and that the livestream could still be canceled.
Trump recounts sensitive information leaked
During his Arizona speech, Trump revisited his account of how sensitive information about Operation Midnight Hammer, the planned June 2025 attack on Iran’s nuclear program, reached the media before the mission was carried out.
According to Trump, the disclosure included the precise departure and arrival times of the American bombers.
“But they leaked that we were leaving at 12:07 from Missouri, and it was in the New York Times, CNN,” he said.
Trump said he subsequently contacted Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, to discuss the potential implications for the operation.
“I said, ‘General, that’s not good, is it?’” Trump recalled.
According to the president, Caine replied: “Not good, sir, but we can do it anyway.”
Trump said he nevertheless decided to change the timing of the mission.
“So I called off the raid,” he told the audience.
The decision, he claimed, was particularly disappointing to the pilots who had been preparing for the operation.
“You know the unhappiest people were the pilots. They were miserable,” he said.
Trump went on to explain that two days later, he decided the attack could proceed — using the same departure time that had previously been disclosed.
“All right, good. Now we can do the raid. Let’s leave it exactly the same time,” he recalled telling his team.
“We used the exact same time,” he added.
According to Trump’s account, returning to the original timing meant the Iranians would be less likely to anticipate the aircraft’s movements.
The president presented the episode as an example of the potential consequences of leaking operational military information and as justification for imposing exceptionally harsh penalties on those responsible.
He did not present new evidence identifying the alleged leakers or independently establishing the circumstances of the disclosures he described.
Trump says the US has eliminated numerous Iranian leaders
Later in the rally, Trump returned to another theme he has raised repeatedly in recent days, joking that the US may have eliminated so many members of Iran’s leadership that Washington is now struggling to determine whom it should negotiate with.
The president began by listing what he described as the destruction of Iran’s military capabilities.
“Their radar is gone. Their anti-aircraft is gone. Their leaders are gone,” Trump said.
“That’s one of the problems. I might have gone too far. I don’t know who the hell to deal with.”
Trump continued his account of the successive losses suffered by Iran’s leadership, claiming that American military operations had eliminated multiple generations of senior officials.
“Their first level leaders are gone. They picked the second level. Their second level leaders are gone. They picked the third level, half of them are gone.”
The comments were delivered in a joking, boastful tone, rather than as an expression of regret over the American campaign.
Trump also claimed that he had been asked to refrain from targeting additional Iranian leaders and had agreed.
“They made me promise not to take out anymore, and I did. I promised them,” he said, without specifying who had made the request.
The president then joked that the leadership losses had made the prospect of assuming power in Tehran particularly unattractive.
“But nobody wants to be the president of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said.
“We hear, we have conversations. We hear them. Who would like to be the president of Iran? Please raise your hand. No, I don’t want to be.”
Returning to the difficulty of identifying a negotiating counterpart, Trump repeated the joke.
“I probably went a little too far. I’m sorry, because I don’t know who the hell we’re dealing with anymore.”
Despite the seemingly apologetic language, the comments formed part of a broader speech in which Trump repeatedly celebrated the effectiveness of American military operations against Iran.
He also reiterated his argument that military action had been necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
According to Trump, before the June 2025 attack, Iran had been just two weeks away from obtaining such a weapon — an assessment he presented as justification for ordering the strikes.
The president argued that the economic consequences of the confrontation, including higher gasoline prices, were a relatively small price to pay for preventing a nuclear-armed Iran.
Trump claims US control of Strait of Hormuz will bring fuel prices down
Trump also addressed the economic consequences of the continuing confrontation with Iran, asserting that the US had established control over the Strait of Hormuz and that more oil was now moving through the strategic waterway than before the conflict began.
He credited the US Navy and the American blockade, which he described as a “Wall of Steel,” for securing the waterway.
The president argued that the military operations had prevented Iran from threatening global security and suggested that energy prices would decline further once the confrontation ended.
“But that’s going to end very soon, and when that ends, your gasoline is going to go down to even lower than it was before,” Trump told supporters.
His comments came amid continuing tensions with Tehran and renewed American warnings against Iranian-backed forces in the region.

‘The Escape’ makes its debut, ‘Shalom’ enchants - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:15:28 UTC
07:15:28 KST

The biggest news on Israeli TV this week is the premiere of "The Escape," the new, all-star series on Channel 12. Based on the opening episode, which can also be streamed on mako.co.il, it’s tense and suspenseful.
It’s also a cautionary tale about why authorities shouldn't look the other way when a cult leader gains too much power. It feels like a mix of The Handmaid’s Tale, "Shtisel," and one of the movies about the 1978 Jonestown massacre.
Keshet 12 produced the series, and Keshet International is set to distribute it internationally.
"The Escape" stars Ido Tako, who just won the Ophir Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance in the movie Where To, as Yoel, a young man born into a sect that, despite a disclaimer, will remind many of the Lev Tahor cult.
Like that group, the cult in the series preaches an extreme version of ultra-Orthodox observance and has moved its members out of Israel and into the Colombian jungle. Yoel has grown up in this cult from a young age, but he is clearly unhappy there.
He sees other members of the group punished brutally for minuscule infractions, such as taking two slices of bread at a meal, and wants a different life for his son, Nachman. The child gazes at the stream by their compound and asks where it flows. When his father explains the concept of an ocean, he is fascinated, and it is obvious he has lived his whole life in this compound.
Yoel lives with the other men, although he is married to Feigi (Naya Beinstock, who appears in the movie Matchmaking 3). Men and women are strictly segregated, except when husbands and wives can “fulfill a commandment” together on the Sabbath.
Yoel does not seem impressed with the group’s leader (Mark Evanir), who talks about blessings and purity but rules with an iron hand. If the title didn’t give it away, Yoel and his family are planning a jailbreak.
Another major character is Carmeli (Yehuda Levi, who became a star over 20 years ago in Yossi & Jagger and has recently appeared in Trust No One and A Body that Works), a Mossad agent who, at the start of the series, is in a Colombian city.
There, he rescues an Israeli arrested on drug charges from a hospital. A complicated backstory involving his family in Israel is hinted at, and he seems to be the latest incarnation of the brave, workaholic, emotionally stunted covert operative we are used to seeing from so many dramas. But Levi’s charisma breathes new life into what might otherwise have been an overly formulaic character.
The series, which was filmed in Colombia, Georgia, and Israel, was created and written by Ariel Cohen for Keshet 12 alongside Yoav and Doron Paz, who also directed. The three collaborated on the movie The Golem, and the Paz brothers also made Plan A and Jeruzalem, the zombies-in-the-Old-City movie.
They carefully create a foreboding atmosphere and make you instantly root for Yoel and his family. In the coming weeks, we'll see what twists and turns "The Escape" has in store for us.
New 'Shalom' film tells story of Jerusalem biblical zoo rhinoceros
The touching movie Shalom, by Meital Zvieli, airs on KAN 11 on October 17 and will then be available on kan.org.il. It tells the story of Shalom, the beloved rhinoceros at Jerusalem’s biblical zoo (officially called the Tisch Family Zoological Gardens), but it's about so much more.
The movie uses the zookeepers’ relationships with the animals very effectively to symbolize the delicate reality of coexistence in the capital. It is beautiful in all the ways a movie can be: moving, wonderfully photographed, and using a simple device to tell a far more complex story.
Shalom came to the zoo just as the 1978 Camp David Accords were being signed. When the film opens, in the early 2020s, he’s tired. The Jews and Muslims on the staff are drawn together by their love for him and their desire to help him when his health begins to fail.
Some may remember the excellent children’s film shown in the Noah’s Ark exhibit at the zoo, and will recognize Rushdi Alyan (the main human protagonist in Shalom) and Gilad Moshe, two of the zookeepers who appear in it and are among the interviewees in both movies. They work together again in this new documentary, and it seems that, against all odds, their bond has grown stronger over the years.
Part of the movie covers the difficult period following the Hamas-led invasion and massacres in Israel on October 7, 2023, and shows how the animals are affected by the missiles fired near the zoo. As the Israel-Hamas War intensifies, Shalom becomes ill, and at the same time, many zookeepers are sent off to fight in Gaza. One of them quips, “The whole world keeps asking me, ‘Where’s Shalom?’”
For many years, I used to visit the zoo in Jerusalem every week with my son, who is on the autism spectrum. I know what it’s like to become attached to these animals and to find calm in this oasis of coexistence and harmony in a city, and a world, roiled by so many conflicts, so I could relate to every minute in this documentary.
But even if you don't share my deep connection to this place or respect for the people who run it, watching Shalom will still be an emotionally resonant experience. Hats off to Meital Zvieli for giving this unique, lovely part of Jerusalem the cinematic treatment it deserves.
New 'Cupertino' series running across Israeli TV providers
"Cupertino" is a new series from Robert and Michelle King, the husband-and-wife duo behind "The Good Wife" and "The Good Fight," and it’s currently running on Hot 3, Hot VOD, Next TV, Yes VOD, and Cellcom TV.
Fans of both shows, especially "The Good Wife," which set a new standard for witty, topical legal drama, have been looking forward to "Cupertino" because it aims to be a cross between "The Good Wife" and "Silicon Valley."
Unfortunately, though, based on the series pilot, which was released to the press, it brings to mind more the clunky, short-lived "BrainDead," a series by the Kings that tried to combine comedy, political humor, and sci-fi horror in a series that didn’t work in any of these genres.
On paper, the premise of "Cupertino" sounds great: Two recently fired lawyers who worked at Silicon Valley tech companies start their own law firm, specializing in defending wrongly terminated Davids against tech Goliaths. It also delves into issues raised by the development of AI.
Mike Colter, who was so good as the charismatic but scary drug lord Lemond Bishop on "The Good Wife," stars as Michael Price, a tech co-founder and lawyer who suddenly finds himself on the street when his partner decides not to share the wealth.
Colter is always good, but here he seems blander than I’ve ever seen him. Blandness is also a problem with his co-star, Rachel Keller as Olivia, a religious Christian lawyer at the same company, who is sexually harassed by her boss but decides to sue because the company’s AI avatar has been based on her.
The jokes and the plotting are painfully obvious much of the time, but I’ll try to keep an open mind and hope things pick up in subsequent episodes.

‘Waves’ captures thrill and tragedy of resistance at Prague radio station in ’68 - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:14:55 UTC
07:14:55 KST

People talk about the concept of resistance to political authority in ways that are often very abstract, but it’s fascinating to see real resistance in practice. The movie Waves, which just opened in Israel, does just that, dramatizing a story of the very sophisticated political opposition to the Soviet Union at a Prague radio station from 1967-1968.
The movie, directed by Jirí Mádl, is based on true events and focuses on two brothers whose parents are dead, Tomás (Vojtech Vodochodský), who is in his 20s, and his teenage brother, Paja (Ondrej Stupka). Tomás is preoccupied with just putting food on the table, while Paja is involved in political activism against Russian control over Czechoslovakia.
Tomás discourages this activism, urging his brother to devote himself to his studies. But Paja is energized by what he hears on Czechoslovak Radio, the international news department, of which is helmed by Milan Weiner (Stanislav Majer), a brave and visionary news editor who inspires his staff and pushes the boundaries of what the station is permitted to report.
When Paja goes to a kind of audition-job interview there, Tomás follows to keep an eye on him.
In a very believable scene, Tomás gets a job as a technician because when a phone rings in the room where they are auditioning, he is the only one to pick it up and bring the message to the editors.
Tomás enjoys his work and respects Weiner and the staff, but is uneasy when government officials pressure him to become an informer. They threaten to take away Paja and put him into an orphanage if he doesn’t cooperate.
The bulk of the movie is about how Tomás manages to play it both ways, giving the secret police just a little information so they will issue warnings but will allow the station to continue functioning.
The situation weighs on Tomás, who is quiet and sensitive, and adds to his worries about his brother. In addition to the personal story of this concerned older brother and that of the ambitious, quirky staff of this rebel radio station, the movie details the events of the Prague Spring, leading up to the Soviet crackdown and invasion in 1968.
The film incorporates news footage seamlessly into the story, which is a beautiful illustration of what it looks like when the personal really does become political. And in a lower-tech era, the tricks they use to keep broadcasting are brilliant.
'A love letter to news radio and newspapers'
MUCH OF Waves is about the exhilaration of resisting, and how exciting it can be to give people the knowledge they need, which is being kept from them, to make their own decisions.
It’s a kind of love letter to news radio and newspapers, and it is set to a soundtrack of classic rock music, which the staff loves, as well as popular Czech songs from the same period.
The ensemble cast is excellent, and Vojtech Vodochodský makes you feel the tension of the untenable position he is forced into very effectively. Majer is suitably charming as the news editor and Tatiana Pauhofová is appealing as a tough translator who has a softer side.
As I watched, it was hard not to think of the Iranian protests in January, in which the government killed tens of thousands of protesters. Some people say that the Iranian people should bring down their oppressive regime on their own, with no outside help.
But Waves, which was the Czech Republic’s official Oscar submission in 2025, depicts a reality in which those who opposed the Soviet-influenced regime had a great many tools at their disposal, such as radio stations and opposition newspapers.
Yet they were still crushed by the reality of the tanks rolling in. It’s sobering to think that the characters in Waves had to live under this regime for another 21 years.
While Waves is entertaining on its own, as a historical drama, it may make you long for the day when there will be a Persian Spring in Iran that will bloom far longer than the one in Prague did.

Texas Attorney-General Ken Paxton spent New Year’s Eve in Dubai with two men wanted for federal charges, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.
The WSJ reported that Paxton, his girlfriend, Tracy Duhon, and Anosh Ahmed and Sameer Suhail, both of whom were indicted months before on federal healthcare-fraud charges, rang in 2025 at a luxury high-rise in Dubai.
Details of the report were contained in court filings and were confirmed by WSJ sources familiar with the matter.
The video provided by the WSJ shows Paxton, Duhon, Ahmed, and Suhail standing on a balcony as fireworks light up the Burj Khalifa.
A federal court in Illinois indicted Ahmed and Suhail in 2024 for embezzling over $15 million from a Chicago hospital, the WSJ reported, citing court records and people familiar with the matter.
Ahmed was also charged as being part of a larger scheme involving at least $195 million in alleged payments from the government for fraudulent COVID-19 tests. He pleaded not guilty to the second charges.
The WSJ noted that Ahmed donated up to $190,000 to Paxton, including $25,000 days after he was indicted.
The pair did not return to the US after their indictments, but have since returned to face their charges.
Ahmed’s attorneys claim in court filings that he was abroad when he was first indicted, and that family health issues delayed his return.
Suhail’s attorneys said that civil matters in Dubai affected his return to the US.
What else has Paxton been accused of?
The WSJ marks the latest in Paxton’s string of controversies, some of which stretch as far back as 2008.
In 2015, he was indicted for felony security charges mere months after he was sworn in as attorney-general. He was accused of encouraging investors to invest in tech company Servergy without disclosing he earned a commission. The case was resolved in March 2024. Paxton paid up to $300,000 in restitution, though he maintained his innocence.
In 2016, an anonymous employee accused him of bribery. Paxton leaned on donations totaling up to $329,000 from family and friends to pay his legal fees for the security fraud case.
In 2020, Paxton filed a lawsuit with the US Supreme Court, arguing that the presidential election results needed to be overturned in four states. Paxton was nearly sued by the Travis County district attorney’s office for refusing to turn over his communications from January 6. He also appeared at the rally preceding the attack on the US Capitol.
That same year, several aides in the Texas Attorney-General’s Office reported him to the FBI, accusing him of abuse of office, bribery, and using his office to help a real estate developer. Paxton and the whistleblowers signed a $3.3 million settlement in 2023, but the settlement was later changed to $6.6 million paid for by the state.
The whistleblower suit led the Texas House of Representatives to impeach Paxton by a vote of 121 to 23 in 2023. Notably, 60 Republicans crossed the aisle to vote in a measure of no confidence against Paxton. He was later acquitted by the state Senate and returned to office later that year.
In 2025, his ex-wife, State Senator Angela Paxton, divorced him after 38 years of marriage, citing adultery. This was after reports emerged of Paxton’s extramarital affairs, including with Duhon.
Talarico leads Texas polls as doubts grow over Paxton
This comes as James Talarico holds a slight lead over Paxton in Texas’s Senate race. If Talarico wins the race, he will be the first Democrat to hold statewide office since the 1990's.
Over the course of the race, Talarico has attacked Paxton’s jet-set lifestyle.
“A party with multiple fugitives and Ken Paxton is still the sketchiest guy in the room,” Talarico wrote in a post on X/Twitter in response to the article.
Talarico has also criticized Paxton over other trips during his tenure as attorney-general, citing reports from the Texas Tribune that stipulate that the attorney-general allegedly brought state-funded security details on his trips, which cost millions.
“Working Texans are already struggling to afford the basics,” Talarico said in a news release, as reported by the Dallas Morning News. “They don’t need Paxton picking their pockets to fund his luxury vacations.”
Paxton adviser Nick Maddux did not directly address the Dubai trip in a statement to the WSJ.
“Like President Trump, Ken Paxton has been politically persecuted for years, and every time, voters have seen through it and sent him back to office because they know he has always fought for Texas,” Maddux told WSJ.
However, some Republicans have noted their misgivings about Paxton.
WSJ noted that before Trump endorsed Paxton in May 2026, Texas Sen. John Cornyn privately told Trump that several pieces of damaging information were likely to surface during the campaign season.
Trump dismissed Cornyn’s concerns and told him he believed that more damaging things would come out about Talarico.
As it stands, Talarico holds about an average 2-3% lead on Paxton, according to polling from The New York Times.

The Armed Forces of Ukraine explained how restrictions on Starlink&apos;s operation are already affecting the performance of combat missions

Unknown Publisher

The Armed Forces of Ukraine explained how restrictions on Starlink's operation are already affecting the performance of combat missions
Kyiv • UNN
SpaceX has restricted the speed of Starshield terminals, causing drones to lose connection in flight. The Ministry of Defense has appealed to the United States, SpaceX, and NATO.
On the night of October 14, SpaceX imposed restrictions without warning on the Starshield military satellite communications system, causing Ukrainian drones to begin losing connectivity during flights. Some Ukrainian Armed Forces units have already had to cancel some combat missions. Defense Express reports this, citing sources in the military and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, SpaceX set a speed limit for Starshield terminals at 160 km/h. After this threshold is exceeded, the terminal loses connectivity. At the same time, the military is recording disruptions even at significantly lower speeds—approximately 72 to 161 km/h.
In particular, when drones fly at speeds of 110–120 km/h, the connection may disappear for 10–20 seconds. Although the drones continue moving, such interruptions significantly complicate controlling them.
The restrictions threaten attack drones and interceptors
The greatest problems arise with high-speed drones, in particular Middle Strike-type drones, which need to reach high speed immediately after launch. Due to the unstable connection, some aircraft may lose the ability to carry out their missions.
The restrictions have also affected interceptor drones. At the same time, the forced reduction in flight speed makes Ukrainian UAVs more vulnerable to Russian countermeasures.
According to a Defense Express source, on October 14 alone, one of the unmanned systems units was forced to cancel some missions because of problems with Starlink.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense confirmed to journalists that the restrictions had been introduced and said it was already in contact with the United States, SpaceX, and NATO partners. The American company has so far provided no official explanations for the reasons behind the changes.

Katie Zacharia claims to be a lawyer. Was she ever actually licensed? - report

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:48:44 UTC
06:48:44 KST

Newly appointed White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia has repeatedly claimed she is a lawyer.
However, several reports have emerged that Zacharia allegedly is not licensed to practice law.
Independent journalist and lawyer Judd Legum found several instances in which Zacharia referred to herself as a lawyer.
Legum found that she called herself a lawyer in Fox News appearances 18 times alone, and frequently referred to herself as a lawyer on her social media accounts.
“As a lawyer, the procedural steps are absolutely critical to get this right,” Zacharia said on an episode of “Fox and Friends First” on August 31.
But neither Legum nor The Washington Post found any bar admissions in any state under Zacharia’s name or maiden name.
Did Katie Zacharia sit the bar exam?
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University’s School of Law in 2011. However, The Jerusalem Post found that her LinkedIn profile states she earned a Juris Doctor degree, meaning she is not licensed to practice law. Her LinkedIn does not list any current or past bar association membership.
If Zacharia did not sit for or pass the bar exam and was licensed, she is not a lawyer by definition.
Zacharia’s LinkedIn page states that she worked as an associate on the international practice team at Chinese law firm Zhong Lun from 2011-2013.
Legum noted in his newsletter that she could plausibly have practiced in China, since the work does not directly involve American courts.
That being said, she could not have sat the bar exam in China because she is not a Chinese citizen, which is a requirement to take the exam, The Washington Post noted.
She also claims to have worked as general counsel for Fix California, a nonprofit founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell.
Generally, a general counsel is an organization’s chief legal officer, meaning Zacharia would have had to engage in the practice of law. Notably, acting as an organization’s attorney in California without a license would be a misdemeanor.
A spokesman for the State Bar of California, where Zacharia resides, told The Washington Post that it “has no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black having been licensed to practice law in California.”
Zacharia evades questions on legal license
The Trump administration has cited her legal work as part of her qualifications for the job.
US President Donald Trump specifically called Zacharia an attorney in his message announcing that she would be stepping into the role.
“Katie is a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney, and a frequent Commentator on outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.
Journalists pressed Zacharia and Trump for more details about her credentials after Zacharia’s first press briefing on Tuesday.
"What state did she pass the bar exam in? You said she is an attorney. Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?" One reporter asked.
“Which state?” Trump asked.
“When I moved to China,” she appeared to say through muffled audio.
The White House did not clarify whether or not she is a licensed, practicing attorney.
“Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law,” the White House said in a statement.

HRW says 31 executed by eastern Libya authorities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:46:42 UTC
06:46:42 KST

Breadcrumb
HRW says 31 executed by eastern Libya authorities
The NGO Human Rights Watch said Wednesday that military authorities in eastern Libya executed at least 31 people earlier this year, the first reported death sentences to be carried out in the country since 2010, according to the group.
Forces under the control of military leader Khalifa Haftar and his clan executed the people between late August and September 10 "following grossly unfair military trials", HRW said in a statement, adding another 50 people in detention were "at imminent risk of execution".
Libya has struggled to regain stability since former ruler Muammar Gaddafi was toppled and killed in 2011, and the country remains divided between the Haftars in the east and a UN-recognised government in the west.
Haftar's forces "are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya's own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians", said Bassam Khawaja, HRW's deputy Middle East and North Africa director.
He called on the international community to pressure the military authorities to halt any future executions.
Khawaja said the country had gone more than 15 years without an execution, but the eastern authorities "shattered that moratorium in a matter of weeks".
"The lives of at least 50 more people now depend on whether Haftar's forces, and the governments that back them, choose to stop this," he added.
HRW said the detainees were being held in a prison about 100 kilometres east of Benghazi.
It is largely under military control and outside the jurisdiction of the judicial authorities, and is frequently accused of human rights violations, torture and ill-treatment.
The death penalty is still in force in Libya for the crimes of murder, terrorism and offences against state security, though in recent years sentences have not been carried out.

Ukraine deposits seeds in Norway's Arctic vault for 1st time since 2022
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:43:41 CST
06:43:41 KST

OSLO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Ukraine has deposited 773 seed samples in the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway's Arctic archipelago, marking its first contribution to the facility since the Russia-Ukraine conflict broke out in 2022, the Norwegian government said Wednesday.
The deposit on Tuesday was part of an international effort that delivered more than 16,000 seed samples from 21 genebanks to the vault, according to a statement from Norway's Ministry of Agriculture and Food.
The latest Ukrainian deposit included samples of buckwheat and other crops, providing an additional safeguard for the country's agricultural genetic resources.
Norwegian Minister of Agriculture and Food Nils Kristen Sandtroen said the latest deposit demonstrated the importance of international cooperation in protecting global crop diversity.
Six international agricultural research genebanks under CGIAR contributed a total of 8,917 samples, while Italy's Council for Agricultural Research and Economics made its first deposit, including historic wheat and rice varieties.
Established by the Norwegian government in 2008, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault provides free long-term storage for backup copies of seed collections from genebanks around the world.
Located inside a mountain on the island of Spitsbergen, the vault now holds more than 1.4 million seed samples belonging to over 130 genebanks, making it the world's largest secure repository of cultivated crop diversity.
The facility is funded by the Norwegian government and operated in partnership with the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen) and the Global Crop Diversity Trust. ■

Archaeologists uncover 23 Roman-era graves in southern BiH
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:43:39 CST
06:43:39 KST

SARAJEVO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists have uncovered 23 graves dating back to the fourth century at a Roman-era burial site near Livno in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), shedding light on burial customs during the late Roman Empire, local news agency FENA reported on Wednesday.
The excavations at the Stitic site in Suhaca, near Livno, have unearthed rare intact ceramic vessels, glass fragments, jewelry, clothing accessories and a coin bearing the image of Roman Emperor Constantine I.
Archaeologist Marija Maric Bakovic, who participated in the excavations, said the site was the oldest cemetery in the Livno area to undergo systematic excavation, with graves preserved in their original positions.
The findings offer insight into burial customs and beliefs during the period. Ceramic vessels and coins were placed in graves as offerings, while some burials contained as many as three vessels. The significance of this practice remains unclear.
Researchers have also found evidence of earlier cremation practices, indicating a transition to the burial of uncremated bodies, as seen in the fourth-century graves at the site.
Further excavations are planned for next year. ■

Feature: Made-in-China toy ball finds place in Finland's beloved "baby box"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:43:27 CST
06:43:27 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Among the tiny clothes, blankets and other essentials packed into Finland's traditional "baby box" for newborns, a soft little ball makes its debut this year. The colorful ball decorated with pictures of animals and fruits has become part of a cherished Finnish welfare package.
Finland's Social Insurance Institution, known as Kela, announced Wednesday that it had begun distributing the 2026 maternity package, which for the first time includes a toy ball made in China.
The package contains 52 items, ranging from baby clothes and bedding to everyday necessities, following an increase in the maternity grant from 170 euros to 210 euros (189.62-234.24 U.S. dollars). Even the cardboard box itself can serve as a baby's first bed.
A SMALL BALL WITH A BIG ROLE
Ten centimeters in diameter, the ball is manufactured in China under license from U.S. toy brand Fisher-Price and imported by Finnish company Toyrock Group, according to Kela.
Priced at around two euros (2.23 dollars), the ball was selected through Kela's competitive public procurement process. According to Finnish news agency STT, Kela rated the winning product as having very high quality, citing its clear, appealing patterns and well-made seams.
The ball may be simple, but its usefulness grows with the child.
Heidi Virrasoja-Prami, marketing and communications coordinator at Toyrock, told STT that even very young babies could enjoy its colorful patterns and practice grasping its soft fabric surface. As they grow older, children can roll it, throw it, or play with their siblings. A rolling ball may even encourage a baby to start moving after it, she explained.
"The beauty of the ball is that it is a really long-lasting toy," Virrasoja-Prami said.
According to earlier procurement reports, Kela plans to purchase balls for approximately 30,000 maternity packages.
A TRADITION THAT SPANS GENERATIONS
Finland's maternity package has a history dating back nearly nine decades. First introduced in 1938 to support low-income mothers, the maternity grant was extended to all mothers in 1949. Over time, the package has become a beloved national tradition, symbolizing the country's commitment to giving every child a good start in life.
Families can choose between the maternity package and a cash grant, with the box remaining especially popular among first-time parents.
Its contents change each year to reflect evolving childcare needs and sustainability considerations. This year's edition also features a peach-colored, space-themed box design called "Imagining the Future."
According to Kela, the new ball is funded through the government's "Finland on the Move" program, which aims to encourage physical activity across all age groups.
Kela specialist Veera Petaja said the ball was intended to promote interaction between babies and parents and encourage them to be physically active together.
The package also reflects an emphasis on sustainability and reuse, encouraging families to give baby products a second life. "When your baby no longer needs the items in the maternity package, you can pass them on," Petaja said in Wednesday's announcement.
MADE-IN-CHINA PRODUCTS HELP NEW FINNISH PARENTS
The little ball is not the only Chinese-made item in this year's parent kit.
According to Kela's official product list, several other essentials, including baby clothes, insulated mittens and booties, and a snowsuit that doubles as a sleeping bag, are also manufactured in China.
Supplied by different companies, these products have found their way into the welfare package that Finnish families have treasured for generations.
As the newest baby boxes arrive at Finnish homes, the little ball made in China is ready for a new journey - from catching a newborn's attention to becoming a playmate as the child learns to grasp, roll and chase.
For Arja Saakslahti, an associate professor of physical education at the University of Jyvaskyla, the significance of adding a ball to the maternity package goes beyond encouraging physical activity.
In an article published on the university's website, she stressed that the simple toy also sends an important message to parents: spend time with their babies and encourage interaction through play.
Perhaps that is where the little ball's greatest value lies. Having traveled thousands of kilometers from China to Finland, it helps bring parents and children closer, adding moments of joy and connection to everyday family life. ■

China's development represents a rise in the strength of the Global South and a boost to the collective strength of developing countries, Wang said, adding that China stands ready to continue close coordination and cooperation with Azerbaijan to safeguard the common interests of Global South countries.
China supports Azerbaijan in playing an important role on multilateral platforms such as CICA and in international affairs, and in making greater contributions to regional and global peace and stability, Wang said.

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as organized crime fight intensifies

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as organized crime fight intensifies
SAN JOSE, Oct 14 - Costa Rica inaugurated a maximum-security prison on Wednesday as it stepped up its fight against organized crime after a surge in killings in what was long one of Latin America's safest countries.
President Laura Fernandez opened the High-Containment Center Against Organized Crime, or CACCO, a prison modeled on El Salvador's mega-prison and a key element of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele's anti-gang crackdown. The facility near the capital of San Jose has a capacity for 5,100 inmates, roughly 20% of the nation's current prison population.
Costa Rica recorded an all-time high of 905 homicides in 2023, according to judicial data. Killings eased only slightly to 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025, remaining well above earlier levels. Authorities have said most murders are linked to disputes among criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and local markets.
"The CACCO will force criminals to face a new model—a tough-on-crime model. Costa Rica will become a global benchmark for prison security," Fernandez said during the inauguration ceremony.
The president also announced a visit to El Salvador on Friday.
Bukele's crackdown is widely credited with sharply reducing gang violence in El Salvador, but rights groups say it has also brought mass arbitrary detentions, due process violations and an erosion of democratic safeguards.
Fernandez said the new prison's impact would depend in part on the judiciary securing more convictions. Her government has clashed with judicial authorities over crime policy and budget cuts, while judges and prosecutors have warned against pressure on democratic checks and balances.
Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar has presented CACCO as part of a broader effort to reassert state control over the prison system, which he says has been infiltrated by organized crime. The first transfers to the prison will take place at the end of October.
Fernandez recently told Reuters that greater US security presence would help Costa Rica confront drug trafficking and organized crime, although current coordination remains focused on patrols, investigations and extradition efforts. REUTERS

Colombia opposition groups launch protest against de la Espriella’s cuts
Former left-wing President Gustavo Petro joined thousands of demonstrators in Bogota in a march against austerity, restored Israel ties.
A coalition of opposition parties, trade unions, indigenous groups and social movements has protested in Colombia against a series of economic and security policies advanced under right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella.
Thousands marched in major cities including the capital Bogota on Wednesday, the first day of a nationwide campaign led by the country’s former left-wing President Gustavo Petro.
Under Petro, Colombia expanded access to public universities, increased the minimum wage and improved labour protections for workers.
Opposition groups say many of those reforms are now under threat, as de la Espriella’s government embraces cuts to government programmes.
Colombia’s Congress has until Tuesday to approve its 2027 fiscal year budget. But as part of the new administration’s austerity measures, allies of de la Espriella are advancing proposals to reduce government spending.
De la Espriella has also pledged to turn Colombia away from his predecessor’s left-wing leanings and towards more free-market policies aligned with those of United States President Donald Trump.
The government issued new rules for police ahead of the protests, handing expanded powers to law enforcement to more quickly deal with protesters who vandalise public property or disrupt access to essential services.
“The right to protest is respected, but there is no right to destroy, attack the security forces, assault others or sow chaos,” de la Espriella said in a social media statement announcing the decree.
He added that “violence, vandalism and blockades that trample on the rights of millions of citizens will not be tolerated”.
Indigenous communities and political groups in rural parts of the country sometimes block roads as part of their protests, with impediments to traffic sometimes lasting weeks.
But critics have pointed out that the protests this week have been largely peaceful.
Many chanted “It will fall”, a reference to the perceived failure of de la Espriella’s government.
A former defence lawyer and millionaire businessman, de la Espriella was a political newcomer when he ran for the presidency this year on a far-right ticket.
He was elected in a June runoff race by a narrow margin. He campaigned on a hardline platform to address crime, immigration and the economy, including proposals to expel millions of migrants from Colombia and shrink the size of the government.
De la Espriella also pledged to backtrack on reforms made under Petro, Colombia’s first left-wing president. He took office in August.
A former left-wing fighter-turned-politician, Petro took part in protests on Wednesday. He was not eligible for re-election in this year’s presidential race; Colombian law currently caps presidents at a single term.
He wrote on social media that the mobilisations were a wake-up call “two months into the start of a tyrannical and imposed government”.
Protesters also expressed concerns about cuts to labour protections and healthcare under the new administration.
“I feel like we have no guarantees and that the little we did obtain … we’re about to lose,” teacher Ester Guerra, 32, told the news outlet AFP in Bogota.
Some demonstrators also took issue with the new administration’s overtures towards Israel. Several carried Palestinian flags, in a sign of solidarity.
On Wednesday, de la Espriella’s government opened a Colombian embassy in Jerusalem, a controversial move as Israel and Palestine have both claimed parts of the city.
Petro had been a staunch supporter of Palestine and had cut relations with Israel over its genocidal war against Gaza. But de la Espriella has moved to restore the severed ties since taking office.
That struck protesters like Jimena Rodriguez, a 20-year-old student, as an effort to ignore accusations of Israeli abuses against Palestinians.
Several noted that de la Espriella’s actions towards Israel mirrored Trump’s, who moved the US embassy to Jerusalem during his first term in 2018.
President de la Espriella “just wants to hand the country over to the United States, to Israel,” Rodriguez said. “I feel dark times are coming.”

According to Bloomberg, the proposed arrangement would see China remove restrictions on Sindlhauser Materials GmbH, a small German company that supplies components within ASML’s semiconductor production chain.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In return, the EU would lift restrictions imposed on the unnamed Chinese company under its 21st sanctions package against Russia. That package targeted several Chinese firms accused of supplying Moscow with key components that could be used in weapons production.
China sanctioned Sindlhauser and 13 other European companies in July in retaliation for the EU measures, Bloomberg reported. Sindlhauser specializes in high-precision manufacturing and advanced coatings for the semiconductor industry and other sectors.
Brussels and Beijing have also agreed to exchange more information and provide warning of future export restrictions, according to people familiar with the talks.
Bloomberg noted that removing Sindlhauser and the Chinese company from their respective restrictions could establish a model for resolving similar sanctions disputes in the future.
The talks come as Europe tries to protect strategic semiconductor supply chains while maintaining pressure on companies accused of supporting Russia’s military-industrial base. ASML, headquartered in the Netherlands, is one of the world’s most important manufacturers of advanced chipmaking equipment.
Earlier this month, an investigation traced Chinese-made electronics, batteries, radio equipment, and other components to a Russian company linked to the Kurier combat robot. Dozens of Russian declarations were identified naming Chinese manufacturers, although it noted that the records did not prove all of the listed equipment was ultimately imported or installed in Kurier systems.

Sanctions are permanent, until Washington decides otherwise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:33:59 UTC
06:33:59 KST

Sanctions are permanent, until Washington decides otherwise
The agreement to supply Russian diesel fuel to the United States has made a considerable political impact, and it comes amid another escalation of the Ukraine conflict during which both sides have been exchanging large-scale missile and drone strikes.
Meanwhile, the European Union has approved its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, while Washington has adopted another round of punitive measures under the so-called Hellish Sanctions Act.
Yet against this backdrop, the US Treasury has issued a general license authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, unloading and import of Russian diesel fuel until April 2027, which, at first glance, appears extraordinary.
In reality, however, such exemptions are a familiar feature of American sanctions policy as they illustrate a fundamental paradox of the US system: exceptionally severe restrictions coexist with considerable flexibility when Washington’s own interests are at stake.
On one hand, sanctions against Russia, particularly those targeting its energy sector, have become increasingly entrenched, and the latest legislation makes their removal considerably more difficult, adding to an extensive framework of federal laws, presidential orders and administrative regulations accumulated over recent years.
On the other hand, the American executive retains substantial powers to authorize exceptions, meaning even the harshest sanctions need not prevent transactions that Washington considers necessary.
The latest exemption is particularly revealing because the administration didn’t need to invoke the waiver provisions contained in the new legislation, given that Section 115 of the Lindsey Graham Act, for example, permits exemptions provided the administration submits a written justification to Congress, so instead, the Treasury employed a much simpler mechanism.
Last week, Bradley Smith, director of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), signed a general license permitting the diesel transactions. Formally, therefore, the decision was taken not by President Donald Trump, or even by the Treasury secretary, but by a specialized department within the department.
There’s nothing unusual about this procedure. Under the sanctions program targeting what Washington calls Russia’s “malicious activities,” more than 100 general licenses have been issued covering a wide range of transactions, meaning another license is hardly a sensation.
Nor should it be mistaken for the lifting of sanctions because general licenses typically have limited validity and can be revoked before their expiry and a change in the political climate, a shift in Washington’s priorities, or an influx of imported diesel into the American market could be sufficient grounds for withdrawing the exemption.
There are precedents for licenses remaining in force for years. During the improvement in US-Belarusian relations in the 2010s, several major Belarusian enterprises benefited from exemptions that effectively suspended certain restrictions, but when relations deteriorated again in the early 2020s, those licenses were withdrawn.
In other cases, licenses serve the entirely technical purpose of allowing companies to complete transactions or wind down existing operations without violating sanctions, which means the distinction between the political significance of the Russian diesel agreement and its legal substance is therefore essential.
No sanctions have been lifted and Washington has merely employed an established administrative mechanism that can be reversed at any moment.
Nevertheless, the episode demonstrates something important about American sanctions policy in that even as Congress seeks to make restrictions against Russia increasingly permanent, the executive branch retains considerable room for maneuver.
The US can impose unprecedented economic restrictions while simultaneously creating exceptions whenever its interests demand them.
The legal machinery is already in place, but what ultimately determines how it is used is political will.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team

The Prime Minister of Armenia proposed exchanging territories with Azerbaijan to finally settle the long-running conflict
Kyiv • UNN
The Prime Minister of Armenia proposed an equal exchange of land to eliminate the enclaves. He also called for opening routes and abandoning claims.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan proposed that Azerbaijan carry out an equal exchange of territories to resolve the issue of enclaves and remove one of the obstacles to peace between the countries. He said this in his address, UNN reports.
Details
Under Pashinyan's proposal, the two states could exchange plots of land of equal size. This would eliminate enclaves—territories that belong to one country but are surrounded on all sides by another.
In addition, the Armenian prime minister called for transport routes and communications between the countries to be opened, as well as for a final renunciation of mutual territorial claims.
Why Armenia and Azerbaijan have been in conflict for decades
The main cause of the confrontation was Nagorno-Karabakh—an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that was predominantly populated by ethnic Armenians until the events of 2023. In the late 1980s, the dispute over the region escalated into an armed conflict and, after the collapse of the Soviet Union, into a full-scale war.
In the 1990s, Armenian forces established control over Nagorno-Karabakh and adjacent Azerbaijani districts. During the 2020 war, Azerbaijan regained a significant portion of these territories, and in September 2023 it restored control over all of Karabakh. After that, more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians left the region.
Despite the end of hostilities in Karabakh, disputes over borders, enclaves, and transport links remained between the states. Pashinyan proposes resolving these issues through a territorial exchange and mutual recognition of sovereignty.

2026-10-14

06:30:13 KST

Bars, clubs and restaurants will offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years in an effort to give them a first step on the ladder into work.
The move comes before the publication of a report on Neets by the former health secretary Alan Milburn, who has warned that the number of young people not in work or education in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervene.
His full review into Britain’s crisis in youth unemployment, including recommendations to the government about how to tackle the crisis, is expected soon after the autumn budget on 28 October.
Working with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), hospitality businesses including the restaurant chains Wagamama, Nando’s and Burger King, the hotel chain Premier Inn and pub chains including Fuller’s and Mitchells & Butlers will offer Neets aged 18 to 24 placements of up to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.
The initiative, which will be launched by Andy Burnham during a visit to a hospitality venue on Thursday, comes after the DWP announced a similar scheme for retailers including Marks & Spencer, Asda, Pets at Home and the John Lewis Partnership last month.
The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said the scheme would help young people “get their first step on the ladder” and build their careers. “With the UK employment rate now the second highest in the G7, this will unlock 100,000 jobs and connect young people with employers ready to take them on and help them build a brighter future,” he said.
Lucy Powell, the education secretary, is expected to announce a review of school exclusion changes, after research showed that students who are persistently absent from school are nearly four times more likely to end up unemployed and not in education or training.
A consultation will gather views on measures to support students at risk of exclusion, improve integration into the classroom and help children stay engaged in the classroom.
Powell said: “Absence and exclusion are too often a path to disengagement, with increased risks of becoming Neet. Too many young people who fall out of education risk being permanently left on the sidelines of work and opportunity.”
Milburn has signalled that Britain’s benefits system should be overhauled, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships. Ministers are understood to be considering sweeping changes to the welfare system, including scrapping a critical disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.
Milburn has previously argued that a national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work.
The chancellor, John Healey, has indicated a readiness to curtail the government’s rising benefits bill, while McFadden has said there is a moral and economic case to shake up the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has made demands for cuts to welfare a central plank of her attacks on the government, telling Burnham in prime minister’s questions (PMQs) on Wednesday that he should cut welfare to fund higher defence spending.
But ministers will be wary of going head to head with Labour MPs, and will hope to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion that forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.

The European Union is so far refraining from using a special mechanism to protect the International Criminal Court (ICC) from the U.S. sanctions imposed by Donald Trump's administration. Details

We have not made any decisions yet. But we continue discussions at all levels
How the EU can protect the court from U.S. sanctions
The blocking statute allows the European Union to counter the effects of foreign sanctions on its territory. In particular, it prohibits European companies and banks from complying with specified sanctions imposed by third countries. The mechanism was previously used in response to U.S. sanctions against Cuba, Iran, and Libya.
Despite having such an instrument, Brussels is currently betting on negotiations. According to EUobserver, at the EU summit on October 15, European leaders plan to call on Washington to lift the sanctions against the ICC.

Halevy warned that the flow of goods into the Gaza Strip would drop by 50%, adding: "Hamas will try to blame Israel."
The dramatic move also followed an increase in direct threats against the lives of merchants who refuse to comply with the terrorist organization's demands. The letter was sent to Mladenov, Maj. Gen. Jasper Jeffers, commander of the International Stabilization Force for Gaza, and Ramiz Alakbarov, the U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the region.
According to the statement, the decision to strike came after members of Hamas' security apparatus arrested the son of a merchant whose father had refused to comply with the terrorist organization's demands for extortion payments and taxes.
According to the IDF, reports received from merchants indicate that Hamas demands a cash payment of approximately 10,000 shekels for every truck entering the Gaza Strip. It also requires merchants to sell require merchants to sell about 30% of their merchandise in cash transactions, a measure designed to enable Hamas to seize the proceeds directly and thereby preserving its grip on power. 
Moreover, the practice directly violates the commitment made by merchants authorized to operate in Gaza to conduct payments exclusively through monitored bank transfers. Reports also indicate that the taxation system has recently been expanded to include secondary merchants and that Hamas intends to impose it even on drinking water supplies.
The merchants' strike directly undermines Israel's ability to meet its commitments. Under the ceasefire agreement, Israel is obligated to allow approximately 600 trucks into Gaza each day, divided roughly equally between international organizations and independent Gazan merchants. Because the private sector accounts for about 50% of all trucks entering the Gaza Strip each week, the strike is expected to reduce the daily flow by approximately 300 trucks, a drop of about 50%.
Three years into the war, Hamas remains standing, managing daily life for Gaza's residents and exerting significant influence over the entry of aid trucks. The IDF has acknowledged that it has so far failed to develop a system that would allow aid trucks to enter Gaza and reach residents without passing through Hamas' hands. There are concerns that the consequences of the strike — a de facto reduction in the flow of goods into Gaza — will intensify international criticism of Israel and further delegitimize its operations in the Gaza Strip.
In his letter, Halevy made clear that Hamas bears full responsibility and called on international officials to act immediately to prevent the terrorist organization from interfering with the mechanism for bringing aid and goods into Gaza and exploiting it to strengthen itself economically and militarily. Halevy also warned that Hamas would exploit the merchants' strike to spread false claims about shortages of goods and Israel's alleged failure to comply with the terms of the agreement.
Raids in the West Bank

During two targeted operations in Ramallah and Yatta, five terrorists who had collaborated with Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) were arrested. According to the IDF and Shin Bet, the "charitable organizations" served as offices for the terrorist groups.
Earlier this week, IDF and Shin Bet forces raided the offices of the Addameer charitable organization in Ramallah. During the operations, suspects were arrested and computers, documents and checkbooks bearing the logos of organizations designated as Hamas-affiliated funds were confiscated. The IDF said Addameer is financed by terrorist funds and operates to provide legal assistance to imprisoned PFLP terrorists. Some of the terrorists employed by the organization took part in the August 23, 2019, terrorist attack at the Dani Spring, in which Rina Shnerb was murdered.
In another operation targeting centers of incitement and terrorism, IDF forces acting on Shin Bet intelligence raided the offices of the Islamic Association for the Care of Orphans, which has been designated an unlawful association, in the town of Yatta in the IDF's Judea Brigade sector of responsibility in recent weeks.
The detainees and seized materials were transferred to security forces for further investigation.
