Turkey seizes control of opposition TV channel as Erdoğan tightens grip on media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:24:05 UTC
06:24:05 KST

Turkish authorities raided the headquarters of Halk TV on Wednesday, one of the country's most popular television channels and among its last remaining independent media outlets. Citing an ongoing corruption investigation, authorities appointed a state trustee to take control of the channel. The dramatic raid interrupted its live broadcast and is seen as an escalation in President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's efforts to suppress criticism and silence Turkey's free press.
The raid on Halk TV's headquarters in Istanbul began early Wednesday morning, with large numbers of police officers seen surrounding the building. The channel reported on its website that "hundreds of police officers" entered its offices while its journalists were barred from entering. The live broadcast was cut off at 6:30 a.m., after which the channel began airing prerecorded programs.
The Istanbul prosecutor's office said the raid and takeover of the channel's management were part of an investigation into its owner, Cafer Mahiroğlu, on suspicion of "bribery, bid rigging and laundering assets derived from criminal activity." Arrest warrants were issued for 17 suspects as part of the investigation, 11 of whom were detained. Authorities also announced that several companies linked to Mahiroğlu had been seized and that the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) had been appointed as trustee to manage them.
Mahiroğlu, who lives outside Turkey and was not in the country at the time of the raid, described it as "a dark day for Turkey." In a video he released, he accused authorities of "taking control of the public's access to information for political reasons." He dismissed the allegations against him as baseless and said seven members of his family had been arrested during the raid.
Özgür Özel, leader of the main opposition New Party (Yeni Parti, YEP), also strongly condemned the raid, calling it further evidence of Erdoğan's dictatorial rule.
"A dawn raid on a television channel, the appointment of a trustee — only dictators do such things," he wrote in a post on X. "Those who appointed trustees to take over local governments and trampled on the will of the people are now appointing a trustee to take control of Halk TV, a channel watched by millions. Because they are I-N-C-O-M-P-E-T-E-N-T and C-O-W-A-R-D-S!"
During Erdoğan's more than two decades of increasingly tight control over Turkey, press freedom in the country has been severely undermined. This year, Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the World Press Freedom Index compiled by Reporters Without Borders. The organization says 90% of the country's national media outlets are under government control.
Halk TV is the fifth major media outlet in recent years to be placed under the control of a state-appointed trustee by Turkish authorities, in a move aimed at controlling its broadcasts and reporting and preventing criticism of Erdoğan's government.
State-appointed trustees have similarly been installed to run numerous local authorities as part of what is widely seen as a broader crackdown on the opposition. That campaign included the arrest last year of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, who was charged with corruption. İmamoğlu is considered Erdoğan's most prominent rival and the opposition's candidate in the next presidential election.
Several other mayors were also arrested, while mounting pressure on the opposition has prompted some opposition mayors to defect to Erdoğan's ruling Justice and Development Party (Adalet ve Kalkınma Partisi, AKP).
Erdoğan's crackdown continued this year when the judiciary, which is under his control, annulled the results of the 2023 internal party leadership election of the Republican People's Party (Cumhuriyet Halk Partisi, CHP) in May. The secular party, founded by modern Turkey's founding father, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, had until then been the country's main opposition party.
The annulment led to Özel's removal as party leader and the reinstatement of former chairman Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, who led the CHP to defeat against Erdoğan and his party in the 2023 elections but is now seen as an ally of the president.
The court ruling sparked unrest, and police even stormed the party's headquarters and forcibly removed Özel, around whom the opposition had rallied following Imamoglu's arrest.
Özel subsequently left the CHP and founded the New Party, which was joined by large numbers of lawmakers who defected alongside him. It is now the largest opposition faction in parliament.
Since being reinstated as CHP chairman by court order, Kılıçdaroğlu has expressed positions more closely aligned with Erdoğan's government. The raid on Halk TV came just days after he, too, criticized the channel's coverage and announced that he had filed a complaint against it with the media regulator.
Nevertheless, following the raid, Kılıçdaroğlu also joined the chorus of criticism, describing the move as an example of "systematic pressure" on opposition-affiliated media.
European officials also criticized the raid, although Europe's growing dependence on security cooperation with Turkey, a NATO member, means that, as in previous cases, the criticism is unlikely to be accompanied by concrete action.
Nacho Sánchez Amor, the European Parliament's rapporteur on Turkey, said Turkish authorities were "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and were seeking to extend their control to 100%.
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory," he warned.

Borisoglebsk air base is actively used by Russian forces to station Su-34 and Su-35 fighter-bombers. These aircraft are regularly deployed to drop guided aerial bombs on Ukrainian positions and frontline towns.
The site also houses storage facilities for guided aerial bombs and large aviation fuel tanks.
Neither the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine nor Russian officials have yet officially confirmed the extent of the damage.
Background:
- In October 2024, Ukraine's defence forces conducted a joint drone operation against Borisoglebsk air base, striking ammunition depots and aircraft parking areas.
- In July 2025, Ukrainian forces attacked the military facility again, damaging infrastructure and aircraft.
- On the night of 7-8 July 2026, units of Ukraine's defence forces conducted another strike on the air base in Voronezh Oblast, destroying a fuel and lubricants storage facility.

OpenAI bugging suspect booked one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia with family before arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:18:13 UTC
06:18:13 KST

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national charged with secretly installing a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI, had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest, federal prosecutors told a judge in a newly unsealed court filing.
Alfozan "has the means — and will have the incentive — to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested," the U.S. Attorney's Office in San Francisco said in the Oct. 8 filing, which asked a judge to seal a criminal complaint against him and a warrant for his arrest.
The filing said the tickets were booked for Oct. 12, from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul.
The judge granted the sealing request, and Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9, the Department of Justice has said.
He has been detained since his arrest.
Alfozan, 35, is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists a prince from that nation's ruling royal family as a fellow partner.
The VC firm, Raed Ventures, says on its website that Alfozan, who lives in the San Francisco area, "is a seasoned technology professional with deep experience in startups, entrepreneurship, and scaling tech companies."
"He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform," Alfozan's bio page on Raed's site says.
Raed, which focuses on investments in the Middle East, announced Alfozan had joined the firm on Feb. 8, 2025, two days after Raed said Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud had joined as a venture partner. A venture partner usually is a consulting or project-based role, not an investing partner or director who is responsible for raising funds or leading deals.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, according to the Department of Justice. The company said it terminated him this month.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that when Saudi tech influencers visited San Francisco in September, "it was Alfozan who welcomed them to OpenAI offices where he gave them tours."
A former CIA official with extensive experience in the Middle East, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the nature of their past work, told CNBC that Raed Ventures is "basically a state organ" of the Saudi government. One of Raed's funds in December 2024 received an investment from Saudi Venture Capital, a subsidiary of SME Bank, which is part of Saudi Arabia's National Development Fund.
In addition to being a venture partner in Raed, the prince, Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, is a member of the ruling Al Saud family, and the managing director and vice chairman of his family's private office, according to his bio on Raed's website.
The former CIA official said that if Alfozan's alleged bugging of OpenAI is part of a state-sponsored espionage effort, it shows that "in the AI and tech boom, even the kingdom of Saudi Arabia has assessed that the risk is worth the gain to engage in economic espionage against a close ally."
The former official also said this incident is "probably the tip of the iceberg."
The criminal complaint against Alfozan does not allege that Raed or its other partners were aware of Alfozan allegedly planting a recording device at OpenAI.
The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California, according to the Department of Justice.
Alfozan is charged in U.S. District Court in San Francisco with one count of using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.
He is being detained pending an Oct. 19 detention hearing, where his lawyer could argue for his release on bond. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, DOJ said.
Alfozan is not charged with corporate espionage or stealing trade secrets.
OpenAI earlier this year held discussions with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the country's sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the AI company.
Raed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNBC has also requested comment from the Saudi embassy in Washington.
Alfozan's criminal defense attorney, William Pernik, told CNBC by email, "At this point, the information provided has been extremely limited, as the charging documents have just been unsealed yesterday."
OpenAI declined to comment on Wednesday about whether it knew about Alfozan's position at the Saudi firm. And the company said it can't share more details about the conference room in question due to operational security concerns.
The company said in a post on X on Tuesday, "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
"We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,"
the company said. "Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
Alfozan, in a recent interview with the podcast Identity Capital about his career, noted that in July 2016, he and other Saudi nationals who were working at various tech companies in Silicon Valley met with their nation's now-de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The prince was visiting Silicon Valley as part of a U.S. tour to promote his "Vision 2030" economic diversification plan.
"One of the issues we discussed was whether we should move back to [the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia] now and bring our technical skills to improve the economy ... or should we work a few more years before we go back in order to gain more experience," Alfozan said in the interview, which was conducted in Arabic, translated by CNBC and posted online Sept. 24.
Bin Salman replied that "the country was undergoing major development and did not have the talent to train the next generation who would carry on those development plans," Alfozan said.
Alfozan added that the group of young workers "decided it was best to continue to learn and develop our skills before taking our knowledge back to [Saudi Arabia] to improve the tech sector."
Throughout the podcast, Alfozan discusses in detail his trajectory from coding in high school in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, to his career in the U.S. At one point in the interview, he refers to himself as an "introvert," who still pushes himself to help other young professionals find success in Silicon Valley.
Days after the podcast was posted, on Sept. 30, a federal criminal complaint alleges that OpenAI staff discovered "a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in" a conference room.
The device, which had a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage, was concealed in toilet paper, according to the complaint.
Alfozan had no authority to enter the conference room, which is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," according to the complaint.
The conference room can be reserved "only by executives and executive assistants," and is typically used "for internal leadership meetings and technical and product sessions, as well as external briefings with government officials and business counterparts," the complaint said.
Closed-circuit TV footage at OpenAI showed Alfozan close to the conference room on multiple days in September at various times, according to the complaint.
The filing also said that in August, and again in September, Alfozan used an AI productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, as well as "external partner meetings."
And a chatbot associated with Alfozan's spouse, which the complaint alleges shared several identifying characteristics with his own account, allegedly submitted detailed prompts about building, customizing, installing and remotely accessing a recording device. Alfozan's spouse, who was not identified in the complaint, has not been charged with any wrongdoing.
After the recording device was found hidden in the TV in the conference room, OpenAI placed a camera in that room, the complaint says.
Alfozan was seen on that camera entering the conference room at about 1:20 p.m. on Oct. 5, and "checking behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted," the complaint alleges.
That same day, the complaint said, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a printer room at OpenAI.
Inside that bag, OpenAI security found his wallet, ID and "another recording device" made by the same Chinese manufacturer, Seeed, which made the device found inserted in the conference room's TV, the complaint says.
The second recording device, like the first one, "had a recording microcontroller," and "had been customized to obfuscate anything stored on the device, such as potentially intercepted audio communications," the complaint said.
Alfozan reported to OpenAI that he had lost the bag, which was returned to him without the second recording device, according to the complaint. He did not inquire about the device, although he asked about certain other items that he said were missing, the complaint said.
"Any attempt to illicitly obtain protected information from U.S. super intelligence and technology companies threatens both American innovation and the national security interests those advancements support," Scott Schelble, special agent in charge of the FBI San Francisco Field Office, said in a statement on Tuesday about Alfozan's arrest, using the Trump administration's preferred term for artificial intelligence.
Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan had a long track record of work experience in the Bay Area.
On his LinkedIn page, Alfozan describes himself as an "Experienced Engineering Lead with 11 years of building scalable and reliable software systems in the data and AI/ML domains."
"Proven track record of leading engineering teams, delivering complex projects and enterprise products. 
Driven by strong project management skills and a passion for cultivating a culture of collaboration and engineering excellence," his bio there says.
Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan was a founding engineer at Nash, an AI firm focused on logistics, according to his LinkedIn page.
And prior to Nash, he worked as a senior systems engineer at Facebook's parent company, Meta, from 2017 through 2022, according to his LinkedIn page. His internships before that included one at Microsoft in 2014, his bio says.
Alfozan studied computer science and engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and data science at the University of California, Berkeley, according to his LinkedIn page.
MIT's media relations office said he was enrolled there from January 2011 through January 2014, and again from February 2016 through May 2016, without receiving a degree.
A UC Berkeley spokesperson said Alfozan attended the school from January 2023 through May 2025, and earned a master's degree.
In 2016, he was a research intern at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia, he said on LinkedIn.
In 2020, he won a $50,000 second prize in the Saudi Covid-19 Challenge, a hackathon event, according to the profile.
Alfozan's home, on a hill in Millbrae, California, overlooks San Francisco Bay with views of Mount Diablo. The small San Mateo County suburb, which is popular with tech workers, is located about 30 minutes south of San Francisco and 25 minutes from Stanford University. No one answered the doorbell of the home Wednesday when a CNBC reporter rang.
The Financial Times reported that Alfozan was "born in the ultraconservative central region of Qassim," but "grew up in Dammam in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province."
The FT also reported that in a documentary about Alfozan that aired on Saudi television, his father said that as a young student in a government-backed program for gifted children to develop skills in mathematics, physics and engineering, Alfozan "would read the encyclopedia cover to cover."
"We are waiting to see what evidence the government has against our client, and look forward to presenting all appropriate defenses in court," Pernik, Alfozan's attorney, said.
"What I can tell you by way of a statement is that, like countless Americans, Mr. Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream," the attorney said. "He spent years studying, working and contributing to an American technological sector that leads the world, a sector built in large part by immigrants like him."
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why," Pernik said.
The lawyer noted that Alfozan is "charged with violating a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent."
"There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us," Pernik said. "Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origins is — and always should be — a protected status under our system of laws."
— Ashley Capoot, Lora Kolodny and Reem Nasr contributed to this report.

Supreme Court sides with Republicans in dispute over cost of campaign ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:16:49 UTC
06:16:49 KST

Supreme Court sides with Republicans in dispute over cost of campaign ads
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The Supreme Court gave political parties and their fundraising committees lower rates for broadcast campaign ads.
- Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson voted to deny the administration’s appeal.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court sided with Republicans on Wednesday and gave political parties and their fundraising committees lower rates for broadcast campaign ads.
Over two dissents, the justices granted a fast-track appeal from the Trump administration and the National Republican Congressional Committee and upheld the use of the GOP-friendly rule in the midterm election.
In a brief order, the court said the issue should be left to the Federal Communications Commission.
The outcome has given Republican candidates an advertising edge in the final weeks of the campaign.
Federal law says a “legally qualified candidate” running for election is entitled to a “lower unit charge” for campaign ads in the 60 days prior to an election.
However, on March 30, the FCC, under Republican control, announced that broadcasters must extend the lower rates to political parties and their joint fundraising committees.
The FCC notice did not explain the basis for this change, and it refused to hold a commission hearing to debate the issue.
But the change was seen as benefiting Republicans.
Democratic candidates have raised more money from direct but limited contributions from individuals, while Republicans have raised far more through party committees that are funded by wealthy donors.
The nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center said the FCC’s rule change was “contrary to the text and purpose of the federal statute and would effectively grant super PACs an advertising discount.”
Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, issued a statement objecting to the change.
“The American public should not have sweeping election-year rule changes forced on them in the dark, on the eve of the election, without a single opportunity for public input,” she said.
Democratic Senate candidates Sherrod Brown of Ohio, Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Roy Cooper from North Carolina objected to the FCC rule change in April and asked for a review.
When no action was taken, they filed suit in federal court. They argued the FCC had no authority to change the law that gave only candidates, not fundraising committees, the benefit of the lower ad rates.
Since then, the two sides have gone back and forth in the courts, with each accusing the other of seeking a late change in the rules.
The U.S. 4th Circuit Court of Appeals in Virginia ruled for the Democrats in a pair of 2-1 decisions.
“Suffice to say that any ‘chaos’ is the FCC’s fault, not ours,” Judge Robert B. King, a Clinton appointee, said on Oct. 7. It “has endeavored to create from whole cloth a new rule entirely outside the purview of judicial review.”
But the Supreme Court stepped in twice to overturn the 4th Circuit and rule for the Republicans.
In an unsigned Sept. 4 order, the court said that the 4th Circuit intervened too soon. The law “makes clear that an aggrieved party must wait for the Commission to resolve its application for review by order before filing a petition for judicial review.”
Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
In September, the FCC did nothing other than to ask for public comments on its March rule change.
Frustrated with the delay, the 4th Circuit issued a second order requiring the FCC to act by Oct. 9.
Last week, in response to an appeal from Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer, Chief Justice John G. Roberts put the 4th Circuit order on hold.
On Wednesday, the full court said the 4th Circuit Court should have left the issue to the FCC.
“Our system of separation of powers does not allow the judiciary to meddle in the workings of a coordinate branch of the government in this manner,” the court said an unsigned opinion.
In dissent, Jackson and Justice Sonia Sotomayor voted to deny the administration’s appeal.

Who Runs the Catholic Church When the Pope Is Hospitalized?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:09:52 UTC
06:09:52 KST

Pope Leo XIV is expected to remain hospitalized for around a week after he had part of his right lung removed in an operation on Tuesday. The Vatican said tests had confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer worldwide.
The Pontiff’s first night in Rome’s Gemelli Hospital was “calm,” the Vatican shared in an update Wednesday morning, and doctors have since said that Leo’s tests show his “recovery is progressing normally.” He has undergone respiratory physiotherapy, has begun walking around his room, and has “resumed eating normally.” Leo will be observed while further tests are performed on his removed cancer tissue, as doctors determine what treatments might be needed next.
Leo, 71, had publicly addressed his health during Sunday prayers in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, during which he said doctors had discovered a “localized nodule” in his lung that required surgery. He thanked everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.
Following the news of Leo’s diagnosis, people across the world have sent their well wishes. President Donald Trump, who has previously criticized the first American Pope, told reporters he wishes Leo "well" and said to "get better fast." European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen wished Leo a “full and speedy recovery,” while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described the Pope as “a source of hope and inspiration for billions around the world.”
As head of the Catholic Church, Leo leads an institution with an immense global following. Figures released in March by the Central Office of Church Statistics of the Secretariat of State show that the number of Catholics worldwide stood at just over 1.422 billion in 2024.
While Leo focuses on his recovery, all papal audiences have been canceled until Oct. 20. His time away from the Vatican has prompted questions about who, if anyone, oversees the church while a Pope is hospitalized.
Here’s what to know about the role of the Pope and how the Vatican will run in his absence.
What is the role of the Pope?
The Pope is the Bishop of Rome and, under Catholic canon law, is described as “the head of the college of bishops, the Vicar of Christ, and the pastor of the universal church on earth,” granting him “supreme, full, immediate, and universal ordinary power in the church.”
Miles Pattenden, a historian of the Catholic Church at the University of Oxford, says the Pope is essentially “the man who makes executive decisions about how the church is to be run [from] the appointment of bishops, cardinals, the canonisation of saints, [to] anything else that involves the Pope's personal legislative or doctrinal authority.”
Beyond his role within the church, the Pope is also a key international figure, frequently speaking out on high-profile topics such as artificial intelligence and immigration, and making apostolic journeys abroad.
In June, Leo made his first major European trip to Spain in honor of Pope Francis, who in the final years of his life had expressed a desire to visit the Canary Islands, a major arrival point for migrants crossing the Atlantic from West Africa into Europe. In September, Leo also embarked on a four-day visit to France.
The Pope is scheduled to take a 12-day trip to Latin America on Nov. 6, which is set to include a stop in Peru, where Leo holds citizenship. The trip is set to go ahead as planned.
TIME has reached out to the Holy See press office for comment.
What happens if a Pope becomes sick, incapacitated, or is hospitalized?
The Vatican has detailed laws and rituals to transfer papal power if a Pope dies or resigns. But none of them apply when he is sick or even unconscious.
Unlike other positions within the church, Catholic canon law does not provide a clear mechanism for transferring the Pope's authority if he becomes unable to carry out his responsibilities. Canon 335 declares that when the Holy See is “vacant or entirely impeded, nothing is to be altered in the governance of the universal church.” The papacy becomes vacant only if the Pontiff dies or resigns, with a resignation required to be “made freely and properly manifested.”
“There is no alternative rule. The Pope is in charge, and there's no mechanism to say the Pope can't be in charge. There's no rules on that,” says Pattenden. "When the Pope is incapacitated, that's a serious problem for the governance of the church.”
In February 2013, Pope Benedict XVI, then 85, gathered the cardinals and announced his resignation as leader of the Catholic Church, citing his “advanced age.” He became the first Pontiff to step down voluntarily in nearly 600 years. Pope Francis confirmed in 2022 that he had prepared a resignation letter shortly after being elected Pontiff in 2013, "in case of impediment due to health reasons." The letter, the contents of which are unknown, was not used, as Francis remained in office until his death aged 88 in April 2025. His final weeks included an extended stay in the hospital as he battled a number of health issues.
“The church doesn't have a process or a procedure like, for instance, the U.S. Constitution, there's no equivalent to the 25th Amendment, and there's no ‘Vice Pope’ like the Vice President,” Pattenden says, remarking on the lack of a deputy as something that can be perceived as a “weakness in the church's constitution.”
As such, “anything that requires [the Pope’s] personal or doctrinal authority” during a hospital stay would have to wait until the Pope is able to address such matters.
Pope Leo, who is fully conscious and already walking around, remains contactable and will likely be able to liaise with church officials, should any pertinent issues arise during his hospital stay. On Wednesday, Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle presided over a mass in place of Leo, and read out a homily prepared by the Pope.
Interestingly, other positions within the church have clearer arrangements in place for periods of incapacity.
For instance, canon law provides for circumstances in which a diocesan bishop becomes unable to govern his diocese, allowing its day-to-day administration to pass to an auxiliary bishop, vicar general, or another designated official.
What does the Roman Curia do?
The Pope already delegates the day-to-day running of the Vatican and church to a group of officials who operate whether he is in the Apostolic Palace or not, and whether he is conscious.
The Roman Curia is the central administrative institution of the Holy See, supporting the Pope in governing the Catholic Church and carrying out its wider responsibilities.
“It has lots of departments, called dicasteries, which continue running according to their present structure and instructions,” says Pattenden. “For instance, there's a dicastery of education that is involved in the running of Catholic universities, setting up links for them, seminaries, and schools, and so on, and there are lots of officials with delegated authority.”
Among the most senior officials is the Vatican Secretary of State, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, whom Pattenden describes as “the second most important person in the Vatican.”
Parolin addressed Leo's surgery early Tuesday, expressing concern, while praising Pope Leo’s calm manner.
Other senior church roles include the Dean of the College of Cardinals—a position recently assigned to Cardinal Tagle. The dean is known for playing a key role in papal transitions and is often considered a top contender himself.
The camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church , a role currently held by Cardinal Kevin Farrell, also takes on specific administrative responsibilities when the papacy becomes vacant following a Pope's death or resignation. The camerlengo helps oversee the Holy See's administration and finances during this period, but notably does not assume the Pope's authority or become an acting Pontiff during hospitalization.
As for now, the Vatican has not indicated that Leo is in any way incapable of performing or delegating his duties.
“It's very clear that Pope Leo wants to be as transparent as possible,” says Pattenden, who notes that “being reminded of the Pope's mortality in this way will cause people to think about the kind of broader questions about what might happen to a Pope who's in ill health.”

Air Force Searching for Next-Gen Perimeter Air Defense Radars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:09:03 UTC
06:09:03 KST

The Air Force is looking to replace the three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations.
A Sept. 21 notice from the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center seeks sources for new technology to continue the Air Route Surveillance Radar-4’s mission and potentially improve its technology.
The notice’s details are classified, but AFLCMC updated the original notice Oct. 13, according to Sam.gov.
The number of radars needed to replace the 44-radar network and the price for those replacements has not yet been determined and will come via market research, Air Force Materiel Command spokesperson Mark Wyatt told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
There is also no development timeline publicly available, though responses to the sources sought notice are due by Oct. 21.
Wyatt said AFLCMC is requesting an instrumented range of 250 nautical miles, identical to the current ARSR-4.
ARSR-4 helps operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. While historically the radar has been very effective at this task, newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly.
“Wind farms are one of many sources of clutter that any solution would have to address,” Wyatt said. “The Air Force is not prescribing any technique to solve this long-standing challenge for radars.”
Interested industry parties can continue to pair their replacement option with the existing Monopulse Maintenance Surveillance Radar or replace that radar with another solution, Wyatt said.
The MMSR works with the ARSR-4 to “interrogate” aircraft transponders it detects by sending out coded radio frequency pulses that the transponder then responds to.
Using the monopulse method, the MMSR can determine an aircraft’s azimuth from a single pulse received from the transponder, instead of needing multiple hits when sweeping the area.
The MMSR is mounted on the ARSR-4, and they rotate together as they monitor the skies.

- Tyndall Air Force Base, Fla.
- Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.
- Watford City, N.D.
- Whitehouse, Fla.
- Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, Cuba
An Aging Platform
The Air Force purchased most of the existing 44 radars in the 1990s, upgrading the previous 1, 2, and 3 models that have monitored the skies since the late 1950s.
The Raytheon-built ARSR-1 entered service in 1958 and was first used to manage the exploding growth of civil aviation. It had a 170-200 nautical mile range. That early system used the Army/Navy/Fixed Radar Surveillance-20 and later variants of the AN/FPS-66. In the 1960s, Raytheon produced the ARSR-2, which improved maintenance and reliability factors. That radar was the AN/FPS-115.
Both the ARSR-1 and -2 ran on vacuum tubes.
Westinghouse Electric Corporation built the AN/FPS-130, the radar base of the ARSR-3, fielding it in the 1970s and extending detection ranges beyond 240 nautical miles; it was incorporated into joint military-civil air defense networks.
The ARSR-4, also built by Westinghouse and commissioned in the 1990s, was the first radar in the family to offer three-dimensional target tracking. That capability allows users to simultaneously measure a target’s range, azimuth, and altitude. The system also provided advanced look-down/clutter rejection capabilities for military operations.
Northrop Grumman acquired Westinghouse in 1996, rolling the company’s radar and electronic warfare programs into its Electronic Systems sector.
While the ARSR-4s monitor the perimeter of the country, Guam, and Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, for the U.S. interior, the FAA manages a network of Common Air Route Surveillance Radars. The CARSR has an estimated 200 nautical mile range.
The complete CARSR system replacement rollout concluded in 2015. The rollout maintained the legacy sites, towers, and mechanical controls while refitting the internal electronics of the radars.
One ARSR-4 location has a strategically vital area to protect: Watford City, N.D., is 165 miles from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., home of the 91st Missile Wing, and 263 miles from Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.—putting hundreds of ICBM silos in its range.
A Larger Network
The ARSR-4 system is one piece of a larger detection system used to track incoming threats.
The Air Force and NORAD used the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77, both of which serve as northern warning systems out to 250 nautical miles. These systems are specifically designed for extreme cold weather, such as in their locations in Alaska and northern Canada.
The Space Force operates the AN/Frequency Precision and Quantization-16 Perimeter Acquisition Radar Attack Characterization System, which tracks missiles and precision space objects out to about 2,000 miles. USSF also operates the AN/FPS-108 COBRA DANE to track missiles out to 2,000 miles and high-altitude space objects at 25,000 miles.
The Space Force’s 20th Space Surveillance Squadron at Elgin Air Force Base, Fla., operates the AN/FPS-85 Phased Array Radar, which can track objects beyond 22,000 miles.
NORAD is also currently building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network.
The Homeland Defense OTHR, which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031.
Canada’s Polar OTHR is expected to cost up to $3.5 billion and is a slice of the nation’s estimated $38.6 billion overhaul of its portion of NORAD.
The polar project is currently in the site procurement phase, with operational deployment planned for 2029 and FOC by 2033.
The U.S. Northern Warning System Modernization project “Crossbow” could cost up to $6 billion, and the system rollout is expected to last until 2028, with the project concluding in 2035.
The High-Altitude and Mobile Near-Space Surveillance Systems has a $4.2 billion contract ceiling and is currently in field testing and initial low-altitude deployments. It is expected to achieve full cloud-based command-and-control network integration by 2028.

Ex-Israeli spy chief sues Netanyahu over October 7

Ex-Israeli spy chief sues Netanyahu over October 7
Former Israeli intelligence chief Ronen Bar has sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation, accusing him of ignoring warnings ahead of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and attempting to shift the blame for the security failures.
Bar, who headed Israel’s Shin Bet domestic security agency during the assault, filed the three-million-shekel (nearly $1 million) lawsuit on Wednesday.
Netanyahu had accused Bar of withholding intelligence and failing to alert troops or evacuate attendees of the Nova music festival. Bar rejected the allegations, arguing that Netanyahu was attempting to deflect responsibility for the attack, which left around 1,200 people dead and saw 251 taken hostage. Israel’s subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,300 Palestinians, according to the enclave’s Health Ministry.
According to the lawsuit, Shin Bet officers began sharing intelligence about unusual Hamas activity with the military late on October 6 and issued a warning at 3:03 am. Netanyahu’s military secretariat was updated at 3:55 am, while Bar’s chief of staff briefed his military secretary shortly after 6 am. Bar denied speaking directly with Israel’s military chief or head of military intelligence that night, contrary to Netanyahu’s account.
Bar acknowledged that Shin Bet had failed to anticipate the scale and timing of the assault and provide adequate warnings. He accepted responsibility for those failures, which contributed to his resignation.
However, he maintained that Netanyahu had been repeatedly alerted to the risk. Bar cited a February 2023 letter warning that Israel’s internal divisions and instability in the Palestinian territories could embolden its adversaries. In July, he said he had personally raised the prospect of an attack, cautioning that intelligence agencies might not be able to predict it.
The filing describes further warnings in September and early October about Hamas’s growing capabilities. Bar also alleged that Netanyahu repeatedly rejected or delayed proposals to target senior Hamas figures, favoring a policy of “quiet at any cost” in Gaza.
According to the lawsuit, the prime minister continued allowing Qatari money into the enclave despite warnings that humanitarian funds were reaching Hamas’ military wing.
Netanyahu rejected the claims, saying Bar could have contacted him through a secure emergency line. Bar said Netanyahu never provided him with his personal phone number.
Netanyahu also said he had submitted nearly 1,000 documents challenging Bar’s account.
His government voted to dismiss Bar in March 2025, citing a loss of confidence. At the time, Shin Bet was investigating allegations that Netanyahu’s aides had promoted Qatari interests, which the office denied. Israel’s Supreme Court later ruled the dismissal unlawful, and Bar resigned in June.
The lawsuit follows reports that Netanyahu received advance warnings from foreign governments. Haaretz reported in September that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed had alerted him to a potential major Hamas operation ten days before the assault. Netanyahu’s office dismissed the allegation as an “absolute lie.”
The Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal have separately reported warnings from Egyptian officials, while the New York Times revealed that Israeli intelligence had obtained a Hamas battle plan known as Jericho Wall more than a year earlier. Netanyahu has denied receiving warnings from Egypt or being shown the Hamas plan.
The political fallout comes ahead of Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections, with Netanyahu accusing his critics of using the October 7 attack for political purposes.

A container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz after an attack – the crew was evacuated in time
Kyiv • UNN
The container ship GFS Pride sank after being struck in the Strait of Hormuz; all 21 crew members were rescued. Another vessel was damaged.
The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank in the Strait of Hormuz after being damaged by a strike involving unidentified munitions. All 21 crew members were rescued. Bloomberg reports this, citing the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, UNN writes.
Details
The vessel came under attack on Tuesday, October 13, while passing through the strait. The impact sparked a fire on board, after which the crew was evacuated. The container ship subsequently sank. None of the sailors was injured.
According to insurance company Allianz Commercial, the total loss of container ships is relatively rare. Between 2016 and 2025, only 33 such cases were recorded worldwide.
Another vessel attacked in the strait
On Wednesday, October 14, another Singapore-flagged container ship, GFS Giselle, was damaged. The strike damaged the vessel's hull, but it was able to reach a safe anchorage under its own power. All 22 crew members remained unharmed.
In addition, the International Maritime Organization reported the sinking of the bulk carrier Cape Dao, which was attacked on September 23. One crew member was killed at the time. The exact date the vessel sank was not specified.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is worsening amid intensified Iranian attacks on commercial shipping. This has already led to increased insurance risks, higher vessel freight costs, and additional pressure on global oil prices.
Last week, the United States also reported destroying a vessel in the Gulf of Oman that, according to the American side, was linked to Iran.

As many as eight US states have filed lawsuits against artificial intelligence company OpenAI, accusing the company of endangering children through its ChatGPT chatbot and misleading parents about its safety.
Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, and West Virginia announced their actions at a news conference on Wednesday, while Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana filed separate lawsuits in their respective state courts.
“OpenAI is hurting kids, and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said according to a statement shared by her office.
“OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide—all while pretending to be their fake friend," she added, saying that the lawsuit is aimed at "protecting our kids and holding OpenAI accountable under our state law.”
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey said the company is endangering children, deceiving parents, and violating state consumer protection laws.
“We must do all we can to protect kids,” McCuskey said, adding that the chatbot lacks adequate safeguards for conversations involving suicide, school shootings, and self-harm.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said OpenAI marketed ChatGPT as safe for minors despite what he described as serious flaws that had led to suicide, violence, and other harm.
“This lawsuit simply holds OpenAI to the same standards under Nebraska law as any other company,” Hilgers said in a statement on US social media company X.
The lawsuits seek to compel OpenAI to comply with state consumer protection laws and stop what the attorneys general describe as dangerous and unlawful conduct.
Addiction among minors
Earlier this year, Florida became the first US state to sue OpenAI, alleging that its flagship chatbot, ChatGPT, caused a range of harms and that the company knowingly released an unsafe product despite warnings about potential risks.
The lawsuit, filed by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, accuses OpenAI of allowing ChatGPT to assist mass shooters, encourage users to commit suicide, impair critical thinking skills and contribute to addiction among minors.
According to the filing, the alleged harms stem from what the lawsuit describes as OpenAI's pursuit of dominance in the rapidly expanding AI sector.
"This litany of harms is driven by Defendants' insatiable quest to win the AI arms race and amass large fortunes, despite knowing the danger of ChatGPT," the lawsuit states.

====================================================================================================

My relative defined ‘genocide,’ honoring him means scrutinizing Pillay’s Israel findings - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:03:47 UTC
06:03:47 KST

When I see the word “genocide” in a headline, I read it with a particular sense of responsibility. Raphael Lemkin, the Polish Jewish lawyer who coined the term and fought to establish it as a crime under international law, was my relative. His name gives me no special authority to decide a legal case. It does give me a responsibility to insist that a word created to protect human beings remain anchored in evidence and law.
That is why Navi Pillay’s appeal to defend international justice deserves a serious response. In an Oct. 12 interview with the Associated Press, the newly named Nobel Peace Prize winner urged support for the international legal system. She also chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza, a conclusion Israel rejects.
I agree that international law needs defending. But defending it requires scrutiny of those who invoke its authority. A Nobel Prize cannot settle a disputed legal conclusion. Neither can a government’s denial.
Raphael Lemkin helped name the destruction of human groups and build a framework to prevent and punish it. The Genocide Convention adopted in 1948 protects national, ethnic, racial and religious groups. Its protections belong to everyone.
That universality depends on precision. Genocide requires evidence of prohibited acts committed with the intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part, as such. The definition encompasses more than killing. It includes serious bodily or mental harm and deliberately imposed conditions of life calculated to bring about a group’s physical destruction, among other acts.
Intent essential for crime of genocide to apply
Intent is essential. It can be established through evidence of conduct and circumstances; perpetrators need not leave a written confession. But devastation alone does not automatically establish the particular intent genocide requires. Nor does a declared military objective automatically disprove it.
Pillay’s commission says it found that intent. A serious challenge to its conclusion must engage its evidence and reasoning. The questions are how the evidence establishes an intent to destroy Palestinians as a group, how competing explanations were assessed, and how statements by officials were connected to decisions and conduct.
These questions go to the basis of a grave conclusion. Asking them is part of taking international law seriously.
The distinction between a commission’s finding and a court’s judgment also matters. An investigative report can document atrocities and contribute important evidence. It is not the same as a judicial determination. The world deserves to know who reached a conclusion, how it reached it, and on what standard.
That distinction does not mean the world must wait for a final judgment before recognizing danger or acting to prevent atrocities. A convention dedicated to prevention cannot become an instruction to intervene only after the destruction is complete.
For Jewish readers, this debate reaches far beyond legal terminology. The Holocaust gives it a particular resonance for Jews, but the convention’s protection was never intended to belong to us alone.
An accusation against a government must not become an accusation against a people
Our history also makes us alert to the danger of collective blame. An accusation against a government must not become an accusation against a people. Jews everywhere must not be made collectively answerable for Israel’s conduct. Palestinians must not be made collectively answerable for Hamas.
That principle obliges us to look directly at Palestinian suffering. A child’s death does not become less terrible because its legal classification is disputed. Families deprived of food, shelter, or medical care do not have to win a terminology debate before their lives matter.
Protecting civilians, allowing and facilitating humanitarian relief, and investigating alleged crimes cannot wait for agreement on a label.
Challenging a genocide accusation does not require declaring every military action lawful. Recognizing civilian suffering does not require accepting every accusation made in its name. War crimes and crimes against humanity are grave crimes in their own right. Genocide is not a measure of whose suffering matters most.
There is danger in both directions. Using the term carelessly can turn it into an instrument of political condemnation. Refusing to consider it when the evidence warrants consideration can abandon people the convention was designed to protect.
A faithful defense of Lemkin’s legacy must confront both. The same discipline must apply whether the accused is an enemy, an ally, or our own government.
I want institutions that investigate allegations rigorously, explain their reasoning clearly and apply standards consistently, including when doing so angers powerful governments. I also want institutions whose conclusions can be questioned without every critic being branded an enemy of international justice.
Public confidence must be earned through evidence, fairness and a willingness to answer difficult questions. Governments cannot claim immunity from that scrutiny. International institutions cannot claim immunity from it, either.
Pillay is right that international law needs defenders. Those defenders should insist that no country is above scrutiny and no institution is beyond it.
My relative helped give the world a word it desperately needed. Our responsibility is to honor both the word and the obligation it created: to recognize genocide when the evidence establishes it, to resist using the accusation as a substitute for evidence, and to protect civilians whether or not that legal threshold is met.
The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of JTA or its parent company, 70 Faces Media.

Most of the protesters at the demonstration were minors.

The incident marked the second attempted break-in at the building within a week. On Monday, protesters gathered at the same location and attempted to enter the premises. The latest incident has once again made the haredi soldiers serving in the building the focus of protests.
The Kodkod program allows haredi men aged 23 and older who are not eligible for combat service to serve in technology-related positions in the IDF. Participants are not required to wear military uniforms, and the program has continued to expand since its launch in 2023.
About 1,000 soldiers currently serve in the program, and about 20% are still undergoing training. According to IDF estimates, enrollment is expected to rise to between 1,100 and 1,200 soldiers by the end of 2026, with hundreds of new recruits joining each year.
Despite the program's expansion, anti-draft protests continuously reach the building where the soldiers serve.

Yisrael Beytenu chairman MK Avigdor Liberman condemned the incident in a post on X/Twitter, calling for the protesters to be arrested and imprisoned.
"At this very moment, dozens of draft dodgers are trying to forcibly break into a military base. Anyone who tries to break into an IDF base is simply a terrorist. They must all be arrested now and thrown in prison."

AI Is Helping Bring Back the Dodo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:00:04 UTC
06:00:04 KST

There are a whole lot of reasons to have a whole lot of concerns about the harm artificial intelligence can cause, which explains why the technology has so many detractors. But even the harshest critics might smile at the news coming out of Dallas-based Colossal Biosciences. There, researchers have just announced that AI may help hasten the return of the extinct dodo, with the flightless bird, which vanished from the world more than 350 years ago, likely walking among us again sometime in the early 2030s. With so few ancient samples of dodo DNA surviving—and that which does exist having degraded over the centuries—the analytic and number-crunching power of AI is just what’s needed to fill in the genetic blanks.
“De-extinction is as much a data problem as a biology problem,” said Colossal CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm in a statement. “[AI] learns how regulatory DNA shapes living birds, then identifies the genetic switches that may have contributed to the dodo’s distinctive anatomy.”
Colossal established its de-extinction bona fides in 2025, when it announced that it had sequenced ancient DNA from the long-extinct dire wolf, used that to rewrite the genome of the extant gray wolf, and brought the Ice Age dire wolf back to life, more than 10,000 years after it vanished. Animals that are also on the company’s de-extinction to-do list include the woolly mammoth, the Tasmanian tiger, the ostrich-like moa, and the antelope-like quagga. The dodo, with its waddling gait, its stubby wings, its goggly eyes, and its preposterous beak, has none of the power, grace, or charisma of those other animals—but that’s part of its charm.
“The dodo never had a chance,” wrote New York Herald Tribune writer Will Cuppy, in his 1941 book How to Become Extinct. “He seems to have been invented for the sole purpose of becoming extinct and that was all he was good for. I’m not blaming the dodo, but he was just a mess. The Portuguese called the birds doudos, or fools, because they would associate with the Portuguese on friendly terms and allow themselves to be hit on the head with clubs.”
But what inspires mockery inspires love too—and it will take plenty of that to bring the dodo back. De-extincting a placental mammal like a dire wolf is a comparatively straightforward process. Colossal researchers first harvested cells from a living gray wolf and made 20 edits to 14 genes, coding for the dire wolf’s white coat, larger size, more powerful jaws, cold weather metabolism, and more. They then extracted the nucleus of that rewritten cell and inserted it into a gray wolf ovum whose own nucleus had been removed. Next, the fertilized egg was allowed to develop into an embryo and was implanted in the womb of a large domestic hound. Just over 60 days later, that mama dog gave birth to a puppy wolf.
De-extincting a bird, which does its gestating outside of any womb, will be harder. For the dodo, the researchers will first harvest primordial germ cells (PGCs)—nascent cells that give rise to eggs and sperm—from the nicobar pigeon, the dodo’s closest living relative. The PGCs will then be rewritten to add dodo traits, in the same way the gray wolf was edited. Those cells will then be injected through the shell of a domestic chicken egg into a microscopic chick embryo. The PGC’s will migrate to the embryonic gonads of the chick-to-be, taking up residence there. When the edited female chick hatches and grows and mates with an edited male, she will lay eggs that will produce not a chicken like her, but a dodo.
“In an ideal world, if we had hundreds of nicobar pigeon [eggs] we would use the pigeon as the surrogate,” says Anna Keyte, Colossal’s avian species director. “But nicobars are seasonal breeders. They only lay for a couple of months out of the year and they usually lay just two eggs in a clutch. Chicken eggs are super easy to get. Some chickens will lay an egg a day. You can just get vastly more surrogate eggs from a chicken than you can from a nicobar.”
But editing the PGCs in the first place will be no small thing, simply because there are so many sites on the dodo genome that code for the species’s traits—especially its ice-cream-scoop-shaped beak. It’s not precisely the genes that the researchers are reading in their work, but the regulatory elements—or the parts of the genome that determine which genes get switched on and off. And for the beak alone, that’s a heavy lift. There are more than 650 regulatory elements associated with beak size and nearly 1,700 with beak thickness and breadth. Worse, the fragmentation of DNA in the ancient samples gives an imperfect record of which of those regulatory switches are to be flipped which way. A new AI platform the company calls GenoMorph can fill in those gaps.
To develop GenoMorph, Colossal scientists built an atlas showing how the genetic switches that control facial development turn on and off as embryos grow in chickens, quail, ducks, and pigeons. They then compared genomes and skull shapes from more than 70 bird species, including the dodo’s closest living relative, the Nicobar pigeon. The result is the list of about 2,350 genetic switches that may help explain the dodo’s unusual beak, which the team is now testing one by one. That work builds on a separate achievement: a remarkably complete dodo genome, assembled from a single well-preserved specimen using software Colossal originally developed for its dire wolf project.
“For an ancient genome, this one is extraordinary,” says Beth Shapiro, Colossal’s chief science officer. “There are a few small holes, but far fewer than we usually see with ancient DNA. We’re really not missing much of the dodo genome.”
The beak might be the most dramatic dodo feature, but there are plenty of others, written in the two billion letters that make up the dodo genome—which is why Colossal scientists urge patience for the five or so years it will take to bring a dodo back into the world.
In the same way that some of the work Colossal did to read and analyze the dire wolf genome helped in the later work developing GenoMorph to read the dodo genome, the dodo work can similarly pay itself forward to reading and editing the genomes of other species to be de-extincted.
“It’s been rewarding to see that an approach developed for the dire wolf is now producing value across another species program,” said Shapiro in a statement. “Every scientific breakthrough becomes part of a scalable technology platform that can accelerate the programs that follow.” For now, the dodo remains biological vaporware—but it’s vaporware that could, before too long, take shape in the 21st century.

Trump Aides Admit the House is a Lost Cause
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Trump White House aides see almost no paths to Republicans keeping control of the House in the midterm elections and are more focused on redoubling their efforts to save the Senate majority.
That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.
It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.
The general expectation is that the House has become a lost cause. Races that Republican congressional leadership once thought they could flip in order to offset Democratic gains are no longer considered attainable.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, has now pulled ad buys in Democratic districts in Michigan and Ohio they were hoping to flip, as well as in the Republican seat being vacated in Nebraska by the retiring Don Bacon. The fund also started canceling remaining ad reservations in two House races where Republicans are seeking reelection in New Jersey and Iowa.
White House aides have shifted their focus to pushing an all-out defense of the Senate majority, which is also looking problematic but to a lesser degree than the House, the sources say. (Polling models and prediction markets agree.)
The aides see the Senate as still in play in large part because early returns for mail ballots have been relatively strong and comparable to 2024 presidential election levels in key Senate battleground states, sources say.
Trump officials at MAGA Inc. have also privately discussed how if Republicans can win some combination of senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, that would form a firewall that complicates Democrats' path to snatching control of the Senate.
Still, Trump officials appear to have conceded they are unlikely to win in North Carolina. Senate Republicans’ campaign arm has paused ad spending in North Carolina since the start of October, mirroring pullbacks by other outside groups.
“President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate,” says White House spokesperson Liz Huston in a statement.
The state of play—retreating from a state like North Carolina, where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair is on the ballot—would have been unthinkable just a few months ago.
But it speaks to the torrid political climate for Republicans heading into the last stretch of the midterm cycle, which appears to worsen by the week as high gas and living prices caused by the Iran war remain sticky in voters' minds.
With 20 days until the election, sources say, Trump officials are looking to get maximum turnout from the MAGA base in November, rather than trying to capture swing voters who polls show are not breaking for Republicans.
"Republicans remain laser focused on winning and protecting and expanding President Trump's majorities,” says Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassare in a statement. “We're thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”
The effort has manifested in a direct voter outreach play with the president crisscrossing the country to reach out directly to his supporters, showing up at rallies in states that should have been reliably Republican.
Trump started the week by hitting the trail in Ohio, where Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown has been polling consistently ahead of Republican Jon Husted, who has weathered negative ads branding him as "the face of data centers."
On Tuesday, the president flew to Wasilla, Alaska—once the home of former governor and vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin—to help the Republican Senate incumbent Dan Sullivan, who has been trailing Democrat Mary Peltola.
And after stumping in Arizona and Kentucky later this week, Trump is set to host a $1 million-per-plate fundraiser dinner for MAGA Inc. at his Mar-a-Lago club, replenishing a war chest that is being emptied at an increasing rate.
Trump has remained steadfast in his belief that he can drive his supporters to vote in November if he hits the trail, as he did in the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, a person familiar with his thinking tells Inner Loop.
But Trump, whose polling continues to be among the worst on record for any president, is not always wanted at rallies. To date, the president has not done a rally in Iowa with Republican candidate Ashley Hinson, who recently began to buck the president and called for measures that would help end the Iran war altogether.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Palantir and London mayor settle lawsuit over UK police contract

Breadcrumb
Palantir and London mayor's office settle lawsuit over UK police contract
US tech firm Palantir and London mayor Sadiq Khan's office have settled Palantir's lawsuit over a decision to block a £50 million ($66 million) contract with London police, both parties said on Wednesday.
Palantir had agreed a two-year contract with the Metropolitan Police to use its artificial intelligence systems to automate certain tasks and for analysing evidence.
But the mayor's office refused to approve the deal, telling the Met Police it had failed to have an open competition for the contract, with reports also quoting a spokesperson for Khan citing concerns Palantir did not align with "London's values".
Palantir's supply of software for the US military and immigration services, plus billionaire co-founder Peter Thiel's political views, have drawn scrutiny as European governments grow increasingly wary about dependency on US tech platforms.
The company was challenging the decision to block the Met contract, but Palantir and the Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime said in a joint statement that they had resolved the case and "withdrawn their allegations against each other".
MOPAC's decision not to enter into the contract "was not based on Palantir's values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company", the statement said.
It added that MOPAC "does not have, and has never had, any policy of not contracting with Palantir" and that it was welcome to participate in any procurement processes.
The settlement comes as Britain is conducting a review of a £330 million National Health Service contract with Palantir, while a parliamentary committee said the company had a "clear mismatch with UK values" and recommended using a break clause, a suggestion Palantir's British CEO Louis Mosley called "irresponsible".

Eight US states sue OpenAI, claiming ChatGPT harms children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:54:28 UTC
05:54:28 KST

Eight US states sue OpenAI, claiming ChatGPT harms children
WASHINGTON – A bipartisan group of eight states said on Oct 14 they had sued OpenAI in courts across the country over harms they say ChatGPT has caused to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users – including teenagers – to harm themselves or others.
Attorneys-general from the states, which include Iowa, Kansas and Arizona, filed the lawsuits independently in state courts, claiming ChatGPT is designed to be agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users.
But the chatbot reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behaviour and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings, the lawsuits claim.
The lawsuits represent the most significant coordinated state action against an artificial intelligence company, adding to a wave of legal challenges OpenAI faces as it prepares for a public listing. Florida’s attorney-general filed the first such state suit in June.
The lawsuits accuse the company of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about the safety of ChatGPT. The states also allege that the company created a public nuisance by endangering the health of their residents.
The lawsuits seek orders forcing OpenAI to make changes to how ChatGPT works. Among other things, the states want the company barred from developing AI models that can improve themselves unless it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.
The states, which also include Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia, are also seeking civil monetary penalties for OpenAI’s violations of state law as well as damages.
A spokesman for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The company is also facing dozens of lawsuits by private plaintiffs, alleging ChatGPT helped users plan mass shootings or other violence. REUTERS

AFRL Partners with Virgin Galactic to Gather Data on Space Weather Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:44:00 UTC
05:44:00 KST

Space tourism company Virgin Galactic announced a new partnership with the Air Force Research Laboratory’s space warfare directorate to collect and share space weather data from the company’s suborbital spacecraft, due for its first commercial flight next year.
The two-year cooperative research and development agreement, which Virgin announced Oct. 14, will provide AFRL with key information about space weather to help researchers understand its impact on satellites and infrastructure that reside on orbit—all gleaned from planned flights of the company’s SpaceShip vehicle. Virgin noted that as part of the agreement, AFRL will “evaluate the integration of sensor systems with Virgin Galactic’s next-generation SpaceShip to collect space weather data during flight.”
“This cooperative research and development agreement will help expand and identify new and additional opportunities for our growing fleet,” the company said.
Understanding space environmental and weather conditions—like solar flares and winds, coronal mass ejections, and geomagnetic storms—is important for government organizations and commercial firms alike. SpaceShip’s suborbital flights offer a chance for AFRL to get more insight into a region where those conditions are perhaps less understood: the mesosphere and lower thermosphere, or MLT. Situated between 60 and 110 kilometers above the Earth, the MLT is too low for satellites to operate, but space weather there can disrupt GPS signals and communications.
Shaun Ard, a senior research chemist at AFRL, said high-quality data about MLT space weather dynamics is limited, and the collaboration with Virgin will help the lab’s researchers “protect and advance space-based systems essential to modern infrastructure and exploration.”
Like previous Virgin Galactic vehicles, SpaceShip is designed to be launched from an aircraft “mothership.” After it reaches altitude and is released from its launch platform, SpaceShip will ignite its own rocket motor to reach suborbital space. The company will launch and land the vehicles from Spaceport America in New Mexico. SpaceShip can carry six passengers.
SpaceShip has been moving through integrated ground testing in recent months, and company officials expect to start flight testing in New Mexico this month.
Virgin envisions SpaceShip as both a space tourism vehicle and a research platform and has aggressive plans to ramp up its cadence following its first commercial flight in February 2027. Once its second vehicle enters service next year, it expects to hit a rate of at least 10 flights per month by the summer, company officials said during an earnings call in August.
“This flight rate is an unprecedented achievement in human spaceflight, and this is made possible with our highly reusable spaceship design,” Chief Financial Officer Douglas Ahrens said at the time. “It’s a beautiful machine with vast potential and now we are approaching the moment when we bring it all together with the ramp of commercial spaceflight operations.”

Families of Trinidadian men killed in US boat strike demand accountability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:42:59 UTC
05:42:59 KST

Families of Trinidadian men killed in US boat strike demand accountability
The Trump administration has killed at least 239 people in boat strikes that critics denounce as extrajudicial killings.
The families of two missing men from the Caribbean country of Trinidad and Tobago have marked the one-year anniversary of their disappearance by calling for accountability from the United States.
Since September last year, the US military has undertaken a campaign of attacking small boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean, on the basis that they were transporting “narco-terrorists”.
But critics have called the boat strikes an illegal campaign of extrajudicial killings.
On Wednesday, the families of Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo issued a statement remembering the two men, who they said were killed in one of the US boat strikes on October 14, 2025.
The families are currently pursuing a wrongful death lawsuit in the state of Massachusetts, supported by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). They have argued that Joseph and Samaroo were fishermen and farm workers, not drug-traffickers.
“The last year has been devastating without Chad in our lives. Chad was the heart of our family. He was loving, generous and caring and always there for us. We all miss him terribly,” said Joseph’s mother, Lenore Burnley.
“A year later, we are still grieving and seeking justice for his death. We will always mourn losing Chad but hope that this lawsuit will be a step towards justice for him and the family.”
Four other people were killed in the attack on October 14, 2025, when a missile struck a vessel returning to Trinidad and Tobago from nearby Venezuela.
The families have said Samaroo and Joseph had been working in Venezuela to support their families.
Both men called their families two days before embarking on the trip home to the islands. They were never heard from again.
The boat strike campaign, launched under US President Donald Trump, has killed at least 239 people since September 2025.
But the US government has provided little evidence to prove its claims that those on board were trafficking drugs. It has also not publicly identified the victims.
In several cases — from Colombia to Ecuador to Trinidad and Tobago — relatives have stepped forward to say that their loved ones were among those killed, and that they were fishermen with no connection to the drug trade.
Separately, the family of Colombian fisherman Alejandro Carranza has filed a complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, accusing the Trump administration of violating his right to life when it allegedly bombed his boat on September 15, 2025.
Samaroo and Joseph’s lawsuit was filed in January and is being heard by a US federal court in the city of Boston, Massachusetts.
“Not a day goes by when our family doesn’t think about our brother Rishi,” said Sallycar Korasingh, Samaroo’s youngest sister.
“Rishi was a good person, loved by his family and community. The last year without him in our lives has been heartbreaking. My brother and family deserve justice. We will continue fighting for answers and the accountability we deserve.”
Legal scholars have noted that, even if those killed were involved in criminal activity, the strikes would still amount to extrajudicial killings.
Under international law, it is generally illegal to use military force for civilian law enforcement. Drug trafficking is not considered an act of war, but rather a civilian crime.
“For a year now, our clients have had to live without their loved ones and without justice in the name of President Trump’s lawless killing campaign,” said Jeff Stein, staff attorney with ACLU’s National Security Project.
The group is representing the families in their lawsuit, along with the Center for Constitutional Rights.
“These illegal strikes at sea have devastated countless families, terrified communities, and made us all less safe,” Stein said. “We won’t stop fighting for accountability. We urge leaders in both Congress and the executive branch to finally end this illegal campaign before anyone else is killed.”
