Neighborhood air pollution linked to slower brain development in early adolescence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:00:52 UTC
05:00:52 KST

An analysis of data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study found that preteens living in neighborhoods with high levels of fine particulate matter or ozone showed less neurocognitive maturation over two years than demographically similar peers in low-pollution areas. Compared with their peers, they showed smaller gains in cognitive task performance, less maturation of brain network organization, and less of the cortical thinning that normally occurs with development. The paper was published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience.
Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development during which the ability to maintain attention, process relevant information, and exercise cognitive control continues to improve. At the same time, the cerebral cortex undergoes major structural and functional changes, including cortical thinning and increasing specialization of communication between brain networks.
Air pollution has attracted growing concern as a possible environmental influence on these developmental processes. Fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, is especially concerning because its particles are smaller than red blood cells and can travel through the bloodstream, while some toxic components may reach the brain through the nasal cavity and the olfactory system. Ozone, a gas found in smog, may harm nerve cells through chronic oxidative stress, and inflammation in the brain has been proposed as another pathway by which pollutants could affect development.
Neuroimaging studies have linked exposure to PM2.5, ozone, and nitrogen oxides with differences in cortical thickness, brain volume, surface area, and functional connectivity in children and adolescents. However, the direction and meaning of these associations have been inconsistent, with some findings suggesting delayed maturation and others appearing to suggest more advanced developmental patterns. Few studies have also examined whether these brain differences are reflected in children’s thinking abilities.
One difficulty is that pollution exposure is closely intertwined with socioeconomic and neighborhood factors, making it challenging to determine whether observed brain differences are caused by pollutants themselves or by other characteristics of the environments in which children live.
Study author Omid Kardan of the University of Michigan and his colleagues set out to isolate the effects of exposure to high levels of PM2.5 and ozone in pre- and early adolescence on brain development and cognitive performance. They hypothesized that high exposure to either pollutant would be associated with slower neurocognitive maturation.
The researchers analyzed data from the ABCD Study, an ongoing longitudinal study of 11,868 children across 21 sites in the U.S. who were enrolled between the ages of 9 and 10.9. The analysis used data from the start of the study and from a follow-up two years later.
The data included resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans, which show how brain regions communicate, structural brain scans, and cognitive tasks measuring attention, working memory, inhibitory control, processing speed, memory, vocabulary, and reading. A total of 3,645 participants had usable data at both time points.
The researchers estimated each child’s exposure from modeled air pollution levels in the 1 km2 area around their primary residence at the start of the study. They used U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards to define high exposure: an annual average above 9 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and a peak ozone level above 70 parts per billion. Low-exposure comparison groups were drawn from children living with less than 7 µg/m³ of PM2.5 or less than 60 parts per billion of ozone.
No participants met the threshold for high exposure to nitrogen dioxide, so that pollutant was not analyzed. The researchers also excluded 40 children who were exposed to high levels of both PM2.5 and ozone, to separate the effects of the two pollutants.
Because pollution exposure is tied to family income and neighborhood, the researchers compared each high-pollution group with a control group matched on household income, parental education, race and ethnicity, sex, and age. The final samples included 348 children with high PM2.5 exposure and 279 matched controls, and 355 children with high ozone exposure and 324 matched controls. The analyses also adjusted for factors including puberty, mental health symptoms, and neighborhood disadvantage.
The researchers combined three measures into a single index of neurocognitive maturation: cognitive task performance, average cortical thickness, and a measure of how closely the organization of a child’s brain networks resembled that of adults rather than infants. Cortical thinning is a normal part of brain maturation in this age range, so greater thinning indicates more maturation.
Children in the low-pollution control groups showed a statistically reliable increase on this maturation index over the two years, but children in the high-PM2.5 and high-ozone groups did not. In other words, the controls showed greater gains in cognitive performance, more maturation of brain network organization, and more cortical thinning than their peers in high-pollution areas. The differences were small, and they held up when the researchers accounted for exposure to the other pollutant.
“As healthy cognitive development is central to multiple domains of resilience and academic achievement, more effort should be directed toward reduction of these pollutants in residential and school areas,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about environmental factors affecting cognitive development. However, the study was observational, and the air pollution data were based on ambient air pollution in the 1 km2 area around each participant’s home, which may not fully reflect their actual exposure. Pollution was also measured only at the start of the study, so the data may not capture moves during the study or exposure earlier in life, including before birth.
In addition, the ozone measure was based on the highest level recorded in a year rather than the EPA’s standard calculation, which may have overstated how many children had high exposure. To create well-matched groups, the researchers also had to exclude 35 children with high PM2.5 exposure who had no demographically similar peers in low-pollution areas, which limits how representative the findings are.
The paper, “Neighborhood air pollution is associated with attenuated neurocognitive maturation over early adolescence,” was authored by Omid Kardan, Chacriya Sereeyothin, Kathryn E. Schertz, Mike Angstadt, Alexander S. Weigard, Marc G. Berman, Mary M. Heitzeg, and Monica D. Rosenberg.

Ukraine’s “Ptashka,” Who Survived Russian Captivity, Receives First Lord Ashcroft Award for Courage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:54:19 UTC
04:54:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s “Ptashka,” Who Survived Russian Captivity, Receives First Lord Ashcroft Award for Courage
Ukrainian servicewoman and former Russian prisoner of war Kateryna Polishchuk, widely known by her call sign “Ptashka” (Birdie), has become the first recipient of the Lord Ashcroft Award for Courage , presented during the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland.
The recognition was announced by Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on October 13.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Polishchuk, who gained widespread recognition for her role in defending Mariupol's Azovstal steel plant during Russia's siege of the city in 2022, received the award in recognition of her courage and continued service to Ukraine.
At the age of 21, she worked as a volunteer paramedic at Azovstal, providing medical assistance to wounded Ukrainian defenders under constant Russian bombardment. She was subsequently captured by Russian forces and spent four months in captivity before returning to Ukraine and resuming her frontline service.
During her participation in the Warsaw Security Forum, Polishchuk addressed Russia's war crimes, the treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war, attacks on civilian cities, Ukrainian-Polish relations, and the importance of continued European involvement in supporting Ukraine.
She also warned European countries about the threat posed by Russia and emphasized the need for a coordinated response to its actions.
“I received an award for exceptional courage. I consider this award not a personal recognition, but an acknowledgment of the courage and strength of every man and woman who defends the world against Russia,” Polishchuk wrote.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha praised Polishchuk's resilience, describing her experience as a reflection of the determination demonstrated by Ukrainian defenders throughout Russia's full-scale invasion.
“Russia tried to break Kateryna, but failed. Her story embodies the strength of spirit of Ukrainians who continue fighting for freedom despite Russian crimes. Kateryna's call sign is Ptashka. Russia tried to put her in a cage, but could not. Because Ptashka proved stronger than Russia. And if Ptashka endured, Ukraine will endure too,” Sybiha said.
The foreign minister also drew attention to the continued detention of Ukrainian soldiers captured during the defense of Mariupol. According to him, more than 700 defenders of Azovstal remain in Russian captivity, with Ukrainian authorities continuing to pursue their release through prisoner exchanges.
Sybiha also condemned Russia's treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war, particularly members of the Azov Brigade, and recalled the killing of at least 53 Ukrainian POWs at the Olenivka detention facility.
He stressed that those responsible must be held accountable regardless of how much time passes.
“The reason for this particular treatment is the unbreakable spirit of our warriors. They embody true Ukrainian courage. That is why the Russians are trying to break them. And that is why we must make every effort to bring them home,” the minister added.
Highlighting the broader scale of alleged Russian violations of international humanitarian law, Sybiha cited United Nations findings indicating that more than 95% of Ukrainian prisoners of war had experienced torture, while nearly all released detainees returned home severely weakened by starvation.
According to the figures cited by the minister, one Ukrainian serviceman lost 77 kilograms during five months in Russian captivity. The UN has also documented 129 executions of Ukrainian prisoners of war and 48 deaths in captivity.
Sybiha further stated that Russia holds Ukrainian detainees at more than 300 locations to which the International Committee of the Red Cross has been denied access.
As of July 2026, at least 38 Ukrainian prisoners of war from the Azov Brigade who survived the 2022 explosion at the Olenivka detention facility have been convicted or are facing prosecution in Russia, the Media Initiative for Human Rights (MIHR) reported on July 28, marking the fourth anniversary of the attack.

US lifts sanctions on Venezuela’s top legislator

US lifts sanctions on Venezuela’s top legislator
Jorge Rodriguez has been removed from OFAC’s sanctions list in latest US push for oil control and bilateral diplomacy.
The United States Department of the Treasury has lifted sanctions on the head of Venezuela’s National Assembly, Jorge Rodriguez, brother of the country’s interim President, Delcy Rodriguez.
The move by US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) comes amid major US-Venezuela energy pacts and other talks with the Latin American country’s government.
The delisting notice was posted on the federal agency’s website on Wednesday, officially removing Jorge Rodriguez’s name from OFAC’s Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) blacklist.
The top lawmaker in the country, Jorge Rodriguez has held the position of National Assembly president since 2021. He was reappointed in January, weeks after the abduction of former President Nicolas Maduro by the US government. He served as vice president under Venezuela’s late President Hugo Chavez, among other posts.
Jorge and Delcy Rodriguez had been sanctioned under US President Donald Trump’s first administration due to their ministerial roles under Maduro, who now faces several federal charges, including a sweeping superseding indictment adding torture to his other alleged crimes.
In 2018, the State Department said that Jorge Rodriguez was given prominent government positions by Maduro “to help him maintain power and solidify his authoritarian rule”.
A source familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that the decision to lift sanctions on Jorge Rodriguez is part of Washington’s wider diplomatic recognition of the interim Venezuelan government, and Trump’s three-phase plan for Venezuela’s stabilisation and political transition.
During a press briefing at the US State Department on Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that the next round of negotiations on Venezuela’s future was scheduled to begin on Wednesday. He also urged all Venezuelan opposition factions to join US-backed political talks with the interim president.
Earlier this year, the US Treasury dropped sanctions against Delcy Rodriguez and later lifted the restrictions on Venezuela’s central bank and its state-owned national airline, signalling Washington’s pivot from economic warfare to backroom bargaining. She has largely complied with Trump’s demands for Caracas to open up its energy industry to American companies.
As interim president, Delcy Rodriguez has promised to hold elections – including in her recent remarks at the United Nations General Assembly – but no firm date has been set. Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado has demanded they take place by July.
Jorge Rodriguez has shepherded several major reforms through the ruling party-controlled legislature since his sister took power, including a law that facilitated the entry of more foreign oil companies, a similar law for the mining sector and an effort to allow private investment for the country’s battered power grid.
Since Maduro’s ouster, Caracas and Washington have cut a deal giving the US access to 17 Venezuelan oil fields, while international energy firms have separately committed to expanding projects in the Latin American country. In August, Trump announced a plan to secure direct US access to a large share of Venezuela’s vast oil to refill the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Macron and Merz hold keys to an EU budget deal — but may be too weak to use them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:52:25 UTC
04:52:25 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron Franco-German Ministerial Council at Augustusburg Palace on July 17, 2026. | Pool photo by Friedemann Vogel/Getty Images
BRUSSELS ― Political pressure is leaving Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz poorly placed to break the deadlock over the EU’s next seven-year budget.
As EU leaders gather for a two-day summit in Brussels from Thursday, the heads of the bloc's two largest countries hold the keys to breaking the impasse between capitals that has persisted for months, as a Germany-led group advocating a smaller budget clashes with those like France which are resisting reductions.
"Delays and persisting divisions in the Council [representing EU governments] are worrying," said Siegfried Mureșan, co-leading the European Parliament's work on the MFF, the multiannual financial framework. "The EU budget can only be built through compromise ... The faster we adopt the budget, the faster we can implement it and become more competitive, safer, help farmers and researchers and protect our borders and cyberspace."
Advertisement
Sealing agreement on the EU's long-term central budget, worth approximately €2 trillion, is the biggest challenge over the next few months facing leaders, all of whom must sign up to the final numbers. While it isn't just up to Macron and Merz, getting the chiefs of the bloc's two most powerful countries to overcome their differences would be a massive step in making all the pieces of the jigsaw slot into place.
But with Macron soon to leave office and Merz under severe pressure domestically, officials and diplomats in Brussels, Paris, and Berlin are playing down hopes of a Franco-German breakthrough this week.
"If the French and German leaders come hand in hand, I think that could change the game," an EU diplomat, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said. "You need [Italian Prime Minister Giorgia] Meloni and [Polish Prime Minister Donald] Tusk, but it starts with Merz and Macron."
While Merz and Macron may talk bilaterally during the summit, according to an Elysée official, there were no firm plans for a more formal sit-down, two EU diplomats said, adding they were expecting them to use the two-day meeting to hash out positions.
Domestic political weakness makes both leaders less likely to yield ground, three EU diplomats said.
Backfiring
For the French president, who leaves office next year, the fear is that making big concessions — like accepting cuts demanded by Berlin — could be weaponized by presidential candidates vying to replace him.
“Macron should not appear too conciliatory” in budget talks, said an ally of the French president. “It would backfire in the presidential campaign.”
Advertisement
Indeed, Macron may be wary of striking a deal that could lead to attacks from far-right leader Marine Le Pen or far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon, both of whom argue that France receives too little value for its contributions to the EU pot.
During a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday evening, Le Pen accused negotiators of speeding up talks as "an attempt to stifle future democratic choices before they even take place" — effectively warning Macron against locking in an agreement before France's April presidential election and votes in other major EU countries, such as Spain, which goes to the polls next month, and Italy, which is due to hold a poll next year.
"All this is not serious," Le Pen told reporters on the 26th floor of The Hotel in Brussels.
It's complicated
Merz faces similar political pressures.
Following humiliating state election defeats to the far-right Alternative for Germany party, the Chancellor is wary of concessions that could be framed as sending more taxpayer money to Brussels. Berlin prefers no deal at all to one that increases the overall budget, Merz said.
But Paris and Berlin's positions may not be as far apart as public statements suggest.
Advertisement
"It’s complicated because France and Germany both need to step outside of their comfort zone," said the Macron ally. "But it will end with a deal between France and Germany,"
France's Europe minister Benjamin Haddad told reporters on Tuesday that discussions should focus on raising money via taxes, or "own resources" as they're known in the EU —such as online gambling levies—rather than "massive cuts."
However, Paris also wants to "stabilize national contributions" ― in other words, keep its own payments level.
Berlin was "open to examine new own resources, but we are more skeptical than the French that it will generate enough money," a German official said.
France is betting that when push comes to shove, Merz will give in to pressure from other countries — and German captains of industry — to abandon his demands for far-reaching cuts.
“I see that there is also a real debate in Germany as well on the fact of having a position that would only be focused on cuts to the detriment of future policies,” an Elysée official said Wednesday. This week, Germany’s industrial lobby BDI and top industry groups urged their government to defend a more ambitious EU budget.
Advertisement
Macron and Merz showed unity earlier this month by jointly urging the European Commission to toughen its stance on China. But they still struggle to agree on another major deal—first reported by POLITICO in July—where Berlin accepts stronger "Made in Europe" rules in exchange for France backing relaxed car emission targets and the 2035 combustion engine ban.
EU Industry chief Stéphane Séjourné told POLITICO on Tuesday he supported the deal to finalize both files. Macron recently called the agreement “imminent,” suggesting progress depended on German coalition talks. But their failure to present an agreement at this week’s Paris car show confirms Paris and Berlin still disagree on terms, with the Elysée confirming negotiations remain ongoing.

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:52:04 BST
04:52:04 KST

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
- Published
Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.
For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.
Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.
But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.
The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless.
"Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."
Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening.
The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
What are Starlink and Starshield?
Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields.
It currently relies on more than 10,000 active satellites, making Starlink the world's largest satellite constellation.
It is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and is the company's biggest revenue driver.
While Starlink is for civilian use, Starshield is its military-grade sister service, designed for the Pentagon.
Starshield relies on the Starlink network, but has greater security like enhanced encryption so that sensitive information can be transmitted without interception.
The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.
How does Starlink work on a battlefield?
Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves. As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in".
This makes them ideal for use on the battlefield.
"It's a connection… that you can basically use pretty fast, you don't need any special equipment, you don't need to prepare, you just go to the field and usually it works," Neo, a soldier with one of Ukraine's drone reconnaissance units, told the Today programme.
"It simplifies our work because we can translate or stream our reconnaissance operations," he added.
The network has become "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", George Barros from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.
In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed.
It is crucial for the effective use of weapons such as drones, which connect to the network so that operators can see their targets in real time, effectively minimising the time between "sensor-to shooter", Barros told the BBC.
Because Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
When it comes to Ukraine's self-defence, it relies on the Starlink network to protect its own skies against incoming Russian attacks, especially jet-powered Shahed drones, Barros added.
Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph (319 km/h), meaning the Starlink restriction made Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.
For Neo, this means that any deliberate restrictions on the Starlink network are "a betrayal".
With no ready replacement for the Starlink network, any speed restrictions or loss of connectivity have major implications for Ukraine defences, and the recent limits have shown how dependent Kyiv is on the network.
While Starlink can provide access nearly everywhere in the world, that does not mean it can be accessed everywhere, and countries must be licenced to use it.
Russia is one place where it is not authorised, although Kyiv has in the past said that Moscow was still getting hold of the terminals and using them in occupied territory in Ukraine.
"If SpaceX obtains knowledge that Starlink terminal is being used by a sanctioned or unauthorized party, we investigate the claim and take actions to deactivate the terminal if confirmed," Starlink said in 2024.
But with tens of thousands of terminals in Ukraine alone, it could be a near impossible task to determine which terminals are authorised and which ones are not.
Why did Starlink restrict drone speeds?
The answer remains unclear.
During a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky had said he hoped it was just a mistake, however, in a later interview with the Financial Times, he said: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will."
Musk said that Starshield is managed by the US government and suggested the Pentagon could be responsible.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X, external. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the president of the United States]."
He added: "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
The BBC has contacted the White House and Pentagon for comment.
The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that left 600,000 without power and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.
Relations between the US and Ukraine have worsened recently, especially since the US announced a deal with Russia to import its diesel into the American market.
Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and in response Donald Trump said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
On Sunday, Trump announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, but three days later, Ukraine said it would resume the strikes, accusing Russia of ignoring it (the Kremlin said it had never agreed to a ceasefire), and the US of withdrawing crucial support.
Zelensky has accused the US of threatening to withhold intelligence if Ukraine continues striking Russian oil facilities. Trump has denied this, but last week told reporters that Zelensky had "better damn well stop" the strikes.
While in London, Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US.
Trump's deal with Russia is his administration's latest effort to lower US fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict, which started in February, has seen prices skyrocket, souring his standing with the American public.

Hundreds of farmers took to the streets of Barcelona with around 200 tractors, buses and private vehicles, calling for urgent action to address what they described as a structural crisis in Catalonia’s agricultural sector.
Wednesday’s demonstration, organised by agricultural union Unió de Pagesos, brought together more than 1,000 agricultural professionals from across the region, according to the union.
Protesters gathered outside the Spanish government’s delegation in Catalonia before marching towards the regional Agriculture Department and the Palau de la Generalitat, the seat of the Catalan government.
“We are prepared not to slacken; it is time to say enough,” said Raquel Serrat, the union’s national coordinator.
Serrat pointed to rising production costs, falling payments to farmers and recent episodes of historic drought, saying the pressures were pushing the sector “against the ropes”.
Farmers demand direct aid and tax relief
Unio de Pagesos said agriculture and livestock farming could no longer depend on temporary measures and one-off subsidies, arguing that long-term solutions were needed to guarantee food sovereignty.
The union is seeking direct aid of up to $18,950 for professional agricultural holdings to help offset the effects of the war in the Middle East.
It has also called on Spain’s central government to reduce taxes on agricultural diesel and value-added tax on agricultural production, introduce dedicated electricity tariffs for irrigation and exempt agricultural machinery from periodic vehicle inspections.
Another key demand is clearer food labelling that allows consumers to identify where products originate.
Import standards and EU funding fuel concerns
The union has raised concerns about alleged breaches of food-chain legislation and imports from outside the European Union that it says do not meet the same standards required of local producers.
Farmers are also worried about proposed reductions in funding under the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), which provides financial support to the bloc’s agricultural sector.
The union argues that the combined pressures threaten the viability of farms and livestock businesses, and has urged authorities to make firm commitments rather than rely on short-term assistance.
Union presses authorities for commitments
No formal meeting with public authorities had been scheduled ahead of the protest, although Catalonia’s Agriculture Department offered to receive union representatives.
Unió de Pagesos said it had already presented its demands through established consultation forums and called on officials to respond with concrete measures.
The demonstration underscores the mounting pressure on regional and national authorities to address farmers’ concerns over costs, market competition and the long-term sustainability of agricultural production.

Russia Builds Military Communications Network Across Belarus Toward NATO and Ukraine — BELPOL
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:49:57 UTC
04:49:57 KST

A new secure military communications system for the Belarusian Ministry of Defense is being deployed across Belarus. It is designed to support the deployment and movement of Russian troops toward the borders of NATO countries.
This is according to the analytical report “The Militarization of Belarus,” presented in Warsaw by the Belarusian association BELPOL and the clandestine Community of Railway Workers of Belarus (CRWB), as reported by Centrum Europy.
The 48-page document was presented the previous day with the participation of Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, leader of Belarus’s democratic forces, as part of the Warsaw Security Forum.
According to the authors, the report was compiled using open sources, materials from the Belarusian underground, and information obtained from Russian generals.
The network under construction is based on radio relay links and directional antennas that allow data to be transmitted over radio channels with minimal risk of interception or eavesdropping.
Specialized equipment is being installed on towers operated by mobile operator MTS, which is 49% owned by Russia and 51% by the Belarusian state.
BELPOL analysts emphasize that the system’s architecture indicates that it is designed to meet Russia’s military needs.
The radio relay network is not being built outward from Minsk to regional centers. Instead, continuous east-to-west routes are being established from the Russian border to the borders of Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Ukraine.
One such route is being laid along the M-10 highway between Gomel and Brest.
BELPOL representative Matvei Kupreichik said the geographical distribution of the repeaters points to preparations to provide infrastructure for the Russian army, while the system’s sole command center is located in Russia.
It was previously reported that in the second half of 2025, Russia deployed a network of repeaters in Belarus to control drones attacking northern regions of Ukraine.
Areas stretching from the Kyiv region to Volyn are at risk of strikes by these Russian drones.

New ‘First Proof’ exam reveals how AI-powered math is a pay-to-play sport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:44:03 UTC
04:44:03 KST

Artificial intelligence models are getting good at math—but only the corporate AIs.
The First Proof project, which aims to objectively evaluate the mathematical reasoning of publicly available AI models, released its third batch of results today. They underline what recent headlines have shown—that some large language models (LLMs) are becoming powerful research tools. They also suggest that proprietary subscription-based models from so-called frontier labs far exceed the math skills of more transparent and accessible “open-weight” models.
“The gap between the open-weight models and frontier models is very large in research mathematics—much larger than in other domains,” says Mohammed Abouzaid, a mathematician at Stanford University and a member of the First Proof team.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In February a team of top mathematicians started First Proof as a rigorous, independent exam for cutting through the proliferation of imperfect “benchmarks” for scoring different models. The AI race to conquer math has accelerated dramatically since those quaint days, when its greatest successes concerned problems that were scarcely connected to actual research. OpenAI’s “slop drop” last week has put to rest scores of more pressing questions, many of which had stood unresolved for decades. And the company’s solution of the Navier-Stokes problem last month convinced many that LLMs are on the verge of superseding human mathematicians—if they have not already.
But these breakthroughs are far from controlled experiments. For the slop drop, OpenAI didn’t disclose the thousands of problems that the company’s new model attempted, most of which it didn’t solve. And that internal model remains completely inaccessible to outside mathematicians, preventing a direct comparison of its performance with others.
First Proof’s mathematicians solicited problems from experts in a broad range of subdisciplines and then selected 10. They asked each model under evaluation to answer the problems as written, with no further human input. Then they had three graders per problem evaluate the answers in a mock “peer review.”
First Proof’s rules require any entrants to be openly available, so OpenAI’s blockbuster new model was excluded. The team tested OpenAI’s GPT 6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, an aggregate model called “ProofCouncil” that combines an Astra agent with other agents to check its work and a similar “harness” built on Kimi K3, the leading open-weight model—one whose inner workings are made completely public, among other entrants. Producers of other major models, including Google, did not participate.
The best performer—ProofCouncil—solved nine out of the 10 research problems in a manner the judges deemed acceptable with “minor revisions” for publication in a peer-reviewed journal. This helped quantify the models’ rapid ascent at math over the course of 2026. (In the round one results that First Proof released in February, the top model got just a few problems correct. And in the round two results released in June, the winner got six or seven.)
For the main skill that First Proof tests—proving well-defined statements—“the models have become very good,” Abouzaid says, “so good that testing the frontier models on this task might not be that relevant in the future.”
Notably, the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, solved exactly zero problems. “It really fell flat on its face,” says Lauren Williams, a mathematician at Harvard University and a member of the First Proof team. “The open models are really, really far behind, so we would urge the community to invest a lot into improving them.”
The First Proof team has received many requests to test open-weight models from mathematicians concerned about privacy after recent high-profile controversies. “I know people who use open-source models exclusively because they’re so paranoid about data leakage with the frontier models,” Williams says.
“We have a lot of questions from mathematicians telling us, ‘I would like to look for alternatives to using OpenAI’s or Anthropic’s models, but I don’t know whether they would work,’” Abouzaid says .
For now, it seems, they don’t.

Sedimentary rocks: why pét nat and cloudy wines are on the rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:00:11 UTC
21:00:11 KST

Centuries ago, Geoffrey Chaucer observed that “ther is no newe gyse that it nas old”. This truth – that there is nothing new under the sun – certainly applies to wine: every year, a well-documented or ancient viticultural practice is repackaged for a mainstream that greets it giddily as an innovation. Orange wine! Wine in kegs! Chilled reds! And, in 2026, cloudy wine, courtesy of Marks & Spencer’s peachy-opaque organic rosé, Trouble (a name that means “cloudy” in French.
Trouble is the first cloudy still wine available in a British supermarket, a development that has seemed inevitable since pét nat – pétillant naturel – hit the big time; it’s an ancestral method of making sparkling wine that involves bottling before fermentation has finished. Typically, pét nats are not disgorged (that is, the dead yeast cells left over from fermentation are not removed), which is what gives them a cloudy appearance. They are also often fresh and tangy, so they suit warm weather, but it’s hard to imagine a better pairing for a pizza takeaway on an autumn evening, and without prosecco’s divisive sherbety notes, to boot. (That said, look out for rustic, cloudy col fondo – bottle fermented, undisgorged prosecco – a hazy, lively and bracing take on the nation’s most popular fizz.) M&S, ever quick on the uptake, has an own-label English rosé pét nat (currently out of stock), while Tesco sells a pét nat chardonnay from Argentina.
The term “clarification” in viticulture refers to several processes that make conventional wines so crystalline – namely fining (where an agent is added to bind haze-forming particles or compounds such as proteins and tannins, causing them to clump and settle) and filtration, which physically removes suspended particles from the wine. There are ways of clarifying that involve neither fining nor filtering, such as racking or settling (as I suspect is the case with Trouble, which hasn’t a speck of sediment). So, cloudy wine can be filtered and an unfiltered wine can be clear. Waitrose has no “cloudy” wines on its shelves, but it does have several unfiltered ones, including surprisingly big players such as Catena malbec.
So why choose a cloudy or unfiltered wine? “There’s texture, there’s fleshiness, there’s rounded fruit,” says Zainab Majerikova, head of wine for the Ottolenghi group, where the three house wines are unfiltered and cloudy natural numbers. “We think this makes them more moreish and a better fit for food with big, complex flavours,” says Majerikova.
I always get the sense that longer contact with lees (those dead yeast cells) makes cloudy wine more food-like; it might be a drink, but there’s a crunchiness to it. For the full effect of its flavours and weight on the palate, Majerikova recommends shaking a bottle of cloudy wine before opening to mix the sediment with the liquid. Either way, she says, cloudiness “brings soul, vibrancy and complexity” to wines for old-fashioned fun.
Four cloudy wines to lift the spirits
Trouble Cloudy Organic Rosé £12 Ocado, 12.5%. A slightly savoury, very drinkable take on a southern French rosé – bring on an Indian summer.
Alma 4 Phos Pét Nat £12 Tesco, 12.5%. Food-versatile pét nat Argentinian chardonnay from the Uco Valley, lightly sparkling and textural.
Alella “La Rumbera” 2022 £32 Dynamic Wines, 11%. A serious unfined and unfiltered skin-contact wine from a legend of Catalonian winemaking.
Ottolenghi Red Wine £26, 10%. This subtly cloudy pinot blend is Ottolenghi’s house red, and might well become mine: a wine you can almost crunch.

Trump sparks outrage over AI tiger video after sharing footage of fatal UK attack
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
US President Donald Trump has sparked outrage after sharing the distressing footage of a 23-year-old man with mental illness being fatally mauled by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in the UK, captioned "Don't ever mess with nature!" This was followed hours later by an AI-generated video of himself taming a tiger. The posts have been condemned as disrespectful to the victim and his grieving family, who have urged people to stop sharing harrowing content of the attack. Vedika Bahl tells us more.
The 23-second video, posted to Truth Social without a caption, shows Trump wrestling with a tiger before appearing to befriend it, set to the song "The Lion Sleeps Tonight". It begins with Trump pointing his finger at the animal and ends with him playfully hugging it. The pointing gesture bears a resemblance to one made by the victim of Saturday's fatal tiger attack in genuine footage.
Earlier, Trump had reposted the distressing real-life footage of the fatal attack, captioning it: "Don't ever mess with nature! President DJT." This post was also amplified by the White House's Rapid Response 47 account on X.
Trump also shared other animal-related videos in his posting spree, including a compilation of animal attacks featuring some AI-generated clips, and another portraying him as a lion while comparing Democratic politicians to jackals.
The victim was identified as 23-year-old William Chapman, who died after entering a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on Saturday. His family described him as "bright, warm and engaging" and said he had lived with severe mental illness for several years, was subsequently prescribed strong medication, and that the coroner will decide if this had a role in his death.
The family has also urged people to refrain from sharing photos and videos: "The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened. The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this."
Trump's posts have prompted widespread criticism online, with users describing them as "sick" and "disgusting". Critics said his caption was insensitive towards the family as they grieve the loss of their son in such tragic circumstances.
British broadcaster Piers Morgan called on Trump to delete the post, describing it as "appallingly tasteless". Others suggested the US president was seeking to distract attention from domestic political issues, although there is no evidence establishing his motive for sharing the videos.
One of the strongest rebukes came from Oliver Coppard, the mayor of South Yorkshire. He said the Chapman family had contacted his office about the distress caused by images and videos circulating online. He accused Trump of using AI to mock the tragedy and the family's suffering for little more than a "cheap laugh on social media".

UK PM promises accelerated delivery of air defence capabilities for Ukraine

UK PM promises accelerated delivery of air defence capabilities for Ukraine
Following a meeting with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reported on an agreement regarding accelerated deliveries of air defence capabilities.
Source: European Pravda, citing Zelenskyy's post on X (Twitter)
Details: These air defence capabilities will be deployed to counter jet-powered Shaheds, which Russia is using to attack Ukraine.

Reform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and election candidates for the party were caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.
Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from an ITV undercover investigation that aired on Wednesday.
Reform leader Nigel Farage has postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex on Thursday morning as the party tries to contain the fallout expected to come from further revelations in the coming days. That will include revelations from undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters.
Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites,” and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
Feeney won seats on Birmingham city council and Solihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”.
Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues.
Feeney was filmed with other candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, talking about where a local mosque might be built. After they make extreme racist comments in the discussion, Feeney says: “Oh god, we’re all going to end up in the papers”.
Chris Whelan announced he had resigned from Reform on 12 October “on personal and health grounds”. Campbell is still in post.
Dean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed separately making a range of comments during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection, including when he discussed what he would do with illegal immigrants crossing the Channel.
Reform has been attempting to pre-empt the impact from the ITV investigation, which will potentially be at its most damaging when footage from inside Reform’s London HQ airs.
The party used a statement issued on Wednesday night to accuse ITV and Hardcash Productions of “extreme methods of deception”.
“They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees,” it said.
The party said that this came at a time when Farage and other members of Reform were “being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation”.
“They have not included this in their report, despite being on notice since March this year. There is currently an ongoing police investigation relating to security breaches against Mr Farage, as is well known,” it added.
Reform said that not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK, adding: “Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.”
The latest crisis to hit the party comes at a time when it has been stalling in the polls and faces problems including the fallout from a different undercover investigation which filmed senior officials discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party.
The outcome is also awaited of a parliamentary standards commissioner investigation into whether Farage should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.
Bridget Phillipson MP, chair of the Labour party, said: “The extreme racism and appalling behaviour exposed by this investigation is truly sickening. Nigel Farage can’t shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples. Every Reform councillor, council candidate or party member found to have made such despicable comments must be thrown out of Reform UK immediately.”

Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:35:55 UTC
04:35:55 KST

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.
The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.
Ahead of a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.
“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”
Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph.
That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.
“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
The two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.
Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.
As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.
Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.
In brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.
Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.
The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.
“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.
Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”
The UK is also set to give £17m in funding towards repairs to the protective roof over the destroyed Chornobyl nuclear power plant which was damaged by Russian drone strike last year.
The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish Guards in full ceremonial uniform.
Musk said the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”

In case you needed more proof that leftists have turned feminism into a joke
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:35:40 UTC
04:35:40 KST

In case you needed more proof that leftists have turned feminism into a joke
In nanny states, men become state-dependent tradbros whose solution to an inadequate allowance is to pitch a fit, women get infantilized, and kids become insufferable. But what happens when someone dares to step out of line?
Enter Louise Montagnon – a 22-year-old master’s student, right-wing activist, and recent municipal National Rally candidate from Bordeaux, who has been all over French media debating the young left-wing activists indulging in synchronized tantrums across France, some burning their schools down to protest the lack of educational space. When a country is sufficiently infantilized, you may as well send young people to fight each other on ideological front lines over problems ginned up mostly by grey-haired men.
Montagnon is refusing to sing the dominant tune. “You are the useful idiots of this movement,” she told 17-year-old Erwan on television. He made his name by publicly draping himself over left-wing leader Jean-Luc Melenchon and kissing him on the cheek, having already mastered the politician’s mannerisms while explaining why student life sucked at his slum of a Parisian school near Montmartre. The academy boasts a majestic courtyard and a €120 million renovation project. His particular hardship was having to put in full days.
Montagnon’s message was that the kid hadn’t seen much of the working world and might want to compare class timetables with her before declaring himself a victim. Her argument is dangerous to the movement because if one person can manage, then why can’t you? And when that person is a young woman, the reality becomes especially inconvenient for young men.
Which would explain the violent reaction to this young woman’s mere existence. “Last year, I had to leave my classes during the year because it was no longer possible for safety reasons,” she said during a media appearance. “When you arrive at university and there are 80 people waiting to kick you out, you are no longer safe.” She also explained that during student elections, the library staff wanted her to leave despite what she described as about 200 “brainless leftists” waiting for her outside.
It has also emerged that back in February, she was reportedly distributing campaign literature when her young female colleague was pushed to the ground and she was thrown up against a wall.
Women’s groups lament the Taliban’s exclusion of girls from education, yet appear conspicuously absent when a young woman in France says that intimidation has interfered with her university life. Women should be able to study and participate in public life without being threatened into submission – but only subject to ideological approval or an adequate score on the most superficial diversity scale, apparently.
Montagnon’s offence is actively denouncing the left-wing status quo, exercising her democratic right to dissent. The very sort of independent thinking that feminism is supposed to celebrate – until the independent thinker backs the wrong party or causes.
She fails the longstanding litmus test to qualify for sisterly support. Feminism has become entangled with identity politics in much of the movement, to the point where a woman on the right can demonstrate intellectual independence, self-determination, and meritocratic qualities, yet still be treated as a threat to the ideological monoculture that became synonymous with the feminist movement ever since it sprang up around left-wing actions in the civil rights era.
Women should work to get ahead, provided they’re of the right sort, say the right things, and frame their achievements as contributions to the collective. Individual initiative is welcome, as long as it doesn’t become an inconvenient example of what can be done without adhering to a left-wing political script. And the collective must remain a perpetual victim. Otherwise, what’s even the point of its existence?
There’s something ironically paternalistic about a movement that champions women’s freedom while demonstrating – through its action or inaction – that it reserves the right to decide which of them are valid.
Turns out that the system that Montagnon is being told to navigate may not even be capable of delivering the meritocratic returns that her hard work warrants. Not anymore. Just look at France’s finances.
The country’s debt has climbed well above the EU’s 60%-of-GDP reference value. Now the government needs to rummage around in the couch cushions to find savings in the hope that ordinary people won’t notice, by scratching a few bucks here and there from health-care reimbursements and by de-indexing pension spending from inflation. Seems that the best outcome that Montagnon can hope for is a worthy spot in a broken system that won’t parasitize her hard work too much.
The state has failed this young woman. Not because she’s a woman per se, but because she insists on living her life like a full-fledged human being without limitations that the left imposes on one’s possibilities – either through peer pressure or its insistence on victimhood. And no amount of lip service to women’s rights will compensate when the most basic conditions needed for self-sufficiency to thrive have deteriorated to the point where the hardworking middle class gets exploited as a cash cow.
Montagnon also happens to have stumbled upon institutional feminism’s most shameful secret: the sisterhood is universal in its advertising, but highly selective in its customer service. And particularly as the broke nanny state fails in its effort to placate the handout-insistent masses, women’s liberation should mean embracing and championing independent, freedom-minded women on the right actively seeking to break those shackles. Otherwise, we’re just arguing over who gets to hold the leash.

&quot;Roof of Europe&quot; has shrunk — Mont Blanc lost more than a metre in height in a year
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:32:56 EEST
04:32:56 KST

"Roof of Europe" has shrunk — Mont Blanc lost more than a metre in height in a year
Kyiv • UNN
Mont Blanc's height has decreased to 4,807.47 metres due to changes in snow and ice. Experts do not associate the annual fluctuations with the loss of glacial mass.
The highest mountain in Western Europe shrank by more than a metre last year. The summit of Mont Blanc in France now stands at 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting the "roof of Europe" 1.29 metres lower than in 2025, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
The mountain is approximately 4,792 metres high, but its summit is constantly shifting as heat, wind and precipitation alter the thickness of the snow and ice at the top. The height recorded by scientists during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than in 2023, when it reached its lowest level in recent times.
Certified surveyors from the National Union of Geometry Experts (UNGE) and the Order of Geometry Experts, who have regularly monitored the summit since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain and drones to create a detailed model of its snow and ice cap.
The data show that the summit has decreased by 3.43 metres from its height of 4,810.90 metres in 2007.
Experts caution against linking year-to-year fluctuations in elevation with the rapid loss of alpine ice caused by fossil-fuel pollution.
"Regarding the mass of ice, it is important to distinguish between changes in elevation above sea level and changes in the total volume or mass of ice," a UNGE representative said. "An increase in the summit's elevation does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained glacial mass, and it does not contradict the documented retreat of alpine glaciers."
Climate deterioration contributed to the hottest summer in Western Europe since records began this year, scarring alpine regions and melting ice at a dizzying rate. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an "explosion in the rate of melting" after confirming that one-fifth of the country's ice had been lost over the past five years, while 5.5% of its volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.
Jean de Garet, president of the departmental chamber of surveyors of Haute-Savoie and leader of the expedition to Mont Blanc, said that the warming trend could be seen with the naked eye across the rest of the Alpine massif, but "at the moment, climate change does not appear to have the same impact above 4,000 metres".
"As we climb, we pass the Brigade Blanche hut before the Tête Rousse glacier," he said in comments to French television channel TF1 on Wednesday. "We saw that the glacier had receded. It literally melted before our eyes, and now in some places we cross a stream rather than a glacier."

The ceasefire that keeps killing children: Gaza one year on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:30:57 UTC
04:30:57 KST

According to the Trump administration, there is a ceasefire in Gaza, since 10th October 2025. This would suggest that no firing is going on, nobody is being killed or injured, no homes, schools or hospitals are being destroyed, and no Palestinians are being detained and taken away from Gaza. It also implies that Gazans are getting enough food, water and medicines and even rebuilding is around the corner awaiting the go ahead signal.
But is this the reality on the ground, or merely the picture the word “ceasefire” is supposed to convey so Mr Trump, desperate for the Nobel Peace Prize can build up his profile on the hope to win it next year?
On the anniversary of the ceasefire itself, at least seven Palestinians, including an eight-year-old girl, were killed by Israeli fire. Since the ceasefire took effect on 10th October 2025, the latest figures says least 1,498 Palestinians have been killed and another 5,306 injured, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry whose figures are usually used by the United Nations. Israeli attacks never really stopped after October 2025, despite the so-called ceasefire. Attacks have also struck shelters housing displaced Palestinians, while much of the enclave’s building stock has already been destroyed or damaged, in many cases repeatedly.
According to Islamic Relief, an aid organization, one Palestinian is killed or injured by Israeli fire every 90 minutes despite the ceasefire.
To put the scale of the killing into an even more horrific perspective, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since October 2023 has killed at least 74,389 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. They include at least 21,976 children, almost 30% of the total. The same sources confirm at least 175,423 injuried and counting.
READ: 4 Palestinians killed, several others injured in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza despite ceasefire
The United Nations has confirmed that Israeli attacks continued throughout the year despite the ceasefire, killing and injuring Palestinians and repeatedly displacing families. According to the UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR), its investigators had verified 1,076 conflict-related deaths between 10th October 2025, and the end of July 2026, including 268 children. At least 331 Palestinians, including 66 children, were killed near the so-called “Yellow Line,” including people who were carrying out ordinary civilian activities and some who were inside their tents. The UN warned that killing civilians who are not directly participating in hostilities is a war crime, regardless of where they are killed. The UN’s October 12 report makes clear that a ceasefire has not brought safety to Gaza’s civilians.
The phantom ceasefire has not brought Gazans the food, clean water, shelter materials and medical care they desperately need.
On 2nd October, the World Health Organisation reported that not a single hospital in Gaza was fully functional, largely because of chronic shortages of medicines and medical supplies.
The median wait for Israeli authorities to approve medical shipments is around 74 days, excluding delivery time, further delaying the arrival of essential supplies. Meanwhile, restrictions on humanitarian goods, shortages of spare parts and funding cuts have continued to undermine water and sanitation services. A year after the ceasefire, Palestinians are still living amid destroyed infrastructure, inadequate medical care and a humanitarian crisis that the ceasefire was supposed to help end. Food supplies improved somewhat earlier in the ceasefire, but they have never reached an adequate level to give the population any real sense of relief or confidence that the severe scarcity they have endured will not return.
READ: Egypt has ‘no hidden agendas,’ ambitions against anyone: President
As another winter approaches, one can only imagine what life on the ground looks like for the over two million Palestinians living in the enclave, most of them displaced from their homes. Although the flow of some supplies has improved since the ceasefire took effect, shelter materials and other essentials remain inadequate, and little has been done to enable people to return home or begin rebuilding their lives—a promise made to them as soon as the ceasefire was confirmed.
According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), 279,000 people are sheltering in 400 flood-prone displacement sites and more than 2,300 unsafe buildings requiring demolition. Nearly 44,000 people are living in these unsafe buildings.
These conditions are particularly dangerous as the rainy season abut to start. Humanitarian efforts remain hampered by Israeli restrictions on the entry of critical supplies, equipment and spare parts, including materials needed to repair water and sanitation infrastructure and prepare shelters for winter. A year after the ceasefire, Palestinians are still struggling to find safe shelter amid the ruins, while reconstruction remains largely stalled. The ceasefire may have reduced the intensity of the war, but it has not given Gaza’s displaced population a realistic prospect of returning to normal life.
A year after the ceasefire was announced, the central question remains: what does a ceasefire mean when Palestinians continue to be killed and injured, families remain displaced, essential supplies are inadequate and reconstruction has yet to begin? The figures documented by Gaza’s Health Ministry, the United Nations and humanitarian organisations make clear that the announcement itself has not delivered the safety and relief that Palestinians were promised.
For the Trump administration and its Board of Peace, the ceasefire may be presented as a diplomatic achievement, but its success cannot be measured by the agreement’s existence or the passage of time. It must be measured by whether Palestinians can live without fear of being killed, obtain the necessities of life and return to their homes.
Until that becomes reality, calling the situation a ceasefire risks disguising the continuing suffering of Gaza’s population rather than bringing it to an end.

Guyanese opposition leader arrested after shots fired outside home of police official

The vehicle later returned, according to a Tuesday statement from the Guyana Police Force, and Narine heard what he believed to be a gunshot as the vehicle approached.
Narine took cover, the statement said, and fired several rounds towards the car, which drove away. Officers later intercepted the vehicle, arresting Mohamed and the other men traveling in it. A search uncovered a firearm and ammunition, the police said.
The government said in a separate statement on Tuesday that Mohamed and his companions had been filming Narine’s residence. It alleged that shots came from their vehicle and said the gun the police found was unlicensed.
Mohamed's office described the shooting as an assassination attempt against Narine. Members of his We Invest in Nationhood party held a press conference on Wednesday to protest what they said was Mohamed's treatment by police. The party said he remains in custody.

The U.S. Department of the Air Force and Northrop Grumman have broken ground on a new final assembly line at Plant 42 in Palmdale, California.
The Air Force press service reported that the project involves constructing more than 90,000 square meters of new production space to expand B-21 Raider stealth bomber production.

NEW DELHI: A false hijack alert created a real scare for security agencies and the 306 people on board Air India’s Frankfurt-Delhi flight on Wednesday, with the Boeing 787 getting diverted to Jaipur as a result where everyone had to wait for hours before they could fly to their destination. It is reliably learnt pilots operating the flight, AI 2030, did not squawk the code 7500 used to convey a hijack or unlawful interference, which has to be punched on a keypad like four letter code to unlock phones.Still the recently installed air traffic control radar system at Mumbai, which is now an enroute ATC due to longer routes taken by Indian aircraft flying between Delhi and the west, somehow conveyed that scary message for the erstwhile Vistara B787-9 (VT-TSE). “Once that happened, Mumbai ATC spoke to the pilots who reported that all operations were normal on the flight. But protocols have to be followed in situations like this and so the plane was asked to divert,” said people in the know.
Why the false scare happened is now the subject of a probe by both aviation and security agencies, with Mumbai ATC’s new systems being looked at closely. Incidentally, air traffic control has been headless as Airport Authority of India’s position of member (air navigation services) has been vacant for some time now and AAI itself does not have a regular chairman.
It remains to be seen how headless AAI’s headless ANS tackles the issue of reportedly false scares that have such an impact on passengers, crew members, security agencies and airline schedules apart from added costs.On landing in Jaipur around 11 am, the plane was parked on a remote bay. There is no button that can be inadvertently pressed. So from the pilot or plane side some error to happen is highly remote,” they say.Senior air traffic controllers say Mumbai ATC has a new system. When a pilot squawks 7500 (hijack), then the colour of this aircraft’s dot on the radar screen turns red and an alarm goes off.In a statement, Air India said: “Air India flight AI2030 operating from Frankfurt to Delhi on Oct 14 was diverted to Jaipur following a perceived security concern. The aircraft landed safely in Jaipur. The relevant security agencies carried out the necessary checks and have cleared the aircraft and crew. All passengers disembarked, underwent security checks, and have since reboarded the aircraft. The flight is expected to continue its journey to Delhi shortly.
