Earth's "vital signs" pushed to record extremes in 2026, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:27:26 UTC
04:27:26 KST

Climate change pushed Earth to its limits in 2026 as certain "vital signs" reach record extremes, report says
Climate change pushed the Earth's environmental system to, and perhaps beyond, its limits in 2026, as several of its "vital signs" reached record extremes, researchers said in a new report on the state of the global climate.
Of the 16 climate markers that researchers consider integral measures of how the Earth is doing, seven are currently at record extremes, while multiple others show evidence of accelerating or abruptly shifting, the report published Wednesday in the peer-reviewed journal BioScience said.
The markers include greenhouse gases, temperature, glacier mass, oceans, wildfires and the planet's energy imbalance, which refers to the difference between the amount of energy the Earth absorbs and the amount it radiates back out into the atmosphere.
Researchers warned in the report that the planet's climate "is moving deeper into uncharted territory."
"Earth's life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits, with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond," the report said. "Across the globe, extreme heat, floods, droughts, storms, and wildfires are no longer rare events but defining features of a changing planet."
A record year
July 2026 broke records as the warmest month ever for the contiguous United States, while the country as a whole was experiencing what turned out to be the hottest summer it had ever seen.
Globally, ocean temperatures also reached new heights in July, the report said, while data show that carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are higher now than at any other time in the last 2 million years. Heat waves scorched Europe, killing an estimated 14,000, and baked portions of the U.S., too, fueling wildfires that burned millions of acres of land.
Climate change appears to be accelerating, and its effects are becoming more intense, the researchers warned. They noted that the patterns they'd observed while compiling the report had raised concerns about their potential to cross a point of no return, one at which their impacts on various ecosystems would be irreversible.
In 2025, coral reefs became the first environmental system on Earth to reach a climate "tipping point," with researchers saying the damage could be permanent.
Global warming is happening more quickly now than it was a few decades ago, according to the new climate report, which said the rate of warming has sped up, increasing from roughly 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade between 1880 and 1970, to 0.19 degrees Celsius per decade between 1970 and 2010, and 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade between 2010 and 2024.
"Rapid destabilization"
Faster warming increases the likelihood of crossing tipping points from which different environments can't bounce back, and it also risks destabilizing the delicate balance between them, researchers said.
For example, greenhouse gas emissions from melting permafrost, wildfires, or other natural sources, which are all triggered by the temperatures associated with global warming, could essentially become a cycle that fuels itself.
Amplified sea ice loss, ecosystem degradation and carbon emissions could also begin to create their own self-perpetuating feedback loop — the crux of the "hothouse" climate trajectory, where various tipping points act as catalysts that push global warming far past humans' control.
"We are witnessing the rapid destabilization of the Earth's climate system," the researchers said. "This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present."
However, the report noted that worsening trends in fossil fuel combustion and other emissions, the main drivers of the extreme changes it centers on, have been accompanied by positive shifts in renewable energy use.
But the researchers emphasized that any progress seen so far "remains far below the scale and speed needed to stabilize Earth's climate system."
"Rapid reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, effective adaptation, ecosystem protection, and transformative societal change remain essential to reducing climate risks and securing a more resilient and sustainable future," they said.

Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.

Two months later, Israel has still not permitted the contract to move forward, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Contractors and trucks are not being allowed to cross into Gaza and begin the work. “Israel won’t open the border,” they said.
A Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment. The Israeli Defense Forces and the Israeli government declined to comment.
Israel’s war in Gaza is one of the eight wars Trump claims to have resolved. He listed it again last week in a screed on social media, protesting that it was unfair he had not won the Nobel peace prize.
The Board of Peace, formed in the wake of an October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, is central to Trump’s claims to have ended the conflict.
Arkel’s planned “mission support site temporary outpost” is decidedly rudimentary: a fortified position of about 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site that was once part of the controversial and now defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, according to the person familiar with the matter. The US-backed GHF operated in Gaza from May 2025 till October 2025 to deliver aid protected by private contractors.
The base would host short rotating deployments of a well-armed force of 150 troops in Gaza, the person said. They would come from a larger component of 500 sent already from Morocco and Kosovo.
But without this contract, the source said, the rest of the Board of Peace program cannot launch. Israel’s refusal to allow Arkel, the contractor, to build the base, essentially cuts the Board of Peace off at the legs.
“You can’t get in without [an international stabilization force (ISF)]. You can’t rebuild,” the person said. “There’s no security. There’s no deliveries of construction equipment. You can’t even start putting utilities. You can’t start putting in basic life-support facilities you know because without the ISF you can’t go in.”
The person familiar with the matter said the Board of Peace believes that Israel’s government will let the project proceed after the Israeli elections, which are scheduled for 27 October.
The controversial Board of Peace has a unique structure. Trump is designated as chair for life. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is an executive board member, as is real estate developer Steve Witkoff, whom Trump has appointed as a mediator in various international disputes.
Though many western democracies have kept their distance from the Board of Peace, 28 countries joined as founding members earlier this year. Kushner has unveiled renderings of a futuristic vision of Gaza, where the city was envisioned as a pristine luxury waterfront resort city with hi-tech skyscrapers looking out over the Mediterranean.
On 23 September the group unveiled what it said was a six-month, $2.45bn plan, as the first step towards reconstruction with a 10-year estimated cost of $71bn.
There were lofty promises and requests for contributions. “Today we can point to real progress,” announced Witkoff.
A US senior adviser to the board, Aryeh Lightstone, announced a new fund would be started. “Your high net-worth donations will go directly to the Palestinian people,” he said. Lightstone has traveled in Trump circles since the president’s first term. He officiated as a rabbi at the 2020 wedding of Trump adviser Stephen Miller to Katie Miller.
Israel has continued strikes in Gaza since the October ceasefire, killing about 1,400 people over that time, according to Gaza health authorities.

The proposed changes cover three pension schemes and the National Social Assistance Programme under the rural development ministry.
NEW DELHI: The Centre on Wednesday approved the continuation of its flagship social security scheme National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) for five years until 2031, while renaming it Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana and dropping former PM Indira Gandhi’s name from three of its sub-schemes.Announcing the decision, I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the “comprehensive social security net” will cover vulnerable groups, including the elderly, widows and persons with disabilities. The scheme with an outlay of Rs 53,428 crore is expected to benefit 3.2 crore people.The revamped programme revises the eligibility criteria for pension for persons with disability (PwD) and increases the assistance provided under the sub-scheme.As per the official release, Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme has been renamed PM Vridhavastha Pension Yojana, the Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme is now PM Vidhawa Pension Yojana and Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme becomes PM Divyangjan Pension Yojana.This comes after the Cabinet approved a new rural employment guarantee scheme, Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin), in December last year, replacing the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA).
Under the revised disability pension sub-scheme, monthly assistance will increase to Rs 375 for beneficiaries from birth to 79 years and to Rs 625 for those aged 80 and above. Till now, beneficiaries aged 18–79 received Rs 300 per month, while those aged 80 and above received Rs 500.The eligibility threshold for benchmark disability has also been reduced to 40% from 80%, bringing the scheme in line with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. Govt said the revision was necessitated by the law, which has also mandated that disability-related assistance be at least 25% higher than that provided under comparable schemes for other categories. The revised scheme is expected to cover more than 27.48 lakh beneficiaries.
The pension amounts under the old-age and widow pension schemes, as well as assistance under the National Family Benefit Scheme, will remain unchanged. The old-age pension ranges from Rs 200 to Rs 500 per month and covers 221.31 lakh beneficiaries, while the widow pension ranges from Rs 300 to Rs 500 per month and covers 67.38 lakh beneficiaries.Under the National Family Benefit Scheme, a one-time financial assistance of Rs 20,000 is provided to a household following the death of its primary breadwinner, provided the deceased was aged between 18 and 59 years. The scheme covers up to 3.59 lakh beneficiaries.

The Nord Stream trial: Ukraine’s strategy of silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:18:27 UTC
04:18:27 KST

The Nord Stream trial: Ukraine’s strategy of silence
The trial of Nord Stream bombing suspect Sergey Kuznetsov is underway in Germany, and the Ukrainian veteran’s defense team have revealed their strategy: say nothing and blame Russia.
Kuznetsov arrived at the Higher Regional Court of Hamburg under heavy security on Wednesday. The hearing is the first of 24 sessions scheduled between now and February, as German prosecutors attempt to prove that the Ukrainian military veteran led the sabotage operation that destroyed the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in September 2022, an act that they say constitutes a war crime.
What is Sergey Kuznetsov accused of?
The allegations against Kuznetsov largely follow the German government’s version of events, which have been drip-fed to Western media outlets in a series of leaks over the last four years. Kuznetsov, prosecutors claim, entered Germany in September 2022 using a forged Ukrainian passport, rented a pleasure yacht with six accomplices, and planted explosives on one of the four undersea lines comprising the Nord Stream project while his team sabotaged the remaining three, all “on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities.
Variations on the story – that the CIA approved or didn’t approve of the operation, and whether or not Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky personally ordered it – have circulated in the media, but Kuznetsov’s alleged involvement remains a constant in most retellings.
American journalist Seymour Hersh has shot down the German story, arguing that the Ukrainian saboteurs would not have been able to transport the requisite deep-sea diving gear and explosives aboard a 15-meter yacht, and almost certainly would have been caught in the act, as NATO was conducting active military exercises in the same area of the Baltic Sea at the time of the alleged sabotage operation. Citing intelligence sources, Hersh maintains that the CIA, working with the Norwegian Navy, used the NATO exercises as cover to plant remotely-detonated explosive devices on the Nord Stream lines.
Where are his accomplices?
Kuznetsov is the only one of the seven alleged saboteurs currently on trial. Another suspect, identified as ‘Vladimir Z’, was detained in Croatia in August and is currently fighting extradition to Germany. According to German media, three civilian divers and the yacht’s skipper – all Ukrainians – remain at large, while a military explosives expert who reportedly took part in the operation was killed in Ukraine in 2024.
What is the evidence against Kuznetsov?
The prosecution did not present any evidence against Kuznetsov at Wednesday’s hearing. However, Germany’s state ARD and NDR broadcasters have published details from the 136-page indictment against him. According to this report, prosecutors intend to focus on:
- A phone call from Kuznetsov to his wife, made in Italian custody last year, in which he defended the bombing as “an official military operation”
- Photographs from tourists and speed cameras placing Kuznetsov in Germany at the time of the alleged operation
- Traces of the military explosives RDX and HMX from the yacht, the ‘Andromeda’
- Internet searches for technical data on the Nord Stream lines and Baltic Sea depths, obtained from Kuznetsov’s phone
What did Kuznetsov say in court?
Kuznetsov remained completely silent throughout Wednesday’s proceedings. His lawyers explained that as Kuznetsov was an officer in the Ukrainian military at the time of the Nord Stream attack, he cannot testify without divulging state secrets. He will remain silent for the rest of the trial.
What did his defense team say?
Kuznetsov’s lawyers did not outright deny their client’s involvement in the attack. Instead, they argued that the evidence linking him to the operation is circumstantial, pointing out that his fingerprints were not among the prints lifted from the Andromeda, and that the prosecution has no eyewitnesses to call.
“It’s the prosecution’s job to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that he was involved,” legal adviser Ilya Novikov told reporters after the hearing. Pressed by a reporter, Novikov refused to say whether or not Kuznetsov was denying guilt. “He keeps silent, and this is his position,” he replied.
Justifying the attack
Kuznetsov’s legal team put far more energy into arguing that the Nord Stream attack – the costliest act of industrial sabotage in history – was justified. “Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor’s infrastructure without harming any human beings?” Defense attorney Nicola Canestrini asked the court. Jes Meyer-Lohkamp, another defense attorney representing Kuznetsov, said that the court should consider whether the pipelines “should have been operating at all in light of Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, and whether action against them could have been justified.”
Nord Stream, Canestrini asserted, was “a weapon in the hand of the Russians.”
Canestrini, an Italian lawyer who specializes in defending war crimes and genocide suspects in The Hague, pushed for the case to be dropped, arguing that Kuznetzov had originally been extradited for “sabotage,” not “war crimes.”
Prosecutors countered that the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines was “attack by military means against civilian objects,” and therefore a war crime.
What happens next?
Canestrini and Lohkamp may be pre-emptively justifying the destruction of Nord Stream in anticipation of some smoking gun evidence tying Kuznetsov to the crime. However, they are adamant that the prosecution has no evidence to draw on or witnesses to call, and that Kuznetsov’s position in the military will protect him from testifying.
“He is not permitted to speak. His two immediate superiors told him that he does not have authorization to make any statements – not even to his lawyers,” Lohkamp told the court, adding that under German law, “Anyone who cannot speak out cannot be convicted.”
As such, the case will ultimately rest on the strength of the prosecution’s evidence. However, with no fingerprints and no witnesses, securing a conviction will be no easy task. Given the fact that a guilty verdict would implicate the Ukrainian military in a war crime against Kiev’s largest foreign donor, a logical next question is whether the trial is set up to fail.
Stick with RT for all the latest news on the Nord Stream trial over the coming months.

Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.
The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings, according to the Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.
But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.
The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.
OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.
The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped and hacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this month one of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.
OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.
The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.
Booming AI salaries have already had a significant effect on housing prices in San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.
In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.

Trump’s new press secretary faces scrutiny over claims to be a lawyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:12:29 UTC
04:12:29 KST

Donald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But when asked after her inaugural press briefing on Tuesday to name the state where she passed the bar exam, she replied curiously: “when I moved to China”.
No public record shows she has ever been licensed to practice law in the US states where she resided, and her answer to reporters’ questions on Tuesday only deepened scrutiny.
Zacharia wasn’t registered in 38 states, as well as DC and the Virgin Islands, where the state’s attorney list was publicly available, according to a review from the Guardian. On Wednesday night, the Wall Street Journal, citing a person with direct knowledge of the matter, reported that Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine University law school in 2011, but did not pass.
Speaking briefly to the New York Times she did not clarify whether she had or had not passed the bar exam, but told the reporter that she had consulted with Pepperdine’s president as to how she should identify herself on TV. According to the Times, she said she was told to stay away from “attorney” or “esquire” but that “lawyer” was appropriate.
After her shaky and widely panned first briefing, a reporter asked Trump which state Zacharia had passed the bar exam in. The president, who had described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment, turned to her and asked: “Which state?” She replied: “when I moved to China”. Zacharia told the New York Times she misheard the question amid the sound of Marine One and believed she had been asked: “Where were you after law school?”
Zacharia’s law degree is real – Pepperdine University confirmed she graduated from its law school – but a degree is not a license. No record has surfaced to prove that she was admitted to practice, according to the report in Popular Information.
In a later statement to the press, Zacharia said she had “practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials”. The White House did not say whether she had passed a bar exam anywhere.
Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile lists her as “general counsel” of Fix California, a conservative group founded by Ric Grenell, a longtime Trump ally and the special presidential envoy for special missions. Zacharia lived in California, but the state bar of California said it had no record of her being licensed in the state.
“The State Bar of California has no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black (or Katie in both instances) having been licensed to practice law in California,” a spokesperson for the California state bar said in a statement. Black is her maiden name.
“Due to confidentiality laws, the State Bar can only confirm whether someone passed the bar exam, not whether they took the bar exam,” it added.
No report alleges that Zacharia has been charged with or has committed an offence.
Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog organization, on Wednesday filed a complaint with the state bar of California, asking it to investigate whether Zacharia misled the public – and potentially violated state law – by describing herself as a lawyer.
“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” said Michelle Kuppersmith, the group’s executive director, in a statement.
California law says anyone “advertising or holding himself or herself out as practicing or entitled to practice law” who is not an active member of the state bar could be punished with a fine of up to $1,000 and up to one year in jail.
“There is a difference between having a JD and being a lawyer, you are licensed as a lawyer by saying that you took the bar,” said Richard Painter, a university of Minnesota law professor and the former chief White House ethics lawyer under the George W Bush administration. “Calling yourself an attorney … it’s a misdemeanor at least.”
Zacharia’s LinkedIn notes that she was remote while at Fix California. But Painter said that was “not relevant – you need to be a member of the bar”.
The profile also says she worked as an associate at the Beijing firm Zhong Lun from 2011 to 2013. Only Chinese citizens can be licensed as lawyers in China, according to Chinese law and legal affairs website China Justice Observer, though foreign staff can work at Chinese firms in other capacities.
The Washington Post, CNN and the independent newsletter Popular Information also found no sign of admission elsewhere, including Texas and Washington DC, where Popular Information said she had worked. The Post found no active or expired admissions under either of her names.
The press office of Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, mocked the exchange on X, asking whether the new press secretary “appears to be a Chinese lawyer”. Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, in the meantime described her briefing performance as “tremendous” and “commanding”.
Zacharia was relatively unknown when Trump announced her selection to be his next press secretary last week, after the departure of Karoline Leavitt earlier this year. In the days since, several outlets have uncovered a series of since-deleted social media posts that promote debunked or baseless conspiracy.
In a series of now-deleted social media posts on X, reviewed by the Guardian, Zacharia fawned over Tesla and Space X founder, Elon Musk.
On 22 May 2022, the new press secretary described Musk, a tech billionaire and Trump ally, as “based”. She went on to explain the term was applied “when you want to recognize someone for being themselves” and “courageous and unique or not caring what others think”.
In another post from the same year, Zacharia also responded to one user sharing a widely circulated picture of Musk and Ghislaine Maxwell, the co-conspirator of the late sex-offender Jeffrey Epstein, at the Vanity Fair Oscar party in 2014, where Zacharia wrote “oh please, he already responded to this #oldnews”.
Musk has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, and has denied knowing Maxwell, claiming the photo which pictures her standing close to him is because she “photobombed” him.
In other now-deleted posts, also from the same period, Zacharia directed various complimentary messages at Musk. “#IstandwithElon,” she wrote in one. In another she praised him for renouncing his support for the Democratic party and saying he would now support Republicans. “Smartest and richest man in the world right here is saying out loud what everyone else is thinking,” Zacharia wrote.
However, last year Zacharia questioned whether Musk could have been trusted “from the beginning” while appearing as a guest on conservative commentator Buck Sexton’s podcast.
“He’s heavily invested in China. A lot of people were questioning his allegiance to begin with. Where is his allegiance completely?” she asked on the show. In late 2025, Musk and Trump had a public falling out of the president’s sweeping domestic policy legislation. They have since reconciled and Musk, according to the New York Times, is spending record sums to help Republicans retain control of the midterm elections this cycle.
The Bulwark previously reported on Zacharia’s since-deleted posts where she called on the administration to “suspend habeas corpus” – the constitutional right to challenge detention before a judge.
Meanwhile CNN also found now-deleted social media posts where Zacharia wrote and reshared comments that accused prominent political figures and Hollywood elites of pedophilia. This includes longtime Democratic operative John Podesta – who was the notable target of the debunked Pizzagate conspiracy – which alleged that several prominent Democrats were part of a child sex-trafficking ring.

UN: Lebanon stability as end of peacekeepers' mandate looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:11:41 UTC
04:11:41 KST

Breadcrumb
UN says wants Lebanon stability as end of peacekeepers' mandate looms
A visiting senior United Nations official on Wednesday reaffirmed the body's commitment to stability in Lebanon as the mandate of its peacekeeping force in the country is set to expire this year.
Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix met officials as well as representatives of countries contributing to the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which counts some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.
"I thanked them for their critical support to UNIFIL and reiterated the UN's strong commitment to supporting peace and stability in Lebanon," Lacroix said.
UNIFIL has served as a buffer between Israel and Lebanon since 1978, but its presence has been unable to prevent several rounds of conflict.
Under US pressure, the UN Security Council last year voted to end UNIFIL's mandate on December 31, 2026.
Lebanese officials have called for the mandate to be extended.
President Joseph Aoun told Lacroix that Lebanon "is keen on UNIFIL staying, considering the importance of the role that it has played from the start of its mission until today", according to a statement from his office.
"The circumstances resulting from Israel's attacks and occupation of southern villages and towns... make the presence of international forces extremely important," Aoun added.
UNIFIL's "withdrawal will create a vacuum that will have negative repercussions on the security situation in the region", he warned.
'Must be heard'
After meeting Aoun, Lacroix said "we know about Lebanon's positions including the letter which it sent to the United Nations requesting a temporary extension of the UNIFIL mandate".
"The positions of the Lebanese authorities must be heard and taken into consideration," he said.
In July, 86 Lebanese lawmakers signed a letter addressed to the UN Security Council calling for UNIFIL troops to remain with an expanded mandate.
Lebanese militant group Hezbollah drew the country into the broader Middle East war in March by attacking Israel, which responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
The looming UNIFIL deadline comes as Israeli forces continue to occupy a self-declared "security zone" that runs around 10 kilometres (six miles) inside south Lebanon along the border.
Violence has decreased since a US-Iran understanding in June, and a US-sponsored Lebanon-Israel framework agreed later that month.
The framework deal involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones", but the process has largely stalled.
Visiting EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told AFP last week that the bloc was in favour of extending UNIFIL's mandate, also warning against a "security vacuum".
France and Italy have said they want to set up a multinational coalition to succeed UNIFIL.

Four Palestinians were killed and several others, including a girl, were wounded in Israeli air strikes across Gaza on Wednesday, according to medical sources.

Around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed, according to the figures cited in the report.

Jewish teachers cancel Italy trip over ‘antisemitic pressure’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:10:19 UTC
04:10:19 KST

Educators from Jewish schools across the US canceled a study trip to Reggio Emilia, Italy, over whether the hosts would require participants to formally distance themselves from Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
The controversy has drawn accusations of antisemitism from Jewish educators and from Italian Jewish community leaders. It has also sparked a political dispute in Italy.
In an email sent to participants on October 9, the American organizers, the Paradigm Project, said they canceled the trip because of “antisemitic pressure being placed on the group.” In a Zoom call with the participants, the organizers also cited safety concerns amid the scrutiny of the Jewish school educators’ personal profiles by pro-Palestinian activists who were agitating for the declaration, a participant said.
Reggio Children considered asking for declarations distancing themselves from 'genocide'
In a leaked audio recording broadcast Monday evening by Italy’s Tg3 TV news program, the president of the host organization Reggio Children, Maddalena Tedeschi, discussed asking participants to sign declarations distancing themselves from the “occupation of territories and genocide.” The recording is of an October 6 meeting of the city’s early childhood education council.
In an interview with the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, Reggio Children spokesperson Francesca Severini said the request, intended to appease local pro-Palestinian activists, had never become an official participation requirement, but acknowledged that the additional wording had been discussed.
The Paradigm Project, a professional development network for Jewish early childhood educators, organized the trip for 68 Jewish educators. A separate delegation of 22 educators from Israel arrived in Reggio and was participating in the program this week.
“Now, more than ever, we must bring back the light and keep the bridge between us strong,” the Israeli educators said in opening remarks Monday.
Reggio Children, an educational organization partly owned by the municipality, promotes the city’s internationally influential approach to early childhood education and provides training for educators. Reggio Emilia Mayor Marco Massari and the city’s education official Marwa Mahmoud did not respond to requests for comment.
Pro-Palestinian activists protest ties to Israel
The cancellation, which came in a phone call from Paradigm to Reggio Children on October 7, follows months of tensions in the city, where pro-Palestinian activists had protested the participating schools’ ties to Israel. During the weeks preceding the trip, activist Cosimo Pederzoli had publicly accused some of the schools of supporting the Israeli military.
At the Oct. 6 meeting, Reggio Children presented a charter, titled “For a Democratic and Participatory Education,” asking visiting groups and partners to uphold human rights, oppose discrimination, reject war, and condemn genocide. The charter, which was approved and is now on the organization’s website, also opposes violations of human rights in occupied territories worldwide, without naming Israel or Gaza.
Severini, the spokesperson, said that activists, teachers and parents had pressured Reggio Children and the municipality to take the charter one step further and require participants to agree to the statement: “I … hereby declare that I distance myself from the occupation of Gaza and the violation of children’s and human beings’ rights in occupied territories as well as every place in the world.”
Severini said that the wording was included as “material for discussion” in a private WhatsApp group. The American organizers were not in the chat, she said, and subsequently received the wording without the context that it would not, in the end, be official language.
Her account contradicts Reggio Children’s earlier public statements. On October 7, the organization acknowledged that the educators had been asked to explicitly distance themselves from the policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in response to concerns raised in the city. Mayor Marco Massari also acknowledged the additional commitment in a public statement, which says, “This Charter will be signed by all delegations visiting Reggio Emilia in the coming months and years.”
In an email to parents, leaders of Wilshire Boulevard Temple’s early childhood centers in Los Angeles said seven of their educators had been scheduled to join the trip and expressed support for Paradigm’s decision to cancel.
“Paradigm, on behalf of our educators and dozens of others, rightfully refused and canceled participation in the study tour and conference, due to the refusal to sign and other security considerations,” read the email. “All participants were notified on October 7, 2026.”
Pesha Kletenik, head of Manhattan Day School, had planned to join the trip. “This was one of the most painful experiences I’ve had,” Kletenik told JTA. “I never felt so targeted as a Jew before in my life. I’m an American citizen. I have one passport. I’ve lived here my entire life.”
Kletenik said she had hoped to adapt the Reggio approach to Jewish teaching and practice, including their model Passover seder, because “it aligns so beautifully with Jewish values.”
Steve Freedman, head of Schechter Bergen in New Jersey, said his school withdrew an educator from a separate trip planned for November. In a letter to families, he criticized the demand for a political declaration while affirming the school’s commitment to the Reggio approach.
The council of the Jewish Community of Modena and Reggio Emilia, a single institution based in nearby Modena that serves both cities, condemned efforts to boycott educational and cultural initiatives involving Jews. It described the conflation of diaspora Jews with Israel’s government as antisemitic.
The Reggio Emilia approach, developed after World War II by educator Loris Malaguzzi and local families, places children’s exploration, expression, and participation at the center of early childhood learning. It gained wider international recognition after Newsweek named one of the city’s preschools among the world’s 10 best schools in 1991.
Severini said Reggio Children’s relationships with American Jewish and Israeli educators stretch back roughly three decades. The Israeli liaison first visited in 1996, she said, and educators from Reggio have also traveled to the United States and Israel.
The organization has hosted educators from all over the world, Severini said, including China, Russia, and Iran. She said she knew of no comparable controversy involving other visiting groups, including previous delegations from Jewish schools.
Reggio Children, she said, hoped to continue its dialogue with the American educators. For Manhattan Day School’s Kletenik, the cancellation stood in stark contrast with the educational values that had drawn her to the approach.
“How are we to navigate rejection by the very experts we collectively idealized, the gatekeepers of the sensitive worldviews and teachings we trusted to nurture our most tender children?” she wrote in a message to her school’s board.

Iranian officials warn US against renewing attacks

The IRGC spokesman stressed that Iran would respond forcefully to any additional military action. “Iran is prepared to respond to any further aggression with greater force than in the past, and the consequences for the United States will be far more painful,” he warned.
Iran increases attacks on vessels in Strait of Hormuz

Bangladesh arrests two for luring locals to fight for Russia in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:02:51 UTC
04:02:51 KST

Bangladesh arrests two for luring locals to fight for Russia in Ukraine
Twenty Bangladeshi victims have been killed after being used by Russia as ‘bait’ to locate enemy positions, police say.
Police in Bangladesh have arrested two people they say are linked to a trafficking network that deceptively recruited locals to fight for Russia in Ukraine.
The suspects, identified as Mizanur Rahman and Abu Taher, trafficked at least 30 people to Russia with false promises of high-paying jobs, Mohammad Asaduzzaman, commander of the elite police force Special Response Battalion, said on Wednesday.
Once abroad, the victims’ passports and phones were taken, and they were handed over to the Russian military, he said.
Seventeen of the trafficking victims, who arrived in Russia in early May, were killed on the first day of deployment after being given minimal training, Asaduzzaman said. A total of 20 Bangladeshis have been confirmed dead.
“Bangladeshis were used as bait to locate enemy positions,” he said. “Russian forces determined their next course of action after the Bangladeshis fell victim to drone attacks.”
In addition to the 20 Bangladeshis killed, two more are being treated in a Moscow hospital while six others are still on the battlefield, police cited a survivor who was injured and managed to return home as saying.
The victims were from poor backgrounds and had paid around $8,000 for the fake jobs that brought them to Russia, Bangladeshi media reported.
Both Russia and Ukraine have recruited thousands of foreign nationals into their armies since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago.
An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army, and officials believe Moscow deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to battle Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region.
Meanwhile, Ukraine says 16,000 foreign nationals from more than 70 countries – including nearly 40 percent from Latin America – are currently serving in its army.
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly last month, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia deceptively recruits people from 47 countries for an “absolutely brutal” campaign and urged countries not to let Moscow “drag” them into the war.
Amnesty International has also accused Russia of using “deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices” to recruit foreigners to fight on the Ukrainian front.
Russia has previously dismissed accusations of coercing foreigners into joining its army.
Amnesty says it cannot conduct inquiries about foreigners in Ukraine’s army as it has no access to prisoners of war held in Russia, which designates the rights group as a “foreign agent”.

As Ukraine struggles with Starlink and US satellite data, Europe has no quick fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:00:57 UTC
04:00:57 KST

As Ukraine struggles with Starlink and US satellite data, Europe has no quick fix
KYIV – As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer any ready-made alternatives.
Ukrainian officials said on Oct 14 the functioning of Starlink’s military-grade service Starshield had been interrupted when terminals were moving at high speed, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defence.
Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that, for the second night running, Ukraine had received no warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.
The reasons for the difficulties were not immediately clear but followed another souring of relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukraine, after Trump announced a deal to waive sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Zelensky to be replaced.
Trump said on Oct 13 that the United States was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, which operates Starlink, said the US government controlled that system’s speeds.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on the social media platform X, using the acronym for president of the United States.
Musk has been a close political ally of Trump.
European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelensky. But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications — provided by SpaceX via Starlink — and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
“That is fairly unique and… what basically that can detect is the heat generated by missiles as they're launched,” said Marc DeVore, an associate fellow at think tank Chatham House. “There is nothing equivalent in Europe.”
No simple Starlink swop for Ukraine, Europe
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Oct 14 following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
But Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, said Eutelsat’s OneWeb network was not well suited to wartime use.
“Its current constellation remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” he said.
“Capacity and performance constraints, combined with the cost, weight, bulk and power consumption of its user terminals, limit its suitability for frontline applications.”
A spokesperson for Eutelsat told Reuters that the company continued to provide connectivity services in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit networks with its partners. It declined to comment further “given the sensitive nature of the situation.”
Von der Ropp also said switching networks would require replacing thousands of terminals, as Starlink and Starshield terminals use proprietary technology and could not simply connect to OneWeb.
Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Ukrainian defence technology startup Buntar Aerospace, said the sudden interruption to Starshield services “highlights to almost every end user both in Ukraine and abroad you can’t rely solely on one solution that can be switched off”.
“You need to have some kind of sovereign capabilities,” he added, so that “you are not subject to somebody’s mood today”.
Fears of over-reliance on US defence technology have grown in Europe in recent years, as Trump has threatened to quit the NATO military alliance just as European leaders see Russia posing the greatest threat to the continent in decades.
European Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a conference hosted by Politico in Brussels on Wednesday that the continent was “quite dependent on American space capabilities”.
“The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities,” he added, mentioning the European Union’s planned satellite constellation IRIS² and urging European countries to work together to avoid frustration.
But that project is years from becoming operational even if everything goes according to plan, causing frustration among European government officials. Germany is developing its own military satellite constellation. REUTERS

US Congresswoman Jayapal slams India's purge of 133 million people from voter rolls, backs protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:00:53 UTC
04:00:53 KST

US Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal has slammed India's removal of over 133 million people — roughly equivalent to the population of Mexico — from electoral rolls via the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process, equating it to US voting rights challenges under the Republic administration and affirming support for non-violent Indian protests demanding free and fair elections.
"I am deeply concerned about the actions of the Indian government to purge 130 million people from the voting rolls. This appears to be a similar playbook to what the Trump administration is doing here at home to undermine voting rights in a democracy," Jayapal wrote on X on Wednesday.
Jayapal was comparing the situation to 2026 US administration’s efforts to audit state voter rolls for non-citizens, which courts have blocked in several cases over concerns about privacy violations and potential disenfranchisement of eligible voters.
The Indian-American House representative expressed her support for youth activists and opposition parties who are demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who they say has manipulated voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling right-wing party.
"Protecting democracies everywhere is essential work, and the Indian people — like the American people — deserve free and fair elections. Non-violent resistance movements are essential in these moments and I stand with the Indian people who are engaging in non-violent protests to counter anti-democratic efforts in India," Jayapal added.
India's Election Commission claims the deletions as targeting dead voters, permanently shifted residents, and untraceable individuals to clean up rolls, but critics including opposition parties and many media reports say the deletion has disproportionately impacted Muslims and other groups who are less supportive of Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
'Basic targets were the Muslims'
Widespread protests have erupted across Indian cities against the exercise, with calls for the chief election commissioner's resignation and Supreme Court involvement, amid claims some living citizens were removed despite opportunities to re-enroll.
In northern West Bengal state for example, over 9.1 million voters—more than 10 per cent of the electorate—were removed from rolls by April 2026. Despite appeals by 2.7 million people, they remain excluded.
In Nandigram area of the state, an analysis revealed that Muslims made up 95 per cent of voter roll deletions in certain lists, despite accounting for only 25 per cent of the electorate.
Non-Muslims, who constitute roughly 75 percent of the population, accounted for just 4.5 percent of deletions, according to data sourced from India’s election commission.
The electoral list revision, which began last year, has led to more than 133 million names being removed from voter rolls, according to media reports. Critics say the exercise has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
According to The Hindu newspaper, Muslims, who make up 13.6 per cent of voters on the draft electoral roll in the capital, New Delhi, accounted for 20.3 per cent of those flagged for "logical discrepancies" and 30 percent of those flagged under five categories indicative of family size by the Election Commissionr's ERONET software.
In northern Bihar state, which didn’t have "logical discrepancy" checks, Muslims accounted for 18.4 percent of deleted electors, in line with their 17.7 percent share in population, the newspaper reported on Wednesday.
Recent investigative reports indicate that BJP agents attempted the mass deletion of Muslim voters from electoral rolls during a statewide revision exercise in India's eastern Odisha state.
Reports across Indian states including Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Madhya Pradesh detail systematic efforts to disenfranchise Muslim voters through targeted voter list deletions, registration hurdles, and discriminatory labelling.
In interview with India Today, former chief election commissioner S Y Quraishi argued that the scale and execution of voter deletions showed bad faith, stating, "Basic targets were the Muslims, and potentially all non-BJP voters."
India arrests 'cockroach' movement members
Meanwhile, two leaders of India's youth-led movement Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), led by founder Abhijeet Dipke, were remanded in custody for five days, as police clamp down on protests against the election commission.
Delhi Police said CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, 30, and Saurav Das, 27, were taken into custody for their "alleged repeated attempts to disturb public peace and violate the law".
Parliamentary opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, from the Congress party, backed the protest leaders.
Rights advocates and critics say Modi's right-wing government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents — allegations the government rejects.
Human Rights Watch said on Wednesday the Indian government must uphold the right of citizens to protest peacefully.
"The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections," it said in a statement.
Home Minister Amit Shah, Modi's powerful right-hand man, has dismissed the protests as localised and accused Gandhi of pursuing an "action plan to protect infiltrators".
"The people of India are not going to fall for your deception," he said, predicting a "resounding majority" for government in the next general election, due in 2029.

Saving Lives on the Front Line: Kyiv Post’s Jason Smart Hits €1M Milestone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Along the roads leading into Ukraine’s front lines, safety is measured in sheer speed. Routes that were quiet thoroughfares months ago are now tunneled under makeshift anti-drone netting, where Ukrainian troops must floor the accelerator to outrun Russian FPV operators actively hunting any moving target. Between regular visits, familiar landmarks vanish: cozy roadside cafes where soldiers once shared coffee are flattened into rubble, and bridges are wiped off the map.
In a battlespace where Russian electronic countermeasures shift constantly and transport vehicles are destroyed daily, off-the-shelf military gear often fails to keep troops alive. Bridging that lethal gap, an emergency pipeline spearheaded by Kyiv Post special correspondent Jason Jay Smart and security analyst Sergej Sumlenny has surpassed €1 million. This effort pooled contributions from 8,585 international donors to rush nearly 2,000 custom-engineered drones, replacement vehicles, and electronic warfare systems directly to combat brigades.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Built Around What Soldiers Need
“We don’t come with a product,” Sumlenny explains. “Instead, we come with the question, what do you need?”
For the German security analyst, rapid frontline adaptation has rendered cookie-cutter tech supplies ineffective. Traditional military supply chains relied on mass-issuing standardized hardware, but the electronic battlefield moves too quickly for a one-size-fits-all approach. A commercial drone that flies reliably in one sector can be rendered completely useless ten miles away by localized Russian jamming.
Russian forces lean heavily on centralized, mass-produced systems, whereas Sumlenny works backward from a Ukrainian unit’s immediate tactical dilemma. His team engineers drones tailored to distinct radio horizons, flight ranges, and payload weights. Rather than shipping boxes through backline depots, Sumlenny personally delivers the systems to combat zones, running immediate field tests and modifying components based on pilot feedback.
Such constant presence has put him on speed dial for frontline commanders whose survival depends on solving unexpected equipment crises in real time.
This direct lifeline proved critical when soldiers from the 93rd Mechanized Brigade contacted Sumlenny after Russian strikes destroyed both of their transport vehicles. With available campaign funds exhausted, Sumlenny initially had to tell the unit he could not help. Then, while they were still on the phone, an unexpected donation from a supporter, in Germany, flashed across his phone’s screen.
“Oh, actually we have money now,” Sumlenny recalled telling the relieved soldiers.
Thousands of Donors Saving Ukrainian Lives
Behind these shipments are thousands of individual donors, largely drawn from Smart’s YouTube audience across the United States, Europe, Australia, and dozens of other nations.
“The soldiers are incredibly appreciative of all the support they receive,” Smart said, reflecting on his visits to frontline positions.
Sumlenny regularly relays donors’ personal messages to the troops, explaining that teachers, veterans, retirees, and families thousands of miles away are personally backing their survival.
Assistance has reached key fighting formations, including the 1st Azov National Guard Corps, the 4th Rubizh National Guard Brigade, the 47th, 67th, and 93rd Mechanized Brigades, the 225th Assault Regiment, and the 501st Marine Battalion. In many cases, the Ukrainian soldiers have recorded video messages, thanking donors, which were later broadcast on Smart’s YouTube channel.
                                
                                    
                                
                                
                                Night behind truck with Ukranian flag: In Kharkiv - with the 225th Assault Regiment. 
                            
Among them, fighters from the Rubizh Brigade thanked contributors after receiving 200 drones, while the 67th Mechanized Brigade’s air-defense unit credited the online community with supplying 22 interceptor drones.
According to Smart, who hosts the largest English-language YouTube channel focused on the inner workings of the Putin regime, reaching his goal of €1 million raised to support Ukraine’s soldiers - more than military medals or other recognitions - is his greatest source of pride from the past four years.
“I am profoundly thankful to all the people who watch the channel and chose to contribute, for keeping abreast of the existential fight in which Ukraine is heroically engaged. The struggle for Ukraine’s future does not stop at its borders; it is one that touches the lives of all of us,” said Smart.
“If the Putin Regime is not crushed now,” continued the American, “we can expect greater wars that will undoubtedly spiral into incalculable costs for countries around the world, especially in the West. By standing with Ukraine today, we are making the world a better place for future generations. This is the fight of our lives.”  
                                
                                    
                                
                                
                                Standing in front of some drones being delivered: In Sloviansk with the 501st Marine Battalion. 
                            
Recognition From Ukraine’s Military Leadership
Beyond his public analysis and fundraising, Smart, who first moved to Ukraine in 2015 at the invitation of the Director of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), has collaborated closely with Ukraine’s defense and security apparatus. Formal decorations have followed from the nation’s senior command, including the Armed Forces’ Medal of Merit, the Medal of Valor in Service to the Military, Third Class, and a medal from the Department of State Protection of Ukraine (ODU), the agency tasked with safeguarding the president and top state officials.
                                
                                    
                                
                                
                                Jason in front of Pyaterka: Ukrainian-occupied Kursk, Russia 
                            
Defense Intelligence Chief Kyrylo Budanov issued an official citation recognizing Smart’s sustained assistance in achieving military intelligence objectives. While still Ukraine’s top military commander, General Valeriy Zaluzhny conferred a commendation for his contributions. Separately, the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security formally acknowledged his work in countering Russian state disinformation.
                                
                                    
                                
                                
                                Jason in armored personnel carrier: At the zero line entering Ukrainian-occupied Russia. 
                            
Urgent Winter Appeal
Following Russian strikes on October 13 and 14 that damaged all three of Kyiv’s municipal heat and power plants, the initiative launched a €25,000 drive to supply frontline units with portable power stations, drones, and medical gear before winter.
Building on contributions from 8,585 international donors, this upcoming push focuses on rushing critical equipment to combat units facing freezing temperatures and ongoing grid disruptions.
Smart noted that supporters can contribute directly to frontline deliveries through the initiative’s PayPal link. Contributors donating over €100 are eligible to receive a commemorative military patch produced in Ukraine.

Netanyahu changed the face of the Middle East. Now he must make it last - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Two days after the Hamas-led massacre of October 7, 2023, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told local leaders in southern Israel: “We will change the face of the Middle East.”
At the time, the declaration sounded like a statement of resolve in the aftermath of a national catastrophe. Hamas had breached Israel’s border defenses, murdered approximately 1,200 people, and taken 251 hostages. Hezbollah was opening a second front from Lebanon, while Iran’s network of armed allies threatened to turn the attack into a wider regional war.
Before October 7, Israel’s security doctrine sought to deter and contain Iranian proxies and avoid the costs of prolonged regional warfare on multiple fronts. I critiqued this approach in my May 2024 report, “Restoring deterrence: destabilizing the Iranian regime,” where I advocated holding the Iranian regime to account for the actions of its terrorist proxies.
The entire defense and security establishment shared the assumption that Hamas could be contained, that deterrence could substitute for a political solution, and that Israel could manage its adversaries through periodic military operations. This conceptzia (rigid assumption) was shattered by the trauma of October 7.
Netanyahu’s response was to promise a fundamental change: not merely to restore the situation that existed before October 7, but to alter the strategic conditions that had made the massacre possible.
Nearly three years later, the regional landscape has changed dramatically. Hamas has suffered extensive military losses. Hezbollah has lost its senior leadership and much of its military infrastructure. Israel has confronted Iran directly, striking targets deep inside the Islamic Republic.
The fall of Bashar al-Assad has weakened Iran’s regional position and disrupted its former strategic corridor through Syria. Israel has also established forward security positions in Lebanon and Gaza intended to prevent hostile forces from rebuilding their capabilities near its borders.
From containment to the dismantling of threats
Israel would now preemptively act against threats before they are manifested by destroying the capabilities of Iran’s proxies, disrupting their supply networks, eliminating commanders, and acting against threats before they could be used again.
The consequences have been visible on several fronts.
In Gaza, Israel dismantled substantial elements of Hamas’s organized military infrastructure, including tunnel networks, command facilities, and weapons installations. In Lebanon, the killing of Hassan Nasrallah and other senior Hezbollah commanders, using an elaborate beeper attack coupled with extensive strikes against their military infrastructure, has been an enormous blow to Hezbollah.
The direct exchanges of 2024 culminated in the June 2025 war, when Israeli forces established air dominance over Iran’s airspace and attacked Iranian military, missile, air defense, and nuclear-related targets. Subsequent American strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities underscored the deepening of the alliance between Jerusalem and Washington that Netanyahu had achieved.
The strategic message was unmistakable: geographical distance, military infrastructure, and the protection provided by regional proxies could no longer be assumed to shield Israel’s adversaries from direct attack.
It was unprecedented for Israel to repeatedly launch airstrikes more than 1,700 km. away from Israel on Houthi-controlled ports in Yemen – primarily Hodeidah Port, alongside Ras Isa and Salif – in response to Houthi drone and missile attacks targeting Israeli territory and Red Sea shipping.
These developments, which demonstrate a substantial transformation in Israel’s operational reach and ability to project power across the region, led me to co-author the report, “Israel 2048: A blueprint for a rising asymmetric geopolitical power.”
For Israel’s new security doctrine to be sustainable, it must consolidate its defense industrial base. After rebuffing former US president Joe Biden, Israel entered Rafah; Biden then retaliated by withholding critical munitions to Israel.
Netanyahu’s response was to turn the crisis into an enormous opportunity, turning Israel into a defense-tech nation by investing in Israel’s arms industry with the aim of becoming an independent weapons-production system and phasing out reliance on US military assistance.
Lebanon and Syria
These developments have shifted the regional balance. Until September 2024, Israel was besieged by Iran’s “Ring of Fire.” Israel began to roll its Iranian encirclement initially with the beeper attack on Hezbollah.
Then, a few months later, the Netanyahu government seized the opportunity of the Assad regime’s collapse in December 2024: Israel carried out hundreds of air and naval strikes and ground incursions across Syria, targeting research and suspected chemical weapons stocks, strategic missile systems, and arsenals that included Scuds, cruise missiles, sea-to-sea missiles, drones, rocket launchers, and weapons/ammunition depots.
Israel further struck fighter jets, attack helicopters, military airfields, radar installations, tanks, and 15 naval vessels docked at the ports of al-Bayda and Latakia. In the process, Israel destroyed an estimated 70% to 80% of Syria’s remaining strategic military assets.
Furthermore, Israel’s ground forces moved past the 1974 disengagement buffer zone into southwestern Syria, to establish a buffer zone at the summit of Mount Hermon. This deprived Tehran of a longstanding partner and an important route for supplying Hezbollah.
This led to other opportunities for Netanyahu’s government, including the possibilities for regional intelligence-sharing, missile defense, and security cooperation with Arab governments concerned about Iranian military power.
Saudi normalization remains a diplomatic objective, in which Israel can offer the Saudi kingdom operational support against the Houthis that can be converted into enduring strategic gains.
As part of CENTCOM, Israel can coordinate with Saudi Arabia to shore up its defenses against Iran and the Houthis – as opposed to Turkey or Pakistan, which, as part of the Mecca Accords with Saudi Arabia, failed to come to its defense. It is a matter of time till this translates into a diplomatic initiative between Riyadh and Jerusalem.
Buffer zones and the new geography of Israeli security
Another important feature of the post-October 7 strategy has been the emphasis on forward defense.
In Gaza and southern Lebanon, as well as in the Syrian separation zone, Israel has sought to create a buffer to prevent Hamas and Hezbollah from reconstituting their capabilities, while providing Israel warning time and intelligence access that would shield its communities from Hamas and Hezbollah attacks.
In July 2026, Netanyahu rebuffed the Trump administration’s pressure to withdraw from the security zone in southern Lebanon, and reaffirmed that Israeli forces would remain for as long as he considered necessary to protect northern communities. This was quite a feat and cannot be taken for granted.
It resulted in Israel advancing past the Litani River and capturing the strategic Beaufort Castle near Nabatieh, only to uncover an extensive Hezbollah tunnel network near the border containing fortified military hardware, in which missiles and drones were stored.
The next phase must be strategic, not simply military
Operational success entails Israel continuing to destroy targets, eliminate commanders, and disrupt supply networks, which will give it freedom of action. Ironically, those calling for Israel to have a long-term strategy and continue to degrade the capabilities of adversaries are the same who conspiratorially claim that this is Netanyahu’s personal war to extend his term in office.
For Israel’s operational achievements to continue and strategically ensure Israel’s security remains enhanced in Gaza and Lebanon, Israel must continue to degrade the capabilities of Hamas and Hezbollah, so that they can be replaced with other factions that are not radicalized.
In Gaza, that means a credible framework that prevents Hamas from reconstituting its military capabilities and establishes workable governance.
In Lebanon, it means a security arrangement that prevents Hezbollah from rebuilding its offensive infrastructure near Israel’s border.
With Iran, it means maintaining the ability to prevent the restoration of acute threats while avoiding an indefinite cycle of escalating conflict.
It is a matter of time until there is another round of military strikes against Iran, which retains its missile infrastructure and is working to restore its nuclear capabilities. The intentions of Syria’s new leadership remain uncertain, and Israel cannot afford to presume enduring quiet on the northern front.
Similarly, it is a matter of time till the Houthis launch rockets and drones at Israel as Iran replenishes its missile infrastructure.
The task now is for Netanyahu to make the gains endure: to translate military reach into deterrence, forward defense into secure borders, battlefield leverage into regional cooperation.
It is precisely Netanyahu’s revolution of Israel’s security doctrine, and Israel’s increased power projection, that serve as a pathway to a lasting regional framework that includes Israel and its Arab neighbors. This will be achieved by Israel leveraging its military strength to recast the Middle East’s strategic landscape.
The writer is a senior research fellow at the Henry Jackson Society in London. Follow him at @BarakSeener

Lithuania freezes the assets of Russian oligarchs Fridman and Usmanov
Kyiv • UNN
Lithuania imposed national sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman after they were removed from the EU list. They were also banned from entering the country.
The Lithuanian government froze the assets of Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman after they were removed from the EU sanctions list. This is stated in a message from the Lithuanian government, reports UNN.
"The government approved a draft resolution submitted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, proposing to freeze the funds and economic resources of two influential Russian businessmen—Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman," the statement said.
As noted, the property of the aforementioned individuals is being frozen, and it is also prohibited to provide them, directly or indirectly, or for their benefit, with funds and economic resources.
"The decision to remove two influential Russian oligarchs from the EU sanctions lists became a sign of weakness. Lithuania's position is different: we are activating the national sanctions mechanism and freezing the property of M. Fridman and A. Usmanov. Sanctions pressure on Russia and those supporting its war of aggression must be intensified," Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said.
The government added that Latvia and Estonia are also imposing national sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov, and that on September 24, 2026, these individuals were placed on the list of foreigners banned from entering Lithuania for a five-year period.
As a reminder

ISTANBUL, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- A series of attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea over the past week has highlighted growing risks to civilian shipping in the region, as Turkish experts called for a broader maritime security framework.
Bulgarian authorities confirmed that one vessel sank on Tuesday 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. A second ship, the Malta-flagged and Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, was struck by three drones 18 nautical miles east of Byala. Its 15-member crew was safely evacuated to the Port of Varna, with five receiving medical assistance.
The incidents followed similar attacks last week, when three Turkish-linked commercial vessels were struck off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, resulting in fatalities.
Experts said the Russia-Ukraine conflict has increasingly threatened commercial shipping in the Black Sea, with attacks on ports and vessels raising security concerns.
A total of 146 commercial vessels were confirmed struck in the Black Sea region between 2022 and 2026, including 82 in 2026 alone, according to data from the Turkish Shipowners' Association.
The human toll has also grown, with 28 of the 37 reported maritime fatalities recorded in 2026 alone, the association said.
The changing nature of the conflict is reshaping the Black Sea into a "multilayered security environment," said Murat Ersavci, a retired ambassador and director of the International Studies Center at the Economic Policy Research Foundation of Türkiye.
He said in a recent assessment for the foundation that the boundary between trade and security was becoming increasingly blurred, adding that a ship's destination, flag, and links to particular companies and sanctions regimes are also becoming part of the security equation.
Ersavci called for a comprehensive maritime security arrangement to ensure safe, predictable commercial navigation, distinguish civilian vessels from military targets, and coordinate efforts among littoral states to protect energy and food shipments.
Canan Tercan, a foreign policy expert at Istanbul Aydin University, warned that the Black Sea risked mirroring the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, where prolonged disruptions have jolted global markets and driven up insurance costs.
Meanwhile, Tercan warned that bringing outside warships into the basin could trigger a wider conflict. "Navigational safety must be secured through an international non-combat agreement, not through naval forces." ■

SANAA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- As escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks put growing pressure on Saudi Arabia, regional actors and the United States are charting different courses, seeking to shape the crisis while avoiding deeper entanglement.
-- Iran has offered to mediate. Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi counterpart Sunday that Tehran was ready to assist in launching Saudi-Houthis talks toward a political solution.
Iran's stance reflects both influence and limits. Though Tehran has long-standing ties with the Houthis, analysts say the group pursues its own agenda rather than taking orders. Abdul-Ghani Al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, told Xinhua the Houthis were signaling to Riyadh that they act in their own interests.
"Iran does not need to control every Houthi decision to benefit from its influence," Yemeni political analyst Muqbil Naji noted. "By offering mediation, Tehran can turn that influence into diplomatic leverage while keeping itself at a distance from direct involvement."
Al Jazeera, citing political analyst Negar Mortazavi, said Iran was seeking to link the Houthi-Saudi conflict to a broader deal with the United States, with Tehran's political objective being "an informal non-aggression arrangement between Iran and its allies on one side and the United States and its regional partners on the other."
-- Israel, meanwhile, has reportedly sought a military opening. Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported Monday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought Saudi approval, through U.S. mediation, for Israel to join operations against the Houthis, a proposal Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman rejected.
Citing sources, the report said Israel believed such cooperation could strengthen ties with Riyadh and advance normalization. Saudi authorities have not commented publicly.
Riyadh insists that normalization with Israel remains tied to resolving the Palestinian issue. The reported overture highlights the gap between shared security concerns and political alignment, analysts say.
"A shared threat can create common interests, but it cannot erase political barriers," Naji said. "Israel may see the crisis as an opening toward Riyadh, while Saudi Arabia has to weigh the wider political cost."
-- Türkiye and Pakistan have taken a third path via the Mecca Alliance for Defense. On Oct. 5, the three members agreed to deploy agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia in response to Houthi strikes.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan reaffirmed Ankara's support for Riyadh Tuesday, while Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reiterated Islamabad's support for Saudi Arabia's right to self-defense Wednesday.
How far those commitments will go remains unclear. Reports have alleged Pakistani participation in strikes against Houthi targets, but Islamabad has denied its jets conducted cross-border operations. Türkiye, meanwhile, is expected to focus largely on defense technology and technical support, while any overseas troop deployment requires parliamentary authorization.
Analysts say Turkish and Pakistani capabilities could strengthen Saudi air and missile defenses and counter-drone systems without drawing either country deep into the conflict. The alliance thus lets Ankara and Islamabad demonstrate solidarity with Riyadh while limiting their exposure to another open-ended Yemen campaign.
-- Washington perhaps harbors the most difficult calculation. U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the Houthis were "behaving very badly" and accused them of seeking to drive up oil prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, highlighting Washington's concern that the confrontation could ripple into global energy markets.
The Trump administration faces pressure to back a key regional partner, but another direct campaign carries uncertain costs after past U.S. military action failed to eliminate Houthi long-range strike capabilities.
Analysts see little U.S. appetite for a prolonged confrontation, yet warn that continued attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could narrow Washington's room for restraint.
"Washington would prefer to contain the crisis rather than inherit it," Naji said. "But that calculation becomes harder to sustain if the conflict begins imposing greater costs on Saudi security, oil markets or U.S. interests." ■
