Reservists lose municipal-tax discounts after wartime protection expires, petition says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:35:20 UTC
03:35:20 KST

Low-income reservists who spent months in IDF reserve service are losing municipal property-tax discounts because their reserve payments push them above income limits, according to a petition Jerusalem’s Hitorerut movement says it submitted to the High Court of Justice on Tuesday.
The movement is seeking to restore a protection that expired at the end of 2025, leaving some students facing full property-tax (arnona) bills after previously receiving discounts of 80%. It argues that the government failed to renew the arrangement despite advance warnings and assurances that it would continue.
One case concerns a Hebrew University medical student who served 425 reserve days from the outbreak of the war through August 6, 2026, including 118 days in 2025. According to the petition, he received an 80% arnona discount in 2025 but was billed the full NIS 5,705.45 for 2026.
His wages from work in October 2025 amounted to just NIS 788, the petition says. Reserve payments and related supplements nevertheless helped bring his recorded annual income to approximately NIS 73,977, averaging NIS 6,165 a month - above the NIS 5,857 ceiling for a single-person household to qualify for an income-based discount in 2026.
Hitorerut argues that the payments did not reflect a lasting improvement in his earnings. After returning to his limited part-time work alongside his medical studies, he faced a full year’s municipal tax without the relief he previously received.
'Reservists should not have to fight twice'
“Reservists should not have to fight twice - once at the front and once against the bureaucracy,” Jerusalem Deputy Mayor and Hitorerut chairman Adir Schwartz said in a statement accompanying the petition.
The dispute concerns income-based discounts, rather than the separate arnona discount available to active reservists. Eligibility depends on household income and size, with national regulations setting the maximum discounts municipalities may grant.
Ordinary reserve compensation counts as income under those rules. For students and other low-paid workers, the minimum payment for military service can substantially exceed their usual wages. Months of service can therefore push them into a lower discount bracket or beyond eligibility altogether.
A temporary regulation allowed municipal councils to exclude those payments when assessing discounts for 2024 and 2025. Jerusalem adopted the arrangement. Hitorerut says its expiration left municipalities without authority to continue excluding the payments in 2026.
The filing describes two further cases. A married reservist and his wife saw their discount fall from 80% in 2025 to 20% in 2026, according to the petition. Another medical student, whose ordinary monthly wages were approximately NIS 2,600-3,000, received a full annual bill of roughly NIS 5,878 after previously receiving an 80% discount.
The movement argues that the result is unequal treatment of students earning comparable wages: those who did not serve can retain their discounts, while reservists lose relief because their previous year’s military compensation is counted against them.
Hitorerut, represented by attorney Matan Gutman, first petitioned over the issue in June 2024. The temporary regulation was published that November.
Extension requested, asks for overpayments to be refunded
In January 2025, the High Court closed that case and awarded the movement NIS 15,000 in costs. Justice Yechiel Kasher found that bringing the petition had been justified from Hitorerut’s perspective and appeared to have contributed to the amendment. He expressly avoided deciding whether the petition would have succeeded had it proceeded to a final ruling.
Schwartz requested an extension in September 2025. Hitorerut says the then-acting interior minister’s office subsequently conveyed approval, but the necessary regulation was never issued. The petition says further demands in August and September 2026 produced only an acknowledgment from the Interior Ministry, with no substantive response from the government offices approached.
A separate change has compounded the problem: An Interior Ministry notice attached to the petition confirms that 2026 eligibility is calculated using average income over 12 months. Applicants can no longer rely on the previous year’s final three months, an option that could help reservists whose service payments fell outside that period.
The movement seeks to restore the exclusion for 2026–2027, retroactive to January 1, 2026, or establish an alternative protecting affected reservists. It also asks for eligibility to be recalculated and overpayments refunded once an arrangement is adopted.
With Jerusalem’s October 31 deadline for discount applications approaching, Hitorerut is also seeking an extension so reservists do not lose the opportunity to apply while the issue remains unresolved. It further asks the government to consider a standing arrangement while emergency reserve call-ups continue.

Morocco opens first state-funded museum dedicated to Jewish culture in Arab world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:35:11 UTC
03:35:11 KST

The new Museum of Moroccan Jewish Culture opened its doors in the city of Fes on Monday, marking the first time in history that an Arab-Muslim country has allocated public funds to establish a museum entirely dedicated to Jewish culture.
According to Morocco's National Foundation of Museums, the 1,700 square meters space invites visitors on a journey into the heart of Moroccan Jewish life and Judaism through a rich and diverse collection of ritual and everyday objects, archaeological, ethnographic and artistic artifacts, archives and rare manuscripts, crafts, traditions, as well as practices and testimonies handed down through the 2500 of Jewish history in the country.
Exhibition galleries display Jewish religious artifacts from Arab World
Local media said the exhibition galleries explore communal institutions, including synagogues, Hebrew schools and rabbinical courts, as well as traditions associated with birth, bar mitzvahs, weddings, funerals and religious holidays. Objects on display include Torah scrolls, prayer shawls, marriage contracts, circumcision chairs, bridal costumes and jewelry.
Traditional crafts also feature prominently, including a reconstructed jeweler’s workshop, tools, silver ornaments, textiles, regional clothing and musical instruments. Audiovisual and digital installations complement the collections, while dedicated spaces will host educational activities for children and school groups.
The front of the building features a brass inscription in four languages: Arabic, Amazigh, Hebrew, and French.
The museum was designed with the involvement of the Moroccan Jewish community, represented in particular by Serge Berdugo, Founding President of the Foundation for Moroccan Jewish Cultural Heritage.
Construction of the museum was initiated by King Mohammed VI during his visit to Fez in April 2019, as part of a program to rehabilitate and showcase the old medina.
The Museums Foundation said the museum "forms part of King Mohammed VI's vision," which places "great importance on preserving and promoting all components of Moroccan identity, in their diversity and complementarity."
The work, completed in March 2023, was carried out by ADER-Fez in consultation with the National Foundation of Museums.
The opening of the Museum of Moroccan Jewish Culture on Monday was attended by Ahmed Toufiq, Minister of Endowments and Islamic Affairs; Khalid Aït Taleb, Wali (regional governor) of the Fez-Meknes region and governor of Fez Prefecture; Serge Berdugo, Founding President of the Foundation for Moroccan Jewish Cultural Heritage; Mehdi Qotbi, President of the National Foundation of Museums; and several other prominent figures, including ambassadors, directors and university presidents.

Alleged Chinese spies targeted former premier and AFP commander via LinkedIn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:34:59 UTC
03:34:59 KST

Alleged Chinese spies targeted former premier and AFP commander via LinkedIn
In short:
The alleged Chinese spies that targeted businessman Alexander Csergo, the first person to be convicted under Australia's foreign interference laws, also approached dozens of other Australians.
The AFP obtained records from the LinkedIn accounts used by the alleged spies as part of its investigation into Csergo.
What's next?
An expert on Chinese intelligence says the approach signals a "fundamental shift" in China's espionage tradecraft.
Two LinkedIn accounts connected to suspected Chinese spies amassed thousands of connections worldwide and approached dozens of Australians working in government, policing and trade with offers of paid consultancy, an ABC investigation has found.
The alleged spies posed as employees of a think tank, offering their targets competitive pay in return for "valuable advice".
Between 2016 and 2025, the alleged spies targeted more than 100 individuals linked to Australia, including former Queensland premier and now Opposition Leader Steven Miles, an Australian Federal Police commander and several senior federal government officials.
Their LinkedIn profiles appeared in the connection records of two LinkedIn accounts presenting themselves as think tank representatives. The accused foreign agents reached out to 58 of those connections, and some recipients shared their personal contact details.
The ABC can reveal the Australians were targeted by the same alleged Chinese spying network that groomed Australian businessman Alexander Csergo, who has been jailed as the first person convicted of reckless foreign interference.
LinkedIn records obtained by the Australian Federal Police (AFP) during the investigation into Csergo show the accounts approached other Australians, including those who worked at government agencies and state trade and investment bodies.
The AFP alleged the operation was conducted by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS), the country's principal civilian intelligence agency. It said the MSS used fake LinkedIn profiles to contact and cultivate potential foreign sources, before requesting information from them.
The Chinese embassy in Canberra rejected the AFP's claims as "entirely groundless".
"We firmly reject unwarranted accusations and vilification against China and hope that the Australian media will observe professional ethics and report in a fair and objective manner," a spokesperson told the ABC in an email.
In June, the Five Eyes alliance, an intelligence-sharing partnership consisting of the USA, the UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, issued a rare joint warning about Chinese intelligence using online job platforms for recruitment "that can provide China with a strategic and tactical advantage over the Five Eyes".
Asked by the ABC if it was aware of or investigating the alleged spying operation, a spokesperson for Australia's domestic spying agency, ASIO, said: "Consistent with long-standing practice, ASIO does not comment on — or confirm — investigations."
Inside the recruitment pitch
In November 2021, while Csergo was living in Shanghai, a LinkedIn account using the name Vera Su offered him part-time work.
The sender introduced herself as being from Nesa Consulting and said the organisation wanted experts to advise on trade between China and Australia.
According to the prosecution case, Csergo subsequently met two people known to him as Ken and Evelyn, prepared reports and received cash payments.
He was convicted in March of reckless foreign interference, an offence introduced under Australia's 2018 national security laws.
The prosecution case was that his conduct involved secrecy or deception and that he was reckless as to whether it supported a foreign principal's intelligence activities.
But an analysis by the ABC of Vera Su's communication records, first obtained by the AFP as part of its investigation into Csergo, revealed how the same LinkedIn accounts sought other people with useful expertise and contacts.
Among those directly approached were people whose profiles listed employment at Austrade — the federal agency that promotes Australian trade and investment — the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Investment NSW, Invest Victoria and Tourism Australia.
The accounts' pitches also sought access to people inside government.
"I wonder if you have special source of information… for example: from important people in the government," one message asked.
Some recipients declined.
One Austrade employee said he could not accept money because he worked for the Australian government, although he offered to introduce people in his professional network.
Former Queensland premier Steven Miles was also connected with the same Vera Su account in April 2021 while he was deputy premier.
The ABC has seen no messages between Mr Miles and the account, and the connection alone does not establish that he received a consultancy offer or provided information. The ABC understands that Mr Miles did not respond to any message from Ms Su.
'Honey traps'
Data reviewed by the ABC shows some Australia-linked targets shared contact details or discussed continuing the exchange outside LinkedIn, including through WeChat, phone calls or meetings.
Business consultant Nick Coyle was dealing with the arrest of his former partner, Cheng Lei, in China on espionage charges when he was approached by the alleged Chinese spies.
"During that time, I was getting many strange approaches," he said. Some were "honey traps", people trying to become "friends", both online and in person.
"I just took the approach — if I don't know them from prior — I would steer clear," he said.
Australian life coach Adrian Cahill also exchanged contact with Vera in 2021. He suspects his background as a former soldier made him a more attractive target.
"I would get those a fair bit," he said. "People write to me saying, 'we've got a job, we've got money, we've got a budget.'"
He said his training helped him recognise those tactics, but people without security experience could be gradually drawn into providing "more and more information".
A 'fundamental shift' in tradecraft
Chinese intelligence expert Nicholas Eftimiades described the state-sponsored fishing expedition as a "fundamental shift".
Professor Eftimiades said China's growing AI capabilities may be playing a role, making mass outreach more efficient and safer for Chinese intelligence officers.
"They can reach out to hundreds of thousands at a time, it's a less expensive proposition to try and get people to work for you," he said.
"We can't keep up with that type of onslaught."
Former US federal prosecutor Vikas Didwania, who has run cases involving Chinese intelligence operations for the US government, said LinkedIn was a "goldmine" for intelligence gathering.
"We have seen on LinkedIn, people post information about what kind of classified information they have access to, what kind of clearances that they have."
Didwania said information obtained from LinkedIn recruits may not be classified, or even useful, but could be part of a process of cultivating sources.
"Over the course of that relationship, you can start to push a little more."
Delicate balance for Australians working with China
In recent years, ASIO director-general Mike Burgess has warned the threat of foreign interference in Australia had reached an "extreme level" and was likely to intensify.
Csergo is the first person convicted of reckless foreign interference under the new threat environment.
During Csergo's trial, the court heard he did not disclose any confidential information. His reports were compiled from publicly available material.
At a sentencing hearing last month, District Court Judge Craig Smith described Csergo as "an otherwise decent man" who had committed "a most serious offence".
He sentenced him to three years and six months in jail.
Judge Smith said it was "fundamental and important" to deter people from becoming involved in activities that could harm Australia's national security.
For Australians working with China, however, the verdict has also redrawn the perilous line between legitimate work with a foreign entity and state-sponsored interference.
Some experts have noted a complicating factor is that China has about 2,000 think tanks, with varying and often opaque ties to the Communist Party and the government.
China's 2017 national intelligence law requires organisations and citizens to support national intelligence work. Some experts argue its practical reach can also affect foreign companies operating in China.
Mr Coyle said Australians working in China had to become adept at "walking and chewing gum".
Mr Didwania said efforts to counter China's spying operations needed to be balanced against the risk of creating a chilling effect.
"How do we differentiate between the great kinds of collaboration versus the collaboration that's really part of an MSS recruitment," he asked.
"It becomes a real challenge."

Brewing in Japan: Price-Fixing Probes Test Consumer Confidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:29:00 UTC
03:29:00 KST

The Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC) is investigating suspected price-fixing in the beer and ice cream industries. While the jury is still out on the hops and frozen milk, Japanese consumer sentiment may already be at stake. How the agency handles these cases could shape consumer confidence in the economy during prolonged inflation.
On September 2, JFTC Secretary General Iwanari Hiroo began a regular press conference outlining the agency’s 2027 budget. What followed was not routine. Instead, Iwanari issued an unusual public warning against cartel-like activity amid rising prices. He said he could not recall a similar warning by the JFTC secretary general in his more than 30 years at the agency.
The statement came as prices for more than 8,000 consumer items were expected to rise during Japan’s autumn price hikes. Rising prices reflect a range of pressures on companies, from high energy prices to domestic logistics challenges. Iwanari acknowledged that price increases were a normal part of economic activity, even if they had a “severe impact” on daily life in Japan. The JFTC is concerned, however, that companies might use rising costs to justify coordinating price increases with competitors.
Five weeks later, the JFTC began investigating the country’s four largest beer companies over suspected coordination of price increases through an industry organization between 2022 and 2025. The move followed a similar investigation launched in June into six ice cream companies over suspected price-fixing.
Like the ice cream probe, the beer investigation has drawn extensive domestic and international media coverage. A Yomiuri Shimbun editorial described the alleged conduct as a “serious betrayal of consumers.”
The investigation could reinforce the broader perception that companies are seeking greater profits during an already difficult economic period. Japanese media have already drawn a parallel between the current investigation and the JFTC’s report on beer pricing in the 1990s, which resulted in no charges.
Japan’s experience of the 1990s also offers a useful reminder of how consumers react to economic uncertainty. In 1997, Japanese wages peaked at 4.67 million yen just as the Asian financial crisis began. These high wages did not necessarily translate into increased spending.
The financial crisis, combined with the domestic policy misstep of raising taxes, contributed to a more defensive consumer mentality. Low- and middle-income Japanese households began to save more as a precautionary move. Consumers increasingly bought only necessities and focused on cost. Retailers cut prices in response, helping bring about “price destruction” (価格破壊). The shift disrupted traditional pricing practices and promoted a more cost-conscious way of consuming.
Today’s economic conditions differ from those of the 1990s. Still, the lessons about consumer behavior remain relevant. In August, Japan had its eighth consecutive month of real wage growth (up 1.5 percent year over year). At the same time, household consumption fell 3.1 percent, marking the ninth consecutive month of declining spending. The divergence suggests that growing purchasing power has not translated into increased spending. The figures suggest consumers may be becoming more cautious throughout 2026.
The government of Japan recognizes the challenge of maintaining consumer confidence and strengthening household purchase power. Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s proposed reduction in the food consumption tax seeks to put more back in consumers’ pockets. Equally important is ensuring companies compete fairly and that prices are not shaped by unlawful coordination.
The JFTC’s investigation addresses this concern and aligns with the goals of the recent Food System Act. The act seeks to promote “reasonable food prices” by basing price formation on the necessary costs of sustainable production, enabling producers to keep operating while still ensuring “stable food security” for the public.
Beer and ice cream are not the same as vegetables, but they do offer daily enjoyment for many consumers. Both investigations will test the JFTC’s ability to prevent collusion and protect fair competition. The outcomes will matter beyond the industries involved and will likely shape public confidence in how prices are set.
The JFTC’s challenge, then, is to ensure companies compete fairly as Japan adjusts to prolonged inflation. If consumer confidence weakens, households may once again become even more defensive in their spending, as they did 30 years ago.

But the restart in July of Yemen's frozen war has brought the fight to its own soil, with Houthi attacks in the Red Sea also harming the kingdom's alternative export route.

Four in five new UK jobs taken by foreigners – report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:22:17 UTC
03:22:17 KST

Four in five new UK jobs taken by foreigners – report
Foreign nationals have filled 80% of new UK jobs over the past decade, while millions of Britons have remained on out-of-work benefits, according to a new report by the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ).
The UK think tank said on Tuesday that British nationals accounted for just 734,000 of the 3.7 million jobs added to payrolls between 2014 and the end of 2025. EU nationals accounted for 408,000 new jobs, while migrants from the rest of the world filled around 2.5 million. 
“Employers have gained unprecedented access to overseas labour while taxpayers have absorbed the growing cost of domestic worklessness,” the report said.
The findings are part of a major inquiry chaired by former UK Work and Pensions Secretary Iain Duncan Smith. The report argues that successive governments have relied on low-skilled migrant labor while millions of Britons have been “written off” by the welfare system.
Since 2020, payroll employment among non-EU nationals has surged by 2.1 million, while the number of people claiming out-of-work benefits has risen by 2.3 million. Much of the employment growth was concentrated in health and social care, administrative services, hospitality and retail. 
“Compounding this, ministers have repeatedly pulled the easy lever of immigration rather than providing a better deal for left behind communities,” Duncan Smith said, urging coordinated reforms to welfare, immigration and regional development.
Around 6.7 million people in England, Wales and Scotland now receive at least one out-of-work benefit, equivalent to roughly one in six working-age adults, according to the CSJ. Since 2019, the number of claimants exempt from requirements to seek or prepare for work has climbed by nearly 1.7 million.
Annual spending on working-age benefits is projected to reach £136.1 billion ($181 billion) in 2026-27.
The report comes amid mounting political pressure over immigration. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly accused successive governments of favoring migrants and minorities over the white working class, demanding tighter border controls and denouncing what he calls a “two-tier” system of unequal treatment.
Britain has also struggled to stop illegal crossings of the English Channel. Some 33,374 people arrived in small boats in the year ending June 2026, down 23% from the previous year, according to the Home Office. The crossings accounted for 88% of detected arrivals via illegal routes.
Public concern remains widespread. An August YouGov poll found that 69% of Britons believed immigration over the previous decade has been too high, while 43% considered it mostly bad for the country, up from 33% in 2016.

Where statutory directions are clear, medical practitioners or medical boards “shall not unnecessarily avoid to attend such emergent cases”, the judge observed in his Oct 6 order.
The petitioner submitted that scans conducted at the gestational age of 12 weeks and six days, and again at 21 weeks and four days, showed no gross congenital anomalies in the foetus. Serious foetal abnormalities were detected for the first time only on Sept 24, when the pregnancy had reached 31 weeks and six days.Doctors, however, refused to undertake MTP without the court’s permission because of the advanced state of pregnancy, prompting the petitioner to approach HC.

Construction costs rose by 25% over the year: will apartments and reconstruction become more expensive for Ukrainians?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:15:46 EEST
03:15:46 KST

Construction costs rose by 25% over the year: will apartments and reconstruction become more expensive for Ukrainians?
Kyiv • UNN
In August, construction work became 25.4% more expensive year-on-year, while volumes for January–August fell by 9.9%. This is increasing pressure on housing prices and reconstruction.
In Ukraine, the rise in construction costs has accelerated significantly. According to the State Statistics Service of Ukraine (the State Statistics Service), in August 2026, construction prices increased by 25.4% compared with the same month last year. The construction of non-residential buildings and engineering structures became the most expensive.
This situation creates additional risks for developers, investors, and the implementation of state reconstruction projects. Rising construction costs may affect apartment prices in newly built developments, as well as the cost of repairs and the reconstruction of housing damaged by Russian attacks.
Why construction work is becoming more expensive faster than overall inflation, how real estate prices are changing, and whether Ukrainians will have to pay more for square meters was examined by UNN.
How construction prices have changed in Ukraine
According to data from the State Statistics Service published on October 12, the construction price index in August 2026 was 101.7% compared with July. This means that the cost of construction work increased by 1.7% in just one month. The increase was even more significant year on year. Compared with August 2025, construction became 25.4% more expensive. For comparison, the annual increase was 23.7% in July and 23.1% in June.
As we can see, prices in the sector are rising at an accelerating rate. Moreover, this is a general trend covering residential, non-residential, and engineering construction.
Which construction segments became the most expensive
Price increases were recorded in all major areas of construction. Over the year, the cost of work on the construction of non-residential buildings rose the most—by 26.4%. In engineering construction, prices increased by 26.1%, while in residential construction they rose by 21.5%. Over the month, prices for the construction of non-residential facilities increased by 2%, engineering structures by 1.6%, and residential buildings by 1.3%.
Among individual types of facilities, transport infrastructure construction became the most expensive in August, rising by 2.1%. The cost of work on the construction of pipelines, electronic communications network lines, and power transmission lines increased by 1.8%.
At the end of January–August 2026, prices for construction and installation work were generally 18% higher than during the corresponding period last year. In the residential segment, the increase was 15.5%; in the non-residential segment, 18.7%; and in the engineering segment, 18.4%.
For comparison, construction prices rose by 5.8% over the whole of 2025 and by 7.9% in 2024, which, according to the vast majority of analysts in the sector, indicates increased price pressure on an industry that simultaneously provides new construction, repairs, and the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure.
Why construction work is becoming more expensive
Construction price growth is significantly outpacing consumer inflation. In August 2026, annual inflation was 8.1%, while construction work became 25.4% more expensive.
Several factors may currently affect the cost of construction projects at the same time:
-  Construction materials. Changes in the cost of metal, cement, concrete, thermal insulation materials, and other resources affect the overall construction budget. 
-  Energy. Electricity and fuel are necessary for the production of materials, the operation of construction machinery, and the transportation of cargo. 
-  Logistics. War-related risks, damage to transport infrastructure, and more complicated supply routes may increase transportation costs. 
-  Labor costs. Higher wages and competition for skilled workers increase the expenses of contracting organizations. 
At the same time, the State Statistics Service did not specify exactly what share of the August price increase was attributable to each of these factors.
The situation in the labor market deserves special attention. According to OLX Jobs, the median salary offered by employers in vacancies in the "Construction and tiling work" category amounted to UAH 38,125 in July 2026. This was approximately 22% more than a year earlier.
For construction companies, the increase in all these costs — for personnel, materials, and the execution of works — entails the need to revise estimates. Such an upward revision may be particularly significant for long-term projects whose budgets were based on previous prices.
Why prices are rising while the volume of work is declining
Despite the substantial increase in costs, the construction sector has not demonstrated a corresponding increase in production volumes. According to the State Statistics Service, in January–August 2026, the output of construction products decreased by 9.9% compared with the same period last year. The value of construction products produced during this period amounted to UAH 156.5 billion.
The largest decline occurred in the construction of engineering structures — 13.7%. Residential construction decreased by 3.8%, while non-residential construction fell by 6.3%. In August, construction volumes were 3.7% lower than in August 2025. At the same time, compared with July, they increased by 12.9%.
Moreover, the situation differed across individual segments. Year on year, August residential construction volumes decreased by 2.3%, while engineering construction fell by 12.2%. By contrast, non-residential construction demonstrated growth of 9.8%.
Will apartments become more expensive for Ukrainians?
The rising cost of construction work creates the preconditions for further increases in housing prices on the primary market. However, the relationship between construction costs and the sale price of an apartment is not direct. A developer may partially pass the additional costs on to buyers, reduce its own profitability, or revise the project’s implementation timeline. But the extent to which the price per square meter will rise will depend on demand, competition, and the financial condition of the particular company.
The situation in Kyiv’s new-build market is illustrative here. According to LUN statistics, as of October 13, 2026, the median starting price per square meter in economy-class new-builds was about UAH 40,500. Over the year, it increased by just 2%. In the comfort class, a square meter cost approximately UAH 56,300, 17% more than a year earlier. In the business class, the median price was UAH 83,300, demonstrating annual growth of 12%. Thus, even within a single city, different real estate segments demonstrate different trends.
Another example is Dnipro, where, according to LUN data as of early October, the median starting price per square meter in economy-class new-builds decreased by 5% over the year, while in the comfort class it increased by 15%.
Therefore, a 25.4% increase in the cost of construction work does not automatically mean that buyers already have to pay a quarter more for apartments. However, persistently high construction costs may create additional pressure on prices in new projects. It is worth noting that the impact on the secondary market will be even less direct, as apartment prices there are largely determined by demand, the condition of the housing, and its location.
How rising construction costs will affect Ukraine’s reconstruction
Rising prices in the construction industry matter both to commercial developers and to state and local authorities implementing recovery projects. These include the reconstruction of damaged residential buildings, schools, hospitals, roads, bridges, heating and water-supply systems, and energy infrastructure.
If a project budget was prepared earlier but the actual costs of carrying out the work have increased, the estimate may need to be revised. With limited funding, this creates a risk of delays or the need to change the sequence in which the work is carried out. For example, if a community planned to restore several facilities within a specified budget, rising construction costs may reduce the number of works that can be financed within the initial budget.
The need to ensure transparency in spending remains an additional challenge. Amid significant price fluctuations, reviewing estimates, substantiating the cost of materials, and monitoring the use of budget funds become particularly important.
Construction has become more expensive in Ukraine: how this will affect people rebuilding their own homes
The rising cost of construction work may also affect households that are repairing damaged apartments or rebuilding private houses. In such cases, additional expenses arise due to changes in the prices of materials, equipment, delivery, and construction workers’ labor.
This issue is particularly sensitive for homeowners who use the state єВідновлення compensation program. According to the program’s official portal, compensation for damaged housing may amount to up to UAH 200,000 for minor repairs, up to UAH 350,000 for major repairs to an apartment, and up to UAH 500,000 for major repairs to a private house. The specific amount is determined according to an established procedure, depending on the nature of the damage. If the actual cost of the necessary work exceeds the approved compensation amount, owners may face the need to seek additional financing.
Therefore, when planning housing restoration, it is important to rely on up-to-date cost estimates and the actual cost of the specific work.
What to Expect from the Construction Market in the Near Future
Experts are currently unanimous: future price dynamics in the construction sector will depend primarily on the cost of materials and energy resources, the availability of qualified workers, logistics, the security situation, and financing opportunities. If contractors’ costs continue to rise, this will sustain pressure on the budgets of new projects and may gradually be reflected in housing prices. However, it is also worth remembering that limited demand does not always allow developers to pass additional costs on to buyers in full. Under such conditions, companies may restrain price increases, offer installment plans, or postpone the launch of new projects.
For state-led reconstruction, the key issue will remain the balance between the amount of available financing and the actual cost of the work. Currently, Ukraine’s construction industry is in a difficult situation: the cost of carrying out work is rising, while overall construction volumes are declining. For the economy, this creates an additional burden on investment and reconstruction projects. For Ukrainians, it poses the risk of a gradual increase in the costs of purchasing new housing and carrying out renovations.

AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:15:00 UTC
03:15:00 KST

Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.
As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.
“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.
Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.
Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.
The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.
In September, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU—who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.
OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.
As with math, Thompson says, we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.
Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.
“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Ukraine’s Warships Join Forces With Britain’s Powerful HMS Dauntless in Major Naval Drills
Five Ukrainian Navy minehunters completed a seven-day training exercise off the southern coast of England, conducting live-fire drills, underwater mine disposal operations, and coordinated maneuvers alongside the British Royal Navy destroyer HMS Dauntless.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Royal Navy on October 12, the training marked the final phase of Exercise Lion Protector, a multinational military exercise organized by the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) to strengthen maritime security and protect critical infrastructure across northern Europe.
The Ukrainian vessels—Henichesk, Mariupol, Melitopol, Chernihiv, and Cherkasy—are currently stationed in Portsmouth as part of Britain’s ongoing military assistance to Ukraine.
Training operations took place in waters near Dorset, Hampshire, and the Isle of Wight, where Ukrainian crews practiced naval gunnery, formation sailing, and the detection and neutralization of underwater explosives.
One of the principal components involved the SeaFox mine-disposal system, a remotely operated underwater vehicle designed to identify and destroy naval mines.
The system uses sonar and onboard cameras to examine suspected explosive devices. Its mine-disposal variant carries an explosive charge, allowing operators to destroy identified threats remotely through a fiber-optic control connection.
The Ukrainian minehunters Chernihiv and Cherkasy conducted live SeaFox operations, successfully destroying simulated mine threats through controlled underwater explosions.
The exercise concluded in the eastern Solent, where all five Ukrainian vessels sailed in close formation with HMS Dauntless, a Type 45 air-defense destroyer. The maneuver tested the Ukrainian crews' ability to coordinate movements and operate safely alongside a significantly larger warship.
The naval training formed the fifth and final stage of Lion Protector, which ran from August through October 2026 and involved forces from the 10-member Joint Expeditionary Force. The training also supports Ukraine’s preparations for future mine-clearance operations in the Black Sea.
Earlier, Ukraine considered deploying its UK-based minehunters to help clear naval mines from the Strait of Hormuz as part of a potential British-French-led operation. The proposal emerged as Ukraine’s warships remained unable to enter the Black Sea due to restrictions under the Montreux Convention.

UN peacekeeping chief says talks on future of Lebanon mission must begin soon
BEIRUT, Oct 14 - UN peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix on Wednesday urged the UN Security Council to begin negotiations on the future of peacekeepers deployed in Lebanon, as Beirut campaigns for an extension to the mandate set to expire at the end of this year.
A UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL has been deployed in southern Lebanon since 1978 but the Security Council last year ordered the mission to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026.
Since a new war erupted in March between Israel and Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, the Lebanese government has campaigned for an extension to UNIFIL's mandate, citing its role in monitoring hostilities and facilitating aid deliveries to villages in Israeli-occupied zones.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres earlier this year presented proposals for a continued uniformed UN presence in Lebanon but no action has been taken yet, Lacroix told Reuters in Beirut.
"These proposals are on the table of the Security Council. There has been no movement in the Security Council until now, but I believe that the negotiations will begin ... shortly, in earnest," he said.
"I think it would be better to have a decision soon rather than later, right? Because that would clarify also the horizon for us, certainly from the more limited point of view of our own planning," he said.
FORCES OPERATE HOTLINE TO EASE TENSIONS
Diplomats say the US is not supportive of an extended mandate for UNIFIL, but Lacroix said it was important to focus on Lebanon’s request and that negotiations at the Security Council could yield a constructive outcome.
Some 7,500 UNIFIL peacekeepers are still deployed at about 50 positions in southern Lebanon, which would be expected to be handed over to Lebanese army troops if no new UN force is agreed.
But since most of those posts lie in territory now occupied by the Israeli military, it remains unclear how Lebanese soldiers could deploy to take over the positions.
Lacroix said that clarity on whether a new UN force would deploy to southern Lebanon would help UNIFIL make sure it does not "leave those positions prematurely before we know what could come next".
In addition to facilitating aid deliveries and monitoring hostilities, the force operates a hotline to ease any tensions between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries.
Lacroix said the deconfliction role was particularly crucial given the presence of Israeli troops in a self-declared security zone deep in Lebanese territory.
He said that Israeli and Lebanese troops in the same geographic area presented "the risk of escalation, the risk of incidents getting out of control" and that "there is a need for a third party to de-escalate". REUTERS

Microplastics are linked to inflammation—scientists might have finally worked out why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:02:43 UTC
03:02:43 KST

Microplastics are a source of extreme concern for health: the presence of these tiny pieces of plastic has been linked to heart attacks, stroke, dementia and brain tumors. But what drives these associations is unclear. Now a study published in Nature offers a tantalizing clue: microplastics interact with water, generating highly reactive molecules.
When microplastics come into contact with water, the water near their surface can become chemically active, generating highly reactive species that can modify nearby substances, including biologically important molecules.
As plastics wear down to microscopic sizes, their surface-to-volume ratio increases dramatically. For example, when a credit card is fragmented into particles some 10 microns in diameter, there is a more than 200-fold increase in its surface area, says Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University and one of the senior authors of the study. As a result, any chemical activity is amplified.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Min and his colleagues examined various microplastics—including polystyrene, polyethylene, polyvinyl chloride, polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate. Plastic surfaces are hydrophobic, meaning they repel water, Min says. Thus, water molecules cannot form the hydrogen bonds they maintain in liquid form. That changes molecular arrangements, and, in turn, the change influences the local electrical environment and chemical reactivity.
The presumed chemical inertness of bulk plastics overlooks the toxicity of their fragmented microscale forms. “For microplastics, this is especially important because fragmentation creates enormous amounts of new surface area,” Min says.
In past research, microplastics have been shown to cause inflammation, oxidative stress and decreased mitochondrial activity. The new study provides a possible mechanism for this, showing that plastic-water interfaces can perturb proteins, cell membranes, and more.
How this might contribute to damage in living tissues in humans is still unclear, Min says. “Ultimately, we hope to connect fundamental interfacial chemistry with quantitative measurements of biological effects, which would help us better understand potential health risks,” he adds.
Martin Wagner, a toxicologist and a biologist at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, who was not involved in the new work, says the study’s findings are exciting. The paper gives scientists a new way to look at the effects of plastic pollution, Wagner says. “It implies microplastics themselves are a source of oxidative species ... and oxidative stress is not a secondary effect of exposure.”

An attorney for Lisa Cook voiced strong doubts that President Donald Trump's committee investigating mortgage fraud allegations against the Federal Reserve governor would be fair and objective.
The lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said the committee is plagued by issues that undermine the appearance of the Fed's independence, including "demonstrably biased members" and "unspecified additional allegations" against Cook.
Those and other issues "would have to be addressed before a hearing could occur" in the probe, Lowell wrote in a letter sent Tuesday to Will Scharf, Trump's aide and counsel.
No such hearing could take place until at least December, weeks later than the initially scheduled date, Lowell insisted.
The letter came three days after Trump slammed Cook as "dishonest" and griped that she was an "automatic no vote" — apparently referring to her opposition to cutting interest rates, which the president strongly desires.
Cook last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its most recent meeting in September.
"She shouldn't be in an important position," Trump said of Cook in those remarks to reporters after returning from a rally in Tennessee on Saturday.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to Lowell's letter that Trump "is performing his constitutional duty in evaluating Lisa Cook's conduct and eligibility to continue serving as a governor on the Federal Reserve."
"The Constitution charges the President with ensuring that the laws are faithfully executed and that the conduct of members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is above reproach," Middleton said in a statement.
An in-person hearing at the White House is currently scheduled for Nov. 5, according to Trump's Oct. 7 presidential memo establishing the "committee of inquiry" into Cook.
Cook's lawyers did not immediately rule out participating in that hearing, and in fact said the Fed governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name," despite their concerns.
But in Tuesday's letter, Lowell said Cook cannot attend a hearing on Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe."
After that, Cook will immediately start preparing for the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee in early December, Lowell said.
The White House did not immediately respond when asked by CNBC if the scheduled hearing would be moved in light of Cook's alleged scheduling conflicts.
Lowell also said he needs time to speak with Cook about issues raised by the White House's most recent correspondence, as well as to prepare her for any possible hearing, "which, because of her being in Asia on Federal Reserve duties, cannot be done until she returns."
"With all of that (and court hearings I have scheduled in November), the earliest date for any hearing would need to be in December following the FOMC meeting," Lowell wrote Scharf.
Trump established the three-member committee two months after reviving his long-running effort to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, from the central bank's board of governors.
The Supreme Court in late June blocked Trump's first attempt to remove Cook, ruling that she was not given sufficient due process under federal law. But that decision did not stop Trump from trying again.
Middleton said in his statement, "The President is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process."
But Lowell wrote Tuesday, "We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee," which comprises three executive branch officials, including top Trump economic aide Kevin Hassett.
Hassett "already has publicly insinuated that the President has 'cause' to fire Governor Cook," Lowell noted, citing the economic advisor's comments from August 2025.
Hassett in those remarks also accused Cook of "making a partisan stance contrary to the independence of the Fed" by refusing to step aside while a Justice Department investigation played out into the mortgage fraud allegations, which Cook denies.
The comments suggest Hassett has already prejudged the case, Lowell told Scharf, "surely belying your assertion that the 'hearing' as proposed would be 'substantive and fair.'"
"A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.

====================================================================================================

How war with Iran is influencing Israeli, US elections - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:55 UTC
03:00:55 KST

Many and varied are the reasons so many people are looking forward to October 28, the day after Israel’s elections, and November 4, the day after the US midterms.
One reason is that election campaigns do not exactly bring out the best in people, and the end of the campaigns in both countries will put an end to bitter partisan rhetoric that only deepens the divides and fuels antagonism.
Campaigns are not great unifiers, and both countries could use more unity. If that is too much to ask, then a little less divisiveness would also be welcome.
Another reason is that war and elections do not go well together. When the two overlap, it becomes difficult to tell what is driving what: Are electoral considerations shaping military decisions, or are battlefield developments shaping the elections?
Sometimes, both.
The first question is particularly pertinent in Israel, where any military action taken now, justified or not, will be viewed through the prism of the campaign. If Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launches an attack against Iran because of steps it is taking or contemplating, a significant part of the country will inevitably see it as an attempt to sway the vote.
Netanyahu pushed Trump to resume strikes on Iran before elections
Consider Israel’s bombing of Iraq’s nuclear reactor in 1981, just over three weeks before that year’s election. The operation was successful, but Labor leader Shimon Peres accused prime minister Menachem Begin of timing it to boost Likud’s electoral prospects. Its proximity to the vote cast a political shadow over an extremely consequential military decision.
Conflicting reports of discussions between Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump illustrate the problem.
On Tuesday, Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu had repeatedly urged Trump to renew attacks on Iran before Israel’s October 27 election and the US midterms a week later. According to the report, Netanyahu cited concerning Iranian nuclear developments, while American officials came away with the impression that he wanted action before the elections.
The Prime Minister’s Office denied that Netanyahu was seeking to start a war before the vote. Netanyahu reportedly told Israeli security chiefs that Trump, not he, had initiated the discussion about renewed fighting before the elections.
A Maariv report over the weekend presented another version: Washington had pressed Israel to strike Iran alone, leaving Israel to assume the political risks of an operation that could have negative consequences for Trump ahead of the midterms.
According to that report, American officials believed Israel would be interested in striking before its own election. The report also said Washington had since backed away from the proposal.
Who was pushing whom? For what reason? And why before the elections?
The reports do not provide a settled answer. They do, however, show how thoroughly the electoral calendar has become entangled with discussion of military action.
There is another layer. Channel 12 reported that Israeli security officials saw no change in the intelligence assessment of Iran that would justify a joint operation in the coming two to three weeks. The same report said IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir warned that renewed fighting could postpone the Israeli elections.
That possibility adds fuel to an already combustible debate. Netanyahu’s opponents have long warned that he might initiate a major military campaign to delay the vote.
And the problem is not confined to Iran.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu visited the seam line in the West Bank and warned that Israel’s enemies were thinking of testing it before the elections. He said the military was prepared for various scenarios, including Palestinian security forces turning their weapons against Israel.
That is a serious threat, one the military needs to prepare for regardless of the date. But when the prime minister explicitly links a security warning to the approaching elections, the political interpretations quickly follow.
Is he deterring an attack? Demonstrating his security credentials? Preparing the public for military action?
Those possibilities are not mutually exclusive. That is precisely what makes the mix so difficult to sort out.
Then there is a question often lost in the argument: Would an Israeli-initiated military operation necessarily help Netanyahu?
Danger comes when every security decision is viewed as a campaign maneuver
If it were successful, it could reinforce one of his strongest electoral assets: his record of confronting Iran. But if it went badly, brought Israeli casualties or dragged the country into another prolonged conflict, the political effect could be very different.
Starting a military operation doesn’t guarantee an electoral dividend. Its outcome matters, as does whether the public believes it was necessary.
Still, until the vote is behind us, any major operation will face an additional question alongside the military ones: Why now?
That question is legitimate. The danger comes when suspicion overshadows everything else, and when every security decision or warning is seen as a campaign maneuver. Israel’s enemies do not suspend their activities because Israelis are going to the polls. On the contrary, they sometimes step up their activities.
A government must remain able to respond, but it must also be able to explain why a response is necessary now.
Then there is the other direction of influence: military action designed to affect an election – an overriding concern now in the US.
Trump has said he will not resume attacks on Iran before the November 3 midterms, ostensibly to avoid shocks to the oil market. The last thing he needs before Americans vote is a sharp rise in gasoline prices.
Iran understands that vulnerability as well.
Reuters reported Wednesday, citing two senior Iranian officials, that Iran was deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to keep oil prices high and influence the US election.
The Iranians would plainly welcome a Republican drubbing and Democratic control of Congress, hoping that a strengthened opposition would make it more difficult for Trump to pursue the war against them.
According to Reuters, Iranian officials are explicitly linking pressure on shipping to the American electoral calendar. The aim is to have developments in the Gulf felt at the American gasoline pump, and then at the ballot box.
Which brings us back to those eagerly awaited mornings after the elections.
October 28 and November 4 will not remove politics from decisions about war. Nor will they resolve the threats posed by Iran or Israel’s other enemies.
They will, however, remove the immediate electoral deadline that now hangs over those decisions and over every interpretation of them.
Until then, voters need to keep two questions in mind: Is military action necessary, and is it happening now because an election is approaching?
The answer could be both, but in the heat of an election campaign and amid heightened regional tensions, the two become difficult to untangle.

====================================================================================================

Psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B leave different fingerprints on the brain, new study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:28 UTC
03:00:28 KST

A new study in rats suggests that three classic psychedelics, psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B, produce distinct patterns of brain energy use, both immediately and a week after a single dose. The findings, published in Nature Communications, challenge the common practice of treating these drugs as interchangeable, though the authors stress that any implications for treating specific mental health conditions remain speculative.
Scientists classify psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B as serotonergic psychedelics because they all bind to the serotonin 2A receptor, a specific protein on the surface of brain cells whose activation is linked to the altered states psychedelics produce. Because they share this primary target, these drugs are often grouped together as potential treatments for mental health conditions like depression and anxiety.
But their chemical structures differ, and they interact with other brain receptors in distinct ways. A 2023 review argued that while these drugs all stimulate the serotonin 2A receptor, their varying interactions with other biological targets could allow them to affect the brain quite differently.
To map these effects, researchers often track how the brain consumes energy. Brain cells use glucose, a simple sugar, for fuel, so measuring where glucose goes can reveal which brain areas are highly active and which are quiet. A 1997 study in humans used this technique, called positron emission tomography or PET, to show that psilocybin increased activity in the frontal cortex.
The research team was led by Mikael Palner, an associate professor at the University of Southern Denmark and head of the Palner Lab, alongside first author Frederik Gudmundsen, now a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University Hospital. “This was the idea of Frederik Gudmundsen, who was a PhD student in my lab at the time,” Palner told PsyPost. “After discussing it back and forth a lot and seeing that many papers and researchers were combining these psychedelic drugs into one bucket we knew we had to test the hypothesis, that serotonergic psychedelics are not just one drug class, but quite distinct drugs.”
The researchers wanted to see if psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B produce similar or different metabolic patterns over time. They focused specifically on two interconnected webs of brain regions. The first is a network linking the outer layer of the brain to deep structures that regulate movement, habits, and compulsive behaviors. The second is a system spanning memory and emotion centers that is involved in fear and anxiety.
Understanding how different drugs alter these networks could provide a biological map for matching specific psychedelics to specific psychiatric disorders. In related work, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that a single dose of psilocybin reduced depression-like behavior in rats for up to 12 weeks, alongside lasting increases in the excitability of prefrontal brain cells.
To test the effects of the three drugs, the researchers divided 48 rats into four groups of 12. Three groups received a single injection of either psilocybin, LSD, or 2C-B, while the fourth group received a saline injection as a control. The researchers gave the rats doses of psilocybin (1 milligram per kilogram), LSD (0.3), and 2C-B (3). In a separate group of nine rats, they confirmed that these doses occupied 51 to 70 percent of serotonin 2A receptors, a level associated with intense psychedelic effects in humans.
Finding the right dose to mimic the human experience yielded an unexpected result. “We compared three different drugs that are often used in humans: LSD, 2C-B and psilocybin,” Palner explained. “One thing was a big surprise and that is how much LSD we need to give a rat per body weight compared to a human.”
Scaled up by body weight, the rat dose would equal about 200 times a typical human dose. “The dose of LSD is 0.3 mg/kg in the rat; in a 70 kg human that’s 21 mg LSD (a regular dose is 0.1 mg),” he continued. “We don’t know why, but the rat has several protective mechanisms towards neurotoxins that may play a role.”
“The dose issue above is a common flaw in animal research with psychedelics and other neuropharmacological drugs for that matter,” Palner added. “One can’t just extrapolate the dose per kg and give the same to a rodent. We need to measure target effects and estimate the correct dose to translate between rodents and humans.”
Each rat underwent three PET scans: a baseline scan before receiving any drugs, an acute scan shortly after the injection, and a long-term scan one week later. During each scan, the rats were injected with the radioactive glucose tracer and allowed to remain awake in their cages for 45 minutes while their brains absorbed the fuel.
Afterward, they were temporarily anesthetized and placed in a PET scanner for 35 minutes to image the tracer’s distribution. The researchers also examined how strongly activity levels in pairs of brain regions tended to rise and fall together across the rats in each group, a rough indicator of how those regions work together.
Because all three psychedelics reduced overall glucose tracer uptake across the brain, which the authors suspect may partly reflect reduced blood flow, the researchers mathematically adjusted the data to look at relative changes. They calculated how much glucose each specific brain region absorbed compared to the rest of the brain. This adjustment allowed them to spot localized spikes or drops in activity relative to the animal’s global brain metabolism.
The acute scans showed that each drug produced a distinct metabolic signature. Psilocybin led to a relative increase in energy use in the dorsal striatum, a deep brain structure involved in habit formation, as well as in the insula, an area linked to emotional processing and bodily awareness. Unlike the 1997 human study, the researchers found no psilocybin-related changes in frontal regions in rats, and a possible strengthening of the link between two frontal areas did not hold up after statistical correction.
In contrast, LSD was associated with widespread decreases in metabolism across the outer layer of the brain, alongside increased activity in the midbrain and emotional centers like the amygdala and hypothalamus. 2C-B shared some features with LSD, including decreased frontal cortex activity and increased activity in midbrain areas that produce dopamine, a chemical messenger linked to reward and motivation, but its midbrain increase was larger and formed a distinct hotspot in a whole-brain analysis. 2C-B and psilocybin both increased activity in the insula.
A week after the single injection, the immediate spikes and drops had mostly faded, but some distinct network changes remained. Psilocybin left a lasting trace of increased metabolism in the insula and strengthened the link between activity in the insula and the prefrontal cortex, the only such network change in the study that held up after statistical correction. Psilocybin and LSD, but not 2C-B, also showed modest lasting decreases across several cortical, limbic, and midbrain areas.
For LSD, most acute metabolic changes had faded by one week, and a possible change in coordination between the cortex and the striatum did not hold up after statistical correction. The drug 2C-B left lasting effects primarily in dopamine-producing midbrain regions, without the sustained cortical effects seen with the other two drugs.
The authors offer what they describe as purely speculative ideas about therapeutic matching. Given their effects on the insula, psilocybin and 2C-B might suit disorders involving anxiety or disturbed bodily awareness; psilocybin’s tentative effects on links involving the orbitofrontal cortex, a frontal region, might make it suited to impulse-control conditions such as obsessive-compulsive disorder; and LSD’s effects on circuits linking the midbrain and striatum might suit substance use disorders. Overall, the results point to drug-specific brain responses rather than a single, universal psychedelic effect.
“Understand that just because one psychedelic drug is reported to do something to your mental health, it’s not necessary that others do the same,” Palner emphasized. “I think with the increased focus and ease of legislation this will be really important to understand.”
“I hope this is taken further and we will see that the right drug is given to the right patients,” he continued. “Whether it’s LSD or psilocybin for depression or anxiety. We need to do the comparison at some point.”
In earlier work, Palner’s lab found that repeated low doses of psilocybin made rats more resilient to stress and reduced compulsive behavior. “We are especially interested in dose reduction and finding the right drug, as our prior experiments with psilocybin microdosing were also interesting,” Palner noted.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Because the measurements were relative to each brain’s overall average, an apparent increase in one region could partly reflect decreases elsewhere. Each drug’s effects were also measured against the same rats’ own baseline scans; the paper does not report statistical tests comparing the drugs directly with one another. And the drugs occupied somewhat different shares of serotonin 2A receptors (51 to 70 percent), so some differences could reflect intensity rather than drug identity.
The study was also small, with 11 or 12 rats per group, and most of the network changes did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. “This is a small study, yet still significant, meaning that the distinct effects are quite robust, otherwise they would drown in noise,” Palner noted. “With rodent work we must balance ethics and significance and justify how many subjects we included.”
Finally, the study was conducted in healthy rats, and no behavior was measured, meaning the links to specific mental health conditions cannot be directly tested here. The emotional and psychological experiences of a psychedelic trip cannot be measured in animals, so the behavioral impact of these metabolic changes remains a topic for future study.
“This was a huge team effort and so many talented young researchers were involved,” Palner said. “I really want to thank them for their time in my lab and wish them all the best in their next adventure.”
Palner disclosed owning shares in Compass Pathways and ATAI, companies developing psychedelic treatments.
The study, “Serotonergic psychedelics induce distinct patterns of metabolic activity and covariance within biologically informed rat brain networks,” was authored by Frederik Gudmundsen, Julia Czurylo, Daniel R. Rijsketic, Camilla Trang Vo, Janika Fortunato, Naja S. Jessen, Sophie Woodruff, Christina Baun, Matthias M. Herth, Vladimir Shalgunov, Boris D. Heifets, Patrick M. Fisher, and Mikael Palner.

This strange sea animal is on menus, but it is disappearing from our reefs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Sea cucumbers can live 100 years, but may not survive our hunger
The alien-looking sea cucumber is a delicacy eaten in soups or consumed for its perceived health and libido benefits.
But a boom in demand since the 1980s has led to overfishing and population collapses in parts of the world, including the Pacific.
Entire species are disappearing from remote Australian reefs, with illegal fishing pointed to as a key culprit.
And there are now concerns that regulators for Australia's legal sea cucumber fisheries are underestimating how long it takes fished stocks to recover.
A new "first-of-its-kind" genetic study, published in iScience, indicates at least one sought-after sea cucumber species lives longer than we thought.
Study lead author and molecular ecologist Sven Uthicke, from the Australian Institute of Marine Science, said the black teatfish (Holothuria whitmaei) could reach 100 years of age.
It was assumed the species, found in Australia's tropical waters but less so in other Pacific countries, only lived five to 20 years in the wild.
Dr Uthicke said the finding meant fishery management needed to revise whether current catch limits were sustainable.
"They're currently assuming that these animals are replaced, basically, 10 times more than they are likely to be,"
he said.
The age a marine species reaches is a major factor for calculating a fishery's environmental sustainability.
Dr Uthicke said the sustainable catch limit for black teatfish and similar species might be lower than we thought.
What are sea cucumbers?
Sea cucumbers are part of a large group of "spiny skin" animals that includes starfish and sea urchins.
Colours and patterns of their leathery skin range from plain browns to vibrant reds and yellows.
Sometimes they have alien-like mouth tendrils, which are actually modified "feet".
Sea cucumbers are believed to benefit the health of coral and seagrass meadows.
"We don't necessarily understand all the ecological services that sea cucumbers provide, but we do know that they are very important in aerating sediment," CSIRO marine ecologist John Keesing said.
Much is still unknown about these weird animals, with few studies into basic biology like how long they can live.
How old do sea cucumbers get?
In the new study, Dr Uthicke revisited a no-fishing zone near Lizard Island in the Great Barrier Reef 24 years after another study he did into the growth rates of black teatfish.
He was surprised to find 31 out of the 76 sea cucumbers from his earlier fieldwork in 2000.
"I'm pretty sure a few of those were over 50, 60 years old,"
Dr Uthicke said.
"We still don't know how fast they grow because the individuals in my study basically did not grow at all over the entire 25 years … and we didn't find any small ones."
As the research was only conducted in one location, Dr Uthicke said other locations and species could be looked at.
But, he said, regulators could use the current findings to manage stocks more conservatively.
Black teatfish stocks have previously collapsed at the Great Barrier Reef and Zenadh Kes (Torres Strait).
As black teatfish are considered globally endangered, the federal environment department has to sign off on any fishing regimes occurring in Australia.
The species is not caught in the regulated Western Australia or Northern Territory sea cucumber fisheries, but it is caught in Queensland fisheries.
A Queensland Department of Primary Industries spokesperson said a recent stock assessment for black teatfish indicated the species was being fished at sustainable levels.
"Future stock assessments will consider all new, relevant information."
An Australian Fisheries Management Authority spokesperson said the new research would be considered when advice was developed for future management settings in the Torres Strait.
They said a past CSIRO survey in 2019–20 found the black teatfish had significantly recovered from historic overfishing and was safe to be fished under a strict harvest strategy.
"Black teatfish is an important source of income supporting livelihoods and the traditional way of life in the Torres Strait," the spokesperson said.
"Torres Strait Islanders have exclusive access rights to black teatfish, which is estimated to be worth over half a million dollars to the local economy."
How much do sea cucumbers sell for?
Dried sea cucumbers can go for hundreds of dollars per kilogram in domestic markets like Hong Kong.
A similar price bracket to other high-end produce like Wagyu beef and foie gras.
Sea cucumbers move slowly, so they are easy to pluck from the water by the basket-load.
Once caught, a sea cucumber is gutted, cooked, salted and dried.
"There's very few other animals that eat them," Dr Keesing said.
"That's the reason why they don't bother hiding themselves too much."
This vulnerability is thought to have led to local extinctions at remote Australian reefs.
Where sea cucumbers are disappearing already
A study led by Dr Keesing last year suggested the golden sandfish (Holothuria lessoni), which was once common at Ashmore Reef, has gone locally extinct, with overfishing the most likely cause.
The reef is located about 200km from Indonesia and 300km from the Kimberley region of Australia.
"Reefs like Ashmore Reef to the north are now sort of fished out so they're [illegal fishermen] looking further south," Dr Keesing said.
At the next reef down, Scott Reef, black teatfish and white teatfish (Holothuria fuscogilva) have reportedly collapsed.
Illegal fishermen have been intercepted as far south as Rowley Shoals, islands west of Broome, in recent years by federal authorities.
Another study earlier this year suggested the white teatfish was no longer in Rowley Shoals and three other species, including the black teatfish, were close to dropping under a critical population threshold for remaining viable.
"That level of fishing just over quite short a period of time has had a very significant impact on those populations," Dr Keesing, one of the authors, said.
"If that can be prevented by greater surveillance, greater consequences for being intercepted, then those populations should recover.
"If that's just allowed to continue … then potentially you could have the Rowley Shoals in the same state as Ashmore Reef."
