What are Iran and Russia's mounting hybrid attacks on Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:55:52 UTC
01:55:52 KST

Iran and Russia-linked hybrid attacks in Europe are mounting, U.K. spy chief says. Here's a look at recent incidents.
London — The head of Britain's top domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture Tuesday of the changing national security threats facing the U.K. and the world.
"We have entered a new era of national security, requiring a new response," he said in his annual threat update at MI5 headquarters in London. "Those who mean the U.K. harm aren't attacking things government owns or controls. They're aiming at people, businesses, communities."
McCallum said that among state threats, "Russia remains aggressor number one," while intelligence analysts have also seen a "major shift" in "Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets."
Both countries, he said, have adopted more and evolving "hybrid tactics" as they target everything from air force bases to synagogues across the U.K. and Europe. Below is a look at some of the incidents that fit that description over the last year alone.
Iran
Iran has used and continues "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites," McCallum said.
But as the U.S. war with Iran nears the eight month mark, analysts have also seen the Iranian regime, "like Russia, attempting to expand their hybrid campaign," he said, leading to more than 50 arrests in the U.K. over the last year alone.
"Sadly, much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities," McCallum said, speaking of incidents this year that included "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but also acts targeting "harder targets, like military sites."
Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.
A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."
These Iran-linked attacks include:
- Liège, Belgium: March 9. An explosive device detonated at a synagogue, causing no casualties. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Rotterdam, The Netherlands: March 13. The firebombing of a synagogue. Attack claimed by HAYI. Dutch authorities say they're investigating Iranian links to the incident.
- Amsterdam, The Netherlands: March 14. A device detonated outside a Jewish school. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Golders Green, London: March 23. Four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer ambulance service set on fire. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Antwerp, Belgium: March 24. A car set on fire in a Jewish quarter of the city. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Paris, France: March 28. 17-year-old allegedly tries to place an explosive device at the Bank of America headquarters. French authorities suspect HAYI was behind the attack, though the link was not confirmed.
- Nijkerk, The Netherlands: April 4. A device detonated outside the premises of a group called Christians For Israel. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Finchley, London: April 15. Molotov cocktails and a brick thrown at Finchley Reform Synagogue. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Park Royal, London: April 15. An attempted arson attack against Persian-language news outlet Iran International. Responsibility for the incident was never claimed. In March 2024, a journalist for the channel, Pouria Zeraati, was stabbed outside his home in London. According to The Guardian, counterterrorism police and security services in Britain believed the Iranian regime used criminal proxies to carry out the attack.
- Hendon, London: April 17. Attempted arson at the former premises of charity Jewish Futures. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Harrow, London: April 18–19. A suspected arson attack at a synagogue in Harrow, then a bottle containing accelerant was thrown at the Kenton United Synagogue a day later. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- Golders Green, London: April 29. Two Hasidic Jewish men stabbed in the north of the capital. Attack claimed by HAYI.
- RAF Fairford, England: Sept. 27. Suspected plot involving British base used by U.S. bombers to strike Iran. Gasoline was found in vehicles, but no viable explosives. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the incident was "almost certainly" directed by Iran.
- Manchester, England: Oct. 2. Two Iranian nationals are charged with terrorism offenses following an alleged plot targeting a Jewish community in the northern city of Manchester.
Russia
For now, Russia remains the biggest threat to security, according to the U.K. spy chief's Tuesday briefing.
"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum said, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia "is using tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."
Incidents linked to Russia this year include:
- Off Vaindloo Island, Estonia: March 19. Russian SU-30 fighter allegedly violates Estonian airspace – NATO scrambles aircraft in response.
- Hutthurm, Germany: March. Authorities thwarted a Russian-ordered assassination attempt targeting the head of a Germany defense company, according to Die Zeit.
- Norwegian waters, near the U.K.: Reported April 9. The U.K. and Norway deployed military vessels to deter Russian submarines found to have lingered for over a month from attacking undersea cables. Over the last few years there have been several incidents of alleged Russian sabotage of such cables.
- Labege, France: June 1. Molotov cocktails thrown at a drone factory that supplies the French and Ukrainian armed forces. French authorities are investigating Russian links, according to Le Monde.
- Leipzig, Germany: Aug. 4. An explosive-laden drone is found near cargo facilities and Ukrainian aircraft. German authorities explicitly attributed the incident to Russia.
- Skarzysko-Kamienna, Poland: August. Fire at a WB Electronics factory that produces drones and other military components. EBU reports that authorities believe Russia used "low-level operatives" to carry out the attack, but authorities do not identify those responsible.
- Tallinn, Estonia: Aug. 15. Arson attack on Milrem Robotics, a defense company that supplies robotic military vehicles to Ukraine. Estonian authorities attributed the attack to Russia in late September.
- Swindon, England: Sept. 9. Joshua Cammidge charged over allegedly sharing locations of drone factories with people linked to Russian military intelligence and offering to carry out sabotage attacks.
- Wola Krobowska, Poland: Sept. 23. Arson attack on a Starlink satellite ground station, which Poland officially blames on Russia in October.
- Lithuania, September. Drone carrying explosive device crossed Belarusian border is shot down by NATO aircraft. Italian defense minister says it "most probably" came from Russia.
- Denmark: Oct. 7. A Danish intelligence official says Russia attempted acts of sabotage against defense industry companies supplying Ukraine over summer.

Lithuania is seeking to extend the deployment of military personnel assisting border guards along its border with Russia until early November, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Wednesday, according to Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT.
Katelynas said he contacted Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas on Tuesday to request an extension of the strengthened border security measures and the involvement of troops.

He said the threat level along the border had not increased but expected that people might try to seek asylum in Lithuania to avoid military service.
The Lithuanian military has said cooperation between institutions to strengthen border security is routine and helps ensure that joint tasks are carried out effectively.
Troops are patrolling areas around border guard stations alongside border officials.
Depending on operational needs, the military may also deploy mobile patrols, mobile observation posts, and military police crews.

Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:54:43 UTC
01:54:43 KST

Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?
Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remain
In his annual speech on threats to the nation, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of the UK’s intelligence service, MI5, warned that AI had the potential to “change the stakes” on existing and even new bioweapons. Here we look at how AI might help in the development of bioweapons and the hurdles that remain.
How could AI help people make bioweapons?
It depends on who wants to make them. One risk is the rogue, unskilled bad actor or terrorist group that works from a garage laboratory. AI chatbots could help them skill up, by compiling relevant information, planning experiments and troubleshooting problems. It’s likely the work would focus on using existing pathogens and toxins.
The other risk comes from well-resourced organisations and nation states that have plenty of skilled scientists, high containment laboratories and all of the equipment and reagents needed to work on bioweapons safely. AI tools could help researchers identify genetic tweaks to make existing pathogens more lethal, for example. This is the more immediate concern, according to Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London. “Here, AI does not remove the need for expertise, it amplifies expertise that is already there,” she says.
A more distant risk comes from highly skilled groups using AI to design completely new pathogens and toxins that are resistant to drugs or have no antidotes.
Have people tried using AI to make bioweapons?
Last year, police in India uncovered a suspected bioterrorism plot in which a doctor and several others drew on AI chatbot queries and AI-driven search, allegedly to help them make ricin, a deadly toxin, using kitchen tools. It is unclear whether the AI’s responses helped, but other accounts suggest the tools can provide relevant and dangerous information.
The AI company Anthropic raised further concerns in September when it reported five cases of scientists in unnamed countries trying to use its Claude chatbot for what may have been dangerous work on viruses or toxins. One red flag, the company said, was that after being blocked, the scientists found workarounds.
In one case, Anthropic said researchers used the chatbot to plan experiments that would introduce mutations in a highly pathogenic bird flu virus to make it adapt and spread more easily in mammals. The work, and the other cases, could signify attempts to make pathogens more dangerous, but such studies are also done in legitimate labs to help researchers spot future pandemics and develop vaccines and drugs to treat disease.
What else has raised concerns?
A flurry of studies has shown how AI tools can provide potentially dangerous information on bioweapons. In a recent exercise at MIT, non-science students were asked if they could get an AI chatbot to help them unleash a pandemic. Within an hour, the chatbots listed four potential pandemic pathogens, explained how to make them from synthetic DNA, and supplied names of DNA synthesis companies that were unlikely to screen their orders. It is easier said than done, however.
In another case, the Stanford University researcher Dr David Relman described how an AI explained how to modify a pathogen to make it resistant to treatment. Another scientist revealed that an AI chatbot had explained how to use a weather balloon to release biological weapons from the sky.
The dual-use nature of biological research can make it hard to distinguish valuable work that could protect health from attempts to develop bioweapons. In 2025, scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratory trained an AI to predict how exceptionally potent neurotoxins from marine snails latch on to human cells, work that could help in the development of antidotes. But the US government became concerned when Chinese researchers drew on the work to develop their own tool to design new toxins. The Chinese researchers said the work was aimed solely at developing drugs.
In April, scientists raised further concerns when they made the first viruses designed by AI. The viruses are a particular type that only invade bacteria, and the work could lead to new medicines, but experts warned that it raised “urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions”.
What hurdles make it difficult?
Most work on bioweapons is beyond the reach of unskilled groups: as well as being highly technical, it is extremely dangerous. While AI chatbots might be prompted to give information on bioweapons, a list of instructions is not enough. “Information is only one part of the problem,” says Lentzos. “Tacit expertise, access to biological materials and equipment, experimental validation, scale-up and delivery all remain substantial barriers.”
Sonia Ben Ouagrham-Gormley, the deputy director of the biodefense programme at George Mason University in Virginia says tacit knowledge – the unwritten knowhow that an AI is unlikely to help with – has been key in the success of historical state-run bioweapons programmes.
Prof Martin Pačesa at the University of Zurich said access to material was critical. “Any graduate physicist could sketch up plans for a potentially more effective nuclear bomb, but where is he going to get a lump of uranium from? Same for bioweapons. If you have access to material and facilities capable of producing them, then AI is not going to make too much difference if you want to do harm.”
What extra measures are needed?
Some AI companies are taking steps to prevent people from using their tools to develop bioweapons, but the majority are not announcing what, if anything, they are doing, says Prof Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We have no formal government policies in place in any country yet to protect against this kind of misuse,” he says.
He wants formal independent evaluations of new AI models before they are released, with any dangers eliminated before the models are made public. And high-risk biological data, such as information on how pathogens might spread more easily, should be restricted. Meanwhile, companies that make genetic material for researchers must screen orders to ensure they are not for the creation of novel, highly dangerous viruses. Some screening already happens, but it is largely voluntary, and can be sidestepped if researchers use AI to design new, harmful genetic sequences that companies are not checking for.

Poland considers reinstating conscription
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:54:16 UTC
01:54:16 KST

Poland considers reinstating conscription
Poland is mulling reintroducing compulsory military service that was abolished in 2009, Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka has said. Her comments came shortly after an opinion poll indicated that over a half of Poles under 24 were against the reinstatement of conscription.
In an interview with RMF FM radio station on Wednesday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka revealed that “discussions at the Ministry of National Defense today cover all possible scenarios.” The official said that she personally is a proponent of universal conscription modelled after the Israeli draft system, where both men and women are called up for service.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka argued that the pool of volunteers should first be exhausted before moving toward the reinstatement of the draft. The Polish deputy defense minister acknowledged, however, that she has “colleagues who are absolutely opposed” to the idea of compulsory military service.
Earlier on Wednesday, RMF FM reported that a recent Opinia24 poll indicated that 46% of respondents were in favor of reintroducing conscription, while 38% were against, with the other 16% undecided. The share of those opposing the draft rises to 53% in the 18-24 cohort. Following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Warsaw has announced plans to expand its military from the current 220,000 personnel to 500,000, including 200,000 reservists, by 2039.
Speaking at a press conference on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called on the European Union to shift to “war-mode” military production.
In recent years, Poland has emerged as one of the most rapidly militarizing EU nations, with its military spending reaching around 4.7% of its GDP. The country has also been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers in its conflict with Moscow, providing Ukraine with weapons, including artillery systems, tanks, armored vehicles, warplanes, and ammunition. Some estimates place Poland in first place among all other Western countries in terms of the volume of assistance provided relative to its own GDP. Poland has also served as a key logistical hub for Ukraine-bound arms shipments from other countries.
Neighboring Germany has emerged as Ukraine’s top backer in Europe in absolute terms, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy. The German government is likewise aiming to increase the number of active-duty troops to more than 260,000 by 2035, backed by 200,000 reservists. In recent months, several politicians in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling coalition have floated the idea of reinstating conscription.
A new military service system introduced in early 2026 requires all 18-year-old men to register for potential service. While enlistment remains voluntary for now, parliament can activate compulsory service if recruitment targets are not met or the security situation deteriorates.
The new model has sparked nationwide student protests, with an estimated 45,000 demonstrators taking to the streets in some 100 cities and towns late last month.
Both Poland and Germany have justified their respective military buildups by claiming that Russia is harboring aggressive plans against NATO member states. Moscow has repeatedly dismissed these allegations as “nonsense” and even suggested providing written guarantees that it has no such plans.
President Vladimir Putin has accused
European NATO member states of openly preparing for war with Russia while using bogus claims. Moscow has also repeatedly warned Western nations against supplying ever more sophisticated weaponry to Ukraine, saying that the bloc is becoming increasingly involved in the conflict with Russia, with potentially dire ramifications.

U.S. special ops test drone laser for longer mortar shots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:53:16 UTC
01:53:16 KST

- A PDW C100 drone carrying a Leonardo DRS STAG-5 laser designator guided mortar engagements beyond standard 120 mm mortar range at Dugway, Utah.
- The Iron Sting validation event, run for U.S. Army Special Operations Command, tested the accuracy and range of new precision mortar munitions.
A small Performance Drone Works quadcopter carrying a Leonardo DRS laser designator guided precision mortar rounds onto targets beyond the normal maximum range of a 120 mm mortar during a recent test for U.S. Army special operations forces at Dugway, Utah, Leonardo DRS said on Oct. 14.
The company said its STAG-5 electro-optical and infrared gimbal with a built-in laser target designator flew on PDW’s C100 drone during the Iron Sting Precision Mortar Validation Event at the White Sage Mortar Range. Repeated engagements were completed at ranges beyond the standard maximum for a smoothbore 120 mm mortar, according to Leonardo DRS, though the company did not give the distances, the number of rounds fired or how close they landed to their targets.
The event was run by the Capability Development and Innovation office, previously known as the Irregular Warfare Technical Support Directorate, for U.S. Army Special Operations Command. Organizers tested the safety, accuracy and extended-range performance of new precision mortar munitions, and let operators try the technology in realistic scenarios.
Leonardo DRS did not name the munitions used. The event shares its name with Iron Sting, a 120 mm mortar round made by Israel’s Elbit Systems that combines GPS and semi-active laser guidance and has been used in combat by the Israel Defense Forces since 2023.
A laser designator marks a target with a coded beam, and a laser-guided munition steers itself onto the spot where that beam reflects. Putting the designator on a drone lets the observer stay well away from the target while still lighting it up, and lets a mortar team engage targets that its crews cannot see.
“The STAG-5 is designed to provide operators with precise, reliable ISR and targeting capabilities that can enhance mission effectiveness across a wide range of operational environments,” said Jerry Hathaway, senior vice president and general manager of the Electro-Optical Infrared Systems business at Leonardo DRS.
Leonardo DRS says the gimbal pairs its laser with day and night cameras so operators can find a target, mark it, confirm the strike and watch the mission from a safer distance.
The C100 is already in U.S. Army service. In September 2024 the service selected PDW’s C100 and Anduril’s Ghost X for its Company-Level Small Uncrewed Aircraft System program, which puts reconnaissance and target acquisition drones in the hands of maneuver companies in brigade combat teams. The rucksack-portable quadcopter can carry about 6.8 kg (15 pounds) of payload and fly for up to 74 minutes.

World Bank announces $93M to reinforce Ebola response in Africa

James Tasamba
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The World Bank has announced $93 million in new funding to strengthen the Ebola response in the African region as the Democratic Republic of Congo battles to contain the current outbreak, according to a statement Wednesday.
The statement said $80 million would strengthen disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, clinical case management, infection prevention and control, and community engagement in affected areas in Congo.
“Health emergencies don’t wait and neither did we,” said World Bank Division Director for Congo Albert Zeufack.
The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Congo has reached 9,066, including 4,381 deaths, since the outbreak declaration in May, according to the latest Health Ministry update.
The epidemic has affected seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and South-Ubangi.
Financing will also help sustain maternal and child health services in Ituri, the epicenter of the disease, so that the outbreak does not increase risks for women and newborns.
It will also help protect livelihoods in affected communities and enable children to continue attending school safely, according to the statement.
Across the region, $13 million in additional financing would strengthen emergency preparedness, response and resilience in 11 regional countries through the Health Emergency Preparedness, Response and Resilience program, said the bank.
In May, after the Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo and Uganda, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned that 10 African countries were at high risk of the outbreak, including South Sudan, Rwanda, Kenya, Zambia, the Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, the Republic of the Congo and Burundi.
While Uganda has been declared Ebola-free, Kenya last week reported its first imported case from Congo.
The World Bank Group has committed $426.6 million to the overall Ebola emergency response to date, through a combination of existing and new grant and concessional financing.

New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:51:25 UTC
01:51:25 KST

The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners.
The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person.
Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation.
The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government.
The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it.
Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement.
The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.
A new urgent procedure will allow ministers to mirror designations already made by the EU, US, Canada or Australia for up to 112 days while a specific separate UK case is prepared.
The new global sanctions regime will come into force on Thursday but will need endorsement by MPs and peers within 28 days.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is pushing through the measures at speed because the Israeli government has vowed to press ahead with an E1 settlement containing 1,234 homes in the West Bank – a development that many observers say would sever a contiguous, viable Palestinian state, so making the so-called two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict near impossible.
The E1 bids close on 19 October but the Israel Land Authority has confirmed that the tender box will not be opened, nor the bids considered, before 19 November, which is after the Israeli election on 27 October.
The British Palestinian Project said the Israeli deferral “does not remove the need to deter commitments being made now, since bidders and their backers commit on 19 October, contracts could still be signed before a new Israeli government is formed”.
The project welcomed the addition of the right to liberty and security of person in the new laws, saying it opens a route to sanctions for serious arbitrary or unlawful detention, including of Palestinian children, and of those responsible for or enabling it. Save the Children estimated in November 2023 that 10,000 Palestinian children had passed through Israeli military detention over the preceding 20 years.
A UN 2026 report on children and armed conflict verified that 981 Palestinian children were detained by Israeli forces in 2025 and 180 of them remained in administrative detention without charge or trial at the year’s end.
The UK has already applied sanctions designations for restrictions on humanitarian aid in Sudan and South Sudan but this is the first time this general power is being applied as part of a new worldwide regime including Israel.
Refusing permits or blocking convoys will be sufficient grounds to apply sanctions, without requiring the obstruction to constitute a formal breach of international humanitarian law – thereby lowering the threshold for action.
Separate work is under way by UK officials in conjunction with European partners on how to outlaw British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.

Suspected Israeli online operations cause alarm in Iran and Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:51:12 UTC
01:51:12 KST

Suspected Israeli online operations cause alarm in Iran and Lebanon
Suspected online espionage triggers intense security crackdowns and counter-intelligence measures in Iran and Lebanon.
Israeli intelligence services are believed to be turning to social media to gather information and recruit potential informants in Lebanon and Iran, according to security experts, using online advertisements and appeals tailored to local audiences.
One Instagram account, presenting itself as belonging to Israel’s foreign intelligence agency Mossad, has published Arabic-language messages encouraging people to make contact through confidential channels.
The account, which is verified and operates under the handle @themossad_official, has posted recruitment appeals in colloquial Lebanese Arabic, including inviting people to explore new opportunities by initiating a private conversation.
The profile prominently features pinned highlight reels with Arabic titles such as “Lebanon” displaying a photo of fighters, “Israel”, “Mossad wants you!”, “Protection”, and “Think about your future”.
In August 2025, Lebanon’s General Security Directorate warned residents against interacting with the Instagram account.
Fake job traps
In Lebanon, where years of economic turmoil have left many residents facing financial hardship, security officials have warned of suspected Israeli intelligence recruitment efforts involving social media.
In January 2025, the Lebanese newspaper Al Akhbar reported that Israeli intelligence operatives were attempting to recruit Lebanese citizens through fake job advertisements offering high salaries, and through direct outreach on WhatsApp.
Retired Brigadier General Mounir Chehade told the newspaper that the recruitment efforts targeted areas with significant support for Hezbollah, including Beirut’s southern suburbs, southern Lebanon and the Bekaa Valley.
Also in January 2025, Lebanon’s General Security Directorate warned against interacting with a Facebook page called SAWA, which it suspected was a Mossad front aimed at recruiting Lebanese citizens.
Similarly, in December 2025, another Lebanese newspaper L’Orient Today reported that the security agency had warned residents against interacting with a social media page calling itself “Unit 504”.
The page claimed to represent the Israeli military’s human intelligence unit and said it was looking for individuals interested in joining its ranks.
The concerns have been accompanied by arrests of people accused of passing sensitive information to Israel. Lebanese authorities were reported in October 2025 to have previously arrested 32 people suspected of giving information to Israel that was used to target Hezbollah leaders.
Targeting Hezbollah’s support base
Academic and political researcher Wissam Nassif Yassin told Al Jazeera that Israeli intelligence uses colloquial Lebanese Arabic on these platforms to avoid arousing suspicion and to facilitate communication.
“The Israeli side focuses on all segments of society because it considers that every person can be penetrated from their own angle, based on the fact that Hezbollah in Lebanon is integrated into the core of Lebanese society,” Yassin said.
“It focuses on the party’s members primarily, then on the resistance environment secondarily, and on the environment surrounding it thirdly.”
While Israel has had notable sucesses in its intelligence operations in Lebanon – including in gathering information leading to attacks on Hezbollah leaders and members, Yassin argued that collaboration with Israel remained widely rejected in Lebanon.
He also pointed to Hezbollah’s own counterintelligence capabilities, arguing that the group has a long history of identifying and disrupting Israeli intelligence activity.
Yassin pointed to the case of Elhanan Tannenbaum, an alleged Israeli spy who was captured in 2000 after being lured abroad, and was released in 2004 in a prisoner exchange deal.
Intelligence war
The use of digital platforms to recruit potential informants also forms part of the longstanding intelligence war between Israel and Iran, which has intensified alongside the military conflict between the two countries.
Hassan Ahmadian, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Tehran, described the current situation as one of the most intense periods in decades-long espionage between the two countries.
“This is an intelligence war. The confrontation between Iran and Israel has continued for decades, but in recent years it has reached its peak,” Ahmadian told Al Jazeera. “Both sides are engaged in intelligence operations. It is an intense conflict that has never stopped.”
Ahmadian said that Israeli recruitment efforts in Iran were sometimes carried out through openly advertised opportunities on social media.
“Israel certainly uses online advertising to recruit people,” he said. “When I was in Iran, I would see advertisements on social media seeking analysts or people to work in security, sometimes offering high salaries and inviting interested applicants to visit a particular page.”
He suggested that openly advertising such opportunities could have a psychological goal beyond recruiting informants, in an attempt to reinforce perceptions of Israel’s intelligence reach inside Iran.
“Israel uses propaganda, but this blatant method is perhaps partly to amplify the Israeli presence,” Ahmadian noted.
The academic also pointed to cases in which Iran had conducted its own counter-operations.
In October 2024, for example, Israeli authorities announced the arrest of seven Israeli nationals accused of spying for Iran by gathering intelligence on military facilities and other sensitive sites.
Separately, the former Israeli Energy Minister Gonen Segev was arrested in 2018 on accusations of spying for Iran. He subsequently pled guilty and was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2019.
Severe legal consequences
Authorities in Lebanon and Iran have threatened severe penalties for anyone interacting with Israeli accounts.
In July, the Iranian newspaper Kayhan reported that Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence had warned of social media accounts allegedly set up by Mossad to extract information and spread fake news following recent security operations. The ministry claimed that Mossad even offered medical advice to people injured during the United States-Israeli war on Iran, in an attempt to gather sensitive intelligence.
In the same month, the Iranian judiciary also warned that sending images or information to networks deemed to be hostile could result in sentences of 10 to 15 years in prison, heavy fines and potential charges of “corruption on Earth”, which carries the death penalty.
In Lebanon, collaboration with Israel carries a penalty of imprisonment.
As the covert conflict expands online, Ahmadian said that there was little indication that the confrontation would ease.
“I do not expect this intelligence war to stop at any moment between the two parties,” Ahmadian said, “it will remain ongoing and will continue to affect the entire conflict.”

01:51:10 KST

In the year 1625, a Lutheran pastor named Joannes Burmeister living in the village of Gülzow in the middle of nowhere, Germany published a small book called "Plautus' Asinaria". It was written in Latin and was in essence an adaptation of a filthy, ancient Roman comedy called "Asinaria" (The Jackass Affair" or "Comedy of Asses") to the biblical tale of King Saul trying to get his daughter's upstart suitor David killed by ordering him to bring 100 Philistine foreskins as a bride-price.
Yes, donkeys do appear in the rip-roaring plot, where Burmeister replaced the morally challenged characters in the original "Asinaria" by the Roman poet Titus Maccius Plautus with the biblical figures. Specifically, the comedy about Roman vulgarians and their horrible antics was retold as the origin story of King David.
We almost never knew this. "Plautus' Asinaria" and actually all the "Christianization" works by Burmeister recasting dirty classic plays with figures from Scripture, would go missing, and stay lost for over 300 years. Come the 21st century, that would drive a professor of classics named Michael Fontaine crazy.
Fontaine had devoted much of his academic career to Plautus and had become, he says himself, obsessed with Burmeister and locating his missing works.
No self-respecting studio would buy the true story of how "Plautus' Asinaria" was survived centuries of war and flame-torching Nazis because it's so implausible, but here we are.
To recap the 3,000-year-old biblical tale, Saul did not want the pipsqueak shepherd as a son-in-law and demanded that David bring him foreskins from 100 (presumably dead) Philistines as a bride-price for his daughter Michal. Saul assumed David would not prevail. It was a reasonable assumption. But the noble David provided 200 to spite the king, and married Michal; and Burmeister took that biblical pearl and went to town.
How did Burmeister's books go missing? Time and many wars, and the Nazi efforts to stomp out other cultures in Europe. How were they rediscovered? Librarians.
Gold in them thar libraries
The first Burmeister offering to resurface was an "inversion" (adaptation) of Plautus' book "Aulularia" ("The Pot of Gold"), which the pastor rewrote in 1629 using the characters in Joshua 2 and 7, rediscovered in the Royal Library in Copenhagen in 2011.
That same year, Fontaine traveled to Copenhagen to celebrate "Aulularia's" rediscovery; made a pilgrimage to Burmeister's village; and then went to Warsaw for a conference on classic comedy to make the formal announcement that Burmeister's "Aulularia" had been found.
But at least two of his other works, including Mater-Virgo, adapting Plautus's "Amphitryon" to the story of Jesus, and "Plautus' Asinaria" seemed to be gone for good. Some fragments of "Mater-Virgo" are circulating and Fontaine suspects "Moscow" is in possession of the whole book; but the "Plautus' Asinaria?" Nothing.
Until this September 15 years later, when Fontaine got an unexpected email from Warsaw. A copy of the Christianized, "inverted Asinaria," possibly the only one in the world, had survived centuries of silverfish, Russian invaders and even Nazis armed with blowtorches, and had resurfaced – on the shelves of the National Library of Poland. The German regime wanted to burn down the building and other major libraries for the sake of better oppression. Burmeister's "Plautus' Asinaria" even had an index card, which was belatedly noticed in 2026 by a senior librarian, Tymoteusz Mikołajczak, while digitizing old records. He wondered what it was, searched the internet for experts on Latin comedy and contacted Fontaine at Cornell.
Why him? Aren't there any Latin experts in Poland? "I'm literally the only guy in the world who would know anything about it," Fontaine explains to Haaretz over zoom, given that he is an expert on Greek and Latin classical literature, and chiefly, the comedies, and had been obsessing over Plautus and Burmeister for years.
Plautus and Terence are the only two Roman comic playwrights whose works survive substantially intact, and one was terrible, Fontaine explains. "Twenty-one plays survive under Plautus's name. Those were the good ones. Terence wrote boring ones."
Possibly Burmeister also found Terence tedious because he also evinced a passion for Plautus, or at least for taking his work and resetting it.
Why would he do that? He was an exquisitely educated Protestant parish priest with a vast intellect living in a tiny village where he had nothing to do all day long, Fontaine explains; and evidently found occupation in substituting characters in bawdy comedies written centuries before Christ with figures from Scripture.
For example, in Plautus' "Amphitryon," Jupiter descends from Olympus, impregnates a woman who gives birth to Hercules, who, in the wider mythology, suffers for humankind, dies and becomes a god. Burmeister noticed parallels with the Christian origin story. "God comes down from heaven, he overshadows Mary, she becomes pregnant and gives birth to Jesus, who suffers for humankind, dies, is buried, and goes to heaven up to God," Fontaine explains. "Burmeister, a devout pastor, said it's basically the same story. He took an ancient sex farce and transformed it into a play about the Bible – 'Mater-Virgo.'"
In "Aulularia," Burmeister retells Plautus' comedy about a miser who finds a pot of gold and becomes pathologically obsessed with guarding it. His parallel is in the Book of Joshua, where Achan steals booty from Jericho in defiance of God's explicit order not to do that, inducing the peeved deity to allow the enemy to crush the Israelites in the battle of Ai.
Now come October 2026, we know what "Plautus' Asinaria" was about too.
In Plautus' original play, a young Athenian named Argyrippus wants money to buy exclusive access to a prostitute named Philanaeum for a year, from her mother. He's aided by his father Demaenetus and some shady slaves. It's a competition because Philanaeum has another suitor and her mother isn't fussed about who wins her. Daddy agrees to help mainly because he wants Philanaeum for himself – sharing is a virtue. Demaenetus has his slaves Libanus and Leonida steal the money from his own wife, but before the twain hand over the money to young Argyrippus, they torment him and his lady love. From there the story gets complicated.
Before the book's rediscovery this September, Fontaine had devoted substantial effort to speculating what Burmeister's version of Asinaria would be about – what biblical story could be matched to this ancient sex farce? He turned out to be "spectacularly right" in one respect, he tells Haaretz – the common theme of the two books was bride-price.
"Of course, I was more than half wrong," he adds. Where? He didn't think a pious Lutheran pastor would keep the foreskins intact, so to speak. He figured Burmeister would replace that detail with a merchant being swindled over animal leather or something.
Not so. "That was totally wrong. They discuss the foreskins as if they're shekels, just a kind of currency," he says. If anything, the Burmeister tale features even more foreskins than the original: 300.
YouTubers would have a thing or two to say about a pastor writing pornographic plays today. Who was Burmeister writing these things for? For the kids, it seems.
How to edify the children
Like his muse Plautus, Burmeister wrote in Latin. His pious comedies closely preserve Plautus' wording, verse meters and sequence of dialogue, with only necessary changes such as Jove to Jova (Jehovah), for instance.
How much parallel can there be between obscene Roman comedies and biblical morality tales? Not much, and the biblical story in Samuel is short. To flesh out his plays, Burmeister added material, Fontaine explains.
In "Plautus' Asinaria," he expanded the role of various people, including Saul's wife Ahinoam, Michal herself, and even featured the obscure biblical figure of Phaltiel, briefly mentioned in the Bible, to whom the vindictive King Saul gave Michal after David fled to exile. Burmeister has David bringing the 200 foreskins taken from Philistines he has killed, as in the Bible, but adds 100 more by making Phaltiel a romantic rival, who buys them from passing soldiers instead of mutilating slain enemies himself. He hopes to use them to win Michal, Fontaine explains.
"Think of Gilderoy Lockhart in Harry Potter, claiming credit for other people's heroic exploits: stolen valor becomes a major theme in Burmeister's play," he says.
He also confirms that other German pastors of the time weren't doing such things.
Why was Burmeister? Why would anybody? Why did he write in Latin, a dead language? Who were these plays, from which pagan gods were cast out but the porn was not, meant for?
He was writing for children, Fontaine says. He was? High school children, Fontaine qualifies. Well, okay then. But why would he write racy plays recast with the stars of Scripture for 17th century German adolescents in Latin, a dead language?
It wasn't exactly dead, he clarifies. "Latin was the language of the western Roman Empire. This was the very late Renaissance period in Germany but people in the education system still used Latin for everything," he explains. "He wrote this play presumably to be performed by high school children, and Latin was the language they studied in."
Aha. The man in the street wouldn't know Latin but it survived in the institutions. Yet don't playwrights write plays for the ticketed among the hoi polloi? "The model isn't Shakespeare performed in vernacular English," Fontaine explains. Burmeister wrote his plays to be performed by the kids in schools, as a way to teach Latin.
Why would Late Renaissance schools teach teenagers using pornographic texts, albeit featuring people of the Book? Maybe because one wants to keep the wildlings engrossed, like one might lure them into learning English using Harry Potter books rather than engineering manuals.
The king is not amused
Beyond his speculated aim of teaching Latin to children in an innovative way, Burmeister may have had another agenda.
"A huge part of the play that Burmeister wrote is taken up with a mirror of princes," Fontaine says, referring to textbooks for the instruction of monarchs, such as Machiavelli's book "The Prince." Sounds like a hoot a minute.
"In his 'Asinaria,' a huge number of characters keep criticizing the king, Saul or David. The play is ostensibly about the bride price but there is extensive discussion of what's fair for a king to do, and how to treat his subjects. It seems to have been an anti-war play," Fontaine adds.
Still doesn't sound funny. Wasn't he writing comedies, like his ancient muse? Yes, but. "A comedy can contain anything from slapstick to fairly serious criticism of society and still end happily, often with a wedding," the professor explains.
Burmeister turned a play considered hilarious in Rome into a biting critique of political leaders and war – "He was writing during a nasty 30-year civil war in Germany, right where he lived," Fontaine clarifies. Yet ultimately "Plautus' Asinaria" is a sacred parody, which was a genre in the Late Renaissance Germany for about 20 years.
It seems however that Burmeister did have some small consideration for his audience.
His play tracks the ancient version, but the priest added two optional scenes printed at the end, of which one is absolutely obscene, Fontaine says. "The wife complains that her husband cannot satisfy her and suggests that the visitor could take his place... Tabellio brings him home for dinner, quarrels with his wife, and gets into a physical fight with her. She grabs her husband's genitals, mocks his impotence, and ultimately demands that he appoint a substitute for his bedroom duties. It's filthy language, in rhyme and full of puns," he adds.
One wonders if Burmeister was married. Fontaine says he wondered that too but can't find the information. He did discover that the poet-priest may have died of the plague.
Coming home
All this was almost lost to posterity.
It was written in the 17th century in Germany. Okay. Copies were disseminated.
In the mid-17th century, Russia occupied eastern Poland, in a campaign known as the Deluge and a century later, Poland was partitioned. In 1794, the Polish rebelled, staging what would become known as the Kościuszko Uprising. It did not go well. The Russians were briefly driven out but came roaring back, and among other things confiscated the Załuski Library as war booty and sent nearly 400,000 books to St. Petersburg.
Among them was "Plautus' Asinaria," Fontaine says. Many books were destroyed in this process but it survived.
Under the restitution provisions of the 1921 Treaty of Riga, which ended the Polish-Soviet War, portions of the old Załuski collections were returned to Poland between 1923 and 1934. Some books remained in Saint Petersburg, but our book was returned, not that anybody seems to have been aware of that.
Times changed again. "Then came 1939, and with it, the Nazis," Fontaine writes in an article about this whole affair. After rolling over Poland, the Nazis decided to reorganize the libraries of Warsaw to be more in keeping with German mores. As the tide of war turned against them in 1944, and following the abortive Warsaw Uprising in 1944, said mores would involve punitively burning books with blowtorches. Yet again "Plautus' Asinaria" survived, likely because, as a foreign-language printed work, it remained at the University of Warsaw Library rather than being transferred to the Krasiński Library building, whose collections the German troops had burned.
Today a demand of severed enemy genitalia to prove devotion would be frowned upon, but it bears noting that the good burghers of Late Renaissance Germany seem to have been undismayed. Fontaine republishes three 17th century engravings of the David affair, showing piles of penises, not foreskins – which presumably would have been difficult to draw in any meaningful way. He wonders if they underlay Burmeister's inspiration.
Was Burmeister's play funny? Eye of the beholder and all that, and even if it didn't end in a wedding complete with cake, one was implied. David and Michal marry offstage during Act III, as Fontaine tells it. "At the end of Act III [part] 1, her mother says she is preparing the wedding; in III [part] 3, Jonathan explicitly describes them as husband and wife." Hilarious stuff.

Germany's AfD and leftist BSW call for end to help for Ukraine

Germany's AfD and leftist BSW call for end to help for Ukraine
BERLIN, Oct 14 - Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the small leftist BSW party joined forces on Wednesday to pass a symbolic motion in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt calling for an end to Berlin's military support for Ukraine.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's national government is Europe's biggest supplier of military aid to Kyiv and has repeatedly restated its support, blaming the war on Russia, which invaded Ukraine in 2022.
The motion was passed on the opening day of the trial in Hamburg of a Ukrainian former military officer charged with blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipeline, which supplied Russian gas to Germany. The government in Kyiv has denied any involvement.
The motion has no practical effect, as state parliaments have no role in foreign policy.
But it raised the prospect that the two parties could reach an agreement allowing AfD state leader Ulrich Siegmund to form a government.
BSW WANTS TO WORK WITH AFD
Last month, the AfD secured its biggest victory in an election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, falling just short of a first absolute majority at state level.
Siegmund has said he intends to seek formal parliamentary confirmation as state premier by the end of the year, though most other parties in parliament have ruled out joining a coalition under the so-called "firewall" policy that aims to isolate the AfD.
BSW, which broke away from the far-left Linke party, whose roots reach back to the former East German communist party, does not want to join a formal coalition with the AfD. But it has said it wants to work with the AfD, with which it shares a desire to restore ties with Moscow and stem immigration.
"The firewall has failed," party founder Sahra Wagenknecht told the news portal t-online. "We will shape policy through shifting majorities and push through as many BSW positions as possible."
Both the AfD and the BSW have been heavily critical of Germany's support for Kyiv, saying it was prolonging the war and the money would be better spent at home.
"What has happened over the last few months and years in this war is, alongside uncontrolled migration, one of the biggest problems of our time," Siegmund said in the debate, which other parties denounced as a "farce". REUTERS

Ukrainian DELTA combat system tested during maritime operations at NATO exercise
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

19:50:00 EEST
01:50:00 KST

Ukrainian DELTA combat system tested during maritime operations at NATO exercise
Ukrainian military personnel have practiced maritime operations using the DELTA battlefield situational awareness system during international NATO exercises, transmitting data in accordance with Alliance standards.
Source: Ministry of Defence of Ukraine
Details: The combat system was tested at the annual REPMUS 2026 (Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems) international exercise, led by the Portuguese Navy.
Unmanned aerial, surface and subsurface systems, as well as radars, were integrated into the Ukrainian combat system.
Quote: "During the exercise, partners and Allies practised the joint employment of unmanned aerial, surface, and subsurface systems and tested interoperability within multinational forces. It is the largest international exercise focused on employing unmanned systems in maritime operations."
Details: According to the Defence Ministry, the Ukrainian team, participating in the exercise for the third time, coordinated its activities through DELTA. In particular, the military and their allies practiced maritime operations, namely reconnaissance, maritime area monitoring, manoeuvring, and escort and simulated engagement exercises.
The Defence Ministry noted that assets transmitting telemetry in line with NATO STANAG 4817 had already been integrated into the Ukrainian combat system.
Quote: "During the exercise, Ukrainian service members also shared combat experience with partners, particularly in the employment of unmanned systems in the maritime domain."
Details: The DELTA system is a Ukrainian situational awareness platform that ensures the collection, processing and display of information regarding enemy and friendly forces in real time, creating a single digital picture of the battlefield. It is an ecosystem of digital military products, which notably includes the Army of Drones.Bonus ( e-points E-points are earned by Ukrainian units for confirmed strikes on Russian soldiers and equipment ) programme, where strikes on enemy targets carried out by units using UAVs are recorded and confirmed.
In early 2026, the Mission Control module was introduced into DELTA, recording data on mission execution, the employment of unmanned systems and the results of combat operations.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that all DELTA users had been granted access to an AI assistant to work within the interface.

German air force fires IRIS-T SLM for first time in Crete
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:49:16 UTC
01:49:16 KST

- The German Air Force completed operational certification of the IRIS-T SLM air defense system with its first live firing at NATO’s Crete range.
- Swedish and German Patriot units and German Stinger crews joined the tactical exercise that followed the certification shot, Diehl Defence said.
The German Air Force has fired its new IRIS-T SLM air defense system for the first time at the NATO Missile Firing Installation on Crete, completing the operational certification the system needed before it can be relied on in German service, manufacturer Diehl Defence said this week.
Air Defence Missile Group 61, the unit based at Todendorf on Germany’s Baltic coast that operates the system, trained at the NATO range in October on linking the full fire unit together: the TRML-4D radar, the Common Tactical Operations Center command post and the launcher with its IRIS-T SLM interceptors. After the certification shot, the IRIS-T SLM was folded into a wider tactical exercise alongside German and Swedish Patriot batteries and German Stinger short-range missiles on the LeFlaSys light air defense vehicle.
“Without the soldiers of Air Defence Missile Group 61, this first firing of the IRIS-T SLM in Crete would not have been possible,” said Lt. Col. Björn Klarl, the group’s commander.
Diehl did not disclose what targets were engaged, how many missiles were fired or the results of individual intercepts.
“The successful system certification firing confirms that IRIS-T SLM delivers reliable performance and a very high hit rate in operation,” said Helmut Rauch, CEO of Diehl Defence.
The system can engage targets out to 60 km (37 miles) and up to 20 km (12 miles) in altitude, according to Diehl, and is designed to protect cities and critical infrastructure against cruise missiles and drones as well as aircraft and helicopters. It sits below Patriot in Germany’s layered air defense, covering medium-range threats while Patriot handles ballistic missiles and longer-range targets.
Ukraine has used IRIS-T SLM in combat since October 2022, when Germany delivered the first fire unit to Kyiv, and the system has since become one of the main tools Ukrainian forces use against Russian cruise missiles and Shahed-type attack drones. Rauch said ten nations now rely on the system, and Sweden, whose Patriot crews took part in the Crete exercise, decided to buy IRIS-T SLM in 2025.
Germany was slower to field the system at home. Berlin ordered six fire units in 2023, and the first was delivered in August 2024, but its entry into service was held up because an ammunition loading crane had not been certified to German standards, Defence Industry Europe reported. The Bundeswehr says Air Defence Missile Group 61 formally put the system into service only in February 2026.
The NAMFI range near Chania was set up under a 1964 agreement among several NATO members and has hosted live missile firings by allied air defense units since 1968, with crews from Nike Hercules and HAWK through to Patriot training there over the decades.

Plan unveiled to increase share of land farmed organically in England to 10%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:49:15 UTC
01:49:15 KST

The government has set an ambition to increase the share of English land farmed organically to 10% by 2036, but concerns remain over how the transition will be funded.
Currently, just 3.4% of England’s agricultural land is farmed organically, one of the smallest shares in Europe. France, for example, farms 10.4% of its land organically, and aims to increase this to 18% by 2027.
Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic veg box company Riverford, said it was a reflection of organic farming having political backing in the EU. Whereas in England, the last organic farming plan was published more than two decades ago.
The government’s new plan, which has been more than three years in the making, sets out a vision for growth in the organic sector, with public procurement – in schools and hospitals, for example – cited as a significant opportunity. The government already has a long-term ambition for 10% of public sector food spend to meet higher environmental production standards. The plan states that the organic sector can play a vital role in achieving this.
The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said the plan was about “opening up opportunities across the sector, from backing farmers already producing organic food to helping others decide whether it could work for their businesses”.
She added: “Organic farming should not be treated as a niche. More people are looking closely at where their food comes from, how it is produced and whether it meets standards they value.”
Haward said public procurement was “impenetrable” for small organic farms, but hoped the plan would be a “catalyst for growth”. However, he said the sector now needed proper backing from the government, including grant funding.
In September, thousands of farmers were left empty-handed after the government’s sustainable farming incentive 2026 (SFI) funding was spent in just six hours. This meant that some farmers who might have been planning to use the funding to transition to organic farming may have missed out.
“SFI needs to be reliable, successful and secure to enable this transition,” said Haward. “It’s hard for any farm to invest in their business if things change, we need some consistency.”
Gareth Morgan, the head of farming policy at the Soil Association, said there had been a lot of discussions with Defra about funding, but in the end “there has been a compromise”.
“There is now an urgent need to reopen SFI to enable farms to move to organic farming,” he said.
Morgan added that increasing the share of land farmed organically could bring down the price of organic food for consumers. “Currently the price of food is subsidised and we don’t pay for the environmental impact. If organic food becomes more mainstream, the price difference will become less,” he said.
Martin Lines, the chief executive of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, said farmers could not rely on government funding alone to make this transition, and said there needed to be “real investment from the supply chain and the private sector, along with fairer prices for farmers for their goods and stronger domestic markets for homegrown produce”.
The National Farmers’ Union, whose members include organic and non-organic farms, said the plan signified a “really positive step forward … for the wider supply chain”.
“Supporting domestic production will strengthen the resilience of our food supply chains and ensure British farmers and growers benefit from opportunities, rather than increasing our reliance on imports,” said Paul Tompkins, the deputy president of the union.
In the plan’s foreword, Eagle said: “Across England, organic farmers, growers and food businesses play an important role in producing high-quality food while caring for soils, wildlife and the rural communities they are part of. In doing so, they also help advance wider goals for nature recovery, cleaner water and greater climate resilience.”
This year has been challenging for farmers because of crop-destroying heat and drought alongside soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran. Organic farms have been found to be more resilient in the face of these extreme weather conditions and are also not affected by rising fertiliser costs.
“Organic farmers are much less exposed to these risks,” Morgan said, adding that the plan was a sign that the government was thinking hard about the pathway for food security.

'Unprecedented': Global Palestine movement vows to drive change

Breadcrumb
'We are driving change': Global Palestine movement hails growing influence worldwide
The global Palestine solidarity movement has reached unprecedented levels of influence, with growing public anger over Israel's genocide in Gaza putting governments under mounting pressure to translate support for Palestinian rights into meaningful political action.
Speaking exclusively to The New Arab, Global Alliance for Palestine (GAFP) secretary-general Anas Altikriti said the movement was gaining momentum worldwide, as hundreds of organisations mobilised across more than 80 countries to mark three years of Israel's war on Gaza.
"This momentum around the world that we've seen build and reach a level was never ever expected – totally unprecedented," he said.
But Altikriti warned that growing international recognition of Palestinian statehood would remain "superficial" unless governments adopted policies to hold Israel accountable for its actions.
"We saw how in late 2025, a catalogue of countries recognised the state of Palestine, how there were Palestinian embassies opened throughout the world – but we insisted then and we insist now that all of this is superficial if not followed with actual policies that first of all hold Israel to account and those who took part in the war crime that we saw and we witnessed."
His comments follow a three-day global solidarity campaign held from 9 to 11 October, which brought together pro-Palestine organisations and campaigners for demonstrations, vigils, cultural events and community gatherings.
The coordinated actions demanded an end to Israel's genocide in Gaza, its decades-long occupation, ongoing settler violence and settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, as well as accountability for governments accused of enabling Israeli war crimes.
Altikriti said the mobilisation reflected growing frustration not only with Israel's military offensives in Gaza, Lebanon and elsewhere, but also with the international community's failure to stop them.
"People are angry beyond what we've known in terms of the crimes committed incessantly and with impunity by Israel and the Israeli government. But also the silence and the tacit complicity of the entire world and here in the UK," he told TNA.
He also urged Britain's government under Prime Minister Andy Burnham to match its changing rhetoric on Israel and Palestinian rights with concrete policies.
"And whilst this new government under Andy Burnham has adopted a new narrative in regards with Israel and the Palestinian rights, we still need to see actual policies being put in place to reflect that kind of anger and frustration that the streets, not only of the UK, but the entire world, feel."
'Of course, we're vilifying Israel'
The growing international movement has also faced criticism from pro-Israel voices, including Israel's Foreign Ministry, which condemned GAFP's global campaign and highlighted a Fox News report describing the activism as "the protest playbook to vilify Israel".
Asked about the Israeli government's criticism, Altikriti responded defiantly.
"Of course, we're vilifying Israel," he said. “Israel is an occupying terrorist state. We made that proclamation time and time and time again, not just myself, not just the Global Alliance of Palestine, but countless Israelis who have themselves seen the poison that Israel creates, not only in Palestine, but throughout the entire world.”
Altikriti argued that Israel's own policies, rather than the activities of solidarity campaigners, were responsible for the growing international anger towards the country.
“The vilification has actually come from Israeli policies itself. Israel has created this. Israel has created the momentum that we see around the world. The anger that people feel, the questioning of American people as to why their tax dollars are being shipped to Israel for them to then kill Palestinian children.”
His comments come as pro-Palestine campaigners seek to sustain international pressure on governments over their diplomatic, military and economic ties with Israel.
Global solidarity reaches new heights
GAFP hailed its three-day mobilisation as a major success, saying it demonstrated the growing reach and influence of the international Palestine solidarity movement.
“Hundreds of organisations and campaigns in over 80 countries around the world do all sorts of activities, whether there are demos, marches, vigils, stands, flag waving or balloon settings,” Altikriti told TNA.
“We count this as a tremendous success, not only for ourselves, the Global Alliance for Palestine, but also all the activist groups and all the campaigns that took part in this, whether under our umbrella or whether independently, we regard this as being an inspiration from the people of Gaza.”
The campaign culminated in a Global Day of Action on Saturday, 10 October, when tens of thousands of pro-Palestine protesters marched through central London.
GAFP estimates that more than 250,000 people joined coordinated actions organised by established groups, including the Muslim Association of Britain (MAB), Palestinian Forum in Britain (PFB), Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC), Stop the War Coalition (STWC), Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) and Friends of Al-Aqsa (FoA).
The mobilisation came as Palestinians marked three years since Israel launched its devastating military assault on Gaza in October 2023.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then.
Despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025, which envisaged the eventual reconstruction of the devastated territory, little progress has been made towards implementing the agreement.
At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the so-called ceasefire took effect.

Netanyahu and Katz warn of PA attack, but security sources say no concrete threat, raising timing questions ahead of elections - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:44:52 UTC
01:44:52 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel
- Defense News
- Israel’s warnings of a PA attack shifts focus from the unresolved Hamas threat - analysis
Israel’s warnings of a PA attack shifts focus from the unresolved Hamas threat - analysis
Netanyahu and Katz warn Palestinian Authority forces could turn their weapons on Israel, but security sources report no concrete threat, raising questions about the timing ahead of elections
As Israel marks three years since the multi-front war launched by Hamas and other Palestinian terror groups on October 7, the various fronts remain open: the IDF continues to conduct near-daily strikes in Lebanon and in the Gaza Strip, where Hamas is still in power; Israeli forces are still deployed in Syria; and the Iranian and Houthi fronts are on pause, but far from resolved.
Last week, the Israeli public was suddenly presented with a new threat. "The IDF is preparing for a scenario in which the Palestinian Authority's security apparatus turns its weapons against Israeli settlers and IDF forces in Judea and Samaria and in communities along the Seam Zone," Defense Minister Israel Katz declared at the weekly cabinet meeting.
"In such an event, we will declare war against the Palestinian Authority, and the IDF will launch a full-scale offensive in accordance with a structured plan formulated and approved by Prime Minister Netanyahu and myself—based on the principles outlined for the IDF."
That's quite a bombshell. Just think about it: tens of thousands of armed Palestinian Authority security personnel deployed throughout the West Bank decide one day to launch an October 7-style attack on dozens of Israeli communities and military bases in Judea and Samaria. The results would be disastrous.
Yesterday, Netanyahu added his own warning. "Our enemies are considering testing us during this period leading up to the elections; we are prepared for any scenario, including a sudden turning of the guns. The IDF has presented a robust plan to me and the Ministry of Defense for such an eventuality; I would advise our enemies not to put us to the test," he said, speaking from the West Bank.
In a post-October 7 reality, Israel's security bodies must be prepared for any scenario, and it's good to know that the country's top leaders are aware of the threat. There is only one problem: there is no indication that such a threat exists. Security sources I've spoken with say the IDF has no intelligence pointing to such an attack, and Shin Bet sources told Israeli media they know of no concrete threat from the PA.
So why the sudden scare, when there is no apparent threat and Israelis have nothing in their power to do about it? There are other possible explanations, from instability within the PA to plain deterrence signaling. But none of them explain the timing. The public first heard of this new threat on October 6, the day before the anniversary of the worst security failure in Israel's history.
Talking about how Hamas is still in power three years after it massacred some 1,200 people and kidnapped 251 more, on their watch, is inconvenient, to say the least, for leaders seeking reelection. So why not shift the conversation to other armed Palestinians, who, apart from a few rogue security personnel, pose no actual threat to Israelis?
Beyond the political cynicism, presenting the PA security forces as an emerging threat is divorced from reality. As you read these words, PA security forces are helping protect Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria. Their contribution to combating Palestinian terror in the West Bank is minimal at best, but their presence and ongoing coordination with the IDF are a net gain for Israel's security.
Could they one day turn on Israel and endanger it? Potentially, yes, and Israel must be prepared for that, especially after October 7. But nothing points to it. The threat posed by Hamas, which is still in power and refuses to disarm, is very real. Talking about that two weeks before the first elections since October 7, however, is politically dangerous. It's far easier to inflate a new threat and divert attention from the failure in Gaza.

Colombia sees nationwide protests against De la Espriella's government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

01:44:14 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres and Laura Gamba
14 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Members of opposition groups, trade unions, Indigenous organizations and social movements took to the streets across Colombia on Wednesday in a widespread protest against the government of President Abelardo de la Espriella.
Authorities reported that demonstrations in some cities escalated into vandalism, roadblocks and clashes with security forces, leaving thousands of commuters stranded due to widespread traffic disruptions.
Law enforcement intervened in multiple cities, including Ibague, to clear blockades and restore order. Clashes erupted during police interventions, with social media footage showing altercations between officers and demonstrators. In one instance in Ibague, a man brandishing a knife threatened officers before being subdued and taken into custody.
Bystanders attempting to block arrests engaged in physical altercations with police officers, resulting in multiple detentions. While preliminary reports confirm several arrests across the country, law enforcement officials have not yet released an official national tally.
The unrest comes a day after President de la Espriella signed a controversial executive decree authorizing police to intervene immediately against violent acts during demonstrations, bypassing previously mandated stages of dialogue and mediation.
Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara confirmed that the government would enforce the new protocol during Wednesday’s national mobilizations.
“The right to protest is respected, but there is no right to destroy, attack security forces, assault others, or sow chaos,” De la Espriella said in a statement announcing the measure.
While the administration maintains that the decree protects peaceful assembly and enables swift action against vandalism and infrastructure blockades, civil rights groups and opposition leaders have questioned whether the rules infringe on constitutional rights to peaceful protest.
Demonstrators are demanding reversals of the administration's economic and social policies, advocating for labor rights, expanded funding for public education and stronger guarantees for civil demonstrations.
Teachers' unions are demanding better working conditions and health care. Student and Indigenous groups want greater protection of their rights.
Demonstrators also voiced opposition to the administration’s foreign policy pivot, specifically rejecting the restoration of diplomatic relations with Israel, which were severed under former President Gustavo Petro, and criticizing closer alignment with the US government of President Donald Trump, which critics view as a threat to national sovereignty.
The mobilizations marked a major test of opposition groups' capacity to challenge De la Espriella's administration.
Former President Petro urged Colombians to join the demonstrations, focusing on the minimum wage and rising food prices.
“If the real minimum wage falls, what we have is a decline in the standard of living of all Colombians,” Petro said in a video on the US social media platform X.

Palestine, Saudi Arabia, Jordan slam Colombia's opening of embassy in West Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:43:51 UTC
01:43:51 KST

Palestine has said that Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem violates international law and UN resolutions.
The Palestinian foreign ministry said on Wednesday the opening constituted “a flagrant violation of international law and relevant UN resolutions and an assault on the Palestinian people and their just and legitimate national rights.”
It stressed that all measures and decisions to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem are “null and void and have no legal effect".
It said that “opening an embassy to Israel in occupied Jerusalem violates international legitimacy resolutions, particularly UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478.”
The two resolutions that were adopted in 1980 affirm the illegality and invalidity of Israeli measures intended to alter the character and legal status of Jerusalem, amid Israel’s enactment of a law annexing occupied East Jerusalem.
The ministry said Colombia’s move also “undermines the international consensus on the city’s legal status and infringes on the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights.”
It warned that the step encourages Israel to continue its “colonial policies and attempts to impose illegal realities on the ground".
The Palestinian foreign ministry urged Colombia to comply with international law and respect relevant UN resolutions, calling on it to “reverse this step to preserve prospects for achieving a just and comprehensive peace.”
Jordan 
In a statement issued following the embassy’s opening, the Jordanian foreign ministry said the kingdom condemns and rejects the move.
The ministry stressed that any measures or decisions aimed at changing the status or legal standing of Jerusalem are “null and void, illegitimate and without legal effect.”
It said the only way to achieve a just and comprehensive peace is to establish an independent, sovereign Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967, lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry condemned and denounced the move, describing it as a “blatant violation of international law and relevant international resolutions.”
It said the move contradicts the established international position on Jerusalem’s legal and historical status.
Riyadh renewed its demand for the international community, including the UN Security Council and all concerned parties, to fulfil their “legal and moral responsibilities” and act urgently to halt “illegal Israeli policies aimed at imposing a new reality by force and undermining prospects for a just and lasting peace.”
Jerusalem remains at the heart of Israel’s dispossession of Palestinians and subsequent occupation of Palestinian lands and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel since 1967, as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.
