Tehran Auto Plaza seeks to turn the automotive world into a destination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:05:21 UTC
01:05:21 KST

Tehran Auto Plaza seeks to turn the automotive world into a destination
TEHRAN – For many motorists, a visit to a car showroom has a specific purpose: to inspect a vehicle, discuss a price and decide whether to buy. Tehran Auto Plaza is being developed around a broader idea, one in which the automobile becomes the starting point for a day of discovery, specialist services, social encounters and new experiences.
Introduced to the media on October 12, the complex is planned as a large-scale automotive destination, bringing together vehicle showrooms, specialist facilities, commercial outlets and spaces for activities beyond buying and selling cars.
The development is designed to accommodate approximately 90 showrooms, alongside workshops, vehicle-tuning facilities, parts and accessories outlets, and services related to vehicle care. Its broader program also envisages cafés, restaurants, shopping opportunities, family-oriented amenities and events intended to attract people whose interest in cars extends beyond ownership.
The idea is to create a place where visitors can encounter different parts of automotive culture in one setting. Some may arrive to explore new models or specialist equipment; others may be interested in vehicle customization, automotive technology, photography or events that bring enthusiasts together.
By combining commercial activity with opportunities for leisure and participation, Tehran Auto Plaza aims to establish a more expansive role for the automobile in the urban experience.
A destination on Tehran’s western edge
Situated along the Lashgari Expressway, which connects Tehran with Karaj, the development occupies a substantial site in the capital’s western corridor. The project materials describe an eight-hectare complex, while other published descriptions refer to a larger combined area for its commercial and service functions.
The layout is intended to distinguish the principal vehicle-display areas from much of the technical infrastructure. The upper section is planned to accommodate the showrooms, while the lower section is intended for workshops, spare-parts businesses, tuning facilities and related automotive services.
This separation gives the project an organizational logic: visitors can explore vehicles in a dedicated display environment while technical work and specialist activities take place in designated areas.
The scale is also central to the concept. Rather than presenting a single brand or a narrow category of vehicles, the development is intended to accommodate a variety of automotive businesses and services. That breadth could make it relevant to first-time buyers, experienced motorists, collectors, families and people simply curious about new developments in the car industry.
Its eventual character will depend on the mix of businesses that become operational and the range of activities available to visitors. Nevertheless, the plan points toward a destination that seeks to bring together commercial, technical and recreational uses rather than treating them as separate experiences.
More than a place to look at cars
The showroom remains the natural starting point, but it is not intended to define the entire visit.
The planned facilities encompass services for different stages of vehicle ownership, including maintenance, repairs, detailing, paintwork inspection, car washing, parts supply and customization. These activities address different interests: a motorist may need a routine service, while another may want to improve a vehicle’s appearance, upgrade its equipment or learn more about specialist products.
Detailing and vehicle-care services, for example, can appeal to owners who take particular care of their cars’ interiors and exterior finishes. Tuning and customization facilities offer another dimension, allowing motorists to explore equipment and modifications suited to their vehicles.
The inclusion of specialist outlets also has the potential to bring together customers and professionals who might otherwise operate in separate parts of the city. For enthusiasts, this could provide opportunities to discover products, compare approaches and exchange knowledge with people who share their interests.
A spare-parts hypermarket is among the facilities planned for the complex, adding a retail dimension to its technical offering. The intention is to make it easier for visitors to find components and accessories while accessing related installation or maintenance services.
The broader proposition is convenience, but also variety. A visitor who arrives with one particular task may discover services or products that were not part of the original plan for the trip.
Where technology meets automotive culture
Technology is another part of the development’s identity. In addition to the proposed automotive super app, the complex envisages opportunities to introduce new technologies, demonstrate specialist equipment and organize activities that bring visitors closer to developments in the industry.
A digital platform could complement the physical experience by helping users discover services, arrange appointments and access information before arriving. It could also help connect visitors with businesses operating within the complex, making it easier to plan a visit around specific interests.
The planned intelligent features and vehicle-related digital services form part of a wider effort to connect the physical and digital sides of automotive activity. For a visitor, this could mean exploring a product in person, obtaining information through a digital service and arranging a related appointment without having to begin the process again elsewhere.
Technology demonstrations and specialist events could give the complex an additional educational role. They may offer opportunities for customers to learn about new equipment, compare products and understand how technological developments are influencing vehicle use and customization.
The effectiveness of this approach will depend on the quality of the content and services provided. Digital tools are most useful when they make information easier to understand and help people take practical action. Similarly, technology events will be more engaging if they provide demonstrations and useful explanations rather than simply displaying products.
A meeting point for enthusiasts
One of the more distinctive aspects of the plan is the intention to host automotive gatherings and specialist events.
Car culture encompasses more than the purchase of a vehicle. It includes the design and engineering of automobiles, the restoration of older models, customization, photography, motorsport-related interests and the communities that form around particular brands or types of cars.
The planned events at Tehran Auto Plaza could provide a setting for these interests to intersect. Gatherings of enthusiasts, specialist presentations and displays of new equipment could encourage people to exchange experiences and become acquainted with developments beyond their usual areas of interest.
Such activities can also create opportunities for automotive businesses to meet customers in a less transactional setting. A product demonstration, technical presentation or themed gathering allows participants to explore an idea before making a purchase or committing to a service.
The proposed program includes events related to emerging automotive technologies and opportunities for brands to introduce products and developments to interested audiences. Test-drive experiences are also part of the wider concept being promoted for the destination.
For the complex, a regular calendar of events could help establish reasons to return after an initial visit. Instead of depending entirely on people who arrive to buy or service a car, it could attract visitors interested in a particular exhibition, demonstration or gathering.
The success of this approach will depend on the variety, organization and regularity of the events. A lively automotive destination needs more than physical space; it needs activities that give people a reason to use it.
A place for families and leisure
The inclusion of cafés, restaurants, shopping opportunities and recreational spaces reflects the project's intention to welcome a broader audience.
For families, these facilities could make a visit more comfortable, particularly when different members have different interests. Someone comparing vehicles might spend time in the showrooms while others take a break in a café or explore other parts of the complex.
For automotive enthusiasts, food and leisure facilities could encourage longer visits and make it easier to attend events or spend time with fellow enthusiasts. For casual visitors, they could help turn the complex into an accessible destination even when there is no immediate intention to purchase a vehicle.
This approach places greater emphasis on the experience surrounding the automobile. The car remains the central theme, but the visit can include dining, social interaction, browsing and entertainment.
The quality of the visitor experience will depend on practical details as much as on the range of amenities. Clear wayfinding, convenient parking, comfortable shared spaces and effective coordination between commercial areas will be important to making a large complex easy to navigate.
Parking is a particularly significant consideration for a destination of this kind, where visitors may arrive in their own vehicles and spend time moving between different facilities. Published accounts of the project describe substantial parking capacity, although the precise figures vary across reports.
If the planned amenities and circulation arrangements work together effectively, the complex could accommodate visits of different lengths and purposes, from a brief stop at a specialist outlet to a longer outing built around a vehicle display or event.
A platform for automotive media and content
Tehran Auto Plaza also envisages a role in automotive media and content production.
The proposed capabilities include professional photography and video production, specialist automotive content, press gatherings and events designed to introduce new products and technologies. These activities could create opportunities for journalists, photographers, filmmakers, reviewers and other content creators to work in a setting that brings different vehicles and automotive services together.
For media professionals, a concentrated range of showrooms and specialist facilities can offer practical advantages. It can make it easier to arrange vehicle photography, record product demonstrations, interview industry representatives and produce material about equipment or services.
The complex could also provide a setting for public-facing content that helps audiences understand technical subjects. Automotive journalism, for instance, can explore not only a vehicle’s design and features but also maintenance, safety, ownership costs and developments in technology.
A dedicated environment for media activities could encourage collaboration among businesses, technical specialists and content producers. It might also give automotive brands additional ways to introduce products to potential customers, provided that promotional material remains clearly distinguished from independent editorial coverage.
The proposed facilities therefore have the potential to support both commercial communication and more informative coverage of the automotive sector. The range and quality of the resulting work will depend on the resources made available and the relationships developed with media professionals.
Employment and business opportunities
Beyond its appeal to visitors, the complex represents an effort to concentrate a range of automotive businesses within one commercial environment.
The planned activities could create opportunities for showroom personnel, mechanics, technicians, parts specialists, vehicle-care professionals, sales staff, hospitality workers, event organizers and media-production teams.
The project’s management has estimated that it could generate more than 2,000 direct jobs, potentially rising to around 2,300 to 2,400, alongside thousands of indirect jobs. These are projections rather than verified employment outcomes, and their realization will depend on the number of businesses that become operational and the scale of their activities.
The concentration of different services could also encourage cooperation among businesses that have traditionally operated separately. A customer purchasing a vehicle, for example, might subsequently use a detailing service, obtain accessories or attend an automotive event at the same destination.
For smaller specialist businesses, being part of a larger complex could offer access to visitors who might not otherwise discover their services. For customers, it could provide a broader choice of providers and make it easier to explore related offerings.
The commercial model will need to balance the interests of the businesses operating within the complex with the expectations of visitors. A successful destination must offer a compelling reason to visit, while providing its occupants with a viable environment in which to operate.
Building a lasting identity
Tehran Auto Plaza enters the market with an ambition that extends beyond assembling showrooms and service outlets. It seeks to establish an identifiable destination around the automobile, bringing together commerce, specialist knowledge, technology, leisure and community activities.
That ambition will be measured by what visitors can actually experience once the planned facilities and programs are operating. The variety of vehicles on display, the quality of specialist services, the accessibility of shared spaces and the regularity of events will all influence whether the complex develops into a destination people choose to revisit.
Its appeal could ultimately lie in the combination of these elements. A place that allows motorists to explore vehicles, obtain specialist assistance, discover new products, meet fellow enthusiasts and spend time with family offers a different proposition from a conventional showroom.
Tehran Auto Plaza is setting out to create such a place on the western edge of the capital. If its commercial, recreational and cultural plans are delivered in a coordinated way, it could give Tehran’s automotive community a new meeting point and offer visitors a more varied way to engage with the world of cars.
The longer-term challenge is to turn the scale of the development into a consistent experience. Its success will depend not simply on how many businesses occupy the complex, but on whether the combination of services, activities and visitor amenities gives people a clear reason to make the journey and return.

U.S. blasts "embarrassing" complaint filed against Lebanon's ambassador
Washington — The Trump administration sharply criticized a legal complaint filed in Lebanon against the country's ambassador to Washington over her reported outreach to her Israeli counterpart, accusing Hezbollah-linked actors of seeking to obstruct U.S.-led efforts to foster diplomatic contacts between the two countries.
The complaint against Lebanese Ambassador Nada Hamadeh Moawad was filed with Lebanon's military judiciary by a lawyer the U.S. described as "pro-Hizbollah," in response to a report in Lebanese media that Moawad contacted Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter after his son was seriously injured in a car-ramming terror attack in the West Bank last month.
"It is embarrassing that a military court is handling a complaint against the Lebanese Ambassador in Washington for carrying out the policy of their legitimate government and engaging in U.S.-led negotiations," a State Department spokesperson told CBS News late Tuesday, in an unusually pointed statement.
The two diplomats have been participating in U.S.-brokered talks aimed at improving relations between Israel and Lebanon — an effort that has faced resistance from Iranian-backed Hezbollah. Lebanon and Israel held their first direct diplomatic talks in decades in Washington in April, with the Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors to the U.S. sitting alongside their American counterparts. Pictures of Secretary of State Marco Rubio with the ambassadors drew scorn from Hezbollah supporters in Lebanon.
"The Lebanese military judiciary should use its limited resources to prosecute Hizballah operatives plotting against the Lebanese government and people instead of working on their behalf," said the State Department official, who also called for the repeal of laws and practices that enable the "politicized targeting" of civilians and diplomats while shielding Hezbollah.
"We have no patience for obstruction," the official said.
That appeared to be a reference to a 1955-era anti-normalization law which was part of a broader Arab League boycott of Israel and prohibits any contact between Lebanese and Israeli citizens.
A diplomatic source told CBS News that the law is outdated and has become a tool used by Hezbollah to suppress those who seek peace and normal relations with Israel.
CBS News has reached out to the Israeli Embassy for comment.
It is unclear whether the complaint against Moawad will result in formal proceedings.
It comes amid a sustained push by the Trump administration to bring the longtime adversaries, still formally at war, closer together. In April, Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted the two ambassadors for direct talks, acknowledging at the time that the U.S. was working against "decades of history and complexities."
In June, the two countries signed a framework agreement meant to lay the groundwork for lasting peace, based on a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon alongside the disarmament of Hezbollah and deployment of Lebanese government forces. Implementation of the agreement has stalled amid disagreements over the sequencing and verification of those steps. The last formal round of talks, held in Rome in August, ended without a breakthrough.
The ambassadors met most recently at the State Department in September, and another round of negotiations is expected this month in Rome.

Done family took £30m dividend from Betfred before warning of job cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:03:10 UTC
01:03:10 KST

The billionaire Done family took a £30m dividend from their Betfred gambling empire, before warning that they would close hundreds of bookies and cut jobs if the government increases tax on high-street slot machines.
The chancellor, John Healey, is understood to be considering proposals to double machine games duty in the upcoming budget, a move that the Social Market Foundation thinktank has said could boost state coffers by up to £460m.
Industry figures, led by the Betfred boss, Fred Done, argue that such a move would result in the closure of vast swathes of the bookmaking and casino sector.
On Wednesday, Done was among industry signatories who signed a last-ditch letter to Healey, warning that the policy could trigger up to 1,470 betting shop closures, 34 casino closures and 15,900 job losses.
The plea, first reported by Sky News, came as Betfred’s holding company filed its accounts at Companies House.
The Warrington-based betting firm won a record £996m from British punters in the year to the end of March 2026, the accounts show, booking a pre-tax profit of £64m.
The strong performance allowed Betfred to pay its shareholders – mainly a series of trusts benefiting the Done family – an interim dividend of £30m, taking the value of shareholder payouts to more than £105m since 2022.
The money is understood to have been reinvested into other Done family businesses, including their burgeoning property empire.
Last month, Fred Done, who founded his first bookies in 1967 and went on to become one of Britain’s richest men, lamented that he “would not wish to be reborn” in the UK.
“They keep saying those with the broadest shoulders should be paying more tax,” he told the Financial Times. “Well, how broad do my shoulders have to be? We paid £400m in taxes as a family last year.”
The Done family, who are collectively worth about £3bn, remain the UK’s biggest taxpayers, according to the Sunday Times Tax List.
Of the £400m they are estimated to have contributed last year, £54m came from machine games duty (MGD), according to the accounts for Betfred Group Holdings Limited.
In theory, that sum would double if Healey follows through with plans to increase the duty rate from 20% to 40%.
However, Done has said such an increase would render hundreds of bookmakers unprofitable at a stroke, forcing him to close them and ultimately reducing the Treasury’s tax take. Casinos have also warned of mass closures.
It is not the first time that Done has threatened mass closures in response to government policy.
Since 2019, the company has threatened to close nearly 1,000 in response to higher taxes or tougher regulation, including the introduction of a £2 cap on fixed-odds betting terminals.
Over that time, the company’s bookmaking estate has shrunk from about 1,620 to 1,293, a decrease of nearly 330. The decline has coincided with a broader shift towards online gambling, with Fred Done appearing in TV adverts urging customers to visit betfred.com.
Campaigners supporting an increase in MGD have focused less on bookies and more on high-street slot machine venues known as adult gaming centres (AGCs), most of which are open 24 hours.
Amid a broader decline in high-street gambling, with the number of bookies steadily shrinking, AGCs have thrived thanks to lax planning and licensing laws, targeting deprived areas in particular for new shop openings.
Andy Burnham has been a vocal critic of AGCs. In August, the prime minister announced measures designed to make it easier for councils to block new venues.
However, some gambling industry figures have warned that AGCs are best-placed to survive a rise in MGD because they have lower overheads than casinos and bookies.
In theory, this means that a rise in the duty could even benefit the sector as rival machine operators retrench. Merkur, the UK’s second-largest AGC operator, has already bid for some of 132 shops that Betfred put up for sale earlier this year.
The Done family declined to comment.

Şahin Demir
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Yemeni government forces said Wednesday that 1,250 Houthi fighters had been “neutralized” during the “Dawn of Yemen” military operation on several fronts.
Yemeni Armed Forces spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said in a statement that government forces conducted 2,309 “precise and direct” strikes using warplanes, drones, field artillery, rocket launchers and sniper units.
He claimed the operations disrupted Houthi defensive lines, command-and-control centers, frontline positions and supply routes, allowing government forces to advance.
The spokesman said more than 460 military vehicles and other pieces of equipment had also been destroyed or damaged.
In the southwestern province of Taiz, government forces continued airstrikes and ambush operations targeting Houthi forces and reinforcements, according to the statement.
Al-Nazili urged residents in Houthi-controlled areas to keep their children away from recruitment campaigns and military positions, and reiterated an amnesty by Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi to fighters who lay down their weapons.
He also accused the Houthis of targeting civilian infrastructure and residential neighborhoods in Taiz.
The Yemeni army also said it captured five Houthi commanders west of Taiz province, including senior commander Akram Amer, who holds the rank of major general.
Separately, the Yemeni army said Tuesday that it had captured five Houthi commanders on the western front of Taiz city.
The 5th Presidential Guard Brigade said in a statement that its forces captured the commanders without providing details about the circumstances or timing of the operation.
The brigade released a video showing five people identifying themselves, but did not specify their positions within the group. Among them was Akram Amer, whom activists described as a senior Houthi commander holding the rank of major general, though his rank and position have not been independently confirmed.
The announcement came amid intensified fighting between government forces and the Houthis in Taiz, particularly on the western and southern fronts. The Dhubab, Hadharan and Jabal Han fronts west of Taiz city have witnessed heavy clashes in recent days, while government forces said they had repelled Houthi attacks and infiltration attempts.
On Monday, Qatar’s Al Jazeera television, citing sources in the government forces, reported that 81 Houthi fighters had been captured during clashes in the Dhubab area. The figure has not been independently confirmed.
The western fronts of Taiz are strategically significant because of their links to roads leading into the city, which has witnessed recurrent fighting between government forces and the Houthis for years.
The Yemeni government launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation earlier this month to retake Houthi-held areas, including the national capital, Sanaa. Government-aligned forces have since announced advances on several fronts, including around the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The operation has been backed by a Saudi-led coalition, which has intensified air operations against Houthi positions. The coalition said earlier this month that 100 fighter jets took part in one phase of the offensive and later announced that 136 military targets had been destroyed.
The escalation follows renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, including cross-border missile and drone attacks and intensified coalition airstrikes in Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognized government from the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened militarily in support of the government in 2015.

Listening to digital jazz might help people manage stress and regulate emotions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:00:19 UTC
01:00:19 KST

New research indicates that listening to digital jazz music through streaming platforms can help people manage their emotions and safely detach from daily stressors. The findings suggest that this specific genre promotes measurable changes in brainwaves and heart rates that support psychological relaxation. The study was published in Acta Psychologica.
Modern life often brings intense academic and professional pressures, especially in highly urbanized environments. To cope with this continuous stress, many adults turn to digital music streaming platforms to alter their moods. Using media to manage how you feel is known in psychology as emotional regulation. People can regulate their emotions in healthy ways, such as reframing a stressful situation, or unhealthy ways, such as suppressing their feelings entirely.
Researchers are particularly interested in a related concept called psychological escapism. This happens when someone temporarily unplugs from their worries by immersing themselves in a digital experience. While escapism is sometimes viewed as a negative habit of avoiding reality, it can also act as a protective mental break that prevents emotional overload. Jazz music, which often features fluid rhythms, improvisation, and a lack of lyrics, is uniquely suited to foster this kind of immersive mental state.
With the rise of automated streaming playlists, genres like lo-fi and ambient jazz have experienced a cultural resurgence. Listeners often rely on algorithms to feed them an emotional ecosystem tailored to their exact state of mind. Researchers wanted to understand how this modern habit of digital jazz consumption affects both the brain and the body.
Yuhao Tian of Shenyang Normal University and Xiaochen Zhang of the Shanghai Institute of Visual Arts focused their investigation on young and middle-aged adults in Guangdong Province, China. This region features a fast-paced economy and a high rate of digital media consumption. The researchers aimed to bridge a gap between the psychological habits of music streamers and the biological reality of how their nervous systems react to audio stimuli.
The researchers recruited 300 adults who regularly used music streaming apps to manage their moods. The participants provided data on their weekly listening habits, including how often they listened to jazz, their average listening duration, and their use of mood-based playlists. They also completed questionnaires designed to measure their emotional regulation skills and their tendencies toward psychological escapism.
The survey results revealed that adults who engaged heavily with digital jazz were better at stabilizing their moods. These frequent listeners favored adaptive emotional regulation techniques, such as rethinking their perspective on a problem, over simply burying negative feelings. Overall, engaging with digital jazz was highly associated with a healthy, restorative form of psychological escapism.
To see exactly what happens inside the body during this escapism, Tian and Zhang brought 50 of the participants into a laboratory setting. The researchers played standardized clips of digital jazz and control tracks, such as ambient or classical instrumental music. The songs had no lyrics and a controlled tempo to ensure the beat did not artificially skew the physical data. While the participants listened, the researchers recorded their brain activity using electroencephalography, or EEG.
The research team also monitored the participants’ heart rate variability and skin conductance. Heart rate variability measures the variation in time between heartbeats, which indicates how well the nervous system is managing stress. Skin conductance measures subtle changes in sweat gland activity, providing a metric for physical arousal. The lab tests showed that listening to digital jazz produced a distinct biological profile compared to the control music.
When participants listened to jazz, their brains showed increased electrical activity in the alpha and theta frequency bands. These specific brain waves are typically associated with a state of relaxed alertness and deep cognitive absorption. At the same time, the participants’ heart rate variability increased, and their skin conductance dropped. This combination of physical reactions points to a calmer autonomic nervous system and lower overall physical tension.
The researchers used statistical techniques to map the relationships between the survey responses and the laboratory metrics. This modeling suggested that the physical responses inside the nervous system partially mediated, in a statistical sense, the link between jazz engagement and emotional regulation. In other words, greater engagement with jazz was associated with calmer physical responses, which were in turn associated with better emotional regulation and greater escapism, though the cross-sectional design means these links cannot be interpreted as cause and effect.
Finally, the researchers conducted in-depth interviews with 22 participants to explore their personal experiences with jazz streaming. The researchers recorded and analyzed these conversations to identify common themes. They wanted to see how the biological data matched up with the subjective feelings of the everyday listeners.
The interviewees reported that digital jazz helped them distance themselves from their stressors without feeling entirely disconnected from the real world. One participant explained, “I never use jazz to get away with reality. It only puts a bit of distance between me and whatever is causing my stresses.” Many participants noted that jazz let their emotions come naturally without being forced into a specific mood.
Some individuals also mentioned that they felt emotionally safe relying on streaming algorithms. They trusted automated playlists to curate the right mood for them during moments of fatigue, reducing the mental effort required to select songs. Another participant noted, “When I feel overwhelmed, I find it work to select music. The algorithm has already been informed about the type of jazz that would pacify me.”
A few limitations should be kept in mind when interpreting the results. The study relies on cross-sectional data, meaning it captures a single snapshot in time. Because of this design, the researchers cannot prove that listening to jazz directly caused the improvements in emotional regulation. It remains possible that people who are already good at managing their stress are simply more drawn to jazz music.
The researchers intentionally recruited participants who already used music to relax, which might inflate the statistical associations found in the data. The study also did not account for baseline personality traits, starting stress levels, or broader musical preferences. Future research would need to track listeners over a longer period and test a wider variety of music genres to see if these benefits hold true across different populations.
The study, “Digital jazz and emotional regulation: A neuroaffective and streaming behavior analysis of psychological escapism,” was authored by Yuhao Tian and Xiaochen Zhang.

Beneath the surface: What Palestinians think about themselves and their future - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

After 48 years of living and working with Palestinians, there is a good chance that I know more Palestinians personally than almost any other Jewish Israeli.
I have spent much of my life in Palestinian homes, offices, universities, refugee camps, villages, and cities. I have known presidents, prime ministers, political leaders, academics, businesspeople, students, activists, and militants. I have negotiated with Hamas leaders and worked closely with Palestinians devoted to peace with Israel.
What follows is not scientific research. These are impressions accumulated over nearly five decades, shaped by thousands of conversations, personal relationships, and attempts to understand what lies beneath Palestinian political statements, slogans, and opinion polls.
Understanding what Palestinians think
My most important observation is that there is often a considerable gap between how Palestinians speak politically and how they live their lives. There is also a gap between the political identity Palestinians feel obligated to project and the questions they privately ask about their society, leadership, and future. I noticed this contradiction decades ago.
In Palestinian political discourse, words such as compromise and concession often imply weakness, surrender, or betrayal. Leaders who speak defiantly and insist on every Palestinian right without qualification may attract greater admiration than those who speak the language of moderation.
Yet many of the same Palestinians demonstrate remarkable moderation in their personal lives. They negotiate, compromise, and cooperate every day. Some of the harshest statements against Israel I have heard came from Palestinians who welcomed me into their homes, treated me as family, and maintained genuine friendships with Israelis.
This is not hypocrisy. For a people who have lived for generations without freedom, resistance is also the language of dignity. Compromise can sound like accepting injustice. Political defiance declares that Palestinians have not surrendered their national rights.
But the language protecting collective dignity can also prevent honest political discussion. Repeating familiar slogans becomes easier than questioning whether they still serve Palestinian interests.
I believe this is where Palestinian society finds itself today.
Traditional political strategies have failed to deliver their promises. Fatah promised diplomacy and negotiations would bring independence, yet its logo still displays rifles and a grenade, hardly symbols of peace. Hamas promised armed resistance would liberate Palestine.
Neither has delivered freedom. The Palestinian Authority has failed to establish accountable democratic government. Gaza has suffered catastrophic destruction, while the West Bank remains occupied and settlements continue expanding.
Palestinians know these realities better than anyone. But acknowledging failure is difficult when national identity has been built around the strategies being questioned.
Beneath the surface, many Palestinians are reassessing their political thinking. They are not questioning whether they deserve freedom but how freedom can be achieved. They are questioning the competence, honesty, and effectiveness of those claiming to represent them.
Consider armed resistance. Palestinian opinion polls have frequently shown substantial support for armed struggle. Israelis often interpret this as evidence that Palestinians prefer violence to peace.
But I wonder about the questions pollsters often do not ask. Would you personally pick up a gun and fight? Would you send your son to fight? Would you risk losing your home, your family, and everything you have built? I believe that support would decline dramatically, perhaps to only a few percent.
The difference between endorsing resistance as a principle and personally accepting its consequences is fundamental.
For generations, Palestinian political culture has celebrated sacrifice, steadfastness, and resistance. These values preserved national identity under extraordinarily difficult circumstances. But there is a difference between honoring sacrifice and asking whether further sacrifices will bring freedom closer.
Gaza has made that question unavoidable. The devastation following October 7 has forced a painful confrontation with political and military choices. Israel bears responsibility for its decisions and actions, but Palestinian leaders must also be accountable for theirs. If Palestinians deny that responsibility then they themselves are denying the political agency they demand.
I believe growing numbers of Palestinians recognize that killing Israelis will not bring liberation. Yet understanding what has failed does not automatically produce agreement about what should replace it.
There is also a profound crisis of representation, made worse by President Mahmoud Abbas's decision to postpone Palestinian elections for another year. The last legislative elections took place in January 2006 and the last presidential elections took place in 2005. An entire generation has reached adulthood without choosing its national representatives. Millions who were children or not even born when Hamas won are still judged for a political choice they never made. They have been denied the opportunity to choose differently.
The official explanations cite Israeli restrictions and difficult circumstances in Gaza, Jerusalem, and the West Bank. These are real obstacles, but if Palestinians must wait for ideal conditions before exercising their democratic rights, they may wait forever.
New political initiatives have begun emerging outside the Fatah-Hamas divide. Samer Sinijlawi's New Path electoral list collected 9,200 endorsement signatures when only 3,000 were required. The New Path is a Palestinian political party with peace with Israel at the top of its agenda. This demonstrates a willingness to organize around alternatives.
Young Palestinians want freedom from occupation but also want freedom from corruption, authoritarianism, and unaccountable leadership. They want to choose, challenge, and replace their representatives rather than inherit their parents' political loyalties. Palestinians cannot renew their national movement while mechanisms for political renewal remain closed.
Palestinians take enormous pride in their steadfastness, attachment to the land, and refusal to surrender their national identity. Remaining on the land, educating children, building businesses, developing institutions, and preserving communities are also forms of resistance. They may establish stronger foundations for independence than another cycle of violence.
Most Palestinians I know do not aspire to become permanent symbols of heroic sacrifice. They want ordinary lives with rights denied for generations: freedom of movement, personal security, political representation, economic opportunity, and national self-determination. They want normality without surrender.
This requires Palestinians to ask difficult questions. What kind of society do they want? What leadership do they deserve? What strategy can achieve independence? How can their national movement serve the people rather than political organizations?
Palestinians must answer these questions themselves. But their political thinking does not develop in isolation. Israeli policies and statements constantly influence Palestinian choices. When Israeli leaders declare that Palestinians will never have independence and that Israel will permanently control their land, they strengthen those arguing that moderation is useless. A Palestinian advocating negotiations must explain what those negotiations could achieve.
Imagine instead an Israeli leader saying: If Palestinians elect leaders genuinely committed to peace with Israel, they will find a genuine partner in Israel. Such a statement would not transform Palestinian society overnight. But it could strengthen Palestinians searching for alternatives to violence, failed negotiations, and the leadership of the past.
After 48 years, I remain convinced that Palestinian society possesses far greater capacity for pragmatism, moderation, and political change than its public rhetoric suggests. Political changes often begin quietly, in private conversations, family discussions, and questions younger generations ask their parents. But those changes must eventually find political expression.
The central question facing Palestinians is not whether they will continue struggling for freedom. It is whether they are prepared to redefine what that struggle should look like, what it should achieve, and who should lead it.
But there is another question: Will Palestinians be allowed to make those choices themselves? Palestinian freedom cannot mean only freedom from Israeli occupation. It must also mean freedom to choose, challenge, and replace Palestinian leaders.
Without both, there can be no genuine Palestinian political renewal. And without that renewal, the prospects for a different future between Israelis and Palestinians become even more distant.
The writer is the Middle East director of the International Communities Organization and the co-head of the Alliance for Two States.

Pleas filed in SC, Delhi HC against de-notification of Jantar Mantar as protest site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:59:39 UTC
00:59:39 KST

A petition has been filed in the Supreme Court against the de-notification of Jantar Mantar.
NEW DELHI: The Indian Youth Congress has moved the Delhi high court challenging the October 11 order de-notifying Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, while a similar plea has also been filed in the Supreme Court.A separate writ petition has challenged the move, arguing that shifting demonstrations to distant locations could undermine the fundamental rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression.The petition in the Supreme Court has been filed by advocate Swaty Singh, according to Live Law.
The application in the high court was filed by IYC president Uday Bhanu Chib on Wednesday in a pending petition over the denial of permission to hold the demonstration at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.The organisation has challenged a standing order issued by Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar on October 11. The order removed Jantar Mantar from the list of designated protest sites and named Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in east Delhi as alternative venues.Delhi Police said a detailed, revised standard operating procedure (SOP) governing protests at the three locations would be issued separately.
Advocate Roopesh Singh Bhadauria filed the latest application after amending the existing petition.
Delhi Police cites Supreme Court directions
During a hearing on October 12, Delhi Police told the high court that its decision to de-notify Jantar Mantar had been taken in accordance with Supreme Court directions.The police argued that the IYC's original plea had become infructuous after three alternative protest sites were designated. However, the High Court issued notice to the authorities on the request to reconsider the matter.The IYC's counsel told the court that the petition would be amended in light of the development, leading to the latest application.The dispute comes days after the Supreme Court, on October 9, asked the government to consider providing an alternative venue for peaceful protests in the national capital. The top court stressed that any such site should have basic facilities for demonstrators.The court was hearing a separate plea challenging proposed restrictions involving Metro stations and the cancellation of trains arriving in Delhi in view of a protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) against Kumar on October 10.
IYC says protest is a constitutional right
The IYC had approached the High Court earlier this month after Delhi Police rejected its request on October 1 to hold a demonstration at Jantar Mantar.In its petition, the organisation argued that the case raises questions about how police authorities can regulate the fundamental rights to freedom of speech and expression, and to assemble peacefully, guaranteed under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution.
“The proposed demonstration arises out of concerns regarding transparency, accountability and functioning of constitutional institutions, and was proposed as a peaceful exercise of the petitioner's right to freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms,” the petition said.The IYC had applied to Delhi Police on September 25, seeking permission for a peaceful demonstration involving around 100 to 150 people between October 1 and October 25.The organisation said it had agreed to follow all lawful conditions relating to security, traffic management, discipline and public order. However, its request was rejected, prompting the legal challenge.
Rajeev Singh is a Digital Content Producer with The Times of India. He covers politics, policies, defence, and conflicts for readers curious to know their implications. He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

The Russian-US deal on supplying Moscow’s diesel fuel to the American and global markets offers “many other” opportunities for bilateral cooperation, said a senior Russian official on Wednesday.
Speaking to journalists on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week, a three-day forum in Moscow, Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev said that his country will continue economic cooperation with the US.
“This involves not only the diesel deal but also many other opportunities for economic and investment cooperation with the US – opportunities that benefit Russia, the United States, and global markets alike,” he said.

He accused many of Russia’s “opponents” of trying to derail the diesel deal, adding that Moscow is in constant communication with the US on the signing of contracts for the deal, which could be signed in the “coming days.”
Last Friday, Trump unveiled a diesel supply agreement following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, under which Moscow agreed to provide fuel to the US and global markets.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the deal as a "gift" to Putin, warning that the easing of restrictions on Russian diesel exports could help finance Moscow's war effort.

Israel’s elections: Netanyahu wants more than victory; he wants to stop others from governing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:59:25 UTC
00:59:25 KST

Opinion polls in Israel tell us many things, but they do not tell the whole story. Sometimes Netanyahu’s bloc appears close to returning to power. At other times, the “change” bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot moves ahead.
But behind these changing numbers lies a more important reality: neither Netanyahu nor his opponents have an easy path to forming a government. This is where the crisis begins.
The problem is not just the number of seats. It is who can turn those seats into a government. Netanyahu knows that his bloc may not reach 61 seats. So his goal is no longer simply to win a clear majority. It is also to stop his opponents from building a majority that can govern. In other words, if he cannot govern, he wants to make sure that others cannot govern either.
This is the real political game.
Polls only offer a picture of the moment, but they cannot decide the final result. Some small parties are close to the minimum share of votes needed to enter parliament. If they cross that threshold, they may add several seats to Netanyahu’s bloc. If they fail, their votes will not translate into seats, changing the whole calculation. This makes figures such as Ofer Winter and smaller right-wing lists part of a wider struggle: will they enter parliament or fall short? And will they help Netanyahu or hurt him?
Netanyahu understands these details well. He manages the right like a chessboard. He wants to weaken rivals within his own camp, but he does not want their votes to go to waste. He wants to limit Ben-Gvir’s growing influence, but he does not want the right to lose valuable seats. He may attack certain figures today, then need them tomorrow to stop the change bloc from forming a government.
These are not ordinary elections. They are a battle for Netanyahu’s political survival.
But the most sensitive factor is not only the right. It is the Arab voter. If turnout among Arab citizens of Israel reaches 65 percent or 70 percent, the whole balance could change. Arab parties cannot form a government on their own. But they could prevent Netanyahu’s return or give the change bloc a chance to govern through direct or outside support.
This is why two numbers worry Netanyahu: the seats won by his Jewish Zionist opponents and the turnout among Arab voters.
If the change bloc cannot reach 60 or 61 seats without Arab parties, it will face a difficult question: will it dare to form a government that depends on Arab support? Or will it step back because it fears a campaign of hostility and accusations?
Netanyahu knows this weak point. The Israeli right has long used hostile messages against Arabs. Any government that includes an Arab party or even relies on its support from outside the coalition, would face fierce attacks from its first day: “an illegitimate government”, “a government supported by Israel’s enemies”, or “a government that puts security at risk”. This language is not new. But it could become even stronger in a tense political moment.
READ: Axios: Netanyahu discussed joint strike on Iran with Trump before Israeli election
Therefore, Netanyahu’s goal may be simple: to create a political deadlock. If he cannot govern, and Eisenkot or the change bloc refuses to rely on Arab support, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would then remain prime minister of a caretaker government. For him, that alone would be a gain.
But the danger goes beyond parliamentary calculations. There is a bigger question: will the elections take place normally? And will Netanyahu accept the results if he loses?
This question is no longer just political speculation.
Some voices in Israel have raised concerns about a scenario similar to 6th January in the United States: rejecting the results, making claims of fraud, mobilising supporters and challenging the legitimacy of the outcome. It may not happen in the same way. But the fact that people are discussing it shows how deep the political crisis has become.
There are also concerns about attempts to disrupt voting, especially in Arab towns. These could involve false information, AI-generated videos, or far-right observers creating tension at polling stations. Security warnings could also be used to frighten people away from voting. In a close election, large-scale fraud is not necessary to change the result. Reducing turnout in certain places may be enough.
This brings us to the role of the police. Trust in the police is already weak, especially among Arab citizens. Crime is widespread, people feel unsafe, and many have little confidence in the police’s ability to protect their communities. If the police are already distrusted in everyday life, what role will they play on a sensitive election day? Will they protect polling stations fairly? Or will they become part of the problem?
These questions make the coming elections a test for Israel’s entire political system. They are more than a contest between parties. Israel often speaks about its democracy. It now faces a simple question: can it manage a normal transfer of power if the result goes against its most powerful political figure?
Netanyahu has built his strength around the idea that he is the only person capable of governing. But he now faces a dilemma: he may be unable to form a government, while finding it difficult to accept someone else doing so.
His battle therefore has two sides: winning votes and deciding whose right to govern is accepted. He wants to present his own victory as legitimate, while portraying a government supported by Arab parties, or formed without his bloc, as a danger to the state.
This is the most dangerous point.
Democracy does not collapse only when elections are cancelled. It can also collapse when election results lose their meaning. It can weaken when Arab votes are treated as unacceptable unless they serve the right. It can break down when one side accepts the result only if it wins. And it can suffer when security becomes a permanent excuse to restrict political life.
Israel’s political situation does not mean that Netanyahu is finished. Nor does it mean that the change bloc has won. But it suggests a new period of political instability. No side has a comfortable majority. Arab voters could become decisive. Small right-wing parties could determine the future of the wider right. And Netanyahu may prefer political chaos to leaving power.
The real question, then, is not simply: who will win the election? The deeper question is: will Israel’s political system accept a result that Netanyahu cannot control?

Israel signs deal with US Pentagon to buy 12 advanced Boeing Apache attack helicopters for the IDF

Israel signs deal with Pentagon for 12 advanced Apache attack helicopters
Boeing’s Apache Echo helicopters are due for delivery early next decade, following government approval and several delays over Israeli budget constraints
Israel’s Defense Ministry and the US Pentagon signed an agreement Wednesday evening for the purchase of 12 advanced Boeing Apache attack helicopters for the IDF, following government approval earlier in the day.
The helicopters are scheduled for delivery at the beginning of the next decade. They will be the Apache “Echo” variant, which the ministry described as the helicopter’s newest and most advanced model.
Defense Ministry Director General Maj. Gen. (res.) Amir Baram instructed the ministry’s mission in the United States to sign the agreement after several postponements granted by the US administration at Israel’s request because of budget constraints.
The ministry said the agreement and its financing framework were developed jointly with American officials, with the effort led by its US mission and Budget Department. It thanked the US administration for its support and flexibility, saying the delays had allowed Israel to bridge funding gaps and proceed with the purchase.
Defense Minister Israel Katz described the acquisition as a key investment in the military’s future capabilities.
“The procurement of the Apache helicopters is a critical step in the IDF's force buildup, one that will strengthen its operational capabilities against a wide range of threats and contribute to the security of the State of Israel in the years to come,” Katz said.
He thanked the US administration and the Pentagon for their cooperation, as well as the Israeli officials who worked to overcome the obstacles to completing the deal.
Baram said the agreement was made possible by “creative solutions we developed together with our American partners, without compromising operational needs.”
He added that the ministry would pursue further agreements for military platforms, munitions and interceptors to support immediate readiness while advancing its force buildup plan for the coming decade.
Boeing Israel President Maj. Gen. (res.) Ido Nehushtan welcomed the agreement, saying the company would work closely with the Israeli government to supply the helicopters to the Israeli Air Force. He pointed to Israel’s selection of Boeing’s KC-46A refueling aircraft and its decision to acquire a second F-15IA squadron as further examples of the defense partnership.
Earlier Wednesday, the government approved an urgent telephone vote to redirect hundreds of millions of shekels earmarked for a five-year development plan for Arab communities toward accelerated defense procurement.
The draft resolution, submitted by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, covers funding for 2027–2029 and cites an “urgent need to expedite defense procurement.” Earlier reporting indicated that the funds were expected to support the Apache purchase.

Norway to provide over US$78m in additional economic aid to Ukraine
Norway will provide Ukraine with an additional 750 million Norwegian kroner (about US$78.5 million) to support the functioning of the state amid the full-scale war.
Source: European Pravda, citing a statement by Norwegian International Development Minister Åsmund Aukrust in an interview with VG
Details: Aukrust stated that the funds will help finance the salaries of public sector workers, social payments and infrastructure recovery.
The funding will be directed to the World Bank's SPUR 2 programme to support Ukraine. The Norwegian contribution will increase the amount of credit funds available to Ukraine.
Aukrust noted that every Norwegian krone contributed could secure approximately three kroner in loan financing for Ukraine. Thus, 750 million kroner (about US$78.5 million) could help raise over 2 billion kroner (about US$209 million) in loans.
The mechanism involves Norway providing the initial funding, with the World Bank using its credit capacity to raise funds on the financial markets, which are subsequently provided to Ukraine as loans.
The minister added that the war is being fought on the front line, but it is also fought every day by ensuring the functioning of society, guaranteeing that children can go to school, and ensuring that nurses treating the wounded receive their salaries.
Background:
- At the end of September, it emerged that Norway was increasing its financial support for humanitarian activities regarding Ukrainian children abducted by Russia, arbitrarily detained civilians and prisoners of war, announcing a new contribution of 25 million kroner (€2.3 million).
- It was also reported that Norway will allocate €90 million to the Ukraine Facility programme to promote reforms in the anti-corruption and energy sectors.

Ankita Bhandari case: 'VIP' question that has brought her parents to India Gate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:54:41 UTC
00:54:41 KST

The family’s demand is that the alleged VIP angle be investigated and that the appointment be halted until the probe is complete.
NEW DELHI: Nearly four years after the murder of 19-year-old Ankita Bhandari in Uttarakhand, questions over an alleged VIP’s role in the case have resurfaced following a controversial political appointment.The appointment of former BJP national general secretary Dushyant Kumar Gautam as Sikkim governor on Monday has prompted fresh outrage from Ankita’s family, who have named him as the alleged VIP in the case. Her parents are now protesting at India Gate in Delhi, demanding that President Droupadi Murmu halt his appointment until the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) completes its probe into the alleged VIP angle.“Dushyant Kumar should be behind bars... I earnestly request the Honorable President not to appoint Dushyant Kumar as governor until the CBI investigation is concluded,” Ankita’s father, Virendra Singh Bhandari, said in Delhi.
Her mother, Soni Devi, said the family was deeply hurt by the appointment and appealed to the President to intervene.“We were deeply pained when we heard the news on the 12th that he (BJP leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam) has now been named Governor.
I appeal to the Honourable President, who is herself a woman and will surely understand my sentiments, to halt the move to appoint this individual as Governor until the CBI investigation against him is concluded,” she said.
The appointment has triggered fresh political backlash, with the Congress accusing the Modi government of protecting Gautam instead of ensuring justice for Ankita’s family. The allegations against Gautam have not been established in court.
What did state government say?
The Uttarakhand government on Wednesday said its legal efforts had ensured that the accused in the Ankita Bhandari murder case remained behind bars, after a court once again rejected their bail applications. It cited the life sentences awarded to the convicts, the constitution of a Special Investigation Team (SIT) and the CBI probe ordered at the request of Ankita’s parents as steps taken to secure justice.The government said the accused were arrested within 24 hours of the incident coming to light, while a chargesheet of around 500 pages was prepared, incorporating evidence and statements from nearly 100 witnesses. It also said the prosecution had consistently opposed bail, ensuring the accused remained in custody during the trial. The case ultimately resulted in life imprisonment for the convicts.The state said it had changed the government counsel three times in response to the family’s demands and ordered a CBI investigation after Ankita’s parents sought one. It added that the family received financial assistance of Rs 25 lakh, while jobs were provided to Ankita’s father and brother.The government also criticised Congress leaders and other organisations for repeatedly raising questions over the alleged VIP angle. It said anyone with concrete evidence should present it to the investigating agencies or the court, rather than making public allegations. The government accused political leaders of attempting to politicise the case and mislead the public.
Congress questions appointment
Congress MP Pawan Khera questioned why Gautam had been appointed governor before the CBI investigation was completed. He alleged that the decision amounted to granting protection to a person facing allegations.“You granted them immunity. You aren't even waiting for the CBI inquiry. What is the pressure to wrap this up so quickly? Who are you shielding? Is there anyone else you need to protect? Who is being blackmailed here—forcing you to appoint someone as a high-ranking official just to grant them immunity? Why risk everything?” Khera said.He accused the government of siding with the person facing allegations rather than the victim’s family.“The very people who are supposed to deliver justice are not standing with the victim. They have sided with the accused—the person facing the allegations...” he said.

Why is the VIP angle still under investigation?

Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee president Ganesh Godiyal alleged that the CBI had made no meaningful progress and had not registered an FIR against the person named by Ankita’s parents. He also announced a one-hour silent fast in Dehradun to protest Gautam’s appointment.The family’s demand is that the alleged VIP angle be investigated and that the appointment be halted until the probe is complete. The allegations against Gautam remain unproven.
Ankita, 19, worked as a receptionist at Vanantra Resort near Rishikesh. She was murdered in September 2022, and her body was recovered from the Cheela canal on September 24.The case involved allegations that she was pressured to provide sexual favours to guests at the resort, which was run by Pulkit Arya, the son of a former BJP leader.Resort owner Pulkit Arya, manager Saurabh Bhaskar and another accused, Ankita Gupta, have been sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder.However, the convictions did not end demands for an investigation into the alleged VIP angle. The registration of an FIR against an unidentified VIP in January 2026 brought renewed attention to the case.Gautam’s appointment as Sikkim governor has now prompted Ankita’s parents to take their demand to India Gate, urging the President to halt the appointment until the CBI investigation is concluded.

Palestine says Colombia’s opening of embassy in West Jerusalem violates international law

Palestine said Wednesday that Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem violates international law and UN resolutions.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry said the opening constituted “a flagrant violation of international law and relevant UN resolutions, and an assault on the Palestinian people and their just and legitimate national rights.”
It stressed that all measures and decisions to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem are “null and void and have no legal effect.”
It said that “opening an embassy to Israel in occupied Jerusalem violates international legitimacy resolutions, particularly UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478.”
The two resolutions that were adopted in 1980 affirm the illegality and invalidity of Israeli measures intended to alter the character and legal status of Jerusalem, amid Israel’s enactment of a law annexing East Jerusalem.
The ministry said Colombia’s move also “undermines the international consensus on the city’s legal status and infringes on the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights.”
It warned that the step encourages Israel to continue its “colonial policies and attempts to impose illegal realities on the ground.”
In addition to Colombia, the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, Fiji, Nauru and Somalia’s breakaway region have moved their embassies to West Jerusalem or opened embassies in the city, a move that runs counter to international resolutions concerning the status of Jerusalem.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry urged Colombia to comply with international law and respect relevant UN resolutions, calling on it to “reverse this step to preserve prospects for achieving a just and comprehensive peace.”
Earlier Wednesday, Colombia opened the embassy in West Jerusalem. The move follows the restoration of its diplomatic relations with Israel in August, after Colombia severed ties with Tel Aviv in May 2024 under a previous government.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel since 1967, as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.

Hidden for 7,000 years: the enigmatic skeleton from Großköllnbach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:51:07 UTC
00:51:07 KST

Was the Stone Age teenager laid to rest in a twisted pose on purpose, or did the body slip in a sloping grave?
Sometimes a dark discolouration in the soil is enough to open a window onto a long-forgotten world. In the Lower Bavarian village of Großköllnbach (Dingolfing-Landau district) just such a clue led to a discovery that is posing new questions for archaeologists: in a pit they uncovered the remains of a person who lived around 7,000 years ago.
But it is not just the great age of the find that makes it remarkable. Above all, it is the unusual position of the skeleton: unlike the burials that were customary at the time, the body lies in a striking, twisted posture. The condition of the cervical spine is also puzzling researchers.
A burial that breaks the mould
The discovery came to light during archaeological investigations in the future Steigäcker IV development area. The excavation team had been examining the site for five weeks when what initially appeared to be a nondescript change in soil colour turned out to be a pit containing human bones.
For district archaeologist Dr Florian Eibl, it is above all the type of burial that is unusual. The people of the Linear Pottery culture (Linienbandkeramik), one of the earliest farming cultures in Central Europe, often buried their dead in crouched burials. The deceased were laid on their side with their legs drawn up, in a posture resembling a sleeping person.
In Großköllnbach, however, the picture is different: the dead person's right leg was bent up extremely sharply, while the left leg was angled outwards. This posture clearly departs from the usual burial practices.
The pit itself also raises questions. Its base was uneven and sloping. In the archaeologist's view, the body may have slipped down the incline after being laid to rest. Individual bones could therefore have shifted or been pressed into the soft clay.
Was the unusual posture therefore intentional? Or did it only arise because of the conditions in the grave?
A young person with striking bones
One thing is clear from the initial examinations: the dead person was an adolescent, as shown by the growth plates on the bones, which had not yet completely fused.
Bones can also provide clues to diseases, injuries and physical strain. The experts are currently paying particular attention to the cervical spine, where a pronounced deformation can be seen. Whether this is due to an illness or a physical peculiarity during life, or only arose because of the position in the grave and after death, still has to be clarified.
A detailed anthropological analysis is expected to provide further clues.
Discovery among clay ovens and age-old longhouses
The skeleton is not the only remarkable find on the site. The excavations are bringing to light an extensive settlement landscape of the Linear Pottery culture. This culture emerged in the 6th millennium BC and marks the spread of the first farming way of life across large parts of Central Europe.
After five weeks of excavation the archaeologists had documented around 150 features. The traces of three large longhouses can be seen in the ground, although at most two of them are likely to have stood at the same time.
Particularly revealing are several preserved hearths and cooking areas, including domed clay ovens whose floors were insulated with tightly packed pebbles. This is where food was cooked, grain was processed and, in all likelihood, an important part of communal life was organised.
Grinding slabs were also discovered. In the archaeologists' view, the stone used for them may have come from areas beyond the Danube or the Bavarian Forest. If this origin is confirmed, the finds would indicate that even the early farmers were procuring and transporting materials over considerable distances.
What happened 7,000 years ago?
The excavation site is not open to the public. The skeleton has now been completely recovered and taken to the district archaeology department for further examination. There the bones are to be studied anthropologically. Only then will it be possible to say in more detail what traces this young person’s life has left, and which questions may never be answered.
Once the scientific investigations have been completed, the district archaeology service intends to share further findings.
Until then Großköllnbach remains a place where the soil reveals not only the traces of an ancient settlement but also the story of a person whose final resting place still poses riddles even after seven millennia.

Europe risks triggering major war if it accepts Russia’s terms, expert warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:50:00 UTC
00:50:00 KST

Europe risks triggering major war if it accepts Russia’s terms, expert warns
Olena Davlikanova, an expert in democratic governance, security policy and strategic forecasting and a senior associate analyst at the Sahaidachnyi Security Center, said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
In her view, the lack of a coordinated and consistent European position toward Moscow remains one of the key risks.
“Europe does not have a common, fully coordinated, rock-solid position on Russia. There are too many forces that want to restore cooperation and return to business as usual, and the risks of this are very high,” she said.
Davlikanova believes European countries must be prepared for Russia to test NATO’s ability to act under Article 5 – not necessarily through a large-scale military invasion, but through a series of coordinated hybrid attacks, including sabotage, cyberattacks and “massive aerial terror.”
She also did not rule out a limited incursion into the territory of a NATO member state, most likely one of the Baltic countries, and the seizure of one or two cities. Moscow could use such a scenario to try to demonstrate that the Alliance is incapable of acting in accordance with the principle of collective defense.
In her view, the main danger is that Ukraine could become a bargaining chip in such a situation. Under this worst-case scenario, Russia would play the “nuclear card,” and some European governments might then say, “Let us talk to Russia; let us negotiate.” Russia, in turn, could respond: “Fine, we can withdraw our troops, but then you must stop helping Ukraine.”
“At that point, if this happens, Europe will open the door to a major war itself,” Davlikanova said.
She stressed that the war is not about Donbas, or even Ukraine or Kyiv. It is about restoring Russian influence in Europe.
Davlikanova also noted that although NATO has significantly evolved in its understanding of modern warfare since 2022, changes to military doctrines, training approaches and exercises are progressing slowly.
She cited the experience of Ukrainian military personnel who take part in exercises and play the role of the simulated adversary. Their experience indicates that some NATO units are still not fully prepared for “War 5.0” – warfare involving integrated systems and technologies. The expert added that instructions written behind a desk and experience gained on the battlefield are two different things.
She also pointed to the slow pace of decision-making in European institutions, describing it as “the greatest vulnerability.”
As reported, Swedish Defense Minister Pål Jonson recently said that Europe had little time left to prepare for a new war with Russia.

Pope Leo’s recovery from a lung cancer operation is progressing as planned, his doctors have said, as the pontiff received good wishes from around the world, including from Britain’s King Charles.
Leo, who had a cancerous mass removed from his right lung late on Tuesday, began walking in his hospital room after respiratory therapy on Wednesday. He was eating normally, his doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritoria said in a statement issued by the Vatican.
A blood test and chest X-ray showed “normal post-operative progress” and the results were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”, they said.
The operation at Rome’s Gemelli hospital confirmed that Leo, 71, has the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma. The Vatican has not yet disclosed the results of further tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.
The cancer diagnosis for Leo, who was elected as the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church in May 2025, has come as a shock.
In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, the pope announced during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup and that it was “well-contained” and had been detected early.
Messages have been sent from around the world. King Charles, who is also being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer, would write to Leo privately, a source told Agence France-Presse. Charles and Queen Camilla met the pope when they travelled to the Vatican in October last year.
Donald Trump, the US president, said: “I want to see Pope Leo get well. I just want to wish him well, get better fast.”
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, wished Leo a full and swift recovery in a message posted on X and said the pontiff was “a source of hope and inspiration for billions around the world”.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said he and his wife, Jeanette, were praying for Leo. The couple met the pontiff at the Vatican in May.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, wrote on X that Leo’s serenity and strength were an inspiration for all. “We hope for his full and speedy recovery,” she wrote.
Before the operation, all of Leo’s appointments until 20 October were cancelled. He went on a papal trip to France in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.
