Thousands of supermarket fridges still exposed after cyberattack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:42:18 UTC
00:42:18 KST

No group has claimed the attack, and experts warn thousands of similarly exposed devices remain online as a separate incident disrupts Dutch grocer Albert Heijn.
French investigators are searching for the hackers who took over refrigeration units at at least 350 supermarkets, forcing staff to throw away spoiled meat and frozen food.
Stores belonging to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché and Coopérative U were among those hit when attackers manually overrode fridge temperatures. The affected stores are a small fraction of France’s supermarkets.
The lack of a ransom demand or claim of responsibility has puzzled investigators, according to a source with knowledge of the probe cited by Reuters. Criminal and hacktivist groups usually move quickly to profit from or publicise their attacks.
France’s cybersecurity agency said the breach affected fridges running software from Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell systems.
Reuters reported it found at least 4,500 Danfoss interfaces visible online on Tuesday, and scanning firm Onyphe said outdated versions were "still widely represented among publicly accessible interfaces".
Danfoss said many affected units had "reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates" or were "running outdated firmware". Serious flaws in older versions of its firmware were detailed in August by security firm Claroty and have since been patched.
Copeland, which owns Dixell, acknowledged the "vulnerability", saying: "We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk."
"This is about basic cyber hygiene," Ken Munro, a partner at British firm Pen Test Partners, told Reuters. "Get it wrong and you get a smelly mess of defrosted food."
He said the attack could be "kids messing around". "If this was a nation state, why affect only a subset of French fridges? There are plenty of other nations with fridges on the internet," he said.
Dutch disruption
In the Netherlands, Ahold Delhaize, which owns Albert Heijn, said it had begun a controlled restart of systems after a cybersecurity incident that started on Sunday. The Dutch cybersecurity watchdog NCSC said it saw no link to the French attack.
Dutch broadcaster NOS reported that Albert Heijn had identified servers in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey used in the attack. NOS stressed this reveals nothing about where the hackers are, as traffic is easily routed through other countries.
Security specialist Pim Takkenberg told NOS the servers were probably used to scout the systems or try to steal data.
NOS also reported that the incident exposed how thin food stocks are. Shops and distribution centres hold around six days’ supply between them, replenished continuously by just-in-time IT systems that can fail and depend on the power grid.
A report by Clingendael and Erasmus University last month advised households to keep eight days of emergency food rather than three. It found that severe weather combined with a major power and IT outage could take two weeks to recover from.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Video footage appears to show mobile fire teams standing on elevated platforms with Verba and Igla man-portable air defense systems, or MANPADS.
Unlike fixed firing positions, the aerial lifts can be moved quickly to areas where Russian forces expect drones to approach.
Once deployed, the platforms raise missile operators above surrounding buildings, trees, and other obstacles, potentially giving them a clearer line of sight and a wider field of fire against low-flying targets.
Similar footage had previously surfaced showing a Russian serviceman armed with a MANPADS standing on one of the elevated platforms, suggesting the concept has moved beyond an isolated experiment.
At the same time, VChK-OGPU claimed that fewer Pantsir air defense systems are now visible at fixed positions around Moscow, including some of the units previously installed on building rooftops.
The channel suggested that those static deployments may have proven less effective than expected against Ukrainian drone attacks, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed.
Moscow is already protected by one of Russia’s densest layered air defense networks. The system includes Pantsir-S1 gun-and-missile complexes, S-400 long-range air defenses, and shorter-range Tor systems, supported by more than 100 prepared positions around and within the capital.
Russia has also constructed dozens of towers and other dedicated structures around Moscow for air defense equipment, as Ukrainian long-range drones have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to reach the capital and its surrounding region.
Tonight, nearly 500 Ukrainian attack drones reportedly targeted Moscow and the surrounding region, in what Russian state media described as one of the largest drone attacks on the Russian capital in the past two years.

Mont Blanc rises by almost two metres, now standing at 4,807.47 metres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:39:46 UTC
00:39:46 KST

An altitude that "is close to the historical value" measured at the end of the 19th century, but still not enough to draw conclusions about the effects of global warming.
Mont Blanc has grown higher. The tallest peak in Western Europe now stands at 4,807.47 metres, almost two metres more than in 2023.
An altitude that "is close to the historical value" recorded at the end of the 19th century, according to expert surveyors in Haute-Savoie who have been regularly measuring the summit since 2001.
However, they are urging caution: this "one-off" reading does not allow any conclusions to be drawn about the effects of global warming. Mont Blanc's elevation varies with the weather, in particular precipitation and winds that shift and redistribute the snow at the summit.
"Today, the summit is really shaped by the force of the winds and by precipitation, even though this year has been particularly dry," explains Mathieu Dragon, a chartered surveyor in Haute-Savoie.
A new technique to study the summit
This year, to refine their observations, the surveyors used ground-penetrating radar to map the ice cap and the rocky peak beneath it.
The data collected will help refine their measurements and track how the roof of Western Europe changes over the coming years.

French Far-Right Leader Marine Le Pen Threatens to Cut Support for Ukraine if Elected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:39:38 UTC
00:39:38 KST

- Category
- World
French Far-Right Leader Marine Le Pen Threatens to Cut Support for Ukraine if Elected
Marine Le Pen has cast doubt on whether France would continue backing EU funding for Ukraine if she wins next year’s presidential election, the Financial Times (FT) reported on October 14.
Le Pen, who is leading in opinion polls, has already pledged to end bilateral financial assistance to Kyiv apart from some operational support and training for Ukrainian soldiers, arguing that France can no longer afford it.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Le Pen had previously been barred from running for public office after a French court convicted her over the misuse of European Parliament funds. That ban no longer prevents her from running in the 2027 presidential election.
Le Pen indicated that, if elected president, she could oppose further EU financing for Ukraine if it required additional French spending, the Financial Times reported.
“The honest thing to do with Mr. Zelenskyy is to tell him, to warn him in fact: listen, we can’t do more, we can’t manage more,” Le Pen told the FT.
She pointed to the EU’s €90 billion ($100.7 billion) loan package for Ukraine, arguing that France’s share amounts to €18 billion ($20.1 billion).
“We’ve already done €90 billion of loans, that’s €18 billion for France. €18 billion is really a lot,” she added.
The EU’s draft seven-year budget includes a dedicated Ukraine financing instrument worth up to €100 billion ($111.9 billion). Le Pen has also threatened to block an agreement on the wider EU budget by withholding half of France’s contribution, FT wrote.
Le Pen maintained that she supported French financial and military assistance to Kyiv after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022 and reiterated her “absolutely total condemnation” of Russian aggression.
She nevertheless reaffirmed her opposition to Ukraine joining the EU, describing membership as “hara-kiri” for France because of what she characterized as a loss of sovereignty and major economic costs.
Asked whether Russia represented the principal security threat to Europe, Le Pen responded: “You know, I can’t read Mr. Putin’s mind and I don’t know his plans.”
France has meanwhile been moving toward deeper military support for Ukraine. Earlier this month, Paris began preparations to train Ukrainian pilots on Rafale fighter jets, with an initial batch of 16 aircraft agreed and plans eventually extending to 100 jets.

Israeli signs deal to purchase 12 Apache helicopter from Boeing after $1B budget cut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:39:20 UTC
00:39:20 KST

Israel has signed a deal to purchase 12 advanced Apache attack helicopters from U.S. aerospace company Boeing for the IDF, after the government approved an allocation of 1 billion shekels (about $323 million)  to the Defense Ministry in a telephone vote.
Defense Ministry Director-General Maj. Gen. (res.) Amir Baram instructed the ministry's delegation in the United States to sign the agreement with the Pentagon following the government's approval on Wednesday. The deal was finalized after the Defense Ministry requested and received several extensions from the U.S. administration because of Israel's budgetary constraints.
The helicopters, scheduled for delivery early in the next decade, will be the AH-64E Apache Guardian, also known as the Echo model, the latest and most advanced version of the aircraft.
The agreement was tailored through a joint Israeli-American effort to meet Israel's operational requirements while addressing the complex budgetary challenges facing the country. The Defense Ministry's delegation in the United States and its Budget Department led negotiations on the agreement and developed the financing arrangement.
The funding will come from postponing Defense Ministry payments on other procurement deals. The reduction in future years' budgets is a technical accounting measure required by the Finance Ministry to enable the agreement to be signed.
Defense Minister Israel Katz welcomed the agreement, describing the acquisition as an important investment in Israel's military capabilities.
"The procurement of the Apache helicopters is a critical step in the IDF's force buildup, one that will strengthen its operational capabilities against a wide range of threats and contribute to the security of the State of Israel in the years to come," Katz said.
"The Israeli defense establishment invested considerable effort and acted with determination to overcome the challenges and complete this agreement, out of a deep understanding of its importance in ensuring the IDF's strength and readiness for future challenges. I thank our partners in the U.S. administration and the Pentagon for their steadfast commitment to Israel's security, and for the cooperation and flexibility that made this agreement possible."
Baram said the deal was made possible by financing arrangements negotiated with the United States that addressed the Defense Ministry's budgetary limitations without compromising operational requirements.
"“The execution of the Apache agreement was made possible thanks to creative solutions we developed together with our American partners, without compromising operational needs," Baram said. "This professional work with the U.S. administration reflects the depth of our strategic relationship and the mutual commitment to Israel's security."
Baram added that the Defense Ministry would continue working to finalize additional major procurement agreements.
"The Defense Ministry will continue working at full pace to sign additional critical agreements, including the acquisition of additional platforms, munitions, interceptors and more," he said. "This is to ensure immediate readiness for any scenario, alongside the implementation of the decade-long force buildup plan, as part of the IMOD's strategy in the face of emerging challenges."

Mexico to require digital platforms to shield minors from harmful content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:39:00 UTC
00:39:00 KST

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Wednesday she would sign a decree requiring social media and streaming platforms to protect children and teenagers from violent, sexual and other potentially harmful content.
The decree, which will step up scrutiny of big technology companies in Latin America's second-largest economy, comes after an attack by two 18-year-old former students on a high school in the northern state of Coahuila in early October left one person dead and wounded three others.
Digital platforms will have one month to come into compliance with the decree, government adviser Luisa Maria Alcalde said.
Sheinbaum added that if companies failed to follow the decree, the government would back a bill to punish platforms.
Officials said they had already met with representatives of Meta, Microsoft, Apple, TikTok, Google, X and Huawei to discuss the matter. Those companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Mexico's move follows a broader global push to protect minors online, with governments in Europe and Australia tightening oversight of digital platforms and US states pursuing a range of child-safety measures.
Brazil has also moved to strengthen protections for children online. Such measures have raised questions over how to protect minors while safeguarding privacy and freedom of expression.
(Reporting by Raul Cortes and Diego Ore; Editing by Aida Pelaez-Fernandez, Anthony Esposito and Joe Bavier)

That Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything is a big help to the PM | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:36:12 UTC
00:36:12 KST

Little things please little minds. And minds don’t come much smaller than some of those in Westminster. If a researcher had come up with a study that showed one element two points higher in value than countless other experiments, it would almost certainly be marked down either as an outlier or “within the margin of error”. At the very least, no conclusions would be drawn until many other experiments had been conducted which had produced similar results. Serious scientific journals would just laugh at you if you asked them to publish your findings.
And yet. In one – just one out of many – recent opinion poll, the Tories have increased their ratings by a couple of points and are now for the first time in years in second place, ahead of Reform. And all of a sudden, Kemi Badenoch is insisting this is incontrovertible proof that the Tories are back in business. All the sins of its 14 years in government have been wiped clean. All hail to Kemi, the new chief. She is the chosen one. And the Conservatives are a government-in-waiting.
You need a certain amount of self-confidence to make it as a party leader. Not to say a touch of the Panglossian. The ability to insist all is well when it is turning to shit. But you can have too much of a good thing. You must at least be within touching distance of reality. And it appears that once again Kemi has jumped the shark. The one good poll has gone to her head and she now believes she is invincible. Nothing can touch her narcissism.
In her early days as Tory leader, Kemi used to crash and burn every week at prime minister’s questions. She considered preparation and research to be beneath her. Instead, she peddled the latest conspiracy theories she had seen on X with a series of scattergun questions. She only started to improve when her minders tried to get her to concentrate for 10 minutes of sustained questions on one subject. Yet over the conference break, Kemi has undergone a brain wipe. She is back in her happy space of making it up as she goes along. No one knows better than Kemi.
Sadly for the Tory leader, Kemi’s approach is also Andy Burnham’s happy place. Much more of this and the prime minister is going to look forward to his Wednesday lunchtime encounters in the Commons. Never look an easy win in the eye. Not because he’s word perfect – there are still a lot of unanswered questions about his involvement with the Manchester City owners – but because there’s an engaging openness to him you seldom find in other politicians. A willingness to answer the questions and to appear as if he’s listening. Mr Congeniality.
It’s also a big help to Andy that Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything. Arguments are always so much simpler when your opponents are deluded. Indeed you couldn’t escape the irony of her insisting that it was Burnham who was consistently mistaken about everything. Even the head of MI5, Ken McCallum, had slapped the prime minister down for suggesting hostile actors had interfered with the Brexit referendum. Kemi can’t bear the fact she might have had the backing of the Russian state in 2016.
Burnham chose to respond to Kemi in the most hurtful way. With kindness. No anger. Just a gentle reiteration of the facts. It was incontrovertible that Russia had tried to influence both the 2019 general election and the EU referendum. The evidence was in front of our eyes. Russian bots selling misinformation all over social media. It was a non-story. And far from correcting him, McCallum had gone out of his way to confirm this.
What the MI5 boss had gone on to say was that it would be better for everyone concerned if we all just dropped the story as it would only give the Russians further encouragement. And who had been keeping the story alive for a third day by bringing it up at PMQs? Take a bow, Kemi. The Tory leader seemingly content to carry on doing the Russians’ dirty work for them. At least Nathan Gill, Reform’s former leader in Wales, had the sense to get paid for this. Kemi was doing it for free. Andy ended by saying he would be delighted to debate whether Brexit had done more harm than good. Kemi shook her head. This isn’t an argument the Tories are keen to have. Their feeling is Brexit is something we all just have to suck up.
After that, Kemi looked a bit lost. Clueless. Scouring her file for something to ask. Instead she just wasted her own and everyone else’s time. First by asking about the budget. As if Burnham was ever going to say: “You know what? Since you’ve asked I might as well give you a heads-up two weeks early.” All Kemi achieved was to make herself look half witted. She ended up sounding a bit hurt. She had hoped that Andy would have spent more time problem-solving than point-scoring. There are days with Kemi when even giving a straight answer comes across as point-scoring.
Earlier in the day, Dominic Cummings had been giving evidence to a Lords select committee on how to prevent rogue actors from entering No 10. That should have been a very short session. Just stop morons like Boris Johnson from appointing people like Dom as his special adviser. Curiously this hadn’t occurred to Dom, nor to the dopey peers interrogating him.
It was a bizarre hour and a half. The sort that gives you mild PTSD. Your mind goes back to all the damage he did to the country during the Brexit referendum and during his year in No 10 and suddenly the horror floods back. Just when your brain has done its best to forget all about him. To consider him a footnote in history. For the record, Dom is as deluded as ever. His main thesis seemed to be that Boris was right to allow him to do whatever he liked but no one else in No 10 should ever be allowed to do what he did. Some things never change. We are well rid of him.

====================================================================================================

Campaigners decry slow progress in repaying victims of carer’s allowance crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:35:51 UTC
00:35:51 KST

Campaigners have urged Andy Burnham to step in after it emerged just a handful of the tens of thousands of unpaid carers who unknowingly racked up huge debts when welfare officials unlawfully changed benefits guidance have been repaid.
The first official update on the carers allowance reassessment exercise launched by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) in April confirms that progress in cancelling wrongful overpayments has started slowly.
Only 2,400 cases (1.04%) of an estimated caseload of 233,300 had been reviewed in the first five months of the £75m three-year scheme, with just 100 carers receiving a total of £40,000. The average repayment to individual carers was £342.
Campaigners said the slow progress was “deeply disappointing” and warned that at current rates it would take about 40 years for the exercise to be completed.
“After years of waiting for justice, only a small number of carers have had their cases reviewed five months into this exercise,” said Helen Walker, chief executive of Carers UK.
“The vast majority still face a lengthy and uncertain wait for resolution, all whilst enduring the ongoing financial hardship caused by these delays.
“There there must be a clear and realistic plan to accelerate progress. With 230,900 identified cases still awaiting review, these figures raise serious questions about whether DWP is on track to deliver within the funding period.”
Sir Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, who has long campaigned on unpaid carer injustices, said: “The carer’s allowance scandal didn’t start on his watch, but the failure to put things right is fast becoming a scandal of its own. The prime minister needs to step in and speed things up now.”
The DWP is understood to have prioritised accuracy over speed in its approach and remains confident it will complete the reassessment exercise on schedule by March 2029. It plans to double the number of staff on the project to 250 by next April.
The reassessment exercise followed an official review by the disability rights expert Liz Sayce published last year which concluded systemic DWP shortcomings had caused hundreds of thousands of carers to unwittingly to run up benefit debts as high as £20,000.
The Sayce review was triggered by an award-winning Guardian investigation, which revealed how hundreds of thousands of unpaid carers were pushed into financial hardship and emotional despair as a result of years of official neglect and failure.
Sayce told the Guardian on Wednesday: “Today’s statistics show that reassessments have started slowly and it’s vital that DWP shares both a robust plan for speeding them up, so people trust they will not have prolonged waits for justice.”
The figures show that DWP has made full repayments to 100 carers totalling £40,000, and reduced overpayment debt incurred by a further 100 carers by a total of £20,000. The amount returned to carers is 41% lower than initially estimated.
The reassessment exercise covers cases where the DWP breached the law by failing to allow carers with irregular wages from part-time work to average their incomes over a year, unfairly exposing them to being penalised for breaching earnings limits.
The Sayce review revealed that the “averaging earnings” problem arose in 2020 after DWP officials quietly changed existing guidance without advising carers or taking legal or policy advice. Many carers who believed they were allowed to average earnings over a one-year period were, as a result, issued with overpayment demands.
Campaigners praised the government for taking action to put right carer’s allowance injustices. But they are also frustrated at the lack of progress on other Sayce review recommendations, including overpayments caused by universal credit faults, and debts caused by officials failing to act on earnings information given by carers.
A DWP spokesperson said: “We are on track to complete the carer’s allowance reassessment exercise within the three years previously announced.
“To support the exercise we have been recruiting and training new decision makers in a rolling programme, ensuring we take the time to assess cases with the accuracy that carers deserve.
“We have plans in place to increase resource at a steady pace over the course of the exercise.”

Container ship sinks near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:35:33 UTC
00:35:33 KST

Two container ships near the strait of Hormuz have sunk after being struck by missiles, amid the sharpest rise in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The increase in attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in an attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.
On Wednesday, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.
“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.
The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day. Hours later, the Antigua- and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, having been hit by a projectile on 23 September, according to data from the International Maritime Organization.
Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship had sunk after hitting a naval mine while making an unauthorised passage through the strait.
State television quoted a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that said the ship was travelling on an “illegal and dangerous route” when it hit the mine.
The ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.
However, UKMTO suggested that both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles, raising questions over Tehran’s account.
Iran has repeatedly warned ships against trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The US military has been guiding ships through the waterway on a route nearer to Oman’s coast.
Ships in the area were reporting an intense series of attacks in recent days, with six vessels attacked on Sunday alone, according to UKMTO’s monitoring.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October. Of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers and two others were crude oil tankers.
The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop-off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.
US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Trump launched his war on Iran, and the Republican party is bracing for punishment at the polls.
According to two Iranian officials, Iran has recently begun using new tactics against vessels it considers to be in violation of its restrictions. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials told Reuters.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials added.
A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Tehran had changed tactics in one significant way. After the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including American naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.

The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile has criticised China’s refusal to recognise Ladakh as a Union Territory of India, calling Beijing’s territorial claims baseless. She argued that China’s territorial claims required historical evidence and maintained that Tibet remained central to the unresolved boundary dispute. “A lasting resolution to the border dispute would be difficult without addressing the Tibet issue,” she said.Tsering further alleged that China’s policies promoting ethnic assimilation and prioritising Mandarin over Tibetan threatened Tibet’s distinct cultural and religious identity.She reiterated that the Tibetan leadership’s Middle Way Approach sought a negotiated settlement that would allow Tibetans to preserve their culture, identity and faith, and urged Beijing to resume dialogue.Tibetan MP Gompo Dhondup also rejected China’s claims over Ladakh and other Himalayan regions, including Arunachal Pradesh, asserting that these territories were integral to India and that Beijing had no right to interfere in India’s sovereignty.Dhondup argued that a free and independent Tibet could serve as a peaceful buffer between India and China along their more than 3,000-kilometre border. He called on New Delhi to reconsider its position on Tibet and repeal its One-China policy, saying stronger support for Tibet would serve both Tibetan aspirations and India’s security interests.
India rejects China’s objections over Ladakh
The latest remarks follow India’s response to Beijing’s objections to the naming exercise. On Tuesday, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reiterated India’s position that Ladakh was an integral part of the country.“It is reiterated that the UT of Ladakh is an integral and inalienable part of India. No amount of denial by the Chinese side can change this established fact,” Jaiswal said.
The exchange followed a notification by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) standardising names for 28 locations and geographical features in Ladakh on official Survey of India maps, including Gogra and Hot Spring, sites associated with the 2020 military standoff.Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning opposed the move, saying Beijing had never recognised the territory as Indian. “The move is illegal and invalid and cannot change the fact that the relevant areas in the western sector of the China-India boundary have always belonged to China,” she said.

Ukraine’s TENCORE and Canada’s Dominion Dynamics will launch production of TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) in Canada for Ukraine and NATO partners.
TENCORE told Militarnyi about the agreement.
During the AUSA 2026 international defense exhibition, TENCORE and Dominion Dynamics signed a memorandum of understanding.
In addition to localizing production, the partnership includes integrating Canada’s AuraNet autonomous control and navigation system.
TENCORE will transfer technology and train Canadian specialists to prepare for full-scale production.
Dominion Dynamics, in turn, will integrate its AuraNet hardware and software suite for command, control and autonomy, and develop a specialized TerMIT variant for operation in extreme Arctic conditions.

The basic TerMIT UGV version is designed to transport cargo, with a range of up to 40 km, a top speed of 15 km/h, and ballistic protection to support logistics missions.
TerMIT versions equipped with the Khyzhak combat module manufactured by UGV Robotics are also available.
In June, it was reported that Germany would also manufacture UGVs for Ukraine under a joint venture between Quantum Systems and TENCORE.

Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:33:52 UTC
00:33:52 KST

Western Europe’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.
The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.
Chartered surveyors from the Union Nationale des Géomètres-Experts (UNGE) and the Ordre des Géomètres-Experts, who have regularly monitored the peak since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain, and drones to create a detailed model of the snow and ice cap.
The summit has shrunk back by 3.43 metres since a high of 4,810.90 metres in 2007, the data shows.
The experts cautioned against linking fluctuations in height from year to year to the rapid loss of Alpine ice being caused by fossil fuel pollution.
“Regarding ice mass, it is essential to distinguish between changes in surface altitude and changes in the total volume or mass of ice,” a UNGE spokesperson said. “An increase in summit altitude does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained ice mass, nor does it contradict the documented retreat of Alpine glaciers.”
Climate breakdown was a factor in western Europe’s hottest summer on record this year, scarring Alpine regions and melting ice at dizzying speed. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an “explosion of melt rates” after confirming that one-fifth of the country’s ice had been lost in the past five years, and 5.5% of volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.
Jean des Garets, the president of the Haute-Savoie departmental chamber of surveyors and the leader of the Mont Blanc expedition, said the warming trend could be seen with the naked eye in the rest of the Alpine massif but that “for the moment, climate change doesn’t seem to have the same impact above 4,000 metres”.
“When we climb, we pass by the Brigade Blanche hut before the Tête-Rousse glacier,” he said in comments reported by the French television channel TF1 on Wednesday. “We’ve seen that the glacier has moved up. It has literally melted before our very eyes and now in some places we’re crossing a stream instead of a glacier.”

US inflation rises before midterm elections, fuelling rate hike fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:31:29 UTC
00:31:29 KST

US inflation rises before midterm elections, fuelling rate hike fears
Economists divided on Fed rate hike as inflation creates uncertainty in run-up to US midterm elections in a tense market.
United States consumer prices jumped in September in the final inflation report before the midterm elections, increasing chances of an interest rate hike later this month.
Annual inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent, up from 3.4 percent in August. On a monthly basis, prices rose by 0.6 percent, according to the Consumer Price Index report released by the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.
Petrol prices led the surge as tensions between the US and Iran, as well as Russia and Ukraine, weighed on global energy prices. Petrol prices rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the CPI monthly increase, according to the BLS. They were up 34.2 percent from the same time a year ago.
“The directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains, driving up the prices of food and fuel,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, an economic think tank, said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.
Petrol prices have continued to climb. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $4.33 ($1.14 per litre), compared with $4.31 a month ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. Diesel prices are higher, at $6.29 per gallon (1.66 per litre), compared with $6.23 a month ago.
In a post on X, Patrick DeHaan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, said, “2026 has now seen more days with average gas prices over $4/gal than any year before: 158 days.”
Shelter costs also jumped 0.4 percent from the previous month, following a 0.3 percent increase in August. Food costs were a bright spot in the report, remaining unchanged overall.
Food away from home, including restaurant meals, rose 0.2 percent, but that increase was offset by a 0.1 percent decline in food-at-home prices, which track grocery costs.
At the grocery store, poultry prices jumped 0.7 percent, fruit and vegetable prices rose 0.5 percent, and juice prices increased 1.1 percent. However, milk prices dropped 2.1 percent and beef prices fell 0.9 percent.
Amid heavy investment in AI infrastructure, prices for computer software and accessories have jumped 28 percent from the same time last year.
“The AI boom is playing a huge part, and we have all read about the hundreds of billions being poured into data centers, AI firms, and models,” Rami Cassis, principal of Parabellum Investment, said in comments provided to Al Jazeera.
Fed pressures
The inflation data comes days before the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision later this month. Last month, the US central bank raised rates by 25 basis points, bringing the target range to 3.75–4.00 percent, the first hike in three years.
Economists are divided over whether the Fed will raise rates again or hold them steady. According to CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, there is a 52.9 percent chance that rates will remain in the 3.75–4.00 percent range, while a 47.1 percent chance of a quarter of a percentage point hike that would bring them to 4.00–4.25 percent.
The inflation data puts pressure on Republicans before the midterm elections on November 3. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that about 78 percent of Americans blamed US President Donald Trump’s policies for price increases.
US markets trended downward following the inflation report. The Nasdaq fell 0.8 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 0.6 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was roughly flat in midday trading.

Reconstruction, resistance, and the battle for Lebanon’s future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:30:02 UTC
00:30:02 KST

Reconstruction, resistance, and the battle for Lebanon’s future
BEIRUT — The announcement by Hezbollah’s Executive Council chairman, Sheikh Ali Damoush, of a new housing assistance program for Lebanese families displaced by the ongoing U.S.–led Israeli attacks comes amid a wider struggle over reconstruction, state authority, and the future of Lebanon.
Damoush declared that “the occupation of some positions by the enemy does not mean that it can establish itself on our land,” arguing that resistance operates differently from conventional armies by exhausting an occupying force until its withdrawal.
He also stressed that changing circumstances do not require surrender, since balances of power can change.
Addressing the humanitarian consequences of the destruction, Hezbollah’s Executive Council chairman announced assistance for families whose homes had been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable: $14,000 for eligible housing units in Beirut and its southern suburbs, and $12,000 elsewhere, including rental and furniture allowances. Initial payments were set at $3,500 and $3,000, respectively.
Damoush described the program as an ethical commitment rather than a substitute for the state’s responsibilities, insisting that assistance should reach affected Lebanese regardless of political affiliation.
“We remain committed to serving our people and doing everything possible for their dignity and honor,” Damoush said, acknowledging that no assistance could fully repay the sacrifices of families who had endured displacement and loss.
The significance of this initiative extends beyond financial assistance; it challenges the narrative that Hezbollah’s political and social capacity was irreversibly diminished.
By organizing housing assessments, establishing specialized committees, and announcing a structured compensation mechanism, the resistance is demonstrating an ability to mobilize resources and maintain a relationship with communities facing prolonged hardship.
This does not resolve the enormous material and economic costs of reconstruction, nor does it remove questions about the program’s funding, coverage, and implementation.
Nevertheless, the initiative illustrates how social organization can remain politically consequential even under military pressure and economic constraints.
The contrast with the Lebanese state is central to the debate; Damoush criticized the Lebanese government for failing to establish a direct assistance program for affected households, distinguishing infrastructure rehabilitation from compensation that enables displaced families to secure housing.
He called on the authorities to stop making concessions, respect constitutional obligations, and return to dialogue with their own citizens.
For devastated southern communities, the central question is not merely who promises reconstruction, but who can deliver it, transparently and equitably.
A state that seeks legitimacy must protect its citizens, restore essential services, and ensure that reconstruction is not conditional on political allegiance.
At the same time, non-state assistance cannot permanently replace public institutions or relieve the government of its obligations.
Damoush also urged solidarity across Lebanon, warning against sectarian hostility and landlords raising rents in response to housing allowances.
His appeal highlights a broader reality: displacement on this scale requires collective responsibility, effective public administration, and safeguards against exploitation.
Four reports recently published by Al-Akhbar in late September and early October 2026 describe a reported US National Security Council proposal linking an internationally supervised reconstruction framework, estimated at $40 billion, with efforts to weaken Hezbollah’s military and political influence.
The proposal envisages a Lebanese reconstruction authority, international oversight, and parallel security and political measures; as presented in these reports, reconstruction is not simply a humanitarian undertaking; it is also conceived as an instrument of political pressure.
The proposed framework seeks to make state-provided services and security alternatives to Hezbollah’s established social networks; its implications therefore extend beyond rebuilding homes to questions of sovereignty, international supervision, and the political conditions attached to financial assistance.
Against this backdrop, Hezbollah’s housing initiative represents a competing approach to reconstruction and community support; its longer-term significance will depend on whether assistance reaches eligible families, whether funding proves sustainable, and whether Lebanon can develop strong institutions capable of protecting all its citizens.
The fundamental challenge remains clear: rebuilding Lebanon must mean more than repairing damaged buildings; it must restore dignity, secure the right of displaced families to return, and establish a state accountable to its people rather than to competing domestic or foreign agendas.

Russia to Sign Diesel Contracts With Washington Soon, Putin’s Money Man Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:30:00 UTC
00:30:00 KST

The Kremlin said on Wednesday that it expects to sign contracts to export diesel to the US in the coming days.
Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund and the Kremlin’s main negotiator with the US, said Moscow is in close contact with the US to finalize the deal.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It will all happen in the next few days… We are in very close, hourly contact with the American side, and everything is moving very quickly,” AFP reported, citing Russian state media.
The comments follow US President Donald Trump’s surprise announcement on Friday allowing Russia to export millions of tons of diesel to the US and global markets. Trump has since demanded that Kyiv stop striking Russian refineries, calling for an immediate energy truce that would protect Russian refineries but not Ukraine’s energy grid.
Dmitriev, born in Kyiv and whose sister reportedly entered Ukraine after 2022, has played a major role in Moscow’s negotiations with the US and is reportedly the chief architect of Washington’s 28-point peace plan, unveiled in late 2025, which repackages Kremlin war goals as peace terms.
Alexander Novak, Russia’s deputy prime minister for energy, confirmed that discussions are ongoing, with some shipments heading directly to the US.
“We are currently working with American colleagues, at both the ministry and corporate levels, on supply contracts,” Novak said, adding that overall volumes could reach 3.5 million tons by the end of 2026.
Peskov: Russia Did Not Break Trump’s ‘Energy Truce’ Because Terms Were Never Set
“Deliveries will be made to global markets, including directly to the United States,” he added.
The overall volume amounts to about half of the US’s daily consumption, according to the BBC, despite sanctions relief running well into April 2027.
Kyiv and Europe have pushed back on Trump’s diesel deal, with President Volodymyr Zelensky saying Kyiv, not Moscow, decides whether diesel leaves Russian ports after Kyiv reportedly wiped out over 40% of Russia’s refining capacity.
On Tuesday, a bipartisan group of 12 US senators signed a joint letter urging Trump to rescind his diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a gift to Moscow and a betrayal of Ukraine.

The strikes targeted a key power plant in the city, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy noted that the Darnytska CHP-4 plant, which supplies the capital with heating and electricity, was targeted by a ballistic missile.
The attack comes just days after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, halting attacks on energy targets.
Since then, the Kremlin’s nightly attacks have nevertheless continued to target energy sites, according to Zelenskyy.
What 'energy ceasefire'?

Meanwhile Russia said it had shot down 900 Ukrainian drones overnight, including 180 near Moscow.

Ukrainian officers warn Starlink slowdown ‘comparable to a nuclear strike against us’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:29:44 UTC
00:29:44 KST

Ukrainian frontline soldiers are alarmed that Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service is reportedly being restricted on fast-moving military platforms, warning of severe operational consequences.
“This is comparable to a nuclear strike against us. All operations are on hold. This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.
The officer commands a medium-range drone strike unit in southeastern Ukraine. The unit relies heavily on Starlink for the operation and navigation of its American-made Hornet drones, used to strike targets at a range of up to 150 kilometers.
Advertisement
“Since last night, all Starlink and Starshield terminals used by our forces have been subject to a speed limit of 100 kilometers per hour,” the officer said.
POLITICO talked to three frontline soldiers, who all spoke on condition of being granted anonymity, as well as a Ukrainian defense ministry spokesperson and the EU's top defense official.
The reported restrictions have revived a question Ukrainian commanders have worried about for years: how much of the country’s battlefield communications can rely on a service controlled by a U.S. company.
Ukrainian soldiers say the restrictions have halted some medium-range drone strikes over Ukraine, disrupting attacks on Russian logistics and leaving frontline Ukrainian troops with less support. The scale of the disruption — and whether it was deliberate — remains unclear.
In a comment on X, Musk said: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," referring to the Starshield division of Starlink that is used for military purposes.
"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX," he added. "Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Advertisement
Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister who has good contacts in Silicon Valley, said late Wednesday: "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored. Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense."
The White House and the Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The restrictions have brought “all medium-range strike operations to a complete halt,” the officer said, including those using mesh-based systems. These rely on a single Starlink-equipped UAV to receive and relay signals to other drones connected through a mesh network, allowing them to strike targets deep inside Russian-held territory or in areas heavily protected by Russian electronic warfare systems.
Such targets include the Donetsk region, the strategically important Novorossiya highway linking Russia to Crimea, the Crimean Peninsula itself, the Kerch area and the Black Sea.
“We can no longer fight effectively to support our infantry on the battlefield. We can no longer strike multiple-launch rocket systems, North Korean-supplied heavy self-propelled artillery positioned deep behind enemy lines, ammunition depots, command centers and other targets,” the officer said.
"The Ukrainian frontline is very much dependent on Starlink-operated mid-strike drones," Iryna Terekh, CEO of Ukrainian missile-maker Fire Point told POLITICO.
Advertisement
Ukraine's devastating campaign
For months, Ukrainian medium-range strike drones have inflicted significant damage on Russian logistics in frontline regions. They have disrupted the supply of fuel, ammunition and other military equipment, slowing Russia's advance.
Members of a special operations unit pilot a reconnaissance drone in the Kharkiv region on Feb. 27, 2026. | Chris McGrath/Getty Images
The officer said he feared that the Starlink restrictions will give Russian troops a critical opportunity to strengthen their positions.
“Starting today, the enemy will build up its logistics routes to Crimea to reinforce its forces there,” he warned.
Two other Ukrainian frontline soldiers operating ground robots and conventional first-person-view drones in the Donbas confirmed to POLITICO that Starlink services for Ukrainian units were abruptly restricted on Wednesday.
“On the night of October 14, without prior notice to the Defense Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals while in motion,” a Ukrainian defense ministry official told reporters in Kyiv.
The official added that the problems occur at speeds varying from 72 kph to 161 kph, "depending on the specific vehicle and unit."
Advertisement
The slowdown in Starlink terminals comes as U.S. President Donald Trump exerts fierce pressure on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries. That follows his deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to release diesel onto global markets — part of Trump’s effort to reduce fuel prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said in a Facebook post.
Asked about the rising American pressure on Ukraine, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a POLITICO event on Wednesday: "Political development sometimes makes strange influence. Elections are coming."
“We are quite dependent on American space capabilities,” Kubilius acknowledged. “The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities.”
The Starlink slowdown was condemned by one of Ukraine’s key European allies.
“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” wrote Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.
Advertisement
Ukraine depends on Starlink
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Starlink has become central to Kyiv's war effort. In the spring of 2022, Ukrainian defenders trapped in the besieged city of Mariupol used satellites operated by SpaceX to send messages to the outside world. Ukrainian units relied on the system to coordinate operations during the fierce urban fighting around Bakhmut in 2023.
To this day, soldiers use Starlink to rapidly adjust artillery fire and navigate naval drones during attacks on Russia's Black Sea Fleet. Ukraine's former army chief, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, once praised the terminals for their "extraordinary utility."
That reliance always carried risk. In the early months of the war, Starlink reportedly shut off terminals that were going to be used in a naval attack on the Russian fleet.
But SpaceX has also acted to favor Ukraine. In February, SpaceX shut down access to Starlink terminals being used illegally by Russia, causing immediate chaos. Ukraine then ramped its own use of the terminals.
Kyiv's armed forces began widely equipping medium-range strike drones with Starlink terminals. Without them, operations would become considerably more complex. The military would, for example, have to calculate terrain elevations and antenna availability itself and install additional communications equipment.
"Starlink allows you not to have to deal with radio physics," a Ukrainian officer with the call sign Jura said in August. "Starlink allows operators to maintain a live video connection with a drone until shortly before impact."
Advertisement
Starlink can also provide so-called "synthetic GPS coordinates," which can help drones navigate when conventional GPS signals are jammed.
A Ukrainian serviceman assembles a drone ahead of a combat mission in the Kharkiv region on May 22, 2026. | Diego Fedele/Getty Images
But Ukrainian officers feared that decisions made in Washington or in the executive offices of American companies could suddenly weaken Ukraine.
"Many of my colleagues and I myself are very nervous about the question of how we would operate without Starlink," Jura said. "We have discussed this question several times among our officers: 'What if Elon Musk or someone at SpaceX switches it off?'"
As Trump has ramped up pressure on Kyiv in recent weeks, Ukrainian officers reported growing problems with Starlink.
One Ukrainian drone pilot, who operates medium-range strike drones, reported severe connectivity problems on Sept. 11 and 12, as well as further disruptions on Sept. 17. He said soldiers from several Ukrainian units had experienced similar problems.
The incidents occurred shortly after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had concluded visits to Kyiv and Moscow. "After few days, the normal work with Starlink come back. But I believe that was the signal," the pilot said.
Advertisement
He argued that Russian jamming equipment could not plausibly have produced such geographically consistent disruptions across multiple sectors of the front.
"So that was, I guess, administered from some office," he said. POLITICO could not independently establish whether the disruptions resulted from deliberate restrictions imposed by the American satellite provider or another technical cause.
The incidents have reinforced concerns among Ukrainian military personnel about their dependence on American-controlled technology.
"The reason is politics and the American option to 'switch off' or critically decrease” U.S. systems, the pilot said.
Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv.Daniella Cheslow and Audrey Decker contributed reporting.

French viewers shocked by Israeli soldiers’ accounts of Gaza in ‘NAZA’ documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:27:26 UTC
00:27:26 KST

French viewers who attended screenings of “NAZA,” a documentary exposing Israel’s killing of civilians in Gaza, said they were shocked by Israeli soldiers’ accounts that reduced Palestinian victims to numbers rather than recognizing them as human beings, Anadolu reports.
Produced by British newspaper The Guardian and directed by Oscar-winning filmmaker Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the documentary was screened in French cinemas on Oct. 12-13.
The film drew considerable interest in Paris on its opening day, with most tickets sold.
French viewers who watched “NAZA” at two cinemas in the capital shared their reactions with Anadolu.
‘I think the filmmakers are very courageous’
A French viewer, Kenzi, said the documentary explained the meaning of NAZA, a term referring to civilian casualties, and left him deeply shocked.
He said Israeli soldiers repeatedly discussed numbers and calculations, almost all of which represented people killed in Gaza.
“We know what is happening, we talk about it, we see it, but not to this extent. And here, it was really shocking to see Israeli soldiers talking about it. Sometimes you could sense regret, sometimes not so much. They spoke quite coldly. So, it really disturbed me. And, I think it was very well made. It went by very quickly,” he said.
Noting that the soldiers compared their actions in Gaza to a video game, Kenzi said: “They talk about artificial intelligence to identify people to kill. At a certain point, you see that they no longer measure the number of people they are going to kill, the collateral damage, the NAZAs.”
He said the soldiers frequently referred to a “system.”
“It seemed as though they had been brainwashed and made to believe that they were on the right side, until they realized for themselves that what they were doing was vile,” he said.
Kenzi recalled the soldiers repeatedly saying they “just wanted to eliminate the enemy.”
“They clearly said that the enemy was children aged 3 to 6, women who had done nothing to deserve this. Often, they wanted to eliminate an enemy leader, and in the end, they killed his entire family except that person,” he said.
Praising the Israeli directors, he added: “I think the filmmakers are very courageous to have initiated a project like this.”
‘It affected everyone in the theater’
Iona, a 23-year-old French viewer, said: “I think the film is extremely important. It is extremely important to have this perspective because we often hear testimonies from victims, but here we have testimonies from the attackers, who put the situation into concrete words.”
She said the documentary could help people understand what was happening and stand on the right side of history, adding that the language used and the questions asked deeply affected her.
“He was not afraid to use the word ‘genocide.’ He asked directly whether it was genocide, and they said yes,” she said, referring to the interviewer.
Iona said she found it shocking that the soldiers did not regard the victims as people.
She also highlighted scenes showing people living normally in Tel Aviv while people in Gaza were dying.
READ: Netanyahu vows to revoke citizenship of those who ‘defame’ Israeli soldiers in Gaza documentary NAZA
“Everything was extremely striking,” she said.
Emphasizing the importance of making such films and allowing everyone to speak, she added: “There was everyone in the theater — young people, older people. You could see that it affected everyone in the theater. There was silence at the end. It was extremely moving.”
She urged people to watch the documentary, ending her remarks with: “Free Palestine.”
‘Reducing human beings to numbers shocked me the most’
Adam, a 27-year-old French viewer, said the documentary left him speechless throughout.
“I was aware of the history and the political issues behind it, of the massacre and genocide taking place in Palestine,” he said.
But hearing testimony from people within the system was still shocking, he added, saying it gave concrete substance to the atrocities.
“Overall, I think the documentary is very well made and presented, because it raises several questions, particularly about the dehumanization of victims through the term NAZA.
Ultimately, the victims, the ‘collateral damage,’ as they like to call them, become nothing more than numbers. Reducing human beings to numbers was what shocked me the most,” he said.
Adam said the massacre in Palestine did not begin in October 2023 and praised the directors’ courage despite pressure from the Israeli government.
‘An interviewer who recognized the disastrous situation in Gaza’
Another French viewer, Yacine, said the repeated emphasis on numbers was among the documentary’s most striking elements.
“They had an interviewer who appeared objective, who had some distance and recognized the disastrous situation unfolding in Palestine and Gaza,” he said, referring to Abraham.
By contrast, he said, the soldiers interviewed appeared conditioned by war.
“There is a real contrast between the images we saw of Tel Aviv, where people seem safe and appear to lead fairly peaceful daily lives, and the images of Gaza at the end of the film, which embody war and destruction themselves,” he said.
“When you see the images, you get the impression that there is almost no life left. People are surviving.”

====================================================================================================

Deadly drone strikes in NATO waters raise stakes for Black Sea trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:27:07 UTC
00:27:07 KST

Krapets resident and engineer Valeri Baronov, 81, shows the wreckage of a drone, which he claims is Russian, a day after suspected Russian drones struck two cargo ships off Bulgaria. | Nikolay Doychinov/AFP via Getty Images
The Ukraine war’s spillover into the Black Sea is creating a growing European security and commercial risk: Drones are hitting ships and killing sailors, grain routes are under strain, and insurers and investors are weighing the cost of operating through Ukraine’s ports.
Five commercial vessels have been hit in Bulgarian and Romanian waters over the past week alone, leaving at least four people dead, several sailors missing and others injured. In response, Black Sea countries Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey have raised the issue at NATO, asking for more focus toward the region and joint support, according to two alliance diplomats.
“The attack within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable. It constitutes a serious breach of maritime and international law and will further jeopardise safe navigation in the Black Sea,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on X after the attacks last week.
Advertisement
Russia has been attacking Ukrainian ports and cities in the area since the start of its full-scale invasion. But the recent strikes have brought the spillover into NATO territory. If they continue, EU leaders will face pressure to protect Black Sea shipping and keep Ukrainian trade moving.
Those questions will be top of mind at Thursday’s European Council summit. According to draft conclusions obtained by POLITICO, leaders are expected to discuss the “immediate restoration of safe passage for grain cargo ships.”
A wider problem
Russia is not the only country using naval drones in the Black Sea. Ukraine has also used them against Russian-linked shipping. In June, a Ukrainian sea drone exploded in Romania’s Constanța port after Kyiv said it had veered off course because of Russian electronic interference.
“The Black Sea situation is quite dangerous because attacks are coming from both [sides],” said an EU shipping representative, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “You have to worry about both.”
Attribution can also be difficult. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Wednesday that investigators still have not proven that Russia is behind the strikes — although some have attributed his reticence to his broadly softer approach toward the Kremlin.
Drone operations by both Russia and Ukraine are likely to continue as long as each has the money and production capacity to sustain them, said Cristian Vlas, assistant research manager for Eastern Europe at the think tank ACLED.
Advertisement
Oleksii Goncharenko, a Ukrainian lawmaker and founder of the Black Sea Security Forum, told POLITICO that a “serious diplomatic initiative” was needed, bringing together Ukraine, Russia and a third-party guarantor, such as Turkey, "to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.”
Grain routes under pressure
The security risk is disrupting routes that carry Ukraine’s harvest to market, with consequences for EU transport links. Black Sea ports are Ukraine’s main export gateway, handling around 95 percent of the country’s grain exports, as well as significant volumes of iron ore. Shipping traffic has fallen as the security risk has grown.
Some cargo is being rerouted to the River Danube, but capacity there has been stretched in recent months as drought pushes water levels to record lows. Operators are trying to add rail capacity, but that risks moving the bottleneck westward to Romania.
Moving more Ukrainian grain overland also risks reviving tensions with farmers in neighboring EU countries, Vlas said. Romanian farmers have worried that Ukrainian produce meant only to transit could stay on the domestic market, he added, while transport operators are already juggling competing demands for capacity.
Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi has warned that millions of tons of unsold grain is piling up, and that farmers who can’t sell won’t be able to afford to resow all their land.
Bulgaria is working with Romania and Turkey on a joint initiative to protect freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, which Radev plans to bring to EU leaders on Thursday.
Advertisement
Following the Black Sea countries' request at NATO, military officials are likely to look into possible options such as shifting counter-drone systems to the region, the two alliance diplomats said. Radev said Sofia will convene his counterparts in Ankara and Bucharest to examine further proposals, while a senior Bulgarian official called for new joint anti-drone systems with Romania, partly financed by the EU.
Investment at risk
The attacks also threaten what had started to look like a renewed bet on Ukraine’s ports. MSC, the world’s largest container line, was among the biggest and newest investors, reportedly acquiring a majority stake in a container terminal at a port near Odesa in May.
Ukraine has also been offering investors a long-term concession at the Chornomorsk terminal near Odesa. This terminal is one of Ukraine's largest planned port public-private partnerships and part of what is expected to be a multibillion-euro reconstruction effort involving European companies.
But people who work in Ukraine’s ports say the case for rebuilding is collapsing.
“No one is ready to invest and rebuild, since you know that tomorrow there will be another missile, another pack of drones,” Oleg Grygoriuk, chairman of Ukraine’s Marine Transport Workers’ Trade Union, said.

U.S. inflation accelerates to 3.7 pct in September as gasoline prices surge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:24:30 CST
00:24:30 KST

A man picks fruit at a store in New York, the United States, Oct. 14, 2026. U.S. consumer prices rose more than expected in September, driven by surging gasoline costs, with annual inflation reaching its highest level since May, the Labor Department said Wednesday. The consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6 percent from August and 3.7 percent from a year earlier. Economists had forecast an annual increase of 3.6 percent. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
NEW YORK, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- U.S. consumer prices rose more than expected in September, driven by surging gasoline costs, with annual inflation reaching its highest level since May, the Labor Department said Wednesday.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6 percent from August and 3.7 percent from a year earlier. Economists had forecast an annual increase of 3.6 percent.
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly CPI increase, and were up 34.2 percent from a year earlier. Overall energy prices climbed 5.2 percent for the month, following a 2.1 percent rise in August.
The surge came as the war in Iran continued to disrupt energy supplies from the Middle East, pushing up fuel costs.
Inflationary pressures also extended beyond energy. Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent for a second consecutive month and 2.6 percent from a year earlier.
"Underlying price pressures are broadening beyond energy," said Anshul Sharma, chief investment officer at Savvy Wealth, pointing to rising shelter costs and airfares as fuel costs are passed on to consumers.
"This is not a good print for the Federal Reserve," said Tiffany Wilding, an economist at PIMCO, who described the pickup in housing inflation as particularly concerning.
The hotter-than-expected report added pressure on the Federal Reserve ahead of its Oct. 27-28 policy meeting, with investors raising bets on another interest rate hike.
U.S. stock futures fell and Treasury yields rose following the release as investors braced for the prospect of higher interest rates. ■

The outages disrupted search, navigation, food delivery and banking services while also affecting corporate clients on Yandex Cloud, including retail giants like Lenta and Magnit.
Key Yandex services like Pay and Cloud did not appear to be fully restored as of Wednesday evening.
Meanwhile, a top executive of state telecom operator Rostelecom stepped up calls for the construction of geographically isolated, decentralized backup data centers to avoid vulnerabilities exposed by the attacks on Yandex.
“Everyone understands today that we need a so-called ‘doomsday’ site, a backup facility where you can always restore your services if something happens,” said senior vice president Valery Yermakov.
President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday convened a cybersecurity meeting with Shadayev, state security officials and top executives, including Sberbank CEO Herman Gref, whose bank’s own data center was hit by drones overnight Wednesday.
Peskov claimed the meeting was not in response to recent “situational” attacks, though Putin urged officials to bolster national digital defenses against growing security threats.

U.S. Air Force AI fighter jet draws 30+ test proposals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:22:14 UTC
00:22:14 KST

- The U.S. Air Force sought three X-62 VISTA test concepts for fiscal 2027 and 2028 but received a final proposal of more than 30.
- The AI research jet also flew an IBM NorthPole chip and third-party autonomy software during HAVE HOLIDAYS tests at Edwards Air Force Base.
The U.S. Air Force went looking for three new flight test ideas for its AI-controlled X-62 VISTA research jet and came away with more than 30, after the first research symposium built around the aircraft drew over 80 participants to Edwards Air Force Base, California, in August.
The three-day meeting at the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School brought together people from industry, academia and the joint force, according to the 412th Test Wing, which released details on Oct. 13. Organizers set out to define three test concepts the X-62 could fly in fiscal 2027 and 2028, but participants submitted a final proposal of more than 30, which the service described as substantial and previously untapped demand for the aircraft.
“We were awed by the level of positive responses and interest,” said Col. Maryann Karlen, commandant of the Air Force Test Pilot School. “This demonstrates, without a doubt, the demand for testbeds like the X-62.”
The X-62, short for Variable In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, is a heavily modified two-seat F-16D that can mimic the handling of other aircraft and host software that flies the jet while safety pilots sit aboard. It became the first X-plane flown by artificial intelligence in combat-style maneuvering, flying against a crewed F-16 in a 2023 dogfight under the DARPA Air Combat Evolution program.
Briefings at the symposium came from DARPA, the Air Force Research Laboratory, MIT Lincoln Laboratory and the Air Force Institute of Technology, among others. Aircrew from an Air Combat Command fighter squadron also shared recent operational experience on getting pilots to trust machine-learning systems.
The jet is now in the middle of a Mission Systems Upgrade funded by the Test Resource Management Center, which adds an advanced radar, more computing power and room for additional sensors. Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, Calspan Corporation, the Air Force Research Laboratory and RTX are working on the upgrade through the Air Force Test Center. Once finished, the X-62 is meant to work alongside VENOM, the U.S. Air Force’s fleet of F-16s converted for autonomy testing at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, and to try out new AI uses for high-priority programs.
Ahead of the expected surge in test work, the school flew a series of short missions it named HAVE HOLIDAYS to work out how to integrate and fly new software quickly. They ran in parallel with HAVE HEAT, an April campaign in which an AI agent on the X-62 autonomously intercepted an airborne target using live infrared sensor data.
One of the HOLIDAYS tests, HAVE BALLDROP, put an autonomous agent from a third party outside the usual prime contractors onto the jet for the first time, drawn from an Air Force Research Laboratory program called xFACTOR. Another, HAVE THANKS, flew BirdBox, an open-architecture laboratory software framework that helps sensors recognize targets at the tactical edge.
HAVE DREIDEL tested commercial runtime assurance software from 3Laws Robotics, which acts as a set of guardrails to stop an autonomous aircraft from breaking limits set by its operators. In HAVE SANTA, engineers put IBM’s NorthPole chip, a low-power processor modeled on the way the brain handles information, inside the VISTA’s computers, where it ran Lockheed Martin Skunk Works’ “Supermassive” simulation and calculated parallel flight trajectories in the air.
