Saudi Arabia’s billions in arms fail to buy security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:20:54 UTC
00:20:54 KST

Saudi Arabia’s billions in arms fail to buy security
TEHRAN - Saudi Arabia spends tens of billions of dollars on arms every year, but is struggling to protect key assets such as airports, refineries and pipelines from missiles and drones fired by Ansarallah, also called the Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF).
Despite acquiring state-of-the-art weapons systems from the United States and Europe and possessing multi-layered air defenses, the kingdom has seen deadly attacks on the main airport serving the capital, Riyadh, over the past week.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired U.S. fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom.
Ansarallah have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses. The approach resembles Russia’s playbook: Moscow has frequently used a mass of drones along with cruise and ballistic missiles in barrages against Ukraine.
Cruise missiles fly at lower altitudes, making them harder to identify and track. Ansarallah have also introduced a new generation of ballistic missiles that are maneuverable.
No single air defense system can guarantee that every incoming threat will be intercepted.
Experts note that the latest Ansarallah missiles, such as the Hatem-2 and the Palestine-2, are fast and accurate.
Last year, an Ansarallah missile evaded Israel’s vaunted air defenses and impacted near Ben Gurion airport. Analyst Amir Bar Shalom told CNN at the time: “They were very accurate, and to be very accurate if you’re launching from 2,000 kilometers, it’s impressive.”
Pandora’s box opened in March 2015
Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Mohammed bin Salman, opened Pandora’s box in March 2015 when he ordered an attack on Ansarallah in support of Yemen’s government, which was aligned with Riyadh. At the time, he vowed that Saudi Arabia would crush Ansarallah within weeks. Despite receiving logistical and intelligence support from the United States, the war against Ansarallah turned into a humiliating ordeal for the Saudi kingdom.
Seven years of conflict with Saudi Arabia -- from 2015 to 2022 -- caused immense suffering in Ansarallah-controlled parts of Yemen, and an economic and transport embargo has continued since.
Ultimately, that led Ansarallah in July to declare they would attack Saudi shipping in the Red Sea – and the campaign of missile strikes began soon afterwards, initially targeting an Aramco oil refinery on the Red Sea coast and Saudi airbases.
Ansarallah are demanding an end to Saudi airstrikes in support of its proxies in Yemen, as well as billions of dollars in compensation from Saudi Arabia.
Iran has offered to mediate between Riyadh and Ansarallah. On Monday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was ready to provide “any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.”
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of Ansarallah’s political bureau, said on Monday that Riyadh had accepted mediation but Ansarallah had rejected truce proposals of two weeks and of one month.
“The battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena,” al-Bukhaiti said. “Every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow.”
Escalation, through even more intense airstrikes, would bring the risk of further missile attacks that would undermine the goal of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to make Saudi Arabia a world-class destination for investment, technology and tourism.
The stakes extend beyond the oil industry. Data centers, desalination plants and airports underpin the kingdom’s technology ambitions, water supply and tourism economy. The crown prince’s marquee investment event in Riyadh later this month will put his pitch to international investors in the spotlight.
But major corporations shied away this week from the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh.
Defeating Ansarallah forces through a ground offensive involving Saudi-backed Yemeni forces seems highly unlikely. Ansarallah forces are entrenched, battle-hardened and know the mountainous terrain. They have inflicted heavy losses on the Saudi-backed forces in the last month.
Last year, the U.S. spent more than $1 billion on a seven-week campaign of air-strikes against them. They eventually agreed not to attack U.S. shipping in the Red Sea but remained very much in place – and in the meantime shot down a number of highly advanced U.S. Reaper drones.
If anything, Ansarallah, who may have as many as 350,000 men under arms, are on the front foot. They have now encircled the city of Taiz, Yemen’s third largest and a vital logistical hub, the Institute for the Study of War said on Monday.
The Saudis are seeking to mobilize an international coalition against Ansarallah. Regional allies have offered help in the way of defensive systems. Pakistan has sent thousands of troops to help defend the kingdom. Egypt has offered whatever support is asked for.
The Saudis may also be able to procure more air defense systems from Europe and the U.S., after running down shipments delivered at the start of the war against Iran.
But the U.S. itself is short of such systems. A report by the U.S. Defense Department’s Inspector-General said the campaign against Iran had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
And with mid-term elections three weeks away, Donald Trump is wary of yet another entanglement in the Middle East. He has been non-committal about direct U.S. strikes against Ansarallah, while not ruling them out.
“U.S. reluctance to get involved stokes the perception that the United States has abandoned a partner at its moment of greatest need,” according to Michael Ratney at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.
Writing before the airport strikes, Ratney – a former ambassador in Riyadh – added: “The kingdom is under attack, and as a political matter, it has to retaliate. But ultimately, we should expect a return to diplomacy – imperfect, unsatisfying diplomacy that nonetheless deescalates the conflict.”
Analysts believe that wealthy Saudi Arabia should swallow its pride and engage in serious dialogue with Ansarallah, whose power has grown despite years of hardship and conflict. Riyadh should have realized by now that security cannot be bought through alliances with Western powers or the purchase of billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Western weaponry, particularly from the United States.

Colombia opens embassy in West Jerusalem despite city’s disputed international status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:17:07 UTC
00:17:07 KST

Colombia opened an embassy in West Jerusalem on Wednesday, becoming the 10th country to establish an embassy in the contested city despite widespread international opposition to moves recognizing it as Israel’s capital, Anadolu reports.
The opening ceremony was attended by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar and Moshe Lion, mayor of West Jerusalem, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry.
Lion said Colombia had become the 10th country to relocate its embassy to West Jerusalem.
The move follows the restoration of diplomatic relations between the two countries in August 2026, after Colombia severed ties with Israel in May 2024 under its previous government.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
READ: Colombia recognises Israeli sovereignty over occupied Golan Heights
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem – occupied by Israel since 1967 – as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.
Israel annexed East Jerusalem in 1980, a move that has not been recognized internationally.
In Resolution 478, adopted in August 1980, the UN Security Council rejected Israel’s measures seeking to alter the character and status of Jerusalem and called on countries with diplomatic missions in the city to withdraw them.
Most countries maintain their embassies in Tel Aviv or surrounding areas rather than Jerusalem, reflecting the city’s contested status and the international position that its final status should be resolved through negotiations.
With Colombia’s move, the number of countries maintaining embassies in West Jerusalem rises to 10, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry.
They include the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Paraguay, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Nauru and Somaliland, which is recognized as independent only by Israel.

President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday urged improving all components of Russia’s digital security system.
Putin said in an address to a government meeting on enhancing cybersecurity via videoconference, which was published by the Kremlin, that Russia is consistently strengthening its sovereignty in all areas, including digital infrastructure.
Putin expressed that with the development of digitalization and “against the backdrop of direct and hybrid external aggression,” cyber threats to spheres such as the economy, logistics and public administration are “reaching a new level.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied any links Wednesday to the government meeting and the Ukrainian strikes.
“No, this is a much more systemic meeting. It is not linked to those ad hoc attacks,” Peskov said at a media briefing in Moscow.

How France's far-right uses Israel to whitewash its antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:16:12 UTC
00:16:12 KST

Breadcrumb
How France's far-right uses Israel to whitewash its antisemitism
Recent revelations have reopened questions about far-right politician Jordan Bardella’s antisemitic statements made between 2013 and 2015. “Banks are all controlled by Jews,” “The Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them and rob them,” and “a Zionist is necessarily Jewish, and deeply so” are among the statements he reportedly made.
Despite irrefutable evidence, the president of the far-right National Rally (RN) has denied these accusations, citing his support for Israel, including an official visit in 2025, as a defence.
Amichai Chikli, Israel’s Minister of Diaspora Affairs, who hosted him during last year’s trip, also publicly defended him.
A history of collaboration
Bardella’s case is taking place against the backdrop of the RN’s attempts to whitewash its links to antisemitism in recent years. But many doubt there has been a fundamental change, especially given its foundations.
Originally, the party was called the National Front (FN) when it was founded in 1972 by veterans of the Nazi Waffen-SS, the collaborationist Milice (the paramilitary organisation set up by the Vichy regime to fight French resistance during World War II), and the Organisation de l’armée secrète (OAS).
Since then, alongside its name change in 2018, it has worked hard to revamp its image to become electable. Its founder Jean-Marie Le Pen – for whom the Holocaust was a “point of detail in history” – was even expelled by his own daughter Marine Le Pen in 2015. The party has also since regularly purged additional ‘bad apples’.
Louis Aliot, a former RN vice-president, explained the party’s intentions clearly in 2013: “It’s antisemitism that stops people from voting for us. That is all there is to it. Once you remove that barrier, you free everything else.”
Now, the RN even claims to be a shield for Jews, notably through support for Israel.
Anti-Muslim politics
But the party did not simply shed its fascist/racist past. It strategically shifted its focus to Muslim, migrants and the left, with the support of an Islamophobic bloc spanning France’s political class and media.
Support for Israel was increasingly conflated with support for Jews, which enabled the weaponisation of antisemitism against all those who expressed solidarity with Palestine, or were visibly associated with the movement.
In fact, the RN started to spew the rhetoric of a “new antisemitism” casting Islam, non-white communities and the left as its principal agents. This was a borrowed strategy that has long been used by Israel to discredit Palestinians and their allies when faced with criticism over its crimes.
The party also found that there was an appetite for such narratives across Western political classes that were particularly invested in fuelling the fire of anti-Muslim sentiments and politics.
What changed since October 2023 is the speed and scale of this process. As scholars Adam Hanieh, Rafeef Ziadah and Robert Knox have argued, the genocide in Palestine has exposed the moral bankruptcy of Western states closing ranks to support Israel, defending the indefensible, and ultimately turning Palestine into a “lightning rod for a much deeper rage about the state of the world” and a “radicalising impulse for political elites” themselves.
Repressing solidarity, legitimising the far-right
In France, solidarity protests have systematically been met with repression and criminalisation. The state’s unconditional support for Israel is equated with defending Jews, and any anti-Zionism that expresses itself on the streets, within political movements, and institutions, is labelled antisemitic.
French President Emmanuel Macron even officially declared this in 2017, which further legitimised the far-right’s targeting of the left.
This was all too visible during a state-sponsored march against antisemitism in November 2023, which was widely seen as a march in support of Israel. Those in attendance included the RN and members of the far-right student organisation Groupe Union Défense (GUD), and members of the French branch of the Jewish Defence League (LDJ).
Those on the left who had taken part were booed and accused of complicity with terrorism.
This was not the only surreal political moment in the last three years of the Gaza genocide, however. Holocaust survivor Serge Klarsfeld, a lawyer who spent his life pursuing Nazi criminals, met Marine Le Pen in 2024 and declared he would vote for her “without hesitation” over the ‘radical’ left.
In 2025, on an official visit to Israel, Bardella knelt inside Yad Vashem, the world’s largest Holocaust memorial. He was also invited to attend a conference ostensibly convened to fight antisemitism, alongside Spanish far-right Vox Party politician Hermann Tertsch, whose father was a Nazi Party member.
Normalising far-right politics
Over the past decade, the left has been progressively isolated and demonised whilst the far-right has been gaining legitimacy. For example, Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s France Unbowed Party (LFI), which has built its electoral success in opposition to a reactionary consensus of neoliberalism, austerity, state racism, and authoritarian politics spanning from parts of the socialist left to the far-right, has faced relentless campaigns accusing it of antisemitism.
Palestine solidarity expressed by LFI and others on the left is seen as pandering to a “Muslim vote” and stoking antisemitism in the poor suburbs.
Disturbingly, the Islamophobic rhetoric being used by the political class and media is not so dissimilar to old antisemitic imagery regarding the infiltration and demographic danger posed by a “foreign” racial group. Muslims in France are painted as endangering a supposedly white, Judeo-Christian civilisation, and terms like “Islamo-leftism” echo the historic fascist conspiracy of “Judeo-Bolshevism”.
Of course, none of this means the far-right is actually cleansed of antisemitism. Just last year, Le Pen stated that she regretted expelling her father and “will never forgive herself.” Also, Bardella recently met with far-right Polish politician Krzysztof Bosak, whose party promotes a “Jews-free Poland.”
Support for Israel and antisemitism are not mutually exclusive, as Bardella’s reported statements remind us: both can rest on the same premise, that Jews form a single, essentialised body whose place is not in Europe but in a Jewish state.
The only difference now is that in France, the same racist matrix once targeting Jews has been redirected to Muslims and non-white people, with Palestine cast as the front line of terrorism and Israel recast as a civilisational and security partner.
Indeed, despite its rebrand, the RN has not broken with its foundational project: a racial-national regeneration through purification, a politics that would crush the labour movement, stop migration and repress any politics that opposed this agenda.
Nevertheless, Israel has found strategic allies among far-right parties across Europe, with whom it shares a fantasy of racial domination, and it seems unbothered by the long-standing history of antisemitism rife within their ranks. It benefits from the image that it is a successful ethnonationalist outpost fighting barbarism and terrorism in the Middle East.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz clearly explained this relationship when he declared Israel was doing “the dirty work for us.”
What is deeply concerning, however, is that the weaponisation of antisemitism and ongoing attempts to discredit those on the left who organise anti-racist and anti-fascist efforts amidst rising hate and oppression only further endanger Jewish communities.

Judge extends White House access for US media outlets amid Trump standoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

15:15:58 UTC
00:15:58 KST

Judge extends White House access for US media outlets amid Trump standoff
CNN, MS Now and Politico can continue to access White House as judge maintains Trump’s ban likely illegal.
A federal judge has extended access to several media organisations that United States President Donald Trump had sought to ban from the White House.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly said Trump likely broke the law in banning journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico from attending White House briefings.
The decision, published late Tuesday, expands on an emergency order issued by Kelly on September 24 that temporarily reinstated access to organisations. It said Trump likely discriminated against the news organisations based on their viewpoints, in violation of the First Amendment of the US Constitution.
He wrote that Trump’s “announcement of the ban and later remarks explaining the reason for it make this a straightforward conclusion: President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him”.
In announcing the ban, Trump had said the organisations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States”.
The Department of Justice subsequently said the reporters’ White House passes were revoked on national security grounds.
In his ruling, Kelly rejected the claim.
“First, there is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision,” he wrote.
The latest order stands until Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during the president’s first term, makes a final determination in the case, or until an appeals court steps in.
Trump has long been a critic of legacy US media and has previously sought to restrict access to certain organisations.
He has also lodged rhetorical attacks on individual reporters both in person and on social media, while launching an array of lawsuits against media companies.
Speaking during an October 8 hearing, Theodore Boutrous, a lawyer for the three banned organisations, said Trump was seeking to “coerce better coverage”.
The Freedom of the Press Foundation was among the groups cheering the latest court ruling.
“But this fight is far from over,” senior adviser for advocacy Caitlin Vogus said in a statement.
“We have every reason to expect the administration will appeal Kelly’s latest order and also continue to prevent CNN and Politico from participating in pool coverage of the president,” she said. “Trump must not be allowed to trample on fundamental First Amendment protections by handpicking his press corps or turning pool duties into a reward for favorable coverage.”

Pope Leo XIV’s recovery from lung cancer surgery is proceeding normally, with blood tests and a chest X-ray showing results within the expected range, the Vatican said Wednesday.
The 71-year-old pontiff underwent surgery Tuesday at Rome’s Gemelli hospital to remove the lower lobe of his right lung after doctors detected a localized nodule. An examination of tissue during the operation confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, the doctors said on Tuesday.

ROME – Pope Leo XIV is out of bed, walking and eating following an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung, and has undergone post-surgery tests which show his progress is “normal”, his doctors said on Oct 14.
Part of the Pope’s right lung was removed in an operation at Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Oct 13 and the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics is now awaiting the results of a biopsy to determine if the cancer has spread.
Blood tests and a chest X-ray meanwhile “confirm a normal post-operative course”, doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora said in a statement released on Oct 14 by the Vatican.
“The values are within the expected range for the type of procedure performed,” they said.
The discovery on Oct 13 that Leo’s nodule was cancerous plunged the Catholic Church into a period of uncertainty.
But a day later, his doctors said his recovery was “proceeding as expected” and the pontiff had eaten both breakfast and lunch, been walking about his room, and had done some respiratory physiotherapy.
“It’s a shock for everyone. We’re in ‘wait-and-see’ mode,” a Vatican source told AFP.
The sporty 71-year-old, who was elected as the first American pope only in 2025, made the surprise announcement that he would be undergoing surgery after Sunday prayers.
Support
Messages of support flooded in from around the world, including from Britain’s King Charles III, who is also being treated for an undisclosed cancer.
Flying outside the hospital north of the Vatican a banner read “Long live the Pope!”
Experts said much would depend on how advanced the cancer was, and whether it had spread, but the Vatican has said it had been detected early and was localised.
The Vatican said the Pope’s recovery should take around a week. All his audiences have been cancelled until Oct 20.
“If we are dealing with stage I or II disease, and recovery is good... the patient can resume a normal life and usual activities within a few weeks,” Alain Gelibter, an oncologist at Rome’s Policlinico Umberto I hospital, told AFP.
Chicago-born Leo is staying in a room on the 10th floor of the building, next to a papal suite with a private chapel that is currently under renovation.
He had entered the hospital smiling and waving on Oct 13.
In the hospital chapel, dozens of faithful prayed for the Pope’s health during the operation.
New uncertainty
The shock news of the tennis-playing Pope’s illness has rattled the Catholic Church.
A Vatican source told AFP the Pope seemed “unwell” after his trip to France at the end of September.
“If this forces him to slow down, it might not be a bad thing, given his very hectic pace,” the source said.
Expert Marco Politi, who has spent decades covering the Vatican, told AFP: “The Church is now in a state of uncertainty. When Leo was elected everyone foresaw a long papacy.”
Hendro Munsterman, a theologian and expert for Dutch newspaper Nederlands Dagblad, told AFP “we have a pope whom everyone described as young, active and athletic. Now, we have a pope who also has his own vulnerabilities, which will change his image.”
His health issues may prompt him to speed up personnel appointments, Munsterman said.
Politi said Leo had been working on “repairing” rifts between various wings of the Church, and many will want him “to continue with this important mission as soon as possible”.
Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, celebrated a mass on St Peter’s Square on Oct 14 that was to have been presided over by the Pope.
The surgery has raised questions about whether Leo will go ahead with a lengthy visit in November to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he worked as a missionary for two decades.
It marks Leo’s first hospitalisation since he became pope on May 8, 2025.
The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo’s predecessor, Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments. AFP

Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:12:46 BST
00:12:46 KST

Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
- Published
Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.
The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.
The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.
- What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis 
  - Published23 hours ago
- Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next 
  - Published1 day ago
- Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says 
  - Published1 day ago
He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits.
Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.
The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.
Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

Mont Blanc: new French measurements, summit 'grows' to 4,807m
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:12:34 UTC
00:12:34 KST

New measurements from Saint-Gervais-Mont-Blanc show Western Europe's highest peak at 4,807.47 metres, almost two metres higher than in 2023. Experts say the change is due to the thickness of the snow and ice cap.
The idea of a mountain growing may sound strange, but that is exactly what happens. Its height can even change in just a few years, as has occurred with Mont Blanc which, according to measurements released in France on Wednesday, now reaches 4,807.47 metres above sea level, almost two metres more than in 2023.
The new calculations were carried out on 17 September by experts from the Haute-Savoie Departmental Chamber of Surveyors, whose territory includes part of the mountain shared by France and Italy.
The results were officially presented on Wednesday in Saint-Gervais-Mont-Blanc, on the French side of the massif, showing an increase of 1.88 metres in three years, reversing the trend of previous years, when the summit had been lower.
Presenting the results, the president of the Chamber of Surveyors, Jean des Garets, recalled that "the summit is in constant motion".
Why Mont Blanc's altitude changes over time
The apparent "growth" is not due to movements of the mountain itself but to variations in the snow and ice cap that covers the top.
The height of Europe's second-highest peak changes according to the accumulation and redistribution of snow, influenced by wind, precipitation, temperature, sunshine and seasonal weather conditions.
For this reason, the periodic measurement campaigns produce different results. Between 2000 and 2010 the height was repeatedly measured at around 4,810 metres. Afterwards, a gradual decrease was recorded.
In 2021 Mont Blanc reached 4,807.81 metres, while in 2023 it dropped to 4,805.59 metres, the lowest figure in recent years. The 2026 measurement, by contrast, puts the mountain back above 4,807 metres.
The Alps' highest peak rises back above 4,807 metres
The new survey confirms that Mont Blanc remains a summit in constant evolution. Compared with the historic figure from 1894, its current altitude is around 27 centimetres higher.
For experts, the succession of measurements is also a useful tool for monitoring the effects of weather and climate conditions on the Alpine environment.

WingXpand unveils swappable brain for drones and rovers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:11:27 UTC
00:11:27 KST

- WingXpand unveiled xPAIR, a swappable control module that runs the company’s aircraft, ground vehicle and watercraft with shared AI and payloads.
- The company says xPAIR has been demonstrated with U.S. Special Forces teams and at U.S. Army events, but has named no customer or price.
U.S. drone maker WingXpand has unveiled xPAIR, a removable control unit that the company says can be moved between its small fixed-wing aircraft, a ground vehicle and a small boat, letting one set of AI software and sensors run uncrewed systems in the air, on land and on water.
The Schaumburg, Illinois, company introduced the system on Oct. 13 and described it as patent-pending. Operators click the xPAIR module into the xRAI aircraft to watch a wide area from above, into the xTRAIL ground vehicle to get closer without sending a soldier, or into the xSAIL watercraft to reach places accessible only by water. WingXpand calls it the first such system in the world, a claim The Defence Blog could not independently verify.
All three platforms share the same threat-detection AI library, communications and payloads, and are run from one user interface. WingXpand says operators can therefore add vehicle types without buying separate control equipment or retraining for each domain, and that the module can fuse data from different vehicles in real time to give a single picture of the area.
“Our military doesn’t need another autonomous system built for one narrow mission,” said James Barbieri, co-founder and CEO of WingXpand.
The company has not released specifications for the xTRAIL or xSAIL, nor said how long it takes to move the module between vehicles in the field or how much a set costs. It also has not named a military customer for xPAIR itself. A company representative told The Defence Blog the technology is already being adopted by the U.S. Department of War, state governments and Fortune 50 companies, and the release says xPAIR and the company’s other systems have been demonstrated with several U.S. Special Forces teams and at U.S. Army events.
WingXpand is best known for the xRAI, a fixed-wing drone with telescoping wings that packs into a backpack and expands for flight. The company added a vertical takeoff and landing kit in 2024 and has worked with Raytheon under a U.S. Army contract to integrate infrared sensors and AI threat detection into the aircraft. It also won the U.S. Army’s xTechSpecialForces competition and has announced contracts with U.S. Special Operations, the U.S. Army and the U.S. Navy, as well as approval for use by Montana state agencies. The company has listed prices for its xRAI aircraft starting at $14,900.
WingXpand says xPAIR is built in the United States and compliant with the National Defense Authorization Act, which bars federal buyers from drones and components made by Chinese manufacturers. The company also pitches the shared core as a way to scale production, arguing that building one common module lets it adjust the mix of air, ground and maritime vehicles as customer demand changes.

Republicans face expanding midterm backlash over Iran war, living costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:11:00 UTC
00:11:00 KST

Republicans face expanding midterm backlash over Iran war, living costs
TEHRAN — Donald Trump says the approaching U.S. elections will not change his position regarding Iran. Republican candidates are already changing theirs.
With three weeks remaining before the November 3 midterms, an unpopular war and its economic consequences are forcing the president’s party to defend Senate seats in states he carried comfortably in 2024, while Democrats press toward control of the House.
The retreat is visible in campaign spending and candidates’ language.
Republican money has been redirected from North Carolina to Kansas. Iowa Senate nominee Ashley Hinson has called for an “immediate end” to the war on Iran, despite repeatedly voting against House resolutions seeking that outcome.
Republicans are spending heavily in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico threatens Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Washington’s military decisions have become liabilities in places far removed from West Asia. Fuel, transportation, and agricultural costs give voters a daily measure of a war Trump continues to promise will end soon.
His party now has to answer for the difference between those assurances and household bills.
Trump’s economic argument undermined
Pew Research Center’s October 8 findings show how sharply public expectations have changed.
Among 5,062 adults that were surveyed between September 28 and October 4, 65 percent disapproved of Trump’s handling of military action against Iran; only 33 percent approved.
Republican and Republican-leaning approval fell from 69 percent in March to 63 percent. Democrats remained overwhelmingly opposed.
The public has also abandoned expectations of a short operation. In March, 43 percent believed the war would end within six months. Now, 47 percent expect it to continue for more than another year, and another 30 percent anticipate six to 12 additional months. Trump’s promises are running against an increasingly skeptical electorate.
Economic concerns help explain that skepticism. 73 percent expressed strong concern about higher gasoline and fuel prices caused by the war. 61 percent of Republicans shared that concern. Fear of American military casualties was almost as widespread, at 71 percent overall.
On October 9, the University of Michigan reported that consumer sentiment had fallen to 46.3, from September’s 48.1. Expected inflation over the next year reached 4.7 percent, compared with 3.4 percent in February before the U.S.-Israeli war began.
These are expectations, not measured inflation, but they show households anticipating further pressure. Lower-income consumers reported particularly steep declines in confidence.
Trump has promised that oil prices would “drop like a rock” once the war ended. For candidates approaching November 3, promised relief offers less protection than prices voters can actually see.
Republicans defend an expanding Senate map
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for outright control, which requires breakthroughs in states Trump won by double digits as well as successful defenses of their own seats.
The opportunity has widened, but the arithmetic remains difficult.
North Carolina provides one of the clearest Democratic openings. Former governor Roy Cooper faces former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley for retiring Senator Thom Tillis’s seat.
Polls published October 13 placed Cooper ahead by eight to 14 points. A major Republican super PAC has shifted resources toward Kansas, where Senator Roger Marshall faces Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton.
Texas demands a far larger Republican investment. Paxton defeated incumbent John Cornyn in the Republican contest with Trump’s backing.
Republicans have spent approximately $210 million on the Senate race, against Democrats’ $39 million, Reuters reported. Yet a ReconMR/Siena survey conducted October 5-8 put Talarico ahead 48-44 percent.
That result deserves attention without being mistaken for a victory. Texas has not elected a Democrat statewide since 1994. Paxton’s difficulties have given Democrats an opening, but Republicans retain enormous resources and a long-established advantage.
In Maine, Susan Collins faces former state Senate president Troy Jackson. A recent Washington Post-Schar School survey placed Jackson ahead 50-46 percent.
Alaska’s Dan Sullivan is defending against former representative Mary Peltola under ranked-choice voting.
In Ohio, former senator Sherrod Brown challenges Jon Husted, appointed after JD Vance became vice president.
Democrats need to protect Georgia and Michigan. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff entered July with nearly $43 million available against Republican challenger Mike Collins’s $2.1 million.
Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed faces former congressman Mike Rogers for retiring Senator Gary Peters’s seat, with recent surveys showing a competitive race despite Democratic leads.
Israel policy and money pouring in
Michigan brings the foreign policy dispute into an unusually direct view. During their debate on October 8, El-Sayed said Israel has lobbied Washington into the Iran war and challenged Rogers’s support for the war. “I don’t want to be pushed into a war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in a war with Iran,” he said.
His argument, which has become increasingly popular, confronts a longstanding assumption in Washington that close military alignment with Israel serves American security regardless of its regional consequences. It also gives anti-war voters a position more specific than general dissatisfaction with Trump.
The fight extends to campaign financing. Senator Bernie Sanders, who for years has tried to create a daylight between the current Netanyahu government and the Israeli regime in general, said in an October 2 post on X that AIPAC planned to spend $233 million "against candidates criticizing Benjamin Netanyahu’s government."
El-Sayed won his primary despite extensive pro-Israel spending supporting opponent Haley Stevens.
Republicans have another powerful financial backer. Reuters reported on October 12 that Elon Musk had spent roughly $366 million during the election cycle, including $276 million since July, to help preserve Republican control.
His interests are tangible: House Democrats have called for investigations into his government contracts and work leading Trump’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency.
Offering accountability without a guaranteed reversal
Republican vulnerability reaches beyond the Senate. Analysts estimate that only 40 to 50 House districts are genuinely competitive, despite all 435 seats being contested.
Redistricting and partisan sorting limit the gains available even in a favorable Democratic year.
In 2018, Democrats gained 41 seats; analysts interviewed by Reuters now anticipate a considerably narrower majority if the party wins. State contests reinforce the uncertainty.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott faces Democrat Gina Hinojosa in a race, producing sharply different surveys. YouGov’s poll, conducted between September 28 and October 5, put Hinojosa ahead 48-47 percent; an earlier Fox News survey favored Abbott 52-47. Neither establishes a decisive advantage.
The October 12 raid of Representative Ilhan Omar’s Washington home added another dispute to the campaign.
U.S. federal agents, this time under Homeland Security Investigations, executed a court-approved warrant in a criminal investigation whose details remain limited.
Omar characterized the raid as a calculated effort to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement, declaring that state intimidation would not silence her.
Ultimately, while a Democratic victory may yield incremental opportunities for limited oversight, it does not guarantee an immediate or automatic end to the war.
The House’s September 15 demand that Trump stop military action or obtain congressional authorization passed 220-204, with seven Republicans joining Democrats, but remains nonbinding.
American electoral discontent is measurable. However, enforceable restraint on American military aggression is still unproven and looks unlikely.
Although domestic electoral discontent can be readily documented, effective and enforceable restraint on U.S. military action remains elusive and improbable.

Netflix is laying off 6% of its workforce, or roughly 1,000 employees, in its biggest cuts since 2022, according to an internal memo seen by Reuters, as the streaming pioneer faces tough competition for viewers from legacy rivals and YouTube.
The bulk of the job cuts would be in Netflix’s product, tech, legal and human-resources teams, the email co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos sent to employees on Wednesday showed.
“Our mission – to entertain the world – is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” they said in the memo.
“Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast.”
Netflix shares, down about 25% so far this year, rose 0.7% on Wednesday. The company had about 16,000 employees at the end of last year.
This year, the streaming company faced doubts about its ability to sustain the growth that disrupted the US media industry by putting pressure on cable TV businesses.
Engagement, or the amount of time users spend on Netflix, has become a key concern for investors as platforms such as YouTube and TikTok attract viewers with free-to-watch, user-generated content that gives them a cost advantage over Netflix.
A failed pursuit of Warner Bros Discovery’s streaming and studio assets earlier this year deepened doubts about Netflix’s strategy. Paramount completed its $110bn Warner Bros acquisition earlier this month to form Skydance.
“They haven’t been able to find like another line of major revenue,” said Ross Benes, a senior analyst at eMarketer, adding the company remained reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a ceiling.
“Eventually, because they’ve kind of nearing a ceiling with that, they’ll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that’s where it’s been more of a struggle.“
Netflix has been trying to expand beyond its subscription business by investing in an ad tier, live programming and gaming.
Its last major round of layoffs came in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs in two rounds after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.
The Wall Street Journal first reported on Wednesday’s memo.

It also launched a crowdfunding campaign to cover the extra costs.
The central Mediterranean crossing from North Africa to Italy and southern France is one of the world's most dangerous migrant routes, used by migrants from Africa and the Middle East seeking to reach Europe, often in overcrowded or unseaworthy boats.
Spanish NGO Open Arms said it had also scaled back its central Mediterranean missions in recent years because of rising fuel costs and Italy's policy of assigning rescue vessels ports in northern Italy. The practice can require ships to sail for two or three days from their operating area, increasing costs and reducing time available for search-and-rescue work.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing, anti-immigration government has repeatedly argued that humanitarian rescue vessels encourage migrants to attempt the crossing.

More than 455,000 individual investors have been affected, it has said.

Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says

Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says
The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after surgery to remove a cancerous growth on his lung.
Pope Leo XIV is out of bed, walking, eating and has undergone respiratory physiotherapy, according to a doctor’s note published by the Vatican a day after his lung cancer surgery.
A blood test and chest X-ray revealed “normal post-operative” progress, doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora said, adding that values were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”.
“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room”, they said, adding that “he resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch.”
“Recovery is proceeding as planned,” the doctors said.
Part of lung removed
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican on Tuesday.
Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment.
The Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”.
A medical statement shared by The Holy See’s press office, following the surgery, noted the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer.
After the procedure, Pope Leo returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled.
The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.

The ex-OpenAI employee allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room".
OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI after it found a hidden recording device in an executive conference room in its San Francisco office, which led to the firing of an employee.
The suspect was identified as employee Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, who was arrested on October 9, about a week after OpenAI discovered the surveillance device. He made an initial appearance in a US court on Tuesday.

Conversations in the conference room "frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," the Justice Department said.

“We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” OpenAI said in a statement posted on X.
The ChatGPT maker said it had “no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data”.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (€200,000) fine, followed by three years of supervised release.

UK’s only naval icebreaker breaks down – Telegraph
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:07:27 UTC
00:07:27 KST

UK’s only naval icebreaker breaks down – Telegraph
The British Navy has been left without its only icebreaker after HMS Protector suffered double engine failure at sea, The Telegraph reported on Tuesday. The breakdown adds to mounting concerns about Britain’s readiness for a major war and persistent funding problems.
HMS Protector, which was originally built in Norway in 2001, suffered simultaneous engine defects while departing Britain and had to be towed back to the Devonport naval base in Plymouth, the report says.
Maintenance failures are suspected, according to The Telegraph, although the full extent of the damage is unclear. If it cannot be repaired, a replacement may not arrive until the 2030s, the paper said.
One Navy source cited by The Telegraph described the incident as a “catastrophic failure.” Former HMS Endurance Commander Tom Sharpe warned that losing the icebreaker would undermine Britain’s presence in the South Atlantic amid renewed tensions with Argentina over the Falkland Islands (Malvinas, as they are known in Argentina) and the Sea Lion offshore oil project, as well as growing competition in the Arctic. 
“These ships cost a tiny fraction of the defense budget yet deliver an outsized effect in presence and soft power,” Sharpe said.
HMS Protector typically deploys to the South Atlantic and Antarctic, conducting hydrographic surveys, supporting scientific stations, and carrying personnel for inspections under international agreements. The vessel, which has a crew of around 88, does not have any heavy weapons but can carry machine guns and embark specialist Royal Marines.
The UK relies on the ship to project its influence in the Antarctic, where its territorial claims overlap with those of Argentina and Chile, though they have effectively been frozen under the 1959 Antarctic Treaty. Britain also operates a separate civilian icebreaker, RRS Sir David Attenborough, but it cannot replace HMS Protector’s naval patrol role.
The reported incident comes after the UK Navy announced in July the retirement of two more Type 23 frigates, leaving the fleet with just five frigates alongside six destroyers. Around the same time, retired Naval Staff chief Lord Alan West suggested that the British fleet has been reduced to the worst state in history.
In March, First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins acknowledged that the Navy is not ready for war, saying it aims to reach that level of preparedness by the end of the decade.
Officials have also sounded the alarm over the hollowed-out military budget, with the Treasury struggling to find £4.7 billion ($6.2 billion) for its multi-year military investment strategy.

Israeli satire show takes jab at far-right's vehement opposition to NAZA documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:07:07 UTC
00:07:07 KST

Israel's SNL-style satire show Eretz Nehederet portrayed NAZA co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor alongside far-right firebrand Tally Gotliv as mythical sirens spouting conspiracy theories and accusations from opposite ends of the political spectrum in an episode aired Tuesday.
The four-minute sketch, a parody of Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster "The Odyssey," follows an Israeli soldier trying to return home after three years of war in the Gaza Strip. It opened the first episode of the show's special pre-election season.
Warning: Spoilers for "The Odyssey" ahead:
מסע החזרה של אודי סאוס מהמילואים הביתה בימוי: גדי פורטנוי אמן ai: דניאל קוץ
The sketch features an Israeli soldier named "Udi Seus" – a play on "Odysseus" – trying to return to his wife and son after 500 days of reserve duty.
Along the way, he encounters Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who continues promising "total victory" and urges him to keep fighting in Gaza, Lebanon and Turkey; a Cyclops-like figure modeled on United Torah Judaism leader Yitzchak Goldknopf, who refuses to support drafting Haredi men into the military; and blocked roads caused by traffic that Transportation Minister Miri Regev, portrayed as a goddess, has failed to manage.
The sketch reaches its climax at what it calls "the most difficult obstacle": the mythical sirens. As they approach, the main character has himself tied down while the other two soldiers block out the voices with headphones.
The three sirens are modeled on Gotliv, who recently left Netanyahu's Likud party to join Itamar Ben-Gvir's far-right Otzma Yehudit party, and NAZA co-directors Abraham and Szor.
The Gotliv character, who in real life is notorious for repeated disruptions during legal and state proceedings, rattles off conspiracy theories, including claims that the IDF chief of staff had prior knowledge of Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack and that Israeli pilots who threatened to stop volunteering for reserve duty during the government's 2023 judicial overhaul were "traitors."
On the other side, Abraham and Szor tell the soldiers: "The pilots are murderers, and you are NAZA criminals" – pronouncing "NAZA" in Hebrew in a way that sounds similar to "Nazi criminals."
As the tied-down soldier screams, Gotliv yells: "That's not impressive; I can scream louder. Now I can scream with Jewish Power!" – a reference to the English translation of Otzma Yehudit.
As the NAZA filmmakers applaud, the screaming soldier asks them to stop. Another soldier references the film's record-breaking standing ovation at last month's Venice Film Festival and says, "We have at least 20-25 more minutes."
Israeli human rights lawyer Snir Klein accused Eretz Nehederet of McCarthyism and said its writers were taking part in a "witch hunt" against the NAZA directors.
"There must be a special place in hell for the group of comedians who are serving Tally Gotliv and her friends under the guise of criticism…" he wrote on X.
"They are just an instrument that allows the Israeli mainstream to feel like it is being critical while it is actually unable to move away from the consensus dictated by the government."
Nir Wolf, TV critic for the right-leaning Israel Hayom newspaper, wrote that the season premiere showed how much Eretz Nehederet caters to the mainstream despite frequent criticism from the right that it is "too leftist."
Wolf said the show had played a major role in "normalizing the insanity" of Netanyahu's coalition by often turning figures such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Tally Gotliv into entertainment.

NGO: Brussels confirms Czech PM’s agri business conflict of interest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:06:52 UTC
00:06:52 KST

NGO: Brussels confirms Czech PM’s agri business conflict of interest
Babiš placed Agrofert in a trust fund before returning to power in an effort to preserve its eligibility for EU farm cash — but Brussels remains unconvinced.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’ links to the agro-chemical giant Agrofert represent a conflict of interest and EU subsidies could be withheld as a result, according to an NGO’s account of a letter it received from the European Commission.
Ahead of his return to power in December 2025, Babiš placed Agrofert in a trust fund in an effort to preserve its eligibility for EU farm cash. However, that appears not to have convinced Brussels. Transparency International Czechia quotes a letter from DG AGRI Director-General Elisabeth Werner, confirming that “the Commission concluded that Mr Babiš’ situation constitutes a conflict of interest” under EU financial regulations.
The trust fund and “measures currently being implemented and notified to the Commission are insufficient” to resolve it, she adds, according to the watchdog NGO, which said it was not allowed to publish the letter.
Advertisement
Babiš has been under renewed scrutiny over Agrofert — a large agro-chemical conglomerate and a major recipient of EU funds — as well as other companies since his return to power last year. Babiš placed the company in a trust fund in a bid to avoid a conflict of interest, but the arrangement has raised questions from both the Commission and the Czech opposition, partly because his children would benefit from it after his death.
Babiš has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. “I don’t own Agrofert, I never will again and I don’t benefit from it in any way. I don’t know what else I’m supposed to do,” he told Czech media last month. “Apparently, even if I shot myself, it still wouldn’t be enough.”
Babiš’ office did not immediately reply to POLITICO’s request for comment about the contents of the letter.
Werner warned in the letter that Brussels would take all necessary steps to protect EU funds, “including the possible interruption of payment deadlines, suspension of payments or application of financial corrections,” according to TI Czechia.
TI Czechia Executive Director David Kotora told POLITICO that he received the letter in September. A follow-up letter from Werner dated Oct. 5 gives the NGO permission to share the contents of the letter without publishing it.
The conflict-of-interest dispute echoes Babiš’ first term as prime minister, when a Commission audit found he still controlled Agrofert. That left Czech taxpayers to foot the bill for EU subsidies deemed to be erroneously paid.
History could now repeat itself as Brussels last month froze €3.18 million in reimbursements to the Czech state for farm subsidies paid out to Agrofert. That followed its earlier May decision that it would not reimburse any paid-out subsidies until doubts about his involvement in the business could be put to rest.
Commission spokesperson Louise Bogey confirmed it had sent a letter to TI Czechia in September, but would not comment on its content. However, she pointed to her remarks at a Sept. 8 midday briefing, during which she said Babiš was in a “potential conflict of interest” and that “the Commission considers the trust fund set up by Mr. Babiš does not sufficiently mitigate this situation.”
Czechia’s agricultural paying agency, which earlier decided that the conglomerate is eligible for EU subsidies despite the Commission’s warning, said Tuesday it had sent clarifications to the Commission this week.
Agrofert spokesperson Pavel Heřmanský said neither Agrofert nor any of its subsidiaries were involved in the communication between the Commission and Czech authorities.
“The cited letter from DG AGRI expresses the opinion of one of the European Commission’s departments. It does not constitute an official position of the European Commission,” said Heřmanský in a statement, adding that “only the Court of Justice of the European Union can provide a binding interpretation of European Union law.”
He added: “We remain convinced that we have received and continue to receive subsidies in compliance with both Czech and European law.”

Croatia's wartime grievances threaten Montenegro's hopes of joining EU by 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:06:30 UTC
00:06:30 KST

Croatia's list of grievances with Montenegro include missing persons, war crimes, prison camps, property seizures and borders. Podgorica has closed 21 of 33 chapters, but Zagreb is blocking progress unless bilateral issues are resolved.
Croatia has warned that a series of unresolved disputes with neighbouring Montenegro, including wartime abuses, property claims and contested borders, could stand in the way of the country's ambition to join the European Union by 2028.
In a document sent to other EU governments on Monday and seen by Euronews, Zagreb set out eight demands it wants Montenegro to address before completing its accession to the bloc.
Montenegro is widely regarded as the frontrunner among countries seeking EU membership, with hopes of becoming the bloc's 28th member by 2028. But its long-running disputes with Croatia, many dating back to the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, threaten to derail that timetable.
“Croatia sincerely wishes to turn the page on this painful chapter of shared history and build a forward-looking relationship with Montenegro. Yet mutual trust and genuine, lasting reconciliation cannot be built without resolving these issues,” the document reads.
Montenegro made further progress towards EU membership on Monday, completing negotiations in three more policy areas – statistics, economic policy and employment – bringing the total to 21 out of 33.
However, Croatia is blocking progress in four other areas, covering transport, foreign relations, fundamental rights and home affairs. Because every existing EU member has a say over the accession process, Zagreb has considerable leverage over its neighbour's membership bid.
The document expands on grievances previously outlined by Croatia's Foreign Ministry in July, many rooted in the wars that accompanied Yugoslavia's collapse.
Among the most sensitive is Zagreb's demand for compensation for around 300 Croatian nationals detained and mistreated at the Morinj prison camp in Montenegro between October 1991 and August 1992. Croatian civilians and prisoners of war were forcibly transferred to the camp during the conflict.
Croatia also wants a memorial plaque at the former camp to remain permanently visible. A large metal frame was installed around it following protests by Montenegrin nationalist groups.
Another demand concerns the fate of 14 people still missing from Croatia's war of independence. Zagreb wants Montenegro to help locate their remains, describing the issue as a “major humanitarian issue that has yet to be resolved.”
A further point concerns war crimes: Croatia wants command responsibility for the crimes against civilians committed at Morinj to be considered in the cases of already convicted war criminals.
Croatia also expects Montenegro to resolve long-standing property disputes dating back to the early 1990s, involving Croatian families unlawfully deprived of their property without adequate compensation.
The paper points out that a 2021 law enabled the restitution of land in a region predominantly inhabited by the Albanian minority, “raising concerns about unequal treatment in comparable cases.”
Zagreb is also calling for the return of the Jadran, a sail training ship which has been under Montenegrin control since Yugoslavia dissolved in 1991.
Finally, Croatia wants the territorial disputes with its neighbour settled, over both the land and maritime border, in line with the Arbitration Commission of the Conference on Yugoslavia.
Croatia itself has an unresolved border dispute with Slovenia, although this did not prevent it from joining the EU in 2013.
“Croatia has consistently encouraged Montenegro to resolve outstanding bilateral issues while actively supporting its EU accession,” the paper continues. “Despite Croatia’s sustained efforts and constructive approach, none of the outstanding issues has yet been resolved.”

Renewed fighting risks ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ in Yemen, aid groups warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:06:18 UTC
00:06:18 KST

Renewed fighting risks ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ in Yemen, aid groups warn
Almost one million people cut off from food aid as health infrastructure overwhelmed by war-wounded.
The humanitarian groups the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the World Food Programme (WFP) have sounded the alarm over the worsening humanitarian situation in Yemen amid ramped-up fighting.
An estimated 800,000 people have been cut off from life-saving food assistance as front lines have rapidly shifted between Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis, according to the WFP.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP’s country director in Yemen.
The crisis is worst in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where an estimated 600,000 people have no access to food assistance, including 200,000 women and children, the United Nations agency said in a statement.
Taiz has been the focus of recent clashes and is hemmed in by Houthi forces, imperiling aid deliveries.
The WFP said that the loss of access is especially alarming given that Taiz has some of the country’s highest levels of food insecurity.
Across Yemen, more than 18 million people do not have enough to eat, it added, while the latest monitoring shows a record 74 percent of households in accessible areas cannot meet their daily food needs.
Casualties flood hospitals
Meanwhile, “overwhelmed” health facilities in Marib, Taiz and along the Red Sea coast were bearing the brunt of the fighting in those areas, according to a statement released by the ICRC, with some receiving more than 700 cases in a single week,
Firas Abu Samra, the ICRC’s health services coordinator, said only a handful of facilities operating in Yemen can provide comprehensive care for the injured.
Front-line hospitals are taking in large numbers of wounded while running short of surgical supplies, anaesthetics, oxygen and medicines, he said.
“Additional pressure on hospitals can mean fewer beds, fewer supplies and less capacity to treat people with conditions unrelated to the conflict”, said Eduardo Toro, an ICRC surgeon at Marib General Hospital.
Christine Cipolla, the ICRC’s head of delegation in Yemen, said the country’s battered health system is ill-prepared to cope with any more fighting.
“Our concern is that the system may have little capacity left to absorb a major surge in casualties,” she said.

Trump says massive oil, gas exploration set to begin in 'our Greenland'
COPENHAGEN, Oct 14 - US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that "massive oil, gas and mineral exploration" was set to begin on Greenland, a contentious statement on a territory that has resisted his efforts to control it and has banned new drilling for crude.
Trump described the Danish Arctic island which is run by a semi-autonomous government as "our new and beautiful Greenland" in a social media post that hailed what he said were US gains from a security deal signed in September.
The Greenlandic prime minister's office declined to comment on Trump's statement.
The Danish foreign ministry and Greenland's ministry of mineral resources did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
TRUMP HAILS US SECURITY GAINS
Greenland has been caught up in a confrontation with Trump who has been saying since 2019 the US should buy or take the strategically located and mineral-rich island for security reasons. On several occasions, he refused to rule out force.
Along with Denmark, the US and Greenland reached an agreement last month to allow the US to boost its military presence on the island - a deal that had appeared to settle the standoff.
The agreement did not allocate any rights for mining or drilling.
"Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform.
"There are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World," he added without naming any specific deals or specific development.
Greenland banned uranium mining in its territory along with all future exploration of oil in 2021.
The government has said it is reviewing whether a Texas firm, Greenland Energy, can use permits predating that prohibition.
The company said in August this year it had plans to drill for oil in 2027 at an untested basin on Greenland's east coast, although it lacked its own permit to do so. The previous owner, ARCO, spent heavily on seismic work in the 1970s but never drilled.
Independent Danish security policy advisor Jacob Kaarsbo said Trump's comments could be seen as a sign that his desire to control Greenland remained unchanged.
"It is extremely dangerous to view this agreement between the Trump administration and Denmark as something that has altered Trump’s intentions," he said.
The 10-page deal between the US, Denmark and Greenland paved the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
"Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," Trump said in his post on Wednesday.
"It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" he added. REUTERS

15:05:53 UTC
00:05:53 KST

It was a flowing speech packed full of precise statistics – but Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK Senedd member, was not quite the gifted orator he had first appeared. The periodic flashing in his spectacles seemed to give the game away as he spoke for five minutes in the Senedd chamber without a glance at his notes.
“Cardiff reviewed 192 roads, following 933 requests, and only four routes have returned to 30mph,” he said as he led the party’s charge to abolish 20mph traffic zones. “£38.3m wasted to implement this policy and up to £8.9bn in an act of economic self-harm.”
It was probably no feat of memory – rather, the Reform member for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr was suspected of using smart glasses that turned his lenses into tiny teleprompters.
In the days afterwards, Senedd members said the issue of smart glasses – popularised by Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta – needed to be dealt with at pace, with explicit guidance developed on their use.
There was no suggestion that O’Connell’s glasses were recording. But it has prompted a fresh debate about the increasingly popular technology, with the House of Commons facing calls to ban smart glasses at Westminster.
The Liberal Democrats wrote to Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, on Wednesday urging him to act amid the “increasing use of smart glasses” on the parliamentary estate. They warned that with Christmas coming, even more people could start using the AI-enabled devices in 2027.
The technology has myriad implications. Anna Sabine, the Liberal Democrat spokesperson for culture, media and sport, said smart glasses could lead to debates becoming increasingly “managed”.
“How much is the quality of what an MP is saying actually down to what they’re getting through the AI glasses?” she said. “It’s a really interesting question.”
She said she had not yet identified anyone wearing smart glasses in parliament but added: “This is the problem: I wouldn’t necessarily know.” A law would help to keep the estate and the work MPs did “private and secure”.
Sabine added: “Smart glasses can record video and take photographs discreetly … creating a particular risk to the existing rules on the parliamentary estate [limiting recording and photography].
“I am regularly in meetings with documents or talking about important, private matters on behalf of my constituents. I am sure you will agree that the details of such cases should never be at risk of being shared because someone is filming or taking pictures discreetly.
“Because smart glasses look like ordinary glasses, and increasingly their recording indicator lights can be covered or disabled, filming could easily go unnoticed by security teams, putting private information at risk.”
A spokesperson for the UK parliament said it was reviewing its policy on the use of camera-equipped smart glasses, as well as other forms of wearable technology, on the parliamentary estate.
The senior deputy speaker of the House of Lords, Lord Ponsonby, told parliament last month that the review “is considering the implications of these emerging technologies and whether additional guidance is required”.
He added: “This work will bring together expertise from those responsible for filming and photography policy, physical and information security, privacy and data protection compliance and accessibility and reasonable-adjustment requirements, ensuring that any future approach appropriately balances security, privacy, operational needs and accessibility considerations.”
O’Connell has been contacted for comment. On Sunday he posted a picture on X of himself wearing a pair of comedy large pink glasses for a breast cancer charity, with the message: “Trialling some new glasses for the chamber this week. Apparently my last ones caused quite a stir.”

German leader insists Ukraine aid is not reducing social spending at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:04:14 UTC
00:04:14 KST

Ayhan Simsek
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday defended his government's financial and military support for Ukraine, rejecting opposition party claims that the aid comes at the expense of social spending at home.
Addressing lawmakers in parliament, Merz said continued support for Ukraine is essential to safeguard peace and security across Europe as Russia’s threats intensify. He argued that military assistance to Kyiv does not reduce funds available for domestic priorities.
“Not a single euro flowing to Ukraine is being diverted from social or educational spending in our country. Not a single euro is missing," Merz said. He added that they had introduced an exception to Germany’s constitutional debt rule to allow defense-related spending to be financed through additional borrowing.
Merz warned that the danger is concrete rather than theoretical. "We see that Russia's readiness to escalate is rising toward Ukraine, toward our Eastern European neighbors, but also toward our own country," he said.
He slammed the right-wing AfD and the socialist Left Party for downplaying threats and fueling division.
"It is incomprehensible to me how those on the far left and far right continue, to this day, to play down the situation,” he said, accusing them of deliberately driving divisions, uncritically spreading disinformation. "One gets the impression you want the chaos because you want to gain party-political advantages from it."
Opposition lawmakers from the AfD and the Left Party have repeatedly argued that billions of euros in support for Ukraine should instead go to domestic priorities such as pensions and infrastructure.
Merz's conservative CDU/CSU alliance is facing pressure as it trails in opinion polls while the right-wing AfD leads. An INSA survey published this week put the AfD at 30%, the CDU/CSU at 18.5%, the environmentalist Greens at 14%, the center-left SPD at 13.5%, and the Left Party at 10%.

Tokyo summoned the Russian ambassador on Wednesday to lodge a protest over Moscow’s arrest of a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, with the foreign ministry urging “fair and impartial treatment.”
Russia has arrested several citizens of what it calls “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for Western intelligence services.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russia’s foreign ministry identified the reporter Tuesday as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, with a spokeswoman saying he was accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory.”
Moscow’s FSB security service said a Japanese national was arrested on the Far East island of Sakhalin – near a disputed cluster of islands – but did not name the individual.
It said the person had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia’s defenses.
On Wednesday, the Japanese foreign ministry said European Affairs Bureau official Kimitake Nakamura summoned the Russian ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev.
Nakamura “lodged a strong protest with the Russian side over the detention of a Japanese national and the issuance of unilateral statements regarding the case,” the ministry said in a statement.
It added that Tokyo had not received any explanation concerning the case.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitri Peskov meanwhile said in a briefing that the security service “is doing its job.”
Ukraine’s Lyman/Vivaldi Offensive Concludes With Solid Terrain Gains, Russian Losses
“If there are spies, they get caught,” he said.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Japan has not been able to contact the individual and did not know about the arrest until the official announcement from Moscow.
Japanese diplomats in Russia have requested “the prompt provision of information” and “humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the Russian announcement but was “still confirming the details.”
“Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority, and we are responding accordingly,” the newspaper said.
Territorial dispute
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national,” and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, TASS and RIA Novosti news agencies reported, citing the security service.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until Dec. 12.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia... to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
This was “not an isolated case,” she added.
The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Media rights group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called for the journalist’s “rights to be respected and for his release,” saying in a statement on X that the gathering of information is part of journalism.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him.
He was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention.
It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.
Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the northeast coast of Japan and to the southwest of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The Kuril Islands – called the Northern Territories in Japan – have been under Russia’s control since the end of World War II, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.
On Wednesday, Japan protested a visit by a Chinese delegation to one of the Northern Territories islands controlled by Moscow and claimed by Tokyo, calling it “absolutely unacceptable.”
The Chinese foreign ministry meanwhile said a delegation visited Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the capital of Sakhalin Oblast in Russia, which is not on the disputed islands.
They “carried out friendly exchange activities with the local side,” ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said.
