Ukraine hits two Russian refineries despite Trump’s demands – Moscow
Ukraine targeted two Russian oil refineries on Wednesday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak has said.
The facilities are in Russia’s Saratov and Ryazan regions, Novak said on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum. He did not specify whether either refinery sustained damage.
“We can see that the Ukrainian side is making no moves towards an energy ceasefire,” Novak said, referring to a limited ceasefire between Moscow and Kiev proposed by US President Donald Trump.
On Sunday, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire. Neither Moscow nor Kiev, however, has confirmed the truce, sending out mixed messages on the matter.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said the announcement “was news” for him, but expressed readiness to stop attacking Russian refineries should Moscow halt strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also declined to confirm the deal, stating that contacts were still ongoing. Peskov also reiterated Moscow’s longstanding position that Russia seeks a long-term peace agreement rather than a temporary truce.
The US president has also accused Zelensky of seeking to “make problems” for the US and the whole world by ignoring demands to stop its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
“Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world. And we told him, do whatever you want, but don’t hit the diesel fuel,” Trump said last week. “And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel. He can do whatever he wants, but he can’t do that. He’d better damn well stop.”
On Friday, the US eased its restrictions on Russia’s diesel trade, allowing it to be sold, delivered, and imported into the US until April 7, 2027.
According to Trump, Moscow agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November, and 1 million more shortly thereafter. Novak confirmed the figures, saying Russia will move to lift its own export restrictions immediately.
According to US media reports, Trump struck the deal after Zelensky repeatedly ignored demands to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. The US president accused the Ukrainian leader of exacerbating the global fuel crisis.
Kiev reportedly asked the US what it would get for stopping its attacks on Russian refineries. The Trump administration suggested that Kiev is receiving enough help and is in no position to demand more.

The incident comes amid another suspected act of sabotage targeting Starlink infrastructure in Europe.
In late September, Militarnyi reported a fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland that provided satellite connectivity to users across Europe, including Ukraine. Polish investigators later determined that the fire had been deliberately set.
Polish prosecutors were investigating the possibility of sabotage on behalf of Russian intelligence services. On October 12, two suspects in the arson were detained in Germany. The Polish government said it considered the incident an act of hybrid warfare and linked it to Russia.

‘The Mind is a Computer or LLM’: We Need to Talk About the Effect of this Simplistic View on our Relationships to our Own Minds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:39 UTC
00:00:39 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
We repeatedly encounter claims that the brain is an LLM, or a computer, or very like one of these things. What effect does repeatedly encountering this debate have on how we understand ourselves? I think it’s worth asking, because, in my view, the debate isn’t one we would be having were it not for the historical circumstances.
I’ve argued against this view plenty. Today, I dig deeper. What effect is it having that many of us believe this view is true? Or, even if we do not believe it, what effect is it having that everywhere we read articles about it, suggesting it is at least possibly true?
My classrooms are tech free this term and I am witnessing more palpably than ever the effect that LLMs are having on our students, but really on our society. As someone who has spent over a decade being nothing short of fascinated with the human mind —yes, I went to undergraduate to enthusiastically pursue psychology only to take a somewhat winded path into Columbia’s philosophy halls for my PhD— I want to bring this theoretical work into a shared practice of exploring and exercising our own cognitive capacities, our own minds. After almost 10 months on Substack experimenting with how to turn my philosophy practical, that day has come.
In this post, I am going to preliminarily sketch my decade+ thinking on brains and minds, and how I think we can use this knowledge to examine our relationships to our own minds in this AI-obsessed age.
Here is my hypothesis: being told on repeat that the brain is a computer of some form (whether in the traditional sense of a something like a digital computer, or, an LLM, see a breakdown here on these views) is having an impact on our relationship to our own cognitive capacities, to our own minds.
There has been much talk about cognitive de-skilling and cognitive decline. These topics are incredibly important, but the question I am asking is a different one.
I’m asking — holding constant whether de-skilling and cognitive decline is a problem for you, and to what extent — whether how we conceive of our minds is impacted, the more we are required to use AI at work, or the more we default towards using it in other aspects of our lives.
Another way to motivate the question is this: most of our mental lives happens below conscious awareness. Assuming this, what kinds of assumptions might we be harbouring about our own minds in the face of how we are told to think about human brains today?
Have we started to believe that LLMs really are better at thinking than us? That they really are more creative than us? Have we started confusing speed, with intelligence? Confident sounding sentences, with knowledge? I think that these are not just questions for research, but conversations we need to be having together and with ourselves.
Let me tell you my unique reasons for believing we desperately need to have these conversations, because it’s rooted in years of thinking about human brains.
I’ve been writing on Substack now for almost 10 months. When I first started out, I did not know what I was doing —I still don’t, obviously — but I did have two general goals. I wanted to share my work in accessible ways, and I wanted to figure out how to turn my insights into something that could make a difference.
I started with the first goal —substantially more achievable — which included writing articles that argued the brain is not a computer, that it’s not an LLM, that mainstream philosophy of mind is also wrong, imho, in how it frames questions of mind, that LLMs do not have language, as well as building a framework that shows why current efforts to understand AI consciousness are, I think, completely off the mark.
Detecting a pattern in any of this? My astute Substack subscribers sure did. Everything I wrote was about what the mind isn’t, what the brain isn’t, and what LLMs don’t have. All my work is showing what’s wrong with the current frameworks.
But what about a positive proposal, Ellen?! Let me explain.
I stand by all of the intellectual arguments I’ve made. And I stand by my decision to only argue negative proposals in theoretical terms (for now, at least). However, today I am in a place where I can explain what the positive proposal might have to look like. All of my thinking here is preliminary of course, but many of you have asked me to push my work into a positive proposal space, and I’m trying to do just that.
Because here’s the thing: There’s a reason that all my intellectual work is about showing where we go awry in our thinking about brains/minds.
It’s because I think there are limits to what we can theoretically or scientifically understand about the mind. Human judgement, human creativity, human thought, I believe we can study aspects of these things scientifically, but I also think that a lot of it escapes scientific frameworks. They are things we have to understand in different ways, through novels, art, or music, for example, or through exercising those capacities for ourselves. Some things about the mind we can only know through experience.
Experiencing these kinds of intellectual moments for myself, for instance, has helped me come to terms with the limits of scientific understanding of minds (though of course, so have the years of study I have done on these topics).
I think back to when I wrote my dissertation, for example, and how there was no way that an LLM could have ever produced it.
The ideas were too sparse in existing literature, the connected thoughts across fields were not well-trodden paths, the intuitions I used to decide what to read, and what not to read, what to focus on, and what not to focus on, could never have been identified by an LLM. I can’t systematise the intuitive knowledge I worked on myself, how could I have even begin to tell an LLM how to do it for me?
And I don’t say these things to toot my own horn. I think every single human being is just like me—infinitely creative and exploratory if given the opportunity, though not infinitely capable of articulating, let alone developing a scientific understanding, of what those intuitive processes look like, or how they work.
But these intuitions and creative urges can be suppressed, if, for example, we never think to exercise them, because —oh, I don’t know — everyone is telling us that LLMs are bigger and better than our own brains… You see where this is going.
With that said, here are some questions I invite you to ask yourself, either by yourself or with others, to see if a broader conversation could happen around these kinds of questions in ways that might help us better relate to AI.
(1) Do I ever think my own mind is inadequate in comparison to an LLM? Why might I think this? This could look like having an idea, plugging it into an LLM, and deciding based on the LLMs response that you don’t want to pursue the idea.
Why exactly might this happen? Why think the LLM is any kind of authority in this situation? What would you have done with the idea prior to the existence of LLMs?
In my view, we shouldn’t compare the ourselves to LLMs, especially not when it comes to our relationship to our own minds and cognitive capacities vs that of LLMs. The human brain should be appreciated on its own terms. Secondarily, we can decide what we think LLMs are good at doing and not doing, where it can help and where it can hinder.
(2) How do you think of the human brain if you were asked about it? Do you think of it as one big computer as you’ve likely seen a lot in the media the last few years? Do you have no conception at all? Whatever ideas you have about the brain, where did you get them? Do you think any of this impacts how you view your own mind?
Sometimes I worry that the simplistic narratives making the headlines will impact our relationship to our minds in daily small ways. For example, the generative capacities of human brains are not understood, though we know the mind is generative from work on language, for instance, and we recognize it intuitively.
The ‘generative’ capacities of LLMs, on the other hand, are well-understood, and the technology produces outputs in an instant. But humans generating ideas can take time. Sitting with an idea. Reading another book that stimulates your mind further and helps you sharpen an idea. Going for a walk, etc.
In the case of our own generative minds, we need patience, we need exposure to an array of ideas, we need reading, we need writing, we need time, and ideally, we need to talk to other humans interested in the same ideas. Being exposed to LLMs that spit out ideas in seconds, might mean that we need to work harder than ever to remember that our brains work differently, and that that’s not a bad thing.
(3) What do you do with inchoate ideas, ideas that are not yet well-formed? Do you let yourself have fragments of ideas, intuitions, or thoughts, and sit with them before being able to clearly articulate what you mean by them? How does your relationship to LLMs influence this process? Does using an LLM help you articulate your ideas more clearly, or does it just give you a thought that feels acceptably like what you were sitting with? Do you hold enough awareness around your thinking to know?
(4) Are there parts of your life that shape your thinking and beliefs in valuable ways that you might not necessarily get from an LLM? Do you pay enough attention to those things? The thought your friend mentioned to you the other day, your child’s curiosity, your partners musings?
(5) Are there things you value about your cognition that you want to preserve for just you, i.e., that you don’t want to outsource to an LLM? Things that give you joy even if the finished product isn’t ‘as good’ or as polished as if you put it through an LLM? Exercising our cognitive capacities as human beings is a good in and of itself. That’s something to bear in mind.
One of the main ideas I keep coming back to in my work is that today, we keep confusing models of the mind with what minds are. One of the deepest consequences of this mistake is that we systematically erase all those parts of our minds that we do not understand, that we cannot neatly fit into the latest, ‘model’ of the mind. Consequently, I am increasingly concerned, we do not pay enough attention to those parts of our mind, and in doing so subconsciously undermine them, through for example not exercising those capacities.
I hope these questions can serve as a way to generate a broader conversation between yourself and others in thinking through these issues.
Thank you for being here. If you found this article valuable, consider a free or paid subscription. You’ll be helping support the existence of rigorous independent philosophical writing on AI consciousness, something we all desperately need today.

Todd Haynes at Lumière Festival: 'It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:37 UTC
00:00:37 KST

"It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely." Euronews Culture sits down with celebrated filmmaker Todd Haynes during this year's Lumière Film Festival.
One of the guests of honour this year at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival is none other than Todd Haynes, one of the most important and singular voices in contemporary American cinema.
The celebrated director and screenwriter of Far From Heaven, I’m Not There, Carol, and May December is known for his pioneering work associated with the New Queer Cinema movement of the early 90s. He then gained acclaim for his films exploring the emotional repercussions of social repression and the unspoken desires revealed by marginalized experiences.
He attends the Lumière Film Festival to present the restored versions of his directorial debut Poison (1991), a provocative exploration of AIDS-era perceptions. He also presents the Julianne Moore-starring psychological drama Safe (1995), marking the first time that these two films have screened in French cinemas since their initial releases.
Euronews Culture sat down with Todd Haynes during the festival to discuss the enduring timeliness of Poison and Safe, his thoughts on the evolving Hollywood ecosystem, as well as his upcoming film De Noche.
Euronews Culture: How does it feel to be at the Lumière Film Festival in Lyon, the birthplace of cinema?
Todd Haynes: Pretty thrillingly natal! No, really, it's a festival I've been hearing so much about for so long. And it really is such a celebration of movies of all kinds, of every genre, of every era. Restorations are presented, artists are attributed, and it's a really remarkable place and atmosphere, and it's so much about just the filmmaking and the films.
There's a retrospective of your films, including two newly restored versions of Poison and Safe. How do you look back on these films, and how do you feel about the fact that there are going to be audiences at this festival who are seeing these two films for the very first time?
I was there for the introduction of Poison. People were asked in the theater who were seeing it for the first time and almost every hand went up! And it was a completely full theatre, so that just demonstrates a kind of interest and curiosity about what's being shown in Lyon, and an audience that is very enthusiastic about it.
So, it's incredibly meaningful. These are my first two features. They are very, very different. Poison came out in the height of the AIDS era and it was among the first couple of films that would join other films in being categorised as the New Queer Cinema. None of which, I don't think, would have been possible outside of that political and socio-economic crisis - the public health crisis of AIDS. In certain times, those kinds of conditions make creating film and documentary, and protest and organised resistance, essential. They drive a kind of urgency that we don't always feel in our medium or our market. That was absolutely true for Poison. And then I made a film [Safe] that also is, in my mind, inconceivable without the AIDS era as a framework. It's a film that takes the place about as far away from the battlefield, if you will, but still engaged. A lot of the themes and issues deal with illness, and the body, and feeling alienated from the world around you...
I had the pleasure of re-watching both films, and that sense of isolation in Safe still feels incredibly prescient.
That’s always surprising and encouraging to hear. I understand how that might be what people could say about Safe. The film was watched again during Covid. There was a lot of discussion about the film and articles that came out were sent to me. And sadly, these issues remain relevant when we're hit by things that are overwhelming and that challenge every single aspect of the way we lead our lives, and the assumptions about how to live our lives that we take for granted.
Both explicitly and implicitly about the AIDS crisis, do you find it heartening or disheartening that Poison and Safe still feel timely? After all, Poison was made at a specific time, and there are many members of the gay, trans, queer communities who continue to feel threatened and continue to express fears...
Absolutely. One does feel at times like we’re in a replay, if not crashing backwards in battles we’ve fought. Battles around reproductive rights, around tolerance and acceptance over queer communities and trans communities. Poison in particular addressed very much that sense of vulnerability that the community was feeling under the siege of AIDS and HIV.
Jean Genet, who's a writer and thinker and poet and playwright who I've always loved - but also derived a certain energy from his attitude about how important it is to remember that being defined marginal... The goal to that is not necessarily to find your way back to the table and become just like everybody else. For him, his queerness, it came out of a criminal background. He liked that homosexuality had this criminal aspect to it. He used that as a way of weaponising his critique of dominant culture. Poison was made at the very end of the 80s and we needed a voice like that.
I'm heartened to see that some of Jean Genet’s books are displayed next to DVDs of your films at the Lumière marketplace...
Oh, I didn’t see that. That’s awesome!
From a European perspective, when you look at present day Hollywood, it’s hard not to see a sense of regression. For instance, to take a recent example, the Paramount-Warner merger feels like it threatens the financing of films from a plurality of voices. What are your thoughts on the evolution of the studio system and Hollywood at the moment?
It's distressing when you see the conglomeration of huge media organizations that one might imagine would provide enough revenue and foundation for risk-taking to still occur. But sadly, that is rarely what you end up seeing. I don't feel it, particularly in the moment, among some of the big streaming companies. There's a sense of wanting to repeat what worked the last time, and keep replicating what the audiences seem to crave. And that's tough.
For my last couple films, we've really gone elsewhere. I mean, we did sell May December, my last feature, to Netflix - and they were a fantastic company, full of incredibly smart people who really believed in the film. But the way we made the film was through the limited amount of investment that we absolutely had to have to get it done so we could all retain our creative freedom and identity. That's how we put together the financing for my current film that I'm finishing now, De Noche. And in that case, I really do want a company fully committed to theatrical release.
Discourse around film and the creation of film feels in jeopardy at the moment. For example, we saw it this year at the Berlinale with the controversy surrounding Tricia Tuttle and the pro-Palestinian speeches made by invited filmmakers. Do you fear or foresee that cultural institutions will become increasingly threatened by political pressure, like in Berlin?
Sure. I think Germany has a unique, specific, and at times contradictory attitudes or laws around how we discuss Israel, for instance. There's this happening on the one hand where speech is kind of being watchdogged and limited, and people have a hard time of just saying that it doesn't have to be about Jewish people to have problems with the policies of Netanyahu, or whoever it may be.
But at the same time, the AfD is rising in Germany... So you have that complete sort of disconnect between these two forces - one trying to make remedy after an incredibly horrific past in history, and then all of a sudden, wanting such extreme change to come into place from completely the opposite direction.
So, Germany is a unique case, but I think we're feeling similar things about a crackdown on content and what is called ideology or point of view in the United States. It's targeted at the media, it's targeted at the news industries, and it's targeted at universities... So it is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely.
To temporarily move away from the doom and gloom, I wanted to share with you that the first film of yours that I saw was Velvet Goldmine (1998), which had a profound impact on me. I remember seeing the trailer for the first time, watching Brian Slade in his feather outfit on stage, hearing the gunshot followed by the needle drop of T. Rex’s '20th Century Boy', and... it still gives me goosebumps.
(Laughs) Awww....
The film turns 30 very soon... How do you look back on Velvet Goldmine and please tell me there’ll be a resotration?
Oh, it's another film that sort of realised or completed a phase of my creative life that was very profound and deep in that whole era of music and the early 70s. And the very interesting relationship between the UK and the US in how that music came to be. Criterion Collection is working on the release of Poison that will coincide with that 30th anniversary. I'm very, very excited about that.
Music plays a big part in your filmography – whether it’s Karen Carpenter, Bob Dylan, The Velvet Underground... I read somewhere that you’re working on a documentary about The Cure...
You know, that was news to me! (Laughs) Somebody brought it up... I mean, I love The Cure and they were formative in my life. Their music and evolution as a band from record to record... But no, it's not something I'm doing, and I'm not exactly sure where that came from! (Laughs)
Can you blame people for trying to manifest this project into existence?
(Laughs) Exactly!
Well, glad we got that cleared up! You mentioned your upcoming film, De Noche... You’ve wrapped, right?
We've wrapped the film and we're in post-production. We're moving from the picture cut to the sound. The whole production was based in Mexico. And this film was a particular struggle to get to this place, so I'm very proud of it.
You mention struggles...
Oh well, it began with the relationship with an actor [Joaquin Phoenix] who came to me for it and we moved forward. We got very close to production two years ago, and then he had a very abrupt or unexpected change of heart and walked away. And so De Noche 1 fell apart. But it was remarkable how the financiers and the investors who were there for that version came back, and demonstrated loyalty to the project and a film that means so much to all of us.
I’m glad De Noche 2 happened, with Danny Ramirez and Pedro Pascal starring. You also worked with Jon Raymond, who you’d previously collaborated with on the miniseries Mildred Pierce. I’m a huge fan of his work with Kelly Reichardt, especially on Old Joy and First Cow, which is a masterpiece in my book.
I couldn't agree more. Jon is a novelist first and has become a screenwriter. I’m so proud to have played even the smallest part in introducing Jon to Kelly when I moved to Portland, Oregon. They met each other, and they really hit it off. Many of his short stories were the first places that she went to in order to resuscitate a career in feature filmmaking that she had kind of put aside. And amazingly, well before she ended up even settling down in the Pacific Northwest, she and Jon really became the chroniclers of that region, its history, of Portland and beyond. So that unexpected move in my life to Portland from New York City... There have been so many rewards from it. And Jon is one of my dearest, closest friends. He's the most fabulous human being.
I can't wait to see De Noche. Is there anything else you can tell us about the film?
I don't know if I've ever quite seen anything like it before as a concept. It sort of begins as a detective story in the late 30s in a very corrupt Los Angeles, and through circumstances and the corruption that these two characters have become embroiled in, they're forced to leave Los Angeles and flee to Mexico. A very inexplicable, unexpected relationship begins to form between the two of them. To get to that point, a lot of dynamics of divisions between them in terms of power and race are overcome bit by bit, step by step, through the exploration of each other as lovers. It ultimately becomes a love story that that leaves you, I hope, longing and wondering what will happen between these two men.
To wrap up, at the opening ceremony of the Lumière Festival, you shared with me that the first film that had a profound impact on you was Mary Poppins. What was it about that film that marked you?
For one thing, it was the sort crown jewel of the Disney experiment, in terms of the films that came out of Disney at that time. The score is so exquisite, the two actors who take the leads are just perfection, it's so beautifully produced... I think for a three-year-old's imagination, there’s something about a maternal subject who comes with unique powers, and also discipline. Just a curious combination of various aspects of that character. I think seeing a movie on the big screen for the first time can't be overstated. The sheer power of that... I think all of those things conjoined to make it a sort of escapable moment of introduction to this medium.
This year has been a very good one in terms of cinema attendance and that being mirrored at the box office. Still, there are cinemas struggling and many fears expressed about the threat that artificial intelligence represents for the creative arts. As broad a question as this is, are you optimistic about the future of cinema?
I have to be optimistic. Because it's a medium I just love. I wasn't able to shoot De Noche on film, as we couldn't afford it, but it will always be my starting point on any film that I make. And what you are seeing among young people is an incredible desire to go out of their houses and leave their home screens and their phones behind and join in the experience of watching a movie on the screen.
You know how we all thought vinyl was going to go away with the introduction of CDs and MP3 and there was a sort of counter movement that was like ‘No, I want to hold it in my hand'... The desire to actually experience it and the warm resonance of hearing vinyl play with a needle on... Sometimes the simplest technology remains the best and the most profound. I hope that continues and I hope we can see that still being played out. It is about younger people and exposing them to what that experience means, and what that's like to share communally in a theatre in the dark.
On that note, Mr Haynes, thank you very much for your time.
The Lumière Film Festival takes place until 18 October in Lyon, France. The restored versions of Todd Haynes' Poison and Safe are being screened, as well as Far From Heaven and I'm Not There. Safe is out now on Criterion 4K UHD Blu-ray.
Todd Haynes' new film, De Noche, finished shooting in April 2026. No release date has yet been announced.

'Americans are seeing their pay totally wiped out' — US inflation surges as midterms loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:11 UTC
00:00:11 KST

US consumer inflation was hotter than anticipated in September, latest government data shows, as Washington's war on Tehran pushed energy costs higher, deepening strains on American households ahead of next month's midterm elections.
The uptick underscores voter worries over high costs of living, and comes as President Donald Trump is campaigning in US states to shore up support for his Republican party as it tries to retain control of Congress.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7 percent year-on-year in September, the Department of Labor said on Wednesday, more than the 3.6 percent analysts forecast according to MarketWatch.
This was a notable acceleration from 3.4 percent in August, in one of the last major economic reports before the November 3 vote.
Inflation picked up pace on a month-on-month basis too, accelerating from 0.4 percent in August to 0.6 percent last month.
The higher-than-expected reading has left analysts divided over the odds of a second straight interest rate hike at the US central bank's upcoming October 27-28 policy meeting.
Economist James Knightley at ING noted that Federal Reserve officials John Williams, Philip Jefferson and Christopher Waller have suggested "that we don't need to see back-to-back interest rate increases," instead leaning towards "a slow and steady" approach.
He expects the Fed will want to be "careful and cautious in terms of its policy tightening."
But traders now see a 51.5 percent chance that the Fed will raise rates by another 25 basis points in October, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. The probability was around 22 percent a day prior.
Already, industries sensitive to interest rates, like housing, are under pressure from steeper borrowing costs.
Yields on US government bonds spiked after the inflation report. The 10-year Treasury yield, which influences rates on mortgage and auto loans, rose to 5.3 percent from 5.2 percent.
Spillovers
Gasoline costs accounted for more than half of the monthly CPI jump, surging 9.1 percent in September, Wednesday's report said.
Energy prices have soared since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, prompting Tehran to block off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas shipments.
Average prices at US gasoline pumps have surged more than 45 percent since the start of the Middle East war to $4.33 per gallon, according to AAA motor club data.
Diesel prices have soared even more, by 67.7 percent, boosting the cost of transporting goods and threatening further spillovers to consumers.
"Again, the Iran-US conflict has led to higher motor fuel costs that everyone is experiencing," ING's Knightley told the AFP news agency.
"The US is also seeing substantial increases in airline fares," he said, adding that this will likely contribute to additional price pressures.
Excluding volatile food and energy prices, core CPI was up 2.6 percent from a year ago.
Although high gasoline and diesel prices drove about half of the September spike in inflation, "it's starting to spill into other areas," warned Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union.
"Airfares, used cars and recreation all had big price jumps," she added. "Americans are seeing their pay totally wiped out by inflation. That's been the case for half a year now."
Long expects that another interest rate hike will be needed, likely in December.
With the underlying US economy remaining strong as massive spending linked to the artificial intelligence buildout boosts demand for chips and labor, economists also caution that higher costs could continue filtering through to households.

Tiny implants can use the body itself to talk to each other
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Tiny implants can use the body itself to talk to each other
The network could let tiny implants sense symptoms and trigger treatments
Medical implants are getting smaller and smarter. But getting them to talk to each other remains tricky.
Now, researchers have developed a way for tiny implantable devices to send electrical signals through the body’s own tissues. The approach could offer a low-power way for implants to work together, with one detecting a symptom and another delivering treatment, the team reports September 24 in Science.
Currently, getting devices to communicate through tissue comes with trade-offs. Some medical devices, such as insulin pumps linked to glucose monitors, use Bluetooth, which relies on radio signals. Receiving those signals requires power even when a device is only listening, increasing the need for battery power and making devices harder shrink. Radio signals also weaken as they travel through body tissue, limiting how far apart communicating devices can be.
The new network called SWANS, the Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System, works differently. A wearable external hub or implant generates an electric pulse that produces a small current in the surrounding tissue. Tiny implants can detect those electrical signals while using almost no power when they are only listening. And without large batteries, those implants can be small enough to inject through a syringe.
To demonstrate how the network works, the team attached motion sensors to the front legs of rats. When the animals moved their front legs, the system’s external hub sent signals through their bodies to neurostimulator implants in the sciatic nerves, causing muscles in the back legs to contract.
The synchronized limbs weren’t really the point. The experiment was designed to show that signals could travel through the body, linking different kinds of devices, says Alex Abramson, a biomedical engineer at Georgia Tech in Atlanta. It was “a proof of concept showing that you can really connect this system to anything.”
Abramson says a network of smart implants could automatically deliver a drug or stimulate a neuron exactly when needed to treat complex conditions like Parkinson’s disease. Simple signals can be sent from one implant to another, while an external hub can coordinate more complex networks of sensors and devices, possibly using artificial intelligence.
Before the new network can be used in humans, researchers will need to show that the electrical signals do not cause unintended problems like heart rhythm disruptions. Such issues have not turned up in the experiments in rats yet, but the technology will need to be tested over longer periods of time and in larger animals, Abramson says.
Materials engineer Amir Alavi says the network’s potential could grow as other technologies improve, including wearables, AI systems and miniature, battery-free implantable sensors like those his lab is developing. “There are now several really interesting directions converging,” says Alavi, of at the University of Pittsburgh’s Swanson School of Engineering. “If those pieces eventually come together, you could have implants that are much smaller, simpler, longer-lived, and more connected than what we have today.”

NATO threats to Kaliningrad affect interests of entire country — Russian MP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:56:45 UTC
23:56:45 KST

KALININGRAD, October 14. /TASS/. NATO’s Deterrence on the Eastern Flank concept, which envisages strikes against the Kaliningrad Region, Belarus, and the environs of St. Petersburg, poses a potential threat to Russia’s overall security, Andrey Kropotkin, Chairman of the Legislative Assembly of the Kaliningrad Region, said in an interview with TASS.
Earlier, media reported that NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich presented the Deterrence on the Eastern Flank initiative at the Warsaw Security Forum.
The initial phase envisages the use of a network of ground drones and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to create an isolated zone and reduce personnel losses. At the same time, long-range missiles are planned to be used against strategic targets: communication centers, command centers, air defense positions in the Kaliningrad Region, Belarus, and the environs of St. Petersburg.
"Of course, it's necessary to distinguish between hypothetical military planning and actual intentions. But when scenarios of direct armed conflict are discussed at such a high level, this requires the utmost responsibility for every word and every decision. I emphasize once again that the Kaliningrad Region is not just a point on a map. It is part of the Russian Federation, where our citizens live, our children grow up, and our businesses operate. And any threats to the region's security affect the interests of the entire country. Russia's position on protecting its sovereignty and territorial integrity is consistent. President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly emphasized the state's readiness to ensure its security. I am convinced that our ‘neighbors’ must understand the consequences of a possible escalation. A direct clash between Russia and NATO cannot be viewed as a routine military-political scenario, as the cost of a mistake could be catastrophic for all of Europe," the lawmaker stated.
The Kaliningrad Region is a Russian semi-exclave, separated from the rest of the country by the territory of EU and NATO member states. Aggressive rhetoric about possible measures against the Russian region has intensified sharply in recent months, with threats of an economic and territorial blockade of the Kaliningrad Region appearing in the foreign press.

Fears over 14 Syrian sailors on ship sunk by drone near Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:56:00 UTC
23:56:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Fears grow over 14 Syrian sailors on board ship sunk by suspected Russian drone near Bulgaria
Fears are growing over the fate of Syrian and Egyptian sailors aboard the HS Dignity, a Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo vessel that sank following a suspected Russian attack off the coast of Bulgaria on Tuesday.
The Syrian Sailors' Union announced that the vessel, which had 16 crew members on board, 14 Syrians and two Egyptians, sank following an attack involving an aerial drone and two unmanned boats.
The ship was travelling between Algeria and the Romanian port of Braila with a crew of Syrian and Egyptian nationals, according to the Bulgarian interior ministry.
The incident comes less than a week after another ship carrying Syrian sailors sank in the same area of the Black Sea.
The Syrian Sailors' Union said search and rescue teams had managed to save five crew members, while the search continued for the remaining 11. Six boats and two helicopters were taking part in the operation.
The union added that it was monitoring developments in coordination with search and rescue authorities and the ship's owner to obtain accurate information about the fate of the missing sailors.
On Tuesday, Bulgarian authorities also reported that a third vessel, the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, had been attacked by drones. Its entire crew of 15 sailors, including seven Ukrainians, was evacuated.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev summoned the Russian ambassador following the drone attacks.
Radev said the Chelsea 3 was "hit by three aerial drones", and that shortly afterwards, the HS Dignity was "struck" and sank.
"We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party; however ... logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of the Russian Federation," he wrote, calling the attack "unacceptable".
Fears grow for Syrian shipping workers
The sinking of the HS Dignity has heightened fears among families of Syrian sailors working aboard commercial vessels, particularly amid repeated attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
Shipping routes near conflict zones have become increasingly dangerous for civilian crews who are not involved in military operations.
About a week earlier, on 6 October, the Alpha Vatan, a Togolese-flagged vessel, was attacked by suspected Russian aerial and naval drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
The attack caused the ship to sink, leaving its crew missing. According to Syrian authorities, ten sailors were aboard the vessel, nine Syrians and one Egyptian.
Moscow denied responsibility for the attack.
On 7 October, Bulgarian authorities announced that they were suspending the search for the Alpha Vatan's crew after rescue teams failed to find any survivors.
The following day, Mazen Alloush, Director of International Relations and Cooperation at Syria's General Authority for Border Crossings, announced that Syrian authorities had sent official memoranda to Bulgaria and the International Maritime Organisation, calling for an investigation into the incident and clarification of the sailors' fate.
Alloush stressed the need for an independent and transparent investigation, expressing Damascus's concern over the suspension of search and rescue operations before conclusive information about the crew's fate had been obtained.
The families of the missing sailors continue to await definitive information about their loved ones, while the sinking of another ship carrying Syrian crew members has raised further concerns over the safety of maritime workers in the Black Sea.
Amid the Russia-Ukraine war, both sides have used aerial and maritime drones to target military and economic assets. The growing threat to commercial shipping has increased the risks faced by civilian crews uninvolved in the conflict.
Agencies contributed to this report.

Fires surge in Brazil’s Amazon, fuelled by El Nino and climate change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Fires surge in Brazil’s Amazon, fuelled by El Nino and climate change
AUTAZES, Brazil – El Nino, climate change and human activity are fuelling a surge in fires deep in Brazil’s Amazon in October, as firefighters race to contain blazes whose smoke is choking residents and causing events to be cancelled in nearby towns.
There were 1,679 fires in Brazil’s Amazonas state in the first two weeks of October, a 253% surge compared to the same period in 2025, according to data from the country’s Amazon surveillance system.
The fires, which officials suspect were set on purpose, have sent plumes of smoke across the sky and provoked states of emergency in at least 36 municipalities across Amazonas, causing respiratory problems for residents.
“Our situation here is critical,” said Luiz Rios, a retired farmer in the state’s Autazes municipality who has struggled to breathe at night, causing his face to swell.
Poor air quality from the fires has cancelled outdoor events in Manaus, the state’s capital and home to over 2 million residents, where public schools closed on Oct 14.
August and September are usually the height of the dry season in the Amazon, when fires become harder to control before the rainy season’s onset usually brings relief in October.
In 2026, however, rains have been slow to bring relief. Scientists and officials point to the El Nino phenomenon, which is predicted to be the strongest on record, and climate change as drivers of the surge in fires.
“Water stress and heat stress are hitting with extreme intensity, creating a potentially dangerous situation that, compounded by human activity, threatens this biodiversity, people’s health, and the productivity of these lands,” said Carlos Durigan, a geographer and researcher at the Amazon Environmental Research Institute.
Brazil’s federal government and civil defence sent aircraft and brigade crews to Amazonas over the weekend to combat the flames.
Brazil’s environment minister, Joao Paulo Capobianco, flew over the state on Oct 11 and spotted fires inside protected forest, which his ministry says points to deliberate arson meant to clear the way for deforestation.
The ministry has promised an investigation.
In the Amazon, fires are rarely natural and are typically set to clear land for farming or ranching. REUTERS

An ancient Chinese math puzzle shows how to win at cards, horse races and gerrymandering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:53:23 UTC
23:53:23 KST

Sun Bin, allegedly descended from The Art of War author Sun Tzu, was a legendary Chinese military strategist who lived more than 2,300 years ago. After one king imprisoned and tortured him, forcing him to use a wheelchair for the rest of his life, he rose to fame as a military advisor for a rival king and lived to record two great victories against his former captor.
One of Sun Bin’s greatest exploits came not on the battlefield but on a racetrack. Like his supposed ancestor, who wrote, “Warfare is a way of deception,” Sun Bin discovered a “way of deception” in horse races that can be boiled down to a simple mathematical puzzle. For reasons that I cannot explain, the most general version of this puzzle remained unsolved and unexamined until 1980, when a college classmate of mine rediscovered it. Thirty years later he told me about the puzzle, and I was hooked. Besides transporting me back to ancient China, solving this problem took me back to my own roots as a mathematician.
I like to approach Master Sun’s problem through several simpler puzzles:
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Puzzle One: Suppose you toss a coin six times. What is the probability of getting exactly three heads and three tails? What if you toss the coin 10, 100 times or any even number of times? How likely are you to get exactly the same number of heads and tails?
Puzzle Two: Now pick an even number, which we’ll call 2N, and a target number, N – k, which is less than N. If you flip a coin 2N times, do you think it is more likely that you will get exactly N heads or that you will get (N – k) or fewer heads? For example, are you more likely to get exactly 10 heads in 20 flips or to get eight or fewer heads in 20 flips? Experiment with different values of k and N and see if you can find a general rule.
The next two puzzles seem, on the surface, to have nothing to do with the first two.
Puzzle Three: Two teams, each with three players, are planning to compete in a match. Each team is supposed to rank its players from best to worst. The number one seed on one team is supposed to play the number one seed on the other, and so on. One coach is honest and ranks their players by true order of ability. The other coach is dishonest and decides to strategically rank their players in a different order. Can the latter coach tilt the odds in their favor? If so, what ranking strategy gives their team the greatest chance of winning the match? What if each team has 10, 100 or N players?
Puzzle Four: The dishonest coach decides to place bets on the individual games rather than the overall team match. For this purpose, they want to know what ranking strategy will give their team the greatest expected number of games won. If there are three players per team, what strategy is optimal, and how many individual games can the coach expect to win? What if there are 10, 100 or N players on each team?
The last two puzzles harken back to a popular legend featuring Sun Bin. According to the story, General Tian Ji and King Wei were planning a friendly series of horse races, and the general asked Master Sun, his trusted retainer, for advice. The wily strategist told Tian Ji to race his best horse against the king’s second best, his second best against the king’s third best and his worst against the king’s best. I call this Master Sun’s strategy. “Just bet heavily, my lord, and I can make you the winner,” Sun Bin said. And indeed, according to the legend, Tian Ji won two out of three races and took home 1,000 gold coins.
That is how the legend goes, but any modern mathematician would be skeptical. Certainly Sun Bin could not guarantee a win. But did the strategy improve Tian Ji’s chances of winning the match? And if so, by how much did it do so? Those questions lead us straight to Puzzles Three and Four.
Before I reveal the answers, we must go back and consider the first two puzzles.
In Puzzle One, the secret to computing the odds of any number of heads lies in the following arrangement of numbers, called Pascal’s triangle:
Each number is generated by adding the two numbers immediately above it; the process can be continued indefinitely. To evaluate the probability of exactly three heads in six tosses of a coin, we look up the third element in the sixth row, which is 20. (Technical note: The top row is traditionally considered to be the zeroth row, and the leftmost element in each row is the zeroth element. So the zeroth element in row six is 1, the first element is 6, and so on.)
We divide 20 by 26, which equals 64, to get the exact probability of three heads in six tosses: 20⁄64 = 0.3125, or 31.25 percent—slightly less than 1⁄3. Are you surprised? More than two thirds of the time, you will not get three heads in six tosses.
As the number of tosses increases, it becomes less and less likely that you will get heads exactly half the time. You can see this visibly from a histogram, in which the height of each bar represents the probability of getting the corresponding number of heads. The peak height of the histogram decreases as the number of tosses, N, gets larger. The appearance of the histogram changes as well: the steps shrink and smooth out into a curve, creating what is known as a normal distribution.
This “view from infinity” provides an approximate—but remarkably good—estimate for the solution to Puzzle One. In 2N flips of a coin, the probability of getting exactly N heads (equal to the peak height of the histogram) is roughly 1⁄√πN. For example, if N = 50, then the probability of 50 heads in 100 tosses is roughly 1⁄√50π ≈ 0.0798, as shown in the figure.
You might wonder at the presence of π, or pi, in the equation, thinking, “What does a ratio between circumference and diameter have to do with flipping coins?” You may also be baffled by the square root. I can’t give you an easy explanation: every proof I have ever seen uses calculus, which is the mathematician’s version of a telescope that gives you a view from infinity.
Puzzle Two is a much more recent variant. It is trickier because we are now comparing the probabilities of two rare events. On one hand, we have an “exceptionally average” result: getting heads on exactly half the tosses. On the other hand, we have exceptionally large deviations from average: the “tail” of the normal distribution. Which one is rarer? It depends on where we start measuring the tail.
For N = 3, we again consult the sixth row of Pascal’s triangle: 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1. We add these numbers from the left and ask when the sum first exceeds the central—and largest—number in the row. We notice that 1 + 6 < 20, so the probability of getting zero or one heads is less than the probability of getting three heads. But 1 + 6 + 15 > 20, so the probability of getting zero, one or two heads exceeds the probability of getting three.
To answer the question for N = 10, we need to compute the 20th row of Pascal’s triangle, which is already kind of tedious. It turns out that the crossover happens at eight heads. That is, we are more likely to get 10 heads than seven or fewer but less likely to get 10 heads than eight or fewer.
To solve the puzzle for N = 100, we would have to compute the 200th row of Pascal’s triangle, and I don’t know anyone (aside from computers) with that kind of patience. But the “view from infinity” gives us a shortcut. The area of the central rectangle is roughly 1⁄√πN. The area to the left of the crossover line can be estimated from the normal distribution. By comparing the two, we can show that the crossover happens at 89 heads.
In general, if the crossover happens at (N – k), then k ≈ √Nln(N)⁄2. (Here “ln” means the natural logarithm.) I’ll call k the “crossover number,” so for N = 100, the crossover number is 100 – 89 = 11. This solution is perhaps slightly less remarkable than our solution to Puzzle One, and for small values of N, the approximation is not as good. But I happen to like it better because I discovered it myself! It also turned out to be a key that let me unlock the solution to Puzzle Four.
A few months ago my wife and I ate dinner with a friend who is always interested in mathematical topics. I told her about Puzzles Three and Four and said that I was writing a book about them. “But where is the mathematics?” she asked me. It was an excellent question, and it brings up a little understood point. Math never arises in the real world in pure and unadulterated form, as you see in textbooks. Math is always hiding behind the scenes. To bring it out into the foreground, you must make a mathematical model of a real-world problem.
In Puzzles Three and Four, the clue is that I’m asking about probabilities. So somewhere there must be a source of randomness. I assume that the source of randomness is the assignment of players to the coaches—that is, the coaches drew the players blindly, as if drawing cards from a deck of 2N cards, with each possible draw being equally likely. You may disagree with this assumption; for example, in the story of Tian Ji, the king may have had access to better horses than the general did. But without making some assumptions, you’ll never get anywhere, and it’s best to start with simple ones. The card game model, which I call One-Round War, allows me to create a table that shows the probability that my ith best player beats the other team’s jth best player, for any pair i and j. Using this table, I can evaluate any proposed strategy and figure out which ones work better for me.
It’s important to note that in One-Round War, both players know the seeding of each card within each hand, so we know which card is our ith best and which is our opponent’s jth best, even though the cards are face down. We do not know the actual card values, though. In a fair version of this game, the players would take turns going first, but I am interested in a wildly unfair version in which I go second every time. That gives me the power to react to my opponent’s moves.
For example, suppose I draw cards {1, 3, 5} and my opponent draws {2, 4, 6}. If I play “honestly,” playing my best (5) against my opponent’s best (6), and so on, I will lose all three tricks. But if I use Master Sun’s strategy, playing my best (5) against my opponent’s second-best (4), and so on, then I will win two out of three.
For the case of six cards, we can show that Master Sun’s strategy wins 70 percent (14 out of 20) of the possible hands. As for Puzzle Four, Master Sun’s strategy will win, on average, 55 percent of the tricks. In both puzzles, Master Sun’s scheme is the best possible strategy utilizing only the ranks of the cards. After 2,300 years, Master Sun’s intuition is vindicated!
There is no evidence that Sun Bin ever considered the problem for N > 3. But modern mathematics gives us the tools to answer such questions. It was precisely this question, the basis of Puzzle Four for an arbitrary N, that my college friend Howard Stern, a fellow math major who passed away in 2016, told me about and that quickly turned into an obsession.
We’ve already seen that Master Sun’s strategy is based on the idea of sacrificing some lower-rated cards against your opponent’s stronger cards so that your remaining cards (the ringers) have a better chance of winning. This approach means that your entire hand consists of two types of cards: sacrificial cards and ringers. Stern proved that the sacrificial cards should always be played in reverse order. (Proving this yourself is an excellent challenge.) Your worst card should be paired against your opponent’s best, and so on. The ringers, on the other hand, should be played in direct order of strength.
After determining this, the devil is in the details. Which cards should you select as sacrificial cards? Which cards should they be played against? How many cards should you sacrifice, and how many should you designate as ringers? These were questions Stern could not answer.
The casual math enthusiast will probably find Puzzle Three to be more accessible than Puzzle Four. It requires no more math than we’ve discussed here, just common sense. Puzzle Four, on the other hand, fascinated and entertained me for a full year. My book Master Sun’s Problem, which came out from Princeton University Press on October 13, contains the full answer. It also tells the full historical story, as well as the tales of some other contributors: Stern, who introduced me to Puzzles Three and Four; journalist Gary Antonick, who let me turn his then column Numberplay in the New York Times into a crowdsourcing experiment; retired engineer Bill Courtney, who solved Puzzle Three; and operations research expert Richard Chatwin, who made a vital contribution to solving Puzzle Four.
Though I don’t want to give away too many spoilers, probably the most stunning discovery was that Puzzle Two and Puzzle Four are the same problem. More precisely, the solution to Puzzle Two is embedded within the solution to Puzzle Four. Remember the crossover numbers from Puzzle Two? We saw that the crossover number for 10 tosses of a coin is two and that the crossover number for 100 tosses is 11. These are exactly the same as the optimal number of cards to sacrifice when using Master Sun’s strategy. It’s another example of the amazing propensity of mathematics to unearth connections between things that did not seem to be related.
For example, if you’re playing a game of One-Round War with 100 cards against 100 cards, you should sacrifice 11 cards and designate 89 ringers. On average, none of the sacrificial lambs will win, but 86 of the 89 ringers will, and you will take the match by an astounding margin of 86 to 14.
Any good math problem should leave more questions in its wake. I deliberately did not include the possibility of upsets in my model. In our card game, the higher card always beats the lower one. But in horse races, the faster horse does not always win. How robust is Master Sun’s strategy under those circumstances?
Also, the scheme reminds me very much of gerrymandering, in which you deliberately lose some electoral districts by a large margin in order to win a lot of districts by a small margin. Can you devise an optimal gerrymandering strategy? In a state with 100 districts, would it be smart to draw a map with 11 losing districts and 89 winning ones? I highly doubt that the solution would translate so directly, but the analogy is worth thinking about.
The world is full of asymmetric or unfair contests. While we may wish there was a way to ensure that justice prevails, perhaps we would do well to take a lesson from ancient Chinese sages who understood how to play the asymmetric contests well.

Earth’s ‘life support systems’ are breaking down, climate scientists warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:53:12 UTC
23:53:12 KST

Earth faces “rapid destabilization” as a result of climate change, an international group of scientists find in the latest edition of an annual checkup of the planet’s “vital signs.”
“This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present,” the authors write.
The report, the latest in a series called the “State of the Climate,” measures 16 key markers of Earth’s climate. Seven of these have reached “record extremes,” says report co-author Christopher Wolf, a research scientist at Terrestrial Ecosystems Research Associates. These extremes include soaring greenhouse gas concentrations, melting sea ice and sea-level rise—driven largely by human activities.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Global warming appears to be accelerating,” Wolf says.
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, a by-product of burning fossil fuels, has reached record-high levels (428 parts per million), as have other greenhouse gases such as methane (1,940 parts per billion) and nitrous oxide (340 parts per billion). The ocean has absorbed a record-breaking jump in heat, which, in turn, has helped fuel unprecedented sea-level rise. At the same time, higher temperatures have meant record losses in the Greenland ice sheet and glaciers.
“Earth’s life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits, with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond,” Wolf and his co-authors write in the report.
Humans are in danger as a result: since September 2025 climate change has fueled myriad natural disasters, including floods in Albania, Bali, Brazil, Columbia, Greece, Indonesia, and Vietnam; heat waves in Europe, India and the U.S.; wildfires in Australia and Florida; and more, the report finds.
The future, the report warns, may be bleak.
“We are increasingly concerned about the risk of crossing climate tipping points that could lead to irreversible changes,” Wolf says.
That could include disruptions to the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC)—the movement of cold and warm water across the Atlantic Ocean, which influences global weather—as well as what the report describes as “irreversible” damage to the Amazon rainforest thanks to the double whammy of global warming and deforestation. Only bold action to reduce fossil fuel use can help halt or reverse this devastation, the authors write.
“The climate emergency is already here, but the future is not yet determined,” Wolf says. “We still have opportunities to avoid some of the worst outcomes through rapid emissions reductions, climate adaptation and broader societal changes. The window for action is narrowing, but it has not closed.”
The report was published in the journal BioScience on Wednesday.

The boys were shooting the weapon out of the conservatory into the garden at targets such as bottles.
Beechey, 18, accidentally pulled the trigger when he was trying to put the safety catch on the air rifle while it was pointed towards Bell’s head.
Connor, from Tadley, Hampshire, was taken to Southampton general hospital but he died two days later from a severe brain injury.

“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives. With today's €2.86 billion disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs, including drones and missiles vital to its defense,” von der Leyen said.
The Commission noted that the urgent delivery of military equipment is particularly important as Ukraine prepares for another winter amid Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion.
According to the statement, the assistance is intended to strengthen the Ukrainian Armed Forces' ability to protect civilians and urban areas from Russian attacks, particularly through improved air defense capabilities.
Overall, since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, the European Union and its member states have provided Ukraine with a combined €231.5 billion (approximately $259.1 billion) in assistance. That amount includes €3.8 billion (about $4.3 billion) financed through proceeds generated by frozen Russian assets, according to the European Commission.
The announcement also comes as the EU advances Ukraine's accession process, with two additional negotiating clusters formally opened during an Intergovernmental Conference in Luxembourg on October 13.
According to Transparency International Ukraine, the decision was announced at a press conference following the meeting. The newly opened areas include Cluster 2, covering the internal market, and Cluster 3, focusing on competitiveness and economic growth.

Russia’s War Budget Is So Huge It Could Almost Build Another International Space Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:50:32 UTC
23:50:32 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s War Budget Is So Huge It Could Almost Build Another International Space Station
Russia has allocated roughly $177.4 billion in 2026 to defense and other expenditures connected to its war against Ukraine, while more than $109.5 billion of its so-called defense budget remains classified, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence on October 14.
The official Russian budget line for “national defense” stands at about $144.4 billion this year. When a broader range of war-related expenditures is included, Ukraine’s intelligence service estimates the total rises to approximately $177.4 billion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Of that defense spending, around $109.5 billion is contained in classified budget items, limiting public visibility into where much of the money is actually going.
Moscow has also earmarked substantial funding to sustain and expand its defense-industrial base. Roughly $189.8 million is allocated to military-industrial development, military-technical cooperation, and scientific and production programs. Those categories receive approximately $73.5 million, $75.2 million, and $41.1 million, respectively.
Additional state support is being directed toward struggling defense companies. Russia has allocated about $24.5 million to reimburse corporate expenses, $5.5 million to prevent bankruptcies, $6 million to offset loan-interest costs, and another $17.9 million for compensation payments to employees.
Ukraine’s intelligence also identified approximately $14.9 million in funding for high-performance computing used in weapons development. Such workloads are carried out at major Russian data centers, including infrastructure operated by Yandex and Sberbank, which Ukraine says links those computing resources directly to Russia’s military-industrial programs.
Another $312 million has been set aside for applied defense research, while approximately $121.9 million is officially allocated to the development and production of various types of drones. Ukrainian intelligence cautioned that this figure does not reflect the true size of Russia’s UAV industry because additional funding comes through private investment, procurement programs, and other channels.
One particularly large allocation is intended for Russia’s National Guard, which is budgeted to receive approximately $8.19 billion for drone purchases.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, those UAVs are expected to serve not only in Russia’s war against Ukraine but also inside Russia itself, including the protection of critical infrastructure, urban patrols, surveillance, and possible use by security forces during domestic unrest.
The scale of military spending becomes especially stark when compared with Russia’s civilian priorities. Moscow’s $144.4 billion official defense budget is more than three times the combined funding allocated to education—about $21 billion—and healthcare, at roughly $22.5 billion.
Ukraine’s intelligence noted that $144.4 billion is close to the estimated $150 billion cost of building the International Space Station. The same amount, it argued, could finance more than 150 modern cancer treatment centers instead.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia was preparing a new round of tax increases expected to extract nearly $44 billion from individuals and businesses through 2029 as the government seeks additional revenue to cover rising military spending and a widening budget deficit.

French minister accused Musk of &quot;online harassment campaigns&quot; against European leaders

French minister accused Musk of "online harassment campaigns" against European leaders
Kyiv • UNN
Jean-Noël Barrot said that Musk uses X to harass European leaders online. He also warned of foreign interference in France's 2027 elections.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot accused billionaire Elon Musk of using his social media platform to organize "mass online harassment campaigns" against European leaders, as he targeted foreign efforts to destabilize the country ahead of next year’s presidential election. UNN reports this, citing The Guardian.
Details
Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role social media has begun to play in the global struggle for democracy. "Forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they use tactics aimed at polarizing public debate," he said.
As a result, he said, "political movements with authoritarian aims" that "play into the hands of declared enemies of democracy" have begun to gain momentum in Europe and North America.
"They are intensifying the polarization of our societies," he added. "Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it," the French minister said.
Barrot cited France’s 2027 presidential election as an example, with far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading in the polls. "The enemies of democracy are doing everything possible to destabilize us," he said. "They are using our divisions, as well as immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, to fuel hatred and tension," Barrot noted.
He cited several other examples, from an unnamed Israeli company accused of creating fake accounts on French social media to influence perceptions of the war between Israel and Gaza, to allegations that Azerbaijan stoked tensions amid deadly unrest in the French Pacific territory of New Caledonia.
Barrot also singled out Musk, the world’s richest person and owner of the social media platform X. "Elon Musk has launched mass online harassment campaigns against European leaders in order to influence the debate, using the virality of his social media platform."
Musk did not respond to a request for comment.
Barrot also cited as an example the protests that have shaken France in recent weeks, when school pupils, students and trade union activists blockaded schools and marched through cities. According to Barrot, these events were exploited by "hostile narratives" from russia, China and Iran, as well as by those associated with the MAGA movement in the US.
Last week, Musk and US President Donald Trump commented on the protests in France, attempting to recast them through the lens of mass migration and dismissing protesters’ demands for improved learning conditions, the publication writes.
Barrot said his government was working to respond to the reality in which paid or commissioned influencers seek to exploit the viral reach of digital platforms. "The Kremlin’s goal is clearly articulated: to put an end to our liberal democracies in favor of a new authoritarianism. Other actors are converging around this goal, seeking to dictate to Europe which democracies are ‘good’ and which are ‘bad,’ based on whether they serve their own interests," he said.
The French minister’s remarks came days after the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was "clear" that russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum.
Barrot said his government would work to counter these efforts by foreign organizations. "We are uncompromising because it is clear to us that they are undermining the fundamental interests of the nation," he said. "We will not tolerate any foreign interference, wherever it comes from. This is a matter of sovereignty."

Uber begins testing self-driving robotaxis in Britain – how drivers, unions and politicians are responding
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Uber begins testing self-driving robotaxis in Britain – how drivers, unions and politicians are responding
Kyiv • UNN
Uber is testing self-driving cars in Manchester without passengers and with a safety operator behind the wheel. The company plans to launch robotaxis in 15 cities by the end of 2026.
Uber has begun testing autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester, seeking to introduce robotaxi services in cities across the UK, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
The first driverless cars are already operating, using technology from partner companies Pony and Verne; Uber recently launched Europe's first autonomous taxi service with them in the Croatian capital, Zagreb.
Uber said it was "delighted to take this first step towards making this technology available to people across the UK".
In social media posts, Verne said it had "begun testing autonomous vehicles in Manchester", while Pony said there were "plans to launch robotaxis in the city" and that testing was already under way.
The testing involves mapping the streets of this city in north-west England; an operator-driver is behind the wheel to ensure safety, and there are no passengers in the cabin.
Limited passenger services began last month in London, although there too an operator-driver was seated in the front of the vehicles (provided by Wayve) in accordance with licensing requirements imposed by Transport for London on private-hire operators.
The publication notes that the next steps have not yet been determined. Resistance to the introduction of robotaxis is growing among Uber drivers, their unions and the capital's politicians. The GMB and ADCU unions said that thousands of drivers could lose their jobs and called for assistance to be provided to those affected.
This week, the London Assembly's transport committee published a critical report calling on the government to devolve powers to regulate autonomous taxi services to the local level.
The document cites "significant uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles", as well as concerns about the impact on public transport and road congestion, safety issues and the accessibility of services for passengers with disabilities.
No official application to launch passenger services in Manchester has yet been submitted; the vehicles are operating under a government licence issued by the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) and the Department for Transport.
A representative of Transport for Greater Manchester said the city aims to make its taxis the safest in the country.
"New technologies are playing an increasingly important role in the development of our city region," they said. "However, their introduction must take place responsibly and safely, with due consideration of what this means for our residents.
Although no applications to launch driverless taxis in Greater Manchester have yet been received, we are aware of potential interest from companies in such activity.
Safety will always remain our top priority, and we need firm guarantees that vehicles posing even the slightest risk to residents will not be operated on our roads".
Uber said it plans to launch robotaxi services in 15 cities worldwide by the end of 2026 — primarily in the United States and the Middle East.

Ex-UK army chef jailed for nearly four years over homemade gun, explosives
LONDON, Oct 14 - A British army chef who was motivated by an extreme right-wing ideology was jailed for nearly four years on Wednesday after he was arrested with a homemade gun and explosives.
Mark Broadhurst, 28, was arrested at his barracks in September 2024 after police discovered online messages espousing racist views, his desire to form a militia and his intention to create homemade firearms and sell them to right-wing groups.
He was in a Telegram group with three other men who last year were jailed for a combined total of 29 years for planning to carry out a terrorist attack at mosques or synagogues as part of what they believed to be a coming "race war".
When Broadhurst was arrested, police found knives and crossbows, black powder, 9mm ammunition and air pistols at his home address, as well as what police described as "an improvised homemade cannon".
Broadhurst pleaded guilty to possession of a firearm and making or possessing an explosive under suspicious circumstances, though he denied he possessed them for the purposes of terrorism.
But a judge ruled that Broadhurst's offences were connected to terrorism and he was sentenced at Sheffield Crown Court to three years and 10 months in prison.
"Mark Broadhurst was clearly interested in violence and developing weapons that had the ability to cause untold harm to innocent people," Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said.
"He was immersed in extremist material and maintained close contact with three now-convicted terrorists inspired by SS tactics and supremacist ideology over a prolonged period." REUTERS

Norway's national economic crime unit said the alleged overbilling targeted the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which provides procurement and logistical support to the alliance's 32 member states and their partners.
The investigation also prompted coordinated searches in Germany and Romania, according to Eurojust, the European Union's agency for criminal justice cooperation.
Investigators suspect that the company submitted fraudulent invoices for shore-based services supporting vessels and their crews during port visits. The company is also accused of using an intermediary to bribe public officials in exchange for favorable treatment in contracts involving the NSPA.
Eurojust estimated that NATO member states suffered losses of approximately 1 million euros, although investigators have yet to determine the full financial impact of the alleged scheme.
Authorities searched the company's premises and several residences in Romania, while German investigators conducted raids at two businesses and a private residence.
The company at the center of the investigation has not been publicly identified.
Marianne Bender, a senior public prosecutor at Norway's economic crime unit, warned that rising global defense spending could create greater opportunities for financial misconduct.
"Defence sector budgets are increasing worldwide, which entails an increased risk of economic crime. This is an area we are monitoring closely," Bender said.
"If NATO has been defrauded, there will be a tough crackdown," she added.
The NSPA coordinates purchases of defense equipment, security systems and logistical services for NATO members and partner countries. The alliance itself does not own military assets such as ships, tanks or weapons.
