Azerbaijan school hijab ban spark protests and rupture with Turkey
New school dress rules introduced across Azerbaijan’s primary and secondary schools this week, which effectively ban the Muslim hijab, have led to 37 arrests and triggered class boycotts, and a nationwide social media campaign while causing a row with the country's longtime ally Turkey.
The newly implemented rules, approved last month, prohibit clothing that the government says violates the “principle of secularism”.
Although the regulations do not explicitly state that they target the Muslim headscarf, videos circulating online have shown girls in hijabs crying after being denied entry to schools under the new uniform requirements.
The amendment to the Descriptions of Uniforms for Students of State General Education Institutions aimed to establish a unified dress code reflecting the country’s “secular principle”, according to the state-run Azerbaijani Press Agency (APA).
Clothing reflecting the “history, culture, and national and moral values of the Azerbaijani people” may be worn during celebrations, subject to approval by the Pedagogical Council, which operates under the Ministry of Science and Education, APA said.
However, this decision to effectively ban the hijab has sparked an outcry.
Local Azerbaijani media outlets reported that students at at least two schools boycotted classes in protest against the restrictions, while pupils also reportedly demonstrated outside schools on Monday.
Azerbaijan’s Interior Ministry told APA that people in Baku had confronted school staff over the uniform requirements, damaged school property and attempted to disrupt lessons.
It said that “37 people were arrested as a criminal investigation had been opened into disturbing public order”.
Meanwhile, social media users based in Azerbaijan have reported difficulties accessing platforms such as Instagram and TikTok, claiming that the sites only work when accessed through virtual private networks (VPNs).
Protests against the uniform policy are ongoing, with critics accusing the authorities of restricting access to social media to suppress dissent.
Azerbaijani authorities have not officially commented on the reported social media outages.
Rupture with Turkey
The controversy has also attracted attention beyond Azerbaijan.
Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, described Azerbaijan’s move as “unacceptable”.
“Leaving a student who covers her head for reasons of faith at the school gate – how can this fit into any conscience, any sense of justice?” he posted on X.
Turkey has been a key ally of Azerbaijan, supporting it in its 2020 war with Armenia, which ultimately led to Azerbaijan regaining control of the Nagorno-Karabakh region.
The ruling Yeni Azerbaijan Party (YAP) hit back on Tuesday, saying Saral’s “irresponsible” comments risked damaging Azerbaijan’s closest relationship on the international stage.
Azerbaijan is a predominantly Shia Muslim country but, after decades of Soviet rule, emerged as one of the most secular states in the Muslim world.
The authorities have imposed restrictions on religious worship and arrested individuals accused of "extremism" in efforts to prevent radicalisation.
Critics have accused the Azerbaijani government of persecuting devout Muslims.
Restrictions on headscarves previously sparked demonstrations between 2010 and 2012, with police dispersing protests and making arrests.
Meanwhile, Azerbaijan’s close relationship with Israel, particularly amid its genocidal war on Gaza, has prompted criticism of the government from Turkish social media users.
Baku’s decision not to leave the UN General Assembly hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address last month drew a wave of condemnation.

Australia, Jordan pledge closer defence ties as Middle East tensions mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:39:44 UTC
23:39:44 KST

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Jordan’s King Abdullah II have agreed to strengthen defence, trade and climate cooperation as the two leaders discussed regional security and escalating tensions in the Middle East during a meeting in Canberra.
In a joint statement on Wednesday, the leaders welcomed plans to deepen defence ties through military training, technology sharing, defence industry cooperation, joint operations and counterterrorism efforts.
They also condemned terrorism and violent extremism.
The talks took place at a time of heightened regional instability, with both leaders stressing the importance of diplomacy and de-escalation.
Leaders reaffirm support for Palestinian statehood
Albanese and Abdullah reaffirmed their commitment to a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, rejected attempts to annex the occupied West Bank and opposed the displacement of Palestinians.
They also called for the full implementation of the Gaza Peace Plan and the unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid to the territory.
Australia condemned Iranian attacks on Jordan and expressed solidarity with the kingdom, according to the joint statement.
The leaders also reaffirmed their support for Syria’s unity and sovereignty, backed Lebanon’s efforts to strengthen state authority and condemned attacks by Houthi militias on Saudi Arabia.
Defence and trade ties in focus
Speaking at Parliament House, Albanese said international cooperation was more important than ever for global security.
“It’s never been more important for countries to work together in the interests of international security,” he said, highlighting collaboration on defence, security, humanitarian assistance, resources and energy.
Abdullah also identified military and intelligence cooperation as areas in which Australia and Jordan could deepen their partnership.
Trade remains another pillar of bilateral relations. Goods and services trade between the two countries totalled $242 million (A348.7 million) in the 2024–25 financial year, according to the Australian Embassy in Amman.
Australian exports to Jordan accounted for $151.1 million (A217.2 million), while imports from the kingdom reached $91.5 million (A131.5 million). Major traded products include meat and fertilisers.
The discussions also covered climate cooperation, signalling an effort to broaden the relationship beyond traditional security ties and expand collaboration across economic and environmental priorities.

Saudi national charged with planting a listening device at OpenAI offices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:39:29 UTC
23:39:29 KST

Saudi national charged with planting a listening device at OpenAI offices
US FBI said Abdulrahman Alfozan was engineer at the tech giant from June 2025.
United States federal agents have arrested a Saudi national and charged him with planting a hidden audio recording device in a conference room at the California offices of OpenAI, where he was working as an engineer.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had been working at the AI company since July 2025, the US Department of Justice said in a statement on Tuesday.
OpenAI discovered the device plugged into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to a criminal complaint filed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).
Following the discovery, the company placed a camera in the room, which captured Alfozan entering last week and checking behind the television where the listening device had been installed, the FBI alleges.
The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete for the best talent and technology with the potential to alter regional economic and strategic dynamics.
Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan and what is he charged with?
Alfozan has been a legal permanent resident of the US since September 2020.
According to a LinkedIn profile in his name, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the University of California, Berkeley. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, it said.
Before he joined OpenAI, he was a venture partner at Raed Ventures, headquartered in Riyadh in Saudi Arabia, which invested “in seed and early-stage startups in Saudi Arabia and MENA”.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the details mentioned in this LinkedIn profile.
Alfozan made his first court appearance on Tuesday on a charge of “using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications”.
It was not immediately clear if he has legal representation. He is expected to return to court on October 19.
If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release.
What happened at OpenAI?
The FBI says a thumb-sized device with a microphone, and which could connect to a camera, had been concealed in toilet paper and placed behind a television set in the conference room. It was installed around September 28, the FBI said. Its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar device in Alfozan’s personal bag.
In a post on X, OpenAI said it had evidence that the employee intended to place other listening devices throughout sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the company said.
The FBI complaint also alleges that Alfozan used an AI productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, despite not having the authority to access these spaces or participate in meetings there.
“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.
Hasn’t OpenAI been accused of helping to spy on civilians?
In an X post by OpenAI explaining how its own systems were used to trap Alfozan, the company said: “Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.”
But AI technology is used not only to catch spying, but conversely, to engage in it as well.
In February 2025, an investigation by The Associated Press found that US tech giants had enabled Israel to track and kill people in Gaza and Lebanon through AI and computing services. The AP reported that the Israeli military had bought advanced AI tools from tech companies including OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, through Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform, to assist with surveillance.
OpenAI denies having a relationship with the Israeli military.
But OpenAI also faced criticism when it signed a deal with the US Department of Defense in February this year to supply its technology to the US military for use in classified settings, including intelligence gathering. OpenAI’s competitor, Anthropic, refused to sign the same deal unless the Pentagon barred mass surveillance of Americans.
There have been several incidents in which OpenAI models have gone “rogue” by independently breaking out of a testing environment and then hacking into other organisations and even government sites, leading to calls for stronger regulations against unchecked AI surveillance.

Japan protests Chinese delegation's visit to disputed Russian-held islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:38:56 UTC
23:38:56 KST

Faisal Mahmud
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Japan on Wednesday protested a rare visit by a Chinese delegation to Russian-controlled islands Tokyo claims are disputed, amid growing tensions over the territory, according to media reports.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi told parliament that Tokyo had lodged diplomatic protests with Beijing and Moscow because of the visit, Bloomberg reported.
“We believe it is completely unacceptable for government officials, business representatives or others from third countries to enter and conduct activities in the Northern Territories in a manner that treats them as though they were Russian territory,” said Motegi.
He said Japan conveyed its position to Russia and China through diplomatic channels on Tuesday, urging both to respond appropriately.
Officials and business representatives from China's northeastern Heilongjiang province visited Iturup, known as Etorofu in Japan, earlier this month to assess potential tourism and aquaculture projects, according to Russian regional authorities.
The visit followed Russian President Vladimir Putin's first trip to the disputed island in August, which Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi condemned as unacceptable.
Tokyo maintains that the Northern Territories, consisting of Iturup, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group, were “illegally” seized by the now-defunct Soviet Union soon after Japan’s surrender in World War II on Aug. 15, 1945.
Russia argues that the seizure was legitimate.
The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty since World War II. Tensions have deepened in recent years amid Japan’s sanctions against Moscow for the Russia-Ukraine war.

Law of the Sea comes to life in the hunt for sanctioned Russian oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:38:09 UTC
23:38:09 KST

Law of the Sea comes to life in the hunt for sanctioned Russian oil
Ukraine’s Western allies are using maritime law to inspect Russian shadow tankers.
Until US President Donald Trump reversed the thrust of his sanctions policy of Russian oil on Friday, Ukraine’s Western allies had been ramping up the use of international law.
Countries sanctioning Russian oil have for the first time enforced boarding and inspection rights under the Law of the Sea this year, experts told Al Jazeera.
“The whole idea now is to disrupt, deter and make it more expensive and costly for Russia to logistically get their oil to market on these ships, and that’s definitely happening,” said Michelle Bockmann, an analyst at maritime intelligence company Windward. She spoke to Al Jazeera on the sidelines of the 49th Conference on Oceans Law and Policy held in Athens.
Some Russian officials believe worse is to come.
“Western countries are trying to organise the interception of our vessels. London and Brussels are drawing up plans to blockade the Baltic Sea and the straits leading into it. Other key shipping routes are also under threat,” Russian Maritime Board chairman Nikolai Patrushev told officials during a visit to China on October 12.
Western sanctions not only ban Russian oil purchases in the sanctioning territories. They forbid Western-insured tankers from selling Russian oil to third parties except at below-market prices, which leaves Russia with little or no profit.
Since sanctions were imposed in 2022, Russia has been exporting about half of its crude oil through a “shadow fleet” of tankers that are not owned or insured by Western institutions, and often do not comply with environmental and safety standards.
It is the right to enforce these standards that allows the United States, United Kingdom and European Union to step up compliance inspections using Article 110 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which allows coastal states to inspect vessels.
That has decreased Russia’s room for manoeuvre in its cat-and-mouse game of circumventing oil sanctions 45 months after the EU, US and other Group of Seven (G7) states imposed them.
“A lot of these ships were using fraudulent registries, and they were stateless,” said Bockmann. Under UNCLOS, she said, “Instead of just hailing them, ‘Hey, what’s your flag? What’s your insurance?’ and then letting them merrily go on their way under the right of innocent passage … they now had a legal basis to board them.”
Shadow tankers have engaged in various illegal practices that exposed them to suspicion and boarding. They have transferred Russian oil from one vessel to another on the high seas to disguise its provenance. They have turned off their trackers to avoid monitoring, falsified their positions, evaded insurance obligations, and flown false flags.
The catalyst for using Article 110 against these practices was the US, which invoked it late last year to board vessels evading US Department of the Treasury sanctions against the export of Venezuelan oil in Operation Southern Spear.
With help from the UK, US Marines seized the Russian-owned Bella I, sanctioned for carrying Iranian and Venezuelan as well as Russian oil, in the North Atlantic last January.
The UK and France have since boarded several other vessels under UNCLOS rules. Although these inspections are few compared to the hundreds of shadow tankers afloat, they have put pressure on the shadow fleet, experts said.
“Article 110 had just been sitting there, not really getting any traction,” said Kristina Siig, a professor of economic law at Aalborg University in Denmark. “The tool has always been there, but it just never got pulled out of the drawer.”
This new adherence to law has had knock-on effects in the shipping industry.
“Due diligence has become the biggest headache in ship management,” said George Xiradakis, a maritime consultant who sits on the boards of several shipping companies in Piraeus, Greece.
Ship charterers and buyers “have to check thoroughly that a ship is in compliance with international standards”, he told Al Jazeera, noting, “The time requirement compared to 2025 has gone up by a factor of several times manyfold.”
The sanctioning nations have pursued the shadow fleet relentlessly.
After being evicted from Western fleets, Russia turned to flags of convenience. The EU, UK and US approached those registries and persuaded them to oust the shadow vessels.
“St Kitts and Nevis were the very first ones in early 2024 … Palau, Gabon, Gambia, Cook Islands, San Marino, Barbados, Comoros, Guinea-Bissau, Sao Tome – they’ve all stopped,” said Bockmann.
Russia reacted this year by bringing many of those tankers onto its own registry.
TankerTrackers.com lists 340 dark or shadow tankers as Russian-flagged. Sanctioning states have responded by using UNCLOS.
Zelenskyy’s ‘sanctions’
Ukraine wants to see all of Russia’s export revenue from fossil fuels dry up, and its President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Trump’s rapprochement with Moscow will prolong the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war.
Kyiv has this year struck at least 26 of Russia’s 30 refineries, causing headaches on the global market.
Russia saw an initial windfall of 31 billion euros ($35bn) this year, after the crisis over the blockage of the Middle East’s Strait of Hormuz raised oil and gas prices worldwide, the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) calculated.
That windfall temporarily bucked a trend of constantly falling Russian oil and gas revenue since the Ukraine war began in 2022. Month-on-month revenues shot up by 52 percent in March.
But Russia’s August revenue from crude oil, refined products and gas all fell by eight percent, following a 12 percent drop in July and a one percent drop in June.
The binary weapon of UNCLOS and national law
The official rationale for inspections is safety, and under UNCLOS “we have a right, we actually have a joint obligation, to try to help each other to police that”, said Siig.
But the agenda that drives these inspections – stopping Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine by interdicting the Russian oil trade – is not enforceable under UNCLOS, she said.
“We are not allowed to tell certain states that they can’t export goods. The only entity that can do that is the UN,” she said. “To enforce sanctions, you have to have state jurisdiction.”
That combination of national and international law makes Denmark and Sweden extremely important.
Together, they control the narrowest chokepoints in the Baltic, where shipping has to pass to enter the North Sea and the Atlantic. So tankers loading crude oil and petroleum products at the Ust-Luga and Primorsk refineries in the Leningrad region have to pass through Danish and Swedish territorial waters, where national laws fully apply, to reach global markets.
The Danish Maritime Authority recorded 292 Russian shadow tanker transits through the Baltic in 2025, and it has progressively tightened its inspection regime.
In February 2025, Danish authorities began compliance inspections on tankers anchored off Skagen, and in April detained the Vietnamese-flagged shadow tanker Vigo after finding its fire safety lax.
In October, Denmark broadened inspections to include ballast systems, fuel quality, emissions, waste management and certificate verification.
“The Danish approach has been to throw the book at [Russia],” said Siig, as Danish authorities now ask for an oil insurance certificate, a sail plan through the Danish Straits and safety documents in addition to an insurance certificate, she said.
Russia ‘acting aggressively towards NATO’
Conscious of the danger of being bottled into the Baltic, Russia has reacted with fury.
On September 14, a Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish helicopter that was inspecting it in international waters south of Gedser, in the Danish Straits.
“Russian forces are increasingly acting aggressively towards NATO military units in the Baltic Sea region,” said a recent Danish Defence Intelligence Service report. “Russia is under more pressure than it has been at any other point during the war against Ukraine. Ukraine’s sustained long-range attacks are causing still more extensive damage deep inside Russia … The Russian economy is on the brink of a major crisis, driven by military expenditures, international sanctions and Ukrainian strikes.”
Denmark is treading carefully as it flexes these provisions of international law for the first time, said Siig. Danish authorities may now be asking for an oil insurance certificate, safety documents, a sail plan through the Danish Straits, and an insurance certificate, but closing off the Strait is not on the cards, she said.
“I have seen no public evidence that such a measure is being considered. Under the ordinary Law of the Sea regime, the Danish Straits are international straits subject to transit passage, and the Kingdom of Denmark has a strong interest in preserving that rules-based system,” Siig said.
“Russia has lost the Baltic,” she noted. “Everybody seemed to be getting along just fine. Then Ukraine happened, and suddenly they got boxed in, geopolitically.”
Ukraine has asked its allies to enforce sanctions even more forcefully. That, said Siig, “might stop the Ukrainian war, and it might start a new one”.

In Phoenix, young ultra-conservatives look to carry on Charlie Kirk’s legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:37:37 UTC
23:37:37 KST

In Phoenix, young ultra-conservatives look to carry on Charlie Kirk’s legacy
From our special correspondent in Phoenix – More than a year after the assassination of far-right influencer Charlie Kirk in September 2025, young activists from the organisation he co-founded, Turning Point USA, are working tirelessly to honour his legacy by rallying the youth vote ahead of the US midterm elections.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
On a cool October evening in the suburbs of Phoenix, capital city of the US state of Arizona, a young ultra-conservative influencer turns his mic on and welcomes the viewers flocking to his TikTok live stream.
“Hi Dylan, great to see you! What’s up, Chase? Thanks to everyone moderating the chat!”
Carson Carpenter, a 21-year-old political science graduate from Arizona State University (ASU) is welcoming participants for an online discussion entitled, “Liberals debate me one-on-one”.
The style of the debate is inspired by Charlie Kirk, a leading figure among ultra-conservative youth who was fatally shot at a speaking event at Utah college on September 10, 2025.
Read moreCharlie Kirk: Trump's fiery far-right 'youth whisperer'
“TikTok live streams aren’t my favourite thing, but at least they bring in a lot of people. There are also a lot of trolls or people who attack me, but that’s part of the game,” Carpenter said with a wry smile, describing his stance as “Jesus First and America Only”.
The debate topic for the evening is particularly explosive: the alleged drugging and gang rape of a female student at Cornell University in 2024 by seven fraternity members.
When an online user joins the discussion on the microphone, Carpenter, in the style of Kirk, immediately attacks him.
“So, you think the accuser is innocent in this case?” he asks him in a deliberately provocative tone.
‘I hope I can carry out his legacy’
Carpenter then accuses the mainstream media of having “protected” the victim. The exchange grows increasingly tense as the disagreement unfolds before hundreds of viewers. Live on air, allegations of gang rape are reduced to a series of provocative questions, in which participants are invited to take sides.
Indeed Carpenter, who has amassed some 19,000 followers on TikTok, has now mastered the mechanics of these online confrontations. He asks controversial questions, takes assertive stances, and finds ways to put his opponents on the defensive.
He uses precisely the same debating tactics that far-right influencer Kirk popularised on American college campuses with his “Prove Me Wrong” concept, inviting students to challenge his ideas on camera. The most incendiary clips would then go viral.
Read moreMan accused of killing Charlie Kirk to face murder trial and possible death penalty
As former president of the ASU chapter of the “College Republicans”, Carpenter worked closely with Kirk, founder of the powerful ultra-conservative youth organisation Turning Point USA.
“I think the Charlie Kirk legacy is just making people apply their thought into reality when it comes to the country as a whole,” said Carpenter, who now heads Off The Record USA, a right-wing media brand he co-founded.
“I hope I can carry out his legacy in the way that he saw it … I don't want to say I would take credit for what his legacy should be, because that can only be determined by him and Jesus.
“There's nobody else that's going to be like Charlie ever,” he added.
The day after his TikTok live stream, Carpenter left his recording studio to head to Paradise Valley Park, in the northern part of Phoenix. He is part of the “CleanUp America” tour organised by Turning Point USA, which carries out a cleanup effort followed by a community festival.
In Phoenix, where Turning Point USA was co-founded by Kirk in 2012, the festival is a must-attend for local young conservatives.
Once the cleanup is complete, participants gather in front of the stage, some still wearing their fluorescent yellow vests. Although the atmosphere is meant to be family-friendly, politics is never far away.
Read moreMAGA civil war steals the spotlight at 'AmericaFest' conference
In a clear nod to US President Donald Trump’s rallying slogan of “Make America Great Again”, participants hand out red caps with the slogan “Make America Clean Again”.
The speakers say prayers, and make repeated references to Christ and the American nation, while participants reflect in silence during the songs.
Kirk himself is frequently honoured. Several minutes of prayer are held in his memory, while a Tesla Cybertruck adorned with his image and the slogan "We the people stand with Charlie Kirk" is parked near the entrance.
‘Big shoes to fill’
On stage, the speakers make one reactionary speech after another. Anthony Watson, a former skeleton racer who competed for Jamaica at the 2018 Winter Olympics and now works with Turning Point USA, insists that the event is not “a forum for debate” and that it is not about “promoting any particular ideology”.
But ultra-conservative influencer Taylor Sharp is not so ideologically cautious. Wearing an “America the Beautiful” cap, he tells the audience that abortion is “the genocide of our children in the womb” and called for Planned Parenthood (Do you need me to ID this or is it obvious?) to be defunded.
In a similar spirit to Kirk, he organises debates on campuses across Arizona in a bid to convince students to join the conservative camp.
For Sharp, who now has more than 168,000 followers on Instagram, Kirk’s death has left a void that no one seems able to fill.
“Kirk was the only one holding this MAGA divide together with civil discourse,” he said.
“Now we have people going after each other on Twitter every single day. And it's like a war room now instead of being peaceful and actually, you know, doing it for the betterment of the movement.”
Indeed, amid the tributes to Kirk, there are growing divisions within the MAGA ranks on issues such as Israel and anti-Semitism.
“There's people that can unify but it's big shoes to fill, you know,” Sharp acknowledged.
“I just don't see that person yet,” he added.
But not all the festival’s participants shared his doubts about a successor to Kirk.
When the American national anthem was played, Daniel Fisher, 26, a strategy director at Turning Point USA, stood to attention with an American flag in one hand and his cap pressed to his heart in the other.
Fisher believes that Charlie’s widow, Erika Kirk, who became president of Turning Point USA immediately after his killing, is his natural heir.
When Erika Kirk made a surprise appearance on stage, she was met with rapturous applause from the audience.
But after speaking for just a few moments, she broke down in tears in the arms of attendees who had come to greet her.
Since her husband’s death, Erika Kirk has taken on an extremely high-profile role, celebrated by her supporters but accused by her detractors of making a spectacle of her grief.
Fisher, however, had the utmost faith in her.
“That was Charlie Kirk's wife, and I don't believe that he made an error when he chose his wife. I feel with God backing her up, she can do the impossible,” he said.
Yet while the festival rallied committed ultra-conservative supporters, it also sought to attract voters beyond its usual sphere of influence.
Daisy Fernandez-Herrera, 22, a master’s student at Grand Canyon University, was one such example.
She described herself as an independent voter and was persuaded by her roommate to make the trip.
“I didn't really have much of an opinion on Turning Point USA,” she confided, wearing a badge emblazoned with “Clean Up America”.
“I heard like a lot of things, but I'm always open for like either side, just like getting my own opinion. I just like their purpose when it comes to their faith, like bringing the community together is always a blessing.
Miles Jetton, 24, a student at the same university, also commented on the religious aspect of the rally.
“I do believe that it is so important to have our foundation in Christ because if you have people … their ideologies are all out of whack, you're going to have a country that's all out of whack. And I think we're starting to see that in America,” he said.
For others, like Ange Perez, 25, the path to Turning Point USA began on social media. An administrative assistant and member of Young Professionals – the organisation’s branch dedicated to networking among young adults – she came across Kirk while scrolling through reels on YouTube.
“I immediately liked his quick wit, his intelligence, his ability to debate, and the strength of his arguments, backed by facts. He’s a role model for me, in a world where I feel that people my age aren’t well-informed enough,” she said.
For Perez, Kirk’s influence extends beyond politics and into religion.
“I wasn't always a Christian, but I became really curious about Christianity when I would hear him talk about it. So then I started going to church,” she said.
My sister invited me and after that I decided to buy my first Bible […] And if everything is true in the Bible, which it is, and if that's where he derived Kirk’s ideas from, then God's ways are good,” she added.
In Paradise Valley Park, participants are packing up. The booths are emptying, and families are heading back to their cars. For Turning Point, the stakes now go beyond TikTok videos and rallies: they have to mobilise supporters into votes on the ground.
As the midterm elections approach, the organisation – which claims to have more than 1,500 campus chapters – is seeking to mobilise its network in support of Republican candidates.
In Arizona, it is backing Andy Biggs, a staunchly conservative Trump ally who is running for governor against incumbent Democrat Katie Hobbs.
Young influencer Sharp, for his part, has no doubt about which direction the state should take.
“Arizona is on a declining … depressing slope that is going into the ground because of Katie Hobbs, he said. She doesn't actually do anything for our state. Andy Biggs is the only person on the ticket that can actually fix this,” he said.
However, Turning Point’s strategy has not gained broad support among ultra-conservatives, even among Republicans, with some criticising the group for backing candidates who are too radical to win over moderate voters.
The organisation also faces another challenge in the erosion of support for Trump among some young voters. Only 49% of 2024 Trump voters aged 19 to 34 continued to approve of his actions in October 2026, according to a study published in early October by the Pew Research Center.
Carpenter, though a MAGA supporter, made no secret of his disappointment with the president.
“Trump has made some mistakes with not just the implementation […] but it's not keeping to the promises of his campaign,” he said.
“And that's why you've seen Gen Z's support wane, right? The war in Iran, the war in Ukraine not being ended, tariffs not being fully implemented, and a whole slew of other things.”
Carpenter expects that the Republicans will be defeated in the midterm elections.
“The people that are saying that Republicans are going to somehow win a supermajority … have not sobered themselves up to the reality of political history in the United States,” he said.

China's yuan loans increase by 11.52 trln yuan in Jan.-Sept. period
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
22:37:35 CST
23:37:35 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 11.52 trillion yuan (about 1.71 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of 2026, central bank data showed Wednesday.
At the end of September, outstanding yuan loans stood at 283.44 trillion yuan, up 4.8 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China (PBOC).
M2, a broad measure of money supply that covers cash in circulation and all deposits, stood at 359.63 trillion yuan at the end of September, up 7.2 percent year on year.
M1, which covers currency in circulation, corporate demand deposits, personal demand deposits and provisions received by non-bank payment institutions, reached 116.76 trillion yuan at the end of September, a rise of 3.2 percent from a year earlier.
China's outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy stood at 468.17 trillion yuan at the end of September, up 7.1 percent year on year, according to the central bank.
"China's major financial aggregates have maintained reasonable growth, with M2 and aggregate financing to the real economy growing at appropriate rates," said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management. "This has helped create a favorable monetary and financial environment for sustained economic improvement."
Since the beginning of the year, the PBOC has introduced two rounds of structural monetary policy measures to address the needs of China's transition to new growth drivers and help financial institutions better align their services with the needs of the real economy.
The latest round of structural monetary policy measures, announced in September, included cutting the one-year interest rate of the Pledged Supplementary Lending (PSL) facility from 1.75 percent to 1.5 percent, expanding the scope of PSL support, and increasing the quota of the relending facility for sci-tech innovation and technological upgrades by 200 billion yuan.
The policy package will channel more funds to areas such as equipment upgrades, strengthen support for sci-tech enterprises, help ease financing constraints on private businesses and reduce their financing costs, said Dong Qingma, deputy head of the Institute of Chinese Financial Studies of Southwestern University of Finance and Economics.
The effects of the September policy package are expected to emerge gradually, with existing and new monetary policy measures working in tandem to provide continued support for high-quality development of the real economy, experts said. ■

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Security forces killed five terrorists and injured four others during an intelligence-based operation in Pakistan's southwest Balochistan province on Wednesday, security sources said.
The operation was conducted in Washuk district, where security forces targeted terrorist hideouts using advanced weapons, the sources told the media.

China's Zhuque-2E rocket launches 10 satellites into space
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

A Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket carrying 10 satellites blasts off from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China, Oct. 14, 2026. China successfully launched a Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China on Wednesday. The rocket lifted off at 7:40 p.m. (Beijing Time) and deployed 10 satellites into their preset orbits. The flight test mission was declared a complete success. (Photo by Wang Jiangbo/Xinhua)
JIUQUAN, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China successfully launched a Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China on Wednesday.
The rocket lifted off at 7:40 p.m. (Beijing Time) and deployed 10 satellites into their preset orbits.
The flight test mission was declared a complete success.
Eight satellites of the 02 group of a "star compute" plan, developed by Adaspace Technology Co., Ltd. (ADAspace) and designed to operate in dawn-dusk orbits, were included in the launch.
According to ADAspace, a commercial aerospace enterprise, these satellites carry high-performance computing payloads, high-speed inter-satellite and satellite-to-ground laser communication payloads, low-light cameras and other equipment.
They will conduct in-orbit verification of key technologies, such as liquid-cooled fluid loops at the 10,000-watt level, ultra-large deployable radiative cooling wings, full-domain laser communication networks and in-orbit training of foundation models.
ADAspace said it intends to carry out in-orbit tests of the 02 group satellites, advance technological iteration, and promote the space computing technology innovation and industry innovation.
The "star compute" plan is an ambitious project by the company to build AI space infrastructure composed of 2,800 computing satellites. The first group of satellites for the plan was successfully launched in May 2025. The third group is scheduled for orbital deployment in 2026. ■

Thailand's industrial confidence rebounds in September

22:36:48 CST
23:36:48 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's industrial confidence improved in September as reduced electricity tariffs helped ease business operating costs and lower living expenses for consumers while the year-end festive season spurred orders, data showed on Wednesday.
The Thai industrial sentiment index rose to 90.7 last month from 89.7 in August as most key components of the index increased, notably operating performance, total sales, production output, and total orders, despite rising cost pressure, according to the Federation of Thai Industries (FTI).
Passenger car sales trended upward, with battery electric vehicle sales surging 100.8 percent year-on-year and plug-in hybrid electric vehicle sales rising 35.3 percent in the first eight months of the year, contributing to the rebound in sentiment, said Pimjai Leeissaranukul, chairperson of the FTI.
Meanwhile, demand for technology products continued to expand, supported by investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers, Pimjai said.
However, she noted that the industrial sector is still facing ongoing risks, especially flooding across central and eastern provinces that damaged commercial operations and housing, hampered freight and input logistics, and created supply-chain bottlenecks in certain sub-sectors toward the end of September.
Based on a survey of 1,330 businesses across 48 industry groups conducted by the FTI, concerns about certain factors declined, namely the domestic economy, government policies, and lending interest rates. Meanwhile, worries about energy prices, the global economy, exchange rates, and access to credit mounted.
The index forecast for the next three months stood at 97.7 in the September survey, edging up from 97.0 a month earlier, reflecting a more optimistic outlook for the industrial sector, partly supported by easing global trade tensions.
Nevertheless, businesses remain exposed to flood threats across several provinces, where the pace and scope of state assistance, alongside post-disaster rehabilitation efforts, warrant close attention, the FTI said in a statement.
The group called on state authorities to adopt proactive flood risk management, including early warning systems and faster insurance compensation, promote energy efficiency initiatives to counter volatile energy prices, and prioritize Made in Thailand certified goods in public procurement, with tax incentives for private-sector use. ■

====================================================================================================

What is potash, and why is the US importing it from Belarus?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:36:48 UTC
23:36:48 KST

What is potash, and why is the US importing it from Belarus?
US reliance on Canadian potash, a key fertiliser mineral, adds to farmers’ cost concerns amid trade tensions.
The United States is preparing to receive its first shipment of Belarusian potash in four years, as President Donald Trump seeks cheaper fertiliser for American farmers amid rising costs linked to the Iran war and a trade dispute with Canada.
A 30,000-tonne shipment of potash is expected to arrive at the Port of New Orleans on Wednesday, according to data from Kpler. The shipment follows Washington’s decision to lift sanctions on major Belarusian potash producers in March, opening an avenue for trade to resume.
Although this shipment from Belarus accounts for only a fraction of the 5.6 million tonnes of potash the US imported last year, it signals a tentative opening of relations between Washington and Minsk.
Trump has said the US is working on a larger agreement to buy Belarusian fertiliser at prices substantially below what it pays Canada, its dominant supplier. But analysts have questioned whether Belarus can compete with Canadian producers on price and expand exports enough to significantly change the US market.
What is potash and why does the US need it?
Potash is a potassium-rich mineral that is a primary fertiliser element. Potassium, an essential plant nutrient, has no substitutes, and potash is widely used in agriculture, including in the cultivation of corn and soybeans.
The US depends heavily on imports to meet its potash needs. Canada accounts for almost 80 percent of US potash imports, according to the US Geological Survey’s 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries. Russia accounts for 12 percent, the second-largest share of US potash imports.
That reliance has made fertiliser supply an economic and political concern, particularly as farmers face rising production costs. In recent months, US farmers have reported higher fuel and fertiliser costs, putting pressure on already tight profit margins.
Trump has reportedly been concerned that financial strain may cost Republicans some of the US farmer vote in this year’s midterms. In 2024, Trump won 78 percent of the vote in farming-dependent counties. At an agriculture roundtable in Wisconsin in June, Trump promised fertiliser prices would “go way down” as the US emerged from the Iran conflict.
Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have added to pressure on global fertiliser markets, particularly for nitrogen-based products. Potash, however, is less directly exposed to the crisis, with the US relying heavily on supplies from Canada.
Trump has argued that buying Belarusian potash could reduce those costs. An additional supplier could also give US buyers more options in a market dominated by Canadian imports.
For farmers, the immediate benefits remain uncertain. Fertiliser is one of several major expenses facing agricultural businesses, alongside diesel fuel and machinery. Even a reduction in potash prices would not necessarily offset increases elsewhere.
Can Belarus offer cheaper fertiliser?
In September, Trump boasted on social media about striking a potential potash deal with Belarus.
“The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said in the post. “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.”
Trump promoted Belarusian potash as a less expensive alternative to Canadian supplies, but the economics of delivering it to American buyers complicates that plan.
Belarus is landlocked, and EU restrictions are affecting its export routes, forcing potash shipments to take a more circuitous path through Russia. The incoming cargo was loaded at the Russian port of Bronka near St Petersburg, according to reporting by the Financial Times.
Those logistical challenges could raise transportation costs and make Belarusian supplies less competitive, even if the product itself is cheaper.
The scale of the exports also matters. A single shipment shows that trade between the US and Belarus has resumed, but it does not mean Belarus can replace a substantial share of Canadian potash or drive down prices across the US market.
However, access to an alternative supplier could give Washington greater leverage in negotiations with Canadian producers, potentially helping US buyers secure more competitive potash prices.
Could Belarus replace Canada as the main potash supplier in the US?
Relations between the US and Canada have been strained since Trump’s second term began, when he unleashed a volley of tariffs on most trading partners, including Canada. His administration initially imposed a 25 percent tariff on many Canadian imports in March 2025, including potash, but reduced that to 10 percent following pushback from agricultural groups and lawmakers. Potash that meets the requirements of the USMCA trade agreement – the trade deal between the US, Mexico and Canada – is exempted. Most Canadian potash imports qualify under the USMCA and remain duty-free.
Trump has maintained that Washington would continue buying from Canada, even as Belarus offered to sell potash at a lower price.
But the viability of Belarus as a major supplier remains unlikely. In September, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko said the country could not supply large volumes of potash fertiliser to the US.
“Even if we wanted to supply [potash] to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes – everything is contracted,” Lukashenko said.
Whether this October shipment becomes part of a much larger deal will depend on the ability to sustain exports and the durability of the diplomatic opening between Washington and Minsk.
Why did the US impose sanctions on Belarus, and why are they being lifted?
The planned shipment marks a significant step in the restoration of trade between Washington and Minsk, which have spent years being at odds over Belarus’s human rights record and its support for Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The US, under former Democratic President Joe Biden, imposed increased sanctions on Belarus in 2021 after Lukashenko’s authoritarian government cracked down on mass protests against its disputed 2020 presidential election. Belarus has also faced Western sanctions for allowing Russian forces to use its territory in the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
But since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, his administration has pursued direct negotiations with Lukashenko. Those talks have led to the release of political prisoners in exchange for lifting US sanctions, creating a pathway towards renewed economic ties.
In March, Belarus released 250 political prisoners under a US-brokered agreement. Washington subsequently lifted sanctions on major Belarusian potash producers and eased restrictions on several financial institutions. In September, US special envoy John Coale announced a further agreement under which Belarus would release 25 prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief.
The rapprochement has opened the door to proposals for deeper commercial cooperation.
On September 29, Lukashenko said he had agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russian state-controlled energy company Gazprom would participate in a project to build a nitrogen fertiliser plant in Belarus. He proposed inviting the US to join the project using American technology, according to the Reuters news agency.
Before this agreement, exiled Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said that a deal with Lukashenko comes with risks.
“Our position is that it is not time to trade with the regime while all the income from potash goes to repression, goes to support of the Russian war machine,” Tsikhanouskaya told AFP in September.
The proposal has not established that Washington will participate in the project. But alongside Trump’s stated interest in buying Belarusian potash, it illustrates how Minsk is seeking to turn improved political relations into broader commercial opportunities.

frame to folly transforms from carnival gateway to neighborhood teahouse in pittsburgh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:35:50 UTC
23:35:50 KST

frame to folly transforms from carnival gateway to neighborhood teahouse in pittsburgh
frame to folly, a collaborativde project between architectural crafts collective, partlab, and neighborhood allies, is a modular timber pavilion developed for different sites and community uses in pittsburgh.
[FEATURED]
modular pavilion shifts from carnival gateway to public furniture
Frame to Folly is a modular timber pavilion designed to be disassembled, transported, and reconfigured for different sites and community uses in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Developed by Carnegie Mellon University’s student-led Architectural Crafts Collective and Pittsburgh-based PARTlab (Laboratory for Radical Participatory Design), the project forms part of a year-long partnership with local nonprofit Neighborhood Allies.
The structure uses a system of vertical timber frames connected by interchangeable infill panels that double as seats, tables, backrests, and awnings. Initially assembled as a gateway for Pittsburgh’s annual Spring Carnival, the pavilion was prefabricated at a shared fabrication space, flat-packed, and transported to the festival site. The frames were joined on the ground and raised into place using a communal technique that required no heavy equipment. Bright orange infill panels were then secured with removable hardware, providing seating, shade, and other amenities for festival visitors.
Reusable timber components adapt to new community setting
After the three-day event, the pavilion was disassembled and moved to the backyard of a neighborhood tea shop, where the same components were reconfigured as flexible public furniture and an open-air teahouse. Built collaboratively by the Architectural Crafts Collective, a student-led design-build collective at Carnegie Mellon University, and Pittsburgh-based PARTlab, the modular system adapts to the new setting while retaining its original components.
At the end of its use at the tea shop, the structure will either be gifted to another community for reconfiguration or disassembled and donated to a material bank operated by the neighboring public library. Through its successive forms and uses, Frame to Folly demonstrates design for disassembly and material reuse, treating architecture as an adaptable system that can respond to changing community needs.
project info:
name: Frame to Folly
architect: Carnegie Mellon University’s Architectural Crafts Collective and PARTlab (Laboratory for Radical Participatory Design)
design team: Sydney Mansavage, Emma Phelps, Tai Le, Gaetan Pelletey, Hazel Buonopane, Jason Asiedu, Neal Lucas Hitch, Kristina Fisher
location: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, US

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia has to build a transparent and clear system for the life and work of foreign specialists, taking into account the needs of all those arriving in the country, CEO of the Agency for Attracting Foreign Talent to Russia Irina Korotkova said.
Earlier, Korotkova said that since the launch of the Time to Live in Russia program, people from 97 countries had submitted 842 applications, with the first seven candidates from China, Jordan, Syria, Canada, Iran, Mexico and Spain already approved.
According to the CEO, interest in the program exceeded the organizers’ expectations. She noted that participants share Russia’s values and are willing to benefit the country.
“Over the past six months, we have observed that the mechanism [of the Time to Live in Russia program] really works and interest in the program has even exceeded our expectations. These are people that share our values and want to benefit our country. For this mechanism to work, we have to create a transparent and clear system for foreign specialists to live and work here. People should consider our country their home, a place where they can realize their potential and where their families will live. Scientists have certain needs, while representatives of creative professions or athletes have others. So each person needs a personalized approach,” the press service of the Agency for Strategic Initiatives (ASI) quoted Korotkova as saying.
Support from day one
Once foreigners receive the special status, they can get a temporary residence permit outside the quota or immediately apply for a residence permit, bypassing the temporary residence stage. The processing of applications will be fast-tracked. The program also helps with relocation, finding a job and settling in Russia.
According to First Deputy Head of the Citizenship and Foreign Citizens Registration Service under the Russian Interior Ministry Konstantin Bukreyev, the ministry helps foreigners who have chosen to move to Russia, including under a decree that streamlines the procedure for obtaining temporary residence permits for those sharing traditional Russian spiritual and moral values. "The Interior Ministry also provides them with advisory and other assistance with paperwork on a priority basis, in a one-stop shop," Bukreyev said.
Program participants’ stories
One participant, Mexico’s Domingo Garcia Martinez Surita, has already been living in Moscow for several years. He worked for big international pharmaceutical companies and is now developing the business for the Russian pharmaceutical firm R-Pharm in Latin America.
"Russia is a wonderful country, it is very safe here. Traditional values resonate with me. I am a Christian, a rather conservative person and I like how Russia values family," he said.
Another participant, Jordanian bioinformatics scientist Tarek Faruni, returned to Russia after working at leading research centers abroad, including Harvard Medical School, McGill University and ETH Zurich. "Russia is a great country. I have lived here before and decided to return, I like Russian culture. My wife is Russian, my son speaks Russian and we want to raise him here," he said.
About program
The Time to Live in Russia program was launched in April 2026, following an initiative to streamline the relocation of foreigners who share traditional Russian values. It is run by the Agency for Attracting Foreign Talent to Russia, a subsidiary of the ASI.
Apart from this program, Russia also has a relocation mechanism under Presidential Decree No. 702, which streamlines the procedure of obtaining temporary residence permits for foreigners who share traditional Russian spiritual and moral values.

Saudi Arabia/Yemen: Civilians must not pay the price of escalation in hostilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:32:28 UTC
23:32:28 KST

Responding to the dramatic escalation of armed hostilities between the Huthi de facto authorities, the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia in recent weeks and the growing toll on civilians amidst ongoing attacks, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Heba Morayef, said:
“The risks to civilians in Yemen and Saudi Arabia are rapidly increasing each day this conflict escalates. All parties to the conflict must ensure civilians are protected and abide by their obligations under international humanitarian law.
“Over the past week, deadly Huthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia have caused significant civilian harm, including a 10 October attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds more- the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in over a decade. The attack came amidst the return of full-blown armed hostilities to Yemen with devastating consequences for civilians there, particularly on the coast and around Ta’iz, Yemen’s third largest city.
Civilians are never legitimate targets. They must not pay the price of further escalation.
Heba Morayef, Amnesty International
“Civilians are never legitimate targets. They must not pay the price of further escalation. The deliberate targeting of civilians or civilian infrastructure, including civilian airports, is prohibited under international humanitarian law and can amount to a war crime.
“All warring parties must immediately refrain from carrying out direct attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks.
“In Yemen, where civilians are already grappling with a severe humanitarian crisis and the impact of years of sporadic bouts of fighting, the conflict will further compound the suffering of the civilian population. It is critical that parties to the conflict take all feasible precautions to avoid or, in any event, minimize harm to civilians and civilian objects, and provide unfettered access to humanitarian aid for civilians in need.”
Background
Recent weeks have seen a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the Huthi de-facto authorities in Yemen, the internationally recognized Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia. The renewed conflict in Yemen is linked to the regional conflict involving the US, Israel, and Iran. The Huthis are supported by Iran and the Yemeni government by Saudi Arabia.
The escalation in Yemen follows the breakdown of a UN-brokered ceasefire in July 2026, following air strikes on Sana’a airport claimed by the internationally recognized government. Between 2015 and 2022, Amnesty International documented gross human rights violations and serious violations of international humanitarian law, including likely war crimes, committed by parties to the conflict, including the Huthi armed group and Saudi-led coalition.
The escalation has been accompanied by intensified ground fighting between the Huthis and Yemeni government forces inside Yemen, including deadly attacks by Huthi forces on civilian areas. While the real death toll is significantly higher, the UN human rights office reported in late September that it had documented at least 32 civilians, including 15 children, killed since August.
Huthi forces have also carried out attacks targeting airports, military installations and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, as well as ships at sea. Between 5 and 11 October, Huthi attacks on civilian airports across Saudi Arabia damaged passenger terminals and civilian aircraft and killed at least 20 people and injured more than 350 people, according to the National.
Saudi Arabia has also resumed its air strikes in Yemen. According to the Yemen Data Project, at least 66 civilians have been killed and 90 injured.
The latest escalation is exacerbating an already severe humanitarian crisis in Yemen where, according to UN figures, at least 18.3 million people are acutely food insecure and more than 2.2 million children under five and 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are acutely malnourished. Access to food and healthcare have repeatedly worsened due to the conflict, warring party conduct and humanitarian funding cuts.

Starshield Connectivity Begins Dropping on Ukrainian Drones at Speeds Above 72 km/h
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:31:41 UTC
23:31:41 KST

On the night of October 14, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals in Ukraine.
According to sources in Ukraine’s Defense Ministry who spoke to Militarnyi, the Defense Forces received no advance notice of the changes.
Starshield is a secure satellite communications system SpaceX developed for government, military, and intelligence users.
Across different unmanned platforms and units, connectivity drops at different speed thresholds, ranging from 72 to 161 km/h. The specific threshold depends on the platform on which the terminal is installed.
Once the terminal exceeds the set speed, it loses connectivity. The restriction affects unmanned systems that rely on Starshield for control and data transmission while moving.
In particular, the changes complicate missions involving drones, including interceptor drones and medium-range strike drones, known as mid-strike drones.
The restrictions also complicate frontline logistics, reconnaissance missions, and the use of drones as communications relays.
As of October 14, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry was in contact with the United States, SpaceX, and NATO partners to establish the circumstances surrounding the restrictions and identify possible solutions.
The ministry is also collecting information from Defense Forces units on how the changes affect terminal operation. Existing backup communications channels are being reviewed as well.
Volunteer Serhiy Sternenko, who supplies drones to the Defense Forces, suggested that SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.
The restrictions may be part of pressure from the Trump administration on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Burnham careful as he meets Zelensky but promises Ukraine won't leave 'empty handed'
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:30:48 BST
23:30:48 KST

Burnham treads carefully with Zelensky visit, balancing Trump and Ukraine
- Published
President Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to London follows a well-trodden diplomatic path in a war now in its fifth year.
For months, US President Donald Trump had been a largely benign presence in the conflict, promising Ukraine greater access to American air defence technology and threatening more sanctions on Russia.
Then last week Trump carried out an abrupt U-turn, lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and calling for Zelensky to be replaced.
Once again Ukraine's leader got on his plane to shore up support among European allies. Today London, tomorrow Brussels.
For the prime minister there was the tricky but now familiar diplomatic task of needing to show solidarity with Zelensky without appearing to criticise Trump.
Burnham's answer was to say and announce as much as he could without exposing himself to questions from journalists asking about Trump's latest betrayal of Kyiv.
So Downing Street issued an embargoed press notice overnight with warm words of support for Zelensky.
It said Burnham would promise to go "further and faster" in helping Ukraine with financial and military aid.
Specifically, the prime minister would pledge to speed up the delivery of lightweight multirole missiles that can help bring down fast jet-powered Russian drones.
There was a military honour guard in Downing Street to greet Ukraine's president, followed by a controlled photo opportunity showing the start of the meeting between the two men.
In No 10, before that meeting, Burnham told Zelensky that Britain stood with him "at this difficult time".
He said it was clear "who the aggressor is" after Russia's attacks on Ukraine's critical national infrastructure. And crucially he praised Zelensky for his "leadership" in being prepared to sit down and discuss Donald Trump's call for an energy ceasefire.
In his reply, Zelensky said it was an "absolutely terrible time" for Ukraine. There was no energy ceasefire, he said, but Russian escalation instead.
He said Ukraine "counted on partnership with the US" but spoke of "some difficulties" and "different surprises" with Ukraine's access to US intelligence and the Starlink satellite network.
Following the meeting, Downing Street said the two men had emphasised how Russia had launched "blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure" after President Trump's call for an energy ceasefire. It was clear, they agreed, "Russia had no interest in peace".
They also discussed how the UK could speed up defensive support for Ukraine ahead of the winter - as well as "retrofitting British capability" on military equipment provided by other allies.
In the House of Commons, at the start of his weekly question time, Burnham used the opportunity to offer what he called his "unwavering" support for Zelensky and promise greater military and financial aid in the future.
But it fell to the Liberal Democrat leader, Sir Ed Davey, to ask the question journalists might have asked if they had the chance.
Sir Ed said the prime minister had studiously avoided commenting on Trump's decision to rip up international sanctions on Russia.
"This House does deserve to know his position, as does frankly President Zelensky and our brave Ukrainian allies," Sir Ed said.
"Doesn't he agree this is yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security?"
In reply, Burnham admitted it was a "very dark and difficult moment" for Zelensky, who was "carrying the heaviest of weights" right now.
But Burnham eschewed the chance to criticise Trump and told MPs this: "What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."
"That is the role I intend to play - it's the right role for me to play - in this moment. I will listen to President Zelensky carefully but he won't be going away from Britain today empty handed."
In other words, do not expect the prime minister to join in the widespread European criticism of Trump.
After the now infamous falling out between Trump and Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025, the UK played a key role in calming the row and bringing both sides back together.
A key player was national security adviser Jonathan Powell, who shuttled between Washington and Kyiv pouring oil on troubled waters. It seems Burnham hopes the UK can play a similar bridge-building role now.
For millions of Ukrainians facing a grim winter potentially with less US support than before, the task could not be more urgent.

US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:29:42 UTC
23:29:42 KST

Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.
US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.
Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%.
Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.
Price increases this year have largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record high last month.
September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990.
The economy has consistently been cited as a top issue for American voters, as rising gasoline prices and persistent inflation have eaten into household budgets. Higher energy prices from the Iran war have cost Americans more than $1,020 per household, according to Brown University, and a total of $133bn for all US consumers.
Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for inflation that is outpacing their earnings, including 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump.
In recent weeks, Trump has attempted to downplay his administration’s role in price increases, pointing to the Iranian government as the cause of the squeeze. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest inflation report.
On Tuesday, Trump posted on social media that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate effort to affect the upcoming elections.
“They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran … in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE,” he wrote.
Later on Tuesday, Trump defended his record on the economy during a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, saying that his support for families has been “substantial”. “Every time they want to try and get me, they say ‘affordability’,” he said.
Heightened inflation will put more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates, its tool to cool prices. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing elevated prices. Higher rates affect the cost of borrowing money, including mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate, applied to the most commonly used loans for home ownership, is up to 7.40%.
“Inflation in the US has come in higher than expected, in a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, in a statement. “The president has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.”

Europe injects 50 bln cubic meters of gas into USG for winter, stockpiling pace slows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:29:26 UTC
23:29:26 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Net gas injection (the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes) by EU countries into underground gas storage (UGS) facilities since the start of the summer season in April 2026 has exceeded 50 billion cubic meters (bcm), according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Consequently, Europe has so far managed to inject only 74% of the volumes required for the upcoming winter into its UGS facilities.
While the average rate of gas injection into EU storage facilities in October remains the highest seen in four years, Europe has already missed the summer months that are most favorable for stockpiling.
As of October 12, European UGS facilities were 73.94% full (14.91 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 83.2% a year earlier. This remains the lowest level for this date since records began in 2011. EU storage facilities hold approximately 80.8 bcm of gas - 11 bcm less than last year's levels and the lowest volume since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that gas stocks in European UGS facilities might not even reach 75%, warning that the region faces a difficult autumn-winter season.
Earlier TASS reported that Europe risks starting the heating season with record-low gas stocks. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU countries may fill their storage facilities to only 70-75% capacity, marking an all-time low for the beginning of the heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU nations must ensure their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% margin of flexibility is permitted in the event of challenging filling conditions. Consequently, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 bcm by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season to meet the filling target. However, anticipating a very mild winter, the European Commission is prepared to lower this threshold to 80% for the current year.

France’s students are angry about more than crumbling classrooms and missing teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:29:13 UTC
23:29:13 KST

Say what you will about France’s high schools, they still produce world-class slogan writers. Here’s a brief selection spotted during three weeks of blockades and marches over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings:
“Pas d’avenir, pas de calme” (No future, no calm). “Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain” (Graduates today, insecure tomorrow). “Vous détruisez notre futur, on bloque votre présent” (You destroy our future, we block your present).
A couple more: “Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs” (Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”). “On n’est pas mal éduqués, on n’est pas écoutés” (We’re not badly brought up, we’re just not being listened to).
Spot the common theme? The protests, which continued this week with more than 160,000 on the streets on Tuesday, might be over very material problems – but beneath them there clearly lies an altogether more existential worry.
This generation fears its future will be one of diminishing prospects, poorly paid, unstable jobs, unaffordable living costs and steadily decaying public infrastructure – the end, in short, of the basic socioeconomic security their parents, mostly, enjoyed.
That was the central theme of a 30-second Instagram post I recorded last week with the Guardian’s social media team and that, at time of writing, had been watched almost 540,000 times – with young people in France the largest single group of viewers.
The same core concerns underlie youth protests elsewhere – notably, ongoing mass housing demonstrations in Spain, where the twentysomethings of Madrid and Barcelona are in revolt at the monthly rental on a one-bed flat costing an entire monthly median salary.
In France, teenagers in Seine-Saint-Denis, a low-income area in the north of Paris, show reporters pictures of broken chairs and desks, holes in walls, leaking ceilings, mould, shattered toilets and defective audiovisual equipment. Some have gone months without key teachers.
The consequence, here, is protest.
As Kitty Sayers, who went to school in France, explained, France’s republic “was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it … The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education.”
This means that in French schools protest is “taught as a legally framed, fundamental right and a civic responsibility”. But the government’s response has also been arguably very French: riot police, teargas, baton charges and stun grenades.
More than 250 pupils have been injured, along with about 100 school staff and 750 police. One teen has lost a hand from a stun grenade, another the sight in one eye, a third his teeth. More than 6,000 people – almost all minors – have been detained.
After a public outcry, the interior minister last week suspended the use of stun grenades. But as Alexander Hurst observed, when pupils complain about the state of their schools “and the response is riot police, the government has lost the plot”.
Wider public support
If the government hoped public opinion would be on its side, it miscalculated. Teachers’ and other unions, parents and university students have marched with the pupils, and a poll this week showed 57% of the public approved of the protests, with 33% opposed.
They come at a particularly delicate time for France’s political establishment. Presidential elections to replace Emmanuel Macron are due next spring, and without a parliamentary majority his government is caught in legislative deadlock.
Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally and the radical-left La France Insoumise of Jean-Luc Mélenchon are weaponising the protests, the former castigating an out-of-control youth, the latter an out-of-control police, and both blaming centrist incompetence.
Above all, the government’s financial room for manoeuvre is all but nonexistent. As Philip Inman pointed out, with a debt-to-GDP ratio and a budget deficit both among the highest in the EU, France has no cash to spare – and the markets are watching.
So while cost-cutting will only provoke more unrest, the absence of it could trigger a boycott of French bonds, or even a default and bailout (although as the economist Paul Krugman says, France “may have crossed from too big to fail to too big to save”).
Ultimately, there seems little doubt France will have to make some of the same painful adjustments to bring its debt back under control that Italy, Spain and Greece made a decade or more ago – and to which French public reaction could be dramatic.
We began with slogans; let’s end with some. The best-known French youth protest – a revolution, more or less – was, of course, May 1968. Comparing its iconic posters with those of today’s demonstrating school pupils is instructive.
In 1968, there was “Sous les pavés, la plage” (Beneath the cobblestones, the beach); “L’imagination au pouvoir” (Put imagination in charge); “L’ennui est contre-révolutionnaire” (Boredom is counter-revolutionary).
Those, you can see, were slogans born out of infinite possibility: a generation that, in overthrowing the old social hierarchies, never doubted its material survival. May 68 was about blowing open the doors of a rigid, outmoded society to grasp a bright future.
Today’s students are fighting to stop the doors slamming shut on them altogether.
